China-Nepal floods: rescuers pull out survivors caked in mud as toll climbs
Nepal has reversed an earlier decision and says it will allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts
Rescuers were on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday. Experts warned that the lake, created after a glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.
Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district. Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site.
The rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said.
“As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travellers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images.

US condemns ‘savage’ gang attacks in Haiti, urges swift deployment of suppression force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:21:01 UTC
05:21:01 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
The US on Friday condemned “in the strongest terms” a deadly gang attack in Haiti's Kenscoff community, calling for stronger security efforts to protect civilians and prevent armed groups from undermining the country's democratic future.
Addressing an UN Security Council meeting, Jennifer Locetta, the US alternative representative for special political affairs to the UN, described the attacks by “terrorist gangs” as “savage” and that Washington mourned the innocent lives lost.
Her remarks came after a gang attack in Kenscoff killed at least 47 people and left dozens abducted.
The attack, which followed months of deadly violence, was another indication of the “dire state” of Haiti's security crisis, Locetta said, accusing gangs of murdering civilians, terrorizing communities, burning homes and destroying families.
Locetta warned that gang coalitions were seeking to prevent Haitians from exercising their right to elect their representatives in future elections.
“Terrorists cannot take democracy hostage for their own selfish and violent ends,” she said, stressing that civilians must be protected from gang violence.
She said the US stood firmly with Haitian authorities seeking to hold perpetrators accountable, end gang impunity, restore state authority and allow Haitians to choose their leaders.
Washington remains committed to supporting Haitian-led security efforts to end gang violence, Locetta said, describing the Kenscoff attack as evidence of why the UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) mission is needed.
“The GSF was not created to issue statements from within a compound wall, or spend our money while Haiti suffers,” she said, urging the force to actively confront armed groups.
Locetta called on troop- and police-contributing countries to deploy personnel to the GSF as quickly as possible and urged UN member states to contribute to its trust fund.
“The GSF needs equipment, resources, and political will to do and finish this job,” she said.
She called on Security Council members to renew the GSF mandate next month, saying the US looked forward to working with Panama, the council's co-penholder, on the renewal.
However, Locetta acknowledged that security operations alone would not deliver lasting stability in Haiti.
She called for credible alternatives to gang violence, accountable governance and greater international investment in infrastructure, capital and job creation to provide opportunities for younger generations.
“The United States stands with Haiti and will continue to work with Haitians and international partners to end this crisis and restore Haiti's stability,” she said.
Haiti is scheduled to hold general elections for the first time in more than a decade on Dec. 13.

Russia destroyed last of Kherson’s heat and power equipment on 26 August. Ukraine’s new defense minister arrived days later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:10:32 UTC
05:10:32 KST

Ukraine's new defense minister went to Kherson Oblast days after Russia destroyed the heat of its main city. Yevhenii Khmara visited the region and met the head of the regional military administration, Oleksandr Prokudin, to discuss the region's most urgent needs, the Defense Ministry reported.
Russia hit the Kherson combined heat and power plant with a glide bomb on 26 August, then struck it again overnight with four more, destroying all the heat- and power-generating equipment that remained, Naftogaz said.
Prokudin has urged residents to leave, warning the city may go without heat and power through the winter. He said that Russia has dropped 170 glide bombs on the oblast since 1 July, more than in the entire first half of 2026.
Air defense topped the agenda
Khmara and Prokudin discussed strengthening defenses against various types of drones and protection against aerial bombs, as well as the safety of roads and critical infrastructure, which are being attacked by Russians day and night. They also addressed giving troops in this direction more capacity to strike the Russian targets that threaten civilians and soldiers.
The needs match the threat Prokudin has described. No region of Ukraine currently has the means to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds or glide bombs, he said, and Russia has begun using both more heavily against Kherson's infrastructure.
The minister met marines and the wounded
Khmara spoke with commanders and troops of the 30th Marine Corps operating on the Prydniprovskyi direction, the ministry said. The talks covered financial support for combat units and larger purchases of strike systems.
"We have taken up the soldiers' requests that need Defense Ministry decisions," the ministry said.
Khmara also visited a medical facility treating wounded troops and presented state awards.
The ministry frames it as direct contact
The Defense Ministry said it plans to keep working directly with troops and the leadership of front-line regions to strengthen the Defense Forces and protect Ukrainian lives.

A familiar business: Russia’s trade missions are replacing GRU spies with the friends and relatives of influential officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:05:30 UTC
05:05:30 KST

Russian trade missions operate in more than 50 countries, and around a third of their staff are career military intelligence officers whose superiors do not work at the Ministry of Industry and Trade, but at GRU headquarters. The spies are tasked with assignments far removed from international commerce. According to a source, Minister of Industry and Trade Anton Alikhanov convinced Putin to replace half of the spies with actual subject-area professionals. But instead, the intelligence officers are simply being subbed out in favor of the relatives and friends of high-ranking officials.
The GRU’s warden for Austria
In August 2025, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, acting on a request from the Ministry of Industry and Trade, dismissed Russia’s trade representative in Austria, 67-year-old Andrei Plotnikov — purportedly due to “the expiration of his fixed-term service contract.”
Ever since the Soviet trade mission in Austria opened in 1921, the post of trade representative has always been reserved for a military intelligence officer. Outside the period of Nazi Germany’s occupation of Austria during WWII, Moscow’s representative in Vienna has always been a professional spy.
Trade representative Plotnikov worked in Austria for four years and gave interviews fairly often about trade turnover between the two countries. However, these conversations were merely cover. Plotnikov in fact held the rank of colonel and doubled as the deputy GRU station chief in Vienna, where he demonstrated solid operational results. Plotnikov’s espionage interests included local politicians and journalists, along with the heads of major firms. He also oversaw the Russian-Austrian Business Council, which stopped operating after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.
“Andrei Nikolaevich [Plotnikov] was fired right after his birthday, and it was an undeserved insult. He’s a very well-known person, and they could easily have signed him to another three-year contract. Look at Alexander Bogatyr, who was in Cuba for nine years, and that was fine,” a source at the Ministry of Industry and Trade complained to The Insider.
At the GRU, Plotnikov was called “our legend,” and his superiors held him up as an example to other staff. When Plotnikov was still a young military intelligence officer, he was sent to West Berlin to serve as the Soviet warden at Spandau Prison. At the time, former close Hitler associate Rudolf Hess was still serving out his life sentence there. In 1987, Hess killed himself, and a version of the story still circulates among neo-Nazi groups that claim he was killed by British intelligence services. Plotnikov wrote a book, The Mystery of Rudolf Hess’s Death: A Warden’s Diary, in which he too arrived at highly questionable conclusions.
After Germany, Plotnikov continued his GRU service and graduated from the Military Diplomatic Academy. He was then assigned to Rosvooruzheniye (now Rosoboronexport, the Russian state-owned defense export agency), where he headed the Southeast Asia desk. From 2003 to 2009, Plotnikov spied in China under cover as a Russian trade mission employee, and before being sent to Austria, he headed Rostec’s representative office in Germany.
Following a series of high-profile spy scandals resulting from reporting by The Insider, Austrian authorities have begun paying much closer attention to Russian diplomats and journalists. The Austrian Foreign Ministry rejected all trade representative candidates proposed by Moscow, forcing the mission to draw on personnel already present in Vienna.
The initial candidate for “chief trader” was Alexander Zherikhov, whose father, Alexander Zherikhov Sr., headed Russia’s customs service from 2004 to 2006 and now holds the post of advisor to the CEO of Gazprom Neft. However, Artem Klimentyev was put in charge of trade instead.
Klimentyev’s mother, Svetlana, is a well-known figure in financial circles, previously working at Mezhprombank and at the Moscow representative office of the now-defunct British company Fort Trading Corporation Limited. Svetlana currently works on the management side of the Moscow Venture Fund.
Klimentyev himself graduated from the Academy of Foreign Trade, and in 2018 his mother arranged for him to become a consultant in the Department of European and North American Countries and International Organizations at the Ministry of Economic Development. From there, he moved to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, where he headed a department until his departure for Austria.
Notably, the reshuffle in Vienna did not help improve trade turnover between the two countries, which in 2025 was down by 74% year-on-year, with a further decline expected for 2026.
Algeria, the gateway to Africa
The dismissal lists at the Ministry of Industry and Trade are drawn up by First Deputy Minister Kirill Lysogorsky, who directly oversees the trade missions. As it turns out, Lysogorsky is far from an outsider to the GRU — a graduate of the Russian Military Academy of the Strategic Missile Forces, he previously headed government departments connected with the defense industry and arms supplies.
“Lysogorsky may be an important figure now, but he used to be just an errand boy running after Deputy Prime Minister Yuri Borisov — together they traveled to half the world,” a source at the ministry told The Insider.
In addition to Plotnikov, in September 2025 career GRU officer Ivan Nalich, Russia’s trade representative in Algeria, was put on Lysogorsky’s “chopping block.” Nalich had worked in North Africa for eight years and had built up an extensive network of contacts among military officers, officials, and public figures. “Algeria is the gateway to Africa,” Nalich said in one interview.
“Trade representative” Nalich also has a classic spy’s biography. In 2003, he graduated from the Institute of Asian and African Studies at Moscow State University, where he appears to have caught the eye of GRU recruiters. After graduation, Nalich took a job at the RIA Novosti state news agency, covering Middle Eastern affairs. In 2005, he moved to Rosoboronexport. Then, from 2009 to 2011, he worked in various positions at Rostec before returning to Rosoboronexport. Nalich subsequently spent five years spying in Morocco before being sent to Algeria as trade representative in 2019.
Nalich seems to have inherited a knack for espionage from his KGB grandfather.
The GRU now has a standing joke that after being fired from the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Nalich will become a backup dancer for his cousin — the well-known performer Pyotr Nalich.
In place of Nalich, Prime Minister Mishustin appointed 56-year-old Alexei Shatilov as Russia’s new trade representative in Algeria. Shatilov had worked for the Presidential Executive Office since the late 1990s in several capacities, and his last post at the Presidential Executive Office was as advisor in the foreign economic activity department of the president’s expert directorate. He had previously worked as trade representative in Algeria and had also spent time in the UAE and Qatar. He is considered to be part of the inner circle of Igor Neverov, head of the president’s foreign policy directorate. Neverov is said to have lobbied for his protégé’s reappointment to Africa.
In a recent interview, Shatilov praised Algeria for its pro-Moscow orientation and encouraged Russian companies to enter the local market. The trade representative did not mention, however, that the country is considered one of the most corrupt in Africa. The initial budget for the highway connecting Algeria with Morocco and Tunisia was $6 billion, but corruption drove the final cost to $17 billion — including $5 billion in kickbacks for local officials.
A comedian replaces a smuggler
In January 2023, Cuba welcomed a new Russian trade representative, Sergei Baldin. Before Havana, he had headed the trade and economic department at the Russian embassy in Portugal and the Russian trade mission in Brazil.
An analysis of Baldin’s activities shows that in Brazil he mainly represented Rosoboronexport’s interests. For example, the trade representative actively negotiated Russia’s entry into the Latin American arms market and took part in Latin America Aero & Defence military fairs in Rio de Janeiro.
Baldin is also credited with the successful negotiations to establish visa-free travel between Russia and Brazil, a development that clearly pleased the GRU and the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). While in Cuba, Baldin spoke in interviews about the good prospects for trade between Moscow and Havana. However, in June 2026, he unexpectedly resigned before his contract had even ended.
As The Insider learned, Baldin had concealed from his superiors at the Ministry of Industry and Trade the fact that he was being prosecuted for smuggling. On May 2, 2021, he flew into Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport from Lisbon and headed for the exit through the green channel. When a customs officer asked whether he had any undeclared currency, Baldin said no. However, during an inspection, officers found nearly $52,000 on him.
Trade representative Baldin concealed from his superiors at the Ministry of Industry and Trade the fact that he was being prosecuted for smuggling
To replace Baldin, Moscow appointed Vakhtang Mosashvili as its new trade representative. His father, Vyacheslav Mosashvili, is a close acquaintance and former Ministry of Transport colleague of Putin aide Igor Levitin.
The younger Mosashvili’s résumé, obtained by The Insider, matches all of the expectations for a member of a nomenklatura family: “Attended a school at the Russian embassy in Belgium, graduated from the law faculty of the Russian State University for the Humanities. Worked at Aeroflot and at trade missions in Hungary and Spain.”
In the Russian mission in Havana, Mosashvili is known as an irrepressible “jokester,” the life of the party at gatherings, and a fan of off-color jokes. The trade representative’s peculiar sense of humor is showcased in his now-deleted account on Odnoklassniki social network, where he wrote about himself: “Three years’ imprisonment under Article 162, Part 1 of the Russian Criminal Code, ‘Robbery,’ served at the PLS penal colony in Solikamsk. Broke, I don’t have a car, I curse, I’m schizophrenic, neurasthenic, asthmatic, I pick my nose, I have dandruff, worms, gonorrhea, I sniff glue, gasoline, and stain remover.”
A few more “trade representatives” from military intelligence also fell under Deputy Minister Lysogorsky’s cuts, but no replacements have yet been found for them. Vladislav Darvay left Moldova in September 2024, and The Insider later published wiretaps which showed that he had organized a visit to Russia by fraudster-oligarch Vladimir Plahotniuc, who stands accused of involvement in running $20 billion in corrupt Russian money through the “Moldovan laundromat”. Plahotniuc met with Kremlin official Dmitry Kozak and discussed interference in Moldova’s elections. However, the plan fell through when Plahotniuc was arrested, Kozak was fired, the Kremlin’s preferred candidates lost the election, and Darvay was barred from entering the country.
In Syria, espionage will continue
In some countries, however, Russian spies have not been replaced by “well-connected” substitutes from the civilian sector. In Syria, for instance, the GRU again managed to appoint one of its own to the trade representative post — 55-year-old career intelligence officer Vladimir Noskov. He replaces GRU officer Georgy Asatryan, who was recalled to Moscow and put forward for an award for the successful evacuation of Russian military personnel and equipment from bases in Syria to Libya.
Colonel Noskov graduated from the Military Diplomatic Academy, was seconded to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and spied in Lebanon, Egypt, and Qatar (facts that did not prevent his son from getting a job at Bain & Company, a U.S. entity closely tied to Anatoly Chubais).
As for his appointment to Syria, it is likely that no one from the “well-connected” crowd, accustomed to a comfortable life, wanted an assignment to that troubled country.

Russian Geran-4 Drone Reaches 960 Km as Analysts Warn 96% of Ukraine Is Within Range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:01:55 UTC
05:01:55 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Geran-4 Drone Reaches 960 Km as Analysts Warn 96% of Ukraine Is Within Range
A Russian jet-powered drone flew approximately 960 kilometers from its launch point on August 28, setting a reported new range record for this type of UAV, according to Ukrainian OSINT analysts from the Oko Hora monitoring group.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The group identified the aircraft as a jet-powered Geran-4 drone. Although the system’s stated range is around 550 kilometers, analysts said operating at high altitude could significantly extend its flight distance.
“Despite the stated range of the jet-powered Geran-4 being around 550 kilometers, flying at an altitude of 5,000–7,000 meters makes it possible to double the range,” Oko Hora analysts said.
Based on the recorded flight, the analysts estimated that approximately 96% of Ukraine’s territory is within the potential operating range of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drones.
The Geran-4 is a jet-powered variant of Russia’s Geran drone family, developed to achieve higher speeds and enhanced flight performance. According to open-source information, the UAV measures approximately 3.5 meters in length, has a wingspan of around three meters, and weighs about 450 kilograms at takeoff.
The drone is powered by a turbojet engine generating approximately 160 kilograms of thrust, providing considerably more power than the engine fitted to the earlier Geran-3.
The upgraded propulsion system reportedly allows the Geran-4 to reach cruising speeds of around 350–500 kilometers per hour, compared with approximately 280–330 kilometers per hour for previous variants. Its previously reported operational range was up to 850 kilometers, with a flight endurance of roughly two and a half hours and a warhead capacity of up to 50 kilograms.
The reported flight comes amid continued large-scale Russian drone attacks on Ukraine. On August 27, Russian forces repeatedly targeted Kyiv and the surrounding region, leaving the capital area under air raid alerts for more than 14 hours and forcing emergency crews to work under the threat of follow-up strikes, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES).

Q&A: The Future of Air Force Cyber Systems and Warfighter Comms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:01:49 UTC
05:01:49 KST

Just over a year ago, in July 2025, the Air Force established a dedicated office on the Air Staff for communications/cyber functions, separate from the intelligence directorate it had long been attached to. The new Warfighter Communications and Cyber Systems directorate now focuses on secure communications, cyber operations, and information technology systems as they support the frontline Airman or Guardian.
The move, leaders said at the time, was a major shakeup necessary to support the service’s need for resilient, reliable communications and cyber operations, and the equipment and personnel associated with those capabilities.
In June, Brig. Gen. Jeffrey A. Phillips took over as Deputy Chief of Staff for Warfighter Communications and Cyber Systems from interim deputy chief Brig. Gen. Joy Kaczor, who filled the role following the retirement of Maj. Gen. Michele C. Edmondson.
Phillips, a prior-enlisted Airman, started his career as a computer programmer and serving six years wearing stripes before commissioning through Officer Training School at Maxwell Air Force Base, Ala., in 1999. He previously commanded the 67th Cyberspace Wing at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, and served as Director of Cyberspace and Warfighting Communications at the headquarters of Air Combat Command at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va.
The one-star now serves a community of about 30,000 enlisted, 3,000 officers, and nearly 100 newly minted warrant officers. He recently sat down with Air & Space Forces Magazine for an interview about where the office stands after a year in operation and his priorities moving forward for the position, the equipment, and the people involved in vital communications and cyber work for the Air Force.
Editor’s Note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.
Q: What is your office doing to modernize both the equipment and support the Airmen in communications and cyber jobs?
A: We have to stop getting stuck in five-year acquisition cycles that end up delivering a product that’s outdated by the time we put it on the battlefield, and so that’s my number one priority. And we’re doing that through a few different lines of effort. Theater deployable communications, or TDC, is really important. We learned in operations like Operation Epic Fury that when we’re out in the field at several locations, we need to be connected at all those locations. So, we need to get that equipment out to the people who need to be connected, and we need to have Airmen out there who know how to operate it or make it simple enough for anyone to operate.
And there’s enterprise communications; those are the foundational networks that we connect back into from the edge, and a lot of those have been underinvested in over the past 30 years, so we’re playing a catch-up game. A big focus for Chief Information Officer Ashley Devoto and me is making sure we can modernize that enterprise network, so I came in with that as my number one priority.
My second priority is the continued evolution of our talent management processes. I think we’ve come a long way in the time that I’ve been part of it, and we need to do that for our enlisted Airmen, our warrant officers, and our officers. In the last few years, we created an executive development forum that all the cyber general officers sit on. It’s really a development team for our colonels. Now all of our general officers mentor all of our colonels.
This year we had what we call our Champions Initiative, and the colonels who were part of our development team were mentors to each O5 and below that we’re meeting on that development team. On the enlisted side, our 1D7 [Cyber Defense Operations] career field has obviously been in a state of flux and change for probably the last 10-plus years, we’ve changed those AFSCs and what they represented several times over that time period, and I kind of put a chalk line in the sand and I said we’re not going to make any more changes until we figure out what’s right, what’s wrong. We get the Airmen the career development courses that they need and then get them the education they need so they can test for promotions on their specialty knowledge tests. So that’s the number two priority.
There are a lot of key partners and stakeholders that we need to work with, so my goal is to rebuild those bridges because we can’t do anything alone. We have to partner with organizations like the Secretariat of the Air Force, the Office of the CIO, and DAF CIO Devoto. We have to partner with our acquisition organization, primarily under Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, and we work with the [Command, Control, Intelligence and Networks Directorate] within AFLCMC primarily for our theater deployable communication and our enterprise IT.
Q: What are some of the key technologies or equipment that your office is helping roll out, use, or upgrade across the communications and cyber areas of the Air Force?
A: Our legacy communication equipment is our Flexible Communication Package, or FCP. It’s been around probably for about the last decade. When you deploy an FCP, the only way a combatant commander can task it is through a unit type code that requires 10 pallet positions on an aircraft, about 40 people, and about 20 short tons to move. It includes things like bulldozers and huge satellite dishes, and it’s been modernized to the point that we don’t need such a big footprint anymore. Our new deployable comm kits—we have two of them: the ACP, the Agile Communications Package, and the Fly-Away Communications Terminal. They’re similar equipment, but a Fly-Away Comm Terminal supports fewer users than an ACP would. So, if we deploy somewhere we need to run command and control applications, we might need more compute and storage power. We can put that on the ACP. If we go someplace where we don’t have terrestrial internet, we can attach a satellite, our commercial satellite comm terminal. So agnostic transport is really big. We can set up a 5G bubble and use that as our transport. That gives us modular equipment so we can reduce our footprint and deploy with a couple of Airmen who know how to use it, providing connectivity for a whole mission-generation force element versus 10 pallet positions and, you know, 20 short tons.
We are in the midst of fielding ACPs. We have a lot of FACTs that are fielded. Now we’re working toward our next-generation ACPs. This technology changes very rapidly, and so keeping up with it is very challenging.
Q: You mentioned work to develop officers; what is your office trying to do for the enlisted and new warrant officers in the ranks?
The 1D7 Cyber Defense Operations career field, for example, has five “shreds.” At different points in time, there have been more or fewer shreds. Those shreds have meant different things, and so you could ask an Airman, or you could ask some senior leaders, “Hey, you know, what’s the definition of a 1D7X1 today? And unless you’re keeping up with the change, which was constant, it was very hard to define it clearly. So, freezing any further changes for Airmen in that career field is crucial because they want that stability, so they can develop more technical expertise and depth.
With warrant officers, we’re not asking them to lead people, we’re asking them to lead efforts. We’re asking them to become technical experts. We’ve put warrant officers in our cyberspace operations career field at the 67th Cyberspace Wing, and we’re starting to put them in the 688th [Cyberspace Wing] and get them into some staff positions as advisors to senior leaders who might not have the technical depth warrant officers have.
Q: How has working in Air Forces Cyber, and the cyber officer’s role, changed over the course of your time in uniform?
A: When I came in, we were support officers. Now we’re operations officers, and I think that’s a huge difference. I was proud of being a support officer. I had a great boss when I was a second lieutenant who pulled me in at Shaw Air Force Base, and he said, “Hey, Munster, this is your role as a communications officer at this base. You’re supporting the SEAD mission.” I said, “Sir. What’s the SEAD mission? He explained it as Suppression of Enemy Air Defenses, and I started to link my service to that mission, and I was very proud of that. As we transitioned to a more of an operational community, I got to lead a cyberspace operations squadron, and I saw how we were out there creating effects that supported whatever the goals of the operation might be, and I’m proud of that too. I think, you know, we’re proving that we are integral to most operations that happen.

‘People are hungry’: Iran braces for new protests as economic crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:00:49 UTC
05:00:49 KST

Iran on Friday marked six months since Israel struck Tehran at 8:10 a.m., dropping, among other munitions, heavy bombs on the compound of then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
Those strikes marked the beginning of a prolonged campaign that has yet to end, although its direction has shifted in recent days under U.S. President Donald Trump, who has described himself as the war’s “great partner.” Washington is now focusing increasingly on economic pressure against Iran, even as Trump continues to post that he is finished being “Mr. Nice Guy.”
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile issued a written appeal to the Iranian public Friday calling on people to “avoid any expression that causes despair.” Trump declared in January that “help is on the way,” but at the time stopped short of attacking Iran, hoping Tehran would halt executions and change course.
That did not happen. About a month and a half later, he joined Israel in the war, following, among other developments, a presentation delivered to him at the White House by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with senior Israeli security officials, including the Mossad chief, watching remotely.
The presentation envisioned accelerating the collapse of the Iranian regime, a goal that has not materialized so far. On Thursday, Mossad Director David Barnea said operations would need to be intensified and expressed optimism that the regime would eventually fall.
The New York Times, however, published testimony Friday from Iranians who said they no longer believe the government is about to collapse. What worries them now is survival. “I can’t describe the level of anxiety about the future,” Negar, an Iranian woman who asked that her full name not be published for fear of the authorities, told the newspaper.
The United States has meanwhile changed course. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was quoted this week as saying that, for now, attacks on Iran would stop and the campaign would become primarily economic.
Washington hopes economic collapse will ultimately force Tehran to accept U.S. demands regarding its nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. But one Iranian interviewed by The New York Times described a very different mood inside the leadership. “The Islamic Republic is convinced that it has defeated the world and that everyone is afraid of it,” he said.
One of the biggest concerns inside Iran is the possibility that gasoline prices, which are heavily subsidized, could rise. Long lines were seen at gas stations this week. “Everyone is rushing to buy and stockpile food, especially Pakistani rice,” Marzieh, a resident of Bandar Abbas, Iran’s major southern port city, told The New York Times. She said even basic goods had already become more expensive.
Several Iranians interviewed by the newspaper said they expected a new round of protests in the near future, despite the regime’s willingness to use live fire against demonstrators and the deadly repression of previous protest waves.
Against that backdrop, Mojtaba Khamenei issued a message praising the government’s performance despite sanctions and pressure from abroad. “I appreciate the measures taken by our government, which were implemented despite the restrictions and plots of the American-Zionist enemy, and despite the sanctions and blockade,” he said.
“Any expression that causes despair or weakens national and public determination should be avoided.”
Fuel prices have proved politically explosive before. An increase in gasoline prices in 2019 brought large numbers of Iranians into the streets. “You cannot stop an economic uprising with anything,” Ismail, a Tehran resident, told The New York Times. “War will not stop it, and violence will not stop it.”
He said Iranians had fallen into a “black hole.”
“People are hungry, confused and unable to find a way out. We are alone, in a catastrophic state of chaos and abandonment.”
Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani also acknowledged the country’s economic distress this week. “We do not deny the economic difficulties, but we will overcome the pressures with wisdom and by maintaining our unity,” she said.
Trump, meanwhile, signaled Thursday that Washington has little interest in returning to negotiations. Asked about his new strategy toward Iran and whether talks were underway, he replied: “We don’t want to talk to them.” Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, he added: “We’re not looking to meet with them either.”
The Wall Street Journal also reported that the administration had “repeatedly” told intermediaries it had no interest in returning to the terms of the June memorandum of understanding with Iran.
A senior Iranian official described the U.S. measures as “total economic war” after the U.S. Treasury secretary this week announced a plan aimed at cutting Iran off from its trading partners as part of what Trump has called an economic “D-Day.”

Short-term SSRI use alters brain connectivity in anxious individuals in unexpected ways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:00:26 UTC
05:00:26 KST

A study of anxious individuals found that 2-3 weeks of escitalopram administration altered the connectivity of their amygdala (a brain region involved in emotion processing and fear) with the dorsomedial cortex (a brain area involved in cognitive processing and regulating emotions) while viewing happy faces, compared to healthy individuals. However, the change was not in the expected direction. The paper was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Anxiety disorders are a group of mental health conditions characterized by excessive fear, worry, or apprehension that is difficult to control and interferes with everyday functioning. They include conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and several specific phobias. Although anxiety is a normal response to threat, in these disorders it becomes disproportionate, persistent, or triggered in situations that are not objectively dangerous.
Treatment typically includes psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of both. The medications most commonly used for long-term treatment are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). These drugs increase the availability of the neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger in the brain) serotonin, or of serotonin and norepinephrine, in the brain and gradually modify neural systems involved in fear, mood, and stress regulation.
Study author Paulina B. Lukow and her colleagues note that connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsomedial cortex regions of the brain likely plays a key role in generating anxiety symptoms. A previous study found that connectivity between these two regions is increased in individuals suffering from anxiety while they are looking at (and cognitively processing) fearful faces, but not when processing happy faces.
The study authors hypothesized that increased serotonin availability in patients after SSRI administration would reverse these changes. In other words, they hypothesized that the connectivity between these two regions of the brain would be reduced after treatment with SSRIs. They conducted an experimental study.
Study participants were 45 individuals suffering from anxiety disorders and 96 healthy participants, included in the study as controls. Each of these two groups of participants was randomly further divided into two groups. In all groups, 74-86% of participants were women. Participants’ average age ranged between 23 and 28 years across groups. All participants were between 18 and 50 years of age.
One group of participants with anxiety was assigned to take one 10mg escitalopram tablet per day with or without food for 2-3 weeks, while the other group of participants with anxiety took an identical-looking tablet with no active ingredients (placebo) for the same period of time. The two groups of healthy participants received the same assignments. Participants did not know whether they were taking escitalopram or placebo. Escitalopram is an SSRI drug commonly used for treating depression and anxiety disorders.
Before the start of the treatment and after the treatment was finished, participants completed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a scan that measures brain activity by detecting changes associated with blood flow) of their brains. While undergoing neuroimaging, participants completed an emotional faces task. In this task, they viewed alternating blocks of happy, fearful, and neutral faces. There were twelve blocks in total, four for each type of emotional face. Participants’ task was to label the gender of the faces shown by pressing a button. The point of this labeling was to make sure that participants were really looking at the faces shown and cognitively processing them while their brain activity was being recorded.
Unexpectedly, the results showed that anxiety symptoms did not improve for participants receiving escitalopram; instead, anxiety levels remained consistently higher in the anxious group compared to healthy controls regardless of the treatment they received. Furthermore, depression symptoms were higher across all participants (both with and without anxiety) who received escitalopram compared to those who received the placebo.
As the study authors expected, after escitalopram treatment, participants with anxiety disorders showed changes in the connectivity between the amygdala region and the dorsomedial cortex in both brain hemispheres compared to healthy controls. However, the change was in the opposite direction compared to what the study authors expected—the connectivity increased, while the study authors expected a decrease.
“These findings suggest that our simple hypothesis of SSRIs inducing a reduction in amygdala-dorsomedial cortex connectivity is incorrect, and the associated brain connectivity may instead increase in the initial weeks of drug administration,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the neural underpinnings of anxiety disorders. However, the study authors note that their participants were recruited from the community rather than directly from mental health services, which may have resulted in the selection of participants with a different symptom profile compared to individuals who seek help for their mental health issues themselves.
The paper, “Brain activation and connectivity after 2–3 weeks of escitalopram administration in anxiety disorders: A randomised trial,” was authored by Paulina B. Lukow, Millie Lowther, Alexandra C. Pike, Yumeya Yamamori, Alice V. Chavanne, Siobhan Gormley, Jessica Aylward, Carlos Escalante Vera, Tayla McCloud, Talya Goble, Julia Rodriguez-Sanchez, Ella W. Tuominen, Sarah K. Buehler, Peter Kirk, and Oliver J. Robinson.

Deal, warning or spy swap? What Russian media are saying about the CIA chief’s Moscow visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:59:53 UTC
04:59:53 KST

Deal, warning or spy swap? What Russian media are saying about the CIA chief’s Moscow visit
On August 25, it was not so much the CIA director as a ready-made story that landed in Moscow: a hulking C-17 military transport, several hours away from the cameras, secret meetings, and a return flight via Riga. By Friday, barely any more facts had emerged. SVR head Sergey Naryshkin confirmed that the talks concerned matters within the intelligence services’ purview, calling the field “sensitive and highly specialized.” Ratcliffe did not meet with Vladimir Putin, but the Russian president was briefed on the talks immediately.
Secrecy, however, abhors a vacuum – especially when the CIA is involved. In just three days, Russian media had sent Ratcliffe to Moscow with a new Ukraine plan, a warning about strikes on NATO weapons plants, and a scenario for nuclear war in the Middle East. Inside the C-17’s cargo hold, they imagined secret equipment, detained intelligence officers, and a mysterious “package” too sensitive to entrust to a phone line.
Every outlet found its own clue in the flight. Some saw the visit as an attempt to head off a looming confrontation between Russia and the West. Others viewed it as a sign that backchannel diplomacy was coming back to life. Still others cast it as an intelligence operation disguised as negotiations. RT breaks down what the Russian press read between the lines of the summer’s most mysterious visit.
Washington probes Russia’s red lines
Gazeta.ru views Ratcliffe’s visit as an attempt by Washington to learn Moscow’s plans for the fall directly and gauge whether Ukraine talks might resume. The outlet does not predict an imminent breakthrough. Grigory Karasin, chairman of the Federation Council’s Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks only of a useful “psychological climate” for keeping contacts alive. Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs, stresses that a visit at this level does not happen without a serious reason.
Political analyst Sergey Markelov offers the most specific theory. In his view, the Americans were looking not for a ready-made peace formula, but for a possible midpoint between the two sides’ maximalist demands:
”The Americans can see that Moscow’s and Kiev’s positions are 100% incompatible. As master negotiators, they are asking whether there is some kind of middle ground.”
Vladimir Vasiliev, a senior researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, offers another hypothesis: Ratcliffe may have acted as Trump’s trusted courier, carrying a message the White House did not want to send through conventional diplomatic channels.
A secret assignment for intelligence diplomacy
Expert magazine treats the visit as a special form of backchannel diplomacy, approaching it from several angles. Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, says the agenda may have included red lines, cybercrime, and terrorism. Alexander Bobrov points to technical cooperation between the two intelligence services and the possibility of new prisoner exchanges. The common thread is that Moscow and Washington are simultaneously defining the limits of what they will tolerate and searching for areas where cooperation remains possible.
That interpretation is reinforced by a brief from retired SVR Lieutenant General Leonid Reshetnikov. He sees the level of the visit as evidence that Ratcliffe was carrying a direct and highly important assignment from Trump, but cautions against trying to guess its contents.
”Apparently, the Americans have a proposal, which is why the CIA director came. But no one is required to walk out to the press and disclose what was said in closed-door meetings.”
Ultimately, Expert leaves the precise agenda open. Ukraine may have been part of it, but not necessarily the only item. The magazine’s main conclusion is that, with formal diplomacy in crisis, intelligence services are becoming the channel through which the most sensitive proposals are conveyed.
Reconnaissance ahead of a major deal
Lenta.ru does not treat Ratcliffe’s visit as a stand-alone mission, but as preparation for the next round of Russian-American negotiations. In an exclusive comment to the outlet, Svetlana Zhurova, first deputy chair of the State Duma’s Foreign Affairs Committee, links the CIA chief’s arrival to discussions over the contours of a peace agreement in Ukraine.
”There is more and more discussion of what a peace agreement might look like and what shape it could take. So… that is the only issue that could be on the agenda.”
The key detail is the expected fall visit by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. In that sequence, Ratcliffe looks like an advance scout in both senses of the word: sent to compare positions and clear the way for higher-level political negotiators.
Trump rushes back to the Ukraine track
Moskovsky Komsomolets describes Ratcliffe’s arrival as a “tough heart-to-heart.” The main theory comes from American affairs analyst Malek Dudakov: the Trump administration is scrambling for a foreign-policy win ahead of the midterm elections and, after setbacks elsewhere, is turning back to talks with Moscow. Ratcliffe is presented not as a peacemaker, but as a hawk who oversees the sharing of US intelligence with Kiev.
”I would not get my hopes up that the visit will produce a breakthrough. In all likelihood, it won’t.”
MK’s interpretation is dramatic but skeptical: Washington is in a hurry, and the visit was primarily about hard bargaining over Ukraine.
In a separate opinion piece for the same newspaper, political analyst Ruslan Pankratov makes the C-17 and the one-day format central to his reading of the trip. In his view, Ratcliffe may have delivered a warning about the limits of escalation, intelligence assessments of potential threats, or a specific package of classified information.
Washington tests whether Russia has reached its limit
Komsomolskaya Pravda casts the visit as an emergency effort by Washington to assess the risk of a direct clash between Russia and NATO’s European members. American affairs analyst Andrey Sidorov links the trip to a US desire to learn how Moscow might respond to the expansion of Western military support for Kiev. Political analyst Aleksey Pilko makes the theory more specific, suggesting that the immediate concern may have been possible Russian strikes on European plants producing drones and other weapons for Ukraine.
”He came to bargain – to find out what the Russian side is thinking.”
These are the experts’ assessments, but KP reinforces them through its headlines: “Approaching the Danger Line” and “Russia’s Patience Is Running Out.” In the outlet’s framing, Ratcliffe did not bring an ultimatum. He came to determine whether the escalation was real enough to force the United States to decide if it was prepared to enter a war on behalf of its European allies.
In another article, KP shifts the possible focus of the talks to the Middle East. Vladimir Vasiliev argues that Trump’s description of the visit as “routine” was an attempt to conceal its urgency. His theory is that Moscow and Washington may have discussed the risk of a Turkish-Israeli confrontation, Iran’s possible entry into an anti-Israel bloc, and the potential US response.
”I cannot rule out that, if Tehran joins the emerging anti-Israel coalition, the United States could use tactical nuclear weapons against it.”
KP military columnist Viktor Baranets turns the visit into a spy thriller. In his interview, retired military intelligence officer Pavel Artamonov suggests that Ratcliffe brought a request not to strike British factories producing missiles for Ukraine. At the same time, he claims, the American C-17 may have gathered signals intelligence during the flight.
”Along the C-17’s flight path, all our military systems were switched off. We left the Americans starved of intelligence, so to speak.”
The Baltic states should be warned, not Moscow
The business daily Vzglyad develops the theory that Ratcliffe may have come to warn Russia, specifying that Washington could be worried about strikes on facilities in the Baltic states working for the Ukrainian military. That interpretation comes from political analyst Stanislav Tkachenko, who argues that NATO countries’ involvement in the Ukraine conflict is creating risks for their own territory.
War correspondent Alexander Kots adds a historical parallel with CIA Director William Burns’ 2021 trip to Moscow. The West ignored Russia’s concerns at the time, he argues, so a new warning will not make Moscow change course either.
”Don’t provoke us, and no one will attack anyone. You can’t talk to us in ultimatums. It doesn’t work.”
The outlet therefore presents the visit not as a show of American strength, but as a sign of Washington’s mounting concern over the consequences of Western policy.
The C-17 mystery: What Ratcliffe brought – and whom he may have taken home
The most important clue was not hidden in diplomatic protocol, but in the aircraft itself. Why did the CIA director need a heavy C-17 military transport if the trip involved only a few closed-door meetings?
Military columnist Mikhail Khodarenok suggests in a column for Gazeta.ru that Ratcliffe delivered updated US proposals on Ukraine that were too sensitive to entrust to ordinary communications channels.
”He flew in, handed over the package, and flew back out. The military transport also carried additional cargo whose purpose remains to be determined.”
Lenta.ru picks up the mystery at the other end of the route. Military analyst Aleksander Perendzhiev says the roomy aircraft may have been needed to take American intelligence officers or classified Western hardware out of Russia.
Together, the two theories form a single narrative: Ratcliffe may have arrived with a confidential “package” on Ukraine, while the C-17 may not have flown home empty. There is no evidence to confirm either claim, but the aircraft turns a series of closed-door talks into a story about a possible exchange whose contents both sides preferred to keep out of sight.
Talks “under the wing” of the intelligence services
In an opinion column, Vedomosti journalists Roman Romanov and Aleksey Nikolsky call the visit an important milestone, but caution against inflated expectations. Ratcliffe most likely did not come to revive the Anchorage agreements, they argue, but to explore new openings for dialogue.
”Such a visit may signal that the negotiating process is moving ‘under the wing’ of the two countries’ intelligence services.”
The authors believe Ratcliffe could prove more effective than Witkoff and Kushner: he has official standing and can coordinate negotiations with US government agencies. Ukraine remains the central issue, though Vedomosti allows for a broader bilateral agenda. The newspaper does not expect a quick breakthrough, however. Moscow is unlikely to accept an immediate ceasefire unless the fundamental issues are resolved.
A secret visit treated as routine business
Unlike many other outlets, Kommersant, Russia’s oldest newspaper, offers no theory of its own and does not consult Russian experts. Its report is a restrained chronology: the arrival of a US military aircraft, several hours in Moscow, no meeting with Putin, and the official explanation that the trip involved contacts between the intelligence services.
”On August 25, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid an unannounced visit to Russia. The purpose of his trip, and whom he met in Moscow, remain unknown.”
The only clue comes from biographical context: Ratcliffe has previously helped arrange prisoner exchanges, while the CIA and SVR maintain a direct line of communication. The visit is therefore presented more as part of a closed working dialogue between intelligence services than as public diplomacy. Still, Kommersant stops short of a definitive conclusion. Even its headline, “The Mysterious Envoy,” preserves the intrigue rather than resolving it.
Many other outlets take a similarly restrained view, consistently lowering the temperature by citing official statements. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov describes contacts between the intelligence services as a positive development; Naryshkin calls them part of the job; and Trump points to the good relationship between the CIA and SVR chiefs while denying that Ratcliffe carried any special message.
”Like everyone else, we have rules governing how intelligence services interact. There is nothing unusual about that.”
That remark by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, quoted by Izvestia, best captures the line taken by most Russian media outlets. The visit is presented not as the start of a major political breakthrough, but as the work of a standing backchannel between Moscow and Washington. Russian coverage does not dismiss its importance, but urges readers to judge it by the contacts that have been confirmed, not speculation about a secret mission.

Timeline: Life of Ratko Mladic, general turned ‘Butcher of Bosnia’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:58:41 UTC
04:58:41 KST

Timeline: Life of Ratko Mladic, general turned ‘Butcher of Bosnia’
Mladic died in prison in The Hague after failed requests by Serbian authorities to secure early release to his home country.
Ratko Mladic, a war criminal convicted for his role in orchestrating the Srebrenica Genocide in 1995 – the first genocide on European soil since the second world war – died in prison in The Hague at the age of 84.
He had been serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity – crimes whose “seriousness” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres restated after his death on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘A true hell’: How three Srebrenica survivors defied death 30 years ago
- list 2 of 3Srebrenica: Genocide on Trial
- list 3 of 3Obituary: Ratko Mladic, war criminal convicted of Srebrenica genocide, dies
“The Secretary-General stands in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladic was found guilty … [and] reiterates his call on all those in position of power to refrain from denying the seriousness of the crimes that have been adjudicated,” Guterres’s spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said in a statement.
On Friday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic accused the UN war crimes court of “uncivilised behaviour” for not allowing Mladic early release, which would have seen him die in Serbia. Earlier this year, Belgrade requested he be allowed to receive medical treatment outside prison, saying his health condition was “serious”.
Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, Mladic was one of the most notorious military commanders of the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia. Under his command, Bosnian Serb forces seized Srebrenica, near the Serbian border, in July 1995, despite the UN declaring the municipality a “safe area”. In the following days, the forces killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys.
Here is a timeline of the major events of Mladic’s life, leading up to his death in detention this week:
1942-1966: Birth and personal life
Ratko Mladic, a Bosnian Serb, was born in March 1942 in the village of Bozanovici in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia (in today’s Bosnia and Herzegovina). His father was a member of a communist-led resistance to the Axis powers in World War II.
In 1966, Mladic married Bosiljka Jedic and later had two children, Darko and Ana.
1965-1991: Military career
At the age of 22, Mladic joined the Yugoslav National Army (JNA) and moved up the ranks. By 1991, he was the head of the Operational Teaching Department of the 9th Corps in Knin (today’s Croatia) and later commanded the Headquarters of the 9th Corps Maritime Division.
1991-1992: Arrival in Sarajevo
The Presidency of the Social Federative Republic of Yugoslavia promoted Mladic to the rank of major-general in 1991 and lieutenant–colonel general in April 1992. He commanded the headquarters of the JNA’s Second Military Area Command in Sarajevo.
1992-1995: Siege of Sarajevo
The Bosnian Serb army, led by Mladic, laid siege to the capital city of Sarajevo.
The longest military siege of a capital city in modern history, it lasted 1,460 days, killing more than 11,500 people. An estimated 480,000 to 500,000 missiles were fired on the city.
July 1995: Srebrenica Genocide
In July 1995, Mladic’s troops captured Srebrenica and Zepa, enclaves under the protection of the United Nations. In what was later termed a genocide, 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed, and between 25,000 and 30,000 were expelled from the area.
July and November 1995: Genocide indictment
Mladic and Radovan Karadzic, political leader of the Bosnian Serbs, were indicted before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) for war crimes committed during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This included the killings at Srebrenica, along with the mass expulsion of Bosniak civilians.
Mladic was charged with 20 offences, including genocide. In 1996, the ICTY issued an international arrest warrant for Mladic and Karadzic.
1997-2011: Life on the run
Mladic remained in hiding after the ICTY indictment, moving to different locations in Serbia.
War crimes prosecutors and media investigations continued to track Mladic’s movement based on rumours, witness interviews, intelligence, and court documents.
In 2001, he reportedly moved to Bosnia and Herzegovina before going back to Serbia.
2011-2016: Arrest and trial
On May 26, 2011, Mladic was arrested in Lazarevo, northern Serbia, at his cousin’s house. He was taken into custody in Belgrade and then transferred to The Hague to be prosecuted by the ICTY.
The trial commenced in June 2011, and closing arguments were delivered in December 2016. Mladic refused a plea deal.
November 2017: Final verdict
Mladic was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2017 over the Srebrenica genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.
June 2025: Release appeal denied
In late 2022, Mladic was hospitalised in “poor health”, his family said at the time.
In June 2025, Mladic had filed a request to be freed, saying he only had a few months to live. His request was denied.
August 27, 2026: Mladic dies
Mladic died while hospitalised in The Hague, after spending approximately 15 years in custody and detention over war crimes in Bosnia.

The Trouble With Trump’s Attempt to Rename Lake Ontario
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:58:01 UTC
04:58:01 KST

As President Donald Trump’s approval rating hit a new low, he turned once again to the art of redrawing the world map. With the stroke of a pen, the President sought to erase over 400 years of cartographic history by renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” through executive order. Trump’s unilateral action requires that the U.S. Board on Geographic Names update its databases to “reflect the renaming of the Lake and remove all references to Lake Ontario.”
Trump’s executive order applies to all U.S. federal maps, documents, and other communications. However, experts suggest that Trump can’t force other countries, international organizations, private mapping companies, or even U.S. state governments to use the new name. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney has already responded in no uncertain terms that Canada will retain the original name of Lake Ontario “today and forever.” New York Governor Kathy Hochul also rejected the use of the name “Lake America” on New York state maps.
As two geographers who have spent decades studying political toponymy, or the politics of place naming, in both the United States and Canada, we are dismayed by the careless nature of Trump’s impulsive use of place renaming as a form of political rage baiting.
Renaming Lake Ontario is part of a larger pattern of using place naming to promote the Trump brand and his “America First” ideology. From the very outset of his second presidential term, Trump launched the so-called “Golden Age of America” by announcing that the Gulf of Mexico would be renamed the “Gulf of America.” This has now been followed with “Lake America,” and Trump even mused about possibly renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, we presume to something along the lines of “American Ocean” or “Ocean of America.”
Over the past year, Trump’s obsession with naming places has given rise to a new term—toponymic narcissism—which refers to the condition of being obsessed with naming places after oneself.
In many respects, Trump tends to approach the world map much like the Greek mythical figure of Narcissus viewed a body of water: as an opportunity to admire the reflection of his own self-image.
The cost of this narcissistic approach to controlling and changing place names is that it obscures how these names should be shared symbolic resources that serve the broader public and not just the ambitions, grievances, or political feuds of a single individual.
The conventional process of naming geographical features along the U.S.-Canada border involves bringing a formal proposal to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names and the Geographical Names Board of Canada, along with their state and provincial counterparts on both sides of the border. There is generally an extensive consultation process to ensure all geographical naming authorities are on the same page before moving forward with a name change. Yet Trump has thrown all of this out the window simply to rage-bait a U.S. ally into submission.
While the standard place naming process is not perfect, it at least establishes an institutional procedure for review, consultation, evidence gathering, and consideration of competing claims before a geographic name is changed. By contrast, what we are witnessing under Trump 2.0 is a unilateral naming by decree or whim with seemingly no public discussion or real government consideration of impacts and consequences.
It is clear to us that Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario is symbolic political theater aimed at diverting our attention away from the fallout of his trade war with Canada. Yet symbols matter. Place naming is a world-making practice that shapes the very foundations of our geographical imaginations and how we come to know and engage with the world.
There is a risk in dismissing Trump’s cartography of mass distraction as a frivolous symbolic tactic, since it can have real consequences for what is taught in classrooms, reconciliation efforts with Indigenous peoples, and the badly needed repair of relations between the United States and Canada.
If there is any hope to be found in the cartographic carnage that Trump is unleashing on the world map, it is that a future president can just as easily reverse these name changes in an attempt to restore America’s world image.

Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:57:50 BST
04:57:50 KST

Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
- Published
Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s.
"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate."
Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory.
Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together.
Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy.
Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors.
In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent.
Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed.
Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination".
In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide".
Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, external, one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group".
The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide.
However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report.
The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated.
But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone".
They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families.
The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment.
They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population".
Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been".
- Greenland contraception scandal victims hear Danish PM's emotional apology 
  - Published24 September 2025
- Denmark apologises to Greenland's forced contraception victims 
  - Published27 August 2025
- ‘Doctors fitted a contraceptive coil without my consent’ 
  - Published8 December 2022
One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.
"It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act."
A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia.
"We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said.
Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together."
Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992.
The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000.
The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities.
In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

Number of missing in Nepal floods passes 2,400 as UNICEF says 17,000 children need aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:56:52 UTC
04:56:52 KST

Rescuers were battling through mud even as the threat of new floods loomed, with emergency teams recovering 586 bodies so far and some of the dead swept downstream as far away as India.
The number of people missing in Nepal and China surpassed 2,400 on Friday, underscoring the scale of the disaster days after a tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept away villages and killed hundreds.
Rescuers were battling through mud even as the threat of new floods loomed, with emergency teams recovering 586 bodies so far and some of the dead swept downstream as far away as India.
The new figures came as Nepal's disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.
Relatives have crowded hospitals in Nepal's capital in a painful hunt for their loved ones, with posters on the walls bearing photos and names of the missing.
"Today is the third day and we don't know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place," Samjhana Thing, 27, told the AFP news agency referring to her brother. "We lost everything. He is our everything."
The US Geological Survey said the disaster, the deadliest for Nepal since a 2015 earthquake, was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.
The deluge of ice and mud also caused huge lakes to form and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to "immediately move to a safe location", saying it had received information that "a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side."
In Tibet, China was forced to suspend its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding on Friday, before saying the threat had eased.
State broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by immense piles of debris began overflowing toward where rescue teams were headed, but later said the water level of the pool had dropped.
Rescue operations were therefore "proceeding in an orderly manner", it added.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who chaired a meeting on rescue efforts, offered Beijing's help to Nepal's emergency operations.
Swept away
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.
The Nepali military located people trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.
"Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel," army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than 100 people trapped in the same area.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.
"The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away," Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, said.
Aid trickles in
Aid began to reach some survivors in Nepal on Friday, as the full scope of the devastation continued to emerge and survivors sought shelter at makeshift army relief centres.
Children who have been separated from their families are being given shelter as attempts are made to reunite them with families.
The UN's agency for children UNICEF said at least 17,000 children are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, while 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged.
The International Red Cross estimates that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in “great need.”
Also on Friday, the European Union promised €2 million in aid for Nepal with European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen writing on X that the "immediate humanitarian aid" would help "deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest."

Nearly 200,000 people forcibly returned to Haiti so far this year, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:54:24 UTC
04:54:24 KST

Haiti receives nearly 200,000 forced deportees, UN says after brutal gang killing
Aug 28 - Nearly 200,000 people were forcibly returned to Haiti in the first eight months of this year, a U.N. official told an emergency meeting of the Security Council on Friday, days after a brutal gang attack killed nearly 50 people near the capital.
The forced return represents at least 20,000 more people than in the same period last year, Indrika Ratwatte, the acting assistant secretary-general for humanitarian affairs, told the meeting.
Sunday night's attack took place days after Haiti received its first U.S. deportation flight since the Trump administration won a legal battle ending Temporary Protected Status for around 350,000 Haitians. On Thursday, another flight arrived with migrants from the U.S. and the Bahamas.
Haitian security analysts have meanwhile warned that the flood of illegal arms entering the country is worsening the conflict that has claimed more than 21,000 lives since 2022.
The U.N. estimates most guns in Haiti originate from the southeastern United States, though many are trafficked into the country through the land border with the Dominican Republic.
Ratwatte briefed the Security Council alongside Carlos Ruiz, the head of the U.N. Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), who warned that without improved security, efforts to advance preparations for the country's first elections in a decade remain "severely constrained and vulnerable to setbacks."
Ruiz said three boys and two girls were among the 47 people killed in the hillside community of Kenscoff near the capital Port-au-Prince on Sunday, where houses were set on fire and people who sought to escape were attacked inside a church.
"This latest heartbreaking episode is a stark reminder of the urgent need to further strengthen international security support for Haiti," Ruiz said.
U.N.-BACKED FORCE'S MANDATE NEARS END
Diplomats argued the attack showed the need to more rapidly scale up the deployment of the U.N.-backed multinational force mandated to help police fight gangs that have massively expanded their influence over the last five years.
Haitian authorities first requested foreign military assistance in 2022, but this was slow to materialize, and a year ago the U.N. mandated a different, larger and more aggressive force to deploy, called the Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The GSF aims to reach a capacity of 5,500 troops by fall this year. The Security Council will vote on whether to renew its mandate at the end of September.
U.S. representative Jennifer Locetta called on the Security Council to renew the mandate.
"The GSF was not created to issue statements from within a compound wall or spend our money while Haiti suffers," she said, adding if more countries bring material support to the force, it could help police fight gangs more efficiently.
"This attack is precisely why the U.N. authorized Gang Suppression Force's mission and mandate matters," she said.
A representative for the Haitian government said Chad, Mongolia and Ivory Coast had agreed to support the force and work was under way for similar agreements with Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Jamaica and Guatemala. The latter two countries had already deployed personnel under a prior iteration of the force. REUTERS

Merz lays into Germany’s most popular party ahead of regional vote
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will stick to its policy of isolating the AfD despite the right-wing party polling at over 40% ahead of regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt. The chancellor claimed that the Alternative for Germany maintains close ties with Russia and thus poses a threat to the “internal and external security of our country.”
The AfD is the largest opposition faction in the Bundestag and the country’s most popular party, with recent surveys indicating that it enjoys the support of 28% of respondents.
The right-wing party campaigns on an anti-immigration platform and is also highly critical of the German government’s support for Ukraine, as well as sanctions against Russia.
Appearing on broadcaster RTL on Thursday, Merz was asked by a businessman from Saxony-Anhalt about the feasibility of the so-called ‘firewall’ policy in a democracy, under which all major parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD. The question came ahead of the regional elections in the eastern region slated for September 6.
The chancellor defended the controversial policy, categorically ruling out a coalition between the CDU and the AfD due to “fundamental” differences.
He claimed that AfD members frequently visit the Russian Embassy in Berlin and maintain the “closest relationship with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin.” Merz also accused the right-wing party of calling into question “our value system” by advocating Germany’s withdrawal from the Eurozone, the EU single market, and the Schengen Area.
The chancellor suggested the possibility of forming a minority government in Saxony-Anhalt, pointing to the situation in both Thuringia and Saxony, where the AfD has also been sidelined, despite coming out on top in the regional elections.
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published by Bild earlier this month indicated that support for Germany’s governing CDU/CSU bloc had dipped to the lowest level in almost five years, at 20%.
The survey also showed that 78% of respondents were dissatisfied with Merz’s government.
Comprised of the Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc and the Social Democratic Party (SPD), the ruling coalition has faced criticism over continued economic stagnation and its failure to deliver on pre-election promises.
The AfD has for years faced significant pressure from regional and federal authorities in Germany. The country’s domestic security agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has designated the party as a suspected far-right extremist entity – a label that permits government surveillance of the AfD. In several regions, local chapters have been subjected to even wider monitoring by the authorities.
