With Fauda’s new season about to drop on Netflix on September 8, you may be looking for some Middle Eastern action drama while you’re waiting, and one option is the classic commando movie The Delta Force, directed by Menahem Golan. It’s available in Israel on Apple TV and streaming platforms around the world.
The movie was released in 1986, when Golan and his producing partner, Yoram Globus, were at the height of their success with their Hollywood company, the Cannon Group, which churned out dozens of action flicks every year. Not surprisingly, many of their movies dealt with terrorism in the Middle East, like Operation Thunderbolt, about the Entebbe rescue.
The Delta Force is a slightly more polished, more international movie, where the heroes are US commandos rather than Israelis, and is loosely based on the 1985 hijacking of a TWA flight. The narration in the trailer goes, “The enemy doesn’t care who they hurt. Not how young, not how innocent, how helpless. Strangers united by the threat of death find the courage to defy their captors. It’s a new age of terror that requires a new breed of warrior. America’s elite anti-terrorist commandos are committed to destroying the enemies of freedom, because the stakes are more than pride, more than honor, more than justice, because they’re fighting to save American lives.”
The Delta Force delivers classic Middle Eastern action
It stars Chuck Norris as Major Scott McCoy, a tough, loyal fighter who quit the military after the fiasco of the US attempt to rescue the hostages held in the American embassy in 1980, in a scene that opens the movie. But Scott is lured back into the game by his commander (Lee Marvin) when a flight en route to Athens is hijacked and flown to Beirut.
Norris was perfect as the ready-for-anything commando, and the cast featured a great mix of American and Israeli stars. The international cast included German arthouse diva Hanna Schygulla, as the flight attendant ordered by the terrorists to separate out the Jewish passengers; Martin Balsam and Rat Pack member Joey Bishop (who makes a speech about how Beirut was once “the Las Vegas of the Middle East”) as two Jewish passengers and Shelley Winters (The Poseidon Adventure) and Lainie Kazan (who played Adam Sandler’s mother in You Don’t Mess with the Zohan) as their wives; Steve James, who plays one of the US commandos, and who married an Israeli model he met making the movie and had a daughter with her who is a singer and who auditioned for The Next Star for Eurovision; disaster movie stalwart George Kennedy as a priest; Susan Strasberg, who was the original Anne Frank in the Broadway production of The Diary of Anne Frank, as a young mother; and Robert Forster, an all-American actor who played the terrorist leader and whose career was rescued from the doldrums a decade later when Quentin Tarantino cast him in Jackie Brown.
The Israeli actors were similarly stellar, including Assi Dayan as an IDF liaison officer who longs to join the action; Shaike Ophir, the actor for whom the Ophir Awards were named, as a Russian Orthodox priest in Beirut with a big secret; Uri Gavriel as a terrorist; Yehuda Efroni as a passenger; and starlet Chelli Goldenberg as a flight attendant.
It’s fun just watching this cast chew the scenery, and there are a few well-staged action sequences, particularly one in which Norris inexplicably rides a motorcycle to confront the terrorists. There are also a few scenes that show that the terrorists are being backed by the Iranian government. As the French say, “Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose.”
Dolly Parton shines on screen
THE WORLD bid goodbye this week to the iconic singer/actress Dolly Parton, whose appealing, self-deprecating persona charmed even those who didn’t usually enjoy her brand of country/pop music. Although she is best known as a singer, she had a movie career, and several of her films are available to stream in Israel. Her best-known screen role is Doralee, the cheerful secretary whose vile boss sexually harasses her in 9 to 5, which is available on Disney+ and Apple TV. This movie will also be remembered for her theme song, which is played during the opening, and the movie itself never quite matches the energy of the song.
But Parton is a delight as the woman everyone considers a dumb blond but who turns out to be as smart as she is cute, and who gets to deliver the unforgettable lines, “If you ever say another word about me or make another indecent proposal, I’m gonna get that gun of mine... and I’m gonna change you from a rooster to a hen with one shot! DON’T THINK I CAN’T DO IT!”
Shame on the unimaginative Hollywood execs for not giving her more and better parts. Other than 9 to 5, her best movie role was Steel Magnolias, where she played the “glamour technician” Truvy, who runs the beauty salon where much of the action takes place. As with 9 to 5, she plays a variation on Dolly’s persona. She also made an appearance in the finale of the Netflix series Grace and Frankie, in which she was reunited with her 9 to 5 co-stars, Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Parton played a “working-class angel” the heroines meet when they go to heaven in a near-death experience.
There are also a few documentaries and concert specials about Parton available on Netflix and Apple TV. The latter service also offers some of Parton’s lesser movies, including The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, where she sings the original version of her song “I Will Always Love You” to Burt Reynolds. That song became an even bigger hit for Whitney Houston, and many of Parton’s songs were recorded by other artists.
The Game offers a psychological thriller
The Game, which is on Yes VOD and Yes London starting August 31, is an old-fashioned psychological thriller series with terrific performances. It tells the story of Huw Miller (Jason Watkins), a police detective who retires in the first episode. His career was derailed when he was chasing a sadistic killer and missed him even though he got close.
While Miller is looking forward to a quiet retirement playing golf with his buddy, everything changes when a new neighbor, Patrick Harbottle (Robson Green), moves in. Harbottle is handsome and charming, but he starts dropping weird hints that convince Miller that he is the killer who got away.
Meanwhile, Harbottle does everything he can to create conflict between Miller and his family, and seems to be playing the long game, while Miller blunders into the increasingly sophisticated traps set for him. None of it is groundbreaking, but it’s solid entertainment.

"All persons seeking to come to Canada must meet the eligibility and admissibility requirements under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Decisions regarding the granting of travel documents are made independently, on a case-by-case basis, by trained officers."

Cancellation of eTA may have resulted from anti-Israel campaigns

HRF then posted: "Victory in Canada. LCP and HRF succeeded in revoking the travel authorization of Arieh King."
HRF files US DOJ request to prosecute King

Russian online marketplace Ozon sold customers $290 million worth of military and dual-use goods over the past year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:24:40 UTC
04:24:40 KST

From August 2025 through July 2026, users of the Russian online marketplace Ozon ordered more than 2.13 million items that could be used for military purposes, paying over 25 billion rubles ($290 million under the current exchange rate), the independent outlet Verstka reports, citing the marketplace’s internal analytics. Journalists identified 33 categories of goods with direct and potential military uses and grouped them into four clusters: military-tactical gear, optics, drones and their components, and firearm parts and accessories.
Military-tactical gear accounted for the largest share. Over the year, users ordered more than 527,000 such items worth 9.14 billion rubles ($106.2 million). Items in this group included body armor, ballistic helmets, tactical vests, protective plates, and neck and shoulder protection.
Nearly 157,700 pieces of body armor were ordered for 5.07 billion rubles ($58.9 million). The average order value was 32,300 rubles ($375). Another 1.48 billion rubles ($17.2 million) went toward the purchase of 81,100 ballistic helmets, and 1.2 billion rubles ($13.9 million) was used to buy nearly 159,000 tactical vests and belts.
Military optics were ordered nearly 350,000 times over the year at a total of 7.22 billion rubles ($83.9 million). This group included optical, collimator, digital, and thermal imaging sights, night vision devices, and thermal imagers. Thermal imaging sights turned out to be the most expensive: more than 28,000 units were ordered at an average price of about 140,000 rubles ($1,600).
Users spent 6.26 billion rubles ($72.7 million) on drones and related products, while about 3 billion rubles ($34.9 million) went toward 554,000 accessories, including frames, propellers, receivers, and cameras for building custom drones. Another 1.15 billion rubles ($13.3 million) was spent on batteries, and about 1.7 billion rubles ($19.7 million) on fully assembled drones.
Components and accessories for small arms were ordered for nearly 2.46 billion rubles ($28.5 million). Weapon grips were the most frequently purchased item — more than 132,500 units for 307 million rubles ($3.5 million). However, the highest revenue in this group came from stocks: 58,500 units were ordered for nearly 605 million rubles ($7 million).
The calculations are based on categories from Ozon’s internal analytics that Verstka classified as military or dual-use goods. These may include items that end up being used for civilian purposes, and the data does not make it possible to identify the buyers or end recipients of the goods. Ozon has thus far not commented on the findings.
Several Ozon logistics centers across Russia have come under aerial attack in recent days following a series of strikes against facilities belonging to its chief competitor in the Russian market, the Wildberries online marketplace. The first confirmed strike on an Ozon warehouse occurred on Aug. 22 in Chapayevsk, Samara Region, leading to a fire and several injuries. In the following days, attacks and the threat of strikes affected the company’s facilities in several more regions, and on Aug. 27, Ozon reported attempted attacks on warehouses in Ufa and Orenburg.

President Donald Trump signs order creating US Space Academy

Unknown Publisher

President Donald Trump signs order creating US Space Academy
The president said graduates of the new academy would serve the US Space Force, NASA and the civilian flight industry.
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order establishing the country’s first-ever Space Academy.
On Friday during an event honoring the four-person Artemis II crew at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Texas, Trump made the unexpected announcement. He described the training facility as “a big deal” and said it would be “top line”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3NASA announces astronauts for Artemis III spaceflight, scheduled for 2027
- list 2 of 3Artemis II crew seen on recovery ship after moon mission return
- list 3 of 3NASA hails success of Artemis moon mission but says more work to do
“I will sign an executive order to begin the process of creating a new national academy. It’s called the US Space Academy,” Trump told the astronauts and NASA employees who gathered to hear him speak.
Trump likened the space academy to other prestigious US service institutions, like the US Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, and the US Military Academy in West Point, New York. Those schools, similar to colleges, prepare a select number of young adults in the US to become officers in the country’s military branches.
“They’re all great. But … we’re gonna have an academy for what the people in this room love the most,” Trump said. “That’s really exciting.”
The order also establishes a new presidential commission that would “advise and assist” Trump in the academy’s creation.
This commission will be led by NASA administrator Jared Isaacman and include top administration officials, among them Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and Russ Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget.
The president said graduates of the new academy would serve the US Space Force, NASA and the civilian flight industry.
“It’ll attract, train and graduate the very best of our nation,” Trump added.
Space has been a significant priority during Trump’s two terms in the White House. In December 2019, Trump signed into law a bill establishing the Space Force, marking the creation of the US military’s sixth branch.
“There are grave threats to our national security,” Trump said at the time. “The Space Force will help us deter aggression and control the ultimate high ground.”
At Friday’s ceremony, Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to each of the four members of this year’s Artemis II crew: NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, along with Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen.
The medal is the highest civilian honour in the US for achievement in space flight.
In April, the Artemis II crew looped around the far side of the moon, taking humans further into space than ever before. The mission was an important step in the Trump administration’s plan to return astronauts to the moon by 2028.
Trump said one of his meetings this past spring was interrupted by news of the crew’s endeavours.
“I was at a very important meeting with the biggest people in the country,” Trump explained. “And somebody said, ‘I’d like to watch Artemis.’ I said, ‘You would? Really?'”
He added that he paused the meeting to accommodate the request. “We actually had a television pulled up, and everybody was spellbound.”
At Friday’s event, the Artemis II crew also presented Trump with a gift: a blue flight jacket with the NASA logo.
“Mr President, when we were in your office and you were so gracious to us – lavishing us with gifts and so much of your time – we had mentioned getting you one of these blue flight jackets,” Glover said to Trump. “And so here we have your jacket today.”
But the future of the Artemis exploration initiative remains unclear.
In May, an unmanned Blue Origin rocket exploded at a launch facility in Cape Canaveral, Florida, causing damage to the site. The incident spurred questions about NASA’s readiness for upcoming missions.
The Artemis III mission was initially expected to return humankind to the moon. But in February, NASA scrapped that plan, instead announcing that Artemis III would focus on running drills in Earth’s orbit, to ensure the safety of future moon missions.
The mission will practice docking with Moon lander models from the private companies Blue Origin and SpaceX.
In June, NASA announced new crew members for the two-week Artemis III mission, scheduled for next year.

====================================================================================================

Where are all the aliens? A new book explores possible answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:23:17 UTC
04:23:17 KST

We’ve been looking for aliens for as long as we’ve been looking up at the starry night sky. Wondering, “What’s up there?” quickly leads to asking, “Who’s up there—and why won’t they come down here and say hi?!”
Astrobiology—the study of life in the universe, from how it began and evolved to how it might take shape elsewhere—is the catch-all scientific field in which researchers grapple with such weighty questions about what’s out there. And, at least when we contemplate the existence of little green men rather than little green microbes, one of astrobiology’s cornerstones is the Drake equation, a seven-factor formula devised by astronomer Frank Drake in 1961 that estimates whether extraterrestrial civilizations are vanishingly rare—or common as dirt.
In the new book Cloudy with a Chance of Starships, Seven Rasmussen, an astrobiologist and devoted Star Trek fan, acts as a tour guide to the astrocurious, showcasing how the Drake equation is more than the sum of its parts—it’s not just a tool for quantifying our chances of first contact but also a tracker of astrobiology’s ever changing frontiers.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Scientific American spoke with Rasmussen about what the latest values for the Drake equation are, how the definition of “intelligent life” is slippery and how our unending search for alien neighbors is like gazing in a cosmic mirror.
What exactly is the Drake equation?
In 1961 Frank Drake had a problem. He had just performed the first-ever search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) by pointing a radio telescope at some nearby stars and was hosting a conference to discuss the project. He wanted to start the discussion with something cool, so he came up with a seven-[term] equation that can tell us how many civilizations we could talk to in the galaxy right now. I love the way the Drake equation is organized so much because it starts off with things that we know pretty well, such as the rate of star formation in the galaxy, and then it wades into thornier things, such as how many planets there are per star. And then it gets into really wild things, such as: What are the odds that a planet hosts intelligent life? And finally, it ends with the average lifetime of a civilization, which is something absolutely unknowable to us at present.
You say at one point in the book that astrobiology is “20 sciences in a trench coat,” which I thought was funny. So what is astrobiology, and what’s in this trench coat?
It really is, though. Astrobiology is the study of life in the universe—both as it occurs here on Earth and as it could occur elsewhere. The reason I love to say it’s 20 sciences in a trench coat is because it really draws upon every single science that we can imagine.
It has astronomy and biology in the name, but astronomy is physics, and biology is chemistry. And a lot of the things that we know about all of these different sciences come from the fossil record, and that’s all geology. And, of course, at the foundation of all these things is math. But there’s also network science in there, and if we’re talking about technological civilizations, then there’s engineering and a whole lot more. It’s really the science that encompasses all other sciences.
Another memorable bit from the book is that the most common phrase uttered by exoplanet scientists is probably a curse word, and after that it’s got to be “oops.” I think that’s an observation that says just as much about the researchers themselves as it does about their field. I’m fascinated by these sorts of peeks into the personalities of the people who are drawn to this kind of science, which is so full of big, unanswered questions. So is there anything else you can tell me about the sort of nerds that choose to become astrobiologists?
Well, it’s definitely a very specific type of nerd. You know, it’s somebody who’s adventurous and curious and, most importantly, okay with studying something for which they may never get an answer. And that’s why I first got into astronomy and astrophysics—I loved it because it was just so big. Astrobiology is this bizarre fabric that pulls and weaves together all the threads of physics and biology and intelligence and philosophy. It’s really beautiful, and it’s all about embracing the unknown.
Yeah, these are folks who are seriously, actually looking for aliens all the time—which is like every kid’s dream of what a scientist does. But the reality, I imagine, is different from the dream: What are we actually looking for when we search for alien life? In the book, you talk about “biosignatures” and “technosignatures,” for instance, but what do those actually look like?
Well, biosignatures are basically any evidence that a living creature, past or present, has interacted with whatever environment or material you’re looking at—like if a rover rolling around Mars finds a fossil. Another example would be gases produced by living creatures that leak out into the air—so-called atmospheric biosignatures, a topic I’ve studied in-depth in my research. Earth’s atmosphere, for example, has lots of free oxygen—but it also has methane, which is a gas emitted by some types of microbes that isn’t thermodynamically stable in the oxygen’s presence. I talk a lot more about this in the book, with the upshot being how, if you see a whole lot of methane on a somewhat Earth-like planet, that could be evidence that Earth-like life is there, too.
So a biosignature is really anything that’s evidence of life, anything produced by a living creature. Conventionally, a technosignature is something that’s been produced by technology, presumably built and used by an alien civilization. The most extreme version of a technosignature might be if the Vulcans from Star Trek came down to Earth in a spaceship and said hello to us. We’d say, “Wow, now that is a technosignature!”
Yeah. “Hey, you got a real nice spaceship there!” That would definitely be a signature of alien technology.
Exactly. Other technosignatures are things like if we detected chemicals in a planet’s atmosphere that are only artificially produced. Probably the biggest example of this we know about is chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), the stuff that [used to make] AquaNet spray out of the can but [was also destroying] Earth’s ozone layer. So if we saw CFCs in an atmosphere, that would be a technosignature—although it wouldn’t necessarily indicate a very intelligent civilization because, as we know, it has very undesirable side effects.
You get at this more in your book, this idea that, if the only astronomically detectable signs of your “intelligence” are related to you severely destabilizing and damaging your environment, then how intelligent are you, really? It’s an interesting question to ponder when we’re looking for signs of alien life.
Yeah. I really took inspiration there from a conversation I had with science historian Rebecca Charbonneau about a concept we call “the cosmic mirror.” The astronomer and SETI researcher Jill Tarter was the first to come up with this, and it basically says that the technosignatures we’re now looking for out in the galaxy are reflective of how we're presently interacting with technology here on Earth. Rebecca gave me this great example of how, after World War II ended, we had all this radio technology we’d invented to spy across the ocean. And astronomers were like, “Well, maybe if someone was trying to contact us from a long distance away, they’d be using radio, too.” So we got radio-based SETI out of that, like the early searches Frank Drake and others performed. And after the laser was invented, we started to think, “Hey, maybe you could use a really big laser to communicate across star systems.” So now we have laser-based SETI programs, too. It’s so remarkable to me, the kind of parallel development of technosignature searches for aliens “out there” with what’s going on, globally and socially, right here.
This relates to something I really wanted to ask you about, which is the Fermi paradox. I loved how you explained in the book that Enrico Fermi was a nuclear physicist “whose only interaction with the SETI community was asking one off-putting question at lunch one time.” Could you walk me through what happened at that awkward lunch and how it gave us this popular concept?
Yeah, so Enrico Fermi, as you said, was a nuclear physicist, and he was part of the Manhattan Project, where the U.S. was racing to develop the atomic bomb before Germany did. And so one day during his lunches with his fellow nuclear physicists, the conversation turned to a recent New Yorker cartoon that lampooned the UFO mania of the time by depicting little green men stealing trash cans in New York City. So they’re talking about this cartoon at lunch, and Enrico Fermi is thinking about it, and the conversation moves on. But then he arrives at the pretty logical conclusion of “Where are the trash-can-stealing aliens?” Dubious UFO sightings aside, if other planets like Earth exist and interstellar communication or even interstellar travel is possible, why haven’t we been contacted yet? And so the Fermi paradox is exactly that question: Where’s everybody else?
Right. And I guess, together or individually, each of the seven terms in the Drake equation could offer some insights about the Fermi paradox’s possible answers. The trouble, as you mentioned, is that our plugged-in values for some of those [terms] are much more certain than for others. Do you think we’ll ever actually figure out, for instance, the average lifespan of technological civilizations or the fraction of planets that they pop up on?
That’s a great question. I’m an optimist—and a Star Trek–brand optimist at that! I believe that, perhaps hundreds of years down the line, when we’ve dealt with climate change and when we’ve denuclearized the world and when we’ve defeated capitalism once and for all, we’ll be able to invent the one thing that will allow us to survey the galaxy, which will be faster-than-light travel. You know, Frank Drake’s equation motivated Star Trek, actually. It was part of the pitch for Star Trek. Gene Roddenberry was like, “I just heard of this new equation that tells us about how much life there is in the galaxy, and here’s a TV show about it.”
I do have to ask you, for “all the peanuts,” as Douglas Adams would say: If you could pick one term out of the Drake equation to know with certainty, which would it be?
It’s got to be fi, the [term] encapsulating the fraction of habitable planets that don’t just develop life but also intelligent life. I want to know: In 100 years, are we going to consider an octopus to be intelligent? Are we going to consider a sperm whale to be intelligent? Will we afford protections for those creatures based on our definition of intelligence? That’s probably the one that, right now, interests me the most.

====================================================================================================

Russia’s Medvedev awaits both positive, negative surprises from AI in few years’ time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:23:05 UTC
04:23:05 KST

MOSCOW, August 28. /TASS/. In the next few years, artificial intelligence (AI) will present both positive and negative surprises, Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Chairman of the Security Council, said as he called this technology a terra incognita.

"Well, artificial intelligence is already joining forces with, so to say, potential partners as it creates bots to breach security systems of certain companies - a task it was not even given <…>. And next we can imagine a totally apocalyptic scenario of where humankind is heading," he added.

Spring scorcher to follow record warm winter for south-east capitals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:21:04 UTC
04:21:04 KST

Spring scorcher to follow record warm winter for Australia's south-east capitals
Australia is wrapping up an exceptionally mild winter, and modelling continues to favour unprecedented heat across the country through spring.
For Sydney and Melbourne, winter has been the warmest on record, with a mean temperature above all previous years in the Bureau of Meteorology's (BOM) meteorological history for both cities dating back to the 1850s.
Canberra also saw its highest ever winter temperatures, while for Adelaide and Hobart, this season will rank as the second-warmest on record.
Climate zones shifting south
Temperatures through winter were so consistently above normal along the eastern seaboard, the weather resembled long-term climates well to the north.
For example, Sydney's mean temperature — the average of all minimums and maximums — was 15.3 degrees Celsius, 2.3C above the long-term average, and only a fraction of a degree below Brisbane's winter climate last century.
In a similar vein, Hobart's mean of 10.4C, equals Melbourne's long-term winter average, while Melbourne's 12.2C was just 0.8C off Sydney's historic winter climate.
Also noteworthy this winter was the lack of extreme cold days and snow.
Brisbane only registered two maximums below 20C, and Canberra just one below 10C.
For our national capital, the coldest day this winter brought a high of 9.5C on July 13 — that's the highest ever, lowest winter maximum, and was 3C warmer than Canberra's typical coldest day of the year.
Sydney's lowest maximum this winter was also a record. A top of 15.5C on June 25 was 3.6C above the typical coldest day, and beats the old record of 14.6C from 1979.
With a lack of polar outbreaks this winter, it goes with the territory that snow was scarce.
It was not only a very poor ski season in alpine regions, but many sub-alpine stretches of the ranges that occasionally see snowfalls missed out completely.
For example, snow did not fall in the Blue Mountains west of Sydney for the fourth consecutive year. Last century, a snowfall or two was nearly guaranteed every winter.
The west coast was relatively cool this winter compared to eastern states, with Perth's temperatures only 0.3C above the long-term average.
Burst of warmth for the start of spring
The source of this year's abnormal heat is complex, and while natural variability and climate change are the main drivers, temperatures are receiving an additional boost from an extreme El Niño event, along with a notable absence of cold fronts arriving from the Southern Ocean.
A similar set of factors that elevated winter temperatures should also be lurking in the background through spring.
And the season will open with a burst of warm north-westerly winds across south-east states, sending temperatures around 5C above normal on the first of September.
Canberra is predicted to hit 21C on Tuesday, and Melbourne and Adelaide 22C, the warmest first day of spring in five years for all three cities.
A warm 25C to 27C is forecast across Sydney for the first day of spring, and while a cooler westerly change will lower temperatures along the southern coastline by Wednesday, the heat will continue to build near the east coast.
Sydney is predicted to reach 27C on Wednesday, 7C above normal for September, while Brisbane is tipped to hit 31C on Thursday and Friday, also about 7C above the long-term average.
Modelling tips record warm season for south
The heat this week is a likely preview of what is ahead through the remainder of the season.
Modelling is forecasting temperatures during the next three months to be the warmest on record for an Australian spring across southern states.
Below is the latest output from the BOM's ACCESS-S model, which is predicting much of our south will see temperatures between 2C and 3C above the baseline 1981 to 2018 average.
However, climate change was already having a significant impact by the turn of the century, which means the forecast converts to a temperature between 3C to 4C above pre-industrial levels.
Considering a 4C above average on a single day is noticeable, when averaged across an entire season, this represents a major shift in the climate.
Another way to analyse the spring forecast is the probability of it being unusually warm, temperatures in the top 20 per cent of years.
According to the BOM's modelling, there is a greater than 80 per cent chance southern Australia will record maximum temperatures in this bracket, while for minimums the 80 per cent plus area is even more widespread, covering around two-thirds of the country.
And forecasts for early summer show no relief.
The map below is a multi-model prediction for January, which is produced by averaging the forecasts from nine meteorological agencies.
The multi-model approach displays a forecast anomaly of 1C to 2C across most of Australia.
Although in this case the baseline used is a more recent, and therefore warmer 1993 to 2016 period, meaning a conversion to pre-industrial levels increases this prediction by another 1.2C

Why so many Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet disaster are pilgrims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:17:56 UTC
04:17:56 KST

Why so many Australians missing after Nepal-Tibet flash flood are pilgrims
Most of the Australians missing after the flash flood that struck the Himalayas on the border of Nepal and Tibet were pilgrims to a spiritually important mountain known as Kailash.
While the identity of many of the 38 missing Australians has yet to be formally confirmed, three tour companies have reported that at least 32 were on trips to visit the remote peak.
Thousands of people from all over the world visit the mountain in south-western Tibet each year, with many travelling via the major highway destroyed on Wednesday by the catastrophic wave of water, mud and rocks.
Mount Kailash holds significance for Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and the Tibetan Bon tradition. Each associates the mountain with different beliefs and sacred histories.
Geographer Emily Yeh, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has conducted research in Tibet, wrote in 2017 that Kailash is associated with the mythical Mount Meru, considered the centre of the world in Hindu and Buddhist cosmology.
According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, the mountain is considered the home of Shiva, the Hindu god of destruction, and Parvati, a Hindu goddess associated with marriage, fertility and motherhood.
Followers of the Tibetan Bon tradition regard it as a seat of spiritual power and associate the region with Tonpa Shenrab, the tradition's founder.
Pilgrims travel to the mountain for purification
India's government operates an official Kailash Manasarovar pilgrimage from June until August or September each year, with routes through the states of Uttarakhand and Sikkim.
Private operators — including several Australian tour companies — also organise pilgrimages via Nepal.
The peak rises more than 6,400 metres above sea level and close to Lake Manasarovar, which is also a significant spiritual site. Pilgrims traditionally walk around the mountain rather than climb it, completing a roughly 53-kilometre circuit.
The circuit is believed to cleanse pilgrims of their sins and can take about three days to complete. Hindus and Buddhists traditionally circle the mountain clockwise, while followers of Bon travel counterclockwise.
At nearby Lake Manasarovar, some Hindu pilgrims bathe in its waters as a ritual of spiritual purification.
Yeh wrote that Tibetan pilgrims stop at monasteries and other sacred sites along the route, touching prayer beads or their foreheads to features believed to bear sacred imprints. Other rituals are meant to test a pilgrim's merit, sin or fortune.
Australians on pilgrimage
Hundreds of people were killed in the disaster and many more remain missing.
Of those missing, at least 540 are foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India headed to Kailash and Lake Mansarovar.
Sadhguru, a hugely popular Indian guru who organises trips to Mount Kailash, released a video in which he said 11 Australians were in a larger group of pilgrims at the immigration centre at Gyirong on the border between Tibet and Nepal when it was destroyed.
He said the group had already visited Kailash and were checking back into Nepal.
A guide sent a message that the group had arrived at the facility only moments before the flash flood struck, he said.
"Literally the entire group was there in the building," he said, fighting back tears.
Queensland woman Kanagamah Sundrasan was reportedly on her way to Mount Kailash when she went missing.
She was one of six Australians who were part of a group organised by tour company Kailash Journeys.
Her daughter Swaatika Kanniah told the ABC her mother was due to arrive the day after the flood hit.
"According to her itinerary, [Thursday] was supposed to be the day she was getting there, basically," Ms Kanniah said.
"It's a very sacred spot, so it was one of her dreams to fulfil.
"She doesn't really go on trips like this. That's why it was very exciting for her to travel and do this thing that she always wanted to do," she added.
Himalayan Glacier, a tourism agency operating in the area, said 15 of the missing Australians were on a religious tour to Mount Kailash it was organising. The group also included people from India, the US, Canada and Singapore.
"They were on a pilgrimage. They were planning to enter China Tibet and go to the Mount Kailash and (Lake) Manasarovar, which is one of the holiest landmarks on earth," chief executive Sagar Pandey told Reuters.
All 15 were Indian Australians, with the youngest an 11-year-old boy, he said.
Mr Pandey said he had flown over the flood zone by helicopter after the disaster and believed there was only a "1 per cent chance" of survival.
"There are no human-made things, no human settlement left. Everything is just flat … I believe that everybody is gone."
Holy day celebrations
It's not just pilgrims to Mount Kailash who were caught up in the disaster.
At least some of those missing were on their way to Lake Gosaikunda for a Hindu holy day, Janai Purnima, celebrated yesterday.
Utsav Aryal, from the Nepalese Australian Welfare Society, said 5,000 to 10,000 mostly Nepali people took the pilgrimage each year for ritual bathing and prayers.
During the festival, devotees take holy dips and participate in religious ceremonies, while shamans perform traditional rites. Hindu men renew the Janai, or sacred thread, worn diagonally across the chest, while priests tie sacred protective threads, known as doro or raksha sutra, around devotees' wrists.
Mr Aryal said many attendees drove on the Pasang Lhamu Highway to the towns of either Dhunche or Syabrubesi before trekking north-east for about three days to the lake.
Local media reported that a bus carrying about 40 passengers headed to Gosaikunda was swept away by the flash flood, with only five managing to jump from the bus and survive.
An Australian colleague's sister, mother and father attended the festival before the flood struck and were stuck, he said.
"They are currently waiting to be rescued but are safe and sound," he said.
Mr Aryal said the highway between Nepal and Tibet had become an increasingly popular trade route and destination for domestic tourists.
"It's not that far from Kathmandu," he said. "It's like two hours' drive. So they very often drive to this place, have a drink next to the towns nearby the river. It was getting more popular.
"Even my parents were there not too long ago, a couple of months ago, travelling to enjoy. [My father] described it as very pretty."

Meanwhile, Spain's interior minister called for calm after Ceuta residents clashed with police during protests against migrants who have remained in the enclave following a mass influx.
Spain has asked the European Commission (EC) for the support from Frontex and Europol to assist with the screening of migrants who are staying irregularly in Ceuta, according to several Spanish media outlets.
Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska has asked the EC for Frontex, Europol and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) to "reinforce the device set up to address the management of the triage and subsequent processing of the personal files of the immigrants who still remain in Ceuta irregularly."
The Interior Ministry also demanded the extension of Operation Minerva, a joint initiative of the Spanish police and the EU border protection agency Frontex.
Madrid ask that that operation run until 2 September until "the situation created in the autonomous city is resolved."
Madrid also asked for the " assistance of the European Union Agency for Asylum in conducting interviews and providing interpreters" in order to triage migrants.
Due to space limitations in Ceuta, this process is expected to be carried out electronically.
The Interior Ministry announced on Friday that Ceuta's border would be reinforced with a package of "extraordinary" measures such as extending the Tarajal and Benzú breakwaters, a permanent system of maritime containment buoys, aerial surveillance with drones, light intervention vessels and remotely operated underwater devices.
At the same time, Ceuta's Assembly unanimously called on the central government on Friday to act "immediately and without further delay" arguing that the city is in an "extreme situation, on the verge of collapse."
The Board of Spokespersons, together with the non-affiliated MPs, unanimously approved on Friday an institutional declaration calling on the government to adopt urgent measures one month after the mass entry of at least 72,000 migrants from Morocco.
"Ceuta has lost its way of life and its calm. We do not have much time to avert disaster," Ceuta's President Juan Vivas warned.
The declaration calls for a return to their countries, "in accordance with the law" of those who took part in the mass entry and are still in Ceuta. It also backs citizens' right to demonstrate, as long as it is done "peacefully and in an orderly manner," and condemns violent incidents recorded in recent days.
"No one can or should take the law into their own hands. The defence of Ceuta and the interests of its people can only be pursued through legality," Vivas said.
Appeal for calm
Meanwhile, Spain's interior minister called for calm on Friday after residents of Ceuta clashed with police during protests against migrants who have remained in the North African enclave following a mass influx.
Tensions have been high in the territory of 80,000 people since at least 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta over several days in July, triggering a Europe-wide migrant alert.
Spain's leftist government says most have since left the enclave of 18.5 square kilometres but thousands remain wandering the streets and sleeping on beaches.
Demonstrations have intensified in recent days, with some protesters clashing with police on Thursday at a beach where migrants have been sleeping. Some of their belongings were burned.
A soldier was injured in a separate incident on Thursday when migrants threw stones at troops, while 12 Moroccan migrants were arrested.
Two more arrests were made after migrants attacked a police officer, sources said.
"Violence is not the answer," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told parliament on Friday.
"I call for calm and an end to any form of violence, because...violence is not the way to resolve any problem with the complexity" of that facing Ceuta, he added.
Right-wing and far-right parties have demanded that all the migrants be rounded up and sent back to their home countries.
Grande-Marlaska accused them of "inciting hatred and confrontation" in Ceuta.
The government has warned that each individual must be identified to determine whether they are entitled to asylum or subject to deportation, while unaccompanied migrant children require special protection.
Ceuta and Melilla, another small Spanish territory in North Africa, form Europe's only land border with Africa.

Aluminum producer Rusal plans to temporarily mothball part of its raw materials production in Russia, the business daily Kommersant said, citing a letter seen by journalists that the company sent to Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
The plan includes the Pikalyovo Alumina Refinery (PGLZ), the Severouralsk Bauxite Mine (SUBR), and the alumina-producing Bogoslovsk and Ural plants, according to Kommersant.
The enterprises generate $800 million in annual losses for Rusal, and the company estimates it will need $1.8 billion in investment to restore its raw materials division.
Rusal asked the government to consider state support for regions and municipalities, promising to “minimize the socioeconomic consequences” of the mothballing.
One source in the metals market told Kommersant the main risk of the mothballing is potential layoffs in the company towns where the plants operate, particularly Krasnoturyinsk, Severouralsk, and Kamensk-Uralsky.
Pikalyovo, a company town in the Leningrad region, became one of the major flashpoints of social unrest in 2009. After the town’s three main employers — an alumina plant, a cement plant, and a chemical plant — shut down, unemployed residents took to the streets and blocked the federal highway between Novaya Ladoga and Vologda. Then-Prime Minister Vladimir Putin traveled to the town. The State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, called what happened in Pikalyovo “an example of irresponsible behavior by business.” The plants’ operations were eventually restored.

Is Israel really 'one step away' from total victory in Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:09:38 UTC
04:09:38 KST

Since the October 7 disaster and throughout two years of war, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly declared that Israel was on the verge of achieving "total victory" over Hamas. He has insisted not only that such a victory was attainable, but that Israeli forces were just weeks away from completing the mission. Time and again, reality has proved otherwise.
Two months into the war, at a Hanukkah candle-lighting ceremony held at the Western Wall on December 7, 2023, Netanyahu declared: "We will soon achieve total victory over the forces of evil and restore security not only to the south but also to the north."
Three months later, at the start of a cabinet meeting in April 2024, he declared: "We are about one step away" from victory in Gaza.
In August 2025, Netanyahu and his security cabinet set five objectives that had to be achieved before the war could end: disarming Hamas, securing the return of all the hostages, the complete demilitarization of Gaza, permanent Israeli security control including the perimeter zone, and the establishment of an alternative civilian administration that would be neither Hamas nor the Palestinian Authority.
A cease-fire agreement was signed last October, but as of August 2026, Hamas has not been defeated. The group has yet to disarm, and Israel continues to control a significant portion of the Gaza Strip – beyond the Yellow Line set out to separate the sides in the agreement – while striking Hamas targets and operatives almost daily, with dozens of Palestinians killed every month. The IDF also assesses that Hamas has used the recent period to rebuild its capabilities.
In January 2026, the Board of Peace was established by U.S. President Donald Trump, an international body led by the United States that is intended to administer the Strip through a Palestinian technocratic committee. In late July 2026, the Board of Peace and Hamas agreed on a framework for disarming the group, which is meant to lead to an Israeli withdrawal and the transfer of Gaza's administration to the Palestinian technocrats. However, the date on which the committee will begin operating has yet to be set, and Hamas remains the de facto authority in areas west of the Yellow Line.
Under the current agreements, the IDF is authorized to control 53 percent of the Strip. In practice, Israel currently controls an estimated 60 to 70 percent of the territory, without international approval.

Second excavation phase at Kashmir Buddhist starts today
Unknown

Excavations for the second phase of the 2,000-year-old Buddhist site at Zehanpora in Baramulla to begin on Saturday
ZEHANPORA (BARAMULLA): Excavations will begin Saturday on the second phase of Zehanpora, a Buddhist site in north Kashmir’s Baramulla. J&K chief secretary Atal Dullo will inaugurate the project.The presence of a 2,000-year-old Buddhist civilisation at the site was discovered last year by Mohamad Ajmal Shah, a professor at University of Kashmir. It gained prominence after PM Narendra Modi mentioned it during his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat on Dec 28 last year.The Prime Minister recalled that people had noticed tall mounds in Zehanpora for years without knowing about their significance. What were first believed to be unusual rock formations were later found to resemble three Buddha stupas seen in photos in a French museum.According to Modi, the blurred photos, thousands of kilometres away, proved crucial as it showed three Buddhist stupas, helping archaeologists connect the dots and reconstruct Kashmir’s ancient past. The discovery reaffirms J&K’s rich cultural legacy.It all began in Oct 2023 when Shah was on a fellowship in France and came across the 100-odd old photos at Guimet Museum showing stupa domes in Baramulla. “I immediately realised I had visited the site.
What struck me was the domes in the photos looked much larger than what we see now,” said Shah, attached to the varsity’s department of Central Asian Studies.Later, Shah requested J&K govt’s department of archaeology to fund the project and it agreed. Shah and his team started digging in Nov last year, initially discovering a hall identified as an apsidal (semi-circular) stupa.Shah and his team also found iron/copper artefacts, needles, decorated objects and other materials. “We identified wall alignments through drone images and excavated precisely at those points. There is a strong possibility that many structures and artefacts still lie preserved beneath the ground,” Shah said.Shah highlighted the possibility that the site was linked to the Fourth Buddhist Council (1st century CE). “Kashmir was a major centre of Buddhism in ancient times. It was here that Hinayana Buddhism evolved into Mahayana Buddhism, giving the religion a new philosophical and cultural form,” he said.
Shah pointed out that the Chinese explorer Hiuen Tsang had mentioned Baramulla in his travel accounts. According to Shah, Tsang spent a night at Uskur, a Buddhist site near Baramulla town and visited several monasteries in the area. “This suggests Tsang must have visited the monastery at Zehanpora as well,” Shah said.

====================================================================================================

What does it mean to be a 'good' man? Ben Vasiliou learned the hard way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

The Interview: Ben Vasiliou wants to talk about how to be a Better Man. Just don't mention the 't-word'
The majority of people who die of suicide in Australia are men, though relatively few say they'd seek help from a mental health professional if they were struggling. We're grappling with a "national crisis" of gendered violence, with one woman killed by her intimate partner every 11 or so days, on average.
Online, manosphere influencers insist that men are in crisis — they're failing to thrive, struggling to find purpose, employment, contentment — because women today have degrees and jobs and independence. They sell advice to get rich quick, to become more handsome by taking hormones and steroids and smashing their jaws with hammers.
Meanwhile, a rising tide of isolation, loneliness and social division is threatening to undermine public health and safety.
These are problems of masculinity gone wrong, says Ben Vasiliou, author of the new book Better Man: Reclaiming masculinity for good. Vasiliou, the chief executive of The Man Cave, which runs healthy masculinity workshops for teenage boys, points a finger at "outdated, rigid stereotypes" — "toxic norms" that tell men to be tough and stoic, squash down pain and fear, never show softness or weakness, never ask for help.
Better Man is Vasiliou's contribution to what has become an urgent, if noisy, conversation about what it means to be a man, and at what cost (Vasiliou himself paid a heavy price for suppressing his true self; he recounts the deep shame and despair he suffered before coming out as gay in his late 20s, when he was married with two children).
It is also a blueprint for change, a guidebook of Vasiliou's ideas for helping a new generation of boys embrace a "more expansive" definition of masculinity so they can enjoy better mental health, better relationships and better lives.
When we meet on a crisp August morning in Melbourne, I'm keen to ask whether being a "good" man is really that different to being a "good" human, and who he'd rather be stuck on an island with: Donald Trump or Andrew Tate.
Have you read a book recently that changed the way you think about a particular issue or yourself?
I recently read the latest and most detailed autobiography of Oscar Wilde. I've never really ventured into his story but the reason why it's staying with me is one, I had the attention span to read 800 pages, which is very rare. And two, it put things into perspective. He was living in the late nineteenth century, and I was able to think about the challenges that were facing the community at that time — particularly around the Industrial Revolution, the Mechanical Revolution, the fight against modernism and contemporary political issues — and how they have showed up today, whether that be with the AI revolution or the weird politics we're seeing around the world.
It just goes to show that humanity has been through these things before; they're different challenges, but they have similar themes about how we progress as a society, how we treat men, how we treat difference, how we treat diversity. Oscar has a similar story to mine. We both married a woman young, had two children young, and although he didn't publicly come out, he was tried for it and sent to jail for being a gay man, and in a way I kind of felt a bit prosecuted when I came out. So I don't know if it changed the course of my thinking, but it gave me a sense of, I'm not the only one that's walked this path, and I'm not the only one to push the boundaries of what masculinity means.
Better Man is essentially an argument that if boys and men embrace a healthier kind of masculinity, if they can learn to challenge rigid stereotypes of dominance, toughness, power and control; if they can learn to express their emotions, it'll go a good way to addressing rates of men's mental illness and suicide, as well as violence against women. You don't like the type term "toxic masculinity" though. Why not?
What I've seen in my work is that by putting the word "toxic" in front of masculinity, it reframes the conversation, and the boys and men that I've worked with and spoken to have a sense of shutting down. I think there's progress in that — we need to encourage critical thinking and get men thinking beyond the binary — but not all masculinity is toxic. There are everyday role models out there living a more expansive version of masculinity, and I think if we take a strengths-based approach to it, men and boys are more willing to step into the conversation about what change is required.
What I've seen is that, and the evidence is clear on this, the more that you adhere to these traditional, outdated forms of what it means to be a man — to be dominant, controlling, aggressive — the more likely you are to experience poor mental health, but also the more likely you are to harm others, and that's super concerning. So I acknowledge that toxic masculinity exists, but it doesn't bring boys and men into the conversation.
What does it mean to be a man in today's world? It's a different conversation. I am a big advocate for trying not to diminish traditional forms of masculinity: living a life of service, being courageous, strength, leadership, provider, protector are actually really beautiful things. But when they're used in isolation they can become harmful. So if we focus on all of that plus a more expansive version of masculinity — where men are caring, compassionate, respectful, set and respect boundaries, promote healthy relationships, believe in gender equity and gender equality, don't believe the rise of feminism is to our detriment — we become whole humans. And that for me is the most important part of the book. The story that I want to tell is that actually, being a great man is actually the same as being a great human.
Are there particular traits you'd single out as being uniquely important for men?
What I'd love to see in the modern man is expression over suppression. It's not as simple as "it's okay for men to cry", although that is true. What we've been passed down is this conditioning that men should bottle things up and be stoic. What we know is that when men are more expressive it builds stronger connections with people, but it also creates this sense of safety that it's alright for men to talk about their shit. That's the thing I want my mates, my colleagues and the men of the world to know: it's okay for things not to be okay.
But we have to go deeper and beyond the slogans and actually create safe spaces for each other as men to lean on each other, so a modern man can be more compassionate when his mate is going through a difficult time and not judge him or police his behaviours when he is perhaps being tender or soft in the way he talks about his emotions. If you are a father, it's about understanding the physical, cognitive, and emotional load that you need to share with your partner, that dads need to be just as present as mums or any other parent. If we set up the right systems and practices, dads should also be able to raise and care for their children and not just be at work providing all the time. Dads that are present emotionally and physically for their kids, able to hold challenging conversations, tackle big issues, be curious and non-judgemental.
More broadly I think men need to embrace the equality of men and women and actually show up 50-50. Men don't just need to be the breadwinner, because families have changed, our understanding of masculinity has changed. Fifty, 100 years ago, women didn't have the ability to get a loan, get a credit card. They weren't treated equally in the workplace. And now they are and actually, because of the way our economy is so cooked, we need both incomes to raise families. So men need to see that being a provider is expected, being a protector is expected, but so is sharing household duty, emotional labour, child rearing, taking care of your parents.
The Man Cave's programs might promote healthy masculinities and improve attitudes about aggression and violence but attitudinal shifts, if they happen, don't necessarily translate to behaviour change or prevent violence per se. Would you agree that's a limitation of programs like yours?
It can be, depending on the design, the curriculum, the length and the facilitation of the intervention. At The Man Cave we're actually seeing behavioural shifts and improvements in really distinct ways. We've worked with 115,000 boys and we have about 12,000 respond to our surveys and evaluation methodology every year. We were [previously] just measuring self-reporting — so like, Are you able to seek help now? Do you have better relationships? We're now surveying the female peers and teachers of those boys, and soon we'll be engaging with parents.
But what we're seeing in the data is that female peers and teachers are reporting that, at least three and six months after our program has finished, there's less misogyny, less homophobia, the boys are more willing to seek help and ask for professional help. Teachers are reporting that they see boys showing up more authentically at school, they're more engaged in their schoolwork.
So yes, absolutely, the evidence base around healthy masculinities and respectful relationships for boys is emerging. We're adding to that research base and we'll have some more research papers coming out over the next 12 months. But we do need more whole of community and whole of school approaches. Our four x one-day workshops are working brilliantly, but to see a sustained long-term impact we need to be engaging with boys long-term.
You write about your own struggle with the "mask of masculinity", part of which involved deciding to come out as gay when you were 28 and married to a woman. How long had you been hiding your true self and what was it costing you?
I think, in a way, my whole life. My mum was a beautiful, courageous woman. I had a really challenging relationship with my dad; I didn't feel safe. And during the early years — so age 10, 11, 12, 13 — there was rapid change happening around me. Dad left and became addicted to heroin. Mum got diagnosed with cancer. So the question of identity kind of just got buried whilst I was in survival mode.
I didn't really understand how much it was eating away at me. The cost was my mental health, my relationships, but I persevered. I just kept going — I got a good job and had the kids and got married and bought a house and once my level of survival started to move to like, Maybe I'm out of poverty now, my world started to open up and I was like, I'm gonna need to deal with my own shit here.
And it honestly came down like a bucket of concrete on my head. I was trying to work through was it sexuality, was it trauma from when mum died, or what dad put us through? I started to put on weight and get depressed and I struggled until I hit breaking point and was like, actually, I'm gay. I was worried about what that meant for me being a man because I didn't want to be judged. But I also had to be really honest with myself about the fact that I'd set up a long-term relationship with my wife at the time; I had children and friends that relied on me.
I was also concerned that I didn't want to be defined by my sexuality — I'm so much more than just being gay. I'm glad now at age 40, 12 years later, that I've got supportive people around me. My ex-wife is still involved in my life and we co-parent and she's ultimately the reason why I survived: because she supported me instead of judging me, and I'm really grateful for that.
What does the process of learning to embrace a more expansive masculinity look like? What are the most important tools in the toolkit?
I think the first thing is self-awareness, to understand how life's journey has shaped who you are today, and to be willing to change. In adulthood we get stuck in this, "I am who I am, you just have to accept me for who I am". Whereas I think that being open and curious to learn is super important. Particularly with technology, everything's black and white, good and bad, ugly and pretty, left and right, and I think that binary is actually harming men and boys. Life is more fluid than that. So being open to change your mind about things, being open to learn and listen to other people — listen to hear, not to judge.
I think being open to personal self-development and seeking help is important. I still go to therapy every Friday morning: I see my therapist, we work through the week's challenges and opportunities. Being able to seek help not just when you're in a crisis, but as an ongoing tool of self-care is super important. Talking about your life, not just the tough stuff but also the good stuff, celebrating the wins, but also being okay with expressing that you might be a bit concerned about the way of the world.
Did you learn anything new while you were writing Better Man?
The first thing I learned actually came from Luke Bateman, when I was trying to articulate how masculine and feminine traits are a spectrum and that we all have them all. I was trying to describe it in a way that was quite binary and Luke said to me, "Actually, what it means to be a good man is also what it means to be a good human, and the more that we move away from trying to fit ourselves into the binary of masculine and feminine, the better humans we become." That was really eye-opening for me. So I reshaped half a chapter.
The second thing I learned was that I'm not the perfect parent. When I reflected back and shared some stories about my own kids while I was writing the book, particularly about my daughter, I realised I've got plenty to learn. I've been a parent for 20 years now and I still don't know it all, and reflecting back on what I was writing, I was like, Oh lord, I really could have made different choices at different points raising my kids.
The third thing I learned was that in such a divisive and polarised world, trying to provide an opinion and provide some leadership around the way we should move forward as men is going to attract a lot of criticism. Being someone who wants to contribute to the zeitgeist and the national conversations about masculinity means that I've copped it along the way. I've copped a lot of critique and criticism and maybe I wasn't prepared for that, but that's part of the journey.
What do people come for you about?
On one hand I get DMs, letters and emails that say I'm trying to feminise boys, that I'm too much of a progressive liberal, that I don't understand men's issues [well] enough and that I'm a lefty feminist who is pushing the feminist agenda. Then on the other side I get, You're a far-right men's rights activist, how dare you platform men and boys, how dare you take away from women and girls, how dare you take away from LGBTQIA+ communities, you're a Trump-loving, Joe Rogan-loving activist and you shouldn't be playing in this space. I hope people read the book because I'm none of those things.
When or where do you feel most like yourself?
Two very distinct places. First, when I'm on the beautiful island of Bali in Indonesia. I think because I started my career in Bali after the bombings, and it was my first professional job. It was also where I learned a lot about social justice and government and corruption. People see Bali as a tourist mecca; I see it as a spiritual home when I go back there and I connect with the people… Just this peace comes over me immediately and I feel really connected to the land, the spirit and the culture.
In terms of my inner comfort, my inner safety, it's our family dinners. We have a big family dinner at least once a month. Just being there in the spirit of my own family, and my sisters who I have this deep, deep relationship with, who I trust implicitly. And we laugh together and we cry together and we trauma-bond together over our crazy upbringing. It doesn't matter where we live or where we are, when we're together it feels like home.
Would you rather be stuck on a remote island with Donald Trump or Andrew Tate?
Both of them. If I'm going to tackle the patriarchy, give it to me all at once. I think that by having them both, I would be able to lean on the opportunity for a bit of groupthink and get them to challenge their own and each other's thinking — because I reckon Trump and Tate don't agree on a hell of a lot. I think underneath all of their bravado and their ridiculous one-liners and their strongman archetype, they're actually both emotionally vulnerable, very, very weak humans who have had a lot of terrible stuff happen to them, and I have this hope and optimism that I would be able to get to them.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Better Man by Ben Vasiliou, published by Simon and Schuster, is out September 1.

Both Trump and Putin feel backed into a corner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
CIA chief's confusing Moscow trip reminds us of the corners Trump and Putin are in
Remember the Central Intelligence Agency? The US intelligence agency which once seemed to wander the world creating wars and instability and inspiring countless thrillers?
You don't seem to hear so much about the CIA these days. Who needs a bunch of shadowy spooks to create world chaos when you have the US president doing it all by himself?
But the CIA has been back in the headlines this week after it was revealed its director, John Ratcliffe, had just made a trip to Moscow, variously described in US media as "mysterious" or "a surprise", to talk to his Russian counterparts.
Intriguingly (as all spooky things invariably should be) that is about all the media reports agree upon.
Different theories on mysterious trip
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow on Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his time in the Russian capital, but that he didn't meet with Putin. Putin was briefed on the talks, Peskov said.
Depending on whether you read the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal or the Washington Post, Ratcliffe may have met with the head of Russia's FSB intelligence service, or the foreign intelligence service, the SVR, or both.
But what is most striking about the reporting of this meeting is the different spin on the apparent reason for the unexpected trip.
The New York Times reported that Ratcliffe went to Moscow "to privately share his bleak assessment of the state of the Russian war against Ukraine, and to urge the Russians to cut a deal before their military and economic situation gets worse".
The Washington Post reported Ratcliffe's trip was "preceded by fresh US intelligence indicating that the Kremlin sees the United States as weakened by the Iran war, offering Russia an opportunity to escalate action against American interests and allies in Europe".
The Wall Street Journal hedged its bets by saying the mission was "so sensitive that even some senior White House officials didn't know about it ahead of time".
Trump, the Journal said, had "personally dispatched" Ratcliffe "after previous rounds of negotiations using other trusted envoys failed to stop the fighting in Russia's war with Ukraine".
"Over the past few months, Moscow has escalated its attacks on Ukraine, boosted support for Iran's regime and resisted American attempts to improve economic ties," it noted.
Putin escalates threats against Europe
The US president has unleashed quite a lot of self-inflicted damage on his country — let alone his political fortunes — in the past week: think a secondary sanctions regime against Iranian trading partners and a trade war with Canada which will hurt US industry and hurt the Republicans in the mid-terms.
Yet these contradictory narratives on the CIA chief's travels to Moscow seem to best highlight the impotent flailing on almost all global issues of the Trump administration, an administration which some analysts still endeavour to argue has a strategy, in the face of repeated signs that it has none. On anything.
Remember when Trump came back to the White House claiming to have a good relationship with Putin and that he could end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours?
Putin, in the same period since Trump's return, has looked like he was winning, and more recently like he was losing.
What Putin does seem to have been doing most recently is escalating his threats against other European countries — a development which potentially makes all of those newspapers' assessments true at the same time.
There's been more covert hybrid warfare, airspace incursions and direct military threats, notably this week against the UK and France.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham had promised Ukraine it would allow the besieged nation access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles. France has also agreed to supply missile technology.
Russia's foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Thursday the two countries were "playing with fire", and of "inevitable catastrophic consequences" for British military installations both within Ukraine and elsewhere.
Trump in a corner on Iran
So now we have two autocrats — Trump and Putin — both stepping up their aggressive language and apparently feeling cornered at the same time.
Both of them are in very tight spots.
Trump has nowhere to go in his conflict with Iran. In fact, he's not able to claim any great victories in any of his foreign policy initiatives.
World leaders seem to be increasingly just ignoring him, or standing up to him — like Canada's Mark Carney this week over tariffs.
Even the "break glass" option of distractions didn't work: possible talks mooted for later this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un got no immediate love from Pyongyang.
That was despite Trump citing his strong personal relationship with the North Korean leader, and the fact it followed Trump's directive to the Pentagon to shorten military exercises with South Korea.
Putin's Russia, meanwhile, has also threatened to attack European defence companies and factories, and has escalated a "shadow war" in Europe.
Intelligence agencies have laid the blame at Russia's door for an attack on a Ukranian military cargo aircraft at an airport in Germany; mysterious fires on drone and munitions factories in Estonia, Italy and Bulgaria; and talk of assassination attempts on drone manufacturers.
That's in addition to a major rise in airspace violations by Russian drones and fighter aircraft, particularly over Poland, Finland and Romania, and an explosive-laden Russian maritime drone floating close to Europe's largest offshore gas project in the Black Sea.
NATO released a statement after its August 12 meeting condemning repeated Russian airspace violations which it said were not only "dangerous and unacceptable" but also observing that they demonstrated "Russia's increasing tolerance for risk".
Loading
'Two to three' week conflict hits six months
While Trump rails against Canada with colourful but pointless moves like unilaterally declaring Lake Ontario will be renamed Lake America, Putin would not need any great secret intelligence sources to assess that, whatever the state of the ground war in Ukraine, the US does seem at a low point in its capacity to do anything about changing the dynamics of that conflict.
Trump could well have got the CIA chief to tell Russian intelligence counterparts, as the Wall Street Journal reported, that the US remained committed to NATO's Article 5, which says that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
But like the rest of the world, the Russian leader would know of the depletion of US military hardware, the damage done to its US bases in the Middle East, and its troop shortfalls, as illustrated by its problems in its aircraft carrier fleet, which have also alarmed allies in our region.
Trump dismissed questions about the Ratcliffe trip on Thursday, saying "he's not going to be attacking a NATO territory".
But the concern that one leader under pressure may escalate pressure on another leader under pressure by opening new fronts in Europe, or increase the pressure by maintaining or even increasing its ties with Iran, are real.
The Trump administration seems equally powerless to control the economic fallout of its own policies on the US economy or for that matter the world economy.
US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent has perplexed financial markets this week with ineffective interventions in the US Treasury bond market designed to bring down long term US interest rates, even as the US Federal Reserve is under pressure to increase rates because of the inflationary impacts of Trump's war in the Middle East and burgeoning debt at home.
This week marked six months of a conflict with Iran which was allegedly only going to take two to three weeks at most.
The fallout from that decision sees Trump, his administration, and global geopolitics instead bogged down in a multitude of strategic and economic quagmires.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.
