Ministry decries new drone legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:21 UTC
01:37:21 KST

The Ministry of Economic Affairs on Thursday expressed regret over the passage of an opposition-backed uncrewed vehicle industry bill in the legislature, warning that the new regulations could hamper the sector’s development.
The legislature on Thursday passed the Act on Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Developing the Unmanned Vehicles Industry, which calls for the central government to allocate NT$240 billion (US$7.59 billion) over six consecutive years through annual budgets.
The ministry would oversee the act, while the Ministry of National Defense would be responsible for military procurement.
Photo: CNA
The Cabinet in June approved the defense ministry’s draft special act on the procurement of domestically developed uncrewed vehicles — which proposed allocating up to NT$210 billion over multiple years — and urged the legislature to pass its version.
The economic ministry said it was concerned that the version would create extra hurdles for development of the drone industry, preventing it from developing new technologies if local drone developers did not get government funding.
The legislature’s version says that the Executive Yuan is required to establish a special committee to coordinate industry policies and review development plans, including funding needs and financing, with more than half of its members to be experts and academics nominated by legislative caucuses, the economics ministry said.
The arrangement could create political gridlock if legislative caucuses delay nominating members or their nominees obstruct proceedings, potentially preventing the committee from operating, it said.
It could also delay government agencies drawing up budgets, as well as defense procurement and industrial development, it said.
The Executive Yuan already holds quarterly interagency meetings with experts to coordinate uncrewed vehicle development, including defense autonomy, industrial development and democratic supply chains, it said.
The mechanism already serves the functions of the proposed committee, while the legislation would only add administrative procedures, it added.
Regarding military uncrewed vehicle procurement, relying on annual government budgets could expose procurement to budget constraints, review delays and cuts, making orders less stable and predictable for the industry, the economics ministry said.
The industry has high research and development (R&D) costs, and technological barriers, making stable government procurement essential for investments, it said.
Taiwan’s drone supply chain comprises more than 274 companies spanning chips, communications, flight controls, navigation, optoelectronics, batteries, motors, materials, systems integration and application services, it said.
Many companies have already invested heavily in funding, personnel and equipment in line with government policy, it added.
Government procurement is intended to share R&D risks with the private sector and spur investment, but unstable orders could increase the financial pressure on companies and undermine business confidence, it said.
Government programs already provide a framework for developing the industry, while the defense ministry can fund military procurement through its regular budget without the legislation, it said.
The act carries more symbolic than practical significance, it added.

EDITORIAL: Labor rights for migrant workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:18 UTC
01:37:18 KST

The Ministry of Labor last week vowed to launch an investigation after Indonesian technicians working on renewable energy projects in Taiwan accused their employer of forced labor and wage theft.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Lin Yueh-chin (林月琴) joined advocacy groups in accusing Singapore-based Sheffield Green Co of changing employees’ contracts and cutting their pay after their arrival in Taiwan.
Workers also said that Sheffield Green, among other companies, failed to give employees time to recover from work-related injuries and pay for their health and labor insurance.
It would be expected that such practices are illegal, yet this case highlights a regulatory gap that leaves foreign workers vulnerable to exploitation. Some companies are taking advantage of Article 51 of the Employment Service Act (就業服務法) — which allows Taiwanese companies to hire skilled foreign workers through expedited work permits — to cut costs and induce foreign employees to accept wages lower than they were promised, while attempting to justify the practice by arguing that these short-term foreign workers are not covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法).
Migrant workers across multiple industries regularly face a long list of abuses — from delayed, reduced or withheld wages, deceptive recruitment and debt bondage to excessively long working hours, lack of rest days and, in extreme cases, physical abuse.
Domestic caregivers, who make up about 30 percent of Taiwan’s migrant workforce, are unprotected by the Labor Standards Act and lack many of the basic protections afforded to other workers, including statutory guarantees on wages, working hours and days off.
Taiwan’s distant-water fishing industry, which relies heavily on migrant labor, has likewise developed an international reputation for worker abuse following reports of hunger, unhygienic living conditions and physical violence aboard fishing vessels. Like live-in caregivers, distant-water fishing workers are also excluded from the Labor Standards Act because they are classified as “overseas employees.”
Migrant workers in the manufacturing sector have also reported exploitative conditions, including excessive working hours, inadequate rest, crowded dormitories, restrictive curfews and deductions from their wages for recruitment fees, accommodation and other expenses.
Victims of abusive employers are left with few options: endure the abuse, leave their jobs and risk losing their legal protections, or speak out. Increasingly, many are choosing the latter.
Earlier this week, Indonesian migrant fishers launched the “Freedom for Fishers Campaign” in Pingtung County, calling for fair wages and employment contracts, safe working conditions, transparent grievance mechanisms and the right to organize without intimidation or retaliation. The campaign is the latest in a series of demonstrations and initiatives by migrant workers and advocacy groups demanding better working conditions and stronger legal protections.
Although demands vary across industries, they share common ground — migrant workers are seeking the same basic legal protections and guarantees that domestic workers have.
Hardly an outrageous request, yet the government has instead prioritized expanding the supply of migrant labor to meet demand and address labor shortages. Meanwhile, the rights and protections afforded to those workers have not kept pace.
On Monday, the Chinese National Federation of Industries urged the government to further ease restrictions on the hiring of migrant workers and double the quota for migrant workers in the general construction sector, highlighting growing labor shortages facing traditional industries.
It is undeniable that Taiwan’s aging population and declining birthrate would only widen labor shortages. However, as the nation comes to terms with the reality that it needs migrant workers, it must likewise recognize that these workers must be afforded fundamental rights. Expanding the former without guaranteeing the latter would only worsen existing systemic problems and deepen tensions between migrant workers, employers and society as a whole.
If Taiwan continues to increase its reliance on migrant labor without addressing the many regulatory loopholes, tightening enforcement and ensuring workers have meaningful avenues to seek help, employers would continue to have opportunities to exploit those vulnerabilities — and there is little reason to believe they would not.
Taiwan cannot expect migrant workers to sustain its economy and care for its aging population while leaving them to bear the cost of the system’s failures. If the nation is going to depend on migrant workers, it must be prepared to protect them — and not simply when their mistreatment makes headlines.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other two
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:18 UTC
01:37:18 KST

The Central Election Commission (CEC) yesterday announced it has approved holding a referendum on nuclear power, but rejected proposals on caning and traffic fines.
The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 14 approved three referendums: introducing caning as a criminal punishment, abolishing the government’s nuclear-free homeland policy and using traffic fines to improve road safety.
The commission met for more than two and a half hours, and ruled that the referendum on caning did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act (公民投票法), CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
The caning proposal, put forward by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeks to introduce caning as a punishment for sexual assault, crimes against children, large-scale fraud and aggravated fraud.
However, caning or similar forms of corporal punishment are not recognized under Taiwan’s criminal justice system, You said.
The CEC therefore determined that the proposal amounted to creating new legislative principles, and was not a referendum on the initiation or repeal of a major policy, as defined by the act, he added.
The proposal involves using state power to inflict physical pain on prisoners and is considered by many countries to be cruel, inhuman and a violation of human dignity, he said.
That would contravene the Act Governing Execution of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (公民與政治權利國際公約及經濟社會文化權利國際公約施行法), which states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, he added.
Of the eight CEC members, seven voted that the caning proposal did not qualify as a referendum, said You, who chaired the meeting, adding that he did not cast a vote.
Regarding the Taiwan People’s Party’s (TPP) proposed referendum on earmarking traffic fines exclusively for road-related purposes, four commission members found that it did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said.
The commission held three rounds of voting, with the same 4-3 split each time, he added.
As for the proposal to repeal Taiwan’s nuclear-free homeland policy, six CEC members supported the referendum, with one abstention, You said.
The CEC ruled that the proposal meets the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said, adding that the referendum vote would be held on Nov. 28, alongside the local elections.
The KMT caucus condemned the CEC’s decision to reject the two proposals, saying that referendums exist to give people a direct say when a country faces major disputes over public policy.
“Yet what has happened now is that whether people want to vote no longer matters, and neither does whether the Legislative Yuan approves the proposal,” it said. “Instead the CEC has decided on behalf of 23 million people: ‘You are not entitled to answer this question.’”
“Is this direct democracy, or the direct confiscation of democracy?” it asked.
The TPP slammed You, saying he had claimed that “referendums submitted by the Legislative Yuan should be approved in principle and rejected only as an exception.”
“Yet he has now turned that exception into a pretext for arbitrarily expanding his powers, abandoning his principles as an academic, enabling the ruling party to flout the law and obstructing the public’s right to initiate referendums,” it said. “Such actions have brought shame on Taiwan’s democratic constitutional system.”
Additional reporting by Lin Hsin-han

DPP China Affairs warns of election interference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:15 UTC
01:37:15 KST

With Taiwan’s year-end local elections approaching, the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) China Affairs Department has warned that cooperating with Chinese election interference could carry a sentence of up to 15 years in prison, while those who report foreign interference could receive rewards of up to NT$20 million (US$632,351).
The department outlined seven types of illegal conduct involving Chinese election interference.
One form of interference is recruiting tour groups at China’s direction. That means accepting Chinese instructions, commissions or funding to recruit borough chiefs, local figures or voters to participate in a tour including transportation, accommodation or meals and asking them to support specific political parties or candidates, the department said.
Photo: Chen Cheng-yu, Taipei Times
Another form of election interference is recruiting people for free or significantly underpriced tours in exchange for votes, which could constitute bribery even without directly receiving instructions from China, it said.
Accepting any travel, accommodation or other benefits in exchange for political support could also be illegal if the person knowingly agrees to vote for a specific political party or candidate, the office said.
Producing or publishing fake opinion polls using foreign funding or at China’s direction to manipulate elections, influence voters or shape cooperation between political parties could constitute election interference, it said.
Assisting China with propaganda by accepting its instructions, commissions or funding to campaign for specific candidates, speak at rallies, hold press conferences, produce promotional materials or conduct media campaigns is also election interference, it said.
Serving as an intermediary to relay instructions related to election interference, such as helping China find, direct or fund people in Taiwan to mobilize supporters, promote candidates or conduct online operations, could also result in penalties, it added.
Lastly, developing organizations or gathering intelligence for China, as well as spying on, collecting or handing over official secrets, could constitute more serious national security offenses, it said.
These seven types of conduct could contravene the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), the National Security Act (國家安全法), the Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法), the Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act (總統副總統選罷法) or the Criminal Code, with penalties of up to 15 years in prison, the department said.
Criminal liability could extend beyond those who accept money to people who recruit others, relay instructions, mobilize supporters, spread propaganda or accept benefits to vote for a particular candidate, it said.
People who encounter suspected election interference should hold onto evidence such as messages, itineraries, payment records, photos and videos, and call 0800-024-099 and press 4 to report them to prosecutors or investigators, it said.
It urged people not to accept benefits, travel to China, follow Chinese instructions nor assist with propaganda to protect democracy, freedom and Taiwan’s right to determine its own future.

HK hears arguments over vigil organizers’ sentences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:12 UTC
01:37:12 KST

Three former organizers of Hong Kong’s annual vigils in remembrance of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown yesterday returned to court to argue over their sentences after being convicted of inciting subversion under a National Security Law imposed by China.
Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人), Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤) and Albert Ho (何俊仁), former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, were charged in 2021 under the law that has effectively stifled the territory’s previously thriving pro-democracy movement.
Lee and Chow, who pleaded not guilty, were convicted on Friday last week.
Photo: AP
Ho earlier entered a guilty plea, which could result in a reduced sentence.
They face a maximum prison term of 10 years and are expected to be sentenced at a later date.
The disbanded alliance also was found guilty on the same charge. It was best known for organizing the only large-scale public commemoration in China that drew tens of thousands of people annually for three decades to remember the crackdown’s victims.
The verdict has drawn concerns from foreign governments.
Critics said the case illustrates a decline in freedoms Beijing promised to maintain when the former British colony returned to Chinese rule in 1997, but the Hong Kong government insisted the court only considered the laws and evidence and that many rights and freedoms are not absolute.
Three government-approved judges ruled the trio of former vigil organizers had intentionally encouraged supporters of the alliance to wait for the right time to carry out “end one-party dictatorship,” one of the group’s core demands, through unlawful means.
The call carried the notion of overthrowing or undermining the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) leadership status, the judges said, adding that the defendants have long held enmity against the party, and they did not genuinely believe their words and deeds would not contravene the security law.
Lawyer Erik Shum (沈士文), who represents Lee and Ho, told the judges that China’s fundamental system did not change because of the alliance members’ promotional work and the CCP was still stable and carrying out its duties, while the defendants’ advocacy work did not involve violence.
Chow insisted she did not do anything wrong and did not deserve even one day in prison.
The verdict was saying that pursuing democracy is a crime, she added.
“If the law truly has no room for our beliefs, then I would rather be a criminal than be a fake person,” she said.
Regardless of whether she is in or outside prison, she would persistently strive to vindicate the 1989 pro-democracy movement, end one-party dictatorship and build a democratic Hong Kong and China, among other goals, she wrote on social media.
The security law calls for sentences of between five and 10 years for convictions of inciting subversion, if the offense is deemed serious. If the circumstances are considered minor, sentences should not be more than five years, short-term detention or other restrictions.

Murder case puts spotlight on postpartum psychosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:12 UTC
01:37:12 KST

The murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a woman who said she experienced postpartum psychosis before strangling her three children, has sparked a debate in the US over maternal mental health.
The 36-year-old nurse does not deny strangling Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months, with fitness bands in their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023. She then jumped out of a second-story window, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down and using a wheelchair.
However, Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, saying she heard a voice ordering her to kill her children.
Photo: The Patriot Ledger via AP
Her lawyers said this was caused by postpartum psychosis.
Prosecutors have rejected her argument, saying she had planned to murder her children and was able to understand the consequences of her actions.
For the past several weeks, dozens of women dressed in pink have come to the court in Plymouth to show their support for Clancy — and to make a statement about women’s health more generally.
Lawyer Kelly Woods said she was attending the trial as a “big advocate” for people who experience postpartum psychosis.
“That is a very under-considered element of this case,” Woods said. “I certainly hope that the medical community can learn from this.”
“I ultimately hope that there is more advocacy for postpartum depression and psychosis,” she added.
Psychiatrists and people close to Clancy, as well as her estranged husband, described her distress during the five-week trial.
The nurse faces life in prison without the possibility of parole if found guilty.
Postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency that affects about one to two women in every 1,000 births, Action on Postpartum Psychosis national training coordinator Sally Wilson said.
Clancy’s case is “an incredibly distressing and rare outcome of postpartum psychosis,” Wilson said.
During closing arguments, Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said the mother had made several pleas for help before the killings and received “lousy medical care” from the doctors she consulted.
“She was doing everything that she could to get help, and for whatever reason, she still slipped through the cracks,” Maternal Mental Health Leadership Alliance executive director Adrienne Griffen said. “That is the question that everybody is asking, is how do we prevent something like this from happening in the future.”
Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy was “suffering from mental illness” and tried to kill herself, but said the killings were planned and particularly cruel.
Right-wing political voices have condemned the level of violence in the killings and the supporters who have gathered outside the courthouse.
“Lindsay Clancy deserves to die for murdering her three children,” podcaster Katie Miller wrote on social media.

The KMT’s failed ‘Taiwanization’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:07 UTC
01:37:07 KST

The “quiet revolution” of Taiwan’s democratization took shape during the 12 years that followed Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) simultaneously becoming chairman of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and president of the Republic of China (ROC). Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) then took the presidential helm in 2000, bringing an end to one-party rule in the ROC, and was re-elected in 2004. He was followed by the KMT’s Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), who served two four-year terms; the DPP’s Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), who also served two terms; and the DPP’s William Lai (賴清德), currently in his first term. Having won just three presidential elections to the DPP’s five, the KMT finds itself gripped by anxiety over its ability to govern the country. The predicament goes back to Ma cementing the KMT’s abandonment of Lee’s political project of Taiwanese localization.
Lee’s politics, which elements within the KMT still steeped in colonial conceptions of Chinese identity labelled as pro-independence, in fact were for a practical localization, or “Taiwanization” of the ROC. This embodied a political realism regarding the ROC’s development in place. Lee also sought to reform the KMT, to cure its colonial hangover, and free it from the confines of party-state ideology. Perhaps this was his way of repaying former president Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國), who appointed Lee as vice president in 1984. Chiang and his father and predecessor, Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石), were fully taken with colonial ideations of Chinese identity. Chiang Ching-kuo’s passing in 1988 presented Lee with the opportunity to make that shift. What remained of “China” in the republic was to be reborn locally as Taiwan.
Like Lee, former Taiwan provincial governor Lin Yang-kang (林洋港) and former vice premier Chiu Chuang-han (邱創煥) were also potential contenders to succeed Chiang Ching-kuo as president. However, they were the epitome of local politickers and bureaucrats; their knowledge and education was confined to navigating the party-state system, and they lacked a broad and ambitious political vision. After Lee assumed the presidency and amid the turmoil of the post-Chiang era, Lin teamed up with the former premier Hau Pei-tsun (郝柏村) to mount an independent challenge in the 1996 presidential election. Former Control Yuan president Chen Li-an (陳履安) did the same with his then-running mate, lawyer Wang Ching-feng (王清峰). Their two tickets won a combined vote share of no more than 25 percent, far behind the 75 percent won collectively by Lee with then-premier Lien Chan (連戰) and the DPP’s Peng Ming-min (彭明敏) with Frank Hsieh (彭明敏). At the time, the Taiwanization of the KMT complemented the DPP.
In the 2000 presidential election, Lien was the KMT’s presidential candidate, but the KMT vote split when former governor James Soong (宋楚瑜) entered the race as an independent, winning more votes than Lien and resulting in the DPP’s Chen Shui-bian taking the presidency. Lien and Soong then ran together in 2004, but lost to Chen Shui-bian once again. Lien not only turned his back on Lee, but abandoned Taiwan in favor of China and reversed the Taiwanese identity that he had previously embraced, at least nominally, under Lee’s influence. This marked a major setback for the localization of the KMT. Then came Ma, under whose rule the KMT’s Chinese self-conceptualization as an exiled colony became even more deeply entrenched. This road, it seems, has been one of no return.
Lee’s direct challenges within the KMT began with the first direct election for Taipei mayor in 1994. Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康) left the KMT to run against the party’s nominee and mayoral incumbent Huang Ta-chou (黃大洲), splitting the vote and allowing DPP candidate Chen Shui-bian to win. At the time, Jaw was a KMT figure on the far right and proponent of the party’s Chinese identity. He loudly and publicly warned that Taiwan faced national annihilation, forming the New KMT Alliance faction in late 1989 to challenge Lee’s localization program. The faction ultimately broke away to establish the New Party in 1993. Meanwhile, KMT members who supported Lee’s approach and hoped for a KMT rooted in Taiwan had formed the pro-localization Collective Wisdom Club faction in 1988, and the Taiwan Solidarity Union was established in 2001. However, after Lee’s death, no Taiwanese localization force emerged from outside the DPP.
After the KMT established its rule in Taiwan in the immediate post-war period, large numbers of Taiwanese elites were eliminated in the 228 Incident, and some local gentry aligned themselves with the regime in its early years. Native Taiwanese political forces within the party-state system came to consist roughly of two groups: one made up of civil servants from the education sector and the China Youth Corps, who mainly became mayors and county commissioners or senior government officials; the other being local councilors and representatives widely regarded as being controlled by organized crime. This was fundamentally different from the DPP, which emerged from the dangwai (黨外, “outside the party”) movement, carried a reformist character, and won broad public support.
The reconvening of two forces — those with a “colonizer syndrome” and strong ideological fixations, and the “colonized syndrome” sufferers driven largely by self-interest within the systems that be — took shape as the DPP moved toward a position of stable political dominance. The KMT ticket for the 2024 presidential election embodied this reconvening, with Jaw, representing the former, serving as the running mate of New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜), representing the latter. The KMT’s predicament can be summed up like this: It has chosen to draw on the very Chinese Communist Party forces that forced it into exile in Taiwan in the first place, rather than becoming Taiwan’s own national party and jointly building a new state. The KMT’s failed Taiwanization is a shadow hanging over Taiwan’s quiet revolution, and the unfinished reality of Lee’s political vision.
Lee Min-yung is a poet.

Taiwan’s AI strategy has a public data problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:05 UTC
01:37:05 KST

Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) chairman Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) uses a sports metaphor to describe the density of electricity demand. A household is a ping-pong ball, ordinary industry a baseball and a science park a bowling ball. A data center is a shot put.
Taiwan is preparing for the shot puts. Four new combined-cycle units at Hsinta (興達) and Taichung (台中), with combined capacity of about 5.2GW, are scheduled to begin supplying or testing on the grid by the end of this year. The Energy Administration’s (能源署) plan adds about 25.98GW of gas-fired capacity between this year and 2035, predominantly fueled by imported liquefied natural gas (LNG).
NUMBERS HARD TO FOLLOW
Photo: Reuters
The figures on the demand side are harder to follow. The government has released estimates for artificial intelligence data centers, but not the project-level information needed to match them with Taipower’s connection data. Power plants, LNG terminals and transmission lines endure for decades. The public record does not show how a request becomes an operating load, or whether the infrastructure is proportionate to the demand claimed.
Officials presenting the national electricity supply-and-demand report in June cited roughly 1.2GW of identified AI data-center demand within the 2035 planning horizon, plus a 2GW to 3GW allowance for faster growth. Taipower tells the Taipei Times that as of July 31, it had received 75 requests from “transmission-level data centers,” representing 4,523 megawatts (MW) of requested capacity. It had agreed to 47 requests totaling 3,331MW, but said about 40 percent of those cases did not proceed to a formal application within the deadline and expired.
The 4,523MW is not active demand, approved capacity, contracted capacity or an energized load. It is what applicants asked for at an earlier stage. Those are different claims on the power system.
TT file photo
Investigative outlet The Reporter (報導者) in April published Taipower data dated from November last year. It recorded 79 transmission-level requests totaling 4,758MW. Taipower had agreed to 40 cases totaling 3,033MW, but more than 70 percent of those cases had expired after the applicants did not initiate the formal application process within six months.
Both datasets might be accurate. They have different cutoff dates and might treat expired cases differently. No published note explains how they fit together.
Natalie Wong (王慧敏) of National Chengchi University tells the Taipei Times that she tried to put them in order. She could not reconcile Taipower’s data with the 1.2GW cited by officials in June and the 303.5 megawatts (MW) known to have been physically connected. The last number is the only one tied to operating infrastructure. Taiwan therefore has several measures of data-center demand, with no public rule for choosing among them.
The 303.5MW is the contracted capacity of four sites receiving power, not their measured consumption. Five more sites were under construction with 567MW of approved supply capacity. These figures are closer to real projects, but still say nothing about hourly use.
Taipower has published an AI estimate before. An August 2024 presentation gave annual figures through 2030, including data centers, and briefly described the method. The Taipei Times could not locate subsequently published annual AI data using the same format.
The June report folded AI data centers and semiconductor expansion into national demand growth of 2.5 percent a year through 2035.
The Energy Administration told the Taipei Times that its forecast draws on applications from AI data centers and semiconductor companies, adjusted for past consumption and efficiency. Its reply did not provide current numbers for AI.
Tseng has separately estimated that semiconductor electricity use could rise from 52 billion kilowatt-hours this year to 110 billion in 2035, approaching 30 percent of national consumption. As of press time, no comparable data is currently available to the public for AI data centers.
Forecasts change. Projects fail, and applicants reserve capacity they never use. That uncertainty is not the problem; keeping its effects out of view is. Outsiders cannot see which assumptions changed or what those changes mean for power plants, terminals and grid reinforcement.
ENERGY SOURCES
Gas generated 47.8 percent of Taiwan’s electricity last year. New units are replacing retiring coal capacity and generation lost after the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春) ceased generating in May last year and entered the decommissioning process. If data center and semiconductor demand exceeds the national forecast, Taiwan must burn more gas, accelerate other generation or reduce demand elsewhere.
Taiwan has no international gas pipeline; all of its natural-gas imports arrive as LNG by sea. Tsai-ying Lu (呂采穎), who directs the energy security and climate resilience program at the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology (DSET, 科技、民主與社會研究中心), said her team is researching Taiwan’s energy security under contingency. That work also needs the size, location and hourly profile of new loads. Neither Taipower nor the Energy Administration appears to publish a current aggregate hourly load profile specifically for AI data centers.
Hydrogen is not yet a commercial alternative. Taipower and Academia Sinica completed a short 10 percent blending test using a 65kW microturbine in 2023. A draft government plan calls for a one-hour demonstration at a 20 percent hydrogen blend in a roughly 5MW system in 2028, but gives no timetable for supplying power stations. Asked how Taiwan would avoid prolonged dependence on LNG, the Energy Administration cited solar, offshore wind and geothermal. Those sources can reduce how often gas units run, but they do not provide a non-LNG fuel for the gas fleet itself.
Geothermal capacity remains below 14MW. Alexander Helling, chief executive of Baseload Capital, a geothermal developer whose Google-backed Taiwan projects aim to add 10MW by 2029, said drilling risk and slow permitting keep projects difficult to finance.
Data centers are concentrated in the north, while much of Taiwan’s generation is farther south. Taipower has encouraged large technology projects to locate closer to generation and in municipalities that support new power infrastructure. The logic is clear enough. The data behind individual siting decisions remain largely internal.
‘ENERGY USAGE STATEMENT’
Under Article 16 of the Energy Management Act (能源管理法), and rules amended in October and November last year, a new or expanded hyperscale or colocation data center planning energy-use capacity of at least 5MW must prepare an “energy usage statement”. The authority handling its permit forwards the statement to the Ministry of Economic Affairs. The review covers efficiency and, under a proposed amendment, industrial benefits. It does not open the connection queue or the demand model used for generation and transmission planning.
In Taoyuan’s Gueishan District (龜山), a resident told The Reporter that locals learned only after construction began that the project was related to AI. Municipal planners cannot plan coherently if they do not know which electricity requests are speculative, agreed, expired or likely to become operating loads.
Wong used the term “deservingness” for this bargain. A city gains electricity and investment by accepting the infrastructure that supplies them. Communities are asked to host infrastructure for a national policy whose demand forecast is not available at that level of detail.
Taipower already holds most of the information needed to clear this up. An anonymized connection queue could show, by municipality and substation area, capacity requested, agreed, expired, contracted and energized. Preliminary requests could be separated from firm commitments without naming customers. The Energy Administration could publish a current range for AI demand, its assumptions and the effects on gas consumption and grid construction.
Taiwan may decide that greater reliance on imported gas is an acceptable price for its AI and semiconductor ambitions. Publishing the underlying data would not settle that choice. It would allow lawmakers, municipalities and host communities to test the same assumptions as the ministries making them.
Romain Blachier is president of Association France-Formosa and an associate fellow at the Fondation Jean-Jaures. He works in renewable energy, consults and teaches energy geopolitics.

Climate change hits trout and salmon in UK’s chalk streams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:03 UTC
01:37:03 KST

A fly fisherman cast his line into the crystal-clear waters of the Itchen, a chalk stream in Hampshire in southern England, home to salmon and trout hit by climate change.
A summer of record-breaking temperatures and drought is threatening the ecological balance of rare chalk streams — rivers formed on chalk beds that are largely unique to England — and the fish that depend on them.
Wading through a branch of the Itchen near Winchester, Piscatorial Society Fisheries Director Robert Wellard, a recreational angler, dipped a thermometer into the clear water, drawing a reading of 17°C.
Photo: AFP
“We should be more around 12°C or 13°C” in August, said Kathryn Boler, manager of the Freshwater Program for the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust.
Chalk streams, which are fed naturally by underground springs filtered through porous chalk bedrock, are known for their clear, cool and mineral-rich waters where fish such as brown trout and salmon thrive.
Out of 200 rivers of this type recorded in the world, 85 percent are found in England, according to the Wildlife Trust, which looks after the UK’s nature reserves.
These unique habitats have been at the forefront of climate change for years, with this summer’s successive heatwaves and bone-dry conditions warming the water, depleting groundwater reserves and reducing river flows.
“This year it’s been unique in the sense that we have had them [heatwaves] pretty much back to back. And so that puts a huge amount of stress on the natural environment,” Wellard said.
During heatwaves, “we’ve seen water temperatures... creeping up well above their normal temperature range,” Wellard said, adding that water temperatures this summer reached levels which start affecting wild fish.
Several angling clubs — which primarily practice catch-and-release fishing — have temporarily limited activity to reduce the stress on the fish.
In water temperatures above 19°C, salmon and trout experience “extra stress on their bodies,” as it reduces the oxygen available in the water and increases the physiological needs of fish, Boler said.
The Itchen chalked up a high of 21.7°C last month, Environment Agency data showed.
Falling river flows in drought conditions also expose the fish to predators.
For Atlantic salmon, which come to chalk streams to spawn and are already classified as endangered, the situation is particularly concerning.
“With the lower flow, salmon are effectively more trapped, and more susceptible to predation from things like harbor seals and cormorants,” said Paul Vignaux, who heads a local association for landowners and anglers in the Itchen.
In 2022, only 180 salmon came to spawn in the Itchen.
Preliminary figures for last year counted 250 individuals — 32 percent of the threshold considered necessary for the species’ conservation, Vignaux said.
This summer was also difficult for young freshwater salmon, the Environment Agency said in its July salmon count of the Itchen and another nearby chalk stream, the Test, with their “abundance and size ... far lower than usual.”
The average temperature of rivers where brown trout live in England is expected to exceed the tolerable limit “at most sites by 2070,” it said.
The critical threshold for salmon is expected to be exceeded in half of their habitats by 2080.
Scientists said climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, drought and other extreme weather conditions.
Combined with river pollution, chalk streams are facing the perfect storm as declining water flows also cause pollutants to become more concentrated.
Scientists, environmentalists and anglers are calling for agencies to restore rivers to a more natural state, reduce water extraction and plant trees to improve shade.
“It’s really essential that as much water as possible stays in the rivers,” Boler said.

A reliable framework could solve drone issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:02 UTC
01:37:02 KST

In the past few years, the development of drones in Taiwan has become the center of multiple needs in the military, civilian and technology sectors. The breakdown in the Legislative Yuan over a special budget bill to fund the domestic development of surveillance and combat drones reflects the high degree of tension between industrial innovation and national security. Conflicting interests and administrative decentralization have made it difficult to design a regulatory framework that can simultaneously ensure security, promote development and maintain government transparency.
Taiwan faces a difficult balancing act in drafting drone-related regulations amid intensifying geopolitical tensions and “gray zone” threats. Relying solely on strict security safeguards is no longer enough to support industrial upgrades. National security agencies insist on stringent control of high-risk areas, flight data transmission and cybersecurity standards. Although such measures might create a strong security barrier, they could also constrain the space for technological development in the domestic industry.
Countries around the world are making drones the focus of innovation, and if legislation places too much emphasis on blanket bans or lengthy review procedures, Taiwanese businesses could miss their window to seize global business opportunities.
The real challenge in regulating drones stems from the failure of coordination mechanisms caused by a decentralized system of authority. The issue involves aviation, telecommunications, transportation, cybersecurity and local governments, but the fragmented approach makes it impossible to effectively address cross-sector risks and the need for information transparency.
The absence of coordinated regulations and legislation would create gaps in oversight, leaving investors and innovation teams at a loss and limiting Taiwan’s opportunity to build a global drone industry ecosystem.
High-risk locations such as airports, ports, hospitals, schools and energy infrastructure require not only cybersecurity and incident reporting mechanisms, but also regulatory guidance for the implementation of innovative technology. Lack of a clear framework for the open flow of data and incident investigations would directly impact confidence in the industry’s development and public trust.
International experience offers a number of valuable lessons. The US and European countries generally adopt a tiered, differentiated management system, establishing technical standards for commercial, consumer and government use, while improving data security and supply-chain screening standards.
Taiwan should establish its regulatory framework around risk classification, cybersecurity standards and supply chain certification to specify requirements for the sourcing of drone components while developing third-party testing and certification capabilities.
Returning to the ongoing deadlock in drone negotiations, if legislation relies solely on a highly restrictive and defensive approach, it would not hinder the transformation of the domestic drone industry, but the nation could miss its opportunity to gain global influence in emerging technologies. Only by building flexibility into the legal framework alongside risk-based regulations, cybersecurity and supply-chain verification, can Taiwan foster independent innovation and safeguard the baseline of public safety.
Edwin Yang is an associate professor at National Taiwan Normal University and chairman of the Central Taiwan Association of University Professors.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. TPP-KMT ties strained by Jhubei mayoral contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is to stand by its candidate in the Jhubei City (竹北) mayoral race, following a breakdown in talks with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) over their competing candidates, TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) said yesterday.
Thursday was the first day that candidates in the upcoming November elections could pick up registration forms.
KMT Hsinchu County Councilor Wu Hsu-chih (吳旭智) picked up a form for the Jhubei mayoral race, raising questions about cooperation between the two opposition parties.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The TPP is planning to field former Hsinchu City deputy mayor Andy Chiu (邱臣遠).
Since last year, the TPP and KMT have worked together on their local election platforms, reaching agreements and coordinating in electoral districts as part of their push for joint governance, Huang told a news conference yesterday.
“Throughout this process, I can say with a clear conscience that the TPP has kept every agreement it has made with the KMT,” he said.
Although the two parties never signed a formal agreement on the greater Hsinchu elections, they had agreed that the TPP would not nominate a candidate for Hsinchu County commissioner and instead support KMT candidate Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩), while the TPP would run its own candidate for Jhubei mayor to give the two parties the best chance of winning, Huang said.
Considering that former TPP chairman Ke Wen-je (柯文哲) is from Hsinchu County, the TPP would have put forward a candidate in the opinion polls if the two parties had not reached a consensus, he said.
Huang said that when he met with KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) on Wednesday, she said that she could not resolve the dispute over the Jhubei race.
Cooperation between the two parties would not work if one side fails to keep its commitments, he said, adding that the TPP would not change course because of the KMT’s internal divisions.
However, there have been no issues so far with bipartisan cooperation in other cities and counties, he added.
Cheng in a news release yesterday said that the Jhubei race is highly unique, with local ties, the makeup of the electorate and the parties’ overall strategy all requiring careful consideration.
Although the two sides made different assessments about the candidates, it does not change their commitment to cooperation, she said.
The KMT and TPP remain committed to working together to win the local elections and meet people’s expectations, she said, adding that they would continue communicating and deepening their cooperation.
In Jhubei, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) plans to field candidate Tseng Sheng-kai (曾聖凱).
Former TPP legislator Li Zhenxiu (李貞秀) on Tuesday announced that she also intends to run in the Jhubei race as an independent, although her eligibility is in question.
Li stoked controversy earlier this year amid questions regarding her Chinese nationality status, and eligibility to run for office and serve as a legislator.
She lost her seat in April after the TPP revoked her party membership.
Jhubei is currently led by Cheng Chao-fang (鄭朝方) of the DPP, who has been tapped to run for Hsinchu County commissioner.

Avoid exposing babies to incense burning: doctor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:02 UTC
01:37:02 KST

Parents should avoid burning incense in areas where babies sleep or spend long periods of time, and ensure thorough ventilation after incense is burned, obstetrician and gynecologist Su Yi-ning (蘇怡寧) said.
Burning incense is part of traditional rites in Taiwan during Ghost Month, the seventh month in the lunar calendar. The Ghost Festival is on the 15th day of the month — which fell on Thursday this year — but people prepare food offerings and burn incense and joss paper throughout the month to honor visiting spirits.
Burning substances releases combustion byproducts and children exposed to incense-burning environments tend to have poorer lung function indicators, Su wrote on his Facebook page on Friday last week, citing studies conducted in Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Photo: Taipei Times
A study in Taiwan found that the frequency of incense burning at home was associated with a higher risk of asthma and wheezing in some children, he said.
A Hong Kong cohort study involving more than 4,000 children also observed a correlation between household incense smoke, reduced lung growth and respiratory illness, he said.
Studies measuring air quality in real household settings have confirmed that incense burning significantly increases indoor particulate matter and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, he said, adding that concentrations are higher in poorly ventilated spaces.
A Taiwanese birth cohort study that tracked more than 10,000 infants found that babies exposed to household incense burning tended to reach certain gross motor development milestones, such as walking while holding onto support and walking steadily on their own, slightly later than average, he said.
While studies found a statistical association between incense exposure and developmental delays, it did not prove that incense burning directly causes developmental problems, he said.
Given that incense exposure can be reduced, there is no reason to unnecessarily increase infants’ long-term exposure, he said.
Families that follow religious or traditional practices that involve incense burning should consider reducing the amount of incense burned and shortening the duration of burning, avoid burning incense in areas where babies sleep or spend extended periods of time and maintain good ventilation afterward, he said.

Taiwan is attracting greater attention in France because of its strategic role in semiconductor production and broader economic development, the new director of the French Office in Taipei (BFT) said yesterday.
Frederic Laplanche, who arrived in Taiwan on Thursday, made the remarks at a media briefing on his second day in the country.
“The strategic importance of semiconductors means that Taiwan is clearly on the map now,” Laplanche said, adding that shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic had highlighted Taiwan’s importance to global supply chains.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Laplanche said France and the EU were seeking greater economic sovereignty by reducing excessive reliance on individual sources for strategically important products.
Taiwan’s democratic system and dependable industrial environment make it an important partner for France and French companies, Laplanche said, describing Taiwan as an “ecosystem of trust.”
Asked about his priorities as BFT director, Laplanche said he hoped to advance economic and technological ties, as well as cultural, scientific and people-to-people exchanges.
Laplanche, who outlined his longstanding personal and professional ties with Taiwan in Mandarin during his opening remarks, first visited the country as a student in 1995 to study its democratization.
He returned in 2004 to help establish the European Economic and Trade Office, where he served as deputy head until 2008, before returning as head of the office from 2011 to 2015.
Laplanche has also served as France’s ambassador to Malaysia and held senior positions at the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs.
Describing himself as a “son-in-law of Taiwan,” Laplanche joked that fate appeared to bring him back to Taiwan once every decade.
He said his latest assignment would allow him to continue building connections between the people of France and Taiwan.
Laplanche also said France would operate a pavilion at SEMICON Taiwan next week for the third consecutive year.
Ten French companies are to exhibit at the French Pavilion, the largest number in the pavilion’s three years at the trade show, he said.

Taiwan places third in Earth science contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:58 UTC
01:36:58 KST

Taiwan placed third at this year’s International Earth Science Olympiad (IESO) after winning two gold and two silver medals, with one student from Taichung earning second place overall.
The 19th IESO, which took place in Turin, Italy, from Aug. 20 to Thursday, drew 160 students representing 41 countries.
Taichung First Senior High School student Wang Yi-cheng (王翌澄) and Kaohsiung Senior High School student Shih Tzu-hung (施子閎) earned gold medals, placing second and sixth respectively.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Education
National Experimental High School at Hsinchu Science Park student Liu Hsin-tse (劉信澤) and Tainan First Senior High School student Huang Ting-yu (黃鼎祐) earned silver medals, placing 20th and 27th respectively.
Since Taiwan began participating in the Olympiad in 2007, it has won a total of 54 gold, 28 silver and three bronze medals, K-12 Education Administration official Yeh Hsin-tsun (葉信村) said.
Wang has enjoyed math and science since junior-high school and found a renewed interest in Earth science after joining a high-school science program.
Earth science is the branch of science most closely connected to everyday life, Wang said, adding that everything from earthquakes to climate change has made him want to better understand how the world works.
The intensive training and fieldwork leading up to the Olympiad not only expanded his Earth science knowledge, but taught him time management, teamwork and how to adapt to unexpected situations, he said.
Taichung First Senior High School teacher Hsu Wei-hsiu (許瑋琇) said Wang often thinks deeper about topics after understanding them, asking questions that go beyond what is covered in class.
Shih, who is from Pingtung County’s Ligang Township (里港), has been interested in Earth science since participating in a junior-high school science fair.
In his first year of high school, he traveled to South Korea to attend an Earth science festival, and exchanging ideas with students from other countries inspired him to compete in the IESO.
Liu has been fascinated by the universe since kindergarten, later studying astrophysics and participating in cosmology research at a university.
Huang became interested in Earth science after taking an after-school astronomy class in fifth and sixth grade.
He fell short in the final stage of the national team selection in a previous attempt, but this year achieved his goal of making the team.
The four members of Taiwan’s team were selected from among 520 students at 95 schools across the nation through preliminary selection, a training camp and a national team selection camp led by National Taiwan Normal University professor Mary Yeh (葉孟宛), Yeh Hsin-tsun said.
Students who win gold and silver medals are eligible for scholarships of NT$200,000 and NT$100,000 respectively, as well as preferential admission to related university programs through guaranteed placement or recommendation, Yeh Hsin-tsun said.

Hualien, Union Bank partner on restoring forest, river habitat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:55 UTC
01:36:55 KST

The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Hualien branch on Wednesday initiated an environmental, social and governance (ESG) partnership project with Union Bank of Taiwan to promote ecological reforestation and river habitat restoration in Hualien County.
The cooperation was established via the forestry agency’s carbon sink and biodiversity ESG project matching platform, making the bank the first ESG corporate partner of the branch.
The bank would adopt 2 hectares of land in the floodplain along the county’s Mugua River (木瓜溪) to help remove invasive species and reforest the land over the next 20 years, the branch said.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Hualien branch
Located at Hualong Revetment’s (華隆護岸) Chuying Levee (初英堤防) near the river, the plot of land is a critical part of the national ecological network, linking ecological corridors from forests to the river, it said.
The region is rich in native ecological resources, the branch said, adding that it has long been promoting ecological restoration there.
However, the floodplain has been invaded by alien species, mainly white popinac, which has formed large areas of monoculture stands that reduced habitats available to native wildlife, it said.
The branch said it has completed ecological restoration by removing white popinacs and reforesting more than 18 hectares of land in the region since 2021.
The effort would continue for the additional 2 hectares of land adopted by the bank to restore indigenous vegetation and the river’s function as a habitat, it said.
Branch Director Huang Chun-tse (黃群策) said the project focuses on long-term ecological stewardship in line with the UN’s sustainable development goals and the spirit of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with the bank committed to managing the 2-hectare site over a 20-year period.
Bank general manager Hsu Wei-wen (許維文) said ecological restoration requires long-term commitment, as tree seedlings cannot turn into a forest overnight.
The bank specializes in financial investment and is investing in a sustainable future for the land near the river to create a more favorable and friendly living environment for native plants and animals, Hsu said.
The bank said it has engaged in wildlife conservation by adopting protected native species such as leopard cats and ring-necked pheasants for more than a decade.
It has also been donating to Shei-Pa National Park’s (雪霸國家公園) ecological conservation and environmental education, it said.
Its cooperation with the Hualien branch on reforesting the river’s floodplain marks a shift in the bank’s ecological action from wildlife species conservation to habitat and ecosystem restoration, the bank said.
The branch said the floodplain ecosystem along the river has improved through years of reforestation and has documented activities of various wildlife species.
The bank’s participation is expected to scale up the restoration benefits and enhance the integrity of ecological corridors and habitat resilience for the river, it said.
Additional reporting by Lee Ching-hui

South Korea, the US and Japan would go ahead with a trilateral military drill next month in response to North Korean nuclear threats, officials in Seoul said yesterday, a day after North Korea vowed to retaliate against what it called US hostilities.
The development further dims prospects for an early resumption of diplomacy between North Korea and the US, despite US President Donald Trump’s recent decision to scale back a major bilateral military drill with South Korea in an apparent goodwill gesture toward Pyongyang.
The Freedom Edge exercise would start on Sept. 7 for a five-day run in the waters off South Korea’s southern Jeju Island, South Korea’s military said in a statement.
Photo: Reuters Photo
The exercise is defensive in nature, and meant to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats as well as promote regional peace and stability, it said.
North Korea has previously slammed the trilateral drill as a “reckless show of strength” that showed its adversaries’ confrontational stance against it.
The drill contained a US intention to lay siege to China and exert pressure on Russia, it has said.
Launched in 2024, the Freedom Edge drill is designed to increase the sophistication of previous exercises with simultaneous air and naval drills geared toward improving joint ballistic missile defense, anti-submarine warfare, surveillance and other capabilities.
Last week, the US and South Korean militaries ended their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise six days earlier than originally planned, after Trump said he had ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the drill.
On Thursday, North Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the US of engaging in “a series of hostile moves” targeting it, including a possible sale of air-to-air missiles to South Korea, vowing that it would “make a serious, immediate and powerful response.”
Earlier this week, South Korea’s Marine Corps said that a biennial joint amphibious landing drill with the US would likely not take place next month as previously scheduled.
The US Marine Corps in June informed it of a constraint in the operational capability of its forces during the drill’s planned period due to the situation in the Middle East, it said.
The US Marine Corps said its “participation level” in the Ssangyong drill was determined in coordination with South Korea and was unrelated to decisions regarding other exercises, adding that it “remains firmly committed to its longstanding partnership” with South Korea.

International experts affirm Taiwan’s anti-corruption efforts, offer recommendations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:55 UTC
01:36:55 KST

Five international experts on the review committee for Taiwan’s third report under the UN Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) said yesterday that Taiwan has established a mature and innovative anti-corruption governance system.
The five-member committee spent two days reviewing Taiwan’s implementation of the UNCAC.
The committee affirmed 41 measures adopted by Taiwan to implement the convention and offered 78 recommendations for improvement in areas including government procurement, combating corruption in the private sector, managing conflicts of interest, political donations, transparency in political lobbying, anti-money laundering policies and the recovery of illicit assets.
Photo: CNA
Committee chair Jose Ungaz said the review demonstrated that Taiwan has found its footing and established a mature and innovative anti-corruption governance system.
The next step is to establish governance systems that are quantifiable and verifiable, and that can demonstrably reduce the risk of corruption, the committee said.
Committee member Gillian Dell said systems Taiwan has adopted, including the Government Procurement Integrity Platform and the Government e-Procurement System, could serve as models for other countries.
However, Dell said Taiwan could improve transparency in national defense, maintain judicial capacity and establish stronger and more stable anti-corruption mechanisms in government procurement processes.
Committee member Duncan Hames said Taiwan’s Enterprise Service Integrity Platform and its practice of considering anti-corruption efforts at state-owned enterprises when determining their eligibility for the Integrity Award demonstrate Taiwan’s commitment to building a culture of integrity in the private sector.
Hames suggested that Taiwan increase the transparency of information on registered companies and improve the reliability of information in government company registry archives. He also said the government should establish a system of criminal liability for legal entities.
Committee member Peter Ritchie said Taiwan has strengths in its prosecutorial system, anti-money laundering and corruption risk assessments, virtual asset management and mechanisms for recovering illicit assets, and should capitalize on those advantages.
Ritchie also suggested that the government share actual case studies and its experiences in handling them with the private sector and other countries.
Committee member Julie Haggie said she was impressed by the high level of government participation in the review and praised Taiwan’s implementation of conflict-of-interest regulations.
However, Haggie said the government could improve the immediate transparency of political donations, political lobbying and lobbying registration.
Minister without Portfolio Lin Ming-hsin (林明昕) said the government’s work would begin following the conclusion of the review. The committee’s recommendations, he said, would serve as references for future anti-corruption policies and legislative drafting.
Taiwan looks forward to presenting the results in its next national report and at the next session of the international review committee, he added.

Plans to build business park on former Nazi camp site in Austria sparks anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:54 UTC
01:36:54 KST

A few crumbling concrete blocks in an overgrown field are all that remains visible of what was once a sprawling Nazi forced labor complex around the Austrian town of Leobersdorf.
Now, plans to build a business park on the site, including a cold storage warehouse and branch of the discount supermarket chain Lidl, have sparked anger in the Alpine nation, which long neglected to address its Nazi past.
“For me, it’s a sad feeling, because a place burdened by history is being built over, sacrificed to the economy,” said Erich Strobl, head of a local campaign to preserve part of the site.
Photo: AFP
After Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, the Weinberglager complex was used for thousands of prisoners of war and forced laborers. It later included the Hirtenberg subcamp of the Mauthausen concentration camp — Austria’s second-largest women’s camp.
About 400 women, mainly from the Soviet Union, but also from Italy and Poland, were imprisoned at the Hirtenberg subcamp between September 1944 and April 1945, and forced to manufacture infantry munitions at a nearby factory complex.
Although some factory ruins survive, the camp barracks and most other structures were gradually demolished, repurposed or destroyed after the war.
However, Bertrand Perz, a historian specializing in the Mauthausen camp, said the Hirtenberg site remains “historically important,” partly because female “prisoners in Mauthausen have been marginalized in the culture of remembrance.”
Plans to build a business park on the plot about 40km south of Vienna, including on land that once formed part of the concentration camp, were first revealed in 2024.
Archeological investigations have identified surviving traces of the former camp complex, but Austria’s Federal Monuments Office concluded that the remains were “not sufficient” for monument protection.
With the bulldozers now moving in, activists have renewed their calls for the site to be preserved.
“A former concentration camp must not be built over with new structures,” the International Mauthausen Committee said.
Standing in front of the site, where gray columns already rise from the ground, Mauthausen Committee Austria board member Josef Pumberger said he felt “grief, anger, rage, that something like this can happen in Austria in the year 2026.”
The project has also attracted controversy, because the land was previously owned by Leobersdorf Mayor Andreas Ramharter, who sold it in 2022 and 2023 for more than 15 million euros (US$17.46 million), according to local media reports.
Austrian company TRA LEO GmbH & Co KG, which bought the plot, said it had offered to support the creation of a memorial on the site.
Lidl confirmed plans to open a store in the planned business park, but said it would not be directly “on the site of the former concentration camp, but on an adjacent plot of land”.
In the aftermath of World War II, Austria presented itself as a victim of the Nazis, ignoring the complicity of many Austrians.
It was only from the late 1980s that the country where Adolf Hitler was born began to examine its responsibility in the Holocaust.
Perz said a debate like the one today around the Hirtenberg site “would have been impossible in the 1980s,” adding that there is now “more sensitivity” toward former Nazi sites.
However, in contemporary Austria, demands for remembrance are increasingly clashing with “the opposite tendency, namely to say: ‘Now this really has to stop,’” he said.
A stele monument was erected in 2024 to commemorate the victims of the Hirtenberg camp, but for Pumberger, that is not enough.
“It is very important to have tangible evidence of the buildings in which the Nazis imprisoned people, tortured them, killed them,” he said. “Otherwise it becomes a virtual act of remembrance, or one that exists only in books and photos and films.”

Nepal orders rescuers to safety after dam bursts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:54 UTC
01:36:54 KST

Nepal yesterday ordered rescuers searching for survivors of deadly floods to get to safety as it reported a debris dam had burst in Tibet, bringing risks of new torrents.
Emergency teams have recovered 472 bodies after a tsunami-like wall of water and mud crashed down on Wednesday, burying homes, smashing bridges and sweeping away vehicles in Nepal and Tibet.
More than 1,400 people are missing, including trekkers in the Himalayas and scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
Photo: AP
The US Geological Survey said the disaster — the deadliest for Nepal since a 2015 earthquake — was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.
The deluge of ice and mud also caused huge pools of water to form.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location,” saying it had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side.”
Separately, China had earlier the same day paused its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding.
A lake formed by immense piles of debris has begun overflowing towards the area that rescue teams were headed, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
“So all rescue teams have been ordered to stand by in place and wait for further instructions,” it said, adding that emergency teams which had earlier accessed the area “have been ordered to withdraw one kilometer.”
At a meeting chaired by Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), leaders underlined “many hidden dangers of glaciers, ice lakes and geological disasters in the surrounding area” and warned that “rescue is facing great difficulties,” Xinhua reported.
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation mean food and water supplies were running out.
The Nepali military had located people trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to retrieve the survivors.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said.
About 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, but efforts were ongoing to extract more than 100 people trapped in the same area, he added.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli Valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck — but he had managed to get out and reach help.
“I survived as I was in the tunnel,” said Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours. “The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away.”
Survivors in a makeshift Nepali hospital endured an agonizing wait for news of their missing loved ones.
Kula Priya, whose eldest son is missing, said she had lost everything when the deluge hit.
“I don’t care for wealth. I just want my son back. If any of you could rescue my son, please do it for me,” she said.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
There are 910 people, including 517 foreign tourists, who are out of contact in Nepal. Indians make up the largest number of missing foreigners, while the US said 90 of its citizens were out of contact.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists and where the only sources of information are Chinese authorities — officials say hundreds are missing and three died.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.

AI debt flood is stoking bond yields, Pimco says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:48 UTC
01:36:48 KST

The flood of debt financing for artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditure is causing “indigestion” in fixed-income markets and fueling yields, but that dynamic should result in decent longer-term returns for investors, Pacific Investment Management Co (Pimco) said.
“There’s too much, too fast” AI-related issuance, Marc Seidner, Pimco’s chief investment officer of non-traditional strategies, said on a podcast with colleagues Pramol Dhawan and Gregory Hall.
It is “very possible” that helped drive the 10-year US Treasury yield to about 4.75 percent earlier this month, the upper end of a multi-year range, in a crowding out effect, Seidner said.
Photo: AFP
Highly-rated large US tech companies including Amazon.com and Alphabet Inc have sold hundreds of billions of dollars of bonds combined this year, putting their debt in competition with the funding of governments that are struggling to repair their finances.
The upshot of it all is not necessarily bad news for fixed-income investors because the AI build-out is driving global growth and productivity, which is naturally going to push yields higher too, said Dhawan, Pimco’s head of emerging markets portfolio management.
“The AI capex story is beyond the US borders,” Dhawan said on the podcast recorded earlier this week. “You’re seeing Taiwanese real growth at 12 percent, [South] Korean growth, gangbusters.”
Seidner and Dhawan were discussing a recent note they published.
Current bond yields offer a “compelling entry point for long-term investors,” they wrote.
For one, investors can lock in yields now at a time when the macroeconomic outlook is far from certain, Seidner said, citing weak consumer confidence data and a recent disappointing jobs report.
“There are enough scenarios where you do really well as bond investors that we shouldn’t get all emotional and worked up about being at the top end of the range” in yields, Seidner said. “Many of us that are in the weeds looking at consumer related debt and other data and statistics worry quite a bit about the lower arc of the K-shaped economy.”

Groups press Merz over China policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:42 UTC
01:36:42 KST

German industry is increasing pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to take a tougher line with Beijing, with companies calling for greater action to address what they describe as unfair competition from Chinese rivals.
The growing assertiveness from German business representatives marks a shift in a country that long resisted trade barriers for fear of Chinese retaliation. How Berlin positions itself will help shape the EU’s broader trade stance toward China, with talks between the bloc and Beijing scheduled for October.
An Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) report published in June said that Chinese manufacturers received three to eight times more state support than OECD rivals relative to revenue, with subsidies accounting for nearly 60 percent of their global market-share gains.
Photo: AFP
Germany’s trade deficit with its biggest trading partner widened by about 22 billion euros (US$25.6 billion) last year to 89.3 billion euros as imports into the European country rose 8.8 percent and exports fell 9.7 percent.
“We need to discuss with China what is happening. If it is confirmed that this is attributable to subsidies or unfair competition, then it is an issue,” said Volker Treier, head of foreign trade at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
The concern is particularly pressing for German automakers such as Volkswagen, which — having been overtaken by local brands such as BYD Co (比亞迪) in China — now face growing competition from Chinese rivals in the European market.
Merz’s coalition has sharpened its language on China, but its messages remain mixed, combining calls to reduce economic dependencies with an insistence that the country remains an important economic partner.
Following signs of division on the matter within his coalition, Merz said on Wednesday that he had asked the Cabinet to work on proposals to address trade imbalances between the EU and China.
“We note that German industry, too, has apparently changed its mind regarding these global imbalances,” the chancellor said, pointing to associations such as the VDA representing automakers, which is reconsidering its previous opposition to protective measures.
Siemens Energy chief executive officer Christian Bruch in June said that treating Chinese imports like European products was “not acceptable,” adding that regulations needed to be put in place and local content quotas considered.
Treier said there were sufficient instruments in the WTO and the EU framework to defend European industry.
“We simply need to streamline and shorten our decisionmaking processes when we decide to act,” he said.
The BDI, representing major German manufacturers, is advocating for the faster application of trade policy instruments, including safeguards and methodological adjustments, such as bundling product groups in anti-dumping and anti-subsidy proceedings.
“The situation is intensifying due to the massive price pressure we face from Chinese suppliers,” BDI executive board member Wolfgang Niedermark said.
“Possible countermeasures by China must be included in strategic considerations, but should not determine or ultimately prevent Europe’s actions,” Niedermark added.
