Population to plummet, council warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:42 UTC
01:36:42 KST

Taiwan’s population is projected to shrink by almost half over the next five decades, intensifying labor shortages and placing a growing drag on economic growth as the technology-intensive economy confronts a rapidly aging workforce.
The population is expected to fall to 12.15 million by 2075, a 48 percent decline from this year, National Development Council projections released yesterday showed.
The decline would fundamentally alter Taiwan’s workforce. From 2037, more than half of the working-age population is projected to be aged between 45 and 64, signaling the end of an era when the economy could rely on a relatively large labor force.
Photo: CNA
The shift threatens to challenge Taiwan’s growth model, which depends on a broad manufacturing workforce and a growing supply of highly skilled workers to support its semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries.
A shrinking pool of workers could make recruitment increasingly difficult, while a growing elderly population would add pressure on social spending and public finances.
The projections also point to a deeper demographic problem — Taiwan is not only losing its population, but failing to replenish it, the council said.
It lowered its long-term fertility assumptions after the fertility rate fell to a record low 0.695 last year, significantly below previous estimates.
The number of women aged 20 to 49 has declined since peaking in 2005, while the proportion of married women in that age group has also fallen.
The shrinking pool of potential mothers is making a sustained recovery in births increasingly difficult, it said.
Taiwan’s population is projected to fall below 20 million in 2045, dropping to 19.98 million.
People aged 65 or older are expected to account for 37 percent of the population, while the working-age population would shrink to 57.9 percent and children to just 5.2 percent, the council said.
By 2075, the imbalance would be even more pronounced, with older people projected to comprise 52.9 percent of the population, working-age people 42.3 percent and children 4.8 percent, it said.
The dependency ratio — the number of children and elderly people relative to those of working age — is projected to rise from 55.2 dependents for every 100 working-age people to 136.6 by 2075, the council said.
The potential support ratio is expected to fall below one, suggesting less than one working-age person for every person aged 65 or older, it said.
The government is preparing the economy for a permanently smaller workforce. It has established a population strategy task force, and in May launched 18 measures covering childbirth support, childcare, education, workplace policies and housing.
Additional policy packages would target elderly people, talent development across all age groups and the recruitment of overseas talent, the council said.
For businesses, the implications extend beyond hiring. Companies are likely to face greater pressure to raise labor force participation among elderly people, attract workers from overseas, and accelerate automation and productivity gains.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:36:40 UTC
01:36:40 KST

Chris Sale on Thursday had thrown 97 pitches through eight innings, a full game for most pitchers in most MLB games, and Atlanta Braves manager Walt Weiss had relievers ready in the bullpen for the ninth inning.
Even so, both knew that Sale was not giving up the ball against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
After learning before the game about the death of a friend, Sale had extra motivation to finish the shutout in Atlanta’s 1-0 win for a series sweep.
Photo: AFP
“He was on a mission,” Weiss said. “You could see it. He was attacking from the first pitch. And not that he doesn’t do that, but you can see he had a different look in his eye. And the look in the eye is always pretty good, but it was even a little bit different tonight.”
That different look meant Weiss already was planning to have Sale return to the mound for the ninth.
Then Sale walked into the dugout after the eighth and announced: “This is mine,” Weiss said.
Photo: AP
Sale said he received a text message before the game saying that his friend Ashley Foss, a financial adviser who worked with Sale’s agent, B.B. Abbott, had died. Sale provided no details.
“If you ever needed more incentive, that’s all you’re going to need right there,” Sale said.
The 37-year-old lefty was dominant in throwing only 60 pitches through five innings and 81 through seven. He allowed just five hits with no walks, throwing 80 of his 109 pitches for strikes.
Sale fanned 11 for his fourth double-digit strikeout game this season and the 95th of his career. The 10-time All-Star ranks seventh all-time. Sandy Koufax is sixth with 97.
Weiss said it was a Hall of Fame-caliber performance by Sale.
“I always talk about how the Hall of Famers are just different, and that’s a perfect example right there,” Weiss said. “Chris knew that we were really thin tonight in the bullpen, so he puts a team on his back and throws a complete-game shutout against the world champions.”
Weiss stuck with Sale even after Freddie Freeman singled to open the Dodgers ninth.
Teoscar Hernandez popped out, pinch-runner Alek Thomas was out at second on Miguel Rojas’ fielder’s-choice grounder and Sale struck out Alex Call for his 17th complete game and first since 2019.
Sale threw a 100.1mph (161.1kph) fastball to Shohei Ohtani in the third inning, reaching triple digits on a pitch for the first time since July 2018 with the Boston Red Sox.
“I’m just thankful to get through it, man,” Sale said. “Like I said, I pride myself on working hard and I pride myself on going out there and giving my team a chance to win.”
Drake Baldwin’s first-pitch leadoff homer in the first inning accounted for the game’s only run.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto (12-8) hurled 6-1/3 innings of one-run, four-hit ball for the Dodgers.

Recent studies suggest that listening to classical music during exercise may help reduce feelings of fatigue and improve physical performance and mental endurance. While upbeat pop and electronic tracks often __1__ a workout, classical music may also offer benefits in certain situations. For example, one study found that female basketball players who trained while listening to classical music showed improvements in agility and free-throw accuracy compared with those who trained without music.
Classical music has also been shown to help athletes find a steady rhythm in motion, which may in turn support smooth and coordinated movement during exercise. Classical pieces with moderate pacing, such as many works by __2__ like Mozart and Vivaldi, may encourage a more consistent workout rhythm. This steadiness makes exercise feel less tiring and helps individuals push through moments that __3__ difficult.
The power of classical music also lies in its emotional range. Slower passages can promote relaxation during warm-ups or cool-downs, while more dynamic pieces may provide a sense of motivation during challenging phases of exercise. This helps create a more enjoyable experience, making workouts feel less like a __4__ and more like an engaging activity.
Photos: AdobeStock I 照片： AdobeStock
Still, can classical music effectively reduce the psychological barriers to physical effort? Some would agree that the answer is __5__ “yes.” Classical music offers more than elegance and entertainment; it can also provide mental, physical, and emotional support. Whether you are preparing for a competition or simply going to the gym, classical music may help make exercise feel easier and more enjoyable.
近期研究顯示，在運動時聆聽古典樂可能有助於減輕疲勞感，並提升身體表現與心理耐力。雖然節奏輕快的流行音樂與電子音樂常常為一場運動鍛鍊營造氛圍，但古典樂在某些情境下也可能帶來益處。例如，有一項研究發現，與訓練時未聽音樂的球員相比，邊聽古典樂邊訓練的女性籃球員，其敏捷度與罰球準確率都有所提升。
古典樂也有幫助運動員找到穩定動作節奏的效果，進而有助於在運動時維持流暢又協調的身體活動。節奏適中的古典樂曲（像是由莫札特和韋瓦第等作曲家所創作的許多作品）可能有助於建立更穩定一致的運動節奏。這種穩定性讓運動感覺較不費力，也幫助人們撐過那些原本可能會感覺困難的時刻。

儘管如此，古典樂真的能有效降低從事體力活動時的心理障礙嗎？有些人會認為答案絕對是「肯定的」。古典樂帶來的不僅僅是優雅與娛樂；它同時也能提供心理、身體與情緒上的支持。無論你是正在準備比賽，或只是去健身房運動，古典樂都可能有助於讓運動變得更輕鬆、更有樂趣。
Words in Use
1. accuracy n. 準確性
During training, Brian improved his shooting accuracy by focusing on his hand movements.
在訓練中，布萊恩透過專注在手部動作而提升了射擊準確度。
2. steady a. 穩定的
steadiness n. 穩定
A steady tempo helps people stay focused on the task.
穩定的節奏能幫助人們持續專注於任務上。
The steadiness of the machine’s movement improved overall efficiency.
機器運作的穩定性提升了整體效率。
3. rhythm n. 節奏
The workers followed a regular rhythm to complete the task efficiently.
工人們依照固定的節奏作業，來高效率地完成任務。
4. moderate a. 適中的，中等的
The teacher spoke at a moderate speed so everyone could follow.
老師以適中的速度講解，讓大家都能跟上。
5. consistent a. 一致的
The melody stays consistent even when the tempo changes slightly.
即使節奏稍微改變，旋律仍保持一致。
Practical Phrases
1. compared with / to. . . 和……比起來
This method is more efficient compared with traditional ones.
這種方法和傳統方法比起來更有效率。
2. push through. . . 撐過……（困難、疲累等）
Alice pushed through the difficulties and finished her work.
艾莉絲撐過困難，把她的工作完成了。
3. lie in. . . 在於……
The problem lies in poor communication among team members.
問題在於團隊成員之間溝通不良。

1. (A) cast a spell on (B) set the tone for (C) keep an eye on (D) pave the way for
2. (A) researchers (B) volunteers (C) philosophers (D) composers
3. (A) would turn out (B) might otherwise feel (C) have yet to get (D) is meant to be
4. (A) chore (B) draft (C) play (D) bond
5. (A) rarely (B) slightly (C) absolutely (D) eventually
參考答案 : 1. B 2. D 3. B 4. A 5. C

From desert foxes to African giraffes, nature has engineered some surprisingly clever cooling systems. One of the most iconic examples involves unusually large ears. Fennec foxes and jackrabbits, both inhabitants of hot desert environments, possess ears that function as natural cooling devices. Severe sleep apnea raises stroke risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:38 UTC
01:36:38 KST

Severe sleep apnea might trigger nighttime urination, raise risks of a heart attack and stroke, a Chiayi County-based surgeon said.
Chiayi Chang Gung Memorial Hospital treated a 30-year-old man who complained of feeling tired during the day, frequent urination at night, and later began wetting the bed, said Tsai Ming-shao (蔡明邵), deputy head of the hospital’s Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery.
When people enter deep sleep, the pituitary gland secretes antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which reduces urine volume, Tsai said.
Photo: Lee Jung-ping, Taipei Times
In people with sleep apnea, repeated airway obstruction and oxygen deprivation during sleep leave the body in a prolonged state of heightened sympathetic nervous system activity, which can disrupt hormonal balance and reduce the secretion of ADH, in turn increasing urine production at night, he said.
Repeated awakenings caused by oxygen deprivation can disturb sleep patterns and could prevent people from waking in time when their brains signal that their bladders are full, resulting in bed-wetting, Tsai said.
Chronic poor sleep can also cause daytime fatigue, resulting in a lack of concentration and sleepiness, he said.
Sleep apnea is not synonymous with snoring, but snoring is a common symptom of sleep apnea, Tsai said, adding that 49.6 percent of people in Taiwan snore.
Chronic sleep apnea can also contribute to obesity and other metabolic problems, increasing the risk of hypertension, myocardial infarction and stroke, he said.
People with sleep apnea are prone to daytime fatigue, persistent sleepiness and a lack of concentration, Tsai said, adding that this could increase the risk of traffic accidents while driving.
Continuous positive airway pressure machines are the standard clinical treatment for sleep apnea, using pressure to keep the airways open, reduce snoring and alleviate oxygen deprivation, he said.
People whose upper airways are narrowed by obesity can reduce pressure on their airways by losing weight and following a diet, Tsai said.

South Africa were well-beaten in the opening fixture of their Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series against old foes New Zealand last weekend, but are unlikely to be as error-prone again in the second Test in Cape Town today.
The world champions had the edge in the scrum battle, the contact area and under the high ball, but despite numerous entries into the All Blacks’ 22, scored one try as handling errors and poor decisionmaking cost them.
The Springboks have not lost two games in a row since 2022 and at home for 11 years, but face a New Zealand side who have their tails up.
Photo: Reuters
The hosts welcome back captain Siya Kolisi from injury, and have gone into “World Cup knockout mode” by picking flyhalf Handre Pollard in the pivot position, while Cheslin Kolbe comes in for Kurt-Lee Arendse.
It suggests a side trying less “frills” with their game-plan and rather focusing on their core strengths.
Coach Rassie Erasmus pulled no punches this week and shouldered much of the blame for the Johannesburg defeat with his technical staff.
“I’m taking responsibility for some decisions we made. The truth is that a lot of the things that we asked from them [the players], they did,” Erasmus told reporters. “The plan didn’t win the game for us, but it’s definitely not the players that lost the game. I think this game was very much lost on decisions I made during the week.”
New Zealand coach Dave Rennie has had two concussion-enforced changes to his starting XV and is without lock Josh Lord and prop Ethan de Groot, while his only other change was to bring wing Leroy Carter into the team.
The remaining Tests in the series are to be played in Johannesburg on Sept. 5 and Baltimore, Maryland, a week later.
Meanwhile, Japan’s top club rugby competition yesterday said that it had watered down plans for an eligibility rule that prompted foreign-born Japan internationals to launch a legal challenge claiming discrimination.
Japan Rugby League One (JRLO) planned to introduce a new rule from next season that would limit the number of players in a matchday squad who had not completed at least six years of compulsory education in Japan, even if they were naturalized citizens.
Players who were born or fully schooled in Japan, or who had a Japanese parent or grandparent, would be assigned to a different category.
A group of 24 foreign-born players, including several who played in Japan’s run to the 2019 Rugby World Cup quarter-finals on home soil, filed a complaint with the Japan Fair Trade Commission and the Tokyo District Court in April arguing that the rule would affect their livelihoods.
The JRLO said it had revised its planned eligibility rules and had reached a settlement with the players over their legal action.
“League One takes seriously the feedback received regarding this system change, as well as the fact that prior explanations and communication with all relevant parties were insufficient, and will reflect this in the future management of the league,” it said in a statement.
The revised rules will see naturalized players continue to be registered in the same category as Japan-born players as long as they have held Japanese citizenship since May last year or earlier.

Prosecutors yesterday indicted nine people for allegedly installing hidden surveillance cameras in eight Dr Shine (光澤) clinics in Taipei and New Taipei City, and secretly recording more than 300 patients — including four minors — while they were exposed.
Investigations into other branches allegedly involved in the case are still ongoing.
The New Taipei City District Prosecutors’ Office is seeking a prison term of 16 years for Dr Shine group operations manager Chen Chih-min (陳志敏), 14 years for company information department head Tang Yung-chieh (唐詠傑) and seven years for surveillance camera supplier Chang Chao-ming (張朝銘).
Photo: Hsu Sheng-lun, Taipei Times
They also proposed seven years for Dr Shine employee Chiang Chin-wei (江勁緯) and unspecified prison terms for five other employees embroiled in the case.
Chen and Tang had abused clients’ trust, shown no remorse, offered no public apology and attempted to deceive police into believing that the devices had been removed years earlier, so they should receive severe sentences, the prosecutors’ office said in the indictment.
Prosecutors also called on Dr Shine owner Wang Chao-huei (王朝輝) to return to Taiwan to face investigation over the scandal.
Wang traveled to China before the incident came to light, but has allegedly shown no sign of willingly returning to Taiwan, even after a wanted notice was issued for him.
Chen and Tang allegedly installed surveillance cameras disguised as smoke detectors or sensor-activated lighting at two Dr Shine clinics in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋); and one each in Sanxia District (三峽), Sanchong District (三重) and Sinjhuang District (新莊), prosecutors said.
They installed the same devices at clinics in Taipei’s Guting District (古亭), Daan District (大安) and Songshan District (松山), they added.
Tang allegedly created a Line group that included Chen and others, and used it to direct efforts to remove surveillance cameras from all branches between May 5 and May 8, prosecutors said.
The installation of cameras allegedly gave Chen and Tang access to private moments when patients were exposed, severely infringing on people’s constitutionally guaranteed rights to privacy and self-determination, prosecutors added.

King Haakon the new face of Norway’s monarchy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:32 UTC
01:36:32 KST

As comfortable in a duffel coat as in ceremonial dress, Norway’s King Haakon is the new face of a monarchy long praised for its modernity and modesty, but now beset by woe and scandal.
Haakon automatically succeeded to the throne yesterday after his father, former king Harald, passed away peacefully earlier in the day. He was due to swear an oath before the government the same day.
He has increasingly seen his family’s affairs plastered across front pages: his wife’s lung transplant, revelations about her ties to convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a rape conviction against his stepson, and the escapades of his eccentric sister and her American self-proclaimed shaman husband.
Photo: NTB / AFP
Haakon, 53, is as modest and measured as most Norwegians — reflecting a society that shuns opulence and ostentation.
Married to Mette-Marit, a commoner who was a single mother, Haakon has focused his attention on issues that concern many of his generation, including environmental protection, and fighting racism and homophobia.
“It’s important that we protect who we are and for Norway to be a country where we’re allowed to love and be with whoever we want,” he said the day after a bloody attack against the gay community in Oslo in June 2022.
He had attended state-run daycare and schools, in line with the wishes of his parents, who were keen to see him grow up among “ordinary” Norwegians.
After secondary school he spent three years in the navy, where he served primarily as an officer on a torpedo boat.
He went on to earn a bachelor’s degree in political science at the University of California in Berkeley and a master’s in international politics at the London School of Economics.
Haakon met Mette-Marit at a 1999 music festival at Kristiansand, Norway. She had a son named Marius, the fruit of an earlier relationship with a man who had a heavy criminal record, including assault and cocaine possession.
The couple went on to have a daughter expected to one day be queen, Ingrid Alexandra, born in 2004, and a son, Sverre Magnus, in 2005.
However, storm clouds were building on the horizon. His sister, Martha-Louise, has repeatedly been accused of exploiting her princess title for commercial purposes. She made headlines by marrying a self-proclaimed shaman, Durek Verrett, in 2024, described as a dangerous “charlatan” by his critics.
Then, Marius was arrested in August 2024 and sentenced to four years in prison in June for rape and assault. He has appealed.
Just days before the conviction, Mette-Marit underwent a lung transplant for the pulmonary fibrosis with which she was diagnosed in 2018.
That came just months after the Norwegian media published troubling revelations about her friendship with Epstein in the early 2010s.
Although he had already been convicted of soliciting a minor, Mette-Marit had been in frequent contact with him, their e-mails indicating a close relationship.
The scandals have tarnished the royal family’s image and weakened its support in the Scandinavian country, although it remains broadly popular.

Supreme Court upholds 28 years for Chiayi bomber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:32 UTC
01:36:32 KST

The Supreme Court has upheld a 28-year prison sentence for a Chiayi City man who planted and remotely detonated an explosive at a temple festival in July 2023, injuring 29 people, including six children and teenagers.
The ruling on Thursday made the sentence against Chao Wei-chih (趙偉志) final. He was initially given a life sentence by the Chiayi District Court, which was reduced to 28 years after the Supreme Court ordered the High Court’s Tainan branch to retry the case.
Chao made the explosive at a rented residence in Chiayi, the ruling said. He packed high explosives and fireworks powder into a metal box, added steel bearing balls and fitted it with a remote-control-led detonator, it said.
Photo: Taipei Times
At around 9:38pm on July 15, 2023, Chao transported the bomb to a temple festival marking the 10th anniversary of the Chiayi and Lienjing Golden Tiger Association in the city’s West District (西區).
He placed the bag in a temporary trash collection area about 4m from the stage before walking about 30m away and detonating the bomb with a wireless remote control at about 9:55pm.
The explosion injured 29 people, including three children and three teenagers. All survived after being taken to hospital.
The Chiayi District Court described the attack as a premeditated, indiscriminate act of violence and sentenced Chao to life imprisonment for illegally manufacturing an explosive with the intent to use it in a crime.
However, in a retrial, the Tainan High Court said prosecutors had failed to prove that Chao, who had a previous interest in explosives, had criminal intent at the time he manufactured the bomb, ruling that Chao had only later decided to use it to harm people.
It therefore sentenced him to 14 years for illegally manufacturing explosives and 18 years for attempted murder of children by an adult, with a combined sentence of 28 years.
The Supreme Court dismissed the prosecutors’ and Chao’s appeals on Thursday, making the sentence final.

Ministry scheme targets labor shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:36:31 UTC
01:36:31 KST

The Ministry of Labor yesterday outlined measures to address worker shortages amid demographic shifts.
The National Development Council’s latest population projections from this year to 2074 show a persistently low birthrate and an aging population.
By 2075, the total population is projected to fall 48 percent from this year to just 12.15 million, while from 2037, people aged 45 to 64 are expected to make up more than half of the working-age population, putting severe pressure on the labor supply, data released by the council yesterday showed.
Photo: Taipei Times
In response, the labor ministry said it has introduced a series of measures to expand the workforce, including job-matching services, incentive programs and policies to attract foreign workers, while balancing the rights of local workers with the labor needs of industries.
The ministry said it has been working closely with industries to address worker shortages, while using public employment service centers across the nation to help businesses recruit workers.
These services include matching jobseekers with employers, organizing recruitment events and contacting potential candidates to arrange interviews based on employers’ needs to help businesses fill vacancies more quickly, it said.
To encourage businesses to recruit unemployed women and older workers, it offers subsidies for retaining older workers, incentives for adjusting working hours, and job redesign programs to help businesses improve working environments and job duties, the ministry said.
These measures are aimed at expanding employment opportunities for older workers and women returning to the workforce, it said.
Starting this year, the ministry has introduced a measure linking the hiring of migrant workers to wage increases for local employees, it added.
In the manufacturing sector, for example, employers can secure one additional migrant worker on their quota for every NT$2,000 raise given to a local employee, on top of the quotas allocated under the “3K5-level” system, it said.
The additional quotas are capped at 10 percent of an employer’s number of workers covered by labor insurance, it said, adding that when combined with other migrant worker application schemes, the overall quota can reach up to 45 percent of insured workers.
The ministry stressed that the expansion of policies governing foreign workers remains subject to the principle of “avoiding any adverse impact on employment for local workers,” while encouraging businesses to raise wages and improve working conditions for local employees.
The policy is intended not only to help industries with critical labor shortages secure the workers they need, but also to ensure that companies improve pay and working conditions for local employees as they bring in foreign workers, it said.
The ministry said it would continue to review and adjust its foreign labor policies to address worker shortages brought about by demographic changes.
While prioritizing the rights of local workers, the ministry would also seek to ensure that industries have a stable supply of workers and work with other government agencies to develop policies for attracting and retaining foreign talent and workers, it said.

Sudan authorities lift Khartoum curfew after two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:32:02 UTC

Breadcrumb
Sudan authorities lift Khartoum curfew, state of emergency after two years
Sudanese authorities have lifted a curfew and state of emergency in Khartoum after two years, allowing residents of the capital to move freely as the government seeks to project an improving security picture, despite warnings from international agencies that serious risks remain.
The measure was announced on Thursday by the government’s Security Affairs Coordination Committee, which said people would be able to travel and work across the city without time restrictions. Previously, movement by people and vehicles had been restricted between 11pm and 5am.
Following a meeting chaired by Khartoum Governor Ahmed Othman Hamza, the committee said security checkpoints and army patrols would remain in place. It advised residents travelling late at night to carry identification.
The committee also barred foreign nationals from entering Khartoum State without valid entry visas or permits.
Authorities introduced the curfew introduced in May 2024, citing deteriorating security conditions in Khartoum amid fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Following the outbreak of the war in April 2023, the RSF seized the presidential palace, Khartoum International Airport and much of the capital and its wider tri-city metropolitan area. The SAF retained a foothold in Omdurman, west of the Nile.
In late September 2024, the army launched a major offensive across Khartoum State. It eventually recaptured Khartoum city at the end of March 2025, pushing out remaining RSF positions from much of the state.
Since then, the government has returned to Khartoum from its temporary administrative base in Port Sudan, seeking to re-establish the capital as the centre of state administration.
Risks remain for returnees
International agencies and analysts have cautioned against treating the army’s recapture of the city, or the lifting of the curfew, as proof that Khartoum is safe or ready for a large-scale return of displaced residents.
In a report released on Friday, the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, described major challenges facing people returning to Khartoum State, as the effects of the war continue to endanger civilian life. The agency highlighted security concerns in some areas of the state, particularly at night, when reports of shootings, theft and drone activity are most frequent.
Drone attacks remain a threat in parts of Khartoum State. On 13 August, RSF drones targeted the capital, prompting anti-aircraft fire from Omdurman as residents reported explosions.
UNHCR also warned of the threat from unexploded ordnance, saying that "safety risks from unexploded ordnance remain present in some areas". It said returnees were confronting "interlinked challenges that constrain their ability to reintegrate sustainably", including unreliable electricity, limited access to basic services and a shortage of adequate housing.

Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:30:59 BST
01:30:59 KST

Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues
- Published
A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered the city of Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa, there have been outbreaks of violence as tensions mount between locals and foreign arrivals.
The Spanish government has been accused by opposition parties of struggling to manage the crisis effectively.
Ceuta's residents have complained of feeling unsafe on the streets, as well as expressing concerns about the burden being placed on public services.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most are sleeping rough on beaches or streets.
Anti-migrant demonstrations earlier this month were largely peaceful, but in recent days they have become increasingly violent.
On Thursday, several dozen locals prevented Red Cross personnel from distributing food and water to the migrants. Afterwards, some set fire to migrant camps on Trampolín beach, the main site where they have been sleeping, and there were also clashes with the police.
Those incidents came hours after the arrest of 12 migrants who were accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, breaking its windows and injuring the four men inside. That same morning there were reports of vigilante groups pursuing migrants through the streets.
Journalists and film crews have also reported being threatened.
"This is a city which has been under pressure, […] which has the right to normality," the mayor of the exclave, the conservative Juan Jesús Vivas, told Antena 3 television.
"The dignity of Spain is a stake right now in Ceuta," he said.
The socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has appealed for calm and accused Vivas's People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox of stoking the tensions.
José María Figaredo, a member of Congress for Vox, is being investigated for a possible hate crime after saying, soon after the migrants' arrival, that they should be "hunted down, one by one".
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told a congressional committee: "We have heard during these weeks rhetoric and comments that contribute to the stigmatisation of immigrants and which feed social division at a moment when what we need is responsibility and statesmanship."
Javier Celaya, who represents Ceuta in Congress for the PP, accused the government of treating "the invaders as victims when the real victims are us, the people of Ceuta".
On Friday, all the parties in the Ceuta local assembly signed a declaration condemning violence.
Earlier this week, the government centralised management of the situation, overriding the local authority, after criticism that it had been slow to respond.
Defence Minister Margarita Robles also apologised to those in Ceuta who "may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared", as the government unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.
Much of the recent ill-feeling in the city appears to be driven by government plans to move migrants into existing public buildings, such as sports centres, in order to be able to process their legal status in an orderly way and return those not eligible for asylum to Morocco.
Many local people, and Vivas, oppose this initiative, due to concerns that it will move the migrants closer to residential areas.
The government is also facing questions about who was behind the mass migrant crossing.
Politicians on the right and the far left have accused Morocco of involvement, pointing to its alleged use of the border with Spain in the past to exert political pressure.
Sánchez and his Socialist Party instead blame people traffickers, insisting that Rabat is a reliable partner which facilitated the immediate return of most of the arrivals.
Nonetheless, the crisis has placed the sovereignty of Ceuta, and its fellow autonomous city Melilla, under the spotlight.
Morocco has maintained a longstanding claim to the territories, which it has reiterated in recent weeks.
Spain's Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he "roundly rejected" such comments by Morocco.
"I don't speak about, nor have I spoken about, nor are we going to speak about Spain's territorial integrity with Morocco or with anyone else," he told the congressional committee.

Reports that US wants big stake in Venezuelan oil and gas spark anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:30:23 UTC
01:30:23 KST

Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.
Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.
On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.
“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.
Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”
Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.
“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.
Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials – despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his head for alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.
Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”
The economist Francisco Rodríguez urged Venezuela’s national assembly to reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.
Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic, sarcastically called the “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.
Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.
Brew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.
“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.
“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”
Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.
That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.
Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.
But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.

Trump vows legal order to break up ‘nasty monopoly’ in US food processing
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump on Aug 28 said he was preparing a legal order to allow farmers and ranchers to be given the right to process their own food aimed at breaking what he called “a nasty monopoly” among the nation’s top processors.
Trump did not name a particular food or industry in his post on Truth Social but said he was “authorising legal documents to be drawn” quickly. Earlier this week, Trump said on the Glenn Beck programme that he would look into whether there are too many beef processing plant regulations.
Beck, who owns a ranch, suggested to Trump that Department of Agriculture regulations were impeding ranchers from processing their own animals, leaving them to rely on the nation’s highly consolidated meat processing industry.
Four companies control about 85 per cent of US meat processing: Cargill; Tyson Foods, JBS USA and National Beef Packing Co.
The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted on X that there would be “big announcements” related to beef processing beginning on Aug 31, including expanding ranchers’ ability to sell across state lines, added support for smaller meat processors and rescinding “outdated guidance.”
Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for more details on the order, which comes as consumers continue to face rising grocery prices ahead of November’s midterm election.
Consolidation fight
Meat is inspected by the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service, which posts inspectors at meat processing plants to ensure products meet federal standards.
Ranchers are generally prohibited by federal law from selling meat from animals they have slaughtered and processed themselves, with some exceptions.
Farm and ranch groups have argued for years that consolidation in the meat processing sector has made it difficult for small producers to stay afloat because there are not many companies competing to buy their cattle, and they must transport their animals to USDA-inspected meat processing plants, sometimes at a high cost.
The Meat Institute, an industry group that represents meatpacking companies, said food safety could be at risk if more ranchers process their own meat.
“Allowing uninspected meat to be sold to unwitting consumers is the wrong approach, and risks undermining this country’s reputation for producing the safest meat products in the world,” the group said.
“If the goal is to lower beef prices for American families, lowering food safety standards is the wrong response.”
The administration of former president Joe Biden attempted to tackle consolidation in meatpacking in part through rules to promote competition and fairer pay for chicken farmers, which the Trump administration has indicated it will rescind.
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have steered funds towards supporting smaller meat processors, in an attempt to offer more options to ranchers.
Trump’s move comes as the nation’s meat processing sector grapples with a 75-year trough in supply as rising cattle costs outpace gains from soaring prices.
Trump also announced last week that more ground beef could be imported into the United States without tariffs.
The Justice Department has also said it is investigating whether meatpacking companies were illegally driving up consumer beef prices. REUTERS

What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:29:12 UTC
01:29:12 KST

KYIV — Before I go to sleep, I make a second bed — my air alert bed.
When the chorus of sirens announcing a Russian attack howls behind my windows and jolts me out of my slumber, I’m trained to jump up and run to my hallway, where this other bed is waiting. There, I usually try to sleep and wait until the attack ends in the morning.
Over the past two days, however, the alerts did not end at sunrise; they droned on into the day and the following night. It’s a nerve-wracking wailing, on top of explosions and the knowledge that your life is constantly under threat.
Advertisement
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.
Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.
But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.
But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.
“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”
As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.
Advertisement
And that is exactly why Russia keeps it going.
“You think we are calling for some kinds of atrocities, while we are aiming to demoralize the public to such an extent that they come out with their little paws raised to meet our troops,” Deputy Speaker of the Russian Duma Pyotr Tolstoy said this week.
That cuts no ice in Kyiv.
A smoke rises above one of Kyiv’s residential districts after a Russian strike on August 27, 2026. | Veronika Melkozerova/POLITICO
“Such statements by a Russian official calling for war crimes and demanding unbearable living conditions for civilians should lead to an ICC arrest warrant. As for ‘raised hands’ — the only reason to raise them is to give Tolstoy and his fellow war criminals the middle finger,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi responded.
Of course, it’s not as if Ukraine isn’t giving Russia a taste of its own medicine.
While peace negotiations have stalled, both sides have turned to total war tactics to the extent their capacity allows. While Ukraine has now also extended its targets from oil depots and military factories to bombing retail warehouses and energy facilities, Russia has embarked on a maximum escalation, attacking civilian housing, postal services, businesses, book and food warehouses — and that list covers only the past couple of days.
Advertisement
In July, the U.N. recorded the highest mortality rates among civilians in Ukraine since March 2022. Russia also reports more civilian deaths caused by Ukrainian attacks, even though, unlike Moscow, Kyiv does not deliberately target civilians but aims to bring the war “where it came from.“
Ukraine’s Deputy Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal best described the situation when talking to me about the attacks on the energy system last month: “It’s like the 12th round and each boxer hopes their rival will fall first.”
While troops on the frontline are largely stuck, with neither side making much progress on the ground, it’s us, civilians, who are being targeted more and more frequently.
Ukrainian military analyst Mykola Bielieskov called it “a mutual driving of each other into the Stone Age, with the hope to do it before the other side does.”
While our soldiers hold the Russian army at the front line, it’s ordinary Ukrainians — with our mental fortitude, our ability to outlive yet another missile, our capacity to adapt and go to work to keep the economy running no matter what — who will eventually decide the outcome of this war, Vyshlinsky said.
“As Mr. Tolstoy said, this is a tactic of deliberate exhaustion of civilians, pushing the rear to accept a war outcome unfavorable to the state,” Vyshlinsky added.
So we must endure until the other fighter falls.
And first, we need to wait for the best words that can boom from our loudspeakers: Air raid alert is over!

Sovereignty on the ballot in Iceland’s EU referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:27:28 UTC
01:27:28 KST

Sovereignty on the ballot in Iceland’s EU referendum
After decades outside the bloc’s periphery, Iceland is about to hold a referendum on reopening membership talks with the EU. Is the Viking nation preparing to trade sovereignty for stability? Or is it climbing aboard a sinking ship?
Icelanders go to the polls on Saturday, August 29 to answer a straightforward, yes or no question: “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”
The referendum is not legally binding, but liberal Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir has pledged to honor its result.
What stage are talks between Iceland and Brussels at?
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009, in the chaotic aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The country’s three biggest banks, Kaupthing, Landsbanki, and Glitnir, collapsed in the same week, and rather than force taxpayers to cover their balance sheets, Reykjavik washed its hands of the problem and let them fail.
The Icelandic krona plummeted, inflation soared, and center-right Prime Minister Geir Haarde resigned. Amid the meltdown, the newly empowered Social Democrats argued that by joining the EU and adopting the euro, Iceland could shield itself from future shocks – even as Iceland recovered far more quickly than EU members such as Greece, Ireland, and Portugal, which were subjected to crippling austerity measures by Brussels, the World Bank, and the IMF in the wake of the crisis.
The Social Democrats won the argument, convincing their left-wing, Euroskeptic coalition partners to vote for application. The left agreed, with the caveat that the final membership deal would be put to the people in a referendum.
Following a change of government, accession talks were shelved in 2013. Iceland, it was reasoned, had emerged from the financial crisis in good shape, and joining the EU would erode the island nation’s sovereignty, potentially diluting its control of rich fishing grounds, with no tangible benefits in return.
How do the polls stand before the vote?
With less than a day to go, the latest polls suggest that the vote will come down to the wire. A poll by market research firm Maskina published on August 25 shows the referendum passing by 51.3% to 48.7%. Two days later, a Gallup poll showed a near mirror inversion of these results, with the ‘no’ side leading by 51.6% to 48.4%. The result in both surveys was inside the margin of error, making the outcome impossible to predict. However, the ‘no’ side has been steadily closing the gap since July, and if the trend holds, could succeed in putting membership talks on ice for the foreseeable future.
The Yes vote: Safety in numbers
The two major parties in Frostadottir’s coalition – her Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir’s Reform Party – support EU membership. Their arguments are the same as they were in 2009, with one key addition: Membership would add a layer of defense against any potential attempts by US President Donald Trump to gain control over Iceland, as he is currently threatening Greenland. Although this is an unlikely scenario, the current US ambassador in Reykjavik caused widespread anger in January when he joked “that Iceland will be the 52nd state and he’ll be governor."
To Foreign Minister Gunnarsdottir, membership provides safety in numbers. “That is so important for us to see a group of like-minded nations stand together on principles and values,” she told AP. “That is also what I’m looking at when I see the European Union in this volatile world.”
Iceland’s six other major parties – from conservatives to centrists to leftists – all oppose membership. In an effort to persuade their voters, Frostadottir has sold the referendum as a zero-risk proposition. A ‘yes’ vote would merely restart talks, she has argued, pointing out that any deal offered by Brussels would still have to pass another referendum. It would also give Icelanders “the option of seeing what an agreement looks like,” she said last month.
Why does the EU want Iceland?
Home to fewer than 400,000 people, Iceland would be the EU’s smallest member state in terms of population. It sits just south of the Arctic Circle between Greenland and the UK, occupying a chokepoint known as the GIUK gap. Russian submarines and naval vessels entering the North Atlantic must pass through the GIUK gap, and with the EU’s foreign policy now bent on confrontation with Moscow, establishing an outpost here is high on Brussels’ list of priorities.
Frostadottir has reportedly warned the European Commission not to interfere in the vote. “The commission never intervenes in national elections or in referenda in any way,” a spokesperson told Euractiv, an outlet that the commission funds.
RT readers will recall that the European Commission has intervened in every national election in the bloc since 2024. This year alone, Brussels imposed online censorship measures ahead of elections in Bulgaria and Hungary. A US House Judiciary Committee report released in early 2026 alleged that the European Commission pressured social media platforms to censor populist and conservative speech during elections in Romania, France, the Netherlands, and Ireland.
While neither Commission President Ursula von der Leyen nor her chief diplomat Kaja Kallas have made the case for joining the bloc publicly, EU-funded media have filled in the blanks. According to Euronews, a ‘no’ vote would “close off a strategic opportunity to expand [the EU’s] positioning in the North Atlantic and Arctic region for generations.”
Is Iceland already embedded in the Western military nexus?
Despite presenting a “strategic opportunity” for the EU, Iceland is not some neutral territory waiting to be claimed. Iceland is a founding member of NATO, hosts the bloc’s air forces at Naval Air Station Keflavik, in return for which the military bloc financed the country’s major ring road, and has a network of radar stations described by the bloc’s officials as “the eyes and the ears of NATO in the north.”
At exercise Northern Viking in Iceland, I saw firsthand how U.S. and Icelandic forces train alongside fellow @NATO Allies to protect vital sea lanes and secure the Arctic, and how Icelandic technology is giving Allied forces an operational edge. Building our readiness and… pic.twitter.com/ZToq3GiBvH
— U.S. Ambassador to NATO (@USAmbNATO) August 21, 2026
Iceland has no standing army, but is a protectorate of the US under a 1951 defense agreement. The annual US-led ‘Northern Viking’ military exercise is currently underway in Iceland, and concludes on September 4.
On top of being fully integrated into the Western military camp, Iceland is already a member of the European Economic Area and visa-free Schengen zone, and has incorporated most EU legislation into its domestic laws.
No: A choice between war and peace
The EU’s militarization has directly harmed the bloc itself, Gunnar Palsson, Iceland’s former ambassador to Brussels, said in August, pointing to the EU’s flatlining economy as a result of its self-imposed embargo on Russian energy.
“The EU is now, for the first time in its history, a direct party to a military conflict in Europe,” Palsson wrote in an op-ed for Iceland’s Morgunbladid newspaper. “The Union’s escalating involvement in the Ukraine war, which is unlikely to lead to an optimal outcome for European countries, has already had a far-reaching impact on their economic situation, their relations with each other and with the outside world.”
The EU Iceland considered joining in 2009 is not the same as the hyper-aggressive, militarized bloc of 2026, he concluded.
‘Left Against the EU’, a social movement founded this year to oppose the referendum, has argued that joining the EU would subjugate Iceland’s foreign policy to the whims of the European Commission, which is “rapidly moving towards militarization.”
“The European Union and NATO have given in to the demands of the arms industry for vastly increased military spending, and it has never been more urgent than now for peace-loving people to withdraw from the warring forces,” reads a policy statement from the group.
“A European army is just around the corner, and Icelanders must seriously ask themselves whether they want to prepare their children and society for the future of serving under the arms of a European military power.”
Should the referendum pass, “Icelanders will become citizens of a union that has a strong political will for militarization and is increasingly involved in conflicts and escalating tensions in Europe,” Haraldur Olafsson, who leads the anti-EU ‘Heimssyn’ movement, warned in May. 
Sovereignty over stocks: Why fish are at the center of the argument
For most Icelandic Euroskeptics, however, the referendum comes down to a simpler issue: fish. Fishing accounts for around 4% of Iceland’s GDP, and a third of the country’s exports. Signing up to the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy risks surrendering control over this vital economic and culturally symbolic sector.
Ireland, another island on the EU’s seaboard, was subjected to these rules when it joined the bloc, and more than five decades later, it is likely that Irish fishermen will demand Icelandic fishermen be treated as they were.
French trawlers are allowed to catch five times more of certain fish in Irish waters than Irish trawlers. “The other countries are making fun of us for the lack of quota we have in our own waters,” Irish opposition leader Peadar Toibin claimed during a parliamentary debate last year.
Any Icelandic politician who trades away sovereignty over the country’s waters would “be expelled from the country,” Eirikur Bergmann, a professor at Iceland’s Bifrost University, told the BBC.
The ‘yes’ side has claimed that Iceland could negotiate exemptions to the Common Fisheries Policy, but no member state has done so to date, and Euroskeptics are unconvinced. Brussels would not even welcome such a debate, never mind find a workable solution.
“Contrary to the government’s claims, membership of the European Union is not a tailor-made agreement where each country chooses the parts that suit it and rejects the others,” Independence Party leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir argued earlier this year. It is unacceptable, Olafsson declared in May, “for a foreign union to legislate on Icelandic resources for its own benefit.”
The EU’s treaties – Rome, Lisbon, Maastricht – “are non-negotiable,” ‘no’ campaigner Sigridur Maria Egilsdottir warned at a rally on August 27. “We wouldn’t show up to the negotiations alone. Brussels would send its most capable team, loaded with conditions, demands and inescapable assumptions that all EU nations have had to abide by.”

How does a murder suspect with ties to Putin get out of pretrial detention within two months?
Businessman Ilya Traber has been released from Moscow’s Lefortovo pretrial detention center, the St. Petersburg-based news outlet Fontanka reported. An investigator ordered his release after his health declined sharply, according to the outlet.

In June 2026, investigators accused Traber and his business partner Vladimir Danilenko of involvement in organizing the 2020 murder of St. Petersburg entrepreneur and municipal deputy Alexander Petrov. Traber was taken to Moscow and sent to Lefortovo; Danilenko was also arrested.

Russia says it launched mobile ICBM from Plesetsk Cosmodrome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:24:29 UTC
01:24:29 KST

Burc Eruygur
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Russia said Friday that it launched a mobile solid-fuel intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the northwestern Arkhangelsk region.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that it successfully conducted the combat training launch of the “nuclear-capable” ICBM, which reached a designated area at the Kura training ground in the Kamchatka region of Russia’s Far East.
“The Strategic Missile Forces practiced the procedure for redeploying a mobile intercontinental ballistic missile launch battery to a remote area, preparing for and conducting the launch,” the statement said.
It added that the purpose of the combat training launch was to confirm the “tactical, technical, and flight characteristics of the missile system.”
The ministry did not identify the missile used in the exercise.
Russia’s Strategic Missile Forces are responsible for the country’s land-based intercontinental ballistic missiles and form a key component of its nuclear deterrent.
In May, the Defense Ministry said it launched a Yars intercontinental ballistic missile from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome toward the Kura training ground during nuclear drills that also involved neighboring Belarus.

Ukraine has built twin-Kalashnikov turret for cheap ground robots. Security Service has already used one to destroy Russian ambushes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:23:53 UTC
01:23:53 KST

Ukraine is bolting the war's most common rifle onto its robots. A company in the Brave1 cluster has developed a turret built around the Kalashnikov that mounts on low-cost unmanned ground vehicles, the state cluster's press service told Defender Media.
Ground robots have become a daily part of the front in Ukraine. Ukrainian units ran 16,676 logistics, strike, and evacuation missions with them in June, up 122 percent since January, and the military has contracted more than 22,000 for 2026, nearly double the 2025 total.
Arming them cheaply is the next step, and the Kalashnikov is the most cost-effective option because it is already the standard rifle across the force.
The robots are already in combat
Ground drones fitted with the turret are undergoing combat testing in Ukrainian units. Fighters of the Security Service Special Operations Center "A" have used one to destroy Russian ambushes set with concealed waiting-mode drones.
The complex is built on a four-wheel chassis with airless tires and an armored body. At the core of the weapon module is a twin turret mounting two Kalashnikov rifles.
The build took under six months
The developers have received a technical assignment and a grant from the cluster to create the turret. The path from idea to finished prototype took less than six months.
Beyond the base version, the turret can be mounted on other wheeled and tracked ground robots. That flexibility is the point: one weapon module across many platforms.
The rifle choice is about scale
The developers chose the Kalashnikov because it is the most widespread small arm in Ukrainian units, according to Brave1. The cluster considers it a simple, effective solution that lets Ukraine quickly scale up strike robots for assaults and for defense against Russian infantry.
Earlier, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said it would buy logistics and strike-ground robotic complexes under a new strategy that calls for sticking to the Defense Ministry's specifications rather than approving models one at a time.

Russian court sentences former Ukrainian presidential adviser Oleksii Arestovych to 11 years in absentia
The 2nd Western District Military Court in Moscow sentenced Oleksii Arestovych, a former adviser to the presidential chief of staff of Ukraine, in absentia to 11 years in prison, the independent outlet Mediazona said on August 28.
The trial lasted a single day and was held behind closed doors. The case stemmed from videos posted on March 17, 2022, in which Arestovych called for “waging a total rail war” against Russia in the occupied territories. It also included an April 8, 2022, publication about Russia’s strike on the Kramatorsk train station.
The court found Arestovych guilty of spreading “fake” claims about the Russian military and of calling for terrorism.
Arestovych resigned from the position in January 2023 and left the country after suggesting that Ukrainian air defense had shot down the Russian missile that destroyed a residential building in Dnipro. Ukraine has since opened two criminal cases against him. In May 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky imposed sanctions against Arestovych.

Top year for the coast, less for Limburg, and Americans love Ghent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:16:59 UTC
01:16:59 KST

Not surprisingly, the weather sent more people to the coast this year, but made them hesitate to book a stay in Limburg. And Americans have taken to Ghent, spending more there than any other group of foreign tourists
Tourism figures show that Flanders’ coastline was bustling this summer, while fewer people turned to recreation-laden Limburg province. We’ll give you one guess why … the weather.
More than six million daytrippers descended on the coast in July and August, and more than 11 million people stayed overnight. July’s 5.6 million overnight stays is an all-time record.
This summer saw a 10% increase in overnight stays compared to last summer, resulting in the highest figures the coast has seen since the Covid crisis. More than 80% of overnight tourists were Belgians.
There are always peak periods, but this summer it was constantly busy.
Ice cream seller Francis De Buck
Because of the consistently warm weather, tourism was also consistent over the two months rather than concentrated in certain weeks or weekends. Restaurants and other catering services were as satisfied as the hotels.
“Normally the first 10 days of July are a bit calmer, but this year the start of the vacation period was immediately busy,” said Francis De Buck, who owns an ice cream and waffle parlour in Blankenberge. “That was because of the nice weather, of course. There are always peak periods, but this summer it was constantly busy. People were here the minute we opened our doors. I estimate that we earned up to 18% more than usual.”
In Flanders’ other popular summer holiday destination – Limburg – there were in fact fewer overnight stays. The province – typically the warmest in Flanders – saw 1.7 million nights booked, a 3.5% decline on last summer. Daytrippers actually increase in the province, however, particularly to hike and to cycle.
“Nearly one million cyclists in two months’ time confirms that cycling is synonymous with Limburg,” said Laura Olaerts of Visit Limburg. “With the heat that we are facing, it’s increasingly important to promote water recreation and forests.”
Ka-ching!
Finally, the biggest share of money spent in Ghent this summer by foreign tourists came from Americans. Whether this means there were more American tourists than other nationalities or that they simply spent more is unclear, but in any case, some 40% of expenditures recorded in Ghent were linked to American bank accounts. A distant second were Dutch tourists at 19%, followed by British tourists at 11%.
Looking at all of East Flanders, Americans also spent more than anyone else in Oudenaarde and in Aalst, though the Dutch outspent them in Sint-Niklaas. The figures come from Worldline and so do not include transactions that were not linked to Worldline payment terminals.

VW eyes defense deal with Israel’s Rafael for Osnabrueck plant: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:15:48 UTC
01:15:48 KST

German automaker Volkswagen is considering entering the defense industry through a potential agreement with Israeli company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, according to media reports Friday.
An agreement involving VW’s plant in the northwestern city of Osnabrueck could be imminent, daily BILD reported.
The plan would involve manufacturing components for the Iron Dome air defense system at the Lower Saxony facility, including trucks, launchers and power generators, Bloomberg reported.
The Osnabrueck plant has been a key concern for VW management as the automaker restructures operations under a cost-cutting program. The T-Roc Cabrio is still produced at the site, but Europe’s largest automaker decided at the end of 2024 to phase out production there next year.
The future of the plant, which employs around 2,300 people, remains uncertain after production ends. The possibility of manufacturing defense components for Rafael at the site has reportedly been under discussion for months.
Major shareholder Qatar reportedly objects to plans
According to Bloomberg, however, VW major shareholder Qatar has raised objections to a partnership with an Israeli company.
The report said a potential solution could involve the state of Lower Saxony taking over parts of the Osnabrueck plant and subsequently establishing a joint venture with Rafael.
No decision has yet been made.
“We are currently examining whether—and in what form—a stake in a potential future industrial solution for the Osnabrück site could be considered,” Lower Saxony Prime Minister Olaf Lies said.
VW’s next supervisory board meeting is scheduled for Sept. 4, when a decision could potentially be made.
Daily Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung reported that the state could invest at least €200 million ($232 million) in the project.
“The specific structures of such a stake are currently still the subject of ongoing reviews and discussions,” a spokesperson for the prime minister said.
“As such, we cannot speculate at this time on either a specific stake amount or a particular investment model.”
Public broadcaster NDR reported as early as March that VW had also held talks with other companies, including German-French defense contractor KNDS.
Volkswagen undergoes restructuring program amid widespread criticism
Volkswagen has been grappling in recent years with sluggish demand, persistently high production costs in Germany, the negative impact of trade tensions with the US, and fierce competition from Chinese electric-vehicle makers.
Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume had said in March that the company will stop manufacturing Volkswagen Group vehicles at Osnabruck starting in 2027 and confirmed talks with several defense firms about shifting the plant for military vehicles production. 
The proposal, since then, has sparked significant controversy within Germany. Volkswagen employees, peace activists and opposition politicians have criticized the plan, arguing the automaker should focus exclusively on civilian production.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative (OFRI) has also organized multiple protests urging Volkswagen to abandon any defense contracts.
Germany’s opposition Left Party called Volkswagen’s planned cooperation with Israel’s state-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems “unacceptable,” citing the Netanyahu government’s ongoing military campaigns across the Middle East, accusing it of war crimes and genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Rafael, meanwhile, has been expanding its European footprint as governments across the continent boost defense spending and procurement following the war in Ukraine.
Although a US-brokered truce went into effect in the Gaza Strip last October, repeated Israeli truce violations have killed more than 1,300 Palestinians across the enclave.
More than 4,300 others were injured ever since. 
Hundreds of bodies of slain Palestinians, meanwhile, have been pulled from under the rubble of destroyed infrastructure.
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel began its genocidal war on the coastal strip in October 2023.

Mongolia Hosts COP17, Urging Global Partners to Action on Climate Issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:15:00 UTC
01:15:00 KST

The 17th Conference of the Parties to the U.N Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) was convened in Ulaanbaatar from August 17-28, bringing together 196 country representatives plus the European Union to negotiate action-based measures on several climate challenges facing the world today. This year’s COP17 included segments on finance, water, land and people, and food systems. Parties agreed on a new initiative that includes $1.3 billion in financing, but failed to approve a new financial mechanism to combat drought.
On August 17, the opening ceremony was attended by Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD Dr. Yasmin Fouad, Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture (and president of UNCCD COP16) Dr. Osama Ibrahim Fakiha, and Mongolia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Batmunkh Battsetseg. The global climate gathering also included a visit by South Korea’s former president, Moon Jae-in, and business leaders from Rio Tinto, Trade Development, Oyu Tolgoi, Asian Development Bank, Global Green Growth Institute, and more.
Welcoming the guests and opening the COP17 gathering, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor stated: “The greatest change we want to see from COP17 is a shift from talk to action, from targets to implementation, and from commitments to measurable results.”
As Fouad, the UNCCD executive secretary, put it in an interview with The Diplomat before the gathering: “COP17 comes at a pivotal moment for global action on land… I believe countries will come to Mongolia with a shared understanding that the challenge is no longer understanding the problem – we know what is at stake. The priority now is implementation.”
In the last two weeks, the Mongolian government, civil society, and environmental organizations cooperated with global financial institutions, policymakers, businesses, and environmental scientists to advance solutions to emerging issues facing not just Mongolia but the globe, including desertification, drought, and land degradation. Building on the progress made at COP16 in Riyadh, governments at COP17 aimed to negotiate practical tools, partnerships, and financing mechanisms needed to help countries turn existing plans into action.
According to the UNCCD, more than 70 countries have now developed national drought plans, compared with only three in 2013 – reflecting growing recognition that drought must be managed proactively rather than only once it becomes a humanitarian and economic crisis.
Desertification, land degradation, and climate change are all interconnected and demand integrated solutions. In Mongolia, the challenge includes extreme climate fluctuations, such as dzud and drought, as well as loss of water, water pollution due to mining activities, as well as mismanagement of rangelands and pastoralism. The combination of these issues in turn becomes additional hindrance to the country’s development.
The last two days of COP17 were designated for all 197 parties to come to some sort of an agreement on a mechanism to combat drought. The Asian Development Bank Partnership estimated $355 billion is needed every year to combat land degradation and drought, yet current investment stands at only around $77 billion, leaving an annual financing gap of $278 billion.
Unfortunately, on August 28, last day of the COP17, parties failed to come to an agreement and passed the issue to the next COP gathering.
One of the main disagreements was whether to establish a new drought protocol initiated by the African Group. The bloc of developed countries – including the European Union, Australia, and the United Kingdom – opposed the establishment of a new drought protocol, preferring to utilize previously agreed multilateral frameworks such as Global Environment Facility and to avoid overlapping agreements.
While drought – and a financial mechanism to combat drought – posed a challenge for the 197 parties to negotiate, rangeland, pastoralism, and water deserve equal attention.
One of the most important segments of COP17 was the High-Level Ministerial Meeting and Finance Day, where delegates, multilateral banks, and participating organizations announce strategic commitments and financial mechanisms focusing on specific issues such as land restoration, rangeland preservation, and invigorating environmentally friendly, green growth.
At the High-Level Ministerial Meeting, Mongolia officially launched the global “Rangelands Flagship Initiative,” which focus on sustainable management and restoration of global pasture lands. The initiative was viewed as one of the most important outcomes of the climate gathering. It will bring together 45 projects across 23 countries, amounting to $1.3 billion in funding, making it the largest investment in the rangelands sector in the history of the UNCCD Convention.
The financial commitments will be assessed by the implementation of individual projects. Participating governments are expected to consider a new policy framework on rangelands and pastoralists designed to increase long-term investment in sustainable rangeland management and strengthen pastoral livelihoods. The initiative also mentioned the establishment of an Eurasian Center for Climate-Resilient Rangelands in Mongolia.
On August 24, Business for Land Forum and Finance Day brought together government, businesses, and investors looking to invest in regenerative landscapes. The Business Council of Mongolia and the UNCCD signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a Business4Land (B4L) platform and Mongolia Hub. The MoU “aims to link consumption, production, and finance through environmental and social standards, as well as financial products focused on preserving natural capital.”
Moreover, Mongolia also signed a Host Country Agreement (HCA) with Global Green Growth Institute to strengthen the legal and institutional framework for climate financing and augmenting investment environments for green projects.
The director of the Protected Areas Policy Department at Mongolia’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, Uranchimeg Tserendorj, stated that for the last 32 years, Mongolia’s Law on Protected Areas has protected land all around the country. The legal framework has allowed the country to protect “20.8 percent of land,” Uranchimeg said.
Mongolia is also seeking a deeper action-based cooperation with both UNCCD and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands. Mongolia’s Environment and Climate Change Minister Sandag-Ochir Tsend met Ramsar Convention Secretary General Dr. Musonda Mumba, “proposing closer cooperation between the Ramsar Convention and U.N. Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) during Mongolia’s COP17 presidency.”
At COP17, mining giants such as Rio Tinto announced their strategy to contribute to Mongolia’s fight against desertification, water pollution, and restoration of forestry by planting 5,000 hectares of forest, investing in renewable energy for company usage, as well as introducing new technology to replenish groundwater. According to the environmental manager of Oyu Tolgoi, one of Mongolia’s largest mining companies, the firm began paying water pollution fees in 2026, a regular quarterly payment of 150-200 million Mongolian tugrik (roughly $42,000 to $55,000). These practices meant to set an example for other mining giants operating in the country.
In the last two weeks, global partners gathered in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia to discuss and negotiate an issue that has long been a focus for climate advocates. Mongolia’s hosting of the UNCCD COP17 is viewed as a step up in its global engagement and contribution and commitment to climate change. Considering the country’s own struggle with wetland loss, drought, rangeland and pastoral management, the platform urged global businesses, government, and civil society to take actions to help contribute solve these challenges.
Although the convention did not reach an agreement on solving drought, it has made progress in promoting and implementing global partnership in climate issues.

US judge questions but won't yet block Trump's new birthright citizenship order
