helen & hard revives viking boatbuilding with whole-tree cabin on norway’s atlantic coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:45:05 UTC
00:45:05 KST

On a rocky headland in Randaberg, Norway, 18 whole spruce trees rise through Helen & Hard’s Cabin Sande, their root systems branching across the ceiling where columns meet beams. Studio founders Reinhard Kropf and Siv Helene Stangeland built the 112-square-meter retreat as their own cabin after twelve years of sketching and refinement. It replaces a 1970s cabin on the same site, where local planning restrictions required the replacement to stay within the earlier footprint and height. From outside, the low form sits close to the rock. Inside, the trees give the home its structure and much of its character.
Helen & Hard looked to Norwegian boatbuilding traditions dating back to the Viking Age for those junctions. Shipbuilders used naturally curved sections where trunk meets root to strengthen the ribs of wooden vessels. For Cabin Sande, each spruce was excavated with its roots intact, cleaned and air-dried for eight months before being scanned. Digital models mapped the irregular forms, then robots milled fitted joints directly from the roots so each tree could work within the column-and-beam system.
Four rows of columns spread across Helen & Hard’s Cabin Sande in a fan-shaped formation, which opens the main room toward the western horizon. Cantilevered roof beams meet in pairs above the space and span a horizontal opening more than nine meters wide toward the Atlantic, leaving the sea view uninterrupted. At the opposite end, the plan narrows toward an entrance facing the garden and morning sun. A long sightline runs straight through the cabin, with vegetation at one end and open water at the other.
The roof projects beyond the glazing to shelter the interior from the Atlantic weather, while concealed tension cables and springs help support the cantilever. Continuous glass wraps much of the perimeter, so changing light and coastal conditions stay visible from across the room. Below, a stone plinth uses rock found on the site, while the planted roof follows the surrounding topography and keeps the building low against the headland.
Cabin Sande sits on a rocky headland overlooking Norway’s Atlantic coast
the timber frame becomes the interior
The main living area occupies the broad center of the plan, with the kitchen along one side and two workspaces along the other. One workspace rises half a level above the bathroom, giving the compact interior a shift in section without breaking up the larger room. The spruce structure continues into bookshelves and benches, then into room dividers and window frames. Columns and built-ins share the same timber language, so the cabin reads as one continuous piece of construction instead of a frame filled later with separate furniture.
Closer to the sea, the broad glass opening pulls the horizon deep into the room. Along the side zones, branching timber creates smaller places for sitting and working while the central space stays open toward the water. The root forms remain visibly irregular after robotic milling, keeping each tree legible in the finished cabin. Digital fabrication works here by accepting those irregularities: the scans make each joint precise while the structure still reads as eighteen individual trees.
eighteen whole spruce trees form the cabin’s branching timber structure
the spruce trees were excavated with their roots intact before digital scanning
a broad opening extends across the living space toward the western sea horizon

Algeria battles scores of wildfires that have killed 12, injured dozens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:44:54 UTC
00:44:54 KST

Yakoota Al Ahmad and Lina Altawell
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Sixty-four wildfires were still burning across 10 Algerian provinces on Friday, most of them in the eastern Jijel province, after authorities extinguished 110 out of 174 fires that erupted nationwide over the past 24 hours.
According to a statement by the General Directorate of Civil Protection, Jijel topped the list of provinces for ongoing fires with 20, followed by Skikda with 14, El Tarf near the Tunisian border with 10, Guelma with six, Annaba with five, and Bejaia with four.
Bouira, meanwhile, is still contending with two fires, while Tebessa, Constantine and Mila are still battling one each.
Emergency teams have continued efforts to extinguish the blazes with aerial support from BE-200 military aircraft, AT-802 firefighting aircraft and Mi-26 helicopters.
Areas where firefighting efforts remain underway include Taxenna, Ziama Mansouriah, El Milia, Ouled Yahia Khedrouche and Chekfa in Jijel, along with areas in Skikda, El Tarf and Annaba.
12 killed, 54 injured
The spate of fires that erupted Wednesday has killed 12 people to date -- five in Jijel, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou, according to Interior Minister Said Sayoud.
Another 54 people have sustained injuries, including six in critical condition, the minister said.
On Thursday, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune declared three days of national mourning, ordering flags to be flown at half-staff in honor of the victims.
On the same day, Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb traveled to Jijel to oversee firefighting efforts and visit the injured and local residents in affected areas.
The fires come amid a severe heat wave affecting North Africa, where authorities say they have mobilized land and air resources with a view to protecting lives and property.
On Tuesday, Algeria’s meteorological service warned of an anticipated heat wave in several provinces this week, with temperatures forecast to reach 49C in some areas.
According to Civil Protection data, around 4,000 fires were recorded in the period from May 1 to July 20, compared with 1,501 during the same period last year, representing an increase of nearly 167 percent.

Alleged Narco-Terrorist Moves to Toss U.S. Indictment on Jurisdictional Grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:42:00 UTC
00:42:00 KST

Reported by
Attorneys for the accused South American drug kingpin Sebastián Marset have filed motions to dismiss all drug trafficking, money laundering, and narco-terrorism charges against him, challenging the U.S. government’s authority to prosecute the case.
Marset is seeking a complete dismissal of the indictment, alleging that agents of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) interrogated him without advising him of his Miranda rights, denied him access to counsel, and brought vindictive charges after he rejected a plea deal. His defense team has also filed motions accusing DEA agents of attempting to extort cryptocurrency from him.
However, Marset’s primary defense rests on a novel jurisdictional argument. His lawyers contend that the United States lacks the authority to prosecute him because the alleged offenses took place outside the country. Prosecutors accuse Marset of leading a massive cartel that shipped cocaine from South America to Europe, with illicit proceeds allegedly wired back to South America through banks in Hong Kong and China.
According to court filings, federal jurisdiction hinges on a single financial transaction. Prosecutors allege that one wire transfer - sent from a Chinese bank to a Portuguese account by Marset's alleged co-conspirator, Federico Ezequiel Santoro Vassallo - routed through a U.S. correspondent bank server located in Richmond, Virginia. Santoro has since pleaded guilty and is cooperating with prosecutors.
Marset’s lead attorney, Robert Feitel, argues that a single automated server transfer is insufficient to establish U.S. jurisdiction, noting that Marset was never physically in Virginia, did not initiate the wire, and could not have known the money would pass through a local server.
“This is the most egregious effort I’ve seen from the United States to assert jurisdiction over things that have nothing to do with them at all,” Feitel, a former federal prosecutor, told OCCRP, adding that he would never have brought charges in Virginia on such grounds. “One transaction, according to the government, came through a Virginia server. We’re talking about one transaction out of 203.”
Marset faces a steep legal battle given the expansive reach U.S. courts typically exercise over international cases with even minimal domestic touchpoints. The U.S. government previously offered a $2 million reward for his capture, and the presiding judge recently denied his request for private visits with his Uruguayan attorney. Still, his defense team remains steadfast.
“To the extent that this case appears to be the first of its kind, it’s because no one else had the temerity” to charge someone based on these facts, Feitel told OCCRP.

The Bigger Bet Behind Nvidia’s $12.9 Billion Hugging Face Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

Nvidia has reportedly agreed to buy popular AI library Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The deal is partly a hedge against an emerging threat: AI companies which consume enormous quantities of Nvidia hardware are increasingly developing chips of their own. In a future where AI becomes centralized in a small group of players with their own chips, those companies could demand lower prices from Nvidia or bypass it altogether.
Hugging Face, an online hub where developers share open AI models and datasets, gives Nvidia a stake in an alternative future, where downloadable AI models allow startups and governments to build systems of their own. Few would have the scale to develop custom chips. (Nvidia and Hugging Face did not respond for comment.)
With roughly 85% of the AI chip market, Nvidia’s share has only one way to go. But a smaller slice of a much larger market could still mean more sales, says Umesh Padval, a Managing Partner at Seligman Ventures. “If the deal goes through, I think it’s a brilliant chess move.”
Nvidia has thrown its weight behind open-source AI in recent months. It successfully lobbied Washington to loosen restrictions on selling its chips to China, which leads in open AI development. More recently, it struck a $6 billion deal with Poolside, to develop an American open alternative. In July, Nvidia helped lead an open letter defending open-source AI and urging Washington not to restrict it. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia boss Jensen Huang wrote in his first post on X.
Meanwhile, Google now exclusively uses its custom TPU chips to train its Gemini AI models. In August, Anthropic hired, Amir Salek, a former TPU team-lead at Google to spearhead a new in-house chip division. The same month, OpenAI shared the first results from its custom chip, Jalapeño. SemiAnalysis, the firm which conducted tests on OpenAI’s chip, said it beat “every Nvidia, AMD, and Google chip we have been able to test.”
“There’s kind of this two-way strategic battle,” says Richard Clode, a technology portfolio manager at Janus Henderson. “On the one hand, Nvidia doesn’t want to be reliant on just three customers, so [it] is deliberately trying, with financing and allocation of chips, [to] encourage other players and neo-clouds. And then vice versa, those hyperscalers don’t want to be completely reliant on just one compute provider.”
Nvidia’s 75% margin means that other firms’ in-house chips do not need to match its performance to save large customers money. Custom silicon has other benefits, too. Nvidia has previously given smaller cloud providers early access to its newest chips, ensuring that the largest players do not dominate supply. Developing chips in-house reduces exposure to those allocations, Clode says, while allowing AI companies to tailor hardware to their specific workloads.
AI companies are not developing these chips completely alone. Google, OpenAI, and Meta have partnered with Broadcom to help turn their specifications into custom silicon.
Those efforts are yet to make a dent in Nvidia’s bottom line. In August, Nvidia reported a blockbuster earnings report with record revenue of $96.2 billion, more than doubling year-over-year and beating Wall Street expectations. Companies like Google and OpenAI continue to buy large quantities even as they develop alternatives. They’ve “poured a lot of infrastructure capex into the existing infrastructure,” says Sriram Viswanathan, a founding managing partner at Celesta Capital and a former Intel executive. Moving to a different architecture, he said, is “a huge lift-and-pour-concrete situation. So I think it’s going to happen over a period of time, but not in one fell swoop.”
He points to Apple as a warning. Apple first developed chips for the iPad and iPhone while continuing to buy Intel processors for Macs. As its expertise matured, its silicon moved into Mac computers and Intel was cut out.
“Nvidia is executing like crazy, so in some ways it’s theirs to lose,” says Sean Lie, co-founder and chief technology officer at AI chip company Cerebras. “But I think we’re seeing a lot of cracks in that armor.”

Tim Cook’s Dark Legacy in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

On September 1, 2026, Tim Cook will hand over control of Apple to John Ternus. He leaves behind one of the most efficient manufacturing systems in consumer electronics, one he helped build as operations chief from 1998.
In China, Cook leaves a second, but related, legacy: workers on Apple lines toiling 60 hours a week or more, often without a rest day and depending on overtime to cover the basic cost of living.
Ternus will have to decide how to handle both of these realities.
At China Labor Watch, we just completed a new investigation into Apple’s supply chains in China. Our conclusion is not simply that Apple’s compliance system fails to prevent violations. Many of the labor conditions that the report identified are baked into the production model itself.
I once asked a worker on an Apple line at a Foxconn factory what he made of the human rights standards Western countries talk about. He called them Western propaganda. What taught him about America, he said, was not standards on paper but the machine-like pace of Apple’s line and pay he was never sure would arrive.
Since 2006 we have investigated Apple’s suppliers in China, publishing 19 reports. I have come to believe blaming Apple alone would be unfair. Apple’s supply chain in China was built on a trade. China needed foreign capital, technology, and jobs. In return, Western firms got cheap labor and speed built on long overtime and extreme scheduling flexibility.
The Chinese government, Apple, and the supplier factories all bear responsibility for the conditions workers face. But Apple has treated allegations of wrongdoing as a compliance problem, rather than the output of its own production model.
Apple’s product cycles are fast, and launches send order volumes sharply higher. Suppliers work on thin margins and must deliver enormous volumes quickly. The component prices are set; equipment costs are sunk. There is only one place left to ensure profits: labor costs. Workers’ hours and income become the buffer, absorbing the volatility Apple itself generates.
Apple’s answer has been to police this through a Supplier Code of Conduct, audits, public reporting and worker training. While these steps do have an impact, the overall pattern is clear: individual violations may be corrected, but the same problems return.
In 2019 we found withheld wages at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant. At the same plant, more than half the workforce was on dispatch contracts, far above the legal cap of 10 percent. Apple disputed most of our findings but acknowledged excessive use of dispatch workers. In 2022 thousands at the same plant clashed with police over pay promised at recruitment; Foxconn apologized, blaming a computer input error. In 2025 we found dispatch workers still being used above the legal cap.
This August we found a full-time assembly worker at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant on a base wage of 2,450 yuan a month, about $363, a little above the city’s legal minimum of 2,350 yuan. To reach 4,200 yuan he has to work 60-hour weeks, totaling roughly 87 hours of overtime a month, against a statutory ceiling of 36.
Raising his base wage by 1,750 yuan, about $260 a month, would let him earn the income he needs on a legal schedule. Even if all 200,000 workers employed at peak operating times received that increase for a full year, the cost would be roughly $620 million – about half of one percent of Apple’s $112 billion in net income in the year to September.
Clearly, Apple can afford to pay more. The discrepancy, then, points to a deeper issue: labor conditions are not given the same priority as output, speed, and profit margin.
Look at how Apple manages suppliers. Yield rates and delivery deadlines are tracked precisely. Missing them can cost a supplier its orders. A labor violation, by contrast, will just produce another audit. Foxconn went through the 2010 suicides and has gone through one labor dispute after another since. To this day it remains one of Apple’s most important partners.
Suppliers know exactly which metrics are most important to Apple.
Apple could have set an enforceable wage floor and made labor conditions matter as much as quality and delivery. It has not.
China has changed, economically and politically. If Apple wants to keep relying on China as its main production base, maintaining the old model now comes at a higher price in both Beijing and Washington. Apple has been willing to pay that price. It has never paid a comparable price to the people who build its phones.
As if the suffering of thousands of workers wasn’t enough, there are other costs as well. When the United States preaches labor rights while its most emblematic company leaves Chinese workers dependent on illegal overtime to live, the contradiction erodes the very labor and human rights standards it promotes.
Cook proved Apple can control how an iPhone is made. He never showed that Apple is willing to take responsibility for the welfare of the people who make those phones. For 20 years Apple’s priorities have been consistent: production first, responsibility second.
On September 1, Ternus inherits the manufacturing system Cook helped create – and the unpaid debt to the workers who power that system. Whether the debt is paid will not be recorded in the next Supplier Responsibility Report, but it will show up in how the worker on the line describes America to everyone he knows.

Libya energy crisis leaves parts of oil-rich country struggling
Long power cuts and severe fuel shortages have disrupted daily life in Libya, a country already plagued by an enduring political deadlock, conflict, and corruption, and home to Africa's largest oil reserves.
As the summer heat peaks, the worst crisis in years has tightened its grip on many Libyans who struggle to stay cool and keep their houses, cars and businesses running.
Experts and United Nations officials say the root of the problem lies in corruption, weak governance and years of inadequate maintenance at power plants.
Libya holds about 48 billion barrels of proven oil reserves and produces roughly 1.5 million barrels a day. It is seeking to raise output to 2 million barrels a day.
But the country only produces a third of the fuel it needs for domestic consumption. Last year, it imported $7.8 billion worth of fuel, according to figures from the National Oil Corporation.
For ordinary Libyans, the crisis has meant spoilt food and stalled businesses amid unbearable heat.
'Poor governance'
Libya has been politically divided for more than a decade, after being plunged into war during the 2011 overthrow of former leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Two administrations are currently vying for power: a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and its rival in Benghazi, backed by military leader Khalifa Haftar.
"Libya produces less than its energy needs during peak periods, and the electricity crisis and fuel shortage are complex, since the country is an oil producer but relies on importing fuel," international relations researcher Bechir Jouini told AFP.
But the issue is also compounded by "the problem of smuggling oil out of the country as well as the failure to implement maintenance programmes for power plants", Jouini said.
He also blamed mismanagement and corruption in the budgets allocated to the energy sector.
"Libya has resources and funds, but it suffers from poor governance and corruption is rampant... despite the allocation of huge budgets to the electricity company," he said.
Hanna Tetteh, the UN envoy to Libya, has also linked the energy crisis to broader failures in the country's institutions.
"The recent widespread electricity outages and public discontent, exacerbated by a prolonged heatwave, have exposed the consequences of institutional fragmentation, large-scale diversion of public resources, underinvestment and uncoordinated decision-making, all of which are essentially failures of governance," the envoy recently told the UN Security Council.
"The contradiction is that this is occurring in a country that does not lack energy resources and has the largest petroleum deposits on the African continent," Tetteh said.
Earlier this month, a key reservoir containing about 4.5 million litres of petrol was targeted by several drone attacks in Zawiya, some 45 kilometres (27 miles) west of Tripoli.
Zawiya has for years been the scene of armed conflict between rival groups who fight over the territory, which is a hotspot for fuel, drugs and migrants trafficking.

Mitri urges unified approach in logging Israeli war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:38:17 UTC
00:38:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon deputy PM Mitri urges unified approach in logging Israeli war crimes
Lebanon's Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri has urged civil society groups and observers to share their documenting of Israeli war crimes in the country, as part of efforts to potentially hold Tel Aviv accountable in future.
Mitri made the remarks after a discussion hosted on Thursday by The Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies in Beirut on "Israeli violations of international humanitarian law".
The session was also attended by Lebanese parliament members, most notably MP Inaya Ezzeddine, MP Ibrahim Mneimneh and MP Michel Moussa.
"We discussed the importance of documenting Israeli violations, the work of the National Committee and the call to enrich it with contributions from the active forces in society", adding that "the dialogue addressed the outcomes of this work and its moral and political impact," Mitri wrote on X after the session.
A press statement distributed by the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies in Beirut said Mitri addressed Israel's crimes and its violation of international human rights law.
The session highlighted the process of documenting Israeli violations of international humanitarian law during the recent war on Lebanon, as well as the methodology and mechanisms adopted by the National Committee for International Humanitarian Law in Lebanon to collect information, document violations and verify them.
Mitri recalled statements by "enemy leaders and their threats to make Lebanon another Gaza".
He also discussed the civilisational and environmental genocide to which Lebanon is being subjected, as well as Israel's crimes against humanity, reviewing the issue of documenting Israeli crimes and violations to work toward prosecuting Israel for its crimes.
Mitri called on civil society groups, and everyone who has worked to document Israeli crimes, to share their research with the Lebanese government to enrich the reports that the government is preparing.
He stressed the need to unify efforts and endeavours on this issue, praising in this regard "the volunteers who are working without pay so far in the National Committee for International Humanitarian Law to document Israeli crimes".
He said the Lebanese government is working to establish a permanent centre to carry out this task.
Regarding the possibility of pursuing Israel before the International Criminal Court (ICC), Mitri said Lebanon is not a party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC, preventing the Lebanese state from taking up a case against Israel there.
At the same time, Mitri said the ICC can, under specific circumstances and through defined mechanisms, accept jurisdiction to consider crimes committed during a certain period, even if the state concerned has not fully joined the Rome Statute.
However, he stressed that the inability of the Lebanese state at present to approach the ICC does not remove the right of Lebanese individuals to pursue Israel before many European courts, such as those in Spain, Belgium and France.
Some European judicial systems allow, under specific conditions, the filing of cases related to international crimes or serious violations.
For his part, Nasser Yassin, director of the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies in Beirut, said the centre in Beirut has worked since the beginning of the recent war on Lebanon to highlight Israeli violations and the cost of the war, particularly the direct and indirect damage to various vital sectors in Lebanon.
It has done so by holding discussion sessions and workshops, as well as preparing and publishing situation assessment reports, position papers and research papers covering the education, health and agriculture sectors.
Yassin stressed the urgent need at this stage to "activate respect for international humanitarian law by respecting civilians and their lives and not targeting health workers or humanitarian service workers".

Syria's al-Sharaa names SDF's Abdi presidential adviser after dissolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:38:00 UTC
00:38:00 KST

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa appointed former SDF ringleader Ferhat Abdi Şahin, also known as Mazloum Abdi, as a presidential adviser Friday, cementing a dramatic political shift just days after the group announced its dissolution and integration into state institutions.
The appointment was announced in a decree signed by al-Sharaa and carried by state news agency SANA.
“Mustafa Khalil Abdi is appointed as adviser to the presidency of the republic,” the decree said, using one of the names by which Abdi has been known.
His appointment comes after he announced Tuesday that the SDF would dissolve under an agreement reached with Damascus in January to integrate its armed units and civilian administration into Syrian state institutions.
Abdi said the move followed “the completion of the process of integrating our forces into the brigades of the Syrian army.”
Syria’s new authorities, which took power after the ouster of longtime dictator Bashar Assad in 2024, have sought to restore central government control across the country after years of fragmentation during the civil war.
U.S. special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack welcomed the agreement Tuesday, describing it as an example of former rivals reaching a diplomatic settlement aimed at strengthening Syrian sovereignty.
Barrack also said securing meaningful government roles for Kurdish figures, including Abdi, would recognize their leadership and contributions to regional stability.
Abdi agreed to integration with Damascus after government forces captured significant territory from terrorist PKK/YPG-led forces during clashes and as Washington strengthened relations with the new Syrian leadership.
In another major step, Syria’s Education Ministry authorized Kurdish-language instruction in public and private schools Thursday in areas where Kurdish citizens constitute a significant share of the population.
The decision allows Kurdish to be taught alongside Arabic and English.
It follows an earlier decree by al-Sharaa recognizing Kurdish as a national language and affirming the national rights of Syria’s Kurdish population, a major policy shift in a country where Kurds have long complained of discrimination.
Abdi said last week that the integration of the Kurdish administration into the Syrian state had been completed but pledged to continue efforts to secure Kurdish rights in the country’s new constitution.
Syria’s Kurdish population is estimated at around 2 million out of roughly 20 million people, with communities concentrated mainly in the northeast as well as in Damascus and Aleppo.

ICE deports Venezuelan father from Texas to West Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

ICE deports Venezuelan father from Texas to West Africa: A situation "I don't wish on anybody"
A 35-year-old Venezuelan man who lived in Texas for years is now nearly 6,000 miles from his wife and 5-month-old American son after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported him to West Africa.
Carlos Tellez Sanchez said he had never heard of Liberia until last week, when he found out he was being deported to the country that sits between Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire just hours before his flight took off. He said he spent the 15-hour flight across the Atlantic in handcuffs, and is now stranded in a remote area of the West African nation.
"I do not understand how a country that considers itself a global hero can act this way towards a human being," he told CBS News in Spanish over a video call.
Tellez Sanchez said he now spends much of his time inside a hotel more than an hour away from Monrovia, Liberia's capital, where he was placed alongside deportees from Brazil, Colombia, Honduras and other countries.
President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration has intensified this summer, with ICE making a record number of arrests. Increasingly, some detainees are being sent to countries that are not their own and banished to far-flung places. Tellez Sanchez, who entered the U.S. illegally five years ago, is one of them.
The Venezuela native had been in the U.S. since 2021 after fleeing his home country. He worked at a car dealership in Dallas during the day and drove for Uber Eats at night to support his family. CBS News could not find any criminal charges or convictions for Tellez Sanchez, beyond civil immigration violations.
In December 2025, Tellez Sanchez was detained by ICE during what he expected would be a routine immigration appointment. He spent eight months in ICE detention centers before his deportation to Africa.
An immigration judge in 2021 granted Tellez Sanchez protection from being sent back to Venezuela, finding that he could be persecuted there. Legally, however, that order did not prevent ICE from deporting him to any other country.
Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration has brokered so-called "third country" deportation agreements with dozens of nations around the world, including some notoriously dangerous places like South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Tellez Sanchez' brother in Dallas, Juan Tellez, said he has no idea why Tellez Sanchez was sent to Liberia and that no one has given him an explanation. He described his brother as a good person and a hard worker who "doesn't deserve what happened to him."
The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to CBS News' questions about Tellez Sanchez' case, including why Liberia was chosen as his country of deportation.
In Liberia, Tellez Sanchez says he has no clear plan.
"It's a very difficult situation," he said, "one that I don't wish on anybody."

In Germany, grapes are being harvested record-early due to the heat: the harvest is expected to be smaller

Unknown Publisher

In Germany, grapes are being harvested record-early due to the heat: the harvest is expected to be smaller
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the hot summer, grapes in Germany ripened several weeks earlier. The drought could reduce the harvest by 30% and make the wine stronger.
In Germany, winegrowers have begun harvesting grapes unusually early—earlier than ever since regular observations began. The reason is a long and hot summer: the grapes ripened several weeks earlier than usual, UNN reports, citing DW.
"Some winegrowers even had to interrupt their vacations because of this," Ernst Büscher, a representative of the German Wine Institute, told Tagesschau on the ARD television channel.
Just a few decades ago, September was the main month for harvesting grapes. Now the timing is constantly shifting. Winegrower Simon Schreiber recalls: "When I began my training in 2010, the harvest took place in the middle or at the end of September. And now it is in mid-August!"
The heat is changing not only the winegrowers' calendar but also the wine itself. The more sun, the more sugar accumulates in the grapes, making the wine stronger. And that is not exactly what the market wants at present: buyers are increasingly choosing lighter wines with lower alcohol content. In addition, intense heat can cause grapes to lose some of the acidity characteristic of German wines.
Nevertheless, winegrowers hope that the 2026 harvest will be good in terms of quality. However, there will most likely be noticeably fewer grapes. Due to the drought, the berries remained small in many regions. Winegrower Johannes Kopp from Sinsheim says that his farm expects around 30% fewer grapes than usual.
This is particularly unpleasant for the industry: winegrowers' costs are rising, while buyers are not prepared to pay much more for a bottle. According to ARD, five euros remains a psychological threshold for many supermarket shoppers. Thus, the current season has turned out to be paradoxical: the grapes ripened record early—but there may be less wine itself.

Germany news: Baltic summit plans hybrid-threat task force
Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026
What you need to know
This blog is now closed. Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 28, 2026:
- Baltic interior ministers meeting in Germany have agreed on a task force to deal with hybrid threats
- The AfD in Thuringia has failed to win a no-confidence vote in the state premier
- Germany's Green Party has warned gas storage levels are far too low
- Germany has seen its earliest-ever grape harvest after an exceptionally hot summer
- Germany's president has paid tribute to Norway's late King Harald

Dobrindt: Security task force and enhanced drone defense agreed at Baltic summit
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that Baltic and European leaders at a special hybrid security meeting agreed to plans to set up a new security task force and to enhance collective drone defense capabilities.
The assembled politicians discussed "urgent security policy questions for a shared future in the Baltic Sea region," Dobrindt said amid the meeting at the Mürwik naval training center in Flensburg on Germany's northeast coast
"Foreign powers are trying to attack our security with hybrid measures, to destabilize our democracies, to weaken our economy," he said. "Drone attacks, cyber attacks, spying, disinformation, arson attacks on critical infrastructure, covert operations and the use of 'disposable agents' are all rapidly increasing in number."
Dobrindt warned that the recent past had shown a pronounced increase in the "quality and intensity" of such attacks and surmised that "we must prepare ourselves for the hybrid threat situation continuing to intensify."
He said the shared goal was to bolster defense against such hybrid threats.
"We want to investigate, deter and defend altogether more quickly," Dobrindt said, saying they wanted to work together to transform the Balitc from a "collective risk area" into a "collective defensive area."
The assembled politicians from Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, Norway and Ireland — the current holder of the rotating EU presidency — had a working lunch at the Mürwik base amid the talks.
They were also taken out on the Baltic Sea in a German Federal Police motorboat.
Germany will stick to 'Lake Ontario' despite Trump's 'Lake America' renaming
Germany intends to continue referring to the body of water between the US and Canada as Lake Ontario, despite US President Donald Trump's decision to rename it as "Lake America" amid his growing rift with Canada.
"This is an American decision to refer to this lake by a different name. For the time being, it has no further implications for other countries," said a spokesman for the German Foreign Ministry on Friday. "As far as we are concerned, it remains Lake Ontario, which is the customary name."
The spokesman went on to argue that "in the US, football is called 'soccer,' but that doesn't mean it's called 'soccer' in other countries as well."
When asked whether the decision could culminate in fresh Trump resentment toward Berlin, the spokesman said that naming of waterways "should not be a reason to harbour political resentment toward anyone."
Earlier this year, Trump and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz engaged in a public rift after the German leader said the US was being "humiliated" at the negotiating table with Iran amid the war. Trump then announced a reduction in the number of US troops in Germany.

Berlin mayor: Hackers trying to blackmail city hall after data breach
Berlin's Mayor Kai Wegner says the city-state's government is being blackmailed by hackers who breached several sectors of its administration earlier in this month.
"Berlin has become a victim of a serious crime," Wegner said, albeit adding that the state "will not allow itself to be blackmailed."
German news magazine Spiegel reports that the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin or just over €2 million (roughly $2.3 million).
As a result of the cyber attack, departments like city planning, construction, housing, mobility, transportation and environment and climate protection were all isolated from the state government network for around a week, starting on August 14.
Among other things, it meant that it was not possible to apply for or pay out housing benefits for several days.
At first, officials said they did not believe sensitive data had been captured. Then on Wednesday of this week, the state government said it was possible that personalized or non-public information might be affected.
According to Spiegel, a ransomware group known as Rhysida is claiming responsibility in a post on the dark web, saying it had secured some 6 terabytes of data and putting a countdown to the time of its publication alongside a demand for 30 bitcoin.
Rhysida gained notoriety in 2023 when it hacked the online information systems of the British Library and published leaked material when it was not paid the bitcoin ransom it demanded.
Finance Minister Klingbeil calls on Trump to end 'irresponsible' Iran war
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is the guest on this Friday's "Interview der Woche" political podcast by public broadcaster ARD.
Much of the interview revolves around domestic policies directly in Klingbeil's ministerial wheelhouse, like the sugar tax, planned income tax reforms, and Germany's difficult economic situation more generally.
But when the discussion turned to fuel prices in Germany, which are nearing their all-time highs from much earlier in the year once again, the Social Democrat (SPD) leader Klingbeil wasted no time in pointing to the external factors in play.
"First of all you have to say that this is the fault of Donald Trump, who started this irresponsible war in Iran," Klingbeil said. "These are the effects, which people are now feeling at the fuel pumps. Therefore the most important thing — and I will be in the US next week for the G20 finance ministers' summit — and the most important message to the US is: Bring this war to an end. That's the first point."
Klingbeil said that the second issue should be to address oil companies "profiteering" as a result of the unrest in Iran and the Gulf, arguing that consumer prices were not a fair reflection of the oil prices or economic fundamentals.
He said he wanted the question of windfall taxes on oil companies to once again be discussed at an EU level.
"The oil companies are making gains on the back of this geopolitical situation," Klingbeil said. "They are filling their pockets and that needs to be stopped, which is why I'm lobbying for the windfall tax and am saying that the proceeds that are raised should be redirected to consumers — which could be achieved by reducing fuel prices."
For a two-month period, Germany dipped its taxes on gasoline and diesel to try to relieve the pressure on prices at the pumps. But this measure expired without renewal in July and prices have since returned close to their highest-ever levels, from earlier in the year. Other smaller factors like the low water levels on the River Rhine impacting freight transport have also played a more minor role in driving up prices in some parts of the country.

Germany risks missing 2026 climate target
Germany is on course to miss its legally binding climate target this year, according to preliminary calculations by the Agora Energiewende think tank.
Greenhouse gas emissions fell by only around 7 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent in the first half of 2026, a decline of about 2% compared with the same period last year.
Agora estimates that Germany will emit around 635 million tons of CO2 equivalent over the full year. That would exceed the country's 2026 limit of 625 million tons.
Germany emitted 648.9 million tons in 2025.
Agora said the decline so far this year was driven largely by weak economic activity and high fossil fuel prices rather than structural progress on cutting emissions.
The think tank said the energy price shock triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had pushed up oil and gas prices and contributed to lower fossil fuel use.
Germany is required to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 65% from 1990 levels by 2030, equivalent to annual emissions of no more than 439 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent.
Agora said meeting that goal would require emissions to fall by an average of around 40 million tonnes a year.

German unemployment remains above 3 million
The number of unemployed people in Germany remained above three million in August despite signs of an improving economy, official figures showed on Friday.
Germany's Federal Employment Agency said 3.061 million people were unemployed, 54,000 more than in July and 36,000 more than a year earlier.
The unemployment rate rose to 6.5% from 6.4% in July.
Adjusted for seasonal effects, unemployment increased by 4,000.
"Even in August, there is little momentum in the labor market beyond the usual seasonal pattern," Federal Employment Agency head Andrea Nahles said, adding that the subdued trend of recent months was continuing.
Unemployment first climbed back above three million in July. Joblessness typically rises during the summer, while Germany's weak economy has also weighed on employment.
There have recently been signs that the economic outlook is improving. The Ifo business climate index rose for a fourth consecutive month in August to its highest level in a year, while German exporters have also become more optimistic.
Germany sees earliest-ever start to grape harvest
Germany's grape harvest has begun earlier than ever recorded following an exceptionally hot summer, according to the German Wine Institute.
"It was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions," institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. "Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays for it."
The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also the first grapes destined for premium wines.
Harvesting is expected to begin "on a large scale" next week.
Büscher said the main harvest was starting one to two weeks earlier than in recent years, which was already earlier than it was decades ago.
"Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it's certainly four weeks earlier," he said.
The harvest could be completed as early as September because many grape varieties are ripening at roughly the same time.
"This will be a very fast harvest," Büscher said.
Growers are also picking grapes early to prevent sugar levels from becoming too high. More sugar generally produces wines with a higher alcohol content, while demand is increasingly for lighter wines with less alcohol.
Prolonged heat can also reduce the fruit acidity characteristic of many German wines.

Protect fossils from hammer-wielding tourists | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:31:20 UTC
00:31:20 KST

I write this while sitting on Charmouth beach in Dorset with my required reading of the Saturday Guardian, as I do regularly. Your editorial (The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status, 21 August) produced a hollow laugh as – this being the centre of fossil hunting on the Jurassic Coast – I am surrounded by armies of hammer-wielding tourists busy smashing the daylights out of any rock available around them. The vast majority have no idea which stone types are likely to bear fossils and don’t report any finds even if they are lucky. Others take carrier bags full of stones back to their cars.
Thus, we have no idea what fossils are being lost to the record every single day here, and so I completely support the suggestion of giving them legal protection. Of course, amateur collecting has a valuable place in unearthing important fossil finds, but only if they are shared and documented. The Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre valiantly tries to educate and inform visitors, but sadly these will inevitably be the minority.
Charmouth is a key part of the designated Jurassic Coast world heritage site, but I can’t think of any others where visitors are allowed, or even encouraged, to bring or rent hammers to wreck the protected features and/or remove them from the site unrecorded. If we want to protect our fossil heritage for future generations to study, we could make a start by regulating this geological vandalism. 
Jill White
Musbury, Devon

There is no proof that this video shows a plane crash in Tel Aviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:31:19 UTC
00:31:19 KST

There is no proof that this video shows a plane crash in Tel Aviv
A video showing an airplane rammed into the side of a building has been circulating widely on social media. While social media users are claiming that the video shows a plane that crashed in Tel Aviv after an Iranian attack, its origin remains unknown and its authenticity highly questionable.
A video that has gone viral on X is said to show a plane crash in Tel Aviv, Israel, after an attack carried out by Iran. The footage, which has garnered more than five million views, was published on August 26 by a fake account pretending to belong to Donald Trump Jr. It is not, however, the official account of US President Donald Trump’s son.
The video shows a plane crashed into the side of a building. The person filming the scene speaks in Russian, saying: “Just now, a plane crashed into a building. Look, it’s stuck there. It’s a huge passenger jet; the windows shattered. My god, this is really happening. I don’t know how long it will hold.”
According to the posts featuring the video, the footage was filmed in Tel Aviv and shows the aftermath of an Iranian attack. However, there is no proof that such an attack actually took place.
No sign of a crash in Tel Aviv
It turns out, this video was already posted online back in March 2026 by the pro-Iranian account Asif Ali. This is the first clue that the video might not be authentic. When we carried out an online search using the keywords “plane crash Tel Aviv”, we couldn’t find a single article about the type of crash shown in the video. No reliable media outlets reported on this crash in August 2026 or when the video was first posted online back in March 2026. When we ran a screengrab of the footage through a reverse image search (check out our handy guide here), we saw that the video hadn’t been shared by any reliable media outlets.
The official X accounts run by the Israeli authorities as well as the city of Tel Aviv also didn’t share anything about a plane crash like the one shown in this footage at any point in 2026 or in previous years.
A video likely generated by AI
The exact origin of this video is difficult to establish. It was also shared back in April 2026 with the same description, but, once again, no trustworthy source was able to confirm its origin.
There are several visual and sonic clues that the video was generated by artificial intelligence.
First of all, there is a crowd of observers gathered in an extremely questionable security area, which seems to have been marked by the authorities using yellow tape. It is directly below part of the plane that seems like it could collapse at any minute and doesn’t align with the security measures usually taken when this type of accident occurs.
Next, if you compare this fire truck to the vehicles used by fire services in Tel Aviv, it is quite different. It doesn’t have the yellow stripes you usually see on fire trucks in Tel Aviv.
Finally, there are no logos or any other distinctive elements on the plane that would help us determine what company it belongs to. This clue, along with the others we identified, suggests that the video was created by artificial intelligence.
When we ran the video through Hiya, a tool for detecting audio produced by AI, it concluded that it was 99% likely that the video’s sound was generated by artificial intelligence.
The latest strikes against Israel were reported on June 7, 2026, when several Iranian missiles were fired towards Israel for the first time since the ceasefire. There is no proof of a link between the video and a new strike on Tel Aviv.

Shells, stalled contracts, and no armor for wounded — Ukraine's new defense minister's problem list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:30:54 UTC
00:30:54 KST

Shells, stalled contracts, and no armor for wounded — Ukraine's new defense minister's problem list
Yevhen Khmara in Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 18, 2026. (Roman Pilipey / AFP / Getty Images)
Bohdan Miroshnychenko
Editor-in-chief of Oboronka
Weapons production in Ukraine has a mountain of problems: short contracts, scandals over ammunition and other complex equipment procurement, inefficient drone purchasing, leaky quality control and oversight of manufacturers' capabilities, export rules that don't work, funding shortages, and more.
All of this ultimately adds up to poor supply for troops at the front.
Neither the dismissed minister Mykhailo Fedorov nor any other "six-month defense minister" has come even close to solving these problems.
To be fair, the task is extraordinarily difficult.
To carry out deep reforms, the head of the Defense Ministry needs not just good ideas and a mandate from President Volodymyr Zelensky, but also the ability to strike a delicate balance among military command, the Presidential Office, members of parliament, the National Security and Defense Council, arms associations, international partners — and to fight off certain corrupt groups with powerful media and political lobbying behind them.
Partly through his own mistakes, partly through resistance from the system, and partly simply for lack of time in office, Fedorov failed to resolve all the industry's long-standing problems — so that burden now passes to his successor, Yevhen Khmara.
Khmara is taking over the Defense Ministry at an extremely tense moment.
Arms companies are anxious over delayed contracting, troops are waiting for clarity on shell, drone, and vehicle deliveries for the second half of the year, and international transfers of weapons and technology for export have been blocked by a poorly written regulation.
Ahead lies the possibility of a new wave of mobilization in Russia — meaning the system needs to run smoothly, with or without Fedorov.
A few chronic problems are particularly prominent. Firstly, public tenders are nearly derailed.
Shifting weapons procurement onto a tender-based system was arguably the previous Defense Ministry's signature reform in the arms sector, since Fedorov's team decided to roll it out much more broadly than it had ever been before. How does it work?
Right now, procurement most often happens "by name" — meaning the General Staff names a specific drone from a specific manufacturer that needs to be bought, and the Defense Procurement Agency (DPA) contracts for it. This approach is efficient in terms of speed, but it creates corruption risks and kills competition.
Under the tender system, military command would provide only technical specifications, while the Defense Ministry would independently seek contractors. This was meant to drive down prices and improve transparency for international partners, who are pouring billions of dollars into Ukrainian weapons production.
It was expected that the Defense Ministry would start large-scale contracting under the tender system as early as summer, but the technical specifications for these purchases were delayed.
By mid-August, only a very small share of the specs had actually been delivered to the Agency. That's what pushed the associations to go public with a warning about a possible breakdown in weapons supply by the end of 2026.
It turned out to be less dramatic than the associations feared. In reality, arms contracting never stopped — not even for a week — and continues to this day. The Ministry kept signing contracts under the old procedure while the new one wasn't yet up and running.
At the same time, part of the funding is left hanging. Babel reports that the Defense Ministry is currently operating with funds from a European loan, which means partners have certain transparency requirements regarding how the funds are allocated. So the tenders still need to get up and running as quickly as possible, regardless.
Secondly, even though drones undeniably dominate the battlefield and have largely replaced artillery in many respects, heavy howitzers still remain irreplaceable in plenty of combat situations: bad flying weather, strikes on massed troops or fortified positions, breaking up assaults or infiltration through tree lines, the need to hit a target quickly, suppressive fire, and so on.
Meanwhile, enemy drones are reaching further and further. In some areas, the kill zone already extends to 20 km (about 12,4 miles), while a standard 155mm shell only reaches 14 km (8,7 miles).
It's become clear that artillery needs to shift to longer-range shells.
In 2026, Fedorov gave total priority to 30+ km (18,6+ miles) long-range shells, as he repeatedly stated publicly. What's the risk here? There are dozens of different 155mm shell types, ranging from the "short" M107 (14-18 km) to extended-range rounds like the HE ER-BT (35 km) — and the longer a shell's range, the scarcer it is on the global market, since propellant charges worldwide are contracted years in advance.
The problem of short contracts isn't new, and no defense minister has managed to solve it.
This hurts not only shell manufacturers but producers of any complex weapon with a long production cycle, since efficient production now requires contracts of at least 12-18 months. The Ministry previously reported introducing long-term contracting, but in practice, it doesn't work — manufacturers still end up investing their own profits into ordering components in advance, with no certainty anyone will buy the finished product.
A similar gap exists in medical evacuation.
The state has contracted tens of thousands of ground robotic systems (GRS) but has barely signed any new contracts for armored vehicles — even though evacuating the wounded requires both working in tandem: the robot crosses the most dangerous stretch, then an armored vehicle quickly picks the soldier up.
Finally, there's the failed export push. Ukrainian arms manufacturers' capacity is running barely half-loaded, so defense companies are asking for weapons exports to be opened up, so they can earn money on the global market and reinvest it into product and production development, along with technology transfer, so they can set up companies abroad, secure new partnerships, and attract more Western funding.
This is especially pressing given the shortage of state orders and the need to develop technology faster than the Russians.
Politically, the question has already been settled — the president made clear a year ago that exports need to be opened up.
But various centers of power still haven't agreed on a concrete mechanism, and who's actually responsible is unclear: the Defense Ministry, the Economy Ministry, the National Security and Defense Council, or individual strategic advisers in the Presidential Office with murky authority.
The rules have changed at least twice since then, and neither version has worked properly, while Ukraine's niche on the global market is gradually being taken over by Western companies.
A vivid example is the "Ukrspecsystems" plant in Britain, whose opening was announced at the level of an international delegation and the ambassador — everyone assumes it's operating — but it still can't start work because it hasn't obtained permission for technology transfer.
All the problems mentioned above can be summed up in a single sentence: the absence of a state strategy for the defense-industrial complex.
As things stand, there's no institutional clarity in Ukraine over who exactly should be thinking about the chronic problems in weapons production and pushing for their resolution at every level of government.

There can be huge comfort in end-of-life preparation | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

00:30:06 KST

Sarah Phillips’ article struck such a chord (What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over work, 13 August). My husband, Dick, died last month with pulmonary fibrosis. His last few months were physically very difficult, but he gained an enormous amount of comfort from sorting out his affairs; he said it was so that the family wouldn’t have a mess to sort out when he had gone.
He changed everything into my name and prepared lists of passwords for our three sons. He passed on his watch to our grandson and his rings to our sons. To do this himself gave him tremendous pleasure.
Dick regarded himself as very lucky to have had 80 years largely free of illness, and he spent his last three years, when he had a terminal diagnosis, making sure that those left behind would be able to manage without him.

Slovak Police Foil Possible Napalm Attack on Factory Producing Drones for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:29:00 UTC
00:29:00 KST

Reported by
Officers from ÚBOK—Slovakia’s Office for the Fight Against Organized Crime—thwarted a potential arson attack on the Skyeton factory near Prešov, which manufactures unmanned systems for the Ukrainian military, police announced earlier this week.
The Ukrainian company's Raybird-3 drones can stay airborne for up to 28 hours and travel up to 2,500 kilometers, operating deep behind enemy lines.
Had the attack succeeded, police said, it would have risked a large-scale fire, endangered the roughly 70 employees who could have been on site, and caused damage worth tens of millions of dollars.
The Slovak Information Service and Military Intelligence played a key role in uncovering the plot, providing information that prompted ÚBOK to launch an intensive investigation. Police identified the perpetrators before the attack could take place and seized a large quantity of incendiary mixture—identified by the Police Force's Institute of Forensic Science as a blend of gasoline and polystyrene commonly known as napalm—along with tools, a mobile phone, an action camera and a hand-drawn plan of the attack.
Three foreign nationals were charged with preparing an especially serious crime of general endangerment, committed as accomplices for hire. Two were detained in Slovakia. German authorities arrested the third under a European arrest warrant issued in an exceptionally short time. Their identities and nationalities have not been made public yet.
When asked for comment, Román Hájek, a spokesperson for the Police Force Presidium, said investigators moved quickly once the tip came in, launching an immediate operational search effort that allowed them to identify those involved before any damage was done. He said officers from the regional police directorate in Prešov also provided significant support during the operation.
"Thanks to the timely intervention of police, no one was injured, and no property damage occurred," Hájek said. He added that the investigation is ongoing and that a change in the case's legal classification has not been ruled out.
In comments to Ukrainian media Skyeton accused Russia of orchestrating the sabotage, noting that Moscow regularly targets the company's domestic facilities as well as its reputation.
"The recent attempted attack on our facility in Slovakia is further proof that Ukrainian defense manufacturers have become a real thorn in their side, and that we are on the right path," the company said.
The case lands amid heightened concern across Europe over sabotage targeting firms tied to Ukraine's defense supply chain, with security officials increasingly describing such plots—often involving foreign nationals recruited for hire—as part of a broader pattern of hybrid attacks reaching well beyond the war's front lines.

Four men plead guilty to London arson attack that destroyed Jewish charity ambulances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:27:04 UTC
00:27:04 KST

Four ambulances run by the Hatzola charity were destroyed in a London neighbourhood home to a significant Jewish population, one of a spate of attacks in the British capital targeting Jewish or Israel-linked locations.
Four men admitted on Friday being behind an arson attack on London ambulances owned by a Jewish charity at a UK court hearing.
British nationals Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, 18, and British-Pakistani Saif Ali, 18, all pleaded guilty to criminal damage linked to the 23 March attack.
Four ambulances run by the Hatzola charity were destroyed in the London neighbourhood of Golders Green that is home to a significant Jewish population, one of a spate of attacks in the British capital targeting Jewish or Israel-linked locations.
Three of the men set fire to the ambulances, while the fourth waited in a getaway car.
The vehicles were parked near a synagogue, and the damage was valued at £1 million (€1.1 million).
Iqbal, Khan and Atshatshi entered their pleas by video link, while Ali, wearing a white shirt, was present in the dock at London's Old Bailey central criminal court.
At a previous hearing, prosecution lawyer Emma Harraway told the court there was strong evidence this was "a premeditated and targeted attack against the Jewish community."
Several antisemitic attacks in London this year targeted synagogues and other Jewish sites.
An Iran-linked group known as Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyah (HAYI) had previously claimed multiple attacks, including the destruction of the ambulances.
The UK government has announced plans to ban HAYI, also known as the Islamic Movement of Companions of the Right, as a national security threat.
Defence lawyers denied the four defendants had any "terrorism" connections to groups proscribed in the UK.
The men were remanded in custody and are expected to be sentenced in spring 2027.
A fifth defendant, Subhan Ahmed, 18, pleaded not guilty to assisting an offender and is due to go on trial at the Old Bailey in January.

Nearly 2,000 missing in Nepal floods as death toll reaches 584
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:25:03 EEST
00:25:03 KST

At least 584 people have died after the Nepal-Tibet flash floods, while nearly 2,000 remain missing in Nepal and hundreds more are unaccounted for in Tibet, according to the latest official figures.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 579 people had died in the country and 1,924 remained missing. Chinese state media have reported five deaths and 558 missing in Tibet.
The missing in Nepal include 517 foreign nationals. Around 4,000 people have been rescued and 15,000 security personnel have been deployed, according to Nepalese authorities.
A Finnish woman remains among those missing. Helsingin Sanomat exclusively reported, citing her spouse, that she works as a postdoctoral researcher at a Finnish university and has lived in Finland for about 10 years.
Finland’s ambassador to Nepal, Petri Puhakka, told HS that the last official sighting of the woman was at the Gyirong border crossing shortly before the flood wave struck the site.
She was travelling with a pilgrimage group organised by the Isha Foundation after a visit to Mount Kailash. The foundation told HS that one Finnish citizen was among a group of about 80 people who remain missing.
The flood began after part of a glacier collapsed near Mount Langtang Lirung on Wednesday, sending ice, rock, mud and water into river systems flowing towards Nepal.
Rescue work was halted for several hours on Friday after a barrier lake created by landslide debris began overflowing. Operations later resumed after authorities judged the immediate risk to be manageable, Reuters reported.
Chinese officials said the rescue had entered a “critical stage”, while Nepalese and Chinese authorities continued to monitor the lake and other hazards.
Nepalese meteorological officials are also examining two nearby glaciers after images appeared to show cracks, the BBC reported. Officials said the cracks do not necessarily indicate an imminent collapse, though both glaciers feed into the same river system affected by Wednesday’s disaster.
Access remains difficult in several areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed. Helicopters are being used to reach settlements cut off by mud and flood damage.
More than 90,000 people are estimated to have been affected, according to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
The Finnish Red Cross announced €500,000 from its disaster relief fund for the IFRC operation in Nepal. The money will support emergency shelter, healthcare, clean water, sanitation, cash assistance and efforts to reunite separated families.
Marko Korhonen, head of international disaster relief at the Finnish Red Cross, said restoring links to isolated communities was essential for delivering aid and helping families obtain information about missing relatives.
