Feature: Five years on, Afghanistan still bears scars of war
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
23:08:27 CST
00:08:27 KST

KABUL, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- An infant, still hungry and unaware that his mother had been killed, reached for her breast after a U.S. overnight bombardment in Bala Buluk district of Afghanistan's western Farah province in 2009.
The haunting scene is described in the newly released English edition of a book by Muhajer Farahi, Afghanistan's deputy minister for publications at the Ministry of Information and Culture, as Afghanistan approaches Aug. 31 -- five years since the last U.S. troops left the country, bringing America's longest war to an end.
The English edition, titled Memories of Jihad: Twenty Years in Occupation, looks back at the two decades of U.S.-led military presence through the eyes of Farahi, chronicling what he describes as years of bombardment, civilian casualties, displacement, destruction, detention and torture.
Five years after the withdrawal, for many Afghans, the scars of war remain.
Farahi said he wrote the book to document what he describes as the realities of the U.S. military presence and its far-reaching consequences for Afghan society.
"The Americans committed widespread acts of violence and atrocities over the past 20 years, from 2001 to 2021. They bombed villages, wedding ceremonies, funerals, religious schools and educational institutions," Farahi told Xinhua.
"They left behind enormous devastation, mostly in remote areas and rural communities. Hundreds of thousands of our compatriots were killed, imprisoned and tortured," he said. "Civilians suffered extensive losses and hardship, and people were displaced from their homes."
Farahi also challenges portrayals of the two-decade U.S. presence that emphasize development assistance and reconstruction projects undertaken during those years while overlooking what he sees as Afghanistan's continued dependence on external support.
"Instead of teaching our people how to catch fish, they preferred to keep providing them with ready-caught fish under their own control," Farahi said.
For many Afghan families, however, memories of those two decades are rooted not in debates over the legacy of the war, but in the loss of loved ones.
Haji Sharif Khan, a resident of Hesarak district in eastern Nangarhar province, still remembers the night in 2019 when his brother, Dr. Nazar Gul, and 12 others from two related households were killed in a U.S. bombing.
Khan said the attack came from multiple directions and continued for hours.
"About six planes came for bombardment from three sides, which continued for over three hours. M4 ammunition, helicopters, jets and even B-52 aircraft were included in this attack," Khan said.
For Khan, the loss was not an isolated tragedy but part of what he sees as a broader pattern of suffering inflicted on Afghan communities during the U.S. military presence.
"The United States had oppressed the whole land of Afghanistan with its plans and programs," he said.
For Miro, another resident of Nangarhar, the ordeal did not end when the bombardment stopped and ground operations ceased.
He recalled that civilians were afraid to approach the scene, help the wounded or pull people from the ruins, fearing that anyone who ventured outside could become another target.
"No one could help anyone. If you went out to help, you would also be targeted," Miro told Xinhua.
Beyond airstrikes and ground operations, the detention of Afghans on various grounds and their confinement in U.S.-run facilities became another deeply contentious chapter of the two-decade war. Thousands of Afghans were held at U.S. military bases in Afghanistan, including Bagram and Kandahar, while some were transferred to the Guantanamo Bay detention facility.
For Khan Mohammad, that chapter remains deeply personal.
The former detainee said he spent nearly two decades in U.S. custody despite maintaining that he had committed no crime.
"They accused me of orchestrating a major conspiracy to attack Jalalabad airport and kill many Americans," Khan told Xinhua. "But I did nothing. I completely denied the allegations."
U.S. troops detained Khan in Jalalabad, the capital of Nangarhar province, in 2006. He was subsequently transferred to Bagram and later to the United States, where he was sentenced to life imprisonment.
Recalling the journey from Afghanistan to the United States, Khan said he was deprived of his senses for much of the trip.
"In Bagram, I was like the other prisoners. Then they transferred me to the United States. The journey was terrifying. They tied my hands and feet, blindfolded me and blocked my ears. The distance was long, and I was in pain the whole time," he said.
After being sent to Washington, D.C., for further interrogation, Khan was imprisoned in California following a court judgment. He was released in January 2025 and returned to Afghanistan as part of a prisoner exchange between the United States and the Afghan interim government.
His release ended nearly two decades in U.S. custody, but the experience, he said, had irrevocably changed the course of his life.
The scars left by the war were compounded by the chaotic final days of the U.S. military withdrawal in August 2021.
Among the Afghans who lost their lives during those days was Zaki Anwari, a 17-year-old promising football player who fell to his death after clinging to a U.S. military aircraft as it took off from Kabul International Airport.
For the Anwari family, the pain of Zaki's death has not faded with time.
His brother, Haji Zakaria, still struggles to contain his grief whenever he sees Zaki's belongings -- his jerseys, boots and football equipment, reminders of the young man's dreams.
"That black day was unbearably painful for us. Regrettably, those harrowing memories are etched into our souls, and we shall carry them to the end of our days," Zakaria said.
On Aug. 26, 2021, amid the final days of the U.S. military withdrawal, a suicide bombing claimed by the Islamic State near the gates of Kabul International Airport killed at least 170 Afghan civilians and 13 U.S. service members.
Two decades of U.S.-led military intervention left Afghanistan scarred by death, destruction and enduring trauma. Night raids, airstrikes and military operations in civilian areas claimed numerous lives, while hospitals, schools, wedding ceremonies and other civilian gatherings were also caught in the violence.
For many Afghan families, the loss of loved ones remains an open wound. Nor did Afghanistan's hardships end with the departure of U.S. troops.
Following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, about 7 billion U.S. dollars in assets belonging to Afghanistan's central bank were frozen by the United States. Sanctions, financial restrictions and declining development assistance added further pressure to an already fragile economy.
Unemployment and poverty rose, food insecurity worsened and development projects stalled, pushing millions of Afghans deeper into hardship.
Five years after the last U.S. troops left Afghanistan, the country continues to live with the consequences of two decades of war.
For millions of Afghans, memories of lost relatives, destroyed homes and years of displacement and hardship have yet to fade, while economic deprivation remains another enduring legacy of a war whose scars Afghanistan still bears today. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: How the mudslide along China-Nepal border happened?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
23:08:21 CST
00:08:21 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- A massive mudslide that devastated the China-Nepal border region was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, experts said, warning that such glacial disasters are becoming more frequent and severe amid global warming.
The mudslide struck Gyirong Port, a major China-Nepal land border crossing in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, on Wednesday morning. As of 3 p.m. Friday, five people had been confirmed dead and 558 others remained missing, according to the latest official statistics.
According to Xinhua reporters at the scene, the silt layer in the core disaster area has reached a depth of over 1.5 meters, posing a high risk of entrapment and adding challenges to the rescue efforts.
THE TRIGGER: A GLACIER COLLAPSE
Satellite imagery and analysis by Chinese geological experts suggest that a high-altitude glacier collapsed in Nepal, triggering the devastating mudslide.
A comparison of satellite images showed that a glacier at an elevation of 5,200 to 5,400 meters had fractured and dragged rock debris along with it, forming a glacial debris flow, said Kang Shichang, director of the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS).
The event presents a classic disaster cascading effect, said Yao Tandong, an academician of the CAS and leader of China's second Qinghai-Tibet Plateau scientific expedition.
According to the experts, after the glacier collapsed, it was not just ice that came down. Vast amounts of ice and rock debris plunged down a mountain river channel, gathering mass and momentum as it moved downstream.
"The further downstream it traveled, the more destructive its force became and the more pronounced the secondary risks grew," Yao said.
"Precisely speaking, this is a chain disaster formed through continuous evolution from a high-altitude ice avalanche to a high-speed debris flow and a mudslide," said Guo Zhaocheng, an expert with China's Ministry of Natural Resources.
WHY THE IMPACT WAS SO SEVERE
Ouyang Chaojun, an expert on mountain hazards and engineering safety at the CAS, summarized three main factors behind the catastrophe: the initial ice-rock avalanche's massive scale and high elevation; its rapid transformation into a fluid debris flow that maintained high speed and depth; and the concentration of local population and buildings on flat riverbanks, leaving people directly exposed to the flow.
According to current assessments, it might have taken only about seven minutes between the onset of the ice avalanche and the mudslide hitting the port, said Guo. Such a narrow window highlights the difficulty of detecting and issuing early warnings for high-altitude, long-distance chain disasters.
Rescuers said the mudslide hurtled downhill at high speed, with no natural obstacles to dissipate its kinetic energy, unleashing massive destructive power when it hit the port.
Guo cited estimates showing that the ice-avalanche debris flow traveled at a speed of about 50 meters per second, an extreme velocity that left people with virtually no time to react.
As an important channel for China-Nepal border trade and a national first-class land port, Gyirong Port normally sees bustling commercial activity, a dense population and extensive infrastructure.
The disaster struck during daytime working hours, when crowds of people were present at the port, a factor rescuers said further raised the risk of casualties.
BEHIND IT: WARMING CLIMATE
Apart from the Antarctic and the Arctic, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and its surrounding areas are the world's largest glacier-covered region, known as the "Third Pole" of Earth.
Similar ice avalanches occurred on the plateau in 2016 and in India's mountain regions in 2021. According to scientists, against the backdrop of global warming, glacial disasters on the "Third Pole" and its surrounding areas are becoming more frequent, more widespread and more destructive.
Glaciers are sensitive to temperature rise. Human-caused climate warming has been the primary driver of the widespread glacial retreat observed globally since the 1990s.
Kang said that continued glacier melting will destabilize the glaciers themselves, make them more sensitive to external disturbances, and increase the frequency and intensify the severity of glacial disasters and their cascading hazard chains.
Therefore, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and curbing global warming are the core of long-term glacier conservation, Kang said. ■

BISHKEK, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China and Kyrgyzstan are good neighbors connected by mountains and rivers and partners on the path toward development and prosperity, Chinese Ambassador to Kyrgyzstan Liu Jiangping has said in a recent interview with Xinhua.

China firmly supports Kyrgyzstan's efforts to safeguard national independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as its policies and measures aimed at ensuring political stability and promoting socioeconomic development. For its part, Kyrgyzstan firmly adheres to the one-China principle and firmly supports China's position on the Taiwan question and on issues related to Xinjiang, Xizang and Hong Kong.
"China and Kyrgyzstan, as good neighbors, wish each other well and have created a model of good-neighborliness, friendship and mutual assistance between our countries," Liu said.
Speaking about practical cooperation, the ambassador noted that China has long been Kyrgyzstan's largest trading partner, its largest source of imports, and its largest source of foreign investment. Last year, bilateral trade reached a record high of 27.2 billion U.S. dollars, up approximately 20 percent year on year. Trade between China and Kyrgyzstan accounted for a quarter of China's total trade with Central Asian countries.
"Kyrgyzstan was one of the first countries to support and actively participate in the Belt and Road Initiative. The high-quality Belt and Road cooperation of the two countries has yielded fruitful outcomes. Major cooperation projects, including the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and the Barskoon-Bedel highway, are advancing rapidly. The Bishkek road network reconstruction project, the new North-South Highway and the Datka-Kemin power transmission line have significantly improved Kyrgyzstan's infrastructure. Aid projects, including a hospital in Osh, have also been implemented, continuing to benefit the local population," Liu said.
Bilateral cooperation in clean energy, modern agriculture and digital economy also continues to expand, she said, adding that a waste-to-energy plant in Bishkek and a 100-MW solar power plant in the Chui region have begun supplying electricity to the grid, injecting new impetus into Kyrgyzstan's green transition.
The ambassador further said that people-to-people exchanges between the two countries in the fields of education, culture, healthcare and youth are constantly increasing. Chinese volunteer medical teams have provided free cataract surgeries and restored sight for over 1,400 cataract patients, and provided free medical care to nearly 20 children with congenital heart defects in Kyrgyzstan.
She also noted that four Confucius Institutes, established through the joint efforts of both sides, have become important platforms for Kyrgyz students to learn Chinese, while the Luban Workshop trains highly skilled technical professionals to contribute to Kyrgyzstan's development and construction. The Chinese Cultural Center in Bishkek has opened, while the large-scale cultural project Happy Chinese New Year in Bishkek has been widely welcomed. The two sides have also strengthened cooperation in joint archaeological research, mutual translations of literary works, mutual screenings of films and TV dramas, and cultural and artistic performances.
"In recent years, exchanges between people from all sectors of the two countries have reached unprecedented breadth and depth. The people of the two countries have been visiting each other frequently, like relatives, further strengthening the public support for China-Kyrgyzstan relations," the ambassador noted.
The continuous strengthening of cooperation between China and Kyrgyzstan under multilateral mechanisms contributes to improving global governance, she said. China and Kyrgyzstan hold similar positions on multiple major international and regional issues and have maintained close coordination and cooperation within frameworks such as the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), and the China-Central Asia Mechanism.
"China sincerely congratulates Kyrgyzstan on its election as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council. China fully supports Kyrgyzstan's work as the rotating chair of the SCO, and supports Kyrgyzstan in playing a greater role in international and regional affairs. Kyrgyzstan fully supports the concept of a community with a shared future for humanity and the four global initiatives proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping," she said.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO. "China and Kyrgyzstan, as founding countries of the SCO, have consistently been practitioners of the 'Shanghai Spirit' and important driving forces behind the SCO's development," Liu said, adding that over the past 25 years, China and Kyrgyzstan have closely cooperated within the SCO, safeguarding common interests and jointly promoting the development and strengthening of the organization.
"I am confident that under the strategic leadership of the two heads of state and the joint efforts of the peoples of China and Kyrgyzstan, the friendship between our countries will be passed down from generation to generation, China and Kyrgyzstan will certainly achieve joint development and prosperity, and the China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future awaits an even brighter future," she said. ■

Rescue operations underway as death toll from mudslide rises
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
23:08:06 CST
00:08:06 KST

Rescuers from the Chinese People's Liberation Army work in a mudslide-hit area near Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, in Xigaze, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Aug. 28, 2026. The death toll had risen to five and 558 remained missing as of 3 p.m. on Friday after a mudslide struck the Gyirong Port along the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, according to the region's emergency management department.
Rescuers are operating around the clock in mudslide-affected areas near the Gyirong Port. (Photo by Liu Yuqin/Xinhua)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- The death toll had risen to five and 558 remained missing as of 3 p.m. on Friday after a mudslide struck the Gyirong Port along the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, according to the region's emergency management department.
At about 4:30 p.m. on Friday, the first team of six members from the Xizang Fire and Rescue Corps and the first group of 15 members with a search dog from the Sichuan Fire and Rescue Corps arrived at the disaster-hit port. They were the first professional rescue teams to reach the core rescue area, the National Fire and Rescue Administration said.
As of 10 a.m. on Friday, a total of 681 fire and rescue personnel and 113 vehicles had arrived at the remote mountainous border area, while 6,612 pieces of rescue equipment and logistical supplies had been dispatched to the town of Gyirong, the administration noted.
According to border inspection authorities in Xizang, an emergency reinforcement team comprising 246 police personnel from Lhasa and Xigaze, the regional capital and the region's second-largest city, respectively, was immediately dispatched to Gyirong Town after Wednesday's deadly mudslide.
Among them were 190 police officers from Xigaze, who took with them more than 300 pieces of rescue equipment, including life detectors and manual breaking tools, to support on-site rescue operations.
A large amount of daily necessities, such as highland barley, rice, flour, drinking water, instant noodles, tents, folding beds, quilts, mattresses, blankets and raincoats have been delivered to the town, the region's emergency management department said.
China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, sent out a 15-member team on Friday equipped with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to conduct on-site surveys to provide accurate data aimed at boosting rescue efforts.
Rescuers on site say operations are extremely challenging due to looming secondary disasters, damaged road infrastructure and communications.
The meteorological department forecasts light to moderate rain or thunderstorms across most of Gyirong County from Wednesday night to Sunday. These downpours could trigger flash floods, mudslides and landslides in vulnerable areas, potentially disrupting rescue work.
The county authorities have also warned that a barrier lake, formed upstream of the port by the glacier collapse, sits in an unstable geological setting and could breach, endangering rescue operations downstream.
Local authorities said a road about three kilometers from the site was destroyed by the mudslide, delaying rescue access and slowing response efforts. Communications and power supply were also cut off, leaving the situation in the core area unknown for a time.
By Thursday afternoon, 499 people affected by the mudslide had been resettled and 555 stranded tourists had also been evacuated.
The mudslide was triggered by the collapse of glacier on the Nepalese side at a higher elevation, said Guo Zhaocheng, an expert with the Ministry of Natural Resources.
It is estimated to have traveled at about 50 meters per second, an extremely high speed leaving people with little time to react, while the affected area stretched more than 20 kilometers, resulting in severe losses, according to the expert. ■

Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital’s civilian supply chains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:07:45 UTC
00:07:45 KST

Russia has spent the past two days repeatedly attacking Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast with jet-powered drones, hitting commercial and logistics infrastructure and disrupting businesses and supply chains around the capital.
The attacks have struck civilian enterprises, food warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals, and warehouses storing books, according to Ukraine’s Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi. Fires have broken out at multiple warehouse sites, while repeated strikes have forced emergency crews to repeatedly stop their work and seek shelter.
The attacks are also affecting the movement and storage of essential goods around Kyiv, with damage to food warehouses and other logistics facilities contributing to supply disruptions and shortages.
Russia expands its aerial campaign against Kyiv
The latest wave comes after Russia dramatically ramped up its use of ballistic missiles against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent months. Now, improved Russian jet-powered drones are being used to sustain repeated attacks on the capital and surrounding oblast.
Russian forces have been launching the jet-powered drones at Ukrainian regions almost continuously for the previous two days.
The pattern has left Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast under prolonged air raid alerts while putting emergency crews under the threat of repeated strikes.
In Kyiv alone, air raid alerts were issued 13 times on 27 August and lasted for more than 14 hours in total.
Across Ukraine, Russian attacks killed 16 people and injured another 50 during the day, Vyhivskyi said.
38 attacks hit Kyiv Oblast
Kyiv Oblast has been among the hardest-hit areas. Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said on Friday morning the oblast had come under 38 Russian attacks since the first strike overnight on 27 August.
In Bucha district, firefighters worked at several locations where Russian drone strikes caused fires at warehouses and damaged vehicles.
At one site, a drone struck again while rescuers were working. After checking the area, emergency crews returned to the site and continued fighting the fire.
Firefighters also extinguished a fire involving 13 passenger cars. A nearby apartment building was damaged by the blast wave, which shattered windows.
At three locations, crews were still working to extinguish fires at warehouse buildings caused by the repeated attacks.
Repeat strikes put rescuers at risk
The repeated attacks have made emergency operations particularly dangerous. Since rescuers began working, air raid alerts in the oblast had sounded 20 times as of Friday morning, according to the DSNS.
Firefighters have repeatedly been forced to stop their work and move to shelters or safe distances because of the threat of another strike, before returning to the fires once the danger passes.
Vyhivskyi said one person was killed and others injured in Kyiv Oblast on the morning of 28 August after civilians remained near a site where crews were clearing the aftermath of an earlier strike despite the threat of another attack.
Commercial sites targeted across Ukraine
The attacks on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast are part of a broader recent pattern of Russian strikes on commercial infrastructure across Ukraine. In recent weeks, Russian drones have hit shopping centers, hypermarkets, warehouses, postal terminals and other civilian businesses.
In Kharkiv, a Russian jet-powered drone struck a closed shopping center in the city’s Kyivskyi district on 28 August, partially damaging the building and starting a fire among equipment and furniture. Firefighters extinguished the blaze despite the threat of repeat strikes. No casualties were reported.
In Zaporizhzhia, another Russian drone strike injured five people and set a shopping center on fire. The blaze covered about 14,000 square meters, and firefighters had to repeatedly take shelter because of the threat of follow-up attacks.
The strikes are adding pressure to Ukraine’s civilian supply and logistics networks, particularly around major population centers. Damage to food warehouses, retail facilities and logistics sites can disrupt the storage and movement of goods, contributing to shortages and delays for businesses and consumers.
Russian drone strike on Kryvyi Rih shopping center kills 15, injures 130. Second attack targeted rescue workers 30 minutes later
Authorities warn civilians to stay away
Ukrainian authorities have urged residents to remain in shelters or other safe locations during air raid alerts and avoid areas where emergency crews are working.
The DSNS warned people not to approach sites where the aftermath of Russian strikes is being cleared, citing the continuing threat of repeat attacks.
Vyhivskyi also urged residents to treat every air raid alert as a signal to move to a shelter or other safe location, warning that no urgent task is worth risking a life.

Questions remain over Israel's role in Bosnia genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:05:41 UTC
00:05:41 KST

Breadcrumb
After Mladić’s death, key questions remain over Israeli support in Bosnia genocide
The death of Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb military commander convicted of genocide and war crimes, has revived unresolved questions about the international networks that supplied and supported the forces under his command during Bosnia’s 1992–95 war.
Mladić died on Thursday while hospitalised in The Hague, where he was in United Nations custody. His convictions for genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war had been upheld on appeal, and he was serving a life sentence.
His death closes the life of one of the central perpetrators of the Bosnian genocide. It does not, however, settle wider questions about foreign military supply, state knowledge and the archives that could help clarify them.
Among the least explored is Israel’s alleged role in supplying or facilitating military assistance to Serbian and Bosnian Serb forces during the war. Israeli human-rights lawyer Eitay Mack and Israeli genocide scholar Yair Auron have sought disclosure of official records concerning Israeli defence exports to the former Yugoslavia, but Israel’s Supreme Court rejected their petition in 2016.
"We collected evidence based on the investigation and testimonies from people that were in Bosnia at the time, and we reached the conclusion that [Israel was] sending arms, despite the UN Security Council embargo and clear knowledge from the Israeli government of the atrocities happening in the war," Mack told The New Arab.
Mack pointed out that the prime minister at the time, Yitzak Rabin of the Labor Party, had been in a coalition with the left, who would push for the government to denounce what was happening in Bosnia.
Despite policy being dictated by what he described as "the most leftist government that Israel ever had", the court upheld an earlier decision not to release information on defence export licences and Defence Ministry decisions concerning the former Yugoslavia between 1990 and 1996. It said disclosure could harm Israel’s national security or relations with foreign countries.
The ruling has resulted in a substantial accountability gap. It neither publicly establishes the scale of any Israeli exports, nor resolves questions about Israeli equipment, training or arms brokering reaching Serbian or Bosnian Serb forces during a period when a UN arms embargo covered the former Yugoslavia.
Mack nevertheless argues the court’s recognition that relevant documents existed – and its decision to shield them – is significant, saying that the stated concern over foreign relations pointed to the sensitivity of the withheld information.
What the court records show
Mack and Auron filed their request under Israel’s freedom-of-information law after years of allegations that Israeli military equipment or assistance reached Bosnian Serb forces during the conflict, particularly given that the UN Security Council arms embargo had formally been in place since September 1991 until late 1995.
The petitioners submitted testimonies from journalists and humanitarian workers who had been in Bosnia, as well as publicly available reporting and historical material documenting Israeli assistance.
Among the material cited was a 2002 Dutch government-commissioned report that referred to allegations that Israeli arms had been supplied in exchange for Bosnian Serb forces allowing members of Sarajevo’s Jewish community to leave the besieged city in 1992.
The same report referred to an investigation into the remains of a mortar grenade at Sarajevo airport in late 1994 that reportedly bore Hebrew letters, as well as a 1995 Israeli television report on private Israeli arms dealers supplying the Bosnian Serb Army (VRS).
"Despite the atrocities, Israel still chose to send arms shipments to the Bosnian Serbian forces, which included ammunition, mortar shells, rifles and rockets," Mack said.
The petition also pointed to references in Mladić’s diaries, portions of which appeared in an International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia judgment in the case of former Yugoslav army chief Momčilo Perišić.
According to the material cited in that judgment, Mladić wrote of an apparent Israeli offer of cooperation against "extreme Islam", with former Bosnian Serb Defence Minister Dusan Kovacevic giving evidence that he was contacted by Israel’s intelligence agency, Mossad, around March 1995, reportedly regarding proposed training in Greece and weapons for a group of fighters.
According to the judgment, Mladić wrote in his diary: "From Israel – they offer joint combat against extreme Islam – offer the training of our men in Greece at their expense. They offer us special weapons for 500 men – snipers for free – they said it came to Bihac, I don’t know whether it was given to Serbia [sic]."
Mack said that the court order dismissed the evidence, arguing that it didn’t know whether the suggestion in the diary had actually been implemented.
A broader pattern of secrecy
For Mack, the questions raised by Israel’s sealed Bosnia-war files are part of a wider pattern in which Israeli courts and state institutions have resisted public scrutiny of defence exports to governments accused of grave abuses.
He pointed to his previous legal effort with Auron to obtain documents on alleged Israeli arms exports to Rwanda during the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. Israel’s Supreme Court also refused disclosure in that case, ruling that the public interest in releasing the information did not outweigh potential harm to national security and foreign relations.
"You can see it in other places," Mack told The New Arab. "I had a procedure regarding the genocide in Rwanda, where the Rwandan government didn’t want to open its own archives and Israel, continuing to be involved in repression and atrocities themselves, don’t have an interest to open these archives."
Mack argued that this reflects a broader weakness in international accountability mechanisms: investigations often concentrate on direct perpetrators while leaving the role of foreign governments, arms suppliers and intermediaries insufficiently examined.
"This is a structural problem when we talk about international justice, where we should also talk about the arms suppliers and foreign actors that are involved in the conflict – not only on those that are directly involved in the offences," he said.
He cited Chad as another example. After Israel and Chad restored diplomatic relations in 2019, the two countries announced cooperation in areas including security. Israeli and international rights groups subsequently raised concerns about the lack of transparency surrounding possible military or security assistance to President Idriss Déby’s authoritarian government, warning that such assistance could be deployed against political opponents, activists and other critics.
For Mack, the continuing secrecy over Bosnia cannot be treated solely as a historical matter. He said the evidence submitted in the case indicated that Israel’s military dealings were undeterred by growing international outrage.
"After the genocide happened, there was still evidence that the shipments continued," he said. "So our conclusion was that Israel did business as usual during the years of the war, and also before and after the Srebrenica massacre that was recognised as genocide."
Mladić was convicted of genocide for the 1995 killings in Srebrenica, in which Bosnian Serb forces murdered more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys after the UN-designated safe area fell. He was also convicted of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including terror and unlawful attacks on civilians during the siege of Sarajevo.
Mack stressed that the failure of the legal bid had not ended public discussion of Israel’s role during the Bosnian war.
"Despite the legal case failing, I think what is good is that both in Israel and outside of Israel, it’s become more common knowledge of the involvement of Israel in the war," he said. "So even if the Israeli government is trying to hide information in the archive, they can’t keep the public silent."
He said his work challenging Israeli arms exports and security ties in multiple countries was intended to demonstrate what he sees as a continuing state practice rather than a collection of isolated episodes.
"What I try to do is raise as many cases of Israeli involvement around the world so that the Israeli public can see that we are not talking about unique circumstances or incidents, but that it’s a pattern of behaviour of all Israeli governments," Mack said.
Mack linked that assessment to the absence of accountability for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
"There is zero accountability in what’s going on," he said. "But I think it’s predictable given how there’s no justice and zero accountability regarding what Israel and Israel’s security forces are doing to Palestinians. So I think it’s logical that we will not see accountability for what Israelis are doing in other countries."

Russia’s Defense Ministry announced Friday that it conducted a successful combat training launch of a mobile, solid-fuel intercontinental ballistic missile from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the northwestern Arkhangelsk region.
The Strategic Missile Forces deployed a mobile launcher battery to a remote area before firing the missile across the country to the Kura test site on the Kamchatka Peninsula, located more than 6,700 kilometers (4,160 miles) to the east.

The latest launch comes less than a week after unverified reports claimed that Ukrainian drones targeted Plesetsk, Russia’s only military spaceport.

More and More Global Leaders Went to Chinese Colleges. Does That Matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

On June 23, 2026, South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok walked onto the campus of Tsinghua University in Beijing, where he had earned a law degree in 2010. “I believe that my time studying at Tsinghua University will remain one of the most beautiful memories of my life, forever cherished and held close to my heart,” he told his hosts. Kim had flown in from Seoul on early morning flights, he recalled, just to make it to class on time. (Kim has since resigned from office to become the chair of the ruling Democratic Party.)
Three weeks earlier, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith had stood in the dormitory room at the Central Party School where he had lived during a month-long program in 2000. “Though the campus has undergone some changes,” he said, “the places where I lived and studied remain just the same.”
Both leaders returned to a Beijing alma mater within three weeks of each other. They are not alone.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the president of Kazakhstan, studied at the Beijing Linguistic Institute (now known as the Beijing Language and Culture University) in 1983-84 and speaks fluent Mandarin. In April 2026, Le Minh Hung took office as Vietnam’s prime minister; in 1996, he had completed a training course on market economy and financial analysis at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics.
With four neighborhood countries now having top leaders who have studied in China, does this mark a new phase in Chinese educational diplomacy in its periphery, or is it little more than a biographical curiosity?
Three forces explain the growing cohort of Asian leaders who spent time at Chinese schools.
First, Chinese universities have risen sharply in global rankings. In the 2026 U.S. News Best Global Rankings, Tsinghua – a public institution that traces its roots back to 1911 – placed sixth globally, accompanied by 10 other mainland institutions in the top 100. A degree from a top institution in China now carries weight both at home and abroad.
Second, and related, education investment has grown steadily. China has maintained public education spending at or above 4 percent of GDP since 2012, a benchmark enshrined in national policy and actively monitored. This is a dividend from decades of economic growth directed back into the education system. Between 2021 and 2024, China invested $539 billion in higher education, building what is now the world’s largest higher education system.
As investment has grown, access has widened, too, for both Chinese and foreigners. Chinese government scholarships – including the Silk Road program for students from Belt and Road partner countries – cover tuition, accommodation, living expenses, and medical insurance. In the 2024-25 academic year, 380,000 international students from 191 countries were studying in China, with Asian students making up 61 percent of that figure.
What does this education actually deliver? Familiarity with the Chinese language and social context, for one. Tokayev’s Mandarin is evident in his public engagements. Thongloun’s Party School curriculum covered party theory and state policy. Kim studied Chinese law, giving him insight into China’s regulatory framework.
Educational history also shapes present-day engagement. Kim’s alumni visit, for example, provided a forum for discussing bilateral cooperation with Tsinghua’s Party Secretary Qiu Yong.
None of this moves the needle on core foreign policy. Vietnam’s “four nos” defense policy and Kazakhstan’s multivector diplomacy are structural features of their geopolitical positions, not likely to change because of a leader’s personal biography. Le Minh Hung has continued Vietnam’s balancing act with Washington and hedging in the South China Sea. Tokayev has maintained Kazakhstan’s close ties with Moscow while deepening economic ties with Beijing. These foreign policy patterns predate these specific leaders – and their Chinese education – and continue today.
But studying in China does matter for diplomacy. Leaders with Chinese training have a better understanding of which institutions produce which decisions, and how China’s leaders think about specific issues. Thongloun said his Party School experience “laid a crucial foundation for leading national development” – what he took from Beijing was the logic behind China’s development approach, applied in Laos.
Should exchanges continue to expand, the share of senior officials in China’s periphery with Chinese training will keep rising. They will act according to their national interests, but with a better grasp of Beijing’s internal drivers. Whether that accumulation eventually shifts policy, or only the quality of communication, is the question to watch.

How family accommodation impacts anxiety and OCD treatment across the lifespan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:00:26 UTC
00:00:26 KST

A recent study provides evidence that family members frequently change their own routines to help loved ones avoid anxiety or obsessive-compulsive triggers, a pattern seen across all age groups. When patients receive intensive treatment that specifically targets these family habits, the initial level of family involvement does not predict how much the patient will improve.
Anxiety disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorder, commonly known as OCD, can cause substantial distress and disrupt daily functioning for individuals of all ages. When a person struggles with these conditions, they often experience intense fear or discomfort in specific situations. Seeing a loved one in pain, family members often step in to help reduce their distress in the moment.
This behavior is known as family accommodation. It can take many forms, such as providing constant reassurance about a feared outcome, participating directly in an obsessive-compulsive ritual, or modifying household routines to help the patient avoid situations that trigger fear.
While well-intended and natural, family accommodation tends to make anxiety and OCD worse over time. By stepping in to help a loved one avoid temporary distress, family members inadvertently reinforce the idea that the feared situation is truly dangerous and unmanageable. This dynamic prevents the individual from experiencing corrective learning. They lose the opportunity to discover that they can tolerate anxiety and handle challenging scenarios on their own. Studies show that this cycle of reliance occurs not only with parents of anxious children but also with romantic partners, siblings, and extended relatives of adults in treatment.
Past research has documented high rates of family accommodation in both youth and adult populations. Most of this prior work looked at patients receiving standard outpatient therapy on a weekly basis, rather than those seeking higher levels of care for complex or severe symptoms. Investigating how these family dynamics operate across the lifespan helps mental health professionals understand whether specialized treatments need to address family behaviors differently for children versus adults.
“This topic was inspired by a collaborative discussion among science practitioners at intensive treatment programs for youth and adults,” said lead researcher Jacqueline Sperling, a clinical psychologist, assistant professor at Harvard Medical School, and co-director of the McLean Anxiety Mastery Program at McLean Hospital. “We recognized that both the pediatric and adult research worlds can be separate, and we wanted to bridge that research gap by exploring patterns across the lifespan.”
Sperling, who is also the author of the book Find Your Fierce: How to Put Social Anxiety in Its Place, and her colleagues examined patients receiving intensive or residential treatment at a single academic medical center. The sample included 67 children and adolescents ranging in age from 8 to 19, along with 131 adults ranging in age from 18 to 76. The youth attended an intensive outpatient program that ran several afternoons a week. The adult participants were enrolled in a partial hospital or residential program, with an average length of stay of about two months.
At the beginning and end of their respective programs, patients and their participating family members completed a battery of questionnaires. These surveys measured the severity of anxiety, OCD symptoms, and depressive symptoms, as well as the extent of functional impairment in daily life. The researchers also measured the frequency of family accommodation using specialized scales. In the youth program, parents reported on their own accommodating behaviors. In the adult program, parents, spouses, partners, or siblings reported on how often they accommodated the adult patient’s symptoms.
During the programs, all patients engaged in cognitive-behavioral therapy that involved gradual exposure to their feared situations. Families were heavily involved in the treatment process to ensure coping skills transferred to the home environment. Clinicians met with family members regularly to teach them how to systematically reduce their accommodating behaviors. For instance, parents were taught how to gradually reduce the amount of time they spent walking an anxious child into school, or how to slowly cut back on answering repetitive phone calls from an adult patient seeking reassurance about their health.
The authors found that family accommodation was highly prevalent across all ages in these intensive treatment settings. At admission, 100 percent of the children or their parents reported some form of accommodation. Similarly, 95 percent of adult patients or their loved ones reported that family members altered their behavior to accommodate the patient’s symptoms. Specific actions, such as providing verbal reassurance, allowing the patient to avoid daily responsibilities, and changing family leisure routines, occurred at high rates for both groups.
“Family accommodation is incredibly common across the lifespan, and that makes a lot of sense given that one’s instincts are to try to support family members,” Sperling explained. “The key distinction, however, is that the support is for the anxiety and OCD and not the family members.”
“The treatment helps families recognize the difference and to offer support in a values-consistent manner instead,” she added.
Despite its presence across the lifespan, accommodating behavior was noticeably more frequent among families of children than families of adults. For example, 60 percent of parents of youth reported providing daily reassurance to their child. In comparison, 24 percent of family members of adult patients reported offering daily reassurance. Family members across both age groups generally reported engaging in more accommodating behaviors than the patients themselves perceived, suggesting that patients might not always recognize how much their families are adjusting to their needs.
When patients first entered the intensive programs, higher levels of family accommodation were associated with more severe anxiety and OCD symptoms, as well as greater impairment in daily functioning. This aligns with the idea that severe symptoms often pull for more family involvement. However, when the researchers analyzed the patients’ progress by the time they were discharged, they found that patients achieved a reduction in symptoms regardless of their initial accommodation levels.
“It was pleasantly surprising that family accommodation levels at the beginning of treatment did not predict less treatment progress by the end of treatment,” Sperling noted. “This finding highlights how working to reduce family accommodation in treatment could help families yield treatment gains.”
A reader might assume from these outcome findings that family accommodation has no negative impact on a person’s ability to recover from anxiety or OCD. This interpretation misses the specific clinical context of the study. The patients were enrolled in intensive treatment programs that actively trained families to stop accommodating the symptoms and taught them alternative ways to offer support. The findings suggest that when treatment directly and effectively addresses family behaviors, a high initial level of accommodation does not stop a patient from getting better. In standard settings where family habits are ignored, accommodation likely remains a barrier to progress.
The study has some limitations to consider when interpreting the results. The participants were drawn from intensive treatment programs that require a large time commitment and often rely on substantial financial resources. This resulted in a relatively homogeneous group of patients, the majority of whom identified as white.
A more diverse sample across different socioeconomic backgrounds might show different patterns of family involvement or face different barriers to reducing accommodation. The study also relied heavily on self-reported surveys, which can sometimes be influenced by a participant’s desire to present their family dynamics in a positive light.
The differences in how the groups were assessed present another limitation. “The treatment programs are not exactly the same, so there could not be a direct comparison of pediatric and adult treatment,” Sperling said.
“In addition, some research measures are just for either youth or adults, so not all of the questionnaires from which data were collected were exactly the same,” she added. “Analogous measures were incorporated to deduce findings.”
Future research could benefit from assessing family accommodation more frequently throughout the treatment process, such as on a weekly basis, rather than just at the beginning and end of a program. This would allow researchers to track exactly how gradual changes in family behavior align with improvements in the patient’s symptoms over time. Utilizing independent evaluators to measure family dynamics, rather than relying solely on patient and relative self-reports, could also provide a more objective understanding of how these behaviors operate and impact recovery across the lifespan.
Moving forward, the researchers want to encourage clinical integration across age boundaries. “I hope that there can be more collaboration among pediatric and adult treatment programs to support development across the lifespan,” Sperling said.
The study, “Family Accommodation of OCD and Anxiety Symptoms Across the Lifespan,” was authored by Jacqueline B. Sperling, Abigail M. Stark, Olivia Woodson, Esther S. Tung, Martha J. Falkenstein, and Jennie M. Kuckertz.

Which are the busiest airports in the EU for commercial flights?

15:00:15 UTC
00:00:15 KST

More than 6.9 million commercial flights were recorded in the EU in 2025, with the highest number of arrivals and departures at Amsterdam Schiphol, Paris Charles de Gaulle and Frankfurt.
Commercial flights in the EU reached 6.9 million in 2025, an increase of 3.8% compared to the year before, new data has revealed.
A report published by Eurostat found that the number of flights in the EU has “risen continuously since 2021”, and by the end of 2025 had “returned to a level similar” to the pre-pandemic figure of seven million recorded in 2019.
In 2025, 91.5% were scheduled flights, defined by Eurostat as a “commercial air service operated according to a published timetable or with a regular frequency open to direct booking by the public”. Meanwhile, non-scheduled commercial flights, which include charter flights and other special services, made up the remaining 8.5%.
The summer months recorded the highest numbers of non-scheduled commercial flights in 2025. There were 648,707 commercial flights in June, of which 11.2% were non-scheduled, rising to 690,855 flights in July (12.3% non-scheduled) and 693,046 in August (11.4%).
Schiphol is the EU's top airport for commercial flights
With 488,000 departures and arrivals, Amsterdam Schiphol in the Netherlands was the EU’s busiest airport for scheduled and non-scheduled commercial flights in 2025. Paris Charles de Gaulle in France was second with 476,000 flights, followed by Frankfurt/Main in Germany with 457,000.
Two Spanish airports, Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas and Barcelona-El Prat, made up the top five with 423,000 and 356,000 flights respectively.
Completing the top 10 were Munich in Germany (329,000), Rome Fiumicino in Italy (320,000), Athens/Eleftherios Venizelos in Greece (271,000), Copenhagen/Kastrup in Denmark (254,000) and Dublin in Ireland (252,000).
Of the top 10 busiest EU airports for commercial flights, the highest shares of non-scheduled flights were recorded at Athens/Eleftherios Venizelos (5.2%), Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas (4.8%) and Copenhagen/Kastrup (4.1%).

- 4. Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport: 423,000

Kyiv ground to a halt for the tenth time on Friday as air raid sirens sounded over the capital. The renewed attacks followed a record 13 alerts that kept the city under warning for almost 15 hours on Thursday.
Russia continued to send waves of drones towards the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Friday, repeatedly forcing residents into shelters and disrupting life across the city for a second consecutive day.
The attacks followed an extraordinary day of disruption on Thursday, when Kyiv spent almost 15 hours under air-raid warnings, with sirens sounding 13 separate times, according to the Foreign Ministry.
“Again and again throughout the day, sirens sounded as Russia launched drones in small groups towards the Ukrainian capital. Each new threat put people at risk and forced them to seek safety,” the ministry said.
The continuing attacks mean Kyiv has already faced at least 23 separate air-raid alerts in less than two days, disrupting work, transport and everyday life.
Ukrzaliznytsia, the state railway operator, said prolonged air-raid alerts caused significant delays, with the disruption expected to continue for at least another day.
No long-distance trains have been cancelled, but some services were running several hours behind schedule as repeated aerial threats interrupted operations.
Russia turns to jet-powered drones
Ukrainian officials say much of the prolonged disruption is being caused by Russia launching small groups of jet-powered drones.
Rather than concentrating them in a single mass barrage, the drones are being sent in successive waves, repeatedly renewing the threat and triggering new air-raid alerts.
“The goal is to exhaust air defences and the population,” Andrii Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said on Friday.
Russia has been stepping up its use of jet-powered drones in recent months. Unlike the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones that have become a regular feature of Russian attacks, some of the newer weapons can reach speeds of up to 500 km/h.
That puts them beyond the reach of many Ukrainian interceptor drones, which typically fly at speeds of up to 300 km/h, potentially forcing Ukraine to use scarce and considerably more expensive air-defence missiles against them.
Between 7am and 7pm on Thursday, Russia launched around 140 attack drones against Ukraine, more than 100 of them jet-powered, according to Ukraine’s Air Force.
The majority were directed against Kyiv.
Warehouses and homes hit
The sustained attacks have caused extensive damage to civilian infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
One person was killed and two others injured in the Kyiv region on Friday, while 14 warehouses, 16 private homes, three apartment buildings and 16 vehicles were damaged, according to regional authorities.
Warehouses and distribution centres have been particularly heavily hit in recent Russian attacks.
Around 90% of Ukraine’s modern storage facilities for goods have been destroyed by Russian strikes, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on Friday.
The destruction will not leave Ukrainians without food, he said, but is forcing retailers to reorganise their supply chains, including by delivering goods directly from producers to shops.
Moscow claims it is hitting military targets
Despite the documented damage to homes, schools, warehouses and businesses, the Kremlin reiterated its usual narrative on Friday, saying that Russia was attacking military and military-related infrastructure.
“Strikes on Kyiv are continuing. They are continuing systematically and deliberately,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
“We continue to destroy the military and paramilitary infrastructure. Our military knows what it is doing and how it is doing it.”

Choking is sold to teens as a safe sexual practice. The research says it never is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:00:04 UTC
00:00:04 KST

When touching someone’s throat, it can only take the pressure of a handshake to cause serious injury, unconsciousness or death. These injuries, which include brain damage and stroke, are often internal and invisible, showing up days or even months after the initial incident occurred. Experts say many who participate in sexual choking are not aware of the risks.
Choking or sexual strangulation is common among young people, says Prof Heather Douglas of the Melbourne Law School. In a 2024 survey of 4,702 Australians aged between 18 and 35, she and her research team found that 57% reported ever having experienced sexual strangulation; 51% reported ever having strangled a partner and 43.9% reported participating in both.
A police investigation into the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney, who is believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, has brought the practice to national attention again this week.
Douglas says their survey found gender differences in prevalence rates. Young women were more likely to report having been strangled (61%) and young men were more likely to report strangling a partner (59%). Among trans and gender-diverse young people the rates were even higher, with 78% reporting ever having been strangled and 74% reporting ever having strangled someone else. Many had positive perceptions of the act – believing it was safe and led to more enjoyable sex. “I don’t think that a lot of young people know how dangerous it is,” Douglas says.
There have been similar findings globally. Dr Debby Herbenick is the world’s leading researcher on sexual choking.
When Herbenick conducted her first nationally representative survey asking about sexual choking in the United States a decade ago, “the data came back and I was just floored,” she says. Only a small percentage of adults in midlife and beyond reported being choked, but for those aged 18-39, “more than a third of them had reported being choked during sex”.
The issue “felt really urgent”, says Herbenick, who is director of Indiana University’s Center for Sexual Health Promotion. When she spoke to her students about it, “they were like, ‘Oh no, it’s OK. We’re all doing the same thing.’
“I think what bothered me about it, and worried me, was I felt like they weren’t making informed choices. They were making choices, but they weren’t informed.”
Choking, or strangulation?
In Australia, when choking results in serious harm, the laws are straightforward. Every state and territory has specific assault laws around strangulation. “Injuries or a strangulation that causes death or really serious harm can’t be consented to,” Douglas says.
But the fact that many young people believe choking is low-risk and enjoyable is a vexed public health issue.
When Women’s Health New South Wales was funded to improve workforce capacity to respond to strangulation, they ran headlong into this problem. Jackie McMillan, a senior project officer, says: “When we started that work, we realised that we couldn’t do that without also talking about sexual choking.”
Physically, strangulation and sexual choking carry the same risks, but “they’re slightly different conversations,” McMillan says.
“If people are calling what they’re doing ‘sexual choking’, it’s because they’re making a distinction between what they see as a consensual sexual practice about freedom of sexual expression, and something that is violence. And if you start in with a language of violence, you often lose those people … They’re not interested in what you have to say. They turn off because they think that what you’re talking about is not what they’re doing.”
Herbenick agrees. “Our research here is very clear that we need to be using the word ‘choking’,” she says. “If people think about what they’re doing as choking, and you call it strangulation, they think, ‘oh, well, I’m not strangling or being strangled. I’m doing choking and choking is safe’.”
When Herbenick has asked young people to describe how they choke in detail, overwhelmingly they describe applying pressure to the neck, and list symptoms like dizziness, seeing stars and shortness of breath. “And so certainly anyone in those buckets has some evidence of doing what we would call strangulation,” she says.
Herbenick’s research includes a partnership with neuroscientists, testing for brain changes in women who have been choked. While there is a large body of evidence about the neurological effects of strangulation in domestic violence contexts, because the subjective experience of choking can be so different, “in some ways I felt like we had to start from scratch,” she says.
For instance, in domestic violence contexts, there is strong evidence that repeat strangulation has more pronounced neurological effects. “But when you look at those multiple versus single strangulation studies, multiple is often like two or three or four times, right? But then if you look at sexual choking, people are often choked, in our studies, an average of 25 times – but sometimes 50 or 100 or 200 or 500 times, because it’s become such a common thing that people do.”
Observations of women who frequently participate in choking and recently participated in choking both suggested it can cause brain injury.
But data on effective public health messaging is still nascent.
Herbenick’s team tried educational messages around the health implications of sexual choking, the importance of receiving specific consent for choking, and messages about the potential legal consequences if an injury occurs. While they found “all three message types were very well received by young adults”, for women, “only the health and consent messages were especially effective” in changing their intentions around choking.
For men to change their intentions, “they needed to know about potential legal consequences in the event of injury or death,” Herbenick says. “It was tough to see, because of course we would like to think that knowing that something could be harmful for somebody’s health would be enough to make a lot of people change their behaviour.” That finding persisted regardless of whether men were choking or being choked.
All the experts who spoke to the Guardian agreed that widespread and robust sexual education that engages specifically with choking is a vital first step in preventing catastrophic health outcomes.
But school systems are not prepared to engage in this level of sexual education, and young people’s information environment, especially on social media, is flooded with misinformation.
“There are some sex educators … who claim that there are safe ways to choke. And there’s just a lot of regular people out there making TikTok videos claiming there are safe ways to choke,” says Herbenick.
“Pornography is one piece of it,” she adds. “Social media is one piece of it. Anyone whose kids are reading fan fiction or … dark romance novels is almost certainly coming across choking.”
On social media, it is often referred to lightheartedly as a “hand necklace” or through memes like “Choke me daddy”.
Non-judgmental sex education
There are no circumstances under which exerting pressure on the soft tissue of someone’s neck is safe; and when drugs or alcohol are involved, the practice becomes even riskier. But this information is not easy to find. McMillan created a website, It Left No Marks, to help combat this void. “We had to build it because it wasn’t there,” she says.
Wellington-based criminology academic Dr Samantha Keene says the tragic death of UK woman Grace Millane in New Zealand in 2020 “put conversations about rough sex and sexual choking or sexual strangulation on the public agenda”. But lately, she says, it has fallen off the radar.
“We know that sexual choking and sexual strangulation is eroticised in a whole range of media … yet we aren’t addressing that in sexual and relationships education.”
“What we know works is having an evidence-based approach,” she says. That means “meeting people where they are” in a non-judgmental way, by giving them access to information that outlines the range of risks associated with this form of sexual practice.
Meeting young people where they are is not a comfortable conversation, Herbenick says. “A lot of parents are thinking, ‘How am I living in a world where I’m supposed to be talking about strangulation during sex, with my … 13-year-old, 15-year-old?’
“I don’t know, but I can tell you that in our studies, when we ask college students how old they were when they first learned about choking, on average the age is 15. Which means that about half of them are learning about it younger than 15.”
McMillan says it takes “endorsement” to deliver this kind of education.
“That’s endorsement from parents. That’s endorsement from the school. That’s endorsement from the principals. We can’t leave teachers out there alone to discuss websites that they can’t even go to without there being a panic,” she says.
“How can we get teachers to talk about pornography if they can’t even visit the sites that the kids are on? We’ve created an impossible situation.”
International research has found that many of the young people who engaged in choking felt some degree of pressure from their partner, or their wider social environment, to do so. “So there’s questions around whether that is true consent, if we say it’s truly free and voluntary,” Douglas says.
Beyond understanding the consequences physically and legally, “what we need to do is make sure that people are skilled up with the things they need to redirect sexual activities to something else they might find pleasurable,” McMillan says.
“And also that particularly young women know sex is meant to be pleasurable. So if you’re not having fun, don’t do that bit.”

Ukraine’s FP-1 Drones Hit Major Russian Oil Refinery More Than 700 Km From Border
Ukrainian forces struck the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery in Russia’s Yaroslavl overnight on August 28, with fires reported at the facility following a drone attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces carried out the strike using FP-1 drones, Ukrainian defense company Fire Point reported on August 28.
OSINT analysts from ASTRA geolocated eyewitness footage and identified the site of the fire as the Slavneft-YANOS refinery. According to the outlet, videos filmed from Yaroslavl’s Dyadkovo district appeared to show two separate fires burning on the refinery grounds.
Yaroslavl regional governor Mikhail Yevrayev had earlier warned residents of a drone threat in the region. In the aftermath of the attack, traffic toward Moscow was temporarily restricted, while several public transport routes in Yaroslavl were adjusted.
Later, Yevrayev said that one person had been killed and 27 others injured in the attack, according to ASTRA.
Authorities also closed two kindergartens in the city due to the need to address the consequences of the drone attack.
About Slavneft-YANOS refinery
Slavneft-YANOS is the largest oil-processing facility in Russia’s Central Federal District, with an annual refining capacity of up to 15 million metric tons of crude oil. Located more than 700 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border, the refinery produces various petroleum products, including gasoline, jet fuel, and lubricants.
The refinery supplies products to major industrial enterprises across Russia’s Central and Northwestern regions. Its customers also include airports, the Northern Railway administration, and facilities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
Several days earlier, Russian oil giant Lukoil has suspended crude processing and petroleum product output at its Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez (NORSI) refinery after a fire triggered by an August 26 drone strike.

Your skin chemistry may affect which mosquitoes most want to bite you
Three disease-carrying species preferred different people based on skin odor and bacteria
Some people seem to get eaten alive by mosquitoes each summer, while others sail through the season with nary a bite.
Certain mosquito species are attracted to, or repelled by, different subsets of people depending on the components of their body chemistry and skin microbiome, researchers report July 30 in iScience. Understanding how mosquitoes choose their hosts could help prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue, West Nile and yellow fever.
“We want to understand what people’s risks are for being bitten because all of these mosquitoes that we studied are vectors of disease,” says Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist at Florida International University in Miami. Manipulating the molecules and bacteria that influence attraction could help scientists create new kinds of commercial mosquito repellents, he says.
Mosquitoes locate their dinners through visual, thermal and scent cues. But human scent is the product of more than a thousand chemicals, many of which are produced by bacteria that live on our skin. That makes it challenging to know which specific cues mosquitoes rely on to find their preferred human hosts.
DeGennaro and colleagues recruited 119 volunteers and exposed three different species of mosquito to each person’s scent. For Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, which feed during the day, volunteers placed an arm inside a device designed to let the mosquitoes smell them but not bite. To observe Culex quinquefasciatus, which feed at night, each volunteer wore a nylon sleeve for several hours to capture their scent, and the researchers placed the sleeve into the apparatus in the dark. For each person or sleeve, the scientists measured how many mosquitoes of each species entered the device to investigate.
Each mosquito species preferred a different group of volunteers, the team found. A. aegypti even showed a slight but meaningful preference for males over females. Though some people had more than one mosquito species find them particularly attractive, no one strongly attracted all three species.
The team also collected samples of the volatile compounds in the air around each person’s arm and of the bacteria living on their skin that may have created some of those compounds. Then the researchers looked for commonalities among the small groups of people who were most and least attractive to each mosquito species, respectively.
Ae. aegypti and C. quinquefasciatus tended to be more attracted to people who had less skin odor overall, the team found. Ae. albopictus was attracted to 13 chemicals with plantlike odors. Certain skin bacteria were present in all three high-attraction groups, including Corynebacterium kefirresdentii, Cutibacterium granulosum and a strain of Staphylococcus epidermis.
Because human odor is so complex, it’s difficult to detect all of the classes of compounds that comprise it, says Maria Elena De Obaldia, a research program manager at the drug developer Regeneron Pharmaceuticals in Tarrytown, N.Y., who was not involved in the work but previously studied mosquitoes’ attraction to humans. (Regeneron is a major financial supporter of the Society for Science, which publishes Science News.) It’s possible there are other compounds that influence attraction that weren’t captured in this study, she says.
Still, the different species’ preferences suggest that each species may have evolved its own way of finding hosts. Those adaptations may have been influenced by the types of host each species feeds on and the time of day that they seek out food, says Alicia Showering, who was not involved in the study. Showering is the CEO of BugBiome, a Norwich, England–based company that develops insecticides from microbes that live on crops.
The team now plans to study how skin bacteria produce odors that are more or less attractive to mosquitoes, says Kaylee Marrero, a mosquito neurobiologist at Florida International University in Miami. That may help researchers develop microbe-based repellants or lures for traps that target the most prevalent species in an area, she says.
“We’re all trying to figure out how to stop people from getting sick,” Marrero says. “Figuring out why [mosquitoes] are biting people is the best way to do that.”
