AI Has Human Doctors Asking: What’s Left for Us?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Don’t be fooled by the question mark in the title of an article published this month in the Journal of the American Medical Association. When the authors, including medical superstar Ezekiel Emanuel and venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, asked, “Will Autonomous AI Exceed AI-Physicians as the Best Medical Care?” they were being rhetorical. Their answer is an emphatic YES. Many in the medical world are begrudgingly coming to terms with the premise that patients can get the best treatment by a hybrid approach where doctors work in consultation with well-trained bots. But this article’s thesis is that AI alone can deliver the best outcomes.
“Review of all published articles on AI in medicine since January 1, 2024, shows that medicine is rapidly approaching the transition point at which AI alone will exceed physicians and physician AI-hybrids in providing the best care at five fundamental medical tasks,” they write. Those tasks include taking medical histories, establishing a diagnosis, identifying what tests are needed, prescribing treatment, and managing chronic diseases. You know, doctoring. AI is now so good, they argue, that clinicians should refrain from meddling, because “humans in the loop degrade AI performance.” Stand back, doc, and let AI do its thing. Which used to be your thing.
Lead author Emanuel—brother of Ari and Rahm, chair of the Department of Medical Ethics and Health Policy at Penn and a renowned oncologist—told me that for many years, he’d dismissed the idea that AI could perform core medical functions. He would run into Khosla at conferences in the 2010s, and the VC would bend his ear about how AI would be doing 85 percent of what doctors did by 2035. It was a hobbyhorse Khosla had been riding for years, writing a 2012 piece in TechCrunch asking, “Do We Need Doctors or Algorithms?”(again, rhetorical) and penning a 101-page treatise in 2016 to that effect. “I said bullshit, there’s no way,” says Emanuel. “What doctors do is too complicated.”
But about a year ago, Emanuel’s friend Robert Wachter sent him galleys of his book A Giant Leap, where Wachter, who is head of medicine at UCSF, outlined a world where first-class medicine would be a collaborative process between AI and doctors, but the masses in “economy class” would mostly make do with AI alone. Emanuel began to think that Khosla might be right. He suddenly flashed on a frightening question: “If AI takes over, what’s left for doctors to do?”
First he needed to validate the premise. He asked Khosla to collaborate, and the VC suggested that his son Neal Khosla join the effort, along with Emanuel’s researcher. Neal runs Curai Health, an online company that uses AI to treat patients, with a staff of doctors to prescribe medicine and handle more complicated issues. (This conflict of interest is disclosed in the paper, along with Vinod Khosla’s relevant investments and Emanuel’s various grants and consultancies.) The coauthors set out to look at all the studies on AI medicine that they could find from January 2024 to the present and concluded that, in many cases, a “superior autonomous AI” will likely surpass humans using AI by 2030. That prediction, they admit, is “unsettling but seems probable.”
Unsettling is an understatement. One of the loudest dissenting voices is John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association, which represents all those doctors who will be worrying about what’s left. When I talked to him, Whyte began by noting what he saw as the paper’s shortcomings, including that some of the studies it surveyed are simulations, not blind experiments, and they don’t all support the article’s conclusion. Notably, a February 2026 Nature article found that in real-life cases, most patients were unable to effectively converse with large language models to access their expertise. Whyte unsurprisingly bristled at the idea of removing humans from the clinical loop. “The AMA does see the potential in these tools, but they have to be utilized in the context of a care plan that’s governed by a physician,” he says.
Emanuel countered that he and his coauthors were careful in their conclusions. “It’s been less than four years since ChatGPT was introduced,” he said to me. “We’re making a prediction for four years from now. You don’t think that [AI is] going to be way more advanced than a doctor?”
Seeking a second opinion, I consulted Wachter. He’s singled out in the paper’s first paragraph as the guy who wrongly argues that AI-only treatment will be “economy class.” (I know Wachter personally.) Surprisingly, Wachter concedes that the authors of the paper have a point. “The argument they’re making is important,” he says. AI is good, he says, and right now AI and humans together are better. “But that can no longer be chiseled into a tablet. There will be times when humans will muck up the performance.”
Wachter is insistent, however, that the unique human attributes of trained physicians are vital and irreplaceable. AI may never be as effective in breaking the news of a grim prognosis than a human, and a patient may well be more likely to be guided to the best path of treatment by a real-life clinician.
Wachter invokes what he calls the doorman fallacy, named after the fear that people who opened doors for tenants in apartment buildings would be out of work once doors could open automatically. In fact doormen perform myriad tasks and are still an invaluable presence in white-glove buildings. Like accepting Amazon packages, feeding pets, and sometimes lending a sympathetic ear to a tenant sharing a gripe. “We’re going to find a version of the doorman fallacy for doctors,” says Wachter. “I can imagine a world where a doctor accepts the AI diagnosis but also performs a lot of other functions that have value.”
What’s being displaced here, though, isn’t something as straightforward as opening a door. It's the hard-won expertise that comes from years of training. You know those scenes in The Pitt where Dr. Robby relentlessly puts his residents on the spot by asking them to come up with instant assessments? That won’t be necessary when AI has the answer on demand. Physicians are on a path to relying so much on AI that their own judgment and knowledge will become less relevant. This “de-skilling” process could accelerate the takeover of medicine by AI, especially as new generations of doctors won’t find it necessary to spend years learning stuff that they can find out by querying an always-on AI expert in the pocket of their lab coat. The AMA’s Whyte admits that this is a concern for him. “A lot of medical schools and residency programs are debating whether physicians in their training can utilize these tools, because if you’ve never learned how to take medical history and do a physical, how will you ever learn?” On the other hand, there’s an argument that ignoring such a compelling tool is a form of malpractice.
So what’s the future for doctors? Vinod Khosla says that we’ll need them, at least in the short term, for surgery and in the emergency room. But in terms of providing expertise and judgment, he says they’re largely expendable, except maybe as debaters with AI to improve those systems. Neal Khosla tells me that the shift is already underway and that he expects that in coming years we will give AI the regulatory permission to prescribe medicine.
Remember the TV series House, where a dyspeptic and rude diagnostic genius decoded baffling conditions while insulting patients and humiliating his hapless acolytes? In the world of AI medicine, a Dr. House would be rendered homeless, because AI will routinely and freely apply its vast knowledge base to the most obscure ailments. The value of human clinicians will be the elements where House was most lacking, like empathy and high-EQ communication. Of course those who perform hands-on procedures are safe from AI encroachment—until the robots figure that out.
Health care is a huge part of our lives, but the debate here goes beyond that sector. The question, “What’s left for doctors to do?” may well be “What’s left for humans to do?” Bill Gates suggests in his recent jeremiad on AI that society might designate some tasks—like doctors counseling patients on how to deal with AI’s prognoses—“human-reserved,” to stave off economic ruin and a run on pitchforks. (Try to sell that solution to corporate shareholders who question the funding of make-work jobs.) At least the misery of the unemployed masses will be mitigated by one bonus: first-class medical advice that’s one click away.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Recently Published Book Spotlight: Death in a Shallow Pond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

David Edmonds is a Distinguished Research Fellow at the Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics at the University of Oxford. He is the author or co-author of eighteen books translated into twenty-five languages, including Parfit, Would You Kill the Fat Man?, and, with John Eidinow, the bestseller Wittgenstein’s Poker. With Nigel Warburton, he co-hosts the podcast Philosophy Bites. In this interview, Edmonds discusses Death in a Shallow Pond, a book that traces the history and influence of Peter Singer’s famous drowning-child thought experiment, its connection to effective altruism and the philosophy of Derek Parfit, and the pressing question of how much we owe to distant strangers.
What is your work about?
Death in a Shallow Pond is, in effect, the biography of a famous thought experiment.
On your way to work, you pass a shallow pond. You hear the cries of a young child, and, turning towards the pond, you notice a toddler flailing about. You look for the parents or babysitter, but there is no one in the vicinity. If you don’t wade in and pull her out, she seems likely to drown. Wading in is easy and safe, but you will ruin the new and expensive shoes you bought only a few days ago and get your suit wet and muddy. What should you do?
Of course, everyone says that you should save the child. How could your shoes be more important than that! Silly question. But then, the inventor of the thought experiment, Peter Singer, makes a contentious move. He says that many of us in the affluent West could easily afford to donate money to a charity that could then be used to save a life. Failing to do so is like worrying about one’s shoes rather than the child in the Shallow Pond.
The book is a history of this thought experiment, published in 1971. It describes the circumstances of its invention (during the Bangladesh Liberation War) and how it became so influential. It also analyzes whether not donating money to charity is really analogous to allowing the child in the pond to drown.
Why did you feel the need to write this work?
I’m not sure I felt a “need” to write it. I had previously written a book about arguably the most famous thought experiment in moral philosophy, namely the Trolley Problem. Death in a Shallow Pond seemed like a natural sister project. And the thought experiment had cropped up in a biography I’d just completed about the English philosopher Derek Parfit. Parfit’s ideas were influential in shaping the global movement—effective altruism—that was inspired by the Shallow Pond. The effective altruism movement encourages people to sign a pledge to donate at least ten percent of their income. The movement stresses that picking the right charities to support is just as important as the amount of money you donate, since some charities are massively more effective than others.
How is the book relevant to everyday life?
It’s very relevant! If Peter Singer is right, then almost all of us should be doing a great deal more than we actually do to help distant strangers. But is he right?
Did you encounter any problems getting yourself published and, if so, how did you overcome them?
I’m very fortunate in that I’ve established a great relationship with my publisher, Princeton University Press (PUP). I think they’re currently the best publisher of philosophy. My editor, Rob Tempio, is a lovely bloke and an excellent editor. Relationships in the publishing world are much undervalued. I’m obviously not present for internal PUP meetings, but it always feels to me as if Rob is batting for his authors. The Shallow Pond was my fourth Princeton book—and because I enjoy working with Rob, I didn’t offer the idea to anybody else. They said “yes” to the proposal quite quickly.
What writing tips do you have?
The best advice I have received was from my co-podcaster, Nigel Warburton. Nigel said that writers often assume that they need to be sitting comfortably at their desk before they put pen to paper, or finger to keyboard: it’s an excuse for a kind of procrastination. But in fact, you can write anywhere. You can write in buses, in cafes, and while waiting for the kids to finish their ballet class or football game. This tip has been hugely helpful to me. Snatch 25 minutes of writing time on a train journey, and it will contribute, in a small way, to reaching the finishing line.
What’s next for you?
I’m planning a book that will tell the history of twentieth-century philosophy and onwards through famous thought experiments and the lives of those who invented them. This seems like a logical next step. I’ve already written books about two thought experiments, and my Parfit biography was quite thought-experiment heavy. The next book will cover thought experiments in the philosophy of mind, language, epistemology, metaphysics, decision-theory, art and science, as well as in politics and ethics.
The post Recently Published Book Spotlight: Death in a Shallow Pond first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Chief of Zelenskyy's office explains why he did not dismiss former head Yermak's deputies

Unknown Publisher

Chief of Zelenskyy's office explains why he did not dismiss former head Yermak's deputies
Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, has explained that he did not dismiss the deputies of his predecessor, Andrii Yermak, after taking office because he believes in institutional continuity, the destruction of which would have brought all processes to a halt while new people learned their jobs.
Source: Budanov in an interview with Ukrainian journalist Nataliia Moseichuk
Quote: "I changed everything, but I did not change the people… First of all, I am a supporter of an institutional approach. An institutional approach means institutional continuity. You cannot ensure institutional continuity by coming in, telling everyone to 'f*ck off', throwing them out and bringing in others… You can do that, but it creates certain problems.
Problem number one is time. It would take at least six months, and many mistakes would be made during those six months… I have no right to experiment, to throw everyone out, destroy all institutional memory, halt all processes and then wait for people to 'figure things out'… I took the classic institutional approach: to manage what is already there and gradually make changes."
Details: Budanov was responding to Moseichuk's question about why, after taking over from Yermak, he had not replaced Yermak's deputies and had "changed absolutely nothing".
According to Budanov, quite a few new people, including military personnel, have joined the President's Office at the middle-management level during this time.
When asked about situations in which military personnel had effectively "hidden" their rank insignia and become civilians, thereby shaping the configuration of power, Budanov said that he remains an active serviceman.
Background:
- On 27 August, Budanov commented for the first time on reports that his name came up in recordings of conversations involving his deputy Iryna Mudra, who is implicated in the latest case brought by the anti-corruption agencies. He said: "Let the court figure out who heard what where."
- In recordings from the anti-corruption investigation known as Operation Forrest Gump, Iryna Mudra can be heard referring to "the leadership" while discussing how to arrange and launder bail money for former minister Herman Halushchenko, a defendant in the Midas case. However, it is not yet known exactly who was referred to as "the leadership" in the recordings.

Nepal’s glacial collapse, Haiti’s latest massacre, and Mladić’s death: The Cheat Sheet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:59:52 UTC
23:59:52 KST

Share & more
Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe.
On our radar
Glacial collapse triggers catastrophic Himalayan flood
A catastrophic landslide and flash flood struck a Himalayan border area connecting Nepal and China’s Tibet region on 26 August, destroying roads, bridges, homes, and hydropower facilities, and damaging the Gyirong Port border crossing. At the time of publication, the death toll had reached 538 in Nepal and five in Tibet, with as many as 1,500 people, including foreign tourists and pilgrims, still listed as missing. The US Geological Survey reported that the landslide was likely caused by a glacial collapse in Nepal, sending a rapidly accumulating mass of ice, rock, river water, and debris 100 kilometres downstream. Experts say climate warming likely played a role by destabilising mountain ice and rock, though the immediate cause of the collapse remains under investigation. Similar surges have become more frequent and intense as Himalayan ice loss accelerates. China suspended rescue efforts on 28 August in areas threatened by further flooding from a debris-dammed lake that has begun to overflow.
In Haiti, a new massacre threatens December’s election
Haiti’s gang violence is continuing to flare and spread. On 23 August, at least 47 people were killed, 22 injured, and dozens kidnapped in Kenscoff, a farming community on the hills overlooking Port-au-Prince. Gang members also burnt houses and raped women, fuelling fears the violence could expand further into the few relatively safe areas around the capital. The massacre comes as Haiti prepares to hold presidential elections next December – the first in more than a decade – and underscores the scale of the security challenge facing a country where the unrest has now displaced nearly 1.5 million people, or 10% of the entire population. Efforts to contain the gangs have so far failed. In September 2025, the UN authorised a UN-backed Gang Suppression Force. Six months earlier, the Haitian prime minister created a special task force to conduct drone strikes against gangs with support from controversial US private military contractor Erik Prince. Neither has managed to restore the security needed for elections. According to the UN, at least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured during the second quarter of 2026, with security forces operations accounting for 40% of the deaths.
Ratko Mladić, convicted of Srebrenica genocide, dies at 84
Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladić, who commanded forces responsible for one of the worst atrocities in Europe since the 1940s, has died in prison in The Hague aged 84. He led a brutal campaign during the Bosnian war, which began in 1992 as Yugoslavia broke apart. Bosnian Serb forces sought to seize territory and establish a separate Serb-controlled state within Bosnia. In the process, Mladić’s forces besieged Sarajevo and murdered more than 8,000 Muslim Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica, despite UN peacekeepers being stationed nearby. After 16 years on the run, Mladić was arrested in 2011 and, in 2017, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted him of genocide for Srebrenica, among other crimes, sentencing him to life imprisonment. Yet some Bosnian Serbs continue to deny his crimes and see him as a protector during the war, a reminder that securing justice for atrocities does not necessarily bring post-war reconciliation.
Liberia begins receiving Trump’s third-country deportees
Twenty deported migrants arrived in Liberia from the United States this week, the first of up to 1,200 deportees – none Liberian – the country has agreed to receive under a deal with Washington. Future arrivals will include nationals from North America, South America, the Caribbean, and other African countries. The Trump administration has deported more than 23,000 people under opaque agreements with 35 countries looking to curry his favour. These forced third-country transfers can occur with no warning, and immigration lawyers describe the practice as a deliberate policy to deny protection and spread fear among people who have been granted – or are seeking – safety in the United States. Cases have included a gay Moroccan woman deported to Cameroon – where homosexuality is illegal – and an Iranian woman with US court protection against being returned to Iran who was sent to the Central African Republic. Although such transfers can amount to refoulement – prohibited under international law when people face persecution or serious harm – US courts have so far allowed them to proceed. A US appeals court ruled in March that the deportations can proceed for the time-being, although a verdict is expected imminently on a legal challenge.
Syria’s Kurdish-led SDF dissolves, but true integration remains elusive
The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) announced its dissolution on 25 August, as part of a plan to integrate its fighters into Syria’s army. The move is a key part of Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s plans for a united Syria – a country that this week was removed from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism. In return for bringing the SDF – a powerful force and key part of the fight against the so-called Islamic State – under state control, analysts say Syria’s Kurds have secured some important concessions, including recognition of Kurdish as a national language, positions for Kurdish civil servants, and the appointment of SDF leader Mazloum Abdi as a presidential adviser. These are significant gains after decades of anti-Kurdish discrimination under the al-Assad regime. But not all Syrian Kurds support the deal, and obstacles remain. Most notably, the future of the SDF’s all-women unit, the YPJ, is unresolved. The all-female militia is important symbolically, politically, and on the ground, and with the Syrian army having no units for women anymore, discussions over the YPJ’s role are ongoing.
El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole raise East Africa flood risk
The Indian Ocean Dipole, a climate pattern involving contrasting sea-surface temperatures in the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean, doesn’t get as much press as its Pacific cousin, El Niño. But it can have a significant impact on weather conditions in East Africa, especially when the two systems work together. With El Niño already established and expected to strengthen through the end of the year, a report by the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) warns that the coming rainy season could bring widespread flooding and displacement, depending in part on how the two climate patterns interact. The DRC report outlines three scenarios for October to December, with as many as 3 million people at risk of displacement in Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan, and Uganda. Kenya, which could face more than a million displacements, is already planning evacuations, mapping out flood hotspots and revamping drainage systems in Nairobi, and urging businesses in areas that could be cut off for months to stock up on essentials. In Somalia, which has the highest projected displacement, the World Food Programme is planning to assist between 800,000 and 1.2 million flood-exposed people, warning that preparations may need to scale up.
Weekend read
And finally…
Russia’s African influence campaign, and the West’s retreat
Russia has been planting ghost reporters and fake experts in African media to advance its strategic interests, according to a new report by Code for Africa and Graphika. The content typically praises Russia’s paramilitary groups and good works, while denigrating Moscow’s geopolitical rivals – especially Ukraine, France, and the United States. So far, so unsurprising. Code for Africa we know does a sterling service around data journalism on the continent, supported by US philanthropies. What’s more interesting is who Graphika is. It turns out they receive their funding from US government military research grants to track foreign disinformation. Which begs the question, what the hell happened to the West’s own influence campaigns? Makes you feel almost nostalgic for the old days, when the US State Department provided golden ticket junkets to Washington for journalists to see democracy in action; when they bothered to groom civil society talent; when the continent felt a little more wooed. Now it all seems shabbier. No romance, just fork over the raw materials.

Nepali families pray for miracles with relatives missing after flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:59:50 UTC
23:59:50 KST

Nepali families pray for miracles with relatives missing after flood
At a Kathmandu hospital, families peer at lists of those who are critical, dead — or have been released.
Kathmandu/Nuwakot/Trishuli, Nepal – Loknath Chaulagain is looking for his 23-year-old nephew Sudarshan at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital.
A bus conductor, Sudarshan was waiting at the checkpoint in Timure, a town bordering Tibet, when the flash flood that devastated parts of Nepal and Tibet struck on Wednesday. His family says a phone call went through to his number at 9:54am local time – after the flash flood struck the border region – but Sudarshan did not pick up the call. Since then, his phone has been unreachable.
The family has been searching for him close to where the floods struck – and now in Kathmandu’s hospitals, where some survivors have been brought. But so far, they’ve had no luck.
They’re not alone. Thousands of families in Nepal are still stranded in the no-man’s land between hope and fear: hopes of an impossible miracle and their worst fears of losing someone they love.
Two days after the flash flood swept away much of what lay in its path along the Bhotekoshi River in the northern Himalayan region bordering Tibet, the full scale of devastation is yet to be ascertained in Nepal. The death toll is on the rise, with nearly 500 bodies recovered. The missing toll is well over 1,000 and is expected to rise further.
The wall of water with ice and mud that surged downstream with fury on August 26 caused maximum damage to Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi in the higher Rasuwa region nearer to Tibetan border checkpoints.
Downstream, it washed away buildings, electric poles, bridges, markets, homes and vehicles that stood in its path in Trishuli and Nuwakot regions.
The usually buzzing Trishuli market is today covered in mud, sludge and debris. Locals, including many Indians who have made the area their home for many years, beg and plead with relief workers to take them to their destroyed homes in earthmovers to retrieve whatever may be left of their belongings.
Helicopters whirred nonstop on Wednesday and Thursday in these areas, trying to rescue people trapped under the rubble or find anyone who might have been washed away and stranded in a dangerous situation. Those rescued with lighter injuries are being treated at the army camp helipad medical unit, while those more badly hurt are being airlifted to larger facilities in Kathmandu.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, people come by and plaster posters on walls with photographs and contact details of missing friends and family.
Other hospital pillars bear lists of those who have been admitted or are in critical condition – or those who have been killed: five-year-old Ishara Tamang in paediatric surgery; 30-year-old Tej Bhadur Tamang in the ICU; 25-year-old male Kusal Magar, listed as dead.
Multiple pairs of concerned eyes study these lists intently, hoping to find their loved ones there.
Among them is Sohan, a young man who does not want to speak to journalists on camera. He is searching for his 42-year-old father, Gyan Bahadur Rana Magar.
“I am too exhausted to talk to anyone. We have been running from one place to another to find any information about my father. Of course we have to keep our hopes alive. How can we let go of hope?” he asks. “Three days on, we are searching and still trying to find him.”
His father went with Indian tourists as a guide to Rasuwa, the border district with Tibet that is one of the worst affected.
When the lists on the pillars offer no answers, people searching for their loved ones head to the mortuary where photographs of some of the recovered bodies have been glued to the gates. Many bodies have been found dismembered; some missing limbs.
When someone finds a hint of familiarity, they inform security officials, who let them in after an identification check to take a look at the body.
Dressed in a red saree and blouse, and wearing a red pothe necklace – a traditional glass-bead necklace worn by married women in Nepal – Lal Kumari is desperately looking for her husband, Arjun Shreshtha.
A tourist van driver in his late 40s, he was swept away by the flood in Rasuwa district.
“I am praying hard,” Kumari tells Al Jazeera. “Every time our phones ring, we hope there will be some good news on the other end. Or that it is his voice that lets us know he is alive and safe. We have not slept at all in the last three days.”
Kumari has three children, including a married daughter and a grandchild, and her only question now is: Could her husband, miraculously, still be alive?

Mladic, who was serving a life sentence after being convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during Bosnia's 1992-95 war, died on Thursday in a U.N. detention facility in The Hague. He was 83.
"We have received nothing from The Hague," Vucic told reporters, adding that Serbian authorities would help arrange a dignified burial for Mladic in Serbia if his family requested it.
The court denied Mladic's request last month to be allowed to return to Serbia to die. It said his health condition was precarious but stable and well-managed at the detention centre.
"We have seen now that The Hague wanted Mladic's death behind bars," Vucic said. "They did not allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, without precedent or justification."
The U.N. body tasked with overseeing residual cases from the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal did not respond to Reuters questions about a possible transfer of Mladic's remains to Serbia.
Serbian media reported that Mladic had expressed a wish to be buried at a cemetery in Belgrade beside his daughter Ana, who died in 1994.
COURT INVESTIGATING MLADIC'S DEATH
The court has opened an inquiry into the circumstances of Mladic's death. A judge appointed to oversee the investigation spent about three hours at the detention facility on Friday but did not make a statement to reporters.
Vucic, a former ultranationalist who served as a minister under late Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic in the 1990s, has rebranded himself in recent years as a pro-European reformer while maintaining close ties with Russia and China.
Mladic was found guilty of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the U.N.-designated enclave.
He was also convicted over the 43-month siege of Sarajevo, during which about 10,000 people were killed.

Explainer-What is visual verification and why does Reuters practice it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:59:21 UTC
23:59:21 KST

Explainer-What is visual verification and why does Reuters practice it?
Aug 28 - Smartphones and social media have transformed journalism by producing a torrent of photos and videos of almost anything that happens where people are present, from holidays to hurricanes, celebrations to crises.
The swift rise of AI has tainted that flow, mixing in highly realistic video and still images of events that never happened or, more perniciously, alternate versions of things that did happen but not in the way depicted.
Reuters confronts this reality with a team of journalists specializing in "visual verification," who search the internet for images of breaking news events – from battlefields to border crossings – and then go through the painstaking process of confirming that those images do depict real events in the times and places they occurred.
Here's a look at how Reuters journalists tackle this challenge head-on, sorting through hundreds of photos and videos per day, of which it might validate and publish a dozen:
WHY DOES REUTERS RELY ON IMAGES FROM THE PUBLIC?
As the world's largest news agency, Reuters has an enormous footprint, with about 2,600 journalists spread over some 200 locations. But the Earth is a vast place and Reuters journalists can't be everywhere – news happens every day at unexpected times and in unexpected places. Videos and photos taken by people who are eyewitnesses to history, verified by Reuters journalists, have become an indispensable part of the file produced by Reuters.
This is in line with the Reuters Trust Principles, which have guided the news agency since World War Two and include directives to provide unbiased, reliable news and to continually develop and strengthen its services.
Verified images sourced from the public have been critical in breaking major news stories from around the world, including providing evidence suggesting that a U.S. missile had been used in a strike on an Iranian girls' school that killed scores of children and in providing detailed looks at the fatal Minneapolis shootings of American citizens protesting President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CAPABLE OF?
AI's ability to generate realistic videos, photos and audio has grown increasingly sophisticated over the past few years. While the fabricated or manipulated images it produced were once littered with visual giveaways – people with unusual numbers of fingers, background text written in unrecognizable letters – what it produces now is far more life-like.
Beyond the technological advances, people who want to use AI to create misleading imagery can feed data into it – photos of real-world people, places and events that the AI can then alter to produce far more convincing images.
Following the U.S. capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, some social media users circulated AI-generated images of Maduro in handcuffs – creating a false image of a real event. Reuters has also reported on AI-generated ads used to provide misleading images about candidates in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.
Even without AI, some social media users will share photos or videos of past events but inaccurately label what they represent – such as taking videos of protests that did occur at a particular place and time in the past and describing them as happening in the present and at other locations – in response to other events.
SO HOW TO TELL FACT FROM FICTION?
The Reuters global visual verification team follows a systematic process to assess whether images found on social media are real, unaltered versions of the events that they purport to portray.
There are a few critical steps in the process. One is to find the person who took the photo or video, confirm that they are who they say they are and if possible interview them to learn more about their experience.
Many images also carry metadata that can confirm where and when they were made and on what device; if that is present it can play an important role in verification.
Reuters journalists on the verification team also compare what a photo or video shows to other known publicly available data and imagery. These include weather reports, satellite imagery, archive and street view imagery. The direction of shadows can reveal the time of day at which a photo or video was taken. Media and official reports on events are taken into account when trying to establish what happened. So too are corroborating images and videos taken by other eyewitnesses that may show the same scene from a different angle.
Visual verification journalists compare their work to assembling a puzzle — once the full picture can be seen, then it is time to publish. Each photo and video is also scanned with several AI detection tools that are trained to look for evidence of AI alteration or generation. These tools are not foolproof – at times our VVT team isn't able to draw firm conclusions from the clues they yield – but such filters are important in spotting traces of AI that may not be visible to the naked eye.
The journalists inside the Reuters newsroom make a judgment call, which gets more challenging by the day. REUTERS

From Huey to Whiskey: How Andrews Is Starting a ‘Significant’ Helicopter Transition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:58:33 UTC
23:58:33 KST

JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md.—The iconic “whup-whup-whup” of the 1st Helicopter Squadron’s UH-1N Hueys still echoes in the skies of the Washington D.C. area, as the choppers flit around the U.S. Capitol, the Pentagon, and elsewhere, carrying senior government officials or training for contingency response.
But on Aug. 27, a new helicopter that first flew half a century after the Huey sat beside the stage for the activation of a squadron that’s a full 57 years younger than the 1st. It was the beginning of the end for the UH-1N—though there is still much to do before the true finale, officials say.
The new 5th Helicopter Squadron, commanded by Lt. Col. Jonathan Bonilla, will take the lead in transitioning the 316th Wing from the Huey to the new HH-60W Jolly Green II, or “Whiskey” as it is commonly called. Earlier this month, the Air Force confirmed Andrews as its “preferred location” to host 26 of the HH-60Ws, combat rescue helicopters that will be modified for the executive airlift mission. During the activation ceremony, Bonilla called it “one of the most significant rotary wing transitions our Air Force has undertaken.”
The mission at Andrews is more than just ferrying VIPs to and from the Pentagon. It’s about being prepared to respond in a crisis to carry leaders and ensure continuity of government operations. Crews are always on alert at a facility just steps away from the flightline at Andrews, prepared to spring into action if the call comes. During the 9/11 terrorist attacks 25 years ago, UH-1Ns were in the air before the Pentagon was struck and provided aid and medical evacuations.
The 24/7 nature of this mission means the 1st Helicopter Squadron can’t just retire its UH-1Ns and then make the preparations to transition to the HH-60W, like most units do when they’re getting a new aircraft. That’s where the 5th Helicopter Squadron comes in.
“As they activate, all of their aircrew members that are currently flying the Huey will begin the transition to the HH-60 Whiskey first,” explained Lt. Col. Kristopher Schmautz, director of operations for the 1st. “And as they convert those aircrews, the 1st will hold down the mission that we are here [to do] as they are getting up to being able to take part of the mission. And then it’ll be a slow transition working with the 5th Helicopter Squadron leadership to transfer some different pieces of our mission, so that we can then convert the members of the 1st Helicopter Squadron to the new HH-60 Whiskey.”
A new squadron will mean about 60 additional personnel at Andrews, but for now, the 5th is a small team, mostly coming from the 1st and with a deep attachment to the UH-1N.
“For about a decade, this is the only aircraft that I’ve known and operated,” Master Sgt. John Griggs, senior enlisted leader of the 5th Helicopter Squadron, said. “So it’s a little bittersweet to to move from something I have such a tenure with, and such a legacy across all the conflicts. … It’s very humbling to be able to see what this helicopter has done for the Air Force, and to be a part of transitioning to a newer airframe, to uphold the same mission.”
Iconic but Old
The Huey gained iconic status during the Vietnam War, and it’s been at Andrews almost as long, with the first helicopter arriving in 1971. Indeed, Schmautz said the 1st Helicopter Squadron has traced the maintenance records on three of its 26 Hueys directly back to Vietnam.
Over the years, the Huey has received some updates. But the Air Force never changed the helicopter’s distinctive two rotor blades—the reason for its famed noise—unlike the Marine Corps’ upgraded four-blade UH-1Y Venom.
The interior also remains remains largely old-school: lots of analog cockpit instruments, exposed wires, and a relatively spartan seating area. The Air Force says the cabin can be modified to accommodate up to 13 people, but on an Aug. 24 media flight, just a few TV reporters with bulky cameras had to squeeze in “like a clown car,” one of the pilots on the flight observed.
Despite a recent rash of precautionary landings in the past two months, Griggs, a flight engineer, says the Hueys are “as safe as they’ve ever been,” and the Air Force’s statistics show major mishaps on the decline over the past decade.
Many of the flights are training for the contingency mission, or learning how to navigate the notoriously complex airspace of Washington. On Aug. 24, the radio rarely stops buzzing with chatter during a brief 30-minute jaunt around the city—a trip that would take hours in typical D.C. traffic.
Nevertheless, the Huey’s age is undeniable. Like many of the Air Force’s older fleets, spare parts are hard to come by as manufacturers either disappear or stop making them. In turn, the fleet’s mission capable rate slipped below 75 percent in 2024, the most recent year of public data. That’s still far higher than many other aircraft, but the first time it’s been below that benchmark in at least a decade.
The time has come for something new, Griggs said. But in the immediate future, the Huey isn’t going anywhere. The HH-60W at the 5th’s activation ceremony isn’t staying at Andrews—it actually belongs to the New York Air National Guard.
The first HH-60Ws actually modified for the Andrews mission will arrive “soon,” a wing spokesperson said, but they could offer no more specific timeline. In the medium term, the goal is to achieve initial operational capability on the HH-60W by 2029 and full operational capability by 2030. So for the next four years at least, the Huey will keep flying.
A New Aircraft
The HH-60W, originally designed for combat search and rescue, offers a few obvious advantages over the UH-1N—it can fly faster, farther, and be refueled in the air. It has a larger cabin, accommodating more people or cargo.
There are other advantages that are harder to see. Schmautz likened the glass cockpit’s upgraded displays to a Tesla car compared to the Huey’s stick-shift transmission. The Whiskey also has a more advanced version of the ADS-B technology aircraft use to broadcast their location to other aircraft and controllers—while the UH-1N sends an ADS-B signal out, it does not have the ability to receive it. The HH-60W can do both. Officials noted that the UH-1N has other systems for situational awareness, but ADS-B is considered the standard.
Lt. Col. James Gray, director of operations for the 5th, said the HH-60W “actually takes some of the load off of the pilot and the crew at times because it’s just a newer airframe.”
Some features of the HH-60W needed for combat rescue, like its externally mounted guns, won’t be needed for the mission at Andrews. But at the activation ceremony, 316th Operations Group Col. Kevin Geoffroy made the case that the combat search and rescue community that uses the HH-60W now has more in common with the units at Andrews than it appears at first glance.
“We both hold quiet, constant vigils, persistently rehearsing our mission and waiting to respond with exceptional speed and skill when our nation calls,” he said.
A New Unit
The idea to put replace the Hueys at Andrews is not new—for several years, the Air Force planned to use the MH-139 Grey Wolf, a modified commercial helicopter, for the job. Budgetary and programmatic developments led the service to abandon those plans last July and pivot to the HH-60W, using backup inventory.
The idea to activate a new squadron was similarly bandied about for a while, Geoffroy said. But it wasn’t until this June that he and wing leadership pitched the idea to Air Force District of Washington leadership. It moved with unusual rapidity through the Pentagon bureaucracy, and now the 5th must figure out how to manage the delicate conversion process.
Gray said one of his first orders of business is figuring out how to get Airmen qualified on the new helicopter.
“I’m very, very eager to figure out how we start to convert the aircrew. There’s a ton of unknowns still, but I have to build a plan that we can at least start to deviate from. So I’m very much wanting to get down in the weeds, know the aircrew and who we’re going to start moving over,” Gray said. “So that’s my focus from an operational standpoint.”
Members of the 5th will initially fly the UH-1N before becoming dual-qualified on the HH-60W. A handful of crew at Andrews already have experience on both the HH-60 and UH-1, Schmautz among them, but there are many who will need to learn the new system or come in from other bases.
Then there are broader questions about how the new 5th Helicopter Squadron and the HH-60W fleet at Andrews will fit within the broader Air Force. The service is in the midst of reevaluating how it does combat search and rescue, a process that got a bit of extra scrutiny with the dramatic rescue of an F-15E crew in Iran this spring.
The HH-60s going to Andrews are coming from backup inventory, not the operational fleet, and officials took pains at the 5th’s activation ceremony to stress that they want to help the combat rescue team, not be a drain.
“We will work tirelessly to be a value-added addition to your team,” Geoffroy said. “We will welcome the aviators who require a break from the heavy burdens of deployment, and in turn, we will prepare our aircrews to become absolute experts in the Jolly Green II.”

South Africa records over 3,400 measles cases
South Africa has recorded 3,462 confirmed measles cases since January 2026, with outbreaks reported in the Western Cape, Free State, KwaZulu-Natal, and Northern Cape, among children aged one to 14 years, the country’s Department of Health said on Wednesday.
Department spokesperson Foster Mohale said the proportion of unvaccinated children under one year old had increased from 12.1% in 2017 to an alarming 36.3% between January and April 2026. This effectively triples the number of completely unvaccinated children and leaves hundreds of thousands of infants at risk of life-threatening illnesses.
Mohale added routine immunisation coverage had fallen severely across all 52 districts in the country, which means that, at current rates, South Africa is unlikely to reach the World Health Organization’s critical 90% coverage threshold for childhood immunisation. He said the consequences of declining coverage include the resurgence of serious vaccine-preventable diseases, erosion of community, or herd immunity, and higher rates of long-term disability and death among infants.
“The majority of cases (70.9%) are in children aged 1–14 years, directly linked to low immunisation coverage,” Mohale stressed.
Mohale added that South Africa has maintained its polio-free status since 2014, while sporadic cases of diphtheria had been detected, primarily in the Western Cape, underscoring gaps in booster coverage and disease surveillance. Pertussis, or whooping cough, cases have also been identified in several provinces, predominantly affecting infants under six months who are too young to be fully vaccinated, Mohale said.
According to spokesperson, this poses severe risks for pregnant women because of the potential for congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). “Unvaccinated children can endanger infants and immunocompromised individuals who cannot be vaccinated, and weak coverage undermines early detection and rapid response to emerging threats.”
Mohale said the department is prioritising an immediate, coordinated national response, including catch-up vaccination campaigns targeting children who have missed doses and under-immunised cohorts in all districts. “Every child deserves protection, and safeguarding them is a collective responsibility,” he concluded.

byunggwon na’s ALIT lamp balances ceramic, wood and light in one quiet composition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:55:14 UTC
23:55:14 KST

Seoul-based designer Byunggwon Na explores the relationship between ceramic, wood, and illumination with ALIT, a lamp reduced to two contrasting materials and a deceptively simple geometry. Beginning with the translucent qualities of ceramic, Na studied how light could pass through, bounce against, and diffuse across its surface before introducing a square wooden column as the project’s only additional material.
The result sets the softly curved ceramic shade directly on top of the timber base, allowing light to fall across both surfaces at once. Rather than hiding the meeting point between structure and diffuser, ALIT makes it the focus: a small material conversation between something solid and rectilinear below and something thinner, lighter, and altogether less obedient above.
Byunggwon Na presents the ALIT lamp | images courtesy of Byunggwon Na
A CIRCLE FOLDS INTO FOUR CURVES
Produced through slip casting, the ceramic shade begins conceptually as a circular plane folded into four quadrants, generating four gently curved surfaces around its perimeter. Its shape sits somewhere between strict geometry and an organic form, with Na likening its silhouette to a maple seed or petal drifting down before eventually coming to rest on the wooden column.
The shade is not permanently attached to the base and can instead be lifted off, replaced, or exchanged with another version. This allows different ceramic pieces to alter the character of the lamp while giving the shade a life beyond illumination: removed from the column, it can work independently as an object or tray. The wooden lamp, meanwhile, continues functioning without it — no complicated assembly or dramatic intervention required.
the colored ceramic shade creates a different atmosphere, with light softly diffusing from beneath
COLOR CHANGES HOW THE CERAMIC GLOWS
Na also experiments with color by mixing pigments directly into the liquid slip before casting, producing ceramic shades whose tone runs consistently through the material rather than being applied later as a colored glaze. While the lighter ceramic versions allow illumination to travel through the shade, the pigmented pieces become opaque, fundamentally changing how the lamp distributes its light.
Instead of glowing from within, these colored shades direct a softer pool of light from underneath, where it interacts with the grain and surface of the wooden column. Across its different configurations, ALIT treats illumination less as something simply switched on and more as another material in the composition — one that shifts depending on what happens to be sitting on top.

EU, 14 countries condemn Israel's seizure of UNRWA facility in occupied East Jerusalem

Mohammad Sio
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
The European Union and 14 countries on Wednesday condemned Israel's seizure of a UNRWA-run facility in occupied East Jerusalem, reaffirming support for the UN agency tasked with providing assistance to Palestinian refugees.
In a joint statement published by the Belgian Consulate-General in Jerusalem, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Denmark, the EU, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Switzerland and the UK all strongly condemned the “unlawful entry” by Israeli forces into UNRWA's Qalandia Training Center on Tuesday and the seizure of UNRWA facilities in East Jerusalem.
The countries, all members of the UNRWA Advisory Commission, noted that UN premises are protected under international law through the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations, and therefore must be respected.
They called for Israel’s “immediate and full compliance” with UN directives allowing UNRWA to carry out its mandated activities without interference.
Signatories further called on Israel “to honor its obligations and to halt all disruptions to UNRWA's activities and operations without delay.”
On Tuesday, Israeli forces expelled UNRWA staff from the center, seized the facility, and raised the Israeli flag in its courtyard.
Israeli military personnel deployed in the streets of the Qalandia refugee camp and the nearby Kafr Aqab neighborhood, where they conducted raids and searches and interrogated Palestinians.
The moves have drawn widespread international criticism.
The Qalandia center includes educational, vocational and health facilities, training workshops, classrooms, dormitories and administrative buildings.
Established in 1952 as UNRWA's first center in Palestine, the facility serves roughly 270 students in 16 vocational specialties, with between 250 and 300 students graduating from the center each year.
Since 1967, Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in violation of UN resolutions.
The latest developments come amid stepped-up Israeli pressure on UNRWA after the Knesset (Israel’s parliament) approved legislation in 2024 restricting the agency’s operations, including a ban on its activities inside Israel.
The controversial legislation took effect early last year.
Last October, the International Court of Justice reaffirmed Israel’s obligation to respect the inviolability of UN facilities -- including those run by UNRWA -- and refrain from interfering with the agency’s operations.
One month later, despite Israeli pressure, the UN General Assembly renewed UNRWA’s mandate for three years, allowing the agency to continue its work until June 2029.

See last night’s ‘blood moon’ eclipse from around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:52:09 UTC
23:52:09 KST

Last night’s near-total lunar eclipse did not disappoint. In the second and final lunar eclipse of the year, our natural satellite transformed into a stunning red-orange “blood moon” as almost all of it fell under Earth’s shadow.
During a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the sun and moon, partially or totally obstructing sunlight on the latter. In this case, more than 96 percent of the moon was covered by Earth’s dark shadow, or umbra, according to NASA, making it a “deep partial eclipse.”
The reddish tone comes from the way Earth’s atmosphere filters light—reddish hues slip through to the other side, while other colors are refracted away, much like a sunset.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Last night’s eclipse began around 9:23 P.M. EDT on Thursday and lasted until about 3:02 A.M. EDT on Friday. The height of the eclipse occurred at 12:13 A.M. EDT, when the moon was 96.3 percent covered in shadow.
We collected some of the best pictures of the event from around the world.
Do you want to catch the next eclipse? While 2027 will see three very subtle, or penumbral, lunar eclipses, the next total lunar eclipse won’t occur until December 31, 2028. But two solar eclipses—when the moon will pass between Earth and the sun—will take place in 2027: a “ring of fire” annular eclipse on February 6 and a total solar eclipse on August 2.

More than 40% of electric vehicle crashes involve pedestrians or cyclists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:51:25 UTC
23:51:25 KST

The percentage of accidents involving vulnerable road users is bigger for EVs than for petrol cars. This is partly due to how quiet EVs are, says traffic institute
More than 40% of electric vehicle crashes involve pedestrians or cyclists
More than 40% of accidents in Belgium involving an electric or hybrid vehicle also involve a pedestrian or cyclist. This is a far higher percentage than the percentage of accidents involving all cars and vulnerable road users, which is 27%. The figures come from Belgian road safety institute Vias.
In the last five years, the number of electric and hybrid vehicles in Belgium has risen from three to 20%. This figure will only continue to grow, notes Vias. The agency points to the lack of noise produced by electric vehicles (EVs) as one of the reasons why they are more likely to be involved in accidents with vulnerable road users.
Car sounds differ
Since 2021, all EVs sold in the EU must be equipped with an Acoustic Vehicle Alerting System (AVAS), which emits a noise when the vehicle is moving slowly or reversing. This was introduce so that when an EV is moving through a parking lot, say, or rounding a corner, vulnerable road users would be alerted.
According to research carried out by Vias, pedestrians do not always hear this sound. The institute conducted a study with 70 people, half of which were visually impaired. The study involved fully electric and hybrid vehicles, as well as petrol cars.
In nearly 40% of cases when the car was moving at 10km per hour, the test subjects did not hear a hybrid vehicle coming. This was 32% for fully EVs and 27% for petrol vehicles.
The results were similar when the speed increased to 20kph. In nearly one in five cases, pedestrians did not hear the hybrid vehicle coming. This was 7% for electric vehicles and 11% for petrol cars.
‘Increase sound levels’
Vias also notes that not all AVAS systems emit the same sounds, so pedestrians don’t always know if the sound is a car or not, especially if there is a lot of background noise. Vias would like regulators to require that AVAS systems are uniform with regards to sound.
“Right now, manufacturers choose the sound themselves,” said Vias in a statement. “We also ask that sound levels increase for cars driving up to 10kph so that people who are visually impaired can hear them.”

Uganda: World's 'youngest monarch' dies aged 34
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

Uganda: World's 'youngest monarch' dies aged 34
August 28, 2026
Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king of the traditional pre-colonial kingdom of Tooro, has died aged just 34, the prime minister of Tooro announced late on Thursday.
"It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV," Tooro's regional leader Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki said on social media.
What is the role of traditional monarchs in Uganda?
Uganda is a republic, ruled by a parliament and a nominally-elected head of state, longstanding President Yoweri Museveni, who's been in power since 1986.
But the country retains several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms as they were constituted in the pre-colonial period. Their power is largely symbolic but they wield considerable cultural and social influence.
Although they were banned after independence from British colonial rule in 1962 by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the nascent country, Museveni reinstated the traditional monarchs in 1993.
Oyo Nyimba was arguably the most recognizable among them, not least because of his unusual story, taking the throne at the age of just 3 in 1995.
What did officials say about Oyo Nyimba's death?
Regional leader Akiiki said that the king had died late on Thursday, without giving a cause of death. He said an official statement with further details, including the funeral and mourning arrangements, would follow later.
He called on the people of Tooro to "remain united, calm and prayerful during this difficult time."
Akiiki also issued one surprising claim about the unmarried young king, who since a very young age had been seen as perhaps Uganda's most eligible bachelor.
"The continuity of the Crown is assured," he said. "His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom."
Ugandan opposition leader Bobi Wine also issued condolences online.
Oyo Nyimba's death triggered an outpouring of grief online and widespread national coverage in Uganda.
Who was King Oyo Nyimba of Tooro?
Born on April 16, 1992, Oyo was the second-born child of the late Omukama Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III and Queen Best Kemigisa Kaboyo, with two sisters.
He ascended to the throne of Tooro, an area in western Uganda near the border to Congo, in 1995 after his father's death.
His unusual status as a modern "boy king" led to considerable interest early in his reign, including from world leaders like former Libyan strongman Moammar Gadhafi, who repeatedly visited Tooro.
Oyo's mother was among his key advisers in his younger years, as was President Yoweri Museveni, who attended his coming-of-age 18th birthday party in 2010 in Fort Portal.
In 2025, the Guinness Book of World Records said he was still the youngest reigning monarch alive, its most recent renewal of the record.
He spent time in the UK at Winchester University to conclude his education. This time away from Uganda prompted a failed challenge to his position in 2015, when his cousin Prince David Kijanangoma declared himself the rightful king of Tooro, accusing Oyo of neglecting the region.
Oyo was known as a lover of sports, and a fan of London football club Arsenal. He took interest in causes including HIV prevention, environmental conservation, tourism and climate change, for instance when he embarked on a hiking expedition in the Rwenzori Mountains in 2022 to try to showcase Uganda's tourism potential and the risks of climate change.
Prior to the news of his death, a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media as saying Oyo had been seriously ill and was seeking medical treatment in the US.

Ransomware group says it stole Berlin data, offers it for auction
BERLIN - A ransomware group said on Aug 28 it was putting up for auction a trove of data it stole from Berlin state agencies, and city officials refused to pay.
The Rhysida group, which researchers say operates from Russia or Eastern Europe, said on its website it took 5.79 terabytes of data including 46,500 contracts as well as emails, phone numbers, passwords and classified information.

The cyberattack on Berlin's network comes less than a month before the city-state holds elections on Sept 20.

Officials could not provide details on the content or scope of the affected data because the extent of the breach was still being examined, Wegner said at a press conference.
Spranger said the city’s election infrastructure had not been affected and that, according to security officials, no data related to the election had been compromised.
Ransomware group targets government
Rhysida has claimed nearly 280 attacks since it emerged in June 2023, according to cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch.
Roughly half of its victims have been in the US, followed by the UK, Canada and Italy, as well as other nations, according to Ransom-DB, a ransomware analysis and tracking service.
The group has repeatedly targeted government institutions, such as the October 2023 hack of the British Library. The group has also claimed attacks on the Chilean army, schools, healthcare facilities and businesses of all sizes. REUTERS
