Takaichi Is No Abe: Japan’s New Conservative Politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:35:00 UTC
23:35:00 KST

For many years, Japan’s current Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has been portrayed by international media as the heir to Abe Shinzo’s political legacy. Her nationalist views, assertive security posture, and close ties to Japan’s conservative movement have made the comparison seem natural.
There is good reason for the comparison. As Michael Green recently argued in Foreign Affairs, Takaichi has continued an important part of Abe’s strategic legacy: strengthening Japan’s defense capabilities, deepening the Japan-U.S. alliance, and responding more assertively to the challenge posed by China. From this perspective, Takaichi represents the continuation of a strategy that seeks to make Japan a stronger and more indispensable U.S. ally.
But strategic continuity should not be confused with political continuity. After roughly 10 months in power, the differences between Takaichi and Abe are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Rather than simply reviving “Abe politics,” Takaichi appears to be developing a new political style of her own: more personalized, more confrontational, and more dependent on emotional mobilization through social media. If Abe represented a conservative politics tempered by strategic pragmatism, Takaichi may represent something closer to a new form of conservative populism.
In other words, Takaichi may be Abe’s heir in grand strategy, but she is not necessarily adopting his tactics. The political methods emerging from Takaichi’s camp suggest a significant change in how Japan’s conservatives seek to mobilize domestic public support.
The controversy over the use of artificial intelligence (AI) during the 2025 Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) leadership election and the 2026 House of Representatives election offers a revealing example. Shukan Bunshun, a Japanese weekly magazine known for exposing political scandals, recently reported that people close to Takaichi’s camp had used AI to produce large numbers of short videos attacking political opponents and circulated them widely online. The revelations triggered a public backlash and created the first serious political challenge of Takaichi’s premiership.
The use of digital technology for political campaigning is hardly unprecedented. What is more significant is how the technology appears to have been used: not simply to communicate policy positions or mobilize supporters, but to amplify political antagonism and shape voters’ emotions. During the Abe era, the prime minister’s office was highly sophisticated in managing the media and political narrative, but Abe generally maintained a clearer distinction between political messaging and outright mobilization through antagonism.
Takaichi’s political operation appears more willing to blur that boundary. This is particularly important because Takaichi has cultivated a direct relationship with voters through social media. Rather than relying primarily on Japan’s established media organizations, she uses X to communicate directly with the public.
According to the Financial Times, Japanese business leaders have become increasingly frustrated with what they see as Takaichi’s unwillingness to listen to views from outside her political circle. They are also concerned that she has become increasingly hostile toward the mainstream media while relying more heavily on social media to maintain her popularity. This approach may be politically effective in the short term. But it also carries potential risks. Social media rewards confrontation, immediacy, and emotional intensity. A political leader who relies heavily on such platforms can easily find herself governing through the logic of mobilization rather than the logic of consensus-building.
A second concern is the uncertainty surrounding Takaichi’s decision-making. In April, the Japanese magazine Sentaku reported that Takaichi had clashed with Imai Nobuya, a senior political adviser during the Abe era, over the possible deployment of the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to the Middle East. According to the report, Imai opposed Takaichi’s reported intention to send Japanese forces to the Strait of Hormuz to support U.S. military operations against Iran.
The details of the episode remain disputed, and the report should therefore be treated with caution. But the broader question it raises is difficult to dismiss: Does Takaichi have the same capacity for institutional and strategic balancing that characterized Abe’s leadership?
Abe was undoubtedly a committed conservative. Yet he was also an unusually pragmatic political operator. He relied heavily on trusted bureaucrats and political advisers, and he understood the importance of reconciling political ideology with institutional constraints and strategic realities. On major security and foreign policy questions, his administration typically sought to balance competing interests before making consequential decisions.
Takaichi’s approach appears more personal. Her foreign policy positions are often closely associated with her own ideological convictions, and she has shown less evidence of the cautious political calibration that was one of Abe’s defining characteristics.
Nowhere is this difference more consequential than in relations with China. Abe is frequently described outside Japan as a China hawk. That description is not entirely wrong, but it misses an important and delicate part of his diplomacy. Despite his nationalist reputation, Abe repeatedly demonstrated an ability to separate ideological commitments from strategic interests. In April 2018, for example, according to a memoir written by a Taiwanese political figure, Abe declined to meet former Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui, who was staying at the same hotel in Okinawa, apparently to avoid unnecessarily provoking Beijing.
In 2019, Abe also sent a private letter to Yasukuni Shrine exploring the possibility of removing the enshrined Class-A war criminals, an effort that would have reduced one of the most persistent sources of friction in Japan’s relations with its neighbors. (I learned of this episode in 2025 while interviewing Kitaoka Shinichi, one of Abe’s key foreign policy advisers, at Stanford University.)
Whatever one thinks of Abe’s broader political legacy, these episodes demonstrate that his conservatism was accompanied by a strong instinct for strategic risk management. He understood that nationalist symbolism could generate domestic political benefits while imposing substantial diplomatic costs.
Takaichi has yet to demonstrate the same degree of restraint. Her approach to China appears to be driven more directly by ideological convictions and political instincts than by a broader strategy for managing Japan’s long-term relationship with its most important neighboring power.
This is precisely where the distinction between Takaichi and Abe becomes most important. Abe sought to strengthen Japan’s alliance with the United States while simultaneously maintaining channels for stable relations with China. His foreign policy was not simply “tough” or “soft”; it was fundamentally about strategic management.
If Takaichi is indeed continuing Abe’s grand strategy by strengthening the Japan-U.S. alliance and making Japan more capable of confronting China, that does not necessarily mean that she is reproducing Abe’s broader approach to statecraft. Abe’s strategic vision depended not only on strengthening Japan’s position, but also on managing the risks created by that stronger position.
Even some of the architects of Abe’s foreign policy now appear concerned about the direction of Japanese diplomacy. On July 2, Yachi Shotaro, the former head of Japan’s National Security Secretariat, wrote in his Nikkei series “My Life History” that the most important challenge facing Japanese diplomacy in the 21st century is its relationship with China. Japan, he argued, must think over the medium and long term about how to build a stable and strategic relationship with China while remaining a U.S. ally and recognizing China as an important neighboring country.
Yachi is hardly a dove on China. After Abe returned to power in 2006, he played a central role in efforts to improve China-Japan relations. According to interview records cited in journalist Funabashi Yoichi’s 2024 book on politics during the Abe era, “Children of Destiny,” Yachi also accompanied former Prime Minister Fukuda Yasuo to China in 2014 and helped facilitate the resumption of China-Japan summit diplomacy.
His remarks therefore reveal something important about the Abe-era foreign-policy establishment. Its members may have supported a stronger Japan and a more robust alliance with Washington, but they also understood that strategic competition with China could not substitute for diplomacy. For them, managing the relationship with Beijing was an essential component of Japanese diplomatic statecraft.
Takaichi’s politics appear to place greater emphasis on confrontation. That difference may ultimately determine whether her premiership can endure. A June poll by Jiji Press put Takaichi’s approval rating at roughly 54 percent, down from around 70 percent at the beginning of the year. For a prime minister who has not yet fully consolidated her political authority, this is hardly an unassailable position. A major scandal, economic setback, or diplomatic crisis could quickly weaken her support.
Takaichi may share Abe’s nationalism, his skepticism toward the postwar liberal order, and his determination to strengthen Japan’s security posture. She may also continue many of the strategic policies that Michael Green and other scholars have associated with Abe’s legacy. But political inheritance is about more than policy positions. It is also about governing instincts.
Abe understood that conservative politics could be sustained only by combining ideology with pragmatism, nationalism with diplomacy, and political mobilization with institutional management. Takaichi appears to be experimenting with a different formula – one that places greater emphasis on personal leadership, social media politics, emotional mobilization, and confrontation with perceived political and cultural opponents.
That does not necessarily mean Takaichi will fail. Indeed, such a political style may prove highly effective in an era of fragmented media and growing public distrust of established institutions. Nor does it mean that Takaichi’s foreign policy is fundamentally incompatible with Abe’s. On the contrary, she may succeed in making Japan an even stronger U.S. ally. But a stronger Japan and a more predictable Japan are not necessarily the same thing.
U.S. policymakers should recognize that Japan is entering a new political era. The question of whether Takaichi is Abe’s successor is ultimately a distraction. What matters is whether she can turn her personalized style of conservative politics into an effective governing system. If she can, Japan’s conservatives may have found a new political formula – one that combines strategic nationalism with populist mobilization and direct communication with voters. If she cannot, the same forces that made Takaichi powerful could also make her government increasingly unstable and expose Japan to unnecessary security risks.

Syria's al-Sharaa appoints SDF commander as adviser after Kurdish force dissolves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:34:43 UTC
23:34:43 KST

The appointment came days after Abdi declared the Kurdish-led force dissolved and integrated into the Syrian army, ending a decade of independent existence in a move Washington called "genuine integration".
Mazloum Abdi, who led the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) until its dissolution this week, was appointed adviser to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, Syria's official news agency SANA announced Friday.
Abdi on Tuesday declared the SDF dissolved and announced the completion of its integration into Syria's armed forces — a process that ended the Kurdish-led force's decade-long existence as an independent military organisation.
US Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack described the SDF's dissolution as "genuine integration" and said assigning influential government positions to Kurdish officials, including Abdi, showed respect for Kurdish leadership and the contribution Kurdish forces had made to regional stability.
Who is Mazloum Abdi?
Born Mustafa Khalil Abdi in 1967 in the Kobani region near the Turkish border, Mazloum Abdi studied engineering at Aleppo University and joined the PKK in the early 1990s, eventually rising through its ranks in Iraq and Europe.
He is known by several names, including Mazloum Kobani, Ferhat Abdi Şahin and Mustafa Halil Abdi. Turkey considers him a terrorist and says he is the subject of an Interpol Red Notice.
Syria analyst Nanar Hawach of the International Crisis Group described him as one of the "experienced cadres of the PKK" who founded the People's Protection Units in Syria after the civil war began in 2011.
Abdi gained international recognition during the battle for Kobani in 2015, when Kurdish forces defeated the so-called Islamic State Group (IS) after months of fighting.
The victory became a defining moment for Syria's Kurds and the beginning of Abdi's close partnership with Washington, which backed the SDF as its primary ground partner against the IS throughout the Syrian civil war.
He is reported to have been close to Abdullah Öcalan, the imprisoned founder of the PKK, who announced in 2025 that the organisation was abandoning armed struggle.
In 2025, Öcalan, whose isolation conditions had been eased following years of requests by Kurdish politicians in Turkey, called on the PKK to lay down arms and abandon armed struggle.
The PKK formally accepted the call and announced it was disbanding as a fighting force, while Abdi said the move did not apply to the SDF.
Recognition from Damascus
The SDF's dissolution and Abdi's appointment are the culmination of an agreement signed in January 2026, which stipulated that Kurdish military and civilian institutions in northern and northeastern Syria would be brought under central state authority.
On 16 January al-Sharaa signed a decree guaranteeing the national rights of Kurds, recognising Kurdish as a national language, declaring Nowruz an official public holiday and granting citizenship to Kurds previously denied legal status — the first such recognition since Syria gained independence in 1946.
By integrating into the Syrian armed forces, the SDF retained aspects of its internal command structure within those brigades during an initial transitional period, though the long-term arrangements remain subject to ongoing negotiation.
Armed clashes in January in which the SDF lost large swathes of territory to Syrian government forces, and the United States' decision to support the new Damascus leadership, pushed Abdi toward a negotiated settlement.
For al-Sharaa the deal is a significant achievement in his effort to extend state authority across all Syrian territory. For the Kurds it marks the end of their de facto autonomous administration in the northeast.
Abdi said political efforts would continue to ensure Kurdish rights were enshrined in the Syrian constitution. "Our struggle to secure our people's rights in the constitution will continue," he said.
Turkey regards the YPG — the main Kurdish component of the SDF — as the Syrian branch of the PKK, which is designated a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the US, the EU and the UK.
Ankara has conducted multiple military operations against YPG and SDF positions in Syria.
Ankara has pressed al-Sharaa to ensure that Kurdish armed groups are fully disarmed and that the YPG's former military structures do not survive within the Syrian state.

Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami revealed a series of initiatives aimed at empowering women
NEW DELHI: Chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Raksha Bandhan announced a series of measures aimed at improving women’s safety, mobility and economic empowerment, including free travel in Roadways buses for women aged 60 years and above.The announcements were made during a Raksha Bandhan programme at Chakarpur Stadium, where women tied rakhis to Dhami. The chief minister said the initiatives reflected the government’s commitment to women’s dignity, safety and self-reliance.Under the new provision, women aged 60 years and above will be able to travel free of cost in Roadways buses. The facility was earlier available to senior citizens above 65 years of age.Dhami also announced that 10 of the 100 electric buses to be operated in Dehradun under the PM e-Bus Sewa will be dedicated to women as Pink e-Buses. He said the facility would subsequently be expanded to other parts of Uttarakhand in phases to provide women with safer and more convenient public transport.The government has also increased the concessional bank loan limit under the Women’s Self-Employment Scheme from Rs 2 lakh to Rs 2.50 lakh.
Dhami said the move was intended to provide women with greater access to capital and encourage them to become employment providers rather than only job seekers.He further announced plans to develop modern, high-tech toilets with contemporary facilities at major public places, markets, tourist destinations and other important locations across the state. The facilities will focus on cleanliness, privacy, safety and convenience for women.Addressing the gathering, Dhami said women’s dignity and safety were among the government’s highest priorities. He said Raksha Bandhan was not only a celebration of the bond between brothers and sisters but also a reminder of responsibility, respect and commitment towards women.
Dhami highlighted schemes including the Nanda Gaura Yojana, Chief Minister Mahalakshmi Kit Yojana, 181 Women Helpline and One Stop Centres. He also said women have been provided 30 percent horizontal reservation in government services.The chief minister said 3.09 lakh women in Uttarakhand had become Lakhpati Didis. He urged them to set a bigger goal of becoming Crorepati Didis and assured them of continued government support.He also highlighted interest-free loans of up to Rs 5 lakh for Self-Help Groups and the Mukhyamantri Sashakt Bahna Utsav Yojana, under which women are being provided better market access for their products.

Can Discussions in Cambridge Help Afghans Build a Post-Taliban Future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

In the past, too many plans for Afghanistan have been designed far from the people expected to live under them. On the surface, the Cambridge Afghanistan Series, organized by the Mosaic Global Foundation, may seem to be more of the same. But the series is genuinely attempting something different, which is not to hand people of Afghanistan another foreign-made political formula, but to create a space in which Afghans themselves can identify the principles, institutions, and sequence required to reclaim their political future.
On September 4 and 5, the Mosaic Global Foundation will convene the fifth Cambridge Afghanistan Series (CAS V) at Jesus College, Cambridge. It will bring together Afghan political voices, civil society actors, human rights advocates, academics, and other stakeholders to discuss pathways toward peace, inclusion, and prosperity.
At CAS III in 2024, six major political factions, including two major armed resistance groups, presented their visions for Afghanistan. An independent examination found that, despite their public divisions, more than 90 percent of their proposals overlapped in substance. CAS IV in 2025 began a more open discussion of the remaining disagreements.
I participated in CAS IV in 2025. I did not see complete unity, nor did I expect it. Afghanistan’s political actors carry different histories, represent different constituencies, bear different grievances, and have different ideas about the state. What I saw was something more modest but genuinely hopeful as major political currents, civil society, and human rights advocates from different ethnic backgrounds and communities gathered to discuss the future of their country and search for an Afghan-led solution.
At a time when the Taliban has tried to erase political plurality inside Afghanistan, the sight of Afghans arguing across their differences, without denying one another a place in the conversation, offered a glimpse of another political culture. At CAS IV Afghans discussed a wide range of topics tied to the future of their country while celebrating their culture with traditional food and music on a night they named “Poetry Night.”
A working group, facilitated by Mosaic, produced a Comprehensive Composite Roadmap, or CCR, at CAS IV in 2025.
The CCR emerged from a process that began at CAS III in 2024. Six major political groups were invited to present their strategic proposals, while an expert panel reviewed 12 roadmaps and proposals in total. The dialogue revealed more than 90 percent overlap among these initiatives in their strategic positions. An independent assessment commissioned by Mosaic subsequently confirmed this finding.
Following that assessment, an Independent Working Group was formed to consolidate the different proposals. It gathered in total 21 roadmaps and proposals from political groups, civil society organizations, and resistance groups and synthesized them into the CCR.
Ahead of CAS V in 2026, the consultation process is continuing and expanding to include specialists, human rights organizations, and religious scholars, or ulema. The aim is to ensure that the CCR incorporates contributions from all strata of Afghan society and reflects as comprehensive and inclusive a range of perspectives as possible.
The CCR rests on three non-negotiable commitments: Afghanistan must have a government chosen by its people, human rights must be respected, and equality – including gender equality – must be guaranteed. Around those commitments, it proposes a broader transition based on national dialogue, regional peace dialogues, and international consensus through a United Nations-led process.
Its central mechanism is a proposed Political Convergence Framework. This would bring together anti-Taliban armed resistance groups, political parties and platforms, civil society and human rights organizations, women’s movements, religious scholars, youth, journalists, professional groups, and diaspora representatives. Its initial responsibilities would include adopting a founding charter, creating a joint secretariat, drafting a detailed transition plan, coordinating internal resistance and civil action, and conducting regional and international diplomacy.
The roadmap then envisages an international conference, the creation of a preparatory committee, the formation of a representative Constituent Assembly, and a merit-based transitional government. The Constituent Assembly would help draft a new constitution and provide legal oversight during the transition. The transitional government would maintain order, build institutions, prepare free elections, and transfer authority to a government elected by the people.
The reason behind this sequencing is the belief that removing the Taliban, by itself, would not answer the fundamental questions that have repeatedly destabilized Afghanistan: Who possesses political authority? How is that authority distributed? How are citizens protected from domination by the state or by one another? How can ethnic, linguistic, religious, and gender diversity be reflected without reducing politics to permanent communal quotas?
To my knowledge, no other current Afghanistan initiative has undertaken this particular task at comparable breadth: placing competing roadmaps side by side, identifying their shared core, preserving the questions that remain disputed, and trying to convert overlapping principles into a common mechanism for action.
Afghanistan’s own recent history provides the clearest warning of why such an initiative is necessary. In 2001, for instance, the Bonn process reduced political reconstruction to a mechanical redistribution of power and a quota system for elite rotation. This meant distributing government positions and political influence among a limited circle of established figures and groups, based on negotiated shares, rather than constructing a genuinely representative system grounded in broad citizen participation, public consent, and accountable institutions. Whatever institutions a conference may establish, an elite bargain is not the same as a durable social contract. CAS must not reproduce another closed agreement among familiar figures in a different foreign conference room. It must connect political negotiation to citizen rights, representative institutions, public accountability, and a fair process for deciding the country’s constitutional future.
Nor should the claim of 90 percent agreement be allowed to conceal the difficult 10 percent where groups disagree. The collected roadmaps still differ over centralization and decentralization, engagement with the Taliban versus struggle against it, the proper role of international actors, the meaning of territorial integrity, and the mechanisms required to correct structural inequality. These are not minor questions. They concern the distribution of power and the identity of the future Afghan state.
That is why CAS V must commit to show how representatives are selected, how women and communities inside Afghanistan influence decisions, how disagreements are recorded, and how the process will communicate with Afghans who cannot enter the Jesus College halls. Women cannot be present merely as symbols while established male politicians negotiate over authority. Civil society cannot be used to decorate a settlement reached elsewhere without them. Those exposed to repression inside Afghanistan must have secure and meaningful channels into the process. Without such commitments, CAS V will become another annual discussion. With them, Cambridge could become the place where the fragmented Afghanistan opposition begins to acquire institutional form.
A conference in Cambridge cannot, on its own, end Taliban rule. A roadmap cannot substitute for political organization inside Afghanistan, nor can international recognition manufacture domestic legitimacy. But the absence of a coherent alternative has long weakened Afghan democratic forces and enabled outside actors to treat Taliban rule as the only available reality. The CCR challenges that fatalism.
The true measure of CAS V will be whether those gathered can establish a fair process for acting together while continuing to disagree. Afghanistan does not need another self-appointed ruler or another elite pact build thousands of miles away. It needs a legitimate path through which its people can recover the right to choose. If the Cambridge Afghanistan Series can help build that path, then a conversation taking place thousands of miles away may still belong, unmistakably, to Afghanistan.

mamuli translates georgian culture and traditions into layered restaurant interior
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:30:48 UTC
23:30:48 KST

Mamuli Reimagines Georgian Identity Through Hospitality Design
With Mamuli, SOIA Design set out to create something more nuanced than a restaurant inspired by Georgia. The goal was to translate the character of Georgian culture into space without relying on familiar decorative symbols or turning heritage into a visual theme. The result is an interior built around interpretation rather than imitation, a warm, expressive environment in Krasnodar, in which traditional references, contemporary craftsmanship, and the rituals of hospitality come together as one experience.
From the beginning, the brief presented a clear challenge. The clients wanted Mamuli to feel unmistakably connected to Georgian culture while remaining sophisticated enough for a contemporary, cosmopolitan audience. They were looking for an interior that could compete visually within a crowded hospitality landscape, but without falling into the predictable language of ethnic or themed restaurants. The space also had to work hard functionally. It needed to transition naturally between intimate dinners, family occasions, wine experiences, and larger cultural events while retaining a strong and recognizable identity. For SOIA Design founders Anton and Ekaterina Baklan, this became an opportunity to approach cultural storytelling from a different direction. Instead of reproducing historical forms literally, the studio extracted ideas, shapes, materials, and associations from Georgian culture and transformed them into contemporary architectural elements.
Subtle Georgian references shape Mamuli’s material interior
The interior communicates its identity through a collection of details rather than a single dominant motif. A warm, earthy palette establishes the foundation of the restaurant. Subtle gold plaster catches and reflects the light, introducing a sense of richness while keeping the atmosphere understated. Above the dining area, custom chandeliers take inspiration from the form of Georgian beehives, turning a cultural reference into an almost sculptural architectural object. Other references are deliberately less obvious. Dark balusters shaped like peppercorns bring the tradition of Georgian spices into the interior through an unexpected, tactile gesture. The result is a form of storytelling that rewards attention: the cultural connection is present, but it does not need to announce itself. Craftsmanship plays an equally important role. Custom wooden elements with zigzag detailing wrap the columns, while tables made from sections of natural tree trunks preserve the irregularity and character of the material. A fireplace incorporated directly into a dining table becomes both a functional element and a theatrical centerpiece, creating a sense of intimacy around the act of gathering. Throughout the restaurant, bespoke furniture, millwork, shelving, and lighting were developed specifically for Mamuli. Rather than treating these elements as background decoration, SOIA Design Studio used them to establish a distinct visual vocabulary for the brand.
the bar counter and shelving were tailor-made to frame the restaurant’s vibrant social life
mamuli extends beyond dining into a social and cultural space
The restaurant was conceived as a flexible social environment rather than a collection of fixed dining zones. Different seating configurations support quiet meals as well as larger communal experiences. A dedicated tasting room provides a more intimate setting for exploring Georgian wine and cuisine, while a stage creates a focal point for performances, tastings, celebrations, and cultural programming. The planning also considers families as an integral part of the restaurant experience. A children’s playroom is incorporated into the overall concept without disrupting the atmosphere of the main dining areas. Even spaces that are often treated as secondary received the same level of attention. The restrooms continue the material language and storytelling established throughout the restaurant, ensuring that the design does not lose its identity once guests leave the main dining room.
Mamuli ultimately operates on several levels. It is a restaurant, but it is also an environment for gathering, celebration, discovery, and cultural exchange. For SOIA Design, the project demonstrates how cultural identity can be expressed without literal reproduction. Georgian influences are embedded into proportions, materials, objects, textures, and atmosphere, allowing guests to experience the spirit of the culture without entering a space built around clichés. The finished interior is intentionally layered. Some references are immediately visible; others reveal themselves through closer observation. Together they create an environment that feels rooted in tradition while remaining firmly contemporary. Mamuli is therefore less about recreating a place from the past and more about imagining how its cultural character might exist today, through architecture, craftsmanship, food, light, and the shared experience of gathering around a table.

Israeli clinic for Gaza children draws mixed reactions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:30:38 UTC
23:30:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Plan to open Israeli clinic in Gaza draws mixed reactions among Palestinians
An Israeli aid organisation is preparing to open a medical clinic for children in a displacement camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis City in southern Gaza, in an initiative that has drawn mixed reactions from residents amid the severe deterioration of the enclave's healthcare system.
The clinic, set up by Israeli aid group Natan for the "Gaza Children's Village" project, will start operations on 1 September, aiming to serve around 10,000 children, the organisation said in a press statement.
According to the group, the facility will offer preventive checkups, vaccinations, primary healthcare, specialist consultations and rehabilitation programs for children with disabilities.
Palestinian doctors and nurses will work at the clinic, while Israeli doctors will provide specialist consultations remotely through telemedicine services, it claimed.
The wider project also includes food distribution, education and psychological support programs. It said the educational activities aim to reject hatred and incitement.
According to Israeli newspaper Haaretz, the clinic cost about $ 200,000 to equip and is being funded through donations from Israelis and Jews around the world.
The initiative comes as Gaza's healthcare system continues to face shortages of medicines, medical equipment and other essential supplies after nearly three years of war.
'Soft power' and political motives
For Palestinians in war-torn Gaza, the involvement of an Israeli organisation has raised concerns about the initiative, despite the medical services it plans to provide.
Abu Mohammed, a displaced father of two, said he supports providing medical care to children but questioned the role of an Israeli organisation in delivering it.
"The problem isn't that Gaza's children receive treatment. Every child deserves it. The question is who caused these wounds in the first place?" he told The New Arab.
He said many Palestinians associate Israel with the destruction and disruption of Gaza's health facilities.
"We don't want our children to die from a lack of medicine, only for Israel to then offer them a clinic," he added.
He argued that increasing the entry of medicines and medical supplies, reopening crossings and allowing patients to travel abroad for treatment should be the priority.
Other residents expressed similar concerns, saying they are worried that humanitarian programmes could also carry political messages.
Ahmed, a young displaced Palestinian, described the project as potentially having an element of "soft power."
"When a child hears that an Israeli doctor is helping him or that an Israeli organisation is providing him with food and medicine, questions may arise," he told TNA.
He also questioned the project's educational and psychological components, particularly its emphasis on rejecting hatred and incitement.
"Who decides what constitutes hatred and what constitutes resistance? Who decides what children in Gaza should learn about the war?" he asked.
Ahmed said children should receive education, food and healthcare without their needs being connected to political or ideological messages.
Parents seek urgent care
For some parents, treatment comes first, particularly those with children suffering from serious illnesses.
Umm Mohammed, whose son has cancer, said her immediate concern was finding treatment for her child.
Her son requires specialised medical care that is difficult to obtain in Gaza, while restrictions on movement have complicated access to treatment outside the Strip.
"Honestly, I don't care much about who this organisation is if it can treat my son," she told TNA. "I'm a mother, and all I want is to see my son live. I don't want to think about politics when my child is sick."
She said her son was too young to understand the political circumstances surrounding his illness.
"He doesn't know who Israel is and who Palestine is. He knows he is in pain and that he needs a doctor," she said.
Her position reflects the dilemma faced by families seeking healthcare in Gaza, where the shortage of medical resources has made access to treatment increasingly difficult.
Palestinian doctors face difficult choices
A Palestinian doctor, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said he would not currently work at the clinic because of its affiliation with an Israeli organisation.
"I am a doctor, and my job is to treat the patient, but I am also living through this war. I know what has happened to the hospitals, doctors and patients," he told TNA. "Under the current circumstances, I don't see myself working for an organization affiliated with Israel."
However, he said his position could change if the healthcare situation deteriorated further.
"If we reach a point where there are no medicines or resources, and this organization is the only one capable of providing treatment for children, I might have to reconsider my position," he added.
"Ultimately, we are doctors, and we cannot stand before a dying child and tell them we won't treat them because of who is providing the medicine."
The doctor said international and neutral health organisations would be a more acceptable option for providing such services, provided they have access to patients and sufficient medical supplies.
Ahed Ferwana, a Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst, also said the project should be viewed within the broader context of the conflict.
He said humanitarian initiatives could influence perceptions of the party providing the assistance, particularly during a war in which Israel has committed numerous violations.
"The issue is not necessarily providing treatment for children, but the context in which the aid is provided, the messages accompanying it and who determines the content of educational and psychological programs," he told TNA.
He argued that allowing independent international organisations to provide healthcare in Gaza would be more acceptable to many Palestinians.
"If Israel is serious about helping the children of Gaza, it is better to allow specialized international organizations to operate and provide them with access to patients, rather than establishing institutions affiliated with it," he said.

Four men admit destroying Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:30:28 UTC
23:30:28 KST

Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing about £1m of damage.
Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, and Judex Atshatshi and Saif Ali, both 18, admitted to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.
Atshatshi, Khan and Iqbal entered their pleas by video link from Wandsworth and Pentonville jails, with Ali in the dock of the Old Bailey on Friday.
Four ambulances belonging to the Jewish volunteer emergency service Hatzola were set on fire on the morning of 23 March while they were parked near a synagogue in Golders Green, an area of north London that has a large Jewish community. Prosecutors said the attack caused about £1m of damage.
The prosecutor, Leo Seelig, suggested the incident had a “terrorist connection” although no mention was made in court of potential proxies working for Iran.
Previously, counter-terror police had looked into the possible involvement of Iranian proxies in the Jewish ambulance arson, as well as other attacks on Jewish sites in London. Most have been claimed online by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right.
However, in April, Iran’s embassy in the UK said it “categorically rejects” allegations of involvement in “violent activities or incidents in the United Kingdom”.
Three of the defendants were said to have set fire to the fully stocked vehicles while a fourth waited in a blue Toyota Avensis. The resulting blaze caused gas canisters inside the ambulances to explode and nearby flats and a synagogue were also damaged by the fire.
The four men were arrested after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.
On his arrest on 1 April, Ali threw his mobile phone out of the window, the court was previously told. The defendant, then aged 17, had been in contact with someone in February with a view to buying a blue Toyota Avensis and had researched online the cost of ambulances.
The prosecution had alleged Ali went on to source the Toyota that was used in the attack, with WhatsApp messages between him and a co-defendant relating to the purchase.
Prosecutors have said they believe the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.
Hatzola is a Jewish charity established in 1979 and run by volunteers, providing free medical transportation and emergency response to Jewish and non-Jewish people in north London.
As well as the ambulances, said to have cost between £240,000 and £250,000 each, four electrical charging stations and cables costing about £5,000 each were also damaged.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb ordered pre-sentence reports for Iqbal and Khan, from Leyton, east London, Atshatshi, from Dagenham, east London, and Ali, of dual British-Pakistani nationality, from Walthamstow.
Remanding them in custody, the senior judge said their sentencing would take place in the spring of 2027 at the conclusion of a separate trial.
At the same hearing, a fifth defendant, Subhan Ahmed, 18, from Walthamstow, pleaded not guilty to a charge of assisting an offender.
Ahmed, who is alleged to have helped to get rid of the car used in the attack, will go on trial at the Old Bailey on 27 January next year.

Andy Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying bill to avoid swaying debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:30:01 UTC
23:30:01 KST

Andy Burnham has told Labour MPs that he will not cast a vote when the assisted dying bill returns to the Commons next month, to avoid influencing the debate.
While supporters of the measure welcomed his move, No 10 officials said the prime minister had no wish to affect the process in either direction, and was just doing what he thought was best to allow MPs to reach their own collective view.
In a separate letter to his ministers on Friday, Burnham warned them against trying to influence the process. When an earlier version of the bill was before parliament, Wes Streeting, the then health secretary who now holds the defence brief, voiced worries about its impact on the NHS.
An original version of the private member’s bill to permit assisted dying in limited circumstances in England and Wales, led by the Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, ran out of time in the last parliament after peers tabled 1,200 amendments.
Another Labour MP, Lauren Edwards, who came second in May’s new ballot for private members’ bills, has tabled a near-identical version to allow adults with less than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.
It has its second reading in the Commons – the first opportunity MPs get to vote on a bill – on 11 September.
Keir Starmer voted for Leadbeater’s bill as prime minister on its second and third readings, while otherwise remaining neutral on an issue seen as a matter of conscience, and where parties gave their MPs a free vote. In his letter to MPs, Burnham said he was taking a different approach.
“The government remains neutral on the question of assisted dying and on the passage of the bill,” he said, stating it was “vital that every view is respected”.
Burnham wrote: “There is no single right position and I have deep respect for MPs on all sides, and the expertise they bring to this debate.”
Saying he had his “own personal views on the issue”, Burnham went on: “However, I am also clear that this is a matter for parliament to decide and my role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not.
“I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote. For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at second reading.”
As the Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham previously said he supported the idea in principle. But in July, he said it would be “very challenging” to introduce the change before palliative care and social care were improved.
Supporters of the bill argue that, with a proposed implementation period of up to four years, there is time for this to happen.
In his letter to ministers, Burnham confirmed that, as is the convention for issues involving conscience, collective responsibility would be again set aside, with frontbenchers free to vote or abstain as they wanted.
MPs should be “able to reach those conclusions without feeling that the government is seeking to influence the debate”, he wrote, adding: “At the dispatch box, I ask that ministers reiterate that this is a question for parliament, on which the official government position is to remain neutral, with the same approach taken outside parliament when dealing with all forms of media, including social media.
“Of course, ministers do not need to resile from their previously stated views when directly asked about them and can correspond with constituents about their previous position, but they should avoid being part of the public debate, and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department’s responsibilities.”
When he was health secretary under Starmer, Streeting used a message to constituents to express doubts about whether the NHS could afford to establish an assisted dying service given other budgetary pressures.
Edwards said: “Andy Burnham is absolutely right to say that people’s personal experiences around terminal illness lie at the heart of the debate and I welcome his view that everyone’s views should be treated with dignity and respect. That is certainly the approach I will be taking and I look forward to what will be a very important debate in two weeks’ time.”
Sarah Wootton, the chief executive of the campaign group Dignity in Dying, said: “We welcome the prime minister reaffirming the government’s neutrality and requesting that ministers do not attempt to influence the debate.
“More and more countries are introducing choice at the end of life. France has just legalised assisted dying. This week Australia completed the set; every single state and territory offers dying people this choice. The will of the public is settled. The will of the Commons is clear, and parts of the British Isles have already moved. On 11 September, MPs must finish what they started.”

Russians are buying their war gear on Ozon. Users of Russia's second-largest online marketplace ordered about $300 million in dual-use and military goods between August 2025 and July 2026, according to internal company data examined by the independent outlet Verstka.
Ukraine is now burning those warehouses down. Its forces struck three Ozon logistics centers covering 314,000 square meters on 24 August, part of a campaign that hit at least four Ozon hubs across southern Russia over several days, Militarnyi reports.
Body armor led the spending
The biggest class by money was tactical gear, six categories covering body armor, helmets, load-bearing vests and belts, armor plates and adapters, and neck and shoulder protection. Users ordered more than 527,000 such items for about $110 million.
Body armor was the single most-ordered product in the class. Almost 157,700 vests were sold for roughly $61 million, at an average of about $388 each.
Optics were the costliest goods
Military optics ranked second by spending and carried the highest prices. Buyers ordered almost 350,000 scopes, night-vision devices, and thermal imagers for about $87 million.
The average thermal sight went for about $1,680, with more than 28,000 ordered. Plain optical scopes were the most common, with over 110,000 orders, followed by almost 99,000 collimator sights.
Drone parts made up the rest
Users also spent about $75 million on drones and drone components. Half of that, roughly $36 million, went to a single category labeled accessories for drones and quadcopters.
That category alone drew 554,000 orders. It consists mostly of the parts to assemble a copter from scratch: frames, propellers, receivers, and cameras.
The first Ukrainian strikes on Ozon started on 22 August. Ozon and Wildberries—Russia’s two largest online marketplaces—and their smaller rivals collectively sell goods and services worth the equivalent of 8.5% of Russia’s GDP and employ 4 million people.

====================================================================================================

LIAA: Predictability of the process and the legal environment are crucial for attracting future investors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:28:46 UTC
23:28:46 KST

The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI), the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia (LDDK) and the Foreign Investors’ Council in Latvia (FICIL) are calling for practical lessons to be drawn from the K2 Ventum case to ensure that the development of major investment projects in Latvia becomes clearer and more predictable in the future.
On 25 August, the Cabinet of Ministers decided not to approve the wind farm project proposed by SIA K2 Ventum. The total value of the project is €560 million, including at least €420 million in planned foreign direct investment. The project envisaged capital investment originating from Latvia, Lithuania and Switzerland.
Investors Assess the Entire Path to a Decision
Investors currently considering major capital investments in Latvia regard a transparent and predictable process as being just as important as the final decision itself – whether the rules are clear, deadlines are respected and institutions act in a coordinated manner.
The preparation of major investment projects takes several years. Even before a final decision is made, an investor commits resources to technical documentation, research, obtaining permits and securing financing.
“Priority project status does not guarantee a positive final decision, but an investor has the right to expect a clear, timely and legally robust process. Every such case also sends a signal to future investors – whether the rules in Latvia are predictable and whether state institutions are capable of acting in a coordinated manner. The credibility of our business environment and our ability to compete for future investment depend on this,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.
The predictability of decision-making is also assessed by international banks and other project financiers. Cases like this can affect the risk assessment of both the specific project and the country’s overall investment environment, increase financing costs and reduce Latvia’s ability to attract future investment projects.
The importance of process quality for companies’ long-term decisions is also emphasised by LCCI, whose members include both domestic and foreign companies.
“Businesses understand that not every project will receive a positive final decision. However, a company that invests for several years in research, documentation and arranging financing must be able to rely on clear conditions and defined decision-making deadlines. If significant issues remain unresolved until the end of the process, the company loses not only the funds and time it has invested – this also affects its willingness to invest in Latvia in the future. A predictable process is not a special privilege for an investor; it is the foundation of a competitive business environment,” says Katrīna Zariņa, Chair of the Board of the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
Legal Certainty Is a Prerequisite for Investment
Legal certainty and legitimate expectations are among the criteria international investors and their financiers consider when assessing a country before committing capital. If state institutions grant priority project status and repeatedly approve a project’s progress, but the final decision is not made within the prescribed timeframe or procedure, this creates a precedent that investors and their legal advisers will factor into the risk assessments of future projects.
In this case, the statutory 30-day deadline for adopting a decision was not observed – the decision was made several months later.
“FICIL is seriously concerned about the decision-making process of the Cabinet of Ministers in the K2 Ventum case. We are not taking a position here on whether the specific project should be implemented or on its environmental impact – our concern is about the quality, timing and predictability of the decision-making process. This is not simply a political decision – it is an administrative act that directly affects the rights and obligations of a specific investor.
“It is therefore particularly important to respect the principles of good governance, legitimate expectations, procedural fairness and legal certainty. It is unacceptable for a decision to be delayed by nine months, causing significant costs and losses to the investor, while the draft decision itself is substantially amended shortly before it is considered.
“Such an approach raises questions about the ability of public administration to ensure a predictable and high-quality process for major investment projects. There is no doubt that the law requires the public interest to be respected, but safeguarding the public interest is not merely a question concerning a specific project – it is also a question of having a high-quality regulatory framework that allows all parties involved to achieve a predictable outcome,” says Jānis Zuļķis, Head of FICIL’s Energy and Industrialisation Working Group.
Impact on Competitiveness and Energy Independence
Latvia’s ability to attract major infrastructure and energy projects is directly linked to its position in regional competition.
The share of wind energy in Latvia’s electricity generation is currently significantly lower than in Lithuania and Estonia, where it is several times higher. In 2024, Latvia generated 276 gigawatt-hours of electricity from wind power, compared with 1,164 gigawatt-hours in Estonia. In Lithuania, wind energy has become one of the main sources of domestically generated electricity.
When choosing between the Baltic states, investors compare not only market potential but also the speed and predictability of administrative and legal procedures in each country. Greater domestic generation capacity could reduce Latvia’s dependence on electricity imports and strengthen the country’s competitiveness in the Baltic region.
The impact on long-term planning and employment is also highlighted by the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia (LDDK).
“Investors who have spent years preparing projects and relying on the process established by the state must not be treated according to the prevailing political climate. This is not merely a decision about a single project, but a signal about the predictability of Latvia’s business environment. If the state creates the impression that the rules of the game can change for political reasons, it becomes a warning to every investor.
“Trust can be lost in a single day, but rebuilding it takes years. The cost of such decisions often extends far beyond a single project. Political responsibility means recognising the long-term consequences of these choices – whether Latvia will continue to be able to attract investment, create well-paid jobs and ensure sustainable economic growth,” emphasises Kaspars Gorkšs, Director General of LDDK.
Practical Improvements Are Needed
LIAA, LCCI, LDDK and FICIL believe that predictable decision-making and adherence to deadlines are prerequisites for Latvia’s competitiveness in attracting investment.
Responsibility for project progress and compliance with deadlines must be clearly defined, while disputed legal issues should be addressed at an early stage. This would allow problems to be identified sooner and provide investors with a clearer path from the submission of a project to the final decision.
The responsible state institutions, together with LCCI, LDDK, FICIL and other stakeholders, should continue seeking solutions to improve the investment environment, accelerate the development of major projects and strengthen Latvia’s position as a reliable investment destination.

Sale of HMS Bulwark to Brazil confirmed by ministers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:26:04 BST
23:26:04 KST

HMS Bulwark is to be sold to the Brazilian Navy, the Ministry of Defence has officially confirmed, formally closing more than two decades of Royal Navy service for an amphibious assault ship whose disposal had been expected for some time.
The department published the confirmation on Friday, framing it around the transition to a new fleet of amphibious transport ships being developed with the Netherlands under a £2.4 billion partnership signed in July.
Lord Coaker, Minister of State for Defence, said: “HMS Bulwark served this country and our allies with distinction for over two decades, and I’m pleased that she will continue her story in Brazilian service, with a nation that has long stood alongside us as a defence partner.”
He said: “This partnership with the Netherlands marks a real step forward for our Armed Forces, giving our personnel the modern, interoperable capability they need to operate alongside our allies for decades to come. It’s also a vote of confidence in British shipbuilding, backing the skills and shipyards that will keep our industrial base strong and our nation secure.”
Bulwark was commissioned in 2005 and based at HMNB Devonport. She served as Fleet Flagship between 2011 and 2015, supported the evacuation of civilians from Lebanon in 2006, and provided maritime security for the sailing regatta at the London 2012 Olympics. Her sister ship HMS Albion remains alongside at Devonport pending disposal.
The decision to retire both ships was announced in November 2024 as part of a package of early withdrawals intended to free money for other priorities, and interest from Brazil has been reported since. Friday’s announcement puts the government’s name to what had until now been expectation.
Under the arrangement with the Netherlands, each nation will operate four of the new vessels. The ships are to be 160 metres long and displace 15,000 tonnes, capable of carrying troops, vehicles and equipment including drones, and are to be built in British shipyards working alongside Dutch industry in a programme the department says will sustain hundreds of skilled jobs.
Their flight decks are being designed around current and future long-range drones and autonomous systems, which the department presents as part of the wider move towards a hybrid fleet, with £1.5 billion confirmed for the amphibious programme in the Defence Investment Plan.
Brazil already operates the former HMS Ocean, sold in 2018 and now serving as the Atlântico, so Bulwark would join a fleet with existing familiarity with British amphibious practice and equipment. The Brazilian Navy has been rebuilding its amphibious and expeditionary capacity around that ship.
The Royal Marines have meanwhile been reorganising around the Commando Force concept, which emphasises smaller teams operating from a wider range of platforms rather than the large-scale landing the Albion class was designed to deliver, and the new ships are being specified with that in mind.

Greek parents brace for back-to-school spending season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:25:46 UTC
23:25:46 KST

Footfall in bookshops and school supply stores is already rising, as parents search for notebooks, stationery, art materials and the rest of the gear pupils will need.
The return to the classroom is approaching, and with it the usual budget exercise for Greek families, who must buy everything their children need for the new school year.
Footfall in bookshops and stores selling school supplies has already started to pick up, with parents looking for exercise books, stationery, art materials and all the other equipment pupils will need.
Prices for basic products are, by and large, close to last year's levels. The final cost, however, can differ significantly depending on the pupil's year group, the school's list, the quality of the products and whether parents opt for branded or more economical items.
According to a market survey by Ertnews Radio 105.8, the cost of basic school supplies for a child in the first years of primary school is estimated at around €100 to €120 this year. This does not include the school bag, lunch box, food container or water bottle.
From €15 to €100 for a school bag
The gap between the cheapest and the most expensive options remains wide.
A school bag can start at around €15, while more expensive or branded models can cost as much as €100.
A classic blue 50-page exercise book starts at around €0.49, while a maths notebook costs between €1.59 and €2.50. Writing notebooks range from roughly €0.80 to €2.
The spread is even wider for two-subject spiral notebooks, which can cost between €1 and €8.
In art supplies, a pad of watercolour paper starts at about €2.25 and can go up to €15, with the average price around €3.50. A set of 12 felt-tip pens, as well as a set of brushes, starts at around €2.50, while the more expensive options can reach €10.
What parents paid in 2025
The comparison with prices recorded a year earlier is also revealing. In September 2025, the Greek Workers' Consumers Association (EEKE) published specific prices for a series of basic school products, following a sample survey of supermarket chains.
In 2025, a 17x24cm two-subject spiral notebook cost €1.64, while an A4 two-subject spiral notebook cost €2.55. A set of 12 fine washable felt-tip pens cost €1.99, and another set of 12 felt-tip pens cost €1.89. A pack of five pencils cost €1.49, four pens cost €1.29, and a compass with a pencil cost €1.49. A set of sharpener and eraser cost €0.99, a 20-centimetre ruler cost €0.36, and a pack of 12 coloured pencils cost €2.85.
These figures are not fully comparable with every product on the shelves this year, as the brand, packaging, dimensions or point of sale may differ. They do, however, give a picture of the level at which basic school supplies were priced in 2025.
It is also worth noting that on 28 August 2025, the Ministry of Development announced, after a meeting with the Hellenic Supermarkets Association, that companies had pledged to keep the prices of school supplies at their 2024 levels.
The ministry's official announcement did not, however, include detailed prices for each product code.
A year on, the picture suggests that in many categories the lowest prices remain at relatively affordable levels. The wide gap between budget and more expensive options, though, means the final bill can easily climb.
For a family with two or more school-age children, even small differences in the price of each item add up, turning preparations for the first day of school into a significant expense for the household budget.

LONDON – Four young British men pleaded guilty on Aug 28 to charges over an arson attack on community ambulances in London, the first of a spate of incidents targeting the capital’s Jewish community earlier in 2026.
Hamza Iqbal, 20; Rehan Khan, 19; Judex Atshatshi, 18; and Saif Ali, 18, appeared at London’s Old Bailey court and admitted a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless as to whether life would be endangered.
The charges relate to the torching of four ambulances belonging to Jewish volunteer emergency service Hatzola on March 23 while they were parked near a synagogue, which prosecutors said caused around £1 million (S$1.73 million) in total damages.
Hatzola is a not-for-profit volunteer emergency service that works alongside Britain’s National Health Service and primarily serves the Orthodox Jewish community.
Pro-Iranian group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya (HAYI) claimed responsibility for the ambulance attack, which was followed by several other arson incidents in the city.
Two Jewish worshippers were stabbed on a street in the Golders Green area of north London in April in the most notable of the incidents, an attack which police are treating as a terrorism attack.
Also, a synagogue and a former synagogue were targeted, as was Persian-language media organisation Iran International and a memorial wall dedicated to people killed in Iran.
British police said at the time that they were investigating possible Iranian links to those arson attacks, with HAYI also having claimed responsibility for some of them.
A charity which provides security for Jewish communities said on Aug 5 that anti-Semitism in Britain remains close to record levels, with almost 2,000 incidents recorded in the first six months of 2026.
This was a rise of 21 per cent compared with the same period in 2025, according to the Community Security Trust (CST), which advises Britain’s estimated 280,000 Jews on security matters.
That was the second-highest figure ever recorded for the first half of a year, the charity added.
The CST said incidents had spiked following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February, with the British authorities since accusing Tehran of using proxies to carry out attacks in Britain and across Europe. Iran has repeatedly denied any involvement. REUTERS

US seeking a deal to make Venezuela its gas pump – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:24:44 UTC
23:24:44 KST

US seeking a deal to make Venezuela its gas pump – media
The US is moving to lock in long-term access to the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves by discussing a 100-year deal with Venezuela, as Caracas plans to leave the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), several outlets have reported.
The idea of quitting OPEC has been discussed during talks with US officials, according to Bloomberg’s sources, although no final decision has been made.
Venezuela was one of five countries that founded OPEC in 1960, alongside Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait. It has effectively operated outside the group’s production quota system for years, while decades of US sanctions and domestic economic turmoil have battered its oil industry and diminished its influence within the organization.
A withdrawal from OPEC would mark a major realignment in Caracas following the January 3 US operation that kidnapped Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Washington has since taken control of Venezuelan oil sales and revenues, with proceeds deposited into US-controlled accounts and Caracas’ access to the funds subject to decisions in Washington.
The US is also seeking a steady flow of Venezuelan crude to its refineries while encouraging American companies to expand their presence in the country’s energy industry. Venezuela currently produces around 1.25 million barrels of crude per day, well below its historic output.
US pushing for ‘massive’ century-long oil lease
Talk of a potential OPEC exit comes as Washington pushes for a major stake in Venezuela’s oil fields. A deal under discussion could lock in several fields for American companies under a 100-year lease and guarantee the resulting crude supplies to the US.
“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” one source told Reuters. A lease is among the legal models under consideration, with individual fields potentially allocated to US producers through auctions or tenders.
A list involved in the negotiations includes 17 fields, spanning undeveloped sites in the vast Orinoco Belt and mature fields around Lake Maracaibo containing roughly 90 billion barrels of proven reserves. Some are currently operated by a small Chinese company under a contract signed during Maduro’s presidency.
The historic deal could essentially more than double US oil reserves by tapping Venezuela, which holds the world’s largest proven crude reserves. “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement,” one US official told Axios. “It is massive.”
‘Donroe Doctrine’
Taking a stake in Venezuela’s reserves would amount to an almost unprecedented US intervention in another country’s economy, Bloomberg noted, while fitting Donald Trump’s so-called “Donroe Doctrine” of expanding American influence across the Western Hemisphere.
Trump has repeatedly asserted US control over Venezuela’s oil since Maduro’s capture in January. Speaking to oil executives that month, he said Washington would decide which companies would rebuild the sector: “You’re dealing with us directly. You’re not dealing with Venezuela at all.” He went further in the spring, publicly floating the idea of turning Venezuela into the “51st state.”
The proposed arrangement could, however, run into legal hurdles. Venezuelan law does not currently provide for leasing oil acreage, while the constitution reserves core industry activities for the state. Recent reforms allow foreign participation through joint ventures and production-sharing contracts, but Caracas has for decades prevented foreign producers from booking Venezuelan reserves as their own.
With details still being negotiated, legal experts say the proposed deal could face constitutional challenges. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright is reportedly expected to travel to Caracas as soon as next week as talks continue.
Another blow to OPEC
Venezuela’s departure would also hand Trump a small victory in his long-running confrontation with OPEC. The US president has repeatedly criticized the group for wielding too much influence over global oil prices and driving up fuel costs for American consumers.
The push comes as the Trump administration faces pressure over high gasoline prices ahead of this year’s midterm elections. Cheaper Venezuelan crude could help ease fuel costs and replenish the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which currently holds around 290 million barrels – about 41% of its capacity.
A Venezuelan departure would come just months after the United Arab Emirates quit OPEC on May 1, seeking greater freedom over its oil production. The move left the organization with 12 members, while UAE state oil company ADNOC subsequently moved to boost crude sales.
Other producers have also pushed back against OPEC restrictions. Iraq reportedly threatened to leave in June unless it was allowed to increase output, although Baghdad later said it had no plans to withdraw. Venezuela and Iran remain exempt from OPEC+ production quotas because sanctions have constrained their output.

"There is no threat of hunger," Vysotskyi added.
The continued destruction of warehouses is forcing businesses to find alternative ways to move and store goods. The most realistic option under the current circumstances is for suppliers to deliver goods directly to production or retail sites, bypassing long-term warehouse storage, according to the minister.
The minister added that some businesses are relocating to other areas, but Russian attacks have already reached some of these relocated facilities.
The minister also advocated for an equal distribution of risks among supply-chain participants when goods are destroyed by Russian attacks, emphasizing that the state is not involved in their commercial or contractual relations.
"There is no state operator involved at any point in the supply and retail chain," Vysotskyi said.
"These are exclusively commercial and contractual relationships between the parties. From our perspective, an equal distribution of risks would nevertheless be fair," the minister added.
A deadly Russian ballistic missile attack on Aug. 5 that killed 17 people also targeted warehouses belonging to several supermarket chains and other civilian businesses, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Telegram.
Since then, some stores have seen limited or no supplies of everyday staples such as vegetables, dairy products, and meat. The situation has been further strained by customers stocking up amid concerns that shortages could worsen.
Despite the intensified attacks on warehouses, Ukraine is not currently facing food shortages, according to officials.
In the same attack, a distribution warehouse belonging to Ukraine's largest online marketplace, Rozetka, was also completely destroyed. It used to process over 100,000 orders a day, according to its co-founder, Iryna Chechotkina.
Meanwhile, the overnight Russian strike on Aug. 28 destroyed 14 warehouses in Kyiv Oblast alone, including facilities storing thousands of books for Ukrainian publishers and bookstore chains.

Russia added Arestovych to its list of “terrorists and extremists” in May 2023 and placed him on its wanted list in October 2023. Moscow’s Basmanny District Court placed Arestovych in pre-trial detention in absentia in February 2024.
