King Harald V of Norway obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:07:11 UTC
23:07:11 KST

King Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017.
The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of the Duke of Edinburgh and the former Greek royal family. The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said.
He was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge.
Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion of Norway in 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in. It is alleged that the royal party was initially turned back at the border, and allowed to proceed only when the driver of their car threatened to ram it through the border post. Within three months, Harald, his sisters and mother had escaped to the US. They spent the war years in Washington DC and Harald thereafter spoke English with a slight American accent.
Meanwhile, Harald’s grandfather and father escaped to England, where they led a government in exile. Famously Haakon, turning up at the BBC to make a broadcast to his people, was asked by a receptionist: “Where did you say you were king of, dear?”
Following the liberation of Norway at the end of the war, the family was reunited and Harald was enrolled first at a state primary and then at Oslo cathedral school. From there he studied at Oslo University and the Norwegian military academy, before following in his father’s footsteps to read history, economics and politics at Balliol College, Oxford, where he also rowed for the college. A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005.
If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968.
Harald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. Although lacking his father’s easy bonhomie, the king attempted successfully – and popularly – to open up the institution and its palace and estates more freely to the public. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26.
The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims.
Harald was treated for bladder cancer in 2003, contracted Covid, had a pacemaker fitted in 2024 and was being treated for the blood disorder haemolytic anaemia.
He is survived by Sonja and their children, Princess Märtha Louise and Prince Haakon, whose wife, Mette-Marit (nee Tjessem-Høiby), was obliged to apologise in February this year for email exchanges with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in which her name was mentioned nearly 1,000 times. The king said that she had not broken any law. Mette-Marit’s son by a previous relationship, Marius, was jailed for four years in June following convictions for two rapes and drug offences.
Haakon succeeds Harald as King Haakon VIII and will adopt the monarchy’s traditional motto: “All for Norway”.

Jungle route turning Indigenous Amazonian children into cocaine couriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:06:56 UTC
23:06:56 KST

At 14, Luis was approached by three men. They gave him a revolver and a backpack loaded with seven kilos of cocaine paste. Then they instructed him to walk three days along a dirt road cutting through dense jungle. It would be the first of three such journeys Luis would make.
"The first time I cried because it was such a long trip. The trail was rough, and we had to watch for jaguars at night," said Luis.
(Luis, a 17-year-old former drug courier was recruited to traffic cocaine base paste near Peru’s border with Brazil. Neil Giardino, Anadolu Agency.)
Luis, now 17, whose real name Anadolu is withholding to protect the minor’s identity, belongs to the Amahuaca, an Indigenous people living in an isolated corner of Peru's far eastern Amazon region called Yurua.
His account is not isolated. Testimony from other Indigenous minors interviewed in Breu indicates an alarming transformation along Peru’s remote Amazon border with Brazil, where a network of jungle roads and clandestine airstrips is carving a cocaine trafficking corridor.
(The remote township of Breu in Peru’s far eastern Amazon has emerged as a transit point in the international cocaine trade. Neil Giardino, Anadolu Agency.)
As the drug trade spreads, it is reshaping this remote frontier, bringing coca crops, cocaine labs, and organized criminal syndicates operating on both sides of the border. It is rupturing Indigenous communities and increasingly putting the lives of Indigenous children at risk, recruiting them not only as drug couriers, but also as consumers.
A remote frontier with little state presence
The sweltering backwater town of Breu where Luis was recruited is connected to the Peruvian Amazon city of Pucallpa by a thread — a dirt airstrip used by light aircraft is only reliably serviceable during the Amazon’s dry season.
During the rainy season, Breu is all but cut off from the rest of the country. Surrounded by dense forest at the edge of Peru’s eastern frontier, the Brazilian state of Acre is roughly 40 minutes by motorboat along the meandering Yurua River.
(From the air, clandestine coca farms and jungle airstrips are visible in remote forests along Peru’s border with Brazil. Neil Giardino, Anadolu Agency.)
For the largely Indigenous population of Breu, the isolation is more than geographic reality: it reflects the limited reach of the Peruvian state, and the vacuum it has created for illegal economies.
In recent years, Breu, Yurua’s regional capital, has emerged as a transit point connecting coca, the raw ingredient for cocaine, from the Andean slopes and Amazonian interior onward to Brazil and Bolivia. Drug traffickers are employing a combination of jungle trails, road networks, rivers, and clandestine airstrips to move cocaine across the border.
Yurua is a multi-ethnic region home to remote Indigenous communities as well as semi-nomadic tribes still living in isolation. Its isolation is, in part, what draws illegal actors to this hidden stretch of the border. Interviews with local government officials, Indigenous leaders, and residents revealed a weak state presence and porous international border have allowed criminal groups to operate with relative impunity on both sides of the frontier.
“We have a worrying issue here in Yurua. Young people are consuming illegal products,” said Breu’s mayor, Manuel Arevalo Mogrovejo. “I’ve heard there are individuals who pass through our region and utilize the roads that exist to move (drugs). But those same drugs are not being produced here. They’re using our region as a corridor.”
That corridor, which straddles the border with Brazil, has seen little state enforcement. The international demarcation line and a police checkpoint marking the border has stood abandoned for over 15 years, according to Yurua’s Indigenous federation president, Fernando Aroni Lozano. During a recent visit to the area, Anadolu confirmed that the checkpoint remains abandoned.
The isolated road traveled by Luis did not begin as a drug route.
It was opened in the 1980s by an oil company, first appearing on satellite imagery in 1987. The road later fell into disrepair, but loggers reestablished it in the 1990s, widening and extending it to reach valuable cedar and mahogany. In the following decade, trails branched out from the main route, allowing loggers to push deeper into the forest to extract the timer and transport it toward the Ucayali River, a major Amazon tributary, and onward to Pucallpa.
(The international cocaine trade is increasingly using remote rivers and streams to move cocaine base paste through the Amazon along the heavily forested Peru-Brazil border. Neil Giardino, Anadolu Agency.)
Deforestation for the creation of road networks is fracturing rainforests. In Yurua, between 2000 and 2021, over 60 square kilometers (23 square miles) were cleared within five kilometers of the road, according to Monitoring of the Andean Amazon Project.
That same road system, first carved through the forest for oil exploration and later logging, is now being revived for the cocaine trade, allowing criminal groups access to a route established decades earlier for extractive industries.
‘Insidious veins’
NASA satellite imagery, research by the University of Richmond, and testimony from Indigenous authorities reveal how the informal UC-105, as the 200-kilometer road is known, has expanded deforestation for coca crops, jungle airstrips, and illegal mining operations. Connecting Breu to Nueva Italia, a logging town along the Ucayali River, the road is now being used to traffic cocaine trade.
"There is no greater impact on the landscapes and livelihoods of the Amazon than roads. And roads are expanding rapidly," said David Salisbury, a professor with the university who has worked in the Yurua region for decades.
Salisbury has led studies on the Yurua road’s impacts on deforestation, land grabbing, illicit crop cultivation, and cultural disruption of Indigenous groups across the region.
"These road networks are not just vectors for deforestation and forest degradation," he said. “They are also insidious veins that bring poison to the cultures; that create opportunities for people to get involved with illegal, illicit activities that are likely not sustainable in the long run, nor beneficial to their communities.”
Despite the presence of illegal actors operating in Yurua, in early 2021, Peruvian lawmakers introduced legislation to incorporate the existing corridor here into a proposed Central Interoceanic Highway linking Pacific ports along Peru’s coast to Brazil. The planned expansion of the Yurua road would run near the Murunahua Indigenous Reserve, a 470,000 hectare (1,815 square mile) protected territory for isolated tribes, putting the reserve and its vulnerable population at risk of encroachment.
While the legislation, which deemed formalizing the road to be "of public necessity," failed to become law, the Ucayali regional government had already incorporated the route into road planning. In the absence of legislative action, on the ground, the road continues to advance.
Advocates have presented the UC-105 as an economic boon that would connect remote communities to markets and bolster international trade with Brazil. Support for the formalization of the road exists among some Indigenous communities in the region, where access to health care and economic opportunities remains all but out of reach.
At the same time, Indigenous organizations, environmental groups, and Peru’s ombudsman have challenged the project on the grounds of environmental concerns and a lack of prior consultation with local communities.
Salisbury told Anadolu that the UC-105 has little basis in geographic reality as an economic corridor connecting Peru and Brazil. The road, he explained, would have to cross through titled Indigenous territories and heavily forested protected areas, while Brazil’s existing road networks remain far from the border.
"This is just an argument to access an area and plunder its natural resources. And also to take advantage of the local people for low-paid itinerant labor and exploitation. And there is also the trafficking of illegal substances," said Salisbury.
In Luis' case, that exploitation took the form of recruitment. The men he said who solicited him, a sibling, and other Indigenous children in Breu were Peruvians.
Luis was approached behind Breu’s market, in a part of town where children are increasingly exposed to "tickets," or rolled cigarettes filled with a harsh cocaine extract made with kerosine and other chemicals.
Luis said he was transported to Pucallpa on a twin-engine plane, then by highway to Nueva Italia where he was handed over the shipment of cocaine. From there, he said, he walked three days through the jungle trail, weighed down with the drugs.
He recalled cold, restless nights gripping his revolver as he drifted in and out of sleep.
(Luis, an Amahuaca Indigenous minor, was given a revolver and a backpack of cocaine which he trafficked through the Amazon. The international cocaine trade here is increasingly targeting Indigenous children as couriers and consumers of the drug. Neil Giardino, Anadolu Agency.)
"That’s how we protected ourselves at night. We took turns keeping watch. They gave us coats, and mosquito nets," said Luis.
On the fourth day, Luis said they made their way back to Breu where his journey began.
"When we arrived, we handed over the drugs and three men paid us. We were lucky because a lot of times, the [drug mules] get into accidents along the way," said Luis. “When we did the handover, they waited with guns in hand.”
Luis said he was paid 1,500 Peruvian Soles, or around $440 – more money than he’d ever seen in his life. He kept quiet about where the money came from, but used most of it to buy household items for his mother.
Illegal economies "provide short-term opportunities for cash. Once you're in those systems, it's also really difficult to get out of them," said Salisbury. As a network of roads and trails moves into the region and expands, he said, the consequences could destabilize not just Indigenous communities, but broader political and economic networks.
Around 40 kilometers into Brazil from the Peruvian border as the crow flies, Spanish-speaking men armed with machine guns allegedly threatened families in the Indigenous Ashaninka community of Apiwtxa in July. Once a paragon of Indigenous-led land conservation and territorial sovereignty, in recent months the Ashaninka here have reeled from expanding criminal routes along the border.
Back on Peruvian territory, Luis said he vowed never to work as a drug courier again.
"I’m going to Pucallpa to finish studying. I’d like to be a leader for my community someday, if god wills it," he said.

The Kuril Flashpoint: Putin’s Visit and the Future of Japan-Russia Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:04:00 UTC
23:04:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the Kuril Islands on August 12. He became the second Russian leader to visit the islands, after President Dmitry Medvedev’s landmark trip in 2010. More recently, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited the islands in 2021.
Putin’s recent visit prompted a protest from Japan, with Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae calling the visit an offense to the sentiments of the Japanese people and unacceptable.
The islands have been the subject of an ongoing territorial dispute between Japan and Russia, both historically and under international law, for over 80 years. Russia calls the islands the Kuril Islands, and Japan calls them the Northern Territories; the volcanic islands lie at the heart of a territorial feud that has prevented the two countries from formally ending World War II, despite signing a joint declaration for restoring diplomatic relations in 1956.
Putin’s recent visit has made it even harder to restore relations between the countries.
There are 56 islands in the 1,300-kilometer (810-mile) archipelago that stretches from Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula to Hokkaido, separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean. Japan claims four of the islands. These include Iturup (Etorofu in Japanese), Kunashir (Kunashiri), Shikotan, and Habomai, the southernmost islands and closest to Japan, just off the coast of Hokkaido. While Russia administers the islands as part of the Sakhalin region, Japan considers the four they claim as part of Hokkaido prefecture and argues that they are “illegally occupied” by Russia.
In 1855, in the first treaty between tsarist Russia and Japan, the frontier between the two countries was drawn just north of the four islands closest to Japan. Twenty years later, a new treaty handed the entire chain to Japan, in exchange for Russia gaining full control of the island of Sakhalin. Japan seized back control of the southern half of Sakhalin during its crushing victory in the 1905 Russo-Japanese War.
In August 1945, as the Soviet Union entered the war with Japan just after the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, the Kuril Islands emerged as a flashpoint. Soviet troops completed their takeover of the islands after Japan surrendered. The Soviet capture of the islands has prevented Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal treaty to end the war, despite repeated attempts over the past 80 years to reach agreement.
In 1956, both Moscow and Tokyo signed a joint declaration that ended their state of war and restored diplomatic relations – though it was not a formal treaty ending the war. As part of the declaration, the Soviet side agreed to transfer Shikotan and the Habomai Islands to Japan. Negotiations continued after the Cold War, producing results such as the 1993 Tokyo Declaration and 2001 Irkutsk Statement, the latter of which reaffirmed the 1956 declaration as the baseline legal foundation for peace talks.
Under Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, talks intensified in 2018, including the drafting of a peace treaty based on the 1956 declaration. However, the process collapsed with the start of the Ukraine war in 2022, when Russia suspended peace-treaty negotiations due to Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow.
The Kuril Islands are far more than a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan; they are a lesser-known strategic fault line in the evolving Indo-Pacific order. Home to around 20,000 people across the chain, the islands are economically and strategically valuable because they are rich in fish stocks and contain deposits of minerals and rare metals, including rhenium, which is used in the production of supersonic aircraft.
For Russia, however, the islands’ greatest value is military. Bases and missile systems on the Kurils help secure Moscow’s Pacific Fleet and reinforce the Sea of Okhotsk as a nuclear bastion. Control of the islands gives Russia year-round access to the Pacific Ocean for its Pacific Fleet, based in Vladivostok, since the strait between Kunashir and Iturup does not freeze in winter. They are also a launchpad for maritime outreach through the Northern Sea Route.
While Russian and Chinese warships recently conducted Joint Sea 2026, an annual bilateral naval exercise, through waters around the Kuril chain, Russian naval forces have also conducted exercises in the Far East.
By tightening its grip on the islands, Moscow is not merely defending territory but also challenging the existing regional balance. This complicates the strategic calculations of the U.S.-led Indo-Pacific alliance, including Japan’s Indo-Pacific outlook, adding another layer of complexity to the evolving region.
For Japan, the dispute is increasingly connected to the wider security challenge posed by a possible Taiwan contingency. Russian military activity in the region could complicate Japan’s ability to focus exclusively on threats closer to Taiwan and the East China Sea.
The implications extend well beyond Russia and Japan. Joint Chinese-Russian naval activity around the Kurils signal growing strategic convergence between Moscow and Beijing. China’s silence and neutral stance on Japan’s territorial claim further strengthens Russia’s position while placing additional pressure on Tokyo.
The timing of Putin’s visit to Iturup Island was notable. It came two days before Japan marked 81 years since its surrender ended World War II. It also came a day after North Korea fired a missile into the Sea of Japan (East Sea) and just days before major South Korea-U.S. military exercises, Ulchi Freedom Shield, were scheduled to begin. The timing suggests a coordinated display of military and geopolitical pressure around Japan, highlighting Japan’s increasingly difficult security environment.
The Kuril Islands dispute is not just a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan but reflects the larger complexity of geopolitical dynamics in the Indo-Pacific Region.
The possibility of peace between Japan and Russia seems bleak at this juncture, after the closing of another window of opportunity for the two countries to engage in a beneficial tradeoff between Russian energy and Japanese technology and investments. The dispute may remain a long-term strategic flashpoint, limiting economic cooperation while intensifying wider geopolitical competition in the Indo-Pacific. This may eventually lead Japan to harden its security posture and deepen its alignment with the U.S. and other Indo-Pacific partners, further reducing prospects for any Japan-Russia rapprochement.

Family says Virginia man missing in Nepal floods was "in his happy place"

Family of Virginia man last heard from at Nepal-Tibet border just before flood hit desperate for info
Anil Goel was among about 10 U.S. nationals at the Rasuwagadhi immigration checkpoint on Nepal's border with Tibet Wednesday morning just before a torrent of mud and floodwater swept away the facility and everything around it.
On Friday, the 67-year-old Northern Virginia resident and former World Bank employee's family was still desperate for information on his whereabouts, as the death toll from the devastating floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border climbed, and at least 1,400 people remained missing.
"We have a photo of our father with his group from the border crossing," Anurag Goel, Anil Goel's son, who works as an engineer in Boston, told CBS News.
The photo sent by Anil doesn't actually show him, but rather at least seven members of the trekking group he was with, posing in front of the immigration office sign. His son believes he may have taken the picture.
Anurag said the family got confirmation that his father's visa was approved at the checkpoint at 8:35 a.m. local time.
Just 35 minutes later, all of the buildings in the area were swept away or covered by a wall of mud and water unleashed by the collapse of a distant rock ledge and the vast Himalayan glacier it had supported.
Goel was on his way to Mount Kailash, about to cross the border from Nepal for a pilgrimage to the sacred mountain in Tibet, when the photograph was taken, his son said.
"We are not sure if they crossed into Tibet," Goel's daughter Manvi Goel told CBS News. "It's possible they did, but my hunch is he was still on the Nepal side when the calamity struck."
Anil Goel is a seasoned trekker and had visited Nepal 10 times previously for hiking expeditions, having embraced the hobby in retirement.
Anurag told CBS News that when he last spoke to his father, he was "very excited, in his happy place."
"For him, it was both — a hiking expedition and a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash," Anurag said.
He said his father fell in love with hiking years ago. He traveled with his wife to the Mount Everest base camp in 2015, and before that he climbed Africa's highest peak, Mount Kilimanjaro.
But "the Nepal region had become his favorite place in the world," daughter Manvi, who lives in California, told CBS News. "Over the years he did many treks. This was his second trek this year. He wanted to take his dear friends from Virginia to understand and explore the region."
Anil documented his treks on YouTube, hoping to attract more people to the region he loved.
On this visit, he was accompanied by 10 other Americans and two Nepali nationals. They were traveling with the Kathmandu-based adventure trekking company Classic Vacations.
Rescue efforts were still ramping up Friday when a swollen glacial lake in the mountains upstream from the affected area, dammed up by debris and filling with meltwater, raised concerns of a possible new inundation looming.
China's state television network said the flood risks from the lake were "manageable," but it was another piece of deeply worrying news for thousands of families like Goel's waiting for word of loved ones.
"We hope for good news but understand the severity of the situation," Anurag Goel told CBS News. "We also want to understand the nature of the rescue work … and raise awareness so that more foreign governments and agencies are able to help."
Authorities said about 1,500 people were still missing on both sides of the border Friday, including as many as 540 foreign nationals from 31 countries. The U.S. State Department said as many as 90 Americans could have been impacted.
Local media in Nepal said the number of missing could be as high as 12,000, but there was no confirmation of that figure from authorities.
Nepal's Foreign Ministry said Friday that it did not need foreign assistance with search and rescue operations, despite offers of help from several countries.

Iceland’s EU referendum: What to know ahead of vote and what's at stake for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:02:48 UTC
23:02:48 KST

Everything you need to know about Iceland’s Saturday referendum on whether the country should negotiate again to join the European Union.
“Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”
This is the question being put to 270,000 Icelanders on Saturday 29 August. From 9am local time, eligible voters will head to the polls to chart their nation's course closer to the European Union — or further away.
The results from the referendum will determine whether the island of 400,000 people should restart negotiations to join the 27-member bloc, or place the revived idea on the backburner for the foreseeable future.
Early polling shows that the results will most likely be down to the wire. An August survey by polling agency Maskína showed a narrow lead, with 51.3% of respondents in favour of restarting talks and 48.7% opposed.
The split indicates tensions over the upcoming plebiscite, which has exposed political fault lines in Iceland covering matters from security to the seas.
Defence remains a particular flashpoint. Iceland is wary of being caught in the crosshairs by Russia’s growing economic and strategic interest in the area, on the one hand, and statements made by US President Donald Trump, who has repeated threatened to annex Greenland, on the other.
But locals are pointing to far more domestic issues that could determine the knife-edge result, from the soaring cost of living to fishing and farming.
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir told Euronews in April that there must be a “balanced discussion” regarding the referendum.
So, what is being discussed, what are the major sticking points, and why does it all matter? Ahead of the vote, Euronews answers your most pressing questions.
What is Iceland voting on?
Saturday’s referendum question will be: “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?” The options will be simply “yes” or “no”.
Crucially, the referendum will decide only whether the government of Iceland should restart accession negotiations with the EU; it is not a vote to determine whether the country should join the EU. That decision would need to be put to a second referendum, as well as being ratified by the 27 EU member states.
Polling stations in Reykjavík will open at 9am on Saturday and close at 10pm that evening. Results are expected to roll through in the hours following.
What is the back story?
Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009, a year after it and other countries were rocked by the 2008 financial crisis. Formal negotiations began in 2010, with membership seen by the Icelandic government as a possible means to shoring up the Icelandic króna.
Yet after two years of lobbying by a Eurosceptic government, the bid was put on hold in 2013.
In the years since, security priorities have shifted dramatically, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 reshaping vulnerabilities across the High North.
Financial calculations have also altered, with many officials such as the Iceland's Finance Minister Daði Már Kristófersson telling Reuters he is hopeful that Iceland joining the EU could boost the country's economy, rocked by high inflation.
Trump’s re-election has also sown discord within the transatlantic alliance and thrown question marks over the US-Iceland 1951 defence agreement. This is a treaty committing the US to support Iceland’s defence on behalf of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), with Iceland accommodating US bases and forces.
Iceland's shift back toward the EU path came in 2024, following Frostadóttir's centre-left government vote into power. After the win, the EU executive confirmed that Iceland's EU application — submitted more than a decade earlier — remains valid.
In early 2026, the country’s prime minister made good on her promise. She announced there would be a referendum to decide whether EU negotiations should restart, with the vote scheduled for 29 August 2026.
What have the campaigners said?
While not a member of the EU, Iceland is a participant in the European Economic Area (EEA). As with Norway, this means Iceland is granted access to the EU’s single market.
EEA membership means Iceland has already adopted a majority of the EU’s rules, equating to roughly 9,000 legal acts. Proponents of a “yes” vote argue that restarting EU negotiations, with the outcome of eventually joining the bloc, would give Iceland a seat at the table when it comes to negotiating these files.
Proponents of “no” argue that Iceland’s EEA membership and access to the single market should be enough, and full membership is not required.
Haraldur Ólafsson, the chairman of Eurosceptic platform Heimssýn,previously told Euronews that since Iceland already adheres to 75% of EU rules, “there is no need for more”.
Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir has remarked that fisheries are the other major issue among "no" voters. Iceland's fisheries industry body, Fisheries Iceland, has raised concerns over a range of EU fish rules, arguing that EU membership would leave Iceland without "the power to act as an independent coastal state".
The EU's Common Fisheries Policy sets catch limits and quotas across member states – a policy that has long strained relations between Reykjavík and Brussels.
The notorious so-called "mackerel wars" stemmed from Iceland adopting a unilateral position on mackerel quotas that the EU considered excessive, putting strain on the country's former EU accession bid.
This slice of Icelandic history is expected to loom large in the mind of most voters, as its fish industries makes up 6.5% of the country's GDP and employs thousands.
What has the European Union said?
"We share values, we know each other very well, we are like-minded, so we are close partners," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said during her visit to Iceland in July 2025.
She used her visit to the Nordic island to trumpet its assets — it shares the same values as the EU, is a member of the single market, and for a mostly pacifist country, maintains robust defences.
It is von der Leyen’s enlargement official, European Commissioner Marta Kos, however, who spelled out Iceland’s EU prospects in more concrete terms. As first reported by Politico, Kos said that Iceland could formalise accession negotiations by 2027, as its former bid remains valid.
When Iceland put its application on hold in 2013, 27 negotiating chapters had been opened. Eleven of those chapters were provisionally closed. The segment on fisheries, however, remained a major thorn in the side of the country's negotiation talks.
However, Kos recently hinted on social media platform Bluesky that Brussels may be ready to find common ground on the delicate issue. "Accession negotiations always reflect the specific realities of each candidate country," she wrote.
How much do foreign threats loom over the ballot?
Magnús Magnússon chairs a platform advocating for closer ties with the EU. He previously told Euronews that the country’s critical infrastructure is under “constant attack” by Russian actors, and it needs to be secured. “There’s a lot of things that the EU can help with in that respect,” he said.
NATO has also acknowledged Russia and China's growing appetite for power in the High North. The alliance in response has since stepped up activity in the region, such as air policing and greater submarine surveillance.
Another boon to the push is to appease Trump, who has argued the US needed the autonomous territory of Greenland for national security reasons, citing increased activity in the area by both Russia and China.
He has often mistaken Iceland for Greenland when repeating his threats, with experts telling Euronews this has sent alarm bells ringing in Reykjavík. It is also no secret that Washington wants to Europeanise NATO and review its security presence across the continent, something that the European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius estimates could cost Europe €500 billion.
The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also acknowledged that the EU and Iceland's security situations are intertwined amid interest from the Kremlin to Beijing.
“From Russian threats to seabed infrastructure to China’s growing interest in the Arctic, addressing these together gives us greater leverage,” Kallas said at a joint press conference from March conference celebrating Security and Defence Partnership between Iceland and the EU.
At the meeting celebrating the pact, aiming to boost defence cooperation between the entities, the country’s foreign minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttirreportedly said that the EEA agreement has provided the strong foundations for this relationship, but that the world is changing. “We must face these changes," she added.
European Policy Centre senior advisor Tobias Etzold has opined that growing doubt over US reliability in the region, paired with an increasingly adversarial Russia, is what reignited the EU referendum debate in Iceland.
And it is the theatre of geopolitics that has injected "fresh dynamism" into a discussion that had lain dormant for more than a decade.

The Dalit enigma: Why Mayawati is going solo in Punjab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:02:37 UTC
23:02:37 KST

The Dalit enigma: Why Mayawati is going solo in Punjab
Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 28, 2026, 19:32 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Mayawati’s solo Punjab gamble tests whether the state’s 32% Dalit population can translate into a consolidated BSP vote.
Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) chief Mayawati has decided to go solo in the upcoming 2027 Punjab assembly election. This move has put the spotlight on a striking contradiction in the state's politics: Punjab has India's highest proportion of Scheduled Castes, but no political party has been able to turn that numerical strength into a durable Dalit vote bloc.On August 25, Mayawati announced that the BSP would contest the polls "alone without any alliance or compromise with anyone", arguing that electoral tie-ups risked weakening the party’s vote share and demoralising its cadre.The decision carries particular significance in Punjab, where BSP founder Kanshi Ram began his political journey and where Scheduled Castes account for 31.94% of the population, according to the 2011 Census.Yet nearly one-third of Punjab's population has never translated into nearly one-third of the vote for the BSP - or any other Dalit-centric political formation.Instead, the Dalit electorate has remained divided across caste, religious, regional and economic lines, allowing the Congress, AAP, SAD and BJP to each build pockets of support within it.That makes Mayawati's 2027 gamble less about the size of Punjab's Dalit population and more about a difficult political question: Can she turn the state's 32% Dalit population into a coherent electoral bloc?
Punjab's number paradox
The numbers explain why every major political party wants a share of the Dalit vote.
Punjab had about 88.6 lakh Scheduled Castes in the 2011 Census, accounting for 31.94% of its population - the highest SC proportion among Indian states. The community is particularly concentrated in the Doaba region, which includes Jalandhar, Hoshiarpur and Nawanshahr.Eight of Doaba's 23 assembly constituencies are reserved for SC candidates, while both Lok Sabha constituencies in the region, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur, are reserved.Across Punjab, 34 of the 117 assembly seats are reserved for Scheduled Caste candidates. But the political influence of Dalit voters extends far beyond these constituencies.
In Punjab, Dalits are divided into several sub-castes and religion.
A 2021 analysis by Lokniti-CSDS professor Sanjay Kumar found that Dalits accounted for more than 30% of voters in 54 assembly constituencies and between 20% and 30% in another 45.In other words, Dalit voters can influence far more than the 34 seats formally reserved for them.But there is a crucial caveat: 'Dalit' is not a single political identity in Punjab.The community comprises several sub-caste and religious groups, including Ravidassias/Ad-Dharmis, Mazhabi Sikhs, Ramdasias and others. Their geographical distribution, religious affiliations, economic circumstances and political histories differ.That fragmentation has repeatedly prevented the kind of consolidated Dalit politics that emerged around the BSP in Uttar Pradesh.Punjab's agrarian structure adds another layer. Land and economic power remain disproportionately concentrated among dominant agrarian communities, particularly Jat Sikhs. As a result, Dalit politics in the state often revolves around land rights, employment, reservation, social dignity and access to common resources, rather than caste identity alone.
From Kanshi Ram's Punjab to BSP's high-water mark
Mayawati pays tribute on death anniversary of Kanshi Ram.
The irony is that Punjab was once among the BSP's strongest political laboratories.Kanshi Ram, born in Punjab, built his early political movement around the mobilisation of Scheduled Castes and other marginalised communities before founding the BSP in 1984.The party's breakthrough in Punjab came in the 1992 election. It won nine of the state's 117 seats with 16.32% of the vote, emerging as the principal opposition party in the House. Six of those nine seats came from Doaba, underlining the region’s importance to the party’s political project.But the breakthrough proved difficult to sustain.In 1997, the BSP's tally fell to one seat, although it still secured 7.48% of the vote. Its vote share then declined steadily — to 5.69% in 2002, 4.13% in 2007 and 4.29% in 2012. By 2017, it had fallen to 1.52%.In 2022, the BSP won just one seat with 1.77% of the vote, contesting as part of its alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal.The steep decline in three decades captures the central problem Mayawati now faces.
How 2022 exposed the paradox
If the BSP's decline showed the difficulty of sustaining Dalit-centric politics, the 2022 assembly election demonstrated how effectively mainstream parties can cut across caste identities.The AAP won 92 of Punjab's 117 seats with 42.01% of the statewide vote, while Congress was reduced to 18 seats.The AAP’s performance was particularly striking in SC-reserved constituencies. It won 29 of the 34 reserved seats, while Congress won four and the SAD-BSP alliance one.The result also undercut the assumption that Congress's elevation of Charanjit Singh Channi as Punjab's first Dalit CM would automatically consolidate the Dalit vote behind the party. Channi became CM in September 2021, just months before the election. His elevation was widely viewed as an attempt to appeal to the state’s huge Dalit electorate.But in March 2022, Congress suffered a dramatic defeat.
SAD and its alliance route
The SAD has historically had its own Dalit support base, particularly among Sikh Dalits.Its alliance with Mayawati ahead of the 2022 election was an attempt to combine the Akali network among sections of the Sikh electorate with the BSP's Dalit support base.The combination, however, failed to produce the revival the two parties had hoped for. The alliance won four seats - three for the SAD and one for the BSP - with a combined vote share of around 20%.BJP's gamble: From alliance politics to going soloThe BJP faces perhaps the most difficult social-coalition challenge of all.Its long-standing electoral arrangement with the SAD ended after the Akali Dal walked out of the NDA at the Centre over the farm laws.The BJP is now trying to establish itself as an independent force in a state where it historically relied heavily on the Akali alliance to provide it with a rural and Sikh social base. That means the party needs to build coalitions beyond the constituencies it traditionally relied on, while also trying to repair its relationship with farmers.Dalit voters are an obvious part of that expansion strategy.But Punjab is not Uttar Pradesh or Bihar. There, the BJP has invested heavily in a social coalition involving non-Yadav OBCs and Dalits. A different caste and religious configuration shapes Punjab’s political landscape, while its agrarian structure and Sikh identity make the BJP’s social engineering considerably more complicated.For the BJP, winning Dalit voters is therefore not simply about adding another community to its support base. It is about constructing an entirely new political coalition in a state where its old alliance no longer provides the same electoral cushion.
AAP's pitch: Welfare, not identity
The AAP has already demonstrated why the size of the Dalit population does not automatically translate into BSP votes.In 2022, the party's appeal cut across caste lines, combining welfare, anti-incumbency and the promise of an alternative to the traditional parties. It also had the 'Delhi model' to demonstrate its pitch.AAP sought to build a political vocabulary around BR Ambedkar, combining Ambedkarite symbolism with a broader welfare narrative.Rather than presenting Dalits as a separate electoral constituency, the party has sought to fold their concerns into a larger promise around government schools, healthcare, jobs, welfare delivery and social dignity.However, now the 2027 election will test whether AAP can retain that support after a full term in government.
Congress has history, but not the Dalit lock
Congress has historically had a strong base among both Hindu and Sikh Dalits in Punjab, but its 2022 performance showed the limits of that advantage. In the 2017 election, the party won 21 of 34 SC-reserved seats; by 2022, after making Charanjit Singh Channi the state’s first Dalit CM and projecting him as its CM face, Congress was reduced to just four reserved seats, while AAP won 29.The setback has not ended Congress's Dalit outreach. In January 2026, Channi himself raised questions within the party over the representation of Dalit leaders, pointing out that several key Punjab Congress positions were held by Jat Sikhs.For Congress, the 2027 challenge is therefore not winning Dalit votes from scratch, but rebuilding a social coalition it once had, without reducing Dalit politics to the Channi factor alone.
Mayawati's real gamble
Mayawati’s decision to contest alone is therefore both ideological and organisational.The BSP has something only a few parties can claim: a political vocabulary explicitly built around Ambedkar, Kanshi Ram and Bahujan mobilisation. Punjab also provides the demographic foundation for such a project.But the party’s electoral history demonstrates the enormous gap between having a potential social constituency and converting it into votes and seats.The challenge is not simply to persuade Dalits to vote for the BSP. It is to persuade different Dalit communities that their interests are sufficiently common to vote for the same party. That is a much harder proposition in Punjab than the 32% figure suggests.
Ready to play a spoilsport?
There is, however, another reason Mayawati’s decision could matter even if the BSP does not return to anything close to its 1992 performance.Punjab’s 2027 contest is shaping up as a fragmented battle involving AAP, Congress, BJP and SAD, although the possibility of a BJP-SAD reunion remains open.In such a contest, even a relatively small but geographically concentrated BSP vote could become consequential.The party’s past performance offers a warning to the larger parties. In 2024, the BSP was reported to have remained a significant factor in parts of Doaba despite its shrinking statewide base, with observers pointing to its potential to influence contests in seats such as Anandpur Sahib, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur.
That is the paradox of Mayawati's Punjab gamble.The BSP may no longer have the numbers to dominate Punjab’s Dalit politics, but it could still have enough votes to disrupt everyone else’s arithmetic.The 2027 election will therefore test not just whether Mayawati can revive the BSP in Kanshi Ram’s home state, but whether Punjab’s nearly 32% Dalit population can finally translate its demographic weight into political leverage - if not as a single bloc, then as the constituency no major party can afford to ignore.
News desk journalist, digital, at The Times of India, with a focus on Indian politics. Over a decade of chasing stories, taming headlines and arguing with commas like they're part of the opposition. Tracks elections, policy pivots, party drama and the fine print of power, where every word can tilt the narrative. Africa's aging autocrats fight to stay in power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:02:00 UTC
23:02:00 KST

Africa's aging autocrats fight to stay in power
August 28, 2026
Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia, for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the United States, the president occasionally speaks of another run for office, even though the US Constitution does not allow it.
From the perspective of Paul Biya, however, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump are still relatively new to office.
Cameroon's president has been head of state since 1982. In 2025, Biya began his eighth term — which is officially due to end on November 6, 2032, just a few months before his 100th birthday.
The 93-year-old has given no official indication that he intends to step down, and the position of vice president remains vacant.
Paul Biya in Cameroon: A loyal leadership circle with one weak spot
During his 44 years in office, Biya has built a stable network of loyal allies that keeps the machinery of government running despite his lengthy absences.
The 93-year-old has now spent two and a half months in Geneva, Switzerland, continuing to issue decrees and make personnel decisions from abroad. In mid-June, his spokesperson denied rumors Biya was receiving treatment in a hospital and stated that the president was in good health.
"There is continuity, but that also means there is little momentum for reform within the government,” Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at consultancy Global Risk, told DW.
And while Biya's power apparatus has helped cushion the impact of the president's long absence, that does not necessarily mean the most influential figures on the ground are united. After all, a post-Biya era is now in sight, and several of his allies are rumored to have ambitions of succeeding him.
"When everyone is lining up to potentially succeed Biya, it also means that the elites may begin challenging one another," Ochieng said. Such rivalry, she warned, could lead to major disruptions, including the possibility of a military coup.
Analyst Levi Mboushou recently voiced similar concerns on DW's AfricaLink podcast.
"Everyone feels the fear and uncertainty, but no one dares to look directly at it because we all have to deal with this repressive regime. You see something, but you say nothing. That is the situation in Cameroon at the moment," he said.
Yoweri Museveni in Uganda: Signs of a dynasty?
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni is only slightly younger, both in age and years in office.
The 81-year-old has been president since 1986 and, like Biya, recently embarked on another term. His succession also remains unresolved, although his son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has recently attracted considerable attention as head of the military.
According to Ochieng, the dynamics in Uganda are complex, not least because military elites and the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) have their own internal power structures.
"Muhoozi has become the most visible figure primarily because he has a strong personality and enjoys the discreet backing of his father. His rise is not the result of support from either the NRM or the military leadership," she said.
Kainerugaba is increasingly emerging as a political figure, including on issues beyond military affairs.
In early July, he ordered the closure of several media outlets. At the time, a source from an international foundation who requested anonymity told DW: "We are witnessing a transfer of power to the president's son."
A similar development has been unfolding for years in Equatorial Guinea, where Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has ruled since 1979, appears to be gradually transferring power to his son.
Known by the nickname "Teodorin," he has served as first vice president since 2016 and now also controls the military.
In June, Teodorin announced the resignation of the entire government on behalf of his father. Observers interpreted the move as a sign that he is gradually becoming the public face of state authority.
Whether Museveni will actually arrange his succession during his lifetime remains uncertain.
Ochieng believes that, in the event of a sudden power vacuum, Uganda could either hold constitutionally mandated elections or follow a scenario similar to that seen in Chad in 2021.
Then-President Idriss Deby was killed in clashes with rebels. The constitution was suspended, allowing his son, Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno, to take power.
Emmerson Mnangagwa in Zimbabwe: Party before people
Zimbabwe also amended its constitution this year, making it far less likely that President Emmerson Mnangagwa could be voted out of office.
In June, both chambers of parliament approved changes extending the terms of parliament and the president from five to seven years. Even more fundamentally, the president will no longer be elected directly by the people but by parliament, where the ruling ZANU-PF party enjoys comfortable majorities.
In July, the 83-year-old Mnangagwa signed the amended constitution into law. However, the opposition and some constitutional experts argue that a referendum should still be held. The government, by contrast, considers the constitutional amendment process complete.
"We are not surprised," Chiedza Mlingwa, deputy spokesperson for the Constitution Defenders Forum, said at the time on DW's AfricaLink podcast.
"The only thing one could be surprised by is the audacity, nothing else. We have observed this pattern since independence in 1980: ZANU-PF works to stay in power. The party does not believe in relinquishing power."
Ochieng noted that countries such as Togo and Cote d'Ivoire have also implemented constitutional changes aimed at preserving power in recent years.
Meanwhile, in Senegal, a constitutional amendment is being discussed amid tensions between former allies at the top of the state, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Speaker of Parliament Ousmane Sonko, both of whom are significantly younger than the continent's other long-ruling leaders.
"Even when legal safeguards exist, if they are not designed in a way that guarantees citizen participation, public debate, civil society engagement, or oversight by other institutions, then it becomes possible for unilateral decisions to be made at the highest levels of government," said Ochieng.
The weakening of institutions to allow individuals to remain in power, she added, is not an African problem but a global one.
Lucy Riley contributed to this article.
This article was originally written in German.

The Cabinet extended the period of legal stay for foreign nationals and stateless persons who defend Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:01:39 EEST
23:01:39 KST

The Cabinet extended the period of legal stay for foreign nationals and stateless persons who defend Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The Government approved a draft law on the protection of foreign nationals and stateless persons who served in Ukraine’s Defense Forces. The period of stay after the end of their contract will be extended to six months.
The Cabinet of Ministers approved a bill that strengthens the legal protection of foreigners and stateless persons who have taken up the defense of Ukraine. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, according to UNN.
Details
The bill was drafted by the Ministry for Veterans Affairs of Ukraine. After completing their military contract, they will have more time to regulate their legal status: the bill provides for increasing the period of lawful temporary residence in Ukraine from three to six months.
The bill proposes:
-  to increase from three to six months the period of lawful
temporary residence after completing a military contract. This will give a person more time to regulate their legal status without haste; 
-  to count the period of military service under contract toward the five-year residence period required to obtain an immigration permit; 
-  to recognize a combatant's certificate, a certificate of a person with a war-related disability, or a corresponding extract from the Unified State Register of War Veterans as grounds for obtaining a temporary residence permit; 
-  to establish a separate immigration quota for foreigners who, for at least four months, together with units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine, performed combat or service missions in areas of hostilities, as well as for those who were held captive; 
-  to introduce an identity document for a foreigner to travel abroad. This is to apply in cases where a person cannot obtain or exchange a passport in their country of origin due to a threat or political circumstances. 
We remind you
The Verkhovna Rada has registered a bill that provides for issuing three-year temporary residence permits in Ukraine to Belarusians who condemn Russian aggression and do not pose a threat to national security, as well as simplifying the process of obtaining citizenship for them.

Principled Caution: Navigating AI in Asian Newsrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

Across Asia, public interest media are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to optimize under-resourced newsrooms. However, these outlets face a high-stakes reality: publishing AI-generated errors, factual inaccuracies, or “AI slop” risks undermining the public trust and credibility central to their legitimacy. At the same time, these media are also aware that they are operating in authoritarian contexts where AI-induced mistakes can lead to legal and political persecution.
Hence, independent outlets in the Asia-Pacific – the media that produce journalism essential to democratic accountability – exercise “principled caution” when deploying AI. They exercise this caution not just because of a desire to maintain their reputation for accuracy. They also do so because there is a real risk of forced state closure, the freezing of assets, or the imprisonment of staff.
This is the core finding of Asia Centre’s latest report, “Principled caution: How AI is used in public-interest media in Asia,” published in partnership with DW Akademie and supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Evaluating media ecosystems across eight Asian countries – Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Myanmar, Pakistan, and Uzbekistan – the study reveals how journalists are managing AI adoption. Rather than blind adoption, Asia’s independent public interest media are approaching AI through a careful and highly selective strategy. In structurally precarious environments where reporting errors can invite censorship, legal action, or operational shutdown, outlets consistently prioritize human editorial oversight over full-scale automation.
The report identifies several key findings:
First, AI usage in newsrooms remains assistive rather than transformative. Outlets primarily use generative AI tools at the preliminary and final stages of editorial workflows, for tasks such as ideation, document summarization, social media adaptation, and headline polishing. The central stages of journalistic work – including original field reporting, investigative narrative drafting, and editorial judgment – remain strictly human-driven.
Second, severe language constraints mean that major global Large Language Models underperform in low-resource Asian languages, including Bahasa Indonesia, Bangla, Burmese, Chittagonian, Dzongkha, Farsi, Jingpo, Khmer, Pashto, and Urdu. These platforms frequently mistranslate context-sensitive terms, flatten cultural nuances, and generate wrong outputs. While translation is the most widely adopted AI task, outputs require labor-intensive human correction.
Third, exiled media from countries like Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Pakistan face distinct operational threats including digital surveillance, internet blackouts, cross-border security risks, and severe financial instability. These pressures leave little mental or institutional bandwidth to experiment with new technologies. Yet, securely tailored automated tools for transcription, translation, and media-monitoring offer an unrealized opportunity to engage diaspora networks and report on repressed homelands without compromising journalists’ digital safety.
Fourth, a sharp institutional deficit persists across newsrooms. Over 60 percent of surveyed newsrooms report that AI adoption occurs via ad-hoc, individual staff experimentation rather than cohesive organizational strategies. Structural gaps, such as the absence of formal editorial guidelines, missing data protection protocols, and a heavy reliance on Big Tech platforms, leave independent media vulnerable to algorithmic bias, privacy violations, copyright risks, and state surveillance.
Fifth, restrictive political and legal environments across Asia impede responsible AI adoption. While state authorities deploy automated systems for online monitoring, surveillance, and synthetic media campaigns, regulatory ambiguity is routinely weaponized to clamp down on media freedoms. Public interest newsrooms face a stark structural asymmetry; political actors deploy AI at scale to amplify state narratives and disinformation, while underfunded independent outlets lack affordable verification tools to counter these attacks effectively.
Looking ahead, AI integration in Asian newsrooms cannot rely solely on off-the-shelf tools built by Western tech monopolies. Long-term media sustainability requires localized AI infrastructure, enforceable newsroom governance frameworks, and open-source language models tailored to the region’s complex political and linguistic contexts. Without this shift toward technological sovereignty, regional media risk becoming mere data points for foreign algorithmic models that operate without local democratic stakes. We must move beyond being passive consumers of black-box solutions and start architecting a digital future that respects our region’s unique socio-political boundaries.
To achieve this, international donors and media development actors must pivot away from short-term, surface-level training sessions. Instead, capital must be redirected toward regional and local entities to lead core technological infrastructure, secure data storage systems, and create collaborative AI hubs specifically designed to serve independent and exiled media. This requires reimagining “capacity building” as the construction of resilient, shared digital architectures that treat cybersecurity as a foundational reporting tool. By financing regional and local based collective defense, we can turn isolated public interest newsrooms into fortified digital outposts capable of weathering persistent state-sponsored surveillance.
Ultimately, the future of journalism in Asia will not be determined by the speed of algorithmic tools, but by whether newsrooms can harness AI without compromising the trust, accuracy, and independence that underpin public interest reporting. In an era of synthetic media floods, human-centric rigor is not a hurdle to innovation – it is our ultimate competitive advantage. Those who prioritize ethical safeguards now will be the only ones to retain audience loyalty when the inevitable global backlash against AI-generated misinformation arrives.
This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Principled caution: How AI is used in public-interest media in Asia”. Download the full report here. For more information about the Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org.

How the stories we tell about ourselves reveal hidden personality disorders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:00:26 UTC
23:00:26 KST

How people construct the stories of their lives offers insight into the severity of their personality disorders. Researchers found that narrating life events with a focus on negative self-change strongly predicted everyday functional impairment. The findings were published in the Journal of Personality.
Psychiatry is currently shifting the way it diagnoses personality disorders. Instead of relying entirely on rigid categories where a patient either has a disorder or does not, newer frameworks use a sliding scale. This dimensional approach focuses on a concept known as the level of personality functioning. It assesses how well a person maintains their identity, sets life goals, and connects with others through empathy and intimacy.
Because identity is heavily shaped by the stories people tell themselves about their past, researchers wanted to see if analyzing these personal narratives could help measure personality functioning. Lead author Kennedy M. Balzen, a psychology researcher at the University of Houston, worked with colleagues Majse Lind, Paulina A. Kulesz, Estefania Fernandez, and Carla Sharp. The team aimed to determine if specific emotional and structural themes in a person’s life story could predict their degree of clinical dysfunction.
The researchers recruited 140 young adults between the ages of 18 and 25. The group included 94 college students and 46 individuals who had either been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder or showed traits of the condition. Borderline personality disorder is characterized by unstable relationships, emotional volatility, and a distorted self-image.
Participants completed an interview where they imagined their lives as a book and described two life-changing events in detail. Trained coders then evaluated these spoken stories for five specific psychological themes. The first theme was agency, which measures how much autonomy and control the narrator feels they have over their life.
The second theme was communion, which tracks feelings of love, belonging, and interpersonal connection. The coders also looked for a trait called exploratory processing. This metric captures how deeply the person analyzed an event’s meaning and worked through their changing sense of self.
Finally, the coders assessed the narratives for growth and deterioration. These two themes measure whether the narrator concluded that the event changed them for the better or revealed a permanent, negative flaw in their character. High deterioration scores suggest the individual believes an event fundamentally damaged them.
Alongside the storytelling interview, participants completed two tools to assess their overall level of personality functioning. The first was a self-report survey where participants rated their own identity and interpersonal struggles. The second was a semi-structured clinical interview conducted by trained graduate students.
This interview format bypasses the biases inherent in self-reported surveys. Participants also took a survey to measure their functional impairment. This assessment tracks a person’s level of disability in daily tasks like cognition, mobility, self-care, and getting along with others.
When comparing the narrative themes to the personality assessments, the researchers observed a distinct pattern. People who exhibited worse personality functioning tended to tell stories with lower levels of agency, communion, and personal growth. These individuals also featured higher levels of deterioration in their stories.
To illustrate narrative deterioration, the researchers highlighted a story from a participant who experienced childhood bullying. The participant described the event as a permanent blow to their ego that made them feel like they could never fit in. The participant said, “I felt like that was a result of my own personal faults, or like something that I lacked in,” and noted that the isolation eventually led to self-harm.
Next, the researchers ran statistical models to see which narrative themes best predicted a person’s level of personality functioning. They found that stories featuring high levels of agency predicted better scores on the self-reported personality surveys. Conversely, narratives high in deterioration predicted worse scores on the clinical interviews.
In fact, individuals who told stories with strong themes of deterioration were nearly three times more likely to meet the clinical threshold for a personality disorder. This threshold was based on the rigorous, interview-rated assessment. The finding highlights how different testing methods capture different aspects of a person’s psychology.
The team also tested whether exploratory processing interacted with growth or deterioration to predict personality functioning. They hypothesized that deep reflection on a negative change would yield different results than deep reflection on a positive change. The data did not support this idea, as deterioration remained the only distinct predictor of personality dysfunction in these models.
Finally, the researchers looked at everyday functional impairment. They used a statistical approach to find the most efficient combination of variables to predict a person’s daily struggles. They found that combining narrative deterioration scores with the results from the self-reported and interview-based personality assessments explained the most variance in functional impairment. The inclusion of narrative deterioration provided predictive power that the standard clinical tools missed.
The study relied on participants self-reporting their borderline personality disorder diagnoses or symptoms, which means some individuals might not have met formal clinical criteria. The tool used to measure functional impairment also captures general life disability, which is not exclusively tied to mental health challenges. Future studies will need to use outcome measures that are directly linked to psychiatric symptoms.
Another limitation involves the coding system used for exploratory processing. The coders had lower reliability when agreeing on this specific metric, which might explain why it did not predict personality functioning in the statistical models. The researchers noted that narrative coding systems were originally designed for typical populations and might need adjustment to fully capture disordered thinking.
It is possible that people with personality disorders simply experience more traumatic life events, which would naturally lead to darker life stories. However, psychological theory suggests the distinction lies in how a person derives meaning from difficult experiences and integrates that meaning into their identity. Still, subsequent studies should account for a person’s history of trauma and abuse to isolate the exact impact of life events on storytelling.
The study, “Life Stories Matter: The Contribution of Narrative Identity to Personality Functioning and Functional Impairment,” was authored by Kennedy M. Balzen, Majse Lind, Paulina A. Kulesz, Estefania Fernandez, and Carla Sharp.

The ‘Asian water tower’ is starting to wobble, computer simulations show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

The ‘Asian water tower’ is starting to wobble, computer simulations show
The Tibetan Plateau is losing stability, a study suggests, as a catastrophic flash flood hit on the Nepal-China border
The study, published on August 21 in Nature Communications, examined the entropy of the region to gauge how much chaos or disorder was building up in a complex system.
Chen Xiaosong, a physicist at the school of systems science at Beijing Normal University and lead author of the study, said on Thursday that from now to the end of this century, “the increase of soil water and the intensification of glacier melting [in the Tibetan Plateau] will constantly trigger such geological disasters”.
Chen’s team examined the plateau’s soil moisture system from 2000 to 2024, which is closely linked to the water and climate patterns affecting nearly two billion people across South and East Asia.

Swiss Abroad face threat to 13th pension payment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Swiss Abroad face threat to 13th pension payment
Swiss citizens living abroad could be excluded from the new 13th state pension payment under a proposal from the right-wing Swiss People’s Party.
A year ahead of the federal elections, the People’s Party is proposing new restrictions on the Swiss diaspora. In a motion, parliamentarian Didier Calame has called for “the 13th pension [payment] to be restricted to beneficiaries who are resident in Switzerland”.
Calame told Swissinfo: “Pensioners abroad are entitled to the OASI [Swiss old-age and survivors’ pension, also known as AHV/AVS], but not to a 13th pension payment. They often deliberately emigrate for economic reasons to countries where the cost of living is lower. So they are saving money.” Calame goes on to say that he has already received reactions from expatriates in Portugal, Thailand and the Dominican Republic. “These are all countries with a low cost of living. You need less money there. That proves I am right.”
Pensions abroad targeted before
Calame came up with the idea for his motion during parliamentary debates on how to fund the 13th pension payment. This is expected to cost the Swiss government CHF4.2 billion ($5.22 billion) this year alone, and then around CHF5 billion ($6.22 billion) annually thereafter. Funding for this has not yet been secured; so far, parliament has only been able to agree on incomplete or temporary funding arrangements.
“Because the financing of the OASI poses a growing challenge, it is essential to concentrate the available funds on those who live in our country and are actually suffering from high prices,” Calame writes in his motion.
During the initiative campaign on the introduction of the 13th pension payment, the People’s Party criticised retirees living abroad. “Swiss citizens living abroad are the most selfish people there are,” declared journalist Markus Somm at the time, acting as an advisor to the People’s Party leadership. Some parliamentarians also spoke of “luxury pensioners abroad”.
Swiss Abroad react with anger
Within the community of the Swiss Abroad, the current proposal – first reported by the news portal cash.ch – has caused outrage. Josef Schnyder, who represents the Swiss Abroad in Thailand, comments: “The People’s Party is making it unmistakably clear where it stands on the Swiss Abroad: paying OASI contributions – yes. Equal rights in old age – no.” Matthias Anderegg, a Swiss Abroad in Thailand, asks: “Are Swiss people worth less as soon as they live abroad? Anyone who has paid into the OASI all their life should be able to spend their retirement wherever they wish, without being disadvantaged.”
Daniel Hunziker, director of the Organisation of the Swiss Abroad (ASO), replied succinctly when asked by Swissinfo: “The ASO rejects cuts to benefits for the Swiss Abroad.”
Will the People’s Party lose the support of the Swiss Abroad with this move, a year before the elections?
“To be honest, I wasn’t thinking about the 2027 elections when I drafted this motion – that’s not how I work. But it could, of course, have a slight impact on this electorate,” said Calame.
Pensions abroad are low
No distinction is made regarding nationality when it comes to pensions paid abroad. They are not only paid to the Swiss Abroad, but two-thirds go to former foreign workers who have returned to their home countries from Switzerland after retirement. “As far as I’m concerned, they are all emigrants. It has nothing to do with the nationality of the pension recipients. The idea behind the 13th OASI was to do something about the rising cost of living in Switzerland,” says Calame.
Both the Swiss Abroad and foreign nationals have seen their numbers rise in recent years, though not at a disproportionately higher rate than the domestic population. The total OASI budget has grown at the same rate.
However, the People’s Party’s focus on pensions paid abroad has so far hardly ever considered the total amount of pensions paid out. During the 2024 initiative campaign, the party already pointed out that almost one in three OASI recipients lives abroad. This is correct, as this chart shows.
However, it is also worth noting that by no means one in three pension francs goes abroad. In fact, it accounts for only 14% of all pension expenditure by the Swiss state.
This is because pensions paid abroad are, on average, much lower. In 2025, the average monthly pension in Switzerland was CHF1,970 ($2,450), while abroad it was CHF702 ($873). Anyone receiving an average pension from abroad would therefore struggle to make ends meet in Switzerland without supplementary benefits. A pension paid abroad costs Switzerland around a third of what a domestic pension does.
Based on the figures for 2025, the potential savings from not paying the 13th OASI pension abroad would amount to around 14% of the new expenditure incurred.
Why the government opposes the pension cut
The Federal Council, Switzerland’s executive body, recommends rejecting Calame’s motion, citing the law – in particular the agreement on the free movement of persons with the European Union (EU) and Switzerland’s social security agreements with other countries. The principle of equal treatment applies in these contexts. “Nationals of the countries concerned have the same rights as Swiss nationals,” writes the Federal Council. “There is no scope for treating beneficiaries living abroad differently from insured persons resident in Switzerland.” Furthermore, the text of the Constitution guarantees all recipients a 13th old-age pension.
In a statement, the international branch of Switzerland’s Social Democratic Party points out that the cost of living abroad is not lower everywhere compared to Switzerland. The Swiss Abroad also often have to take out private health insurance, which can be significantly more expensive, particularly as they get older. “If such private insurance is not available, they have to cover a considerable proportion of their healthcare costs themselves,” writes Co-President Christophe Margot. “This is another reason why they are reliant on the 13th OASI pension.”
The maximum annual state pension in Switzerland for an individual currently stands at CHF32,760 ($40,729), including the 13th payment. The amount depends on the duration and level of pension contributions made during a working life.
