Families of 33 missing Britons rush to Nepal as fears grow of more floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:39:36 UTC
22:39:36 KST

Families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing, as fears mount over the risk of a second wave of flooding in the region.
The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 538 people, while more than 1,500 remain missing.
Among them are hundreds of foreign tourists who were visiting the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims for its natural beauty and religious significance.
Relatives of missing Britons have shared their devastation as they desperately try to reach their loved ones who were last seen in the Rasuwa district, where power and communication lines are down. Many are scrambling to book flights to Kathmandu, the Nepalese capital.
 On Friday, authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, posing a risk of “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed after debris blocked a river at the site was also rising and at risk of bursting.
Rescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes. Many were seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.
In a video on YouTube, Jaggi Vasudev, known as Sadhguru, a spiritual leader who founded the nonprofit Isha Foundation, told followers at the foundation’s camp at Saga in Tibet, China, that 80 members of an Isha group returning from Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists, were missing, including nine British people.
Among them was Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51. Her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC that completing the pilgrimage was “her dream”.
 Neetu’s nephew, Anmol Goyal, said she had been travelling with a friend, and that her last known location was at the immigration centre on the Tibet-Nepal border. He said she had been added to the Nepalese government’s official list of missing persons.
The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of them are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Goyal said her husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.
“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”
The Telegraph reported that an NHS psychiatrist, Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims on Isha Foundation’s journey to Mount Kailash. The group’s last-known location was an immigration centre in Timure, in the mudslide’s direct path. 
 His wife, Manjula Atmakur, who arrived in Kathmandu to search for him on Friday, told the newspaper she was disappointed by the British government’s response to the disaster.
Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers in its group who were unaccounted for.
Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list. “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there,” he said. “She must be in trauma.”
 Also missing are an A-level student from Surrey, Spandan Sahu, 18, and his father, Santosh Sahu, 46, the chief executive of the UK pharmaceutical technology company Charac; Spandan’s mother, Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44; and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.
Mahadev Semwal, a friend of Sahu’s for about 15 years, said: “I had WhatsApp communication with him on Monday: they were going to Nepal then Manasarovar in Tibet.
“When I heard on Wednesday about the flooding, I lost contact with him – when I am trying to message him it is getting delivered but not read.
“Our heart says they are safe somewhere. It’s possible because the communication is jammed.
“But when you see the videos, it is unbelievable. It feels so bad.”
Also confirmed missing was Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse from Dartford, Kent, who left for Nepal last Saturday on a religious journey.
 Deepesh Patel told the Press Association that his parents, Bipin Patel, 66, and Mala Patel, 60, from Coventry, were missing after flying to Nepal on 22 August for a pilgrimage. His brother Anant Patel told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information on their whereabouts.
Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he had not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.
“We’re not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week,” Kolagatla added.
Tatjana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she had not been able to contact her sister, Julija Jakovicka, who was attending a yoga and meditation retreat near the Nepal-Tibet border when flash flooding hit.
Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he had not heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, or sister-in-law, Ankita Chandra, 35, who had gone on a pilgrimage.
Ranjan added: “We don’t know if they crossed the border … We don’t have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated.”
The tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said it had been unable to make contact with a party of 12 Britons aged 13 to 65 who had booked a tour to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and were in the vicinity when the flash floods hit.
Sunil Amin, from Croydon in south London, shared with the Daily Mail the “horrible, horrible feeling” of repeatedly trying to phone his wife, Hema Amin, 63, who was on a pilgrimage with Alpine Eco Trek from Nepal to Tibet with her sister. “I’m devastated,” he said.
The Trekkers’ Society, which organises tours across Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage had gone missing. The organisation confirmed that four men and boys aged between 14 and 50 and five women aged 40 to 53 were unaccounted for.
Himalayan Glacier US said it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff, including two Britons, who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, regarded as the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.
The tour operator Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – who were travelling with it.
 Leaf Holidays, which runs Himalayan treks and expeditions from Kathmandu, wrote in a Facebook post that its group of 55 travellers remained missing, including four British citizens, Tara and Babar Gurung and Thaneswar and Tejkumari Gurung, who have not been heard from since Tuesday.
Twelve of the missing British citizens were on a tour to Mount Kailash led by Nabhi Nandan Das, a 64-year-old Hindu priest who works at the Sanatan Mandir and community centre in Surrey, the Telegraph reported. He is understood to have been leading 11 Britons on a tour that was due to visit Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, two Hindu holy sites in Tibet.
Pramod Poudel, who runs a Nepalese street food company in Sussex, told the Daily Mail his wife, Sumitra, mother, Tulisa, brother Pradip and uncle Madav were all missing. His father, Purusottam, has been found alive.
The Non-Resident Nepali Association in the UK launched an emergency fundraising appeal on Thursday and more than £12,000 has been raised.
Rajendra Pudasaini, a nurse in Essex who is president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said Nepal was witnessing an “irreplaceable loss” and Nepal was “paying the price for global warming”.
Pudasaini told BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme that many of his family members were missing. “My godson, we found the body yesterday morning, you know, he (was) just buried under the mud at his house, and yes, lots of other dead bodies being found.”
He added: “It’s a very difficult situation to describe, actually.”

'Preposterous': Lawmakers Reject Trump's Renaming of Lake Ontario Amid U.S.-Canada Trade War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:38:19 UTC
22:38:19 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Lake Ontario will continue to be called by that name despite President Donald Trump signing an Executive Order directing for it to be renamed as “Lake America.”
“The name is more than 400 years old, pre-dating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” said Carney on Thursday. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms.”
Insisting that Canadians are aware of the “naming reality,” Carney rejected Trump's directive for the lake, which borders the Canadian province of Ontario and the U.S. state of New York.
The name change is the latest jab in an escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada after talks collapsed last week, leading to tariffs being imposed by both countries.
The order applies to U.S. federal references of the lake and does not determine how Canada—or others—refer to the body of water.
The “Lake Ontario” moniker has also firmly been rejected by many in the U.S., including New York’s Gov. Kathy Hochul, who simply stated: “New York won’t be calling it that.”
With tensions between the Trump Administration and Canada reaching new heights, here’s what to know about how lawmakers on both sides of the lake have responded to the Executive Order.
How Canadian lawmakers have reacted
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, a vocal critic of the U.S. President, insisted “it’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world, now and forever.” In agreement, Ontario lawmaker Marit Stiles said: “It will always be Lake Ontario.”
Patrick Brown, the mayor of Brampton, Ontario, described the name change as “preposterous,” telling CNN: “We’re still going to call it Lake Ontario, I think many of you [Americans] will still call it Lake Ontario.”
“The only person who is going to have a trouble with what to call it is your President,” Brown continued. “If our Prime Minister wanted to rename the Mississippi, you’d probably get a chuckle out of it. It’s having the same reaction in Canada.”
Pierre Poilievre, Canada's main opposition leader, staunchly pushed back on Trump’s directive. “Lake Ontario is and will always be Lake Ontario, and no Executive Order will change that. It doesn't belong to President Donald Trump to rename on a whim,” he said.
“It's Lake Ontario, buddy,” said Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston, referring to the name change as “some real foolishness.”
Elsewhere, Toronto mayor Olivia Chow vowed that Trump's "antics won't weaken our resolve as Canadians."
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew likened Trump to an “over the hill” rock band. “He thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he’s trying to bring back that,” he said, referencing how Trump signed a similar order last year renaming the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.”
City councillor Brad Bradford, who is currently running for mayor of Toronto, said if he’s elected, he’ll push to rename Trump’s home state the “Province of New York.”
Referring to D.C.’s actions as "ludicrous," Bradford insisted “you can try and change the name of a lake, but you can’t change the spirit of our city, our province, or our country.”
What U.S. Democrats have said about the name change
Rep. Tim Kennedy of New York referred to the trade war as "illogical" and accused Trump of distributing "juvenile" rhetoric. “Lake Ontario will always be Lake Ontario,” he said.
Former First Lady and 2016 Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton stated “it’s Lake Ontario” in response to the news.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland argued the move was “more evidence we elected a toddler as President.”
Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan announced plans to introduce a bill, titled the "Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act," that would nullify the name change.
Denouncing the President's directive, Dingell said: “Donald Trump can sign all the Executive Orders he wants, but it will always be Lake Ontario. Canada is not our enemy. It is our neighbor, our ally, and one of Michigan’s most important economic partners. It is a friendship that no stroke of a pen can erase.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told his social media followers: “Donald Trump picked a fight with Canada that is costing you money. Instead of fixing it, he is spending your tax dollars to rename Lake Ontario.”
Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona queried the directive while referencing the cost of living crisis, asking: “How does changing the name of a lake help the American people? They can’t afford their lives right now.”
Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, who is running for Governor, referenced the lake that straddles her own state when responding to the news, saying: “On behalf of the great Lake Superior, I call that superiorly stupid. We’ve had enough of Trump’s tariff taxes.”

Over three-quarters of Lithuanians support introducing universal military service — survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:37:13 UTC
22:37:13 KST

VILNIUS, August 28. /TASS/. More than three-quarters (76%) of Lithuanian residents support the idea of introducing universal military conscription, a survey conducted by Norstat and commissioned by the Visuotine gynyba association showed.
"The idea of reviving the practice of general conscription was supported by 76.3% survey participants," association president Tomas Godliauskas said.
As many as 23% of respondents favored sticking to the existing rules, while 14.5% of those surveyed voted for a professional army without conscripts. The military cannot currently enlist all men of military age due to underdeveloped infrastructure, so Lithuania makes decisions on military recruitment based on a computerized random selection, like in a lottery.
In 2015, the Baltic republic restored compulsory military service, abolished in 2008, citing geopolitical concerns. Initially it was reinstated for a five-year period to prepare sufficient reserve troops, but parliament later decided to make conscription permanent. Politicians also propose making it universal.
The survey was conducted among 1,501 respondents earlier this month.

Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:36:07 UTC
22:36:07 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead.
The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger.
In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine.
The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered.
Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.
The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later.
“It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN.
The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning.
“In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living.
However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element.
Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin.
“The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska.
The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland
Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023
Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death.
However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown.
The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks.
This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community.
Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth.
Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose.
“It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.”

Greek F-16s intercept Turkish drone over northern Aegean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:34:14 UTC
22:34:14 KST

The Turkish drone reportedly operated in the wider maritime area between Samothrace and Lemnos, immediately triggering surveillance and interception procedures.
The Hellenic Air Force was immediately put on alert after a Turkish unmanned aircraft (UAV) was detected entering the Athens Flight Information Region (FIR) and violating Greek national airspace.
It is reported that the Turkish drone flew over the wider sea area between Samothraki and Lemnos, triggering the immediate activation of established surveillance and interception procedures.
The Greek response was swift. A pair of F-16 fighter jets from the Air Force took off, tasked with locating, identifying and intercepting the Turkish UAV. The scramble of the Greek aircraft highlights Athens' operational readiness in the face of any activity that breaches its airspace.
A particular cause for concern was that the Turkish UAV approached an area close to the terminal runway of Alexandroupoli Airport at the very moment when an Aegean passenger aircraft was preparing for take-off.
Cooperation between the Civil Aviation Authority and the Greek fighter jets enabled the UAV to be driven away without compromising the safety of the passenger flight.
For precautionary reasons, however, the passenger aircraft was instructed to follow an alternative flight path and maintain a low altitude until it had cleared the area. It then continued its journey as normal to "Eleftherios Venizelos" Airport.
The incident takes on added significance because of its timing, occurring just a few hours after fresh statements from the Turkish Ministry of Defence about the possible creation of a UAV base on Rhodes. Ankara had argued that such a development could adversely affect "peace and stability in the Aegean", while hinting at the possible adoption of "necessary measures".
In Athens, the recent incidents are being assessed in their entirety, as officials consider whether they form part of a coordinated effort by Turkey to send political and military messages or signal a broader shift in its posture in the Aegean.
The fact that Greek F-16s had to be scrambled to intercept the Turkish unmanned aircraft reinforces concerns about a possible resurgence of provocative actions on the ground, with the Greek side closely monitoring Ankara's next moves.

Former senior Chinese legislator handed death sentence with reprieve
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:33:53 CST
22:33:53 KST

NANJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Jiang Chaoliang, previously a senior national legislator and Party chief of central China's Hubei Province, was on Friday sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve for accepting bribes.
Jiang was a member of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC), China's top legislature, and vice chairperson of the NPC Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee.
After the two-year reprieve period expires, the sentence will be lawfully commuted to life imprisonment without commutation of sentence or parole, said a verdict from the Intermediate People's Court of Nanjing City in east China's Jiangsu Province.
The court also ordered that Jiang's political rights be deprived for life and the confiscation of all his personal property.
From 1995 to 2025, Jiang took advantage of his official positions to provide assistance to relevant units and individuals in matters such as business operations, project contracting, loan financing and personnel promotion. In return, he illegally accepted money and property totaling more than 746 million yuan (about 110 million U.S. dollars), according to the verdict.
Jiang's bribery amount was particularly huge, and his conduct caused especially significant losses to the interests of the state and the people, for which his crimes warranted the death penalty in principle, the court said.
However, Jiang truthfully confessed his crimes after being taken into custody, voluntarily disclosed criminal facts not yet known to the investigators, offered information on other criminal cases, admitted his guilt, showed remorse and actively returned illicit proceeds. The bribes he received had been recovered. The court thus imposed a lenient sentence on him, the verdict noted.
The case was heard publicly by the court on May 28. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence, while Jiang and his defense counsel cross-examined the evidence and made their arguments. Jiang made a final statement in court, pleading guilty and expressing remorse. ■

Economic Watch: China's smart-driving firms seek place in global cars
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:33:52 CST
22:33:52 KST

CHENGDU, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- The latest Mercedes-Benz GLE SUV made its global debut at this year's Chengdu Motor Show, with an assisted-driving system jointly developed with Chinese autonomous driving technology provider Momenta.
The new long-wheelbase GLE is also set to later adopt Momenta's R7 World Model, a self-improving physical AI engine. Mercedes-Benz first invested in the Chinese startup in 2017, and their cooperation has expanded in recent years.
For decades, foreign automakers followed a fixed business pattern: introducing overseas-developed models and technologies into China and making targeted adaptations for local consumers. However, as software and artificial intelligence gain growing importance in modern automobiles, this industry dynamic has undergone a notable shift.
Other global automakers such as BMW, Volkswagen and Toyota are also partnering with Chinese companies in the field, as China's fast-moving auto market produces a new crop of tech suppliers.
A NEW SUPPLIER LANDSCAPE
The booming and fast-evolving Chinese market serves as the core driver of this transformation. Once largely confined to vehicles priced above 300,000 yuan (about 44,229 U.S. dollars), advanced assisted‑driving features have gradually spread into the 150,000- to 200,000-yuan vehicle segment and, in some instances, even lower‑tier markets.
At the ongoing Chengdu Motor Show 2026, the 29th edition, in southwest China's Sichuan Province, urban navigation assistance and automated parking -- two of the most capable such functions -- have become standard features on newly launched models.
The shift is taking place as new-energy vehicles (NEVs) take a larger share of China's auto market. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, NEV sales reached 1.56 million units in July this year, accounting for more than 60 percent of monthly new vehicle sales for the first time.
As NEVs spread across more price segments, Chinese automakers seek to differentiate their products through smart‑driving functions.
This rapid adoption, paired with fierce competition among carmakers, has allowed firms including Huawei and Momenta to see their technologies gain wider application across electric‑vehicle systems, intelligent driving and smart cockpits.
Compounding this shift, a structural mismatch between legacy R&D rhythms and China's fast‑paced NEV market also creates growing hurdles for traditional Chinese-foreign joint ventures, for which, a conventional vehicle‑development cycle once ran 48 to 60 months.
"In NEVs, we indeed did not keep pace with China's overall development speed," said Yang Xian, deputy general manager of FAW‑Volkswagen's Jetta brand.
FROM CHINA PROJECTS TO GLOBAL AMBITION
For Momenta, teaming up with international automakers within China represents only part of its global ambition.
The company is pursuing overseas expansion along two parallel tracks: tagging along with Chinese automakers such as Chery as they enter foreign markets, and delivering cross‑border, global vehicle programs alongside international partners including Mercedes‑Benz, General Motors, Toyota and Hyundai, said Gu Gongyao, Momenta's vice president.
In July, Momenta won approval from Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) for Level 4 autonomous‑driving road tests nationwide, a key milestone in its European expansion. Per the standard six-tier autonomous driving classification system, Level 4 vehicles are capable of full autonomous operation within designated scenarios without requiring a human backup driver.
Momenta is not alone in testing how far technologies forged in China's hyper‑competitive domestic market can go global. Other Chinese autonomous‑driving firms are taking divergent overseas routes.
Baidu's Apollo Go has rolled out fully driverless commercial ride‑hailing services in Dubai. WeRide runs commercial robotaxi services across the Middle East and has struck plans with Danish mobility provider GreenMobility to launch autonomous shared‑mobility services in Denmark. Pony.ai, meanwhile, operates autonomous‑mobility services with ComfortDelGro in Singapore while advancing robotaxi projects in Dubai and Qatar.
Such ventures, however, also illustrate why global expansion entails much more than simple software exports.
Traffic codes, data‑governance requirements, safety standards and road conditions differ sharply across markets. A system extensively trained and validated on Chinese roads still demands further verification and adaptation before deployment elsewhere, while commercial roll‑out hinges on securing local regulatory clearance.
Industry observers say the partnership between Mercedes-Benz and Momenta offers one example of how Chinese smart‑driving firms are building ties with global automakers and validating their technologies overseas. However, whether this translates into sustained roles within global vehicle programs remains to be seen. ■

Feature: Survivor from Nepal's floods recounts devastation as mud-choked terrain hinders rescue
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

KATHMANDU, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Hira Bahadur Dikshit, a resident of Dhungebazaar, a settlement swept away by the floods in northern Nepal, was still in shock as he looked at the devastated area that was once a bustling town.
The flood, triggered by the collapse of a glacier on the Nepalese side at a higher elevation on Wednesday, left a trail of destruction across riverside areas in Nepal, killing hundreds of people and damaging infrastructure.
Dikshit said he had never witnessed such a devastating flood in his life.
The entire settlement of Dhungebazaar, located in Bidur municipality of Nuwakot district, was swept away by the flood. The settlement, which stretched along the riverbank, was once a bustling town.
"I ran to higher ground on a nearby hill when I heard that a massive flood was approaching," he said. "But many people in the settlement could not save themselves."
On Thursday, when journalists visited the area, it was difficult to find any trace of the houses that had stood there before the disaster. A large swath of land around the once-important town was submerged in muddy water.
Similarly, a settlement along the Trishuli River in Devighat, another area of Bidur municipality, was swept away by the flood. Virtually no traces remain of many structures along the riverbank.
Thick mud and waterlogged ground have left the area extremely unstable. People and livestock are believed to be buried beneath the mud and debris, although there was no immediate official estimate of how many people may have been buried.
There were no official figures available regarding the number of houses that were destroyed or buried in the disaster.
At the Nepal Army Training Center in Bidur municipality, family members of missing people have been seen anxiously waiting for news of their loved ones, many with tears in their eyes.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction Management Authority said that as many as 538 bodies had been recovered from flood-hit areas as of 15:00 local time on Friday, with 977 people still missing. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China urges the Japanese government to speed up the destruction process of the abandoned chemical weapons (ACWs) and restore a safe living environment for the Chinese people at an early date, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said Friday.
It is reported that a civic group in Japan held an exhibition in Yokohama City to expose the Japanese military's wartime production and use of poison gas and its waging of gas warfare against China and Southeast Asian countries during WWII. After Japan's defeat, some chemical weapons were left behind in China, continuing to cause harm to local people.
In response to a media inquiry, Lin told a regular press briefing that during WWII, Japanese militarists developed and used chemical weapons on a large scale in China and other Asian countries, which constitutes a blatant violation of international law and has caused untold suffering on multiple countries.
In China alone, there are more than 2,000 cases of Japanese forces using chemical weapons, causing more than 200,000 Chinese military and civilian casualties, according to Lin.
After Japan's defeat, in an attempt to cover up its crimes, a large number of chemical weapons were left behind in China, resulting in more than 2,000 casualties so far and posing a serious threat to Chinese people's lives and the ecological environment, he added.
Lin said that the Japanese government has demonstrated insufficient sincerity and given inadequate input in fulfilling its obligations of the Chemical Weapons Convention concerning the complete destruction of the ACWs, and the destruction process is seriously lagging behind schedule.
China urges the Japanese government to fulfill its responsibility under relevant convention, face up to the just call from visionary people in its own country and victim neighboring countries, and comprehensively and faithfully fulfill the requirements of international convention and the memorandum of understanding (MoU) between the two governments to speed up the destruction process.
"To remove the hazardous ACWs is Japanese government's unshirkable historical responsibility and due obligation under international law," Lin said. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: From robot dogs to homegrown seeds: how technology is transforming China's vegetable powerhouse
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:33:33 CST
22:33:33 KST

JINAN, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- In a greenhouse in Shouguang, east China's Shandong Province, a robot dog patrols the aisles. Its cameras scan bell pepper leaves for early signs of disease -- spotting problems days before they become visible to the human eye.
Shouguang, a county-level city under Weifang, Shandong, is the country's vegetable powerhouse. With an annual production of 5 million tonnes, it grows enough vegetables to feed more than 40 million people -- over 30 times its own population.
For decades, the city has supplied vegetables to dining tables across China. Now, technology is reshaping its vegetable-production sector, with the changes rippling far beyond the city itself.
ROBOTS TRANSFORM GREENHOUSE FARMING
Growing vegetables used to be backbreaking work. Yield and quality depended on the constant tracking and adjustment of ventilation, lighting, irrigation and fertilization in greenhouses -- tasks that were largely carried out manually. But with the help of a highly automated system, farmers can now monitor and control greenhouse conditions with just a few taps on a smartphone.
The robot dog and its synergy with other unmanned equipment have been the transformative forces. Equipped with high-definition cameras, the quadruped robot detects crop diseases caused by pests or unfavorable microclimate earlier than human worker can. Once an anomaly is detected, specialized robots move in to spray pesticide or fertilizer. The timely intervention has reduced the use of these agrochemicals by 35 percent, according to Wang Yihong, operations manager of Weifang Yuntu Tech Co., Ltd., the developer.
The high-tech greenhouse, due to its precise management of temperature and humidity, boosted production by 5 to 15 percent and improved overall efficiency by 20 to 30 percent, said Li Guangju, a senior agronomist with the local agriculture and rural affairs bureau.
"Robot dogs are becoming increasingly popular on large farms," said Wang, adding that they can cover a daily service area 10 times larger than human growers. The firm has since extended the project beyond Shandong, into central China's Henan Province and northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.
Today in Shouguang, 85 percent of newly built greenhouses are empowered by Internet of Things technology, which facilitates smart agriculture, according to local agricultural and rural affairs bureau.
TECHNOLOGY POWERS PRECISION BREEDING
While bustling robots are the most visible face of Shouguang's transformation, a deeper revolution is taking root in its laboratories, where cutting-edge science is turning seed development into precision engineering.
Though being a vegetable powerhouse, Shouguang once relied heavily on imported seeds. With international seed companies holding a dominant market position, local growers faced volatile profits. To break free from this dependency, local seed companies ramped up their own innovation efforts.
Shouguang Sanmu Seed Co., Ltd., once a simple seed distributor, has evolved into a comprehensive biotech enterprise. Working with universities and research institutes, it has developed a tomato variety that slashes production costs by three-quarters. It now holds 97 national plant variety rights and has developed over 260 varieties.
At the Shouguang Vegetable Research Center co-established by the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences and the local government, scientists are using whole-genome selection to slash breeding cycles by nearly a third. In just seven years, the center has developed 41 new vegetable varieties.
To date, a total of 315 proprietary varieties have been developed in Shouguang, accounting for about half of the province's total, and the market share of domestically bred seeds in Shouguang has climbed from 54 percent in 2010 to over 70 percent today.
SEEDS OF CHANGE
The transformation in Shouguang reflects a broader national drive in agricultural innovation. Sci-tech progress now contributes more than 64 percent of China's agricultural growth, securing the country's place among the world's leading agricultural innovators.
Infrastructure for modern farming is expanding rapidly. In 2025, China added about 5.05 million hectares of newly built or upgraded high-standard farmland, bringing the total to over 66.7 million hectares. Meanwhile, the comprehensive mechanization rate for crop cultivation and harvesting reached 76.7 percent.
As physical infrastructure advances, technology and expertise are spreading across regions. Expert workstations, training programs and cross-provincial technical advisory teams are helping disseminate advanced practices nationwide and accelerate the adoption of smart agricultural systems.
China's agricultural technology is reaching far beyond its borders, benefiting populations worldwide. Shouguang Vegetable Industry Development Center is involved in more than 300 agricultural projects in over 40 countries, using Chinese-designed systems ranging from automated irrigation to climate-controlled greenhouses, said Zhang Linlin, deputy director of the center.
In the Abu Dhabi desert, for example, a joint venture produces 7 tonnes of fresh vegetables daily, demonstrating that these technologies can succeed even in more challenging environment.
The future of Shouguang's vegetable industry lies in boosting productivity and cutting overall costs through the adoption of new technologies, crop varieties, business models and equipment, Li said. ■

Japan spends record 15.4 trln yen in July-Aug. to support currency
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:33:31 CST
22:33:31 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Japanese authorities spent a record 15.4 trillion yen (about 96.5 billion U.S. dollars) over the past month to stem its home currency's slide, the Finance Ministry said Friday.
Ministry data showed that the market interventions happened between July 30 and Aug. 26 but did not specify exact dates, with the amount topping the previous monthly record of 11.73 trillion yen logged in the April-May period this year.
A Japanese government source has confirmed that the country's authorities intervened in the currency market on July 30 to buy yen after the unit hit 163.99 per U.S. dollar, its weakest level in around 40 years, on July 23.
On Aug. 3, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that the two governments had jointly intervened to boost the yen during New York trading hours on July 31, marking the first coordinated move in 28 years.
The July 31 intervention led the U.S. dollar to plunge briefly to the lower 155 yen range, but it has since regained ground, now hovering at the 159 yen level. ■

Rescue operations underway as death toll from mudslide rises
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:33:26 CST
22:33:26 KST

Rescuers from the People's Armed Police Force carry out search and rescue work on a riverbank area 2.2 kilometers from the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, in Xigaze, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Aug. 28, 2026. The death toll had risen to five and 558 remained missing as of 3 p.m. on Friday after a mudslide struck the Gyirong Port along the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, according to the region's emergency management department. Rescuers are operating around the clock in mudslide-affected areas near the Gyirong Port. (Photo by Liu Shuang/Xinhua)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- The death toll had risen to five and 558 remained missing as of 3 p.m. on Friday after a mudslide struck the Gyirong Port along the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, according to the region's emergency management department.
At about 4:30 p.m. on Friday, the first team of six members from the Xizang Fire and Rescue Corps and the first group of 15 members with a search dog from the Sichuan Fire and Rescue Corps arrived at the disaster-hit area of the port. They were the first professional rescue teams to reach the core rescue area, the National Fire and Rescue Administration said.
As of 10 a.m. on Friday, a total of 681 fire and rescue personnel and 113 vehicles had arrived at the remote mountainous border area, while 6,612 pieces of rescue equipment and logistical supplies had been dispatched to Gyirong Township, the administration noted.
China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, sent out a 15-member team on Friday equipped with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to conduct on-site surveys to provide accurate data aimed at boosting rescue efforts.
By Thursday afternoon, 499 people affected by the mudslide had been resettled and 555 stranded tourists had also been evacuated.
According to border inspection authorities in Xizang, an emergency reinforcement team comprising 246 police personnel from Lhasa and Xigaze, the regional capital and the region's second-largest city, respectively, was immediately dispatched to Gyirong Township after Wednesday's deadly mudslide.
Among them were 190 police officers from Xigaze, who took with them more than 300 pieces of rescue equipment, including life detectors and manual breaking tools, to support on-site rescue operations.
A large amount of daily necessities, such as highland barley, rice, flour, drinking water, instant noodles, tents, folding beds, quilts, mattresses, blankets and raincoats have been delivered to the township, the region's emergency management department said. ■

Profile: Ballet dancer-turned Russian scientist bridges global teams at China's Science Island
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:33:21 CST
22:33:21 KST

HEFEI, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- From the ballet stage to a nuclear fusion laboratory, Russian research administrator Viktoriia Saklakova has found her new rhythm on Science Island in eastern China, coordinating international teams working on the world's most advanced fusion experiments.
The 36-year-old serves as the head of international cooperation at the Institute of Plasma Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (ASIPP). Based on Science Island in Hefei, Anhui Province, she is responsible for coordinating exchanges, joint experiments, and talent programs for researchers from over 50 countries.
Inside her office, Viktoriia navigates a constant stream of emails in Chinese, Russian and English. Just meters away sit two of China's major fusion devices: the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST), the world's first fully superconducting tokamak device nicknamed China's "artificial sun," and the Burning Plasma Experimental Superconducting Tokamak (BEST), China's next-generation "artificial sun" under construction.
Since she joined ASIPP in 2023, it has become part of her monthly routine to host dozens of foreign experts. "I want to help China's 'artificial sun' make more friends."
Viktoriia's connection to China dates back two decades. She first visited northeast China's Heilongjiang Province in 2006 and later performed as a ballet dancer there. The experiences inspired her to learn Chinese, pursue a physics master's degree at the Harbin Institute of Technology, and eventually earn a doctorate from the University of Science and Technology of China in Hefei.
After graduation, Viktoriia decided that remaining on Science Island, a leading global hub for nuclear fusion research, would be her best choice. Over the past three years, she has helped broker partnerships between ASIPP and institutions including the International Atomic Energy Agency and Russia's Joint Institute for Nuclear Research.
Fusion research requires tight global coordination. Viktoriia noted that EAST's experimental schedule is divided into three time slots to accommodate researchers across Asia, Europe, and the Americas.
To keep projects on track, she often works late into the night, fielding messages and joining video conferences across multiple time zones. For many scientists, she acts as more than an interpreter; she coordinates device access, facilitates joint research, and helps young researchers find opportunities in China.
China's fusion program has accelerated in recent years. EAST has set multiple world records, and ASIPP has completed several key procurement packages for the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) project.
"China's progress in controlled nuclear fusion has amazed peers globally," Viktoriia said, attributing the momentum to long-term strategic planning and an open approach to international collaboration.
Beyond connecting established researchers, Viktoriia is also cultivating the next generation. Starting in the summer of 2024, she began organizing an international student summer camp, bringing young participants to Science Island to gain firsthand experience with China's fusion research.
Maxim Andreev, a master's student at the Moscow Power Engineering Institute, attended this year's camp. He said the experience solidified his plan to pursue a doctorate at ASIPP.
"Cross-border cooperation will greatly advance fusion energy for all humanity," he said.
Looking ahead, Viktoriia aims to expand her network of partner institutions and facilitate more joint experiments on next-generation devices.
"Fusion is a generational endeavor," she said. "Here in China, I'm willing to dedicate my lifetime to it." ■

Head of Zelenskyy's office says elections during war pose serious threat
Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office, has said the current political situation in Ukraine amounts to tension but not yet a crisis. He urged Ukrainians to avoid internal division and said elections should be postponed until after the war.
Source: Budanov in an interview broadcast on 28 August on the national joint 24/7 newscast
Quote: "Elections during war, apart from technical problems, carry a serious threat… Elections during war call their results into question to some extent. Because not everyone can vote normally. Questions start being asked: some people voted, others could not, how many were unable to vote, and so on.
And in a society that is not entirely united, this creates grounds for, say, one particular oblast simply to say: 'Sorry, we are for Ukraine, but we do not recognise all this, and until everything is sorted out, we will remain autonomous.' This is a path towards the state breaking apart."
Details: Budanov recalled the events of 1918, when Ukrainians "lost their state in an instant".
Budanov said he views current events in Ukraine as "tension" rather than a "crisis".
He urged all sides in the confrontation to "calm down a little and look at the situation in Ukraine more broadly", adding that there is always a way out.
Budanov said the war should be ended first, and only then should the process of political renewal be launched.

Switzerland's Beznau nuclear power plant back online after heatwaves force shutdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:30:21 UTC
22:30:21 KST

Reactor 1 was first brought online in 1969 and Reactor 2 in 1971, making it one of the oldest nuclear plants in the world.
The Beznau nuclear power plant in Switzerland, which was shut down multiple times over the last two months due to summer heatwaves, is fully operational again, Swiss energy company Axpo said on Friday.
Axpo said the second reactor at the Beznau plant in northern Switzerland, Europe's oldest nuclear power plant still in operation, went back online on Thursday.
The heatwaves that hit Europe sent temperatures soaring in the Aare River, which the site uses for cooling.
Reactor 1 has been back in operation since 21 August and Axpo said it had now reconnected the other to the grid, which is "now gradually returning to power operation and is expected to reach full capacity within approximately two days."
Reactor 2 was taken offline on 4 August for refuelling, during which 20 of the 121 fuel assemblies in the reactor core were replaced.
The plant had been shut down in June and again in July due to the unusually high temperatures in the Aare, which drains nearly half of Switzerland and flows into the Rhine.
Several European nuclear power plants had to reduce their output or temporarily shut due to summer heatwaves.
Nuclear energy accounts for just over a third of Switzerland's electricity production.
The country has four ageing nuclear reactors, including the two at Beznau, which produce around a tenth of Switzerland's electricity demand.
Reactor 1 was first brought online in 1969 and Reactor 2 in 1971, making it one of the oldest nuclear plants in the world.

Schools can now hold back final year pre-schoolers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:30:16 UTC
22:30:16 KST

Schools in Flanders can now require children to repeat the third year of pre-school rather than leaving it up to the parents, a decision that will better prepare children to enter primary school, say experts
Starting from the 2026-27 school year, children in the third year of pre-school can be required to repeat the year. Currently, parents can choose to follow the pre-school’s advice to hold the child back or not, with the result that many kids are not ready to enter the first year of primary school, according to education experts.
Once children are in primary school, the decision to have a child repeat a year is with the school, not the parents. The largest percentage of schoolchildren in Flanders repeating a year can be found in the first-year, with 5.6% of them repeating the year.
This figure drops with every passing year, but the biggest drop is between the first and second year pupils. Only 3.2% of pupils in their second year are repeating it.
Parents choose to enrol them in the first year of primary school even if we advise against it
“It’s in that first year that the foundations are laid for learning – counting to 10, knowing all the letters, forming words,” explains Mieke Goos, an education professor at UHasselt. “Lacking those building blocks at the end of the first year is the main reason pupils are held back.”
Selina, a first-year teacher in Antwerp has to tell at least one child a year that they will not be moving on to the second year. “These are often pupils who we wanted to hold back in pre-school,” she says, “because we knew they weren’t ready for primary school.” But their parents “choose to enrol them in the first year of primary school even if we advise against it”.
Not all fun and games
The parents often see the difference between pre-school and primary school as very black and white, she continues, with pre-school seen as a playground. “That perception is unfortunate because the third year of pre-school is very focused on starting to learn.”
In the third year, kids learn how to listen, to do exercises, to sit at a workspace. “The new minimum standard for pre-schoolers will hopefully make it more clear that we also have expectations of pre-schoolers,” says Selina, “and that they can learn a great deal by repeating this third year.”

A tiny Rhodope village draws visitors from around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:29:51 UTC
22:29:51 KST

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
A tiny Rhodope village draws visitors from around the world
Dimitar Ralev on how Kosovo, with just 29 residents, is turning visitors into friends – and new neighbours
Friday 28 August 2026 14:03
Friday, 28 August 2026, 14:03
Dimitar Ralev
PHOTO Personal archive
Font size
There are villages in Bulgaria with only a handful of residents, while others have been completely abandoned. Yet there are also places that seem to have found their own way of bringing life back – not through flashy attractions, but through tranquillity, authenticity and a personal touch. One of them is the picturesque village of Kosovo in the Rhodope Mountains, where tourists have long been regarded not simply as guests, but as friends.
As of December 31, 2025, Bulgaria had 1,280 settlements with between one and 49 residents, while 192 had no inhabitants at all, according to the National Statistical Institute. The reasons vary, but are most often linked to the search for work and better opportunities – something many people believe they can find only in the big cities or abroad.
PHOTO selokosovo.com
The story of Hristo and Svetla Ralev, both engineers – Hristo in electrical engineering and Svetla in software – is different.
After more than 15 years living and working in Venezuela, where they raised and educated their two children, they decided to return to Bulgaria. Looking for a quiet place where they could change their way of life, in 2004 they came across Kosovo, about 50 kilometres from Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second-largest city, on the road between Asenovgrad and Smolyan and just five kilometres from the spa resort of Narechenski Bani.
Neither had any previous connection with the village. Gradually, however, they fell in love with Kosovo and restored three of its old houses, turning them into small guest properties welcoming visitors from Bulgaria and abroad.
PHOTO selokosovo.com
There are different stories about how Kosovo got its name. It appears not to come from the Bulgarian word for blackbird, kos, but rather from the way the village lies koso – at an angle – across the mountain slopes. Anyone exploring Kosovo and its surroundings should therefore be prepared for steep streets and paths.
PHOTO Personal archive
Neither had any previous connection with the village. Gradually, however, they fell in love with Kosovo and restored three of its old houses, turning them into small guest properties welcoming visitors from Bulgaria and abroad.
A decade after his parents first came to Kosovo, their son Dimitar joined them. He returned from Venezuela after graduating from university and spending some time in Caracas as a teaching assistant in mechatronics and robotics. The economic problems in the South American country, which had begun under President Hugo Chávez (1999–2013), prompted him to look for his future in Bulgaria.
PHOTO selokosovo.com
Together with his cousin Gergana Lyutskanova, who studied tourism in Switzerland and later worked in the sector in Barcelona and the Cayman Islands, Dimitar began helping his parents welcome and accommodate visitors.
“Gergana is the one with professional experience in the industry,” Dimitar Ralev says. “So we try to apply her experience and what we have seen being done around the world. She doesn’t live permanently in Kosovo as I do, but she gives us the valuable perspective of a professional who can see the bigger picture and knows how to keep things moving, which is very important.”
PHOTO selokosovo.com
For Dimitar, the way guests are treated is particularly important in a place like Kosovo. If a particular service or product is unavailable in a small mountain village, that need not become the visitor’s problem. What matters more is offering a suitable alternative so that the experience remains a pleasant one.
And the approach appears to work. The Ralev family have made friends from different parts of the world. Some return to Kosovo every year; others have even decided to buy property there.
PHOTO selokosovo.com
“We don’t even call them tourists any more, but friends. They not only come every year, but several of these families now own properties in Kosovo and use them as holiday homes. We also know a woman who retired with her husband in Germany, and this year they moved to the village permanently.”
Many of the visitors are mixed Bulgarian-foreign couples and families. They often combine a visit to the Bulgarian partner’s home town with a few restorative days, or perhaps a week, in the Rhodopes.
PHOTO selokosovo.com
“We have also had guests from South America, although they are more of an exception. It comes as a big surprise when they arrive in a little village like this in the Rhodopes and someone welcomes them who not only speaks Spanish but also has a connection with South America. We had that happen with visitors from Peru. The woman was Bulgarian and the man was Peruvian, and they were very surprised to find someone in the Rhodopes speaking Spanish with a Latin American accent.”
Although Kosovo remains a small village, the number of people living there year-round has gradually increased in recent years – particularly striking against the broader demographic picture in Bulgaria’s villages.
PHOTO Personal archive
“Last winter there were around 15 of us, because several families have bought properties and moved here permanently. In summer and at weekends, quite a few people come from Sofia, Plovdiv and Burgas. They have holiday homes here and want to get away from everyday life for a while.”
And perhaps that is Kosovo’s greatest asset – its ability to make you slow down.
Kosovo’s history goes back centuries. Settled in the 17th century, it reached its heyday in the middle and latter part of the 19th century. Many of its surviving stone houses with their distinctive stone-slab roofs date from Bulgaria’s National Revival period. The livelihoods of local people – transporting goods for hire, livestock farming, agriculture and masonry – enabled them to build large, spacious homes with high stone walls and carved ceilings. Cobbled streets and bridges appeared too, and remain part of the village landscape today.
Туристи от цял свят откриват магията на родопското село Косово
PHOTO selokosovo.com
Among Kosovo’s landmarks are the Church of the Dormition of the Mother of God, built in 1851, the old school dating from 1889, the chapels of St Nedelya and St Peter, the watermill and blacksmith’s workshop, as well as its many preserved National Revival houses.
The area around Kosovo also offers plenty of opportunities to explore the cultural and historical heritage of the Rhodopes. Nearby are Bachkovo Monastery and Asen’s Fortress, the Wonderful Bridges rock formations about 30 kilometres away, and the thermal springs of Narechenski Bani, six to seven kilometres from the village. The climate is another attraction: summers are cool, while winters are relatively mild, with severe cold and blizzards uncommon.
PHOTO selokosovo.com
All this makes tiny Kosovo a village rich in history, architecture and atmosphere. And although official figures showed just 29 residents at the end of 2025, perhaps the most encouraging thing is that some of them have chosen Kosovo not simply as a holiday destination, but as their home – proof that the road to a better life does not always lead to the big city. Sometimes it leads to a small village nestled among the slopes of the captivating Rhodope Mountains.

‘Undeveloped Moroccan’: Netanyahu’s wife hit with ‘extreme abuse’ lawsuit
Sara Netanyahu, the wife of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has repeatedly humiliated and abused a former household worker, at one point calling him an “undeveloped Moroccan,” a new lawsuit claims. The controversy adds to a years-long trail of remarkably similar allegations, painting a picture of intolerable conditions at the residence.
On Tuesday, Ynet reported that Rami Ben-Hamo, who worked at the residence from 2023 to 2025, is seeking 450,000 shekels ($150,000) in a lawsuit filed with the Jerusalem Regional Labor Court. While the complaint has been formally filed against the Prime Minister’s Office, the alleged abuse is overwhelmingly attributed to Sara Netanyahu.
According to Ben-Hamo, he sometimes worked from around 7:30 AM until the early hours of the following morning, clocking 60 to 80 hours of overtime a month. He claims to have “suffered extreme abuse” from the prime minister’s wife, adding that she made him clean her handbag and the soles of her shoes, repeatedly wash his hands between tasks, and endure screaming and humiliation when cleaning or household chores were not performed exactly as she wanted.
At one point, Netanyahu allegedly called him an “undeveloped Moroccan,” declaring: “I am the prime minister’s wife. You will do what I tell you.” Ben-Hamo claims the ethnic insult was repeated and that he sometimes had to beg her in tears to stop.
The complaint also alleges that Ben-Hamo was kept at work after the start of Shabbat – the weekly Jewish day of rest between Friday and Saturday evenings – despite Netanyahu knowing he observed the tradition. After suffering a cardiac event at work and undergoing catheterization in 2025, Ben-Hamo says her treatment of him became even harsher.
When Ben-Hamo wrote a resignation notice, saying he wanted to leave because of the mistreatment, the Prime Minister’s Office “refused to accept this note and demanded that the plaintiff change the wording so that it said he wanted to leave for personal reasons.”
Netanyahu’s office dismissed the allegations as “fake news,” calling it a politically motivated “witch-hunt” ahead of the October elections.
However, the recent controversy fits a pattern of strikingly similar grievances about Sara Netanyahu. Just several weeks ago, former residence worker Yehiel Ohev-Ami, 61, sued her for 300,000 shekels ($100,000), claiming that Netanyahu repeatedly insulted and yelled at him, and “once ordered him to clean the kitchen floor while crawling.”
In addition, Netanyahu allegedly wished him cancer and death after Ohev-Ami went out on a smoke break, and even “diagnosed” him with autism. The prime minister’s office has denied the accusations.
In May, Israeli media reported that another former employee reached a settlement with her staffing company after alleging repeated humiliation, including an incident in which Sara Netanyahu threw olives and tomatoes at her during breakfast.
In 2016, a Jerusalem labor court awarded former residence caretaker Meni Naftali 170,000 shekels ($57,000) after accepting his claims that Sara Netanyahu’s fostered “abusive employment conditions,” including verbal insults and unreasonable demands.
According to multiple media reports, Sara Netanyahu – a psychologist by training – enjoys immense political influence and essentially has veto powers on appointments to key positions. Earlier this month, former chief of staff Yoav Horowitz suggested that in terms of politics, “Sara Netanyahu and Bibi Netanyahu are one; it’s impossible to separate between them.”

NTA gets 3 senior officers amid exam overhaul

The Centre has brought in three senior officers, including an IPS officer at NTA
NEW DELHI: The Centre has brought in three senior officers, including an IPS officer, at the National Testing Agency (NTA), giving the embattled examination body fresh administrative muscle as it undergoes one of its biggest personnel and security overhauls following controversies over NEET-UG and UGC-NET.IPS officer Ravi Kumar Singh and IAS officer Prasanna Venkatesh V have been appointed directors at NTA, while Amit Samdariya, a 2016-batch Indian Revenue Service (Customs and Indirect Taxes) officer, will join as joint director. The appointments were cleared through separate personnel ministry orders dated August 27.The induction comes days after NTA began a wider revamp that includes removing around 600 experts from its examination panels, onboarding a fresh set of specialists and introducing a four-tier scrutiny mechanism for question papers.The agency is also strengthening examination security, recruiting additional officials and moving to new premises where security is proposed to be reinforced with CISF deployment. The measures were reviewed recently by Union education minister Pralhad Joshi as the government sought to tighten both the academic and operational ends of the examination process.NTA has been under sustained pressure since the NEET-UG paper leak controversy, which triggered nationwide protests and intensified scrutiny of how high-stakes examinations are secured and administered.
More recently, it was forced to order fresh UGC-NET examinations in English, commerce and sociology after multiple errors and repeated questions were detected in the June papers, adding a question-paper quality problem to its security challenges.Against this backdrop, the appointment of officers drawn from the police, administrative and revenue services marks another step in the attempt to strengthen NTA's institutional capacity.The personnel ministry has directed all three officers to take charge within three weeks. The orders state that failure to join within the stipulated period would trigger the process of debarment from the Central Staffing Scheme.The staffing changes are unfolding alongside a broader examination-reform exercise. A high-powered task force headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani has begun seeking suggestions from students, parents, teachers and other stakeholders on reforms to the public examination system, with the consultation open till September 13.
The task force is examining examination security, institutional processes, technology, infrastructure, accessibility and student well-being, while the changes within NTA are focused on immediately strengthening the agency responsible for conducting some of the country’s largest entrance and eligibility tests.

Waymo in Munich: Could autonomous vehicles make Europe's roads safer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:27:08 UTC
22:27:08 KST

Waymo is bringing driverless taxis to Munich, its third city outside the US, as data suggests autonomous vehicles are far safer than human drivers.
Following technology news about Europe on social media can be frustrating, as positive news is often overshadowed by complaints that consumers lack access to the latest innovative technologies and services due to a plethora of regulations from Brussels.
The autonomous vehicle (AV) sector, however, looks positive in Europe this year — the United States’ leading autonomous vehicle company, Waymo, just announced that Munich will be its latest addition to its ongoing global expansion.
While Waymo already offers services in dozens of cities across the United States, it recently began its international rollout, with London, Tokyo and Munich as the first three cities abroad.
This is not the first good news for Europe’s consumers, lazy drivers and AV-enthusiasts this year.
Yael Ossowski recently pointed out that a Dutch decision to greenlight Tesla’s Full Self-Driving Supervised (FSD) led to a domino effect of approvals, with Danish, Lithuanian and Estonian regulators quickly following suit and giving Tesla owners more choice in how much they trust their car's semi-autonomous features.
AV taxis are 12 to 20 times safer than human-driven taxis
Waymo coming to Munich’s streets is not just good news for passengers dreading the music choice of local taxi drivers but also has wider implications for road safety.
Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman suggested early on that machines will ultimately be better and safer than humans at decisions about navigation and driving. A few years later, we do have hard data to back this up.
Data from major US cities show that AV-taxis are between 12 and 20 times safer than human-driven taxis, helping prevent many accidents and injuries.
Given that we still have around 20,000 road fatalities in Europe every year, where 67% of all accidents happen due to the drivers’ fault, it should be in the interest of consumers and policymakers to reduce this by enabling cutting-edge technology.
With Munich taxi fares from the airport to downtown ranging from €80 to €90 per trip, AV taxis could be a game-changer for many passengers across the EU, especially those living in remote areas with no access to public transport or many late-night flights.
Although, in the past, ride-hailing apps have created a competitive challenge to traditional taxis, the expansion of AV taxis can add to it, ultimately making rides more affordable for average consumers.
Companies like Waymo should also not be seen as competitors to the car industry but as companies that program and build your driver.
Especially for the German automotive industry, this might be a huge opportunity to partner up and plug into the AV ecosystem so that, one day, visitors from all over the world can be chauffeured in a driverless, locally manufactured BMW or Audi through Munich.

The HACC Appeals Chamber refused to transfer Kolomoiskyi’s case to another court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

The HACC Appeals Chamber refused to transfer Kolomoiskyi’s case to another court
Kyiv • UNN
The HACC Appeals Chamber did not transfer to another court the case involving Kolomoiskyi and five former PrivatBank employees. They are accused of misappropriating UAH 9.2 billion.
The Appeals Chamber of the High Anti-Corruption Court refused to transfer to another court the case of Ihor Kolomoiskyi, the former ultimate beneficial owner of PJSC CB "PrivatBank," and five other individuals—former employees of the banking institution suspected of misappropriating more than UAH 9.2 billion belonging to the bank. This was reported by the HACC Appeals Chamber, according to UNN.
On August 28, 2026, a panel of judges of the HACC Appeals Chamber considered a motion by the defense of the former ultimate owner of the Ukrainian bank and a top manager of the institution to transfer the case from the HACC to another court. Following consideration, the panel of judges of the HACC Appeals Chamber refused to grant the motion
As the court recalled, according to the investigation, the individuals are accused of misappropriating property on an especially large scale as part of an organized group, legalizing (laundering) property obtained through criminal means, and official forgery (Part 5 of Article 191, Part 3 of Article 27, Part 3 of Article 28, Part 1 of Article 366, Part 3 of Article 209 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
It should be noted that this concerns case No. 991/10098/26, in which, according to the investigation, in January–March 2015, the ultimate beneficiary of "PrivatBank," who was then head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration, organized a scheme to misappropriate the bank's funds in order to subsequently finance a controlled offshore company and increase his own stake in the institution's authorized capital. To this end, the bank was artificially compelled to pay the said controlled company more than UAH 9.2 billion under the pretext of an alleged repurchase of its own bonds at an inflated price.
Subsequently, for the purpose of legalization, part of the amount—more than UAH 446 million—was transferred to the accounts of three related legal entities under the guise of securities purchase and sale transactions, and later to the accounts of two more. Ultimately, the funds reached the personal account of PrivatBank's ultimate beneficiary. He disposed of them at his own discretion, contributing them to the bank's authorized capital to comply with the requirements of the National Bank of Ukraine.
As a reminder
On August 7, the Podilskyi District Court of Kyiv imposed a preventive measure on Ukrainian oligarch Ihor Kolomoiskyi, who is an accused in the case concerning the misappropriation of more than UAH 9.2 billion from "PrivatBank." The Ukrainian businessman will remain in a pretrial detention center until November 9, 2026.

Brigadier General Talaei-Nik said that the recent wars, despite their losses, had also created opportunities for political, social, scientific, industrial and defense-related progress. He added that the defense industry had built strategic stocks of weapons, equipment and ammunition before the war, while production continued during the war through a network of about 9,300 knowledge-based and private companies. According to Talaei-Nik, these companies support two-thirds of the defense industry, and production of some equipment increased several-fold.
He said that Iran’s arms production has more than doubled since the 12-day war, with several-fold increases targeted for some products. He also added that Iran is moving toward a leading global position in areas such as long-range and cruise missiles and drones, while arms exports will continue based on available surplus.
The Defense Ministry spokesperson stressed that Iran produces more than 1,000 types of weapons, equipment and ammunition, with defense self-sufficiency exceeding 90 percent. He said that the defense industry has moved beyond reverse engineering and achieved indigenous technologies and designs in some areas.
He described Iran’s resilience as the main “surprise” of the war, saying the enemy had expected the country’s military, defense, economic and social capabilities to collapse in the early days, but the opposite occurred.
Talaei-Nik said that Iran’s defense strategy remains combined and asymmetric, combining the preservation and strengthening of deterrence with offensive approaches within a defensive framework to prevent the enemy from seizing the initiative. He added that strengthened counter-drone defenses and lessons learned after the 12-day war significantly reduced Defense Ministry casualties in the subsequent war.
He stressed that additional surprises in weapons, equipment, technology, and tactics have been prepared in line with the principle of surprise and will be revealed on the battlefield.
MNA
