What Does Japan Think of the Sudden Cut to South Korea-US Joint Drills?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

On August 16, U.S. President Donald Trump scaled back military drills with South Korea. In a social media post, he cited three different explanations for the move: the cost of the exercises to the United States, his supposedly friendly relations with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and his displeasure over perceived lack of South Korean support for the U.S. war effort against Iran.
After Trump’s intervention, the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, which started on August 17, only ran through August 21 instead of the originally scheduled August 27. In practice, the first phase of the exercise – focused on defense – was preserved while the second phase – focused on counterattack – was canceled. In addition, live-training exercises were replaced with simulations.
According to the South Korean new agency Yonhap, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told the legislature that “Neither our government nor U.S. officials knew what President Trump wrote on his Truth Social account.” In a meeting with the National Assembly Committee on Foreign Affairs and Unification, Cho said, “We were not notified in advance.”
On August 24, the United States canceled the biennial Ssangyong drills, a large joint amphibious landing exercise, scheduled for September. This time, the justification was constraints on force availability caused by the Iran war. This announcement was not as abrupt, as the U.S. Marine Corps had officially notified Seoul back in June that its force availability would likely be constrained.
On August 28, the United States, South Korea, and Japan announced that they will conduct the annual Freedom Edge drills, joint military drills to test readiness against North Korea’s missiles and nuclear weapons threat, from September 9 to 11.
What is Japan’s perspective on the latest developments in the South Korea-U.S. alliance?
Japan’s initial reaction has been muted. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro responded to the announcement by saying: “As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States, and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region.” The statement, however, did not actually criticize the U.S. decision to scale back joint exercises.
Although Japanese leaders have been publicly quiet, this incident highlights several points of concern that have existed since the second Trump administration.
First, it could indicate a more aggressive move by Washington to resume talks with North Korea. Japan would always have been wary of a North Korea-U.S. deal that advanced U.S. security while sidelining Japanese concerns. For example, a hypothetical deal could cut back on Pyongyang’s long-range missiles, which can reach the United States, but do nothing to reduce its stockpile of short-range missiles, which can reach Japan. The threat to Japan remains persistent, as North Korea fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles on August 20; this was the third ballistic missile test in August.
There is also a question of whether the United States will maintain denuclearization as a policy objective, and what Japan will do vis-à-vis North Korea if the United States abandons it. Conservative Japanese leaders also have a vested political interest in the return of abductees, an issue that might get ignored in a North Korea-U.S. deal.
Japanese analysts worry about a more emboldened North Korea, though at the same time they doubt the likelihood of a U.S. overture to Pyongyang succeeding. But experts have failed to predict many aspects of this administration’s foreign policy.
U.S. overtures to North Korea, reciprocated or not, will likely be reflected in the three strategy documents currently being revised in Tokyo: the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Defense Buildup Program. Japan intends to finish updating these documents by the end of the year. Tokyo could also, much more quietly, consider nuclear weapons for itself if questions about the credibility of the U.S. nuclear deterrent being to mount.
Another worrying aspect of Trump’s social media post is the signal that the United States is prepared to more explicitly make assistance in the Iran War a condition of continued support. Certainly, there are different dynamics between the South Korea-U.S. alliance and that between Japan and the United States. For one, Japan has long relied on its constitutional and legal framework to avoid entanglement in U.S. wars. However, the Trump administration may be less sympathetic to such justifications. If they cannot force Japan to support U.S. military operations in the Strait of Hormuz due to Japan’s constraints, Washington may demand concessions from Japan in other areas, such as reduced joint exercises or increased host nation support.
This administration has shown a tendency to link security and economic issues in a way that previous administrations usually did not (i.e., reducing the benefit of the training exercise to its financial costs). The timing is particularly worrying for Japan as Tokyo begins negotiations with Washington over host nation support. A sudden demand for a large increase is certainly possible.
Trump’s decision – announced on the same day Ulchi Freedom Shield began – makes it clear that U.S. military exercises can be scaled down on a moment’s notice. Japan has its own exercises with the United States, Keen Sword, in October. Though it is expected to be smaller than the 2024 iteration due to U.S. deployments in the Iran war, it could be scaled back even farther. Trump could use the same three-fold justification he used against South Korea to cancel or scale down these exercises.
In a related concern, Trump’s rationale for the decision showed his susceptibility to accepting autocrats’ talking points. Trump appears to have bought Kim’s argument that the training exercises are aggressive, while the U.S. and South Korean governments have long maintained that these exercises are defensive. It’s odd, to say the least, to see a U.S. president describing actions by the South Korea-U.S. alliance as “totally inappropriate and hostile” and North Korea as “unthreatening and respectful.”
Finally, there is real concern about what it would mean for U.S military readiness on the Korean Peninsula and in the Indo-Pacific more broadly if training exercises become scaled back or more erratic.
Alliance readiness is a key concern. While North Korean soldiers are returning to the peninsula after having real world battle experience in the Russia-Ukraine war, the best that the U.S. and South Korean soldiers can do to prepare is live trainings. Yet these live trainings are being replaced by simulations at the same time the enemy is “training” by engaging in real combat.
A U.S. Department of Defense official said in a statement that “These adjustments preserve essential readiness and training objectives,” and “There will be no degradation to U.S. training objectives.” But saying the sky is pink does not make it so.

Nilekani panel seeks public ideas to fix exam system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:25:10 UTC
22:25:10 KST

NEW DELHI: The high-powered task force set up by the Centre to overhaul India’s public examination system has opened a nationwide consultation Friday, seeking suggestions from students, parents, teachers and other stakeholders on making high-stakes tests more secure, transparent and student-friendly.The panel, headed by Infosys co-founder and technology expert Nandan Nilekani, was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi last month amid heightened scrutiny of the examination system following the NEET-UG paper leak controversy and youth protests over alleged lapses in test conduct.The announcement had come a day after the Centre accepted the demands raised by the youth-led CJP, whose protests over the NEET leak included calls for then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters.“The High-Powered Task Force on Reforms in Public Examinations wants to hear from students, parents, teachers — every citizen,” a senior official said on Friday.The public consultation will remain open till September 13, with citizens allowed to send suggestions through WhatsApp, a dedicated website, email and a toll-free number.Officials said the task force is examining reforms across the examination chain — from institutional processes and question-paper security to use of technology and strengthening of examination infrastructure.
It will also look at measures to improve accessibility and inclusion, while factoring in student well-being during the examination process.“The objective is to develop a public examination system that is robust, secure, transparent, equitable and future-ready,” the official said.
The exercise assumes significance after repeated controversies surrounding national-level entrance and eligibility examinations raised questions over paper security, examination management and the ability of testing agencies to respond quickly to irregularities.Apart from Nilekani, the task force includes former ISRO chairman S Somanath, former Intelligence Bureau director Tapan Deka, IIT Madras director V Kamakoti, former education secretary Anita Karwal and logistics expert Amrit Lal Meena.The panel is expected to recommend both immediate safeguards and longer-term structural changes in the way public examinations are designed, administered and secured.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Friday offered condolences to victims of the deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border.
Lai said in an X post that he was sending his thoughts and prayers to everyone affected by the floods and mudslides, per CNA. He offered his deepest condolences to families who had lost loved ones.
Lai wished for recovery and reconstruction efforts in the affected areas to proceed safely and swiftly.
A flash flood swept through communities along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday after a glacier collapse sent a torrent of water, rock, ice, and mud through Himalayan valleys, per Reuters. It destroyed roads, bridges, and other infrastructure.
More than 390 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal and Tibet, and more than 1,400 were missing, according to the Associated Press.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot has summoned US Ambassador to Belgium Bill White for the second time this year after a mocking Instagram post, Politico reports.
In an Instagram post, US President Donald Trump’s spokesman in Belgium asked, alongside an apparently AI-generated image of Belgian Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke on a pack of cigars, “Who is the biggest loser in Belgium?” The cigar box’s lid, in a clear mockery of the health minister’s efforts to change the warning labels used in alcohol advertisements, reads “Harms every joy in life.”
In a statement to Politico, Prévot said it was unacceptable for the ambassador to use such offensive language against a member of the government. He also confirmed that he had summoned White to explain himself.
A spokesman for the Belgian Health Ministry declined to comment on the situation.
The Belgian brewers’ union is protesting this week
against a law proposed by Vandenbroucke that would change the warning label from “alcohol abuse causes health damage” to “alcohol causes health damage.”
White was previously summoned to the Foreign Ministry in February after he accused Brussels of anti-Semitism when it opened an investigation into three Jewish mohels in Antwerp who were suspected of performing circumcisions without proper medical qualifications. He called the investigation “nonsense” and pressured Vandenbroucke to intervene.
Conner Rousseau, the leader of Vandenbroucke’s Vooruit party, responded to White’s post on Instagram, saying the ambassador knows nothing about healthcare and is only doing what “Daddy Trump” wants.

BERLIN, August 28. /TASS/. A meeting on Iran in Istanbul involving the foreign ministers of the E3 - the United Kingdom, Germany and France - as well as Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey has been postponed, DPA reported, citing sources in the German government.
According to the agency, the meeting was postponed because of a scheduling conflict involving one of the participants. A new date has not yet been set.
DPA reported earlier that the foreign ministers of Germany, Turkey, France and the United Kingdom were due to meet their counterparts from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in Istanbul on August 30. Germany and Turkey initiated the talks.
The ministers had been expected to discuss ways to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the regional security situation. The participating countries wanted the meeting to signal to the United States the need to continue negotiations with Iran.
The situation in the Black Sea and Ukrainian grain exports were also to be discussed in Istanbul.

Sofia gets seven minehunters from Belgium and the Netherlands for a sea Russia mined
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:20:42 UTC
22:20:42 KST

Bulgaria will add seven minehunter ships to its navy under two agreements with Belgium and the Netherlands, Reuters reported. Parliament cleared the acquisition on 26 August, and the vessels are meant for a sea where mines have drifted since Russia invaded Ukraine. They will work within a three-country task force whose mission widened this summer beyond mine clearance.
Russia's invasion turned the Black Sea into hostile water for civilian shipping: mines drift out of the fighting, strikes fall on port after port, and grain leaves through whatever routes are still open. Mine clearance is the slow work that keeps those lanes usable at all, and every hull committed to it widens the area the navies bordering that sea can actually cover.
What parliament approved
Three of the hulls come through a sale the Netherlands agreed with Sofia, and they carry the gear for locating mines and mine-like objects and blowing them up. The remaining four arrive under a three-way handover deal signed by the two donor countries and the recipient, according to Reuters.
Before the three sale ships change hands, the Dutch will put their systems back in working order and raise how much they can do at sea. The bill for the yard work on all seven, up to the level the alliance requires, falls to the buyer. Alongside the ships, a signed memorandum provides for training the crews and supplying spares and extra kit.
Belgium and the Netherlands, together with the UK, handed Ukraine five mine countermeasure vessels in April, described at the time as the core of a future large-scale Black Sea clearance operation.
A task force that grew
Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye signed the agreement creating a joint Mine Countermeasures Task Group in January 2024, and the group began work that summer. Three other states hold coastline on the same sea: Georgia, Russia, and Ukraine.
"Bulgaria is part of the mine countermeasures group established together with our colleagues from Türkiye and Romania, and it is working in excellent coordination to clear the maritime areas of the three countries," Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said.
At a NATO summit in July, the three agreed to expand the force so it also protects critical infrastructure. Romania's national defense strategy had already flagged risks to Black Sea infrastructure.

Outspoken ex-commander who clashed with military leadership says drugs were planted in his car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:20:17 UTC
22:20:17 KST

Outspoken ex-commander who clashed with military leadership says drugs were planted in his car
Oleksandr Shyrshyn, a former battalion commander in Ukraine's 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade, said on Facebook on Aug. 28 that cannabis had been planted in his car in an apparent attempt to implicate him in the illegal production and possession of drugs.
Shyrshyn previously criticized Ukraine's senior military leadership during Oleksandr Syrskyi's tenure as commander-in-chief. Syrskyi was dismissed on July 22.
In one instance, Shyrshyn called the command's orders during the Kursk operation in Russia "idiotic" on May 16, 2025, and later resigned. Syrskyi subsequently ordered that Shyrshyn be deemed "undisciplined."
"Weed was planted on me. It was all very interesting and very much planned," Shyrshyn wrote on Aug. 28 on Facebook.
The service member said he was stopped in Kharkiv while driving past the scene of a traffic accident. Police searched his car and found drugs hidden in the center armrest.
"I don't use that armrest because it's on the back seat. I opened it and there was some kind of package inside. I took it out, and (the police officer) asked, 'What is this?' I said, 'I don't know.' I opened it, and there was weed with scales and a bunch of small bags," Shyrshyn told Ukrainian media outlet Babel.
Shyrshyn said the presence of the small gram scales alongside the cannabis could be used to accuse him of intending to distribute drugs.
According to Shyrshyn, the police were acting on a tip, and "suspicious" people resembling Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) officers were standing around the site where his car was searched.
National Police and the SBU did not comment on the accusations at the time of publication.
Shyrshyn did not specify who he believed had planted the drugs in his car but suggested that Oleh Shyriaiev, commander of the 225th Separate Assault Regiment, could be involved. The two have been in a longstanding conflict.
"I have no conflict with anyone else except the 225th and 425th," Shyrshyn said, adding that a "series of other events" had taken place before the search and said he would provide more details later.
During Syrskyi's tenure, both the 225th Separate Assault Regiment and the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelia" were not attached to any corps and reported directly to the higher military command. The units operated in some of the most dangerous sectors of the front and often suffered heavy casualties, raising concerns about the rationale behind their deployment.
Journalist Anna Kaliuzhna said a "large amount" of cannabis had been planted in the service member's car in advance, with an attempt apparently made to disable the vehicle's alarm beforehand.
"Police were waiting at a specific location and told (him) exactly what to open," Zhulak said on Facebook.
The journalist also suggested that the incident may be linked to the command of the units directly overseen by Syrskyi, which Shyrshyn had criticized.
Allegations of violence against servicemen have surfaced in both the 225th and 425th regiments. In July, Ukrainian media outlet Texty published audio recordings in an investigation that purportedly captured Shyriaiev ordering that Ukrainian soldiers be shot if they abandoned their positions without authorization.
A separate investigation by Ukranian media outlet Babel into the 425th "Skelia" Regiment identified several alleged cases of harsh treatment and torture of soldiers, along with a high rate of non-combat casualties.
Shyrshyn, known by the call sign "Genius," said in May 2025 that flawed decisions by the military command were causing excessive losses of personnel, equipment, and territory due to a systemic disconnect from troops on the ground.
An internal investigation followed, and Syrskyi subsequently declared Shyrshyn "undisciplined," a designation referring to service member who fail to follow orders, violate military regulations, or undermine the army's combat effectiveness. Syrskyi, who was then commander-in-chief, said Shyrshyn was seeking "attention or self-realization."
In February 2026, a court overturned the disciplinary reprimand imposed on Shyrshyn by the military command.

Dutch spy agencies to get more powers against foreign enemies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:19:41 UTC
22:19:41 KST

Dutch spy agencies to get more powers against foreign enemies
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands’ two intelligence agencies are to gain new powers to track and disrupt “obvious adversaries” such as Russian hackers, Chinese spies and Iranian operatives without asking permission in advance, under a draft law published by the cabinet.
The domestic intelligence service AIVD and military intelligence service MIVD would no longer need prior sign-off to follow an individual hacker online. “By then they have already gone,” said defence minister Dilan Yesilgöz.
Once a foreign service is formally designated an adversary, the agencies could pursue anyone thought to be working for it, with a watchdog checking afterwards whether their actions were lawful and able to halt operations it considers inappropriate.
The plans have raised concerns about the privacy of Dutch citizens. Yesilgöz said oversight would remain in place. “Putin and his cronies do not deserve our privacy, but the people of the Netherlands do,” she said.
The bill would also let the agencies work more closely with Dutch banks, universities and online platforms, warn them of risks and, in some cases, demand information from them. Interior minister Pieter Heerma, who is responsible for the AIVD, declined to name specific organisations.
It follows the previous cabinet’s abandoned plan to screen 8,000 foreign researchers and students for espionage risks, which was judged unworkable. Oversight of the two agencies would be merged into a single body.
The draft is open for public consultation before it goes to parliament.

Valmiki scam: Karnataka minister B Nagendra resigns; breaks down on camera
Unknown

Valmiki scam: Karnataka minister B Nagendra resigns; breaks down on camera
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 28, 2026, 18:49 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
B Nagendra broke down during a press conference while announcing his decision
NEW DELHI: Karnataka planning and statistics minister B Nagendra resigned from the state cabinet on Friday amid mounting pressure over the alleged Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation scam.He also broke down during a press conference while announcing his decision.Nagendra stepped down within 25 days of assuming office after being re-inducted into the cabinet on August 3. He said he had tendered his resignation to chief minister D K Shivakumar."Today I am voluntarily tendering my resignation as the minister," an emotional Nagendra told reporters.
He said he had taken the decision with a heavy heart to ensure that the party leadership was not embarrassed.Nagendra alleged that he was being targeted as part of a conspiracy and said the BJP could not intimidate him through central investigating agencies."They (BJP) can't scare me with ED, CBI," Nagendra said.He also alleged that "Manuwadis", in an apparent reference to the BJP, were targeting him because they did not want a tribal person in the country to grow."Manuwadis targeted me as they didn't want a tribal person in the country to grow," he alleged.
Nagendra also challenged the BJP to defeat him in Ballari in the "court of public opinion". He said he was prepared to resign as an MLA and face elections if the BJP was ready to take him on.The resignation marks the second time Nagendra has stepped down from the cabinet over the controversy. He had earlier resigned as tribal welfare minister in June 2024 when the issue first surfaced.
Pressure after cabinet re-induction
Nagendra was re-inducted into the Karnataka cabinet on August 3 and given the planning and statistics portfolio. His return triggered fresh demands from the BJP and JD(S) for his removal over the alleged diversion of funds from the state-run corporation.Earlier on Friday, Nagendra had said he would meet chief minister D K Shivakumar and discuss the matter in detail."If a situation arises where my actions cause embarrassment to the party, then I will..." he had said, alleging that the developments were part of a "conspiracy".The opposition BJP and JD(S) had been protesting his re-induction into the cabinet and alleging his involvement in the alleged Rs 89 crore scam.The two parties had also staged repeated protests inside and outside the Karnataka legislature during the recent monsoon session, which was curtailed by three days and adjourned sine die on August 24 amid continued disruptions.The BJP and JD(S) had planned a foot march from Raichur to Ballari from September 1 to 10, demanding Nagendra's resignation.
What is the Valmiki Corporation case?
The controversy dates back to May 2024, when P Chandrasekharan, then an accounts superintendent with the Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation, died by suicide and left behind a six-page note alleging irregularities and unauthorised transfers of corporation funds.
Subsequent investigations found that Rs 89.63 crore had been transferred from a corporation account to a Union Bank of India account and later moved to multiple other accounts, triggering a major political controversy.Nagendra, who was tribal welfare minister when the issue surfaced, resigned from the cabinet in June 2024.He had previously rejected reports that he would resign and maintained that the allegations against him were "politically motivated". Just two days ago, he had dismissed media reports claiming that he had offered to step down.His resignation on Friday came amid renewed political pressure on the Congress government over the alleged Valmiki Corporation scam.

Qatar pledges support for efforts to end Libya’s political division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

Qatar pledges support for efforts to end Libya’s political division
Qatari minister meets eastern army chief in Benghazi amid efforts to bridge longstanding political divisions in Libya.
Qatar’s minister of state has pledged his country’s commitment to ending longstanding political division in Libya during a visit to Benghazi.
Minister of State Mohammed bin Abdulaziz al-Khulaifi met with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the self-styled Libyan National Army, which is aligned with the unrecognised eastern-based government, on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Libya rivals test a new path towards unity, 15 years after Gadaffi downfall
- list 2 of 3Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
- list 3 of 3Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
Libya has been split since 2014 between the Tripoli-based government of National Unity, led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and the Haftar-backed eastern administration of Osama Hammad.
The visit, during which al-Khulaifi expressed Qatar’s support for Libyan unity and sovereignty, comes as the country faces the challenge of implementing a recently agreed election pact.
The two officials discussed regional developments and “topics of common interest,” the Qatari Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Al-Khulaifi affirmed Qatar’s support for “a political process that reflects Libyans’ aspirations while aiming at preserving the country’s sovereignty,” according to the statement.
He also stressed the need for continued dialogue and reconciliation to build consensus and pave the way for stability.
Qatar will keep engaging with Libyan parties and leaders to back United Nations efforts towards a political agreement, al-Khulaifi added.
He earlier told Al Jazeera he had discussed ways to support the political process and national dialogue with leaders in Tripoli.
Election pact
Libyan negotiators agreed last week to an initial election pact aimed at ending years of political division within the country.
A document obtained by Al Jazeera Arabic shows the “4+4” committee’s deal, initiated in Tunisia, rewrites the laws governing presidential and legislative elections and sets a 24-month deadline to hold them.
The committee drew four members each from the eastern House of Representatives and the Tripoli-linked High Council of the State.
The pact, however, is on shaky ground, with people from both sides saying they were left out of talks or had not seen the final text.
The United Nations labelled the deal an important step and says the full agreement will be published once it is formally signed.
The UN and other mediators have spent years trying to resolve the split by arranging elections. However, the implementation of the pact is viewed as challenging, due to divided state institutions, legal voids, and lingering political mistrust.
Libyan legal expert Al-Mahdi Kashbour told Al Jazeera that there appears to be a gap between the powers of the parties that signed the agreement and the institutions with the authority to implement it.
Libya political analyst Elias al-Barouni stressed that the pact does not make any concrete plans for the country’s elections. Even if legal hurdles are cleared, the problem then shifts to who governs Libya in the interim, he added.

Hainan establishes international aerospace data service center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:18:01 UTC
22:18:01 KST

HAIKOU /China/, August 28. /TASS/. South China’s Hainan Province established an International Aerospace Data Service Center during an aerospace forum held in Wenchang on the island’s eastern coast. Participants in the event also signed major agreements.
According to the Hainan International Media Center, the forum, held on August 24-26, saw “a series of major contracts signed to establish infrastructure for regular commercial launches.” The administration of the local space city signed strategic and framework agreements with 17 companies, including the commercial rocket division of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation.
In addition, Hainan Space Group signed memorandums with six companies, including China Galaxy Securities. These agreements cover a range of areas, from satellite manufacturing and finance to space tourism. They are expected to lay a solid foundation for frequent launches under commercial projects.
The event was organized by the Wenchang International Aerospace City Administration with the support of relevant government agencies and a group of leading Chinese banks. During the conference, experts, investors, and officials focused on issues including the development of reusable launch vehicle technologies and leveraging the advantages of the Hainan Free Trade Port for the aerospace industry. Other topics included low-Earth-orbit satellite internet, financial support for projects and a new tourism ecosystem. Another key practical outcome of the forum was the opening of a joint laboratory for intelligent computing satellite constellations.
The projects are expected to transform Hainan into a highly developed aerospace hub of global significance powered by advanced digital technologies. According to Liu Hongjian, Chairman of Hainan Space Group and head of the province’s international commercial launch center, the island is rapidly developing a world-class aerospace science and industrial cluster.
Wenchang Mayor Cao Shuyu, for his part, highlighted Hainan’s unique advantages in launch efficiency, logistics, and safety monitoring in rocket stage drop zones. He noted that the local industrial cluster makes it possible to significantly reduce costs, and provides capabilities for rocket assembly and data exchange, satellite manufacturing and the development of space tourism. The official recalled that the province’s spaceport has carried out 11 launches since the beginning of this year. Construction of new launch pads is proceeding at an accelerated pace. According to Cao, major projects planned for the next five years include deploying satellite constellations, implementing a crewed lunar program, and launching heavy-lift rockets into orbit.

A judge in the Sverdlovsk region has disqualified the liberal Yabloko party’s list of candidates from the upcoming regional assembly elections, the court said Friday.
The regional ban follows Russia’s Supreme Court ruling last week to reject Yabloko’s final appeal against a nationwide ban barring its candidate list from the State Duma elections next month.
The Sverdlovsk Regional Court ruled in favor of a lawsuit filed by the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), which accused Yabloko of a range of violations that include those cited in the Supreme Court ruling.
LDPR claimed Yabloko committed copyright infringement, overspent its funds and shared content on banned platforms like Instagram and Facebook. Konstantin Kiselyov, who leads Yabloko’s Sverdlovsk region list of candidates, argued that the same accusations can be leveled against the other parties running in the elections, including LDPR.
“Each party and their leaders are on these banned social networks. I come across official state agencies there, and they can’t live without them,” Kommersant quoted Kiselyov as saying in court.
Yaroslav Shcherbakov, another Yabloko member in the Sverdlovsk region, also accused LDPR of openly calling for the elimination of its political competitor.
Yabloko’s Yekaterinburg branch said it would appeal the ruling.
The Sverdlovsk region is the fifth in Russia where Yabloko has had its list of candidates barred from running in the regional assembly races in September, either through court rulings or rejections by local election commissions.
Yabloko faces the risk of being stripped of its official registration due to legal requirements to field candidates in at least 20% of regional assembly elections or 10% of gubernatorial races every seven years, according to exiled journalist Farida Rustamova.

Analyst: Estonia won't shake fiscal deficit any time soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Analyst: Estonia won't shake fiscal deficit any time soon
If both the debt burden and interest costs continue to grow faster than revenues, the government will eventually have to intervene, either by introducing new or higher taxes or by cutting spending, LHV analyst Triinu Tapver said.
Tapver told ERR that the key indicators in the Ministry of Finance's latest macroeconomic forecast are fairly similar to LHV's forecast, updated in mid-summer, which projects economic growth of 2.2 percent and inflation of 3.3 percent this year, followed by 2.6 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively, next year, assuming the external environment stabilizes.
"I am currently updating our summer forecast and various risk scenarios. Overall, however, I still expect growth in consumption and investment to accelerate. Investment will initially be driven primarily by government investment in defense and infrastructure. An important distinction needs to be made here, however, because a large share of defense equipment is purchased from abroad, meaning a relatively small proportion of that money actually enters the Estonian economy," Tapver said.
She noted that defense spending is primarily an investment in security rather than an economic stimulus comparable to conventional investment. Private-sector investment has yet to gain clear momentum, but gradual growth could also be seen there next year.
Improved consumption should support state budget revenues through value-added tax and excise duties.
"However, it is difficult to assess the scale of that impact. Around 85,000 people have not yet begun applying their tax-free allowance on an ongoing basis and their future behavior will affect how much of the additional income goes into consumption and, from there, into tax revenues," the analyst said.
The Ministry of Finance forecasts that consumer spending will grow more slowly than incomes in 2026. Given that higher earners also gained more in euro terms from the income tax change, Tapver said some of the additional income could go into savings or toward paying off existing obligations rather than consumption.
"Therefore, we cannot assume that higher net incomes will immediately translate into a comparable increase in consumption and tax revenues," she said. "This brings us to the main pressure point in the state budget. On the one hand, defense spending and other more permanent expenditures are increasing; on the other, growth in budget revenues is being constrained by the income tax change and declining revenue from the sale of CO2 emissions allowances."
While improved consumption will support revenues from consumption taxes, Tapver said this may not be enough to offset rising expenditures.
"At present, it appears that the budget deficit will persist, meaning that both the debt burden and interest costs will continue to rise. If interest rates remain higher going forward, servicing new debt will also become more expensive," the LHV analyst said.
Overall, continued improvement in the economy can therefore be expected, but so can structural pressure on the state budget. Tapver noted that if spending and the debt burden grow faster than revenues, intervention will eventually be necessary, either by increasing revenues through new or higher taxes or by cutting spending.
Tapver pointed out that several important spending decisions for the coming years have yet to be made, meaning the budget's actual trajectory could differ significantly from current forecasts.
"The positive side is that the economic recovery, improving consumption and expected growth in private-sector investment are creating a more favorable environment for the budget than before. If economic growth becomes more broad-based, the tax revenue base will also improve. In the longer term, however, we should be able to use better years to rebuild a sufficient fiscal buffer before the next economic downturn," Tapver said.
--
Editor: Karin Koppel, Marcus Turovski

Germany's grape harvest starts earlier than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Germany's grape harvest starts earlier than ever
August 28, 2026
Germany's main grape harvest has begun earlier than ever recorded after the country's exceptionally hot summer accelerated ripening across its wine-growing regions, the German Wine Institute said on Friday.
The record-early harvest continues a trend seen in recent decades, with higher temperatures affecting when grapes ripen, as well as their sugar and acidity levels.
Where and when is the harvest starting?
"This was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions," institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. "Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays because of it."
Harvesting is already underway across Germany's wine regions, from Saxony in the east to Lake Constance in the south.
The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also the first grapes destined for premium wines.
The main harvest is expected to begin "on a large scale" in the first week of September.
Compared with recent years, the main harvest has begun around one to two weeks earlier, according to Büscher.
"Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it is certainly four weeks earlier," he said.
Why is the harvest so early?
The hot, dry summer caused grapes to ripen unusually quickly, while many varieties are reaching maturity at roughly the same time.
That means the harvest is also expected to proceed rapidly and could be completed by the end of September.
"This will be a very fast harvest because almost all varieties are ripening at the same time," Büscher said.
Climate change has brought some advantages for Germany's wine industry over the years. Warmer conditions have allowed growers to experiment with grape varieties better suited to warmer climates and have made wine cultivation possible in some new areas.
But increasingly long and frequent periods of heat and drought also pose challenges.
Growers are closely watching both sugar and acidity levels. Leaving grapes on the vines too long in hot conditions can push sugar levels higher, producing stronger wines with more alcohol.
High temperatures can also reduce the fruit acidity that gives many German white wines their characteristic freshness.
What will the 2026 vintage be like?
Growers are pleased with the quality of the grapes harvested so far.
"The grapes are still very healthy," Büscher said, adding that this pointed to aromatic white wines. Producers are also expecting deeply colored red wines.
However, the overall harvest is expected to be below average because dry conditions have left grapes smaller than usual.
Significant rainfall in the coming weeks could accelerate the harvest even further.

Italy's sixth brutal heatwave will

Dutch court hands life sentence to Rwandan man for genocide role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:17:34 UTC
22:17:34 KST

Dutch court hands life sentence to Rwandan man for genocide role
Eugene N. was convicted for his part in a massacre at a stadium in which 3,000 Tutsis were slaughtered.
A Dutch court has sentenced a Rwandan man to life in prison for his role in the murder of thousands during the 1994 genocide in the Central African country.
The Hague district court found Eugene N guilty of war crimes and genocide on Friday, and issued the sentence.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thirty-two years on, young Rwandans reflect on progress, pain and hope
- list 2 of 3Rwanda: The genocide against the Tutsi
- list 3 of 3Amputee football grows in Rwanda, fostering unity and resilience
Judges called his conduct a “significant lack of respect for human dignitiy and for human life,” and said that only a life sentence would serve justice “to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families”.
Named only as Eugene N, the suspect helped ransack and burn homes in two mostly Tutsi communities, before taking part in a mob that descended on roughly 3,000 Tutsis sheltering in a stadium in Mbazi in April of 1994.
He directed the Hutu attackers to let no one escape and threw a grenade into the crowd, the court said. Survivors of the initial attack were later beaten and hacked to death.
Eugene N, variously reported to be 66 or 67 years old, fled the Netherlands in 1998 and later became a Dutch citizen. Rwanda sought his extradition in 2014, but the Netherlands’ law shields nationals from being handed over.
Prosecutors opened their case in 2020, questioning more than 30 witnesses before arresting him in 2024.
Eugene N denied his involvement, his defence portraying him as having tried to stop the violence and lost dozens of relatives himself. His representatives called him “a broken man”.
Prosectutors countered, “If the horrific crimes of the suspect … do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?”
Rwanda’s 1994 genocide killed more 800,000 people, mostly Tutsis, in roughly three months of violence directed by Hutu ethnonationalist leaders.
A United Nations tribunal prosecuted leading organisers, but European courts have since pursued lower-level suspects under universal jurisdiction, which allows atrocities and war crimes to be prosecuted regardless of where they occurred.
Dutch courts have convicted other genocide suspects, and in some cases, extradited them to Rwanda.

8 civilians killed in drone strike in Sudan’s North Kordofan: Rights group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:17:30 UTC
22:17:30 KST

Adel Abdelrahim and Lina Altawell
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Eight civilians were killed and dozens injured in a drone strike on the Um Sharu area of Sodari locality in Sudan’s North Kordofan state, a Sudanese rights group said Friday.
The independent Emergency Lawyers group said in a statement that a drone targeted civilians Thursday while they were traveling in the area, killing eight and injuring dozens, according to an initial documented toll.
The strike also destroyed four civilian vehicles, the group said, adding that the drone returned and targeted civilians again as they attempted to evacuate the wounded.
Emergency Lawyers said there was no military presence in the area and that no armed clashes were taking place at the time.
The group condemned the attack, warning that it would further worsen civilian suffering and deprive the wounded of necessary medical care.
It said the attack constituted “a violation of international humanitarian law” and could amount to a war crime.
The group did not identify who was responsible for the strike, while there was no immediate comment from the Sudanese army or the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as of 1200GMT.
Sudan’s three Kordofan states — North, West and South — have witnessed clashes between the army and the RSF since Oct. 25.
Since April 2023, Sudan has been gripped by a war between the army and the RSF that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,630 Troops, 3 Tanks, and 55 Artillery Systems in One Day
Ukraine’s General Staff reported that Russian forces lost approximately 1,630 personnel, 55 artillery systems, and three tanks over the previous 24 hours as of August 28.
According to Ukrainian military estimates, Russia’s cumulative personnel losses since launching its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, have risen to around 1,483,780.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine also estimates that Russia has lost 12,307 tanks, including three in the latest reporting period, along with 25,237 armored combat vehicles and 48,749 artillery systems.
Other reported losses include 2,067 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,593 air defense systems, 440 aircraft, and 354 helicopters.
The General Staff further estimates that Russia has lost 2,420 unmanned ground systems and 485,024 operational-tactical UAVs, including 16 and 1,657, respectively, over the past day.
Ukraine puts Russia’s cumulative losses in other categories at 5,060 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 140,741 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,604 pieces of special equipment.
Meanwhile, the General Staff recorded 250 combat engagements between Ukrainian and Russian forces across the front during the previous 24 hours.
At the same time, Ukrainian forces continued targeting Russian military infrastructure behind the front. Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Nebo-U radar station at the Millerovo military airfield in Russia’s Rostov region, the 429th Achilles Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade reported on August 27.

US ICE agency to spend $16.7m on electric shock gloves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:15:38 UTC
22:15:38 KST

US ICE agency to spend $16.7m on electric shock gloves
The much-criticised immigration agency has agreed a contract for 6,000 pairs of gloves that will deliver painful shocks to control resisting detainees and protesters.
The United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency is to spend $16.7m on 6,000 pairs of electric-shock gloves.
A notice on a federal database published on Thursday showed that the much-maligned agency, which has been the face of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has agreed a no-bid contract with Kentucky-based firm Compliant Technologies for the supply of the gloves, alongside support equipment and services, over the next six months.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Most Americans say Trump has gone too far on US immigration: Poll
- list 2 of 3US deports nearly 2,300 Mexicans to Guatemala over Mexico’s objections
- list 3 of 3Trump plans largest mass visa cancellation in history: Who will it affect?
ICE stated in its procurement notice that the “de-escalation devices” will be used when dealing with detainees and protesters.
Officers will deploy the equipment in “high-tension environments”, including during arrests, while transporting combative detainees, and when managing civil disturbances outside detention facilities, the agency said.
“It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties.”
The agency said the shocks would help officers handle aggressive inmates, prevent escape attempts, force people to expose hidden hands for handcuffing, and manage crowds.
ICE added that the gloves offer an alternative to “more severe force” such as firearms, noting they would be used under “approved policy, training, and accountability standards”.
Civil rights pushback
The agency has concluded the contract despite mounting opposition from civil rights advocates and Democratic lawmakers, who contend officers cannot be trusted to use the technology responsibly.
Critics note that ICE officers already face intense criticism over their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing Trump’s immigration policies.
The American Civil Liberties Union said giving immigration agents “a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability”.
Fatal shootings by ICE agents of two US citizens in Minnesota earlier this year spurred protests and widespread criticism. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since Trump took office.
The procurement notice was posted hours after a group of US senators urged the agency to scrap the purchase in a letter to its acting director.
“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant scepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter read.
The lawmakers warned the technology carries “substantial risks” during civil arrests if deployed without clear limits, proper training, and independent oversight. They called on ICE to publicly disclose how officers will be trained and how the use of the gloves will be documented and internally reviewed.
The Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, dismissed the criticism.
“Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers,” the agency said in a statement.

Federer to be inducted into tennis Hall of Fame
Roger Federer is back – on the tennis court and in the spotlight. Following a special appearance in New York, he will be inducted into his sport’s Hall of Fame on Saturday in Newport, Rhode Island.
The term Hall of Fame is not as common in Europe as it is in North America, and particularly in the US. Even those who know nothing about a particular sport realise that if someone is in the Hall of Fame, they are among the greatest in their field. It comes as no surprise that Roger Federer is to be inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport this week – naturally in his very first year of eligibility.
The way his induction is being celebrated says a great deal about the status of the now 45-year-old from Basel. When he was told the good news in November, it was the manner in which it was delivered that stirred emotions for Federer. During the live broadcast, which reached him while he was surrounded by 50 junior players in Biel/Bienne, no fewer than 33 members of the Hall of Fame offered their congratulations – from Chris Evert to Stefan Edberg, and from Martina Navratilova to Rod Laver. Pat Rafter even joined in at 3am Australian time.
More
Roger Federer is not eternal, but he changed tennis forever
This doesn’t happen to everyone who receives this honour. “Hearing all these heroes at a moment like this means a great deal to me,” Federer admitted, visibly moved. The Basel native generally keeps a low profile on the tennis scene; he is nowhere near as visible as, say, John McEnroe, Boris Becker, Evert or Navratilova.
Now, however, he is once again being given a fitting send-off in America. For an exhibition match with McEnroe, Andy Roddick and Andre Agassi in New York, he even picked up a racket in public once again. The fans in the huge arena at Flushing Meadows – where he won five US Opens in a row from 2004 to 2008 – were absolutely thrilled. And an unprecedented drone show captured Federer bathed in bright light over Manhattan.
However, he also made it clear that a comeback is out of the question. “I’m glad you asked,” he said with a smile. “But no, there are far too many obstacles.” He feels comfortable. “But I can hardly find the time to play an exhibition match, let alone go on a professional tour. I’m done with that. Now I’m just a fan and I’m enjoying watching the game.”
More
Roger Federer: ‘You cannot be alone at the top’
Only the second Swiss
The first man to have won 20 grand slam titles is enjoying the week in the US surrounded by his entire family. Parents, wife, children – they’re all there.
As is customary in other sports, a tennis player becomes eligible for induction into the Hall of Fame five years after retiring or after their “last genuine competitive match”. In Federer’s case, this was the 2021 Wimbledon quarterfinal, which he lost to Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz. He is only the second Swiss player after Martina Hingis (2013) to be inducted in Newport.
The official ceremony will take place on Saturday evening local time in the historic holiday resort favoured by wealthy industrialists in the late 19th century. The question of who will deliver the laudatory speech is now adding to the excitement. Some are tipping Rafael Nadal, whose career is so closely linked to Federer’s. There could well be tears once again.

Lithuania’s sole ammunition maker begins €36m expansion, eyes sales in Asia, Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:11:00 UTC
22:11:00 KST

Lithuania’s sole ammunition manufacturer and the only such producer in the Baltic states began construction on a €36-million second production line that will double the factory’s capacity and open the way for exports to Asia and Africa.
Giraitės ginkluotės gamykla, or Giraitė Armament Plant, currently employs about 120 people. The expansion is expected to increase its workforce to 200, with the additional 80 employees to be hired beginning in the fourth quarter of this year.
“The company has been limited in its growth in recent years because it could not produce more ammunition,” CEO Mindaugas Kurauskas told reporters at the plant in Giraitė on Friday. “That is why a decision was made at the state level to invest in a second line, and today we officially begin construction.”
The second line is expected to be installed in the third quarter of 2027, with both lines operating at full capacity from 2028. Production capacity will rise to 500 rounds per minute, twice the current level.
“Lithuania certainly does not need that much ammunition, so we are taking major steps to expand our geography. Africa and Asia are the main regions where we would like to focus,” Kurauskas said.
The company has already established a presence in the Middle East, which Kurauskas said it had “conquered” through the quality of its products.
The factory will continue producing the same two ammunition calibres but plans to expand its product range, including the ability to manufacture training rounds.
Kurauskas said the Lithuanian military’s use of the factory’s ammunition is confidential.
The expansion will include enlarging production and storage facilities from about 5,500 square metres to 7,900 square metres and constructing a new hazardous waste area. The project is being proposed for designation as a project of importance to the state.
The company says the new line will not produce anti-drone ammunition.
Giraitė began producing anti-drone rounds earlier this year, with trial batches sent to Sweden and France. Military organisations in the Czech Republic, Estonia, Belgium and Israel have also expressed interest in testing them.
Kurauskas said the factory has received €700,000 worth of orders for the anti-drone ammunition from foreign customers, though he declined to identify the countries.
“If there are actual orders, it means there is a desire to continue having and testing (the ammunition) and training soldiers,” he said.
The factory is also in discussions with foreign defence companies over potential cooperation, including possible applications for ammunition used against drones. Kurauskas declined to comment on the negotiations, citing their sensitivity.
He said the plant has secured gunpowder and other materials needed for production for about a year despite shortages on the global market.
“The global ammunition market had a major shortage in 2022, but at this point we are seeing stabilisation,” Kurauskas said. “It is difficult to say what will happen next year, but we hope our quality will prevail.”

Barrister Syed Iftikhar Ali Gillani of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) was elected prime minister of Pakistan-administered Kashmir on Friday after securing 30 votes in the regional legislature.
Gillani defeated Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) candidate Sardar Mukhtar Ahmed Abbasi, who received 14 votes, Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper reported.
He succeeds PPP leader Raja Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, who had served as prime minister since November 2025. Rathore took office after a no-confidence motion ousted his predecessor, Chaudhry Anwarul Haq.

The PML-N has won 25 of the 38 directly elected seats so far, while the PPP secured 12, according to Dawn.
Born in Muzaffarabad in 1980, Gillani studied at SOAS University of London and was called to the bar at Lincoln’s Inn in 2005. He first entered the regional assembly after winning a by-election in 2011.
Gillani retained his seat in 2016 and served as education minister for five years. After electoral defeats in 2021 and this year, he returned to the assembly on Aug. 24 through a seat reserved for technocrats and professionals before being nominated for the premiership.

Get Fresh Estonia, which sells berries and fruit under the No Bananas brand, has filed for bankruptcy amid a sharp deterioration in its finances.

Even Cuba's stray cats are feeling the heat as crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:09:13 UTC
22:09:13 KST

Even Cuba's stray cats are feeling the heat as crisis deepens
HAVANA, Aug 28 - Cuban Gabriela Lopez runs a rescue center called Aldameros that would melt the heart of any cat lover. Cats of all shapes and sizes slink about, purring after being fed and caressing the legs of workers.
But all is not well here.
The communist-run island early this year plunged into unprecedented economic and social crisis as stiffened U.S. sanctions and a fuel blockade imposed by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump have pushed the population of 9 million people to the brink.
The center, like the population at large, has little water now, despite its central Havana location, just a couple hours of electricity daily and costs are soaring alongside inflation, says Lopez.
“Before, we could store food for a few days, but now we live day to day because we have no (cold storage). As for water, we have to maintain good hygiene, but there are problems with supply," she says, exhausted by the seemingly endless problems she rattles off in an interview.
"These are small issues that, when you look at them as a whole, add up to a major problem."
Animals, she says, are just the latest casualty of deepening shortages that have begun to impact virtually every facet of life in Cuba.
Still, the cats strolling about the center look unfased despite the problems in their midst. At lunch time they meow and push their way to plastic bowls of pureed scrap chicken, fish and vegetables. After the mid-day meal, they roll over, belly up, and rub their backs on the floor.
But Havana-based veterinarian Daniel Hernandez says the problems go far beyond what meets the eye, as the country`s clinics struggle to keep medications and vaccines on hand amid deepening shortages.
"The biggest problem we face is a steady power supply, (to maintain) refrigeration for medications such as vaccines and other drugs that require a cold chain to ensure they function properly," Hernandez said. "This is really stressful."
Rising costs, meanwhile, have forced volunteer centers like Lopez`s Aldameros to seek alternative food supplies, often unsuccessfully. Businesses that once donated food scraps now seek to sell them instead, she said.
"They realized there was a market," Lopez said.
To make matters worse, prices soar while donations have dried up alongside the country`s tourism sector, says Claudia Diaz, a volunteer coordinator for Cubans in Defense of Animals (CEDA), a non-governmental group of animal rights activists.
“With fewer tourists coming (to Cuba), we have lost a significant source of income both in the form of supplies and cash," Diaz said.
Those donations, she says, once underpinned pest control campaigns, helped centers like Aldameros stay afloat and promoted animal rescue and vaccination campaigns.
"We`re doing everything we can to stay open," said Lopez. "But it's hard (in these conditions) without any help." REUTERS

HMS Bulwark to transfer to Brazilian Navy as UK turns to future of amphibious ships
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

HMS Bulwark to transfer to Brazilian Navy as UK turns to future of amphibious ships
HMS Bulwark is to be sold to the Brazilian Navy, ending more than two decades of service with the Royal Navy, as UK focus turns to the future of amphibious assault ships.
- 
    Landing Platform Dock Ship closes two decades of Royal Navy Service.
- 
    Transfer follows UK and Netherlands £2.4 billion amphibious ship agreement signed in July 2026.
- 
    Agreement advances Royal Navy’s transition to a hybrid Navy with £1.5 billion investment confirmed in the Defence Investment Plan.
HMS Bulwark, one of the Royal Navy’s two Albion-class amphibious assault ships, was commissioned in 2005 and went on to play a central role in operations around the world, including amphibious deployments, humanitarian assistance missions and multinational exercises with allies and partners.
Her sister ship, HMS Albion, remains alongside at HMNB Devonport pending disposal.
The transfer comes as the UK and Netherlands confirmed a new £2.4 billion maritime partnership in July 2026 to deliver a fleet of new amphibious transport ships, replacing the capability provided by the Albion class.
The future ships will be built in UK shipyards, working alongside Dutch industry, as part of a programme that is expected to sustain hundreds of highly skilled UK jobs. At 160 metres in length and displacing 15,000 tonnes, they will be capable of transporting troops, vehicles and equipment, including drones, wherever they are needed.
Minister of State for Defence, Lord Coaker said:
  HMS Bulwark served this country and our allies with distinction for over two decades, and I’m pleased that she will continue her story in Brazilian service, with a nation that has long stood alongside us as a defence partner.
This partnership with the Netherlands marks a real step forward for our Armed Forces, giving our personnel the modern, interoperable capability they need to operate alongside our allies for decades to come. It’s also a vote of confidence in British shipbuilding, backing the skills and shipyards that will keep our industrial base strong and our nation secure.
Based at HMNB Devonport, HMS Bulwark served as the Royal Navy’s Fleet Flagship between 2011 and 2015, supported civilian evacuation operations from Lebanon in 2006, and provided maritime security for the Sailing Regatta at the London 2012 Olympics.
The flight decks of the future UK-Dutch amphibious fleet are being designed to operate current and future long-range drones and autonomous systems, supporting the Royal Navy’s transition to a hybrid Navy and the wider ambitions set out in the Defence Investment Plan to integrate uncrewed and autonomous technology across the fleet.
The programme will form the backbone of a strengthened UK-Netherlands amphibious force, with each nation set to operate four vessels, delivering a shared and interoperable capability that reinforces NATO’s northern and Atlantic flanks.

Chimpanzees have been hurling rocks at the same trees for more than a decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
13:07:11 UTC
22:07:11 KST

Chimpanzees have been hurling rocks at the same trees for more than a decade
- Date:
- August 28, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Some chimpanzees in West Africa repeatedly throw rocks at particular trees, creating piles of stones that can remain in use for more than a decade. Researchers think this unusual behavior may be cultural and could serve as a form of communication, territorial signaling, or something more symbolic. Camera traps and audio recordings are now being used to reveal who throws the stones and how nearby chimpanzees respond.
- Share:
Walking through the savanna-woodland landscape of Boé National Park, Guinea-Bissau, you might encounter a tree covered in gnarled scars, with an accumulation of rocks surrounding its base.
The chimpanzees may have left the area, but you are lucky nonetheless, because you have stumbled upon evidence of a rare — and potentially cultural — chimpanzee behavior: accumulative stone throwing.
Video recordings show wild western chimpanzees, usually adult males, throwing rocks at specific trees and repeatedly returning to these trees to perform the behavior.
[See video link after end of article.]
While throwing, the chimpanzees pant hoot — a loud, long-distance communicative signal — and sometimes repeatedly hit their hands and feet on the tree in a behavior called buttress drumming.
We have just returned from a field site in Guinea-Bissau where we collected data to help us investigate the social and ecological context of accumulative stone throwing to determine what these chimpanzees are trying to communicate.
Given our evolutionary relatedness to chimpanzees, we hope accumulative stone throwing can help us understand the emergence of complex communication and stone tool use over the course of human evolution.
A cultural behavior
Pant hooting and buttress drumming are both part of the male chimpanzee display, suggesting that accumulative stone throwing might represent a modification of this common behavior. It is likely a cultural behavior due to its limited distribution, and because the availability of rocks and trees does not guarantee the presence of an accumulative stone throwing site.
Previous research suggests that accumulative stone throwing is likely communicative or may even have a symbolic purpose, with sites marking important locations within the chimpanzees’ territory.
However, we still don’t know what accumulative stone throwing sites might mean to the chimpanzees themselves nor why they do it. While some primates use stone tools to access food, for instance to crack open nuts, accumulative stone throwing is a rare example of stone tool use in a social context. It has been observed in only four chimpanzee groups in West Africa to date.
Setting up camp
We traveled to the remote Boé chimpanzee territory in Guinea-Bissau and based ourselves in Béli, a small village where, in collaboration with local people, the Dutch non-governmental organization Chimbo maintains a compound. Visiting researchers and tourists can stay here and use a workspace with solar-generated electricity.
From Béli, we cycled and hiked 22 kilometers into the savanna-woodland to establish a bush camp with our two field assistants, Djei Baldé and Balu Séra, and a master’s student from the Great Ape Behaviour Lab, Taylor Tippett.
The Boé chimpanzees performing the behavior are unhabituated; they are not used to humans, meaning that we cannot observe individual chimpanzees on foot because they will run away. Instead, we collected behavioral data using camera traps and recording devices.
We set up two video cameras at each accumulative stone throwing site and placed the recording devices strategically to capture audio data from the areas around these sites.
Our campsite bordered the Fefine, a large river that flows even in the dry season. In a landscape like the savanna-woodland where water sources are scarce, rivers like the Fefine are important for wildlife and humans alike. We captured several of our neighbors on cameras set up near the riverbank.
Chimpanzee nests
On an average day, we woke up around 6:30 a.m. and ate a small breakfast before heading to a set of two to five sites. There, we replaced the SD cards and batteries on the cameras, made sure the devices were working well and collected any additional data needed, including measurements of the tree and 3D scans of rocks thrown at the tree for later analysis.
Along the way, we recorded observations of chimpanzee nests, feeding signs, vocalizations and sightings.
The video and audio data we collected will allow us to investigate the social traits of accumulative stone throwing, including the age and sex of the stone thrower and the audience (other chimpanzees nearby who might react to the throw). This information can help us determine what chimpanzees are trying to communicate.
We found that most of the sites first identified by the Pan African Program, and revisited by our team in 2017, were still in use during our recent trip to the field, meaning that chimpanzees can use these sites for over a decade.
The threat of bauxite mining
As many primate species face threats from human activities, cultural behaviors and the maintenance of rich cultural repertoires can help them adapt to environmental changes and provide support for conservation.
On top of its potential communicative importance and intrinsic value as a cultural behavior, accumulative stone throwing involves durable primate material culture, the loss of which would constitute the erasure of primate heritage.
Unfortunately, chimpanzee habitat in Guinea-Bissau is threatened by extractive industries, particularly industrial mining. While in the field, we encountered bore holes from bauxite mining exploration.
Bauxite mining represents a significant opportunity for economic growth and development in Guinea-Bissau. It can also cause habitat destruction and pollution with severe detrimental effects for chimpanzees, other wildlife and the local people — as it already has in neighboring Guinea.
Environmental oversight and regulations are much needed, especially given the added challenges of unstable governance in Guinea-Bissau.
By studying and bringing attention to chimpanzee cultural behaviors like accumulative stone throwing, we hope to support chimpanzee conservation and the maintenance of biodiversity more broadly, as well as the preservation of primate cultural materials for future research and education.

Beijing has formally removed former senior officers Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli as members of China’s supreme military command.
The two generals have been under investigation for alleged discipline violations since January and were officially stripped of their positions on the Central Military Commission (CMC) at a meeting of the National People’s Congress’ Standing Committee on Friday.

Their sudden downfall left the country’s top military command with only two members, Chinese President Xi Jinping and vice-chairman Zhang Shengmin, who is in charge of disciplinary affairs within the armed forces.

Waving Chinese national flags and singing the military anthem are sights more commonly associated with state-sanctioned patriotic rallies. Yet on the night of August 18 along Chongqing’s Nanbin Road, young men used these patriotic symbols while marching against a seemingly bizarre enemy: teenage idol trainees of a boy-band talent agency and their female fans.
What began as a localized dispute outside the headquarters of Shidai Fengjun (also known as “Time Fengjun,” or TF Entertainment), an agency that helped pioneer China’s idol-trainee industry, rapidly escalated into a prolonged public disturbance. For days, the area around the agency saw escalating street violence, culminating in a heavy police presence and roadblocks.
The confrontation offered a glimpse into a broader dynamic in contemporary China: how online male grievances can spill into the streets, how nationalist symbols can be mobilized in gender conflicts, and how authorities struggle to contain the resulting unrest.
The trouble began on August 15, when groups of male short-video livestreamers and “anti-fans” (黑粉) repeatedly gathered outside Time Fengjun’s office building. Many appeared to be seeking online traffic and attention. They burned and tore down fan posters, blocked company vans, and confronted the company’s young trainees, some reportedly as young as 11. They livestreamed the confrontations while shouting “jiahao” (嘉豪), a derogatory internet term mocking young men who try too hard to appear “cool.” The chant appeared intended as a deliberate provocation.
The incident took on a broader gender dimension after a viral video clip circulated on August 17. The footage captured a female fan throwing a small object (variously reported as a power bank or water bottle) at a male provocateur, who responded by splashing water at her and appeared to move toward her aggressively. When police on site immediately detained the male provocateur but did not detain the female fan, online male communities erupted in fury.
Accusing police of giving women preferential treatment, commenters began using terms such as “maternal law enforcement” (秉母执法, bingmu zhifa), a pun on binggong zhifa (秉公执法, “impartial law enforcement”), and “Chongqing maternal public security” to portray local authorities as biased in favor of female fans.
Driven by this digital rage, crowds of young men marched down Nanbin Road on August 18, demanding the release of the detained men. They wrapped their grievances in the language of patriotism, waving Chinese national flags and singing the national anthem and the military anthem “Strong Army Song” (《强军战歌》) as they marched.
Patriotic rhetoric gave the confrontation a broader political frame. Some protesters portrayed the predominantly female fan community as a symbol of what they saw as a feminized and “decadent” youth culture, casting their confrontation with the fans as a fight to “realize justice.”
As the marchers gathered around the building, the confrontation turned physical. Livestreamers chased, kicked, and assaulted female fans. Videos circulating online showed ordinary women and girls caught in the confrontation. In some footage, female fans were surrounded, cornered, shoved, kicked, or splashed with liquid. Chinese-language media also reported that a mother and daughter were among those assaulted, although their relationship is difficult to independently verify from the footage.
In response, Time Fengjun suspended its trainees’ offline sessions on August 18, but faced intense criticism from female fans for failing to protect them and remaining silent about the violence.
As the physical crowds swelled, the conflict spilled back online into more serious digital harassment. Online vigilantes doxed female fans on site, leaking their personal identities. The harassers used AI tools to splice the victims’ faces onto non-consensual pornographic images, which were then printed on flyers advertising prostitution and distributed both online and in person.
Facing several days of increasingly visible unrest, local authorities moved to contain the confrontation. Physically, police blocked roads and used municipal buses to disperse and evict the male protesters. Online, videos about the incident, and posts and searches containing terms such as “bingmu zhifa” appeared to face censorship on major Chinese social-media platforms.
On August 20, the Chongqing Public Security Bureau released a brief statement. It downplayed the gender-targeted physical and digital violence, dryly framing the multi-day unrest as a minor “fandom dispute” involving “water-throwing and chasing.” It offered “legal education” to participants and called for “civilized fan activities.”
By reducing the confrontation to a fandom dispute, authorities restored temporary order while leaving the gender grievances that fueled the conflict largely unaddressed. The Chongqing confrontation illustrated how online male grievance can move rapidly from digital spaces into the physical world, especially when it becomes entangled with broader anxieties over gender and masculinity.
Meanwhile, censorship on Chinese social media platforms makes it increasingly difficult to document and verify such incidents domestically, leaving overseas platforms such as X and Threads as important sources of evidence and further widening the information gap between China and the outside world.

Three endangered jaguar cubs have
been born at a Naples zoo due to the rising tropical-style heat
in the last four years.
                                    
                                       
				The latest offspring at risk of exticntion, Parthenope, was born
in May and went on show for the first time Friday
"This is an extraordinary success for the Naples Zoo, especially
considering that the species is considered 'Near Threatened' by
the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature) and
that it is the only breeding pair in Italy," said Fiorella
Saggese, curator of the park.
                                    
                                       
				She added: "Events like this serve to remind us how crucial it
is to protect animal species even in contexts outside their
native geographic range.
                                    
                                       
				"Zoos play a fundamental role in this: by managing animals in
controlled environments, they promote the conservation of the
species' genetic variability, that mix of genetic variants
(alleles) that increases the likelihood that, in the face of
environmental changes—climate, availability of resources,
emergence of pathogens, habitat modifications, etc.—some
individuals will survive."
The European and global zoo network collaborates to ensure the
species' conservation through projects with local communities.
                                    
                                       
				Like her two siblings, Parthenope will also leave for a new
destination as soon as she is ready to leave her mother, but the
Naples Zoo's owners have announced some important news this
year.
                                    
                                       
				"We are ready to build a bridge directly with South America,"
announced Giulia Floro Flores, one of the zoo's founding
members, "and collaborate with local conservation centers to
protect the species comprehensively.".

Uzbekistan tests US-China AI rift with bid to join rival tech bloc
