Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 500, thousands still missing
Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026
Rescue workers have resumed a search for hundreds of people still missing two days after catastrophic flash flooding hit the border between Nepal and China.
Their efforts were briefly put on hold on Friday after a lake formed by debris began overflowing, threatening areas already devastated by the disaster.
"We have received a notice saying that the lake has broken its banks," Narendra Pariyar, the most senior bureaucrat of the hard-hit Rasuwa district, told DW. "We can see that the level of water in the river is rising."
Residents in Nepal's border district of Rasuwa were seen fleeing up hillsides as they braced for a surge in river levels, Reuters reported.
Authorities later said the threat had eased but that they were closely monitoring the situation.
Meanwhile, Nepal said the death toll had risen to 579, up from 390 a day earlier. China has updated its earlier count of three to five deaths in Tibet.
More than 2,000 are still believed to be missing, including over 500 foreigners from more than 30 countries.
Nepal: WHO and Red Cross warn disaster is 'not over'
The International Red Cross estimated that over 93,000 people have been directly affected by the catastrophe and are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.
"We're of course very concerned about a secondary flood," said spokesman David Fisher at a press briefing in Geneva, adding that Red Cross relief trucks had been blocked by the lake which formed following the landslide.
Kamal Kishore, Head of the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, warned of further "cascading hazards that might unfold" and said: "The disaster is not yet completely over. It is still unfolding in some ways."
The World Health Organization (WHO) warned of the risk of disease in the wake of the disaster.
"Following a disaster of this scale, displacement, overcrowding and disruption to water, sanitation and health services can increase the risk of infectious diseases, including diarrhoea and respiratory illnesses," said spokesman Tarik Jasarevic.
What is the latest update from China?
Wednesday's disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse that sent rock and meltwater surging into rivers below, left a new danger in its wake: a barrier lake formed upstream by debris dams.
China's Ministry of Water Resources said the lake held roughly 2 million cubic meters of water as of Thursday and was expected to receive another 3 million cubic meters — equivalent to about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — over the following three days, with peak flow expected around September 1.
Chinese national broadcaster CCTV said the lake's barrier sat more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from Gyirong Port, the border crossing that was engulfed by the initial flood, and is at an elevation roughly 1,000 meters (3,280 feet) above it.
The country had mobilized an eight-member engineering team to survey the lake by air and build 3D models of the site. Engineer Chen Hanxiao described the difficulty of the terrain: "After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it," he told CCTV.
He said the team's general strategy was to dig a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, though the channel's exact width and depth would depend on calculations of water flow and how quickly the lake continued to fill.
Their survey found the lake to be about 150 meters long and 40-50 meters deep. Continuing rain in the area, which is forecast to last through the coming week, has further destabilized the surrounding soil and rock.
On Friday afternoon, Chinese state media reported that the first professional rescue teams had reached the "core rescue site" or the area wiped out by a mudslide.
What did Nepal say about search and rescue?
Nepal's Foreign Ministry said Friday it does not need foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations, despite offers of help from several countries with nationals still missing. 
 
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said Nepal's security agencies were managing the response.
 
"The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don't require such help," he said. 
 
Hundreds of foreign nationals remain unaccounted for, including from South Korea, which has already sent a response team and plans to dispatch a disaster relief unit. South Korea's Foreign Ministry confirmed that Nepal had indicated it was not yet ready to accept foreign rescue teams, adding, "South Korea will keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter." 
 
Seoul has pledged $1 million (€860,000) in humanitarian aid through international organizations, after reporting nine of its nationals missing and 10 stranded after a hydropower plant they were working at was hit by the flood. 
 
According to local media, India, China, the United States, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have all asked Nepal's government for permission to send their own search-and-rescue teams to assist.

Hong Kong launches first regional mediation platform for medical disputes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
11:03:47 UTC
20:03:47 KST

Hong Kong launches first regional mediation platform for medical disputes
New Healthcare Dispute Resolution Centre online platform provides both virtual and face-to-face services for patients and doctors
Hong Kong has launched the first regional mediation and arbitration platform dedicated to medical and healthcare services as part of the city’s efforts to resolve local and cross-border disputes and strengthen its bid to become an international legal services hub.
The Healthcare Dispute Resolution Centre, a non-profit organisation set up in 2024, announced its new online platform on Friday, providing both virtual and face-to-face services for patients and medical practitioners to settle conflicts through mediation and arbitration.
“Disputes, whether they are related to medical errors, patient rights or contract issues, often turn into litigation that takes time, incurs high costs, and goes toe to toe. Litigation not only harms the relationship between patients and healthcare providers, but also wastes precious public resources,” centre chairman Samuel Kwok Po-yin said at the launch ceremony.
“As cross-border use of medical services becomes more frequent, the new website and platform will become a hub for resolving medical and healthcare disputes in Hong Kong and in the Greater Bay Area.”
The bay area refers to Beijing’s initiative to link Hong Kong, Macau and the nine Guangdong cities into an economic powerhouse.
Kwok said that, compared with court litigation procedures, mediation and arbitration would take less time and cost less, while cases would be kept confidential and dealt with based on professional knowledge.

Is Nepal facing another devastating flood from a new lake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
11:02:10 UTC
20:02:10 KST

Why Nepal faces another flood threat from a new lake on China border
Glacier collapse in Nepal triggered flash floods, mudslides and a barrier lake where a landslide dammed the river.
Two days after a glacier collapse sent a catastrophic flood roaring through parts of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, a newly formed river has broken the banks, and a renewed flood threat is looming.
The river breach on Friday halted rescue operations in the area after flash floods and mudslides caused by glacial collapse from the Himalayas led to 469 confirmed deaths. More than 1,000 people remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet.
A lake has formed by the buildup of debris at the border of Nepal and China at the flood site, and as it continues to rise, it increases the flood risk.
What happened?
On Friday, officials in Nepal’s Rasuwa district said they had been notified that the barrier lake had begun to overflow.
“We can see that the level of water in the river is rising,” Narendra Pariyar, Rasuwa’s most senior official, said.
He added that it is currently unclear how high the water level is. “We do not know how big it is and how high is its water level. We can see that the level of water in the river is rising.”
Scientists say this disaster has created not one but two new lakes. One has formed high up near the glacier, where meltwater is now trapped.
The other, much larger and more dangerous lake sits on a river in Nepal, where a huge landslide blocked the valley and dammed the river.
What was the threat?
Nepali and Chinese authorities warned on Thursday that the lower lake had formed due to the buildup of debris at the site of the flood.
The lake is rising in level, which means it can burst, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) warned.
Chinese authorities said they have mobilised an engineering team of eight members to carry out aerial surveys and 3D modelling of the barrier lake, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Friday.
However, there are challenges when it comes to accessing the site.
“After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it,” one of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, told CCTV on Thursday evening.
Where is this lake?
The lake is near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers on the Lhende river system in Nepal.
It is flowing upstream of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that carry water south towards Kathmandu, The Kathmandu Post reported.
How was this lake formed?
The glacial collapse which led to the Wednesday flash floods also caused mudslides, pushing rock, ice, mud and debris into river systems.
“The new lake appears to be an avalanche-induced barrier lake. The ice-rock avalanche deposited a huge volume of rock, ice and debris in the river valley, blocking or severely constricting the drainage,” Pawan Bhattarai, assistant professor at the civil engineering department of Nepal’s Kathmandu-based Tribhuvan University, told Al Jazeera.
“Water then accumulated behind this natural barrier, forming the lake. Satellite imagery and even some Chinese media reports has confirmed the barrier lake.”
These immense piles of debris blocked river channels, creating a natural dam and hence causing this lake to form.
“The satellite images and drone videos taken show two lakes formed after the event. One is formed in the upper part and other in the Lehende river,” Nitesh Khadka, a Nepali researcher and physical geographer who specialises in glacial floods, told Al Jazeera.
Khadka explained that the upper lake – the one in China – formed when the melted glacial water pooled and prevented natural drainage.
“The lake on the Lehende is formed when land/mudslide blocked the flow and water got impounded. It’s a natural process and can’t be prevented,” Khadka added.
“If it poses a danger, safe and control breaching could be done but it also seems infeasible due to complex terrain.”
Meanwhile, the terrain where the mudslide barrier lake – on the Nepal-China border – has formed is remote and steep, where it is also very difficult to bring crews or heavy machinery.
“The avalanche and formation of the natural dam itself were probably not preventable,” Bhattarai explained.
“However, the consequences could potentially have been reduced through better satellite monitoring, rapid detection of river blockage and lake formation, real-time river monitoring, timely evacuation, and strong Nepal-China transboundary early-warning systems.”
Why is it such a big risk?
When sudden lakes form, the surrounding area is not in a position to hold it. Additionally, when a barrier lake is held behind only by loosely packed rocks and mud, even moderate overflow can erode the barrier and trigger a sudden, destructive outburst flood downstream.
“The danger is not just the lake itself, but the possibility of sudden dam failure. In a steep valley like this, even a short-lived breach can generate a fast-moving debris-laden flood with very little warning for downstream communities,” Bhattarai said.
China’s Ministry of Water Resources estimated on Thursday that the lake is holding about 1.5 to 2 million cubic metres of water and warned that about 3 million cubic metres more could flow in over three days.
This is the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
“It is a threat, because if a formed lake suddenly breaches it may cause another flood; it may mobilise the sediments that will hamper search and rescue operation and will also put dangers to those surviving in the hydro tunnels,” Khadka said.
This means that if the lake causes a flood, the flood will pick up mud and rocks, making the water even more destructive and making it harder for teams to search for the missing.
Khadka added that this also poses a threat to workers or engineers in hydropower tunnels downstream, or the displaced flood survivors in the vicinity. If a sudden flood rushes down, it could slam into these tunnels and power stations, trapping or injuring anyone who is still there.
“We may not be able to stop the natural process completely, but we can reduce the flood risk through continuous monitoring, safe lowering of the lake where feasible, early warning and timely evacuation downstream,” Bhattarai said.
What’s the status of rescue efforts?
Rescue efforts have been impeded due to the floods and mudslides.
In the hard-hit Rasuwa district, they were paused on Friday since the barrier lake broke its banks. However, after the brief pause, the efforts were resumed. China’s state broadcaster CCTV said on Friday that the risks from the overflowing barrier lake were “manageable”.
According to a World Health Organization (WHO) official on Friday, six health facilities have been damaged by the floods, and eight health workers are missing.
Nepal has said it does not need help from abroad.
“The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, Foreign Ministry spokesperson, said on Friday.
Has this happened before?
While this exact barrier river has not formed before, glacial collapse and glacial lake outburst floods have happened before in the Himalayas.
“Similar cascading events have happened before. Nepal’s 2012 Seti flood is an important example, where rockfall, temporary river blockage and a rock-ice avalanche combined to generate a destructive flood,” Bhattarai said.
“The exact mechanism in Rasuwa is still being investigated, but the broader process is not unprecedented.”
Simply put, a glacial collapse refers to when a large mass of glacier ice detaches from its bed.
This sometimes involves millions of cubic metres of ice, rock and water, which can transform into a highly mobile ice-rich avalanche or debris flow.
Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF) refer to the sudden and catastrophic release of vast volumes of water from melting glacier-fed lakes.
In July 2016, the lower part of a valley glacier in Tibet’s Aru Range detached, sending about 68 million cubic metres of ice down the mountain and killing nine herders and hundreds of animals. This was located in far western Tibet, near the Pangong Tso region along the India-China border. Two months later, a nearby glacier collapsed, releasing about 83 million cubic metres of ice.
In November 2022, about 40 million cubic metres of glacier ice detached from the Bukadaban Feng glacier in the Kunlun Mountains on the northern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, in China’s Qinghai province. An ice avalanche crashed into a lake below, creating a 13-meter (42ft) high wave, according to analysis by the European Space Agency.
GLOFs have also hit northern Pakistan. In May 2022, a flood hit the Hassanabad area of Hunza Valley after a sudden breach of an ice-dammed lake formed by the surging Shishper Glacier.

Xi extends condolences over mudslide disaster in Nepal

20:01:50 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday sent a message of condolences to Nepali President Ram Chandra Poudel over a mudslide disaster that hit Nepal recently.
In his message, Xi noted that a severe mudslide disaster occurred recently at the Gyirong-Rasuwa border crossing between China and Nepal, causing heavy casualties, leaving people missing and resulting in property losses.
On behalf of the Chinese government and people, Xi expressed deep condolences to the victims and sincere sympathies to the bereaved families, the injured and people in the disaster-stricken areas.
Xi noted that China is making every effort to search for and rescue missing persons, relocate and resettle affected people, provide prompt medical treatment to the injured, minimize casualties and prevent secondary disasters.
China and Nepal, Xi said, are connected by mountains and rivers and share a common destiny, adding that China is ready to actively assist Nepal in its rescue efforts and provide support and assistance to the best of its capability.
Xi also expressed his belief that both peoples will be able to work together to overcome the disaster and rebuild their homes as soon as possible.
On the same day, Chinese Premier Li Qiang sent a message of condolences to Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah. ■

Timeline: U.S.-Israel-Iran war -- key events of past 6 months
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:01:35 CST
20:01:35 KST

CAIRO, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Friday marks six months since the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Although the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in June, raising hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough, negotiations aimed at resolving differences and ending the conflict have since stalled. Last month's escalation in fighting, coupled with new U.S. sanctions on Iran, has further reduced the likelihood of a near-term resolution.
The following is a timeline of the conflict starting from Feb. 28:
Feb. 28:
--- The United States and Israel launched joint military strikes against Iran, killing Iran's then Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.
-- The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) launched retaliatory operation, firing missiles and drones at U.S. military bases in the Middle East and targets in Israel.
March 2:
-- Lebanon's Hezbollah said it had launched rockets and drones toward Israel. The Israel Defense Forces said it launched "forceful" airstrikes across Lebanon in response, noting it began operating "against Hezbollah's decision to join the campaign."
March 3:
-- Deputy Commander of IRGC's Navy Mohammad Akbarzadeh said the Strait of Hormuz was under Iran's full control.
March 8:
-- Iran's Assembly of Experts announced that Mojtaba Khamenei, son of Ali Khamenei, was selected as Iran's new supreme leader.
March 12:
-- In his first public remarks, Mojtaba Khamenei called for the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and urged neighboring countries to shut down U.S. bases.
March 13:
-- U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. military carried out bombing raids against military targets on Iran's Kharg Island, a key oil export hub that handles most of the country's crude shipments.
March 21:
-- Trump threatened to hit Iran's energy infrastructure unless Tehran fully reopened the Strait of Hormuz within 48 hours. He then twice postponed the attacks, first by five days and then by 10 days, on March 23 and 26, respectively.
-- The United States and Israel attacked Iran's Natanz uranium enrichment facility, while Iranian missiles struck targets in southern Israel.
March 24:
-- Israel's Channel 12 reported the United States had sent Tehran a 15-point peace plan, via Pakistan, in an attempt to end the war.
March 28:
-- Yemen's Houthi armed forces said they had launched a barrage of ballistic missiles targeting "sensitive Israeli military sites" in southern Israel. Local observers said the attacks appeared to signal the Houthis' formal entry into the widening regional conflict.
April 3:
-- Iranian forces shot down a U.S. F-15E Strike Eagle over southwestern Iran, triggering a large-scale U.S. combat search-and-rescue operation involving special forces and aircraft. One crew member was rescued quickly, while the second was recovered after an extended search, with additional U.S. aircraft lost during the operation.
April 6:
-- Iran rejected the 15-point peace plan, but delivered its response via Pakistan in a 10-point document, while calling for a permanent end to the conflict.
April 8:
-- Iran and the United States agreed to a two-week ceasefire. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later said the arrangement did not include Lebanon. Israel launched its heaviest bombardment of Lebanon since the start of the war.
April 11:
-- Senior U.S. and Iranian officials held talks in Islamabad, Pakistan. Despite intensive talks, the two sides failed to reach an agreement.
April 12:
-- Trump said that the U.S. Navy would start to blockade ships attempting to enter or leave the Strait of Hormuz.
April 16:
-- Lebanon and Israel reached a 10-day ceasefire agreement brokered by the United States. The deal marked the first pause in more than a month of fighting between Israel and Hezbollah that had killed over 2,000 people.
April 23:
-- Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to destroy any Iranian boats laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
May 3:
-- The United States launched "Project Freedom" to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. The operation was later suspended by Trump, citing progress in negotiations with Iran.
May 15:
-- Israel and Lebanon agreed to extend their ceasefire by 45 days.
May 23:
-- Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran and the United States are working to finalize an MoU, after Trump said his administration was "in final stages of" peace talks with Iran.
June 3:
-- Israel and Lebanon agreed to implement a ceasefire. The two sides also agreed to advance the creation of "pilot zones" in Lebanon where Hezbollah will be excluded.
June 7:
-- Israel launched airstrikes on the southern suburb of Beirut, Lebanon's capital. Iran responded by firing multiple waves of missiles at Israeli targets.
June 11:
-- Iran's main military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, announced the full closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
-- Iran launched missile and drone attacks against U.S. military targets in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan, in retaliation for the U.S. attacks.
June 14:
-- Pakistan announced that the United States and Iran had reached a peace agreement following intensive negotiations, with both sides later confirming the deal.
June 18:
-- The United States and Iran signed an MoU, launching a 60-day negotiation period aimed at reaching a final agreement.
June 26:
-- The U.S. Central Command conducted strikes against Iran as "a powerful response" to the alleged Iranian drone attack on a commercial vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz a day earlier.
June 28:
-- IRGC fired ballistic missiles and drones at U.S. military facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain in response to U.S. airstrikes.
July 1:
-- An informed source told Xinhua that indirect talks between the United States and Iran were underway in Doha under the mediation of Qatar and Pakistan, focusing on the implementation of the MoU.
July 8:
-- The United States launched strikes against 80 Iranian targets, and in response, Iran's IRGC attacked 85 U.S. military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait, in a new round of escalation of regional tensions.
-- Trump said that the ceasefire with Iran "is over," and he did not want to deal with Iran anymore.
July 18:
-- Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi said that Iran ceased the fulfillment of its obligations under the MoU.
Aug. 3:
-- Trump said talks with Iran are "going on right now," adding that "this is a last chance."
Aug. 17:
-- The 60-day window that Washington and Tehran set for themselves to hammer out a final peace agreement expired.
Aug. 19:
-- Trump announced what he described as "the most crushing economic operation ever taken" against any country providing a lifeline to Iran after reportedly instructing his top envoys to halt their conversations with Iran the day before.
Aug. 23:
-- Iran's senior security official Mohsen Rezaei warned that the country will consider any state's participation in or support for the U.S. anti-Iran economic operation as an "act of war."
Aug. 24:
-- U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country.
Aug. 28:
Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said that diplomacy with the United States can get back on track if Washington realizes that pressure against Tehran does not work. ■

France's Q2 GDP revised down to flat growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:01:29 CST
20:01:29 KST

PARIS, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- France's gross domestic product (GDP) was revised down to zero growth quarter on quarter in the second quarter of 2026, from a preliminary estimate of 0.2-percent growth, according to revised data released Friday by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE).
Household consumption rebounded by 0.3 percent in the second quarter, following a 0.3-percent decline in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, government consumption increased by 0.4 percent, up from a 0.3 percent rise in the first quarter.
Exports rebounded strongly, rising 2.9 percent in the second quarter after falling 3.0 percent in the previous quarter, driven in particular by an increase in aeronautics exports. Imports increased 1.1 percent after declining 0.6 percent in the previous quarter.
Foreign trade made a positive contribution of 0.6 percentage points to GDP growth in the second quarter, reversing a negative contribution of 0.9 percentage points in the previous quarter, according to INSEE.
INSEE said the revisions reflected a further deterioration in agricultural production compared with the information available at the end of July, as well as stronger-than-expected prices for market services, which were not fully known at the end of July.
The institute also further revised down France's GDP growth in the first quarter to a 0.2-percent contraction from the 0.1-percent contraction reported in May. ■

New WHO global center in China to accelerate worldwide push to end tuberculosis epidemic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:01:18 CST
20:01:18 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- A new World Health Organization (WHO) global collaboration center for tuberculosis (TB) research and innovation was established in China on Friday, aiming to offer Chinese expertise to the global campaign of curbing the world's deadliest infectious disease.
The center was officially inaugurated at the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) in Beijing. It will focus on scientific and technological innovation, disease surveillance and other areas of TB prevention and control.
"China has made significant progress in reducing the burden of TB and is playing an increasingly important role in the global TB response," said Tereza Kasaeva, director of the WHO Department of HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections.
According to the WHO World TB Report 2025, the total TB incidence in China dropped significantly to 49 per 100,000 population in 2024. This has made China a country with moderate to low TB prevalence.
Kasaeva said the new center could serve as an important platform for global innovation, research, technology exchange and capacity building, helping translate scientific advances into practical solutions.
Zhao Yanlin, head of the National Center for Tuberculosis Prevention and Control under the China CDC, said the center will serve five core functions.
They include developing, evaluating and promoting new diagnostic technologies, anti-TB drugs, vaccines and digital health tools; contributing to the formulation and revision of WHO guidelines and standards on TB; providing international training and capacity building in laboratory testing and epidemiological investigations; conducting global TB surveillance, risk assessment and data sharing; and establishing multilateral platforms for technical exchanges and joint research, according to Zhao.
According to WHO data, TB remains the world's leading cause of death from a single infectious disease, despite decades of efforts to control it. The establishment of the new center comes as the international community works toward the goal of ending the global TB epidemic by 2030.
Since 2012, China has seen a continuous decline of TB, with both the incidence and mortality rates dropping by approximately 30 percent, while maintaining a national cure rate exceeding 90 percent. ■

China's data economy hits 6.78 trln yuan amid AI boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:01:01 CST
20:01:01 KST

GUIYANG, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's data industry continued to expand rapidly in 2025, supporting the development of the fast-growing artificial intelligence (AI) sector, according to official data.
The scale of China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan (about 1 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, up 15.7 percent year on year, showed figures released at the opening of the 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo on Friday.
Data-related software products, including AI application software, and data resource products, including token services, had a combined output value of 4.99 trillion yuan, accounting for 73.6 percent of the industry's total.
As of this month, more than 126,000 high-quality datasets had been built nationwide, with a total volume exceeding 1,815 petabytes, an increase of more than 89 percent from March.
"AI development is heavily driven by data," said Liu Liehong, head of China's National Data Bureau. "Wherever AI advances, we push forward the construction and application of high-quality datasets."
The expo is being held in Guiyang, capital of southwest China's Guizhou Province. Guizhou is a key hub for China's national "East Data, West Computing" project. This national strategy operates similarly to a power grid, shifting the heavy data processing demands of China's economically bustling eastern coast to resource-rich western regions. Crucially, the project utilizes the western region's abundant green energy such as wind and hydropower, making it a major milestone in green technology and carbon reduction.
By late July 2026, Guizhou housed 50 key data centers, with total computing capacity reaching 176.57 EFLOPS. Nearly 98.4 percent of this capacity was dedicated specifically to AI-related computing.
EFLOPS, or ExaFLOPS, is a unit of computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
Themed "Token: A New Path to Value of Data Elements," the expo has attracted 372 domestic and international companies and over 16,000 registered guests.
The rapid growth of China's data industry is backed by years of policy efforts. In 2019, China became the world's first country to formally recognize data as a factor of production, followed by the establishment of the National Data Bureau in 2023. ■

Armenia no longer considers Russia a strategic partner: PM

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has said that there are grounds to no longer consider Russia a strategic partner of Armenia.
Speaking at a news conference in the capital Yerevan on Aug. 27, Pashinyan accused Moscow and the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) of failing to “implement its security obligations,” meaning Russia’s refusal to interfere in Armenia’s 2022 escalation with Azerbaijan.
“After the events of September 2022, how can we say that there is a strategic partnership?” Pashinyan said, responding to a question about why Russia was not described as a strategic partner in the Armenian government’s 2026-2031 program.
“If we now write ‘strategic partnership,’ you will ask why Russia and the CSTO did not fulfill their security obligations in September 2022. What should I answer you?” he said.
The Armenian government’s 2026-2031 program instead says that dialogue aimed at mutually beneficial, multi-sector cooperation with Russia will continue as Armenia transforms its relations with Moscow “in the new conditions of establishing peace in the region” and pursues a balanced foreign policy.
Presenting the program to parliament, Pashinyan said the transformation of Armenian-Russian relations was a natural process following the establishment of peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan.
In response to Armenia’s claims, Russian officials have repeatedly said the security obligations did not extend to Karabakh, which is internationally recognized as the territory of Azerbaijan, and that they only concern Armenia’s territory itself.
Armenian and Azerbaijan fought a series of cross-border wars in the Karabakh region within Azerbaijan since the late 1980s. Baku fully liberated its territory in 2023.

Netherlands orders Saab mobile camouflage systems
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:47 BST
20:00:47 KST

The Netherlands Ministry of Defence has signed a multi-year agreement with Saab covering the Barracuda Mobile Camouflage System, with an initial order placed for equipment to be fitted to Royal Netherlands Army Fennek reconnaissance vehicles and Panzerhaubitz self-propelled howitzers, according to the company.
The agreement announced by Saab on 27 August will allow the Netherlands to place further orders for the camouflage system over its duration. Options are also included to extend the equipment to additional vehicle types in the Dutch Army fleet.
Saab said deliveries associated with the first order will take place over the coming years. The company did not disclose the value of the agreement in its announcement.
The Barracuda Mobile Camouflage System is designed to be fitted directly to military vehicles and reduce their detectability across multiple parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. According to Saab, individual installations are tailored to the vehicle concerned and can be produced in camouflage patterns intended for woodland, urban or Arctic environments.
The system forms part of Saab’s wider Barracuda camouflage family, which includes products intended to reduce the visual, near-infrared, thermal infrared and radar signatures of personnel, vehicles and fixed positions. Mobile camouflage systems are designed to remain fitted while vehicles are moving and operating rather than being limited to static concealment.
Henning Robach, head of Saab’s Barracuda business unit, said in the company’s release: “We are proud to support the Royal Netherlands Army with our advanced multispectral camouflage solutions, helping to protect its vehicle fleet from detection across the modern sensor spectrum, strengthening survivability and mobility on the battlefield.”
The first Dutch vehicles covered by the agreement include the Fennek, a wheeled reconnaissance vehicle used extensively by the Royal Netherlands Army, and the Panzerhaubitz 2000, the tracked 155mm self-propelled artillery system operated by Dutch forces.
Both vehicle types can operate relatively close to the forward area and are potentially exposed to a growing range of surveillance systems. Modern battlefield reconnaissance increasingly combines optical cameras, thermal imagers, radar and uncrewed aerial systems, placing greater emphasis on reducing vehicle signatures across several sensor bands rather than relying solely on conventional visual camouflage.
The Netherlands operates Fennek vehicles in several configurations, including reconnaissance and command roles. Developed jointly for German and Dutch requirements, the platform is designed around a low profile and wheeled mobility, with specialised sensor equipment fitted to reconnaissance variants.
The Royal Netherlands Army also operates the Panzerhaubitz 2000, commonly known as the PzH 2000, as its principal heavy self-propelled artillery system. The German-designed vehicle carries a 155mm gun and has served with several European NATO armies.
Saab said the Barracuda system supplied under the new agreement will be adapted specifically to the vehicles on which it is installed. The modular nature of the agreement also gives the Dutch Ministry of Defence the option to bring further elements of its vehicle fleet under the same arrangement in future.

In Ceuta, a month after the influx of migrants, protesters set fire to their camp and clashed with police
Kyiv • UNN
Demonstrators in Ceuta set fire to a migrant camp and demanded that the migrants be returned to Morocco. Spain's government is under pressure because of the migration crisis.
Protesters set fire to a migrant camp in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in North Africa on Thursday and demanded the migrants’ immediate return to Morocco, UNN writes, citing dpa.
Details
According to DW, protesters in Ceuta on Thursday not only set fire to a migrant camp, but clashes with police also broke out. The unrest occurred a month after a massive influx of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish enclave.
Television footage from Benitez Beach, where migrants had been camping for weeks, showed civilians repeatedly throwing objects into the fire.
Police separated the demonstrators from the migrants, who retreated to the pier. Earlier, demonstrators had tried to stop Red Cross vehicles carrying food and water for the migrants.
At the end of July, up to 80,000 migrants arrived in Ceuta en masse from Morocco, many of them by sea. According to official data, at least 96 people died. Most of the migrants returned shortly afterward, but several thousand remain in Ceuta.
Spain’s conservative opposition called for their return. However, international agreements and a Spanish court ruling prohibit collective deportations and require individual assessments of cases.
Unaccompanied minors are entitled to special protection. It is believed that around 1,500 children and adolescents are among the migrants, and 500 of them are considered particularly vulnerable, mostly girls, who are planned to be transferred to mainland Spain.
The left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is facing growing pressure over the crisis, while the opposition accuses him of inaction and abandoning the residents of Ceuta.
The country’s government has also provided contradictory accounts of whether the authorities were warned about the mass arrival.
Spain’s Defense Minister Margarita Robles said that the CNI, the intelligence service under the jurisdiction of her ministry, had warned the authorities a day before the influx.
Meanwhile, the country’s Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska and other government members stressed that there had been no warnings of an influx on such a scale.
Sánchez is due to address parliament about the crisis next week.

====================================================================================================

Couples who share awe-inspiring experiences report greater relationship flourishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
11:00:13 UTC
20:00:13 KST

Experiencing feelings of awe alongside a romantic partner is linked to greater relationship satisfaction and depth. A recent study suggests that these shared moments of wonder foster a stronger sense of connection and relational growth, providing benefits beyond what individual experiences of awe offer. The research was published in The Journal of Positive Psychology.
Awe is an emotion triggered by encountering something vast that challenges a person’s existing understanding of the world. This feeling can arise from seeing a breathtaking natural landscape, listening to a moving piece of music, or experiencing a moment of profound scientific insight. Compared to simple happiness, awe tends to be a self-transcendent emotion. It reduces a person’s focus on themselves and encourages open-mindedness.
A 2022 review detailed how experiencing awe shifts attention outward, fostering social connection, a heightened sense of meaning, and prosocial behavior. Expanding on these personal effects, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 indicated that awe increases a person’s motivation to pursue their authentic self, driven by these very feelings of self-transcendence.
While prior research highlights the personal benefits of awe, studies focusing on individually induced awe in romantic contexts have yielded mixed results. The authors of the new study reasoned that awe might be most impactful for couples when it is a shared experience. Sharing emotional events is known to intensify feelings and help partners build intimacy.
“My research focuses on awe and its relationship to psychological depth,” said lead author Matteo Perini, a PhD candidate in social and cultural psychology at the Behavioural Science Institute at Radboud University. “One idea that has become central to my work is that awe may be one route into depth: by confronting us with something vast that goes beyond our current frame of reference, it may push us to revise our mental models and engage with things at a deeper level.”
“This study extends that question into romantic relationships: can awe, when experienced together, help two people connect more deeply?” Perini added.
The research involved two online studies. The first study recruited 198 adults who were in a romantic relationship. To participate, individuals had to be currently in love and report high levels of passionate love. The participants completed questionnaires measuring their general tendency to experience awe in daily life, the awe they experienced specifically with their partner, and their overall relationship satisfaction.
The scientists also measured self-other overlap, which is the degree to which a person feels their own identity merges with their partner’s identity. Participants indicated this overlap by adjusting a digital image of two circles, one representing themselves and the other representing their partner, until the circles reflected their perceived level of connection.
The authors found that shared awe positively predicted relationship satisfaction, passionate love, and self-other overlap. When the researchers looked at general awe and shared awe together in the same statistical model, only shared awe remained a positive predictor of these relationship outcomes. A person’s general tendency to experience awe on their own did not account for unique positive variance when shared awe was considered.
To expand on these initial findings, the researchers conducted a second study with 306 romantically involved adults. In this group, participants did not have to report being currently in love. The scientists measured the same concepts as the first study but added new variables to capture different layers of relationship depth. These included relationship flourishing, which reflects a meaning-oriented dimension of relationship growth, such as seeking out shared purpose rather than just feeling pleasant.
The team also measured a person’s willingness to sacrifice for their partner and relational quiet ego. Relational quiet ego describes a state of reduced self-focus combined with greater perspective-taking and inclusivity within the relationship. To ensure shared awe was distinct from simply having fun together or doing novel things, the researchers also tracked shared amusement and the frequency of awe-related activities, such as visiting unfamiliar locations or attending collective events.
The results of the second study indicated that shared awe was a strong predictor of relationship satisfaction, even when accounting for shared amusement and the frequency of awe-related activities. Shared awe also positively predicted self-other overlap, willingness to sacrifice, relational quiet ego, and relationship flourishing.
The scientists analyzed how shared awe might link to relationship satisfaction through these different psychological pathways. They found that the association was primarily explained by indirect pathways involving relationship flourishing, self-other overlap, and a willingness to sacrifice. Relationship flourishing emerged as the strongest pathway, suggesting that shared awe is closely tied to a sense of shared meaning and relational growth. Relational quiet ego did not provide unique explanatory value in this specific model.
“I was surprised by how strongly shared awe was related to relationship flourishing,” Perini told PsyPost. “In our second study, shared awe alone accounted for about half of the variance in flourishing, which was considerably stronger than I had expected.”
“Sometimes these strong correlations are observed because two scales are very similar to each other, but in this case the two measures were substantially different, one about shared experiences of awe, and the other about meaning and growth in the relationship,” he explained.
Interestingly, when shared awe was accounted for, a person’s individual tendency to experience awe became negatively associated with relationship satisfaction.
“I would treat that particular finding cautiously until it is replicated, but it raises an interesting possibility,” Perini said. “Awe may be especially beneficial for a relationship when it becomes something partners share, rather than something one person primarily experiences outside the relationship.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that awe promotes a deep sense of psychological overlap and unity with large social groups. The new study suggests a similar merging process happens on an interpersonal level between romantic partners.
“I wouldn’t translate this into ‘couples should constantly chase spectacular experiences,'” Perini noted. “But it does suggest that there may be value in making room for wonder together, whether through nature, art, music, travel, learning something new, spiritual experiences, or simply encountering something familiar in a different way.”
The data relied solely on self-reported questionnaires from one partner in the relationship. The authors recommended that future studies collect data from both partners to see how they might agree or differ in their perceptions of shared wonder.
The researchers also noted a few details about the study’s design that affect how the results can be interpreted. “The biggest caveat is that the two studies in this paper are cross-sectional and rely on self-report, so they cannot establish that shared awe causes better relationships,” Perini explained. “The reverse is also plausible: people who are already in satisfying and deeper relationships may simply be more likely to experience their lives together as awe-inspiring.”
“Since completing this work, however, we have also run a separate experiment in which dyads were exposed to awe, and we observed that participants in the awe condition were able to connect at a deeper level,” Perini said. “Those results are not part of the present paper and we are still preparing them for publication, but they provide experimental support for the broader idea that awe can affect interpersonal depth, rather than merely being correlated with it.”
Moving forward, the researchers hope to explore the exact role these shared emotional experiences play in long-term romantic bonds. Observing couples in their daily lives or testing awe-inducing activities over time could help determine whether awe fundamentally changes the level at which people reflect and connect.
“We are currently preparing another paper on what we call partner-induced awe: the experience of feeling awe toward one’s own romantic partner,” Perini said. “Our findings suggest that this may matter even in long-term relationships.”
“To me, this pushes against the idea that awe belongs only to spectacular, once-in-a-lifetime experiences, or that it is something we direct toward powerful or distant people,” he explained. “In long-term relationships, that capacity may be particularly valuable because familiarity can so easily turn into taking the other person for granted.”
The study, “United in wonder: shared awe is associated with satisfaction and depth in romantic relationships,” was authored by Matteo Perini, Lou Mier, Hein van Schie, Jasper de Groot, and Johan Karremans.

Guidance: Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:05 BST
20:00:05 KST

Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
Guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme for veterans who served under, and were impacted by, the Ban on LGBT personnel in HM Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
Documents
Details
LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Data detailing scheme progress which will be shared on a monthly basis.
Data as of 24/08/26:
Total individual applicants*: 1,696
*Applicants may have more than one case due to there being two payment types.
Total decisions made on cases: 2,145
Value of total payments made: £57,808,000
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme was recommended by the LGBT Veterans Independent Review which was published in July 2023.
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme is a payment scheme open to those who served under and were directly impacted by the Ban on LGBT personnel serving in the Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
This page provides information and guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, including eligibility and how to apply.
Types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments
There are two types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments:
1. LGBT Dismissed or Discharged Payment. This payment is for those who were dismissed or administratively discharged because of the Ban, including officers who were ordered or instructed to resign or retire by their respective Service Board.
2. LGBT Impact Payment. A payment to recognise other experiences of those who served under the Ban, as outlined in the Financial Recognition Payment Types and Tariff Table. (LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme Rules, Annex B).
Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above before starting an application.
How to Apply
Online applications
The Ministry of Defence encourages all eligible applicants to submit their applications online.
An app for the scheme can be accessed on Defence Gateway from 13 December 2024.
This platform will ensure that your data and any uploaded documents are secure. The app dashboard will keep you updated about the status of your application.
The online application process has two steps:
Step 1: Register for a Defence Gateway Account so you can access the online Financial Recognition Scheme application form.
Step 2: Sign in to your Defence Gateway account and submit your Financial Recognition Scheme application form via the Financial Recognition Scheme app.
Hard copy applications
If you would prefer to submit a hard copy (paper) application form, read scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above.
Hard copy application forms can also be obtained from Veterans UK.
Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Help with applying to the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion have partnered with the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme to provide support to veterans who are applying to the scheme.
These charities can assist with completing the application form, provide guidance on writing the necessary evidence and answer any questions applicants may have.
Royal British Legion
- Email: info@britishlegion.org.uk
- Phone: 0808 802 8080
For more information on the support the Royal British Legion can offer, visit Royal British Legion - Applying for restorative measures for LGBTQIA+ Veterans.
Fighting with Pride
For more information on the support Fighting with Pride can offer, visit Fighting with Pride LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme.
Veterans Welfare Service
Additional support is also available from the Veterans Welfare Service (VWS) who provide information, guidance and support to veterans and their families, as well as supporting veterans through a network of case managers across the UK and Republic of Ireland.
To find out more, visit Veterans Welfare Service or contact the Veterans’ Helpline using the details below.
- Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
- Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
- Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Other restorative measures
For information on non-financial restorative measures visit LGBT veterans: support and next steps.

He Scraped All of Their Art for AI. Now He’s Collaborating on a Tool to Help Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Since early 2023, photographer Jingna Zhang and a small crew of volunteers have worked tirelessly to maintain an image-sharing social media and portfolio app called Cara. So far, it has attracted about 1.5 million artists. What drew them to the platform? A shared opposition to the unauthorized use of their work to train AI models and a desire to publicize their art while avoiding exploitation by Big Tech.
But while Cara filters out AI images and offers some minimal protective features, preventing scrapes themselves is nearly impossible. And just this month, beginning on August 13, Cara was subjected to three major scrapes, which spiked its server fees and alarmed creators who had migrated there from platforms like Instagram, where all content is explicitly available to Meta as training data.
The first of these incidents came to light when the individual responsible took to the subreddit r/DefendingAIArt to announce he had obtained a 12-terabyte archive of 12 million works from Cara—more or less its entire library of publicly available images. “It was a fun project,” he wrote under the handle MandarinDawnPoppy994 in his since-deleted post, saying the process cost him less than $10.
“We actually found out about it through our users tagging us,” Zhang tells WIRED, since the scraper was “gloating and looking for other people to join him to do something with the dataset on Reddit,” sparking a fierce debate across AI-related forums about the ethics of what he had done. “I just feel it's targeted and very hurtful,” she adds, noting that “laws are not caught up on” protections against such data harvests, meaning that scrapers can often justify it as technically legal. (Zhang is separately part of two ongoing class actions brought by visual artists, one against Stability AI, Midjourney, and others and the second against Google, alleging that the companies’ image generator tools were trained on their copyrighted work.)
In a surprising turn of events, however, the person who grabbed all the art off Cara would turn out to regret his stunt and agree to collaborate with Zhang on a new open-source tool to protect artists.
In the meantime, unfortunately, other scrapers continued to take advantage of Cara’s vulnerabilities and minimal resources. While a number of AI proponents objected to going after Cara, a few were apparently emboldened by MandarinDawnPoppy994 to carry out what Zhang sees as “copycat” attacks.
A second scraper pulled about 8.5 million links from Cara, as well as metadata like usernames, titles, and tags, and uploaded these to Hugging Face, the AI developer platform. After Hugging Face was bombarded with takedown requests, it responded in a statement that while it would issue a notice to the user, “CaptiveDreamer,” to remove the personal metadata, it could not do the same for the URLs, since “no copies of the artworks are hosted here,” and the links “point to the copies the artists published on Cara.” The company concluded that “further copyright reports on the same basis will not change this outcome.”
Finally, on August 22, a third scraper obtained 123,000 images from Cara, along with text posts and user bios that included personal information, sharing it all on a site called Academic Torrents. Zhang then launched a GoFundMe for legal fees, setting a goal of $120,000, explaining that the money would go toward exploring any and all strategies of defending Cara through cyber and copyright laws. As of Thursday, she has raised more than $100,000, and she says Cara is actively looking for any additional legal assistance.
Zhang is frustrated not only by the scraping but also by the confusion around what she and the Cara team can realistically do to shield artists from malicious actors, saying that some users have already deleted their portfolios and abandoned the site. “We have done the right things within limits without making it horrible to use,” Zhang says of the app’s current safeguards, including some new temporary measures like login gates—which, she adds, aren’t really a solution to an ongoing, internet-wide problem.
And Zhang worries that people blaming her for the string of attacks may not understand that Cara has almost certainly been scraped before, like any other site; it cannot guarantee complete security. “If it makes them feel better, deleting your work and leaving Cara, I support that,” Zhang says of those leaving. “But I don't want to give people the misconception that if they go somewhere else, they are safer, because they're not. Bigger platforms get scraped more, so that makes me feel worse.”
Yet Zhang, who is quick to remind WIRED that she is not a tech founder except by accident, has a newfound ally in this battle: the person who kicked off this month’s scraping frenzy. After a Cara user confronted him and eventually persuaded to delete his dataset, she got in touch to understand his motivations and confirm the deletion. “He felt very bad to see how hurt people were,” Zhang says. “So he decided to help us.”
“Heft” is a student in North America with a background in software and an interest in digital preservation and archival projects. (He requested that we refer to him only by one of his screen names due to doxing and death threats he says he received over the Cara situation.) In a conversation over Discord, Heft tells WIRED that scraping Cara was originally nothing more than a technical project and that he had no intention of making the data public.
Heft says he nevertheless “made a foolish decision to attempt to ragebait with the dataset on Reddit” and “was carried away by trolling in the comments.” He knew it would provoke artists on Cara but did not anticipate the sheer anguish in that community. He saw people “sharing how they were having panic attacks over the scrape, how they deleted their entire portfolios from the internet.” In direct conversations with artists, he gained a greater appreciation of how personal their work was to them and how much they valued their ownership of it.
“In retrospect, not only deliberately targeting Cara but presenting it the way I did in the post was cruel and thoughtless,” Heft says. “I missed the consequences that this would have beyond causing a bit of anger.”
He notes that while he was initially curious as to whether the data could be successfully used in AI training, he never believed it would, since 12 million images “is not a lot to train an image model” and “most commercial AI labs train from large-scale web scrapes” available from open-data organizations like LAION. Random users may dump troves of data on Hugging Face, says Heft, but he considers it “highly unlikely that OpenAI or Anthropic is scanning every new Hugging Face dataset to train on.”
Once shaken out of this theoretical mindset and moved to make amends, Heft joined Cara’s Discord server as a troubleshooter and has been identifying why a number of proposed fixes are unlikely to be successful. “He’s just helping us, you know, taking the time to explain” the structural weak spots that allow for scraping, Zhang says. When a certain tool or design comes up in the conversation, Heft lays out how he can “just break through in like a few minutes, literally,” she says.
Because Heft is “of the belief that no site can be made truly ‘unscrapable,’” as he puts it, he and Zhang are collaborating on a countermeasure that can make a difference after the fact.
The tool, Lantern, allows artists to create a “one-way fingerprint” for their images without storing them on the platform. It “regularly scans new publicly available AI image datasets,” Heft says, and if an artist’s work appears in one, “the artist receives a notification and a link to the dataset so they can request removal or potentially submit a takedown notice.”
Lantern is just getting off the ground, and it’s the kind of imperfect workaround inspired by a regulatory vacuum. But Zhang and Heft are aiming to give artists a little more control and a sense of awareness about how content gets hoovered up across the web, regardless of whether a website forbids this in its terms of service, as Cara does. Plus, since it’s open-source, anybody can contribute to the code.
Zhang’s biggest hope for the fallout from the scraping spree is that it might draw the attention of policymakers looking beyond questions of copyright, which is just one piece of a complicated puzzle.
“Getting attacked by AI is just going to become so, so commonplace,” she says. And most of the time, the attacker won’t say sorry—let alone try to set things right.
Update, Friday August 28 at 2 pm: This story was updated to clarify the process by which Cara’s leadership team connected with Husk after he scraped the site.

CCTV: We notice that the rescue work in the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong County is still ongoing, could you share with us the latest developments?
Lin Jian: The Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee held a meeting on August 28 to deliberate, plan and deploy work on rescue and relief efforts after a devastating mudslide hit Gyirong County, Rikaze City of Xizang Autonomous Region. General Secretary Xi Jinping chaired the meeting.
At the beginning of the meeting, Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the CPC Central Committee, President of the People’s Republic of China and Chairman of the Central Military Commission, proposed that all participants stand for a moment of silence for those who lost their lives in the disaster.
It was noted in the meeting that the mudslide in Nepal had caused heavy casualties and left many missing at the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County. In the wake of the mudslide, the CPC Central Committee gave high priority to the disaster response, and General Secretary Xi Jinping immediately made important instructions, setting out clear requirements for rescue operations and emergency response. Entrusted by General Secretary Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Premier of the State Council, travelled to the disaster-hit area to visit those affected and the rescue teams, and provide on-site instruction on rescue and emergency response efforts. Zhang Guoqing, Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Vice Premier of the State Council, also rushed to the site to oversee the operations. Under the strong leadership of the CPC Central Committee and under the instruction of the State Council working group, the Xizang Autonomous Region, the Ministry of Emergency Management and other relevant departments, as well as other professional rescue forces, including firefighting and rescue teams and China Anneng Group, acted swiftly. The People’s Liberation Army and the armed police forces responded immediately to the call and arrived at the affected region in a timely manner. Rescue and relief efforts were carried out in an intensive and orderly manner, while the resettlement of affected people and follow-up work were launched and advanced across the board.
It was underlined in the meeting that the disaster happened in a high-altitude, cold region, where valleys are steep and the climate is highly volatile. There are still many glaciers and glacial lakes in the surrounding areas, with considerable geological hazard risks, posing enormous difficulties for rescue and relief efforts. All relevant parties must uphold the principle of putting people and human life first, and ensure that all work is carried out with firm and effective measures and sound and efficient approaches. Sound rescue plans must be formulated, and all-out efforts must be made to search for and rescue missing people from China and abroad. Joint consultations among multiple departments must be strengthened, monitoring and early-warning efforts must be enhanced, close attention must be paid to the stability of the barrier lakes and surrounding mountains, and effective measures must be taken to prevent secondary disasters. On-site personnel management must be strengthened to ensure safety throughout the entire rescue operation. Proper arrangements must be made for affected people, and careful and thorough efforts must be made in providing compensation, relief and other follow-up assistance. We will provide emergency assistance to disaster-hit areas in Nepal, and carry out international rescue cooperation .
We will earnestly act on the guiding principles of the meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, and make all-out efforts for rescue operations, emergency response, and other work related to foreign countries.
Reuters: I would like to ask a follow-up question concerning the landslide in Tibet. Are you able to update us today on a breakdown of the nationalities of the casualties? And in particular, are there Indian tourists or pilgrims who have been affected on the Tibetan side?
Lin Jian: As I said yesterday, relevant information is under further verification. We have informed relevant countries’ embassies in China and will stay in contact with them.
China Daily: Results of the Cook Islands parliamentary general election show that the Cook Islands Party led by incumbent Prime Minister Mark Brown won majority seats, securing another term for Mr. Brown. What is China’s comment and expectation for its relations with the Cook Islands?
Lin Jian: China congratulates Prime Minister Mark Brown on winning another term. China highly values its relations with the Cook Islands, and stands ready to work with the new government to further deepen political mutual trust, expand practical cooperation in various fields, and strive for greater progress of the comprehensive strategic partnership featuring mutual respect and common development for the benefit of both peoples.
The Paper: It is reported that, a civic group in Japan held an exhibition in Yokohama City on Japanese army’s wartime poison gas use. The exhibition aims to expose Japanese military’s wartime production and use of poison gas and its waging of gas warfare against China and Southeast Asian countries during WWII. According to the exhibition, after Japan’s defeat, some chemical weapons were left behind in China, continuing to cause harm to local people. Japanese visitors interviewed at the exhibition said that conducting chemical warfare was an atrocity committed by the Japanese military, and they never learned about this history at school; Japanese forces committed such evil acts, and it is a disgrace for the country. They also said that is why they want to erase it from history; This history must be made clear. We must become people capable of distinguishing right from wrong, they added. What’s your comment?
Lin Jian: During WWII, Japanese militarists developed and used chemical weapons on a large scale in China and other Asian countries, which constitutes a blatant violation of international law and has caused untold suffering on multiple countries. In China alone, there are more than 2,000 cases of Japanese forces using chemical weapons, causing more than 200,000 Chinese military and civilian casualties. After Japan’s defeat, in an attempt to cover up its crimes, a large number of chemical weapons were left behind in China, resulting in more than 2,000 casualties so far and posing a serious threat to Chinese people’s lives and the ecological environment.
Despite long-existing evidence of the crimes against humanity, Japanese right-wing forces distorted history and falsely claimed that the abandoned chemical weapons (ACWs) have gradually become “not harmful” and that “the legal statutes of limitations for liability have passed.” The Japanese government has demonstrated insufficient sincerity and given inadequate input in fulfilling its obligations of the Chemical Weapons Convention concerning the complete destruction of the ACWs, and the destruction process is seriously lagging behind schedule.
To remove the hazardous ACWs is Japanese government’s unshirkable historical responsibility and due obligation under international law. China urges the Japanese government to fulfill its responsibility under relevant convention, face up to the just call from visionary people in its own country and victim neighboring countries, comprehensively and faithfully fulfill the requirements of international convention and the MOU between the two governments, speed up the destruction process, and restore a safe living environment for the Chinese people at an early date.
AFP: On the U.S. and Iran, U.S. President Donald Trump yesterday hinted that his administration might be preparing sanctions targeting Chinese institutions over the links to Iran. This is part of U.S. efforts to isolate Iran. What is your response to Donald Trump?
Lin Jian: On the Iran situation, we always believe that dialogue and negotiation is the only viable way out. China opposes illicit unilateral sanctions. This position is consistent and clear.
The Hindu: Two questions on the mudslides. First, has there been any official determination on what actually caused this tragedy? And secondly, there were reports this morning that all 555 stranded tourists had been evacuated. I was just wondering if you had any information on whether there were tourists from India who have been evacuated and also if there are some who are still missing?
Lin Jian: We noted that experts and official institutions of China and Nepal have made preliminary assessment on the cause of the disaster. According to their analysis, the disaster has been triggered by a collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. For more details, please refer to the information released by competent authorities.
On your second question, I have made response just now. Relevant information is under further verification. We have informed relevant countries’ embassies in China and will stay in contact with them.

Europe injects 39 bcm of gas into storage facilities for next winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:57:43 UTC
19:57:43 KST

MOSCOW, August 28. /TASS/. Net gas injection - the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes - by EU countries into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities has exceeded 39 bln cubic meters since the start of the summer season in April 2026, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Thus, Europe has so far managed to inject only 58% of the volumes needed for the coming winter into its UGS facilities.
As of August 26, European UGS facilities were 63.8% full, 17.24 percentage points below the five-year average for that date, compared with 76.5% a year earlier. This is the lowest level for this date since records began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold around 69.7 bln cubic meters of gas, 14.3 bln cubic meters less than a year earlier and the lowest level since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that gas inventories in European UGS facilities may not even reach 75% by the next heating season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas inventories. The average pace of replenishing gas inventories at EU UGS facilities in July was among the lowest since records began in 2011 and accelerated only slightly in August. At the current pace, Europe may have its storage facilities only 70-75% full by the start of the fall-winter period, which would be an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full each year between October 1 and December 1. A 10% flexibility margin is allowed in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bln cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 fall-winter period to meet the storage target.
The pace of storage filling this year has been significantly affected by Europe losing the "battle" with Asia for available supplies on the liquefied natural gas market during the Middle East conflict, higher fuel prices, and extreme heat in June and July. During such hot summer periods, demand for electricity to power cooling and air-conditioning systems rises sharply. Gas is one of the main sources of electricity generation, alongside nuclear, wind and solar power.

Majority of student rooms priced well over the legal limit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:56:56 UTC
19:56:56 KST

Majority of student rooms priced well over the legal limit
Louis Gore-Langton
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The majority of student rooms on the Netherlands’ biggest rental platform, Kamernet, are being advertised at prices well over the legal limit – an average of €239 a month, and more than €400 in Amsterdam – investigative outlet Argos has found. Local councils are not intervening and say they have no power to do so.
Argos compared rent on 2,637 ads against the maximum each room is legally allowed to charge. Six in ten rooms were priced above the legal maximum over July and August, with landlords of overpriced rooms asking an average of €239 a month more than the rules permit.
In some cities, like Amsterdam, where the average room costs nearly €1,000 a month, 97% of the rooms Argos sampled were above the cap, by an average of €421 a month. In Utrecht the figure was 72%.
Utrecht and Nijmegen issued no fines and lowered no rents last year, while Rotterdam and The Hague were the exceptions, acting far more often.
Amsterdam council reaction
 Since the Affordable Rent Act 2025 was introduced, which caps prices by a points system based on a room’s size and features, councils have been required to intervene – something the investigation found is not being done in many cities.
A spokesperson for Amsterdam council housing executive Zita Pels told DutchNews that the council cannot take legal action on advertising alone – an illegal rent must already be in force before it can do something. So students must first get into an illegally high rental contract before they can be helped.
The spokesperson also said the council “strongly opposes” the way people “shamelessly” exploit the housing crisis in Amsterdam, but that it unfortunately cannot do more about the advertising problem.
They also said the council itself advertises on rental platforms, attends student events, and visits tenants at home, because many people are reluctant to report overcharging for fear of losing their room.
In March, Amsterdam council also imposed a €45,000 penalty on the manager of a student complex in Amsterdam’s Zuidoost district for a range of violations, the council highlighted, including excessive rents. The landlord can still object.
There is a tenant advice foundation called !Woon that the council subsidises. Its 2025 report records more than 19,000 contacts about rent or service charges and 575 reports of serious landlord misconduct, and lists cases it has won, including 21 rulings against a single landlord, one of which cut a rent from €1,076 to €280.
The council’s own enforcement report to councillors, published in May, shows direct action on rents is a small part of the picture. Of 726 complaints under the new rental laws in 2025, 96 concerned rent levels; 167 were passed to !Woon and 102 fell outside the rules. The bulk of the council’s 1,836 enforcement outcomes last year involved empty or misused homes, not overcharging.
