Inside Meta’s Push to Put Robots to Work in Data Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:56:22 UTC
19:56:22 KST

Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.
Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”
At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.
Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II, and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.
But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don't have a chance to do this,” he said.
Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry they sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.
Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.
“More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things,” says Paul Golding, who oversees so-called physical intelligence at the chipmaker Analog Devices.
The growing use of robots has received little attention from the activists driving a powerful nationwide movement against data centers. Tech companies often tout jobs for humans as an upside to the developments that can be used to justify tax breaks for them. In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates what is now its largest data center campus, which employs hundreds of workers. The company opened the facility in 2014 and has several years left of a property tax break that allows it to save tens of millions of dollars annually, which the city has viewed as a worthwhile trade-off for having its cachet upped by having Meta jobs.
In Altoona, Meta worker group chats have taken on a demoralized tone, “saying we’re all going to be gone in a few years anyway because of the robots,” a person familiar with the discussions says. Even if adoption of robots proves slower than anticipated, some worry the quality of jobs available is trending downward. Two of the workers say that Meta is developing AI software and other technologies that they believe will allow it to hire lower-skilled—and thus, lower-paid—workers and centralize some roles in areas such as Denver, Colorado, that are more financially advantageous to the company.
“They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting,” one Meta data center worker says. “They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.”
Meta contends its need for skilled workers remains robust. This year, the company launched a long-term program to train thousands of people annually from any background in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing work at no cost to them. Meta is even guaranteeing employment in states such as Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas for those who complete the training. It also partnered with building trade unions to fund apprenticeship programs.
But as communities rethink data center tax breaks and weigh putting new rules on the industry, the prospect of robots replacing at least some jobs may need to become a bigger concern. Altoona Mayor Dean O'Connor tells WIRED he hasn’t given much thought to robots taking jobs at Meta’s data center, though he frames automation as inevitable. “We will deal with it as it comes,” he says.
Tripping Cables
In a 2023 YouTube video, Meta touted that it was using a self-driving tugger robot to transport heavy server racks within its data centers as well as a wheeled, barcode-reading robot developed in-house to track inventory. The next year, Microsoft and Google unveiled separate investments in robots for their data center operations, and Amazon last year discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
Pursuing robotics for “economically valuable tasks,” like “replacing a faulty server rack,” is “absolutely something we're looking into at Microsoft,” Ashley Llorens, a managing director for the company’s research accelerator, tells WIRED.
Meta’s tugger and inventory robots are now operating in a number of the company’s data centers, including in Iowa and Virginia, according to the people familiar with the projects. They say the robots generally work well, though there are limitations.
The inventory bot is now also being used for failure inspections, but it can’t differentiate between green and red indicator lights on equipment because its camera only detects grayscale, meaning human checks are still required to assess some breakdowns. The device also struggles with corners and traversing the cables that are often in the path of its wheels. Because there aren't that many of them, the robots need to be moved between buildings, which requires a door-opening human who maneuvers the robot with a remote control.
Two sources also describe the inventory bot as too slow. One says Meta previously explored using drones as a faster alternative, but ultimately didn’t pursue the idea.
Inside the Testbed
The Altoona data center campus is often where Meta prototypes new technologies. “What they do here in Altoona, they take to their other sites and put that in place there,” says O’Connor.
Since last June, Meta has been trying out a pair of dual-armed Watney robots for some cabling work at one of its Altoona buildings, according to one of the people familiar with the company’s efforts. The robots are supervised by humans and can’t work as fast as people yet, but they show promise.
After Watney launched in 2023, it put out a demo of a laundry-folding robot that it claimed could also handle janitorial work inside businesses. The San Francisco startup quietly pivoted to data center robots early last year, according to archived copies of its website.
Meta is testing additional robots in New Albany, Ohio, at the company’s newest data center campus known as Prometheus. Four-wheel robots “with a scissor-lift-style riser and a six-axis arm on top” made by the automation giant ABB are being used there to reseat parts and, eventually, they may take on other tasks with diminishing human oversight, a person familiar with the product says.
But the idea that robots will prevail over humans isn't guaranteed. “There's been a lot of pilots and demos, but no provable working solution,” says Helen Oleynikova, CEO of Exclaim Robotics, which is developing prototypes to replace broken parts and reset cables in data centers.
At Meta’s data centers, some workers have complained about the amount of downtime the robots need to recharge their batteries, according to the people familiar with the matter. Meta has also acknowledged internally that robots aren’t equipped for certain tasks, such as the intense cabling work required to run an Nvidia GB300 supercomputer. “Things have been designed for human hands forever to make everything a five-minute repair,” says one former Meta employee. “Redesigning everything will take time.” But the robots are getting prepared.
Will Knight contributed to this story.

He had prevented Tutsis from escaping and threw a grenade into the crowd
A Dutch court on Friday handed a life sentence to a 66-year-old man for his role in the massacre of 3,000 Tutsis during the 1994 Rwanda genocide.
During the violence that took place in April 1994, terrified victims sought refuge in a football stadium in Mbazi, southern Rwanda, only to be systematically slaughtered.

“Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families,” the court said.
His actions were committed with “genocidal intent”, said the presiding judge handing down the verdict.

NATO Could Face “Punch After Punch” in Potential Russian Missile Attack Amid Patriot Shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:51:00 UTC
19:51:00 KST

- Category
- World
NATO Could Face “Punch After Punch” in Potential Russian Missile Attack Amid Patriot Shortage
American Patriot missile stockpiles stationed across Europe have fallen to critically low levels as a direct result of ongoing military engagements with Iran, according to statements from government officials.
The reduction in available interceptors raises major operational concerns for regional defense networks that rely heavily on these surface-to-air systems for airspace protection, as reported by AP on August 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Military stockpiles face mounting pressure as defense capabilities are diverted to manage active security threats linked to Iran. The depletion of these stockpiles highlights growing strain on international supply chains and existing defense reserves held by allied forces throughout the European continent.
The vulnerability created by these shortages extends directly to potential allied operations.
"In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, NATO could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth,” the US defense official said.
When Russian forces fire ballistic missiles at Ukraine, air defense systems have only minutes or seconds to detect and intercept the incoming targets. The limited response time leaves cities increasingly exposed to high-speed missiles, which dive steeply toward their targets at several times the speed of sound.
Ukrainian officials state that the US-made Patriot defense system is the sole weapon in their inventory capable of stopping these specific threats, such as Iskander-M, S-400, and Zircon missiles. However, Ukraine operates too few batteries and interceptors to provide comprehensive coverage.
Unlike cruise missiles that navigate like pilotless aircraft, ballistic missiles are launched as rockets before making rapid descents. This trajectory sharply reduces the window available for defenders to track and neutralize warheads.
When a Patriot battery is absent, out of position, or depleted of ammunition, alternative Ukrainian defenses cannot effectively substitute for it. Furthermore, tactical combinations of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, drones, and decoys force defenders to track multiple incoming objects and strictly ration their remaining interceptor stocks.
Global supply shortages exacerbate the defense deficit inside Ukraine. Recent military operations involving US and Israeli forces against Iran have consumed high volumes of Patriot and THAAD interceptors. This has reduced the overall US Patriot inventory by an estimated 65% from prewar levels.
While production capacity is expanding—with Lockheed Martin aiming for 2,000 PAC-3 MSE interceptors annually by 2030 and a new production facility opening in Germany—current output cannot immediately fulfill global demand.
Consequently, Ukrainian forces are seeking long-range capabilities to target Russian missile launchers and infrastructure on the ground before weapons can be launched.
European nations struggled to locate available Patriot interceptor missiles to support Ukraine ahead of anticipated winter strikes by Russian forces. Kyiv sought hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors as international supplies became severely constrained.
In July 2026, Ukrainian air defense forces shot down only 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, while another 40 failed to reach their targets. Germany had previously provided three complete Patriot systems and arranged two additional units, the Netherlands assembled one system featuring five launchers.
Poland transferred five interceptor missiles, and Ukraine requested up to 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Greece. Allied efforts subsequently gathered slightly more than 20 missiles after Germany offered five extra rounds if other partners supplied 20.

Tigers, jaguars, bison found in raid on fuel smugglers near U.S. border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:49:45 UTC
19:49:45 KST

Tigers, jaguars, bison among 135 exotic and endangered animals found in raid on fuel smugglers near U.S. border
Mexican authorities said Thursday that they had rescued Bengal tigers, mandrills, hyenas and even a camel during raids on a fuel smuggling ring in the northeastern state of Tamaulipas, on the U.S. border.
The 135 animals found at a ranch also included lions, buffalo, sulcata tortoises, spider monkeys, jaguars, an American bison and a green macaw.
Thirty-five of the animals, including the green macaw and sulcata tortoise, are classified as endangered species.
Mexican authorities regularly rescue exotic animals from properties owned by wealthy drug traffickers. Some Mexican drug cartels are known to house exotic cats as symbols of power and, occasionally, to dispose of their enemies. According to a 2023 U.S. indictment, some victims of a Sinaloa cartel faction were "fed dead or alive to tigers."
On this occasion, however, the military found them during an operation targeting fuel smugglers.
Smuggling gasoline and diesel from the United States into Mexico and reselling it tax-free is a huge money-maker for organized crime gangs, including drug cartels.
During these latest raids on five properties, the military seized 18,000 gallons of diesel, fuel tanks, pumps, firearms, and tools.
One person was arrested.
Mexican authorities cracked down on fuel smuggling in 2025, when high-ranking navy officers and officials were implicated in the illegal trade.
Some 10 billion liters of black market fuel were seized at that time in Tamaulipas.
The attorney general's office on Thursday formally charged Fernando Farias, a high-ranking officer who was expelled last week from Argentina, with fuel smuggling.
A former governor of Tamaulipas, Ernesto Ruffo, was also recently arrested on charges of fuel theft.
Fuel smuggling a growing problem
Fuel theft — more commonly known as huachicol in Mexico — has risen to the second most profitable revenue stream for Mexican cartels behind drug trafficking, according to the U.S. Treasury.
U.S. officials allege that some cartel members steal fuel and crude oil from Pemex by bribing insiders, tapping pipelines, siphoning refineries, hijacking tanker trucks, and intimidating employees.
The stolen fuel is then sold across Mexico, the United States and Central America, while crude oil is smuggled north via complicit brokers — frequently disguised as "waste oil" to evade taxes and environmental scrutiny, the U.S. Treasury discovered.
Once inside the United States, the oil is then funneled to unscrupulous importers along the southwest border, sold at deep discounts on U.S. and global markets with proceeds quietly funneled back to the cartels.
U.S. authorities have even accused the Jalisco New Generation cartel of operating its own service stations.
The United States has been cracking down. In June, the U.S. Treasury imposed sanctions on two Mexican men and nine companies involved in transportation, financial services and real estate, accused of being tied to a cartel-linked fuel theft ring.
In December, the Treasury Department imposed sanctions on a violent Mexican fuel-theft cartel and its imprisoned leader, nicknamed "The Sledgehammer."

====================================================================================================

GTA has always raised anxieties over video games and violence—here’s what the science actually says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:46:00 UTC
19:46:00 KST

On October 22, 2001, millions of gamers got an entirely new way to wreak havoc: Grand Theft Auto III. In the landmark video game, players could hit pedestrians with cars, shoot rockets at police, and rob and steal to their hearts content. And that’s just scratching the surface of all the audacious crimes one could commit in the game’s explorable world, Liberty City.
The backlash was tremendous. Lawsuits accused the makers of the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) franchise, Rockstar Games and Take-Two Interactive, of inspiring real-life murders and assaults. Parents and pundits fretted that the GTA series and other hyperviolent franchises such as Doom and Call of Duty promoted actual violence—a worry that, at the time, was backed by numerous high-profile scientific papers.
The furor wasn't enough to kill GTA. And now, almost a quarter-century later, gamers are anxiously awaiting the next installment in the franchise, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6). Yet even though it has a new extended trailer out on Netflix that shows all sorts of fresh crime scenes, the game is generating far less anxiety today than its predecessors did before.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The lack of moral panic is in some ways proportional to the actual danger. Yet what’s inescapable is that numerous scientific studies published in the past 30 years do suggest a link between violent video games and aggression. But that doesn’t mean the connection should be overstated—and evidence suggesting the opposite also can’t be ignored.
“Exposure to violent media, including violent video games, is not the only risk factor, and it’s not even the most important risk factor,” says Brad Bushman, a professor at the Ohio State University, who previously served on former president Barack Obama’s committee on gun violence.
“Probably the most important risk factor is provocation. If you provoke somebody, they’re very likely to respond in an aggressive way, whereas if they play a violent video game, maybe they will, maybe they won’t,” he says. People’s socioeconomic status, IQ score, alcohol consumption, and level of narcissistic traits and even hot temperatures can all influence violent behavior, he adds.
Chris Ferguson, a psychology professor at Stetson University, has conducted research finding that while video games can stress players out, that doesn’t necessarily lead to aggressive behavior.
Anyone who has ever played an online shooter knows the experience can be frustrating. Ferguson says playing games can affect emotional states, but the effects don’t tend to last.
“To the extent that people may have an emotional reaction to a game, it doesn’t usually last that long because it doesn’t matter,” he says.
Still, Bushman argues, the evidence suggests that these supposedly fleeting frustrations do matter. Research needs to account for how aggressive a person is to begin with to get a better picture of how a video game might influence them, he says.
“People who play violent video games become numb to violent images, their brain activity is reduced, and they think aggression is no big deal,” Bushman says. “If aggression is no big deal, then they don’t have such a problem aggressing against other people.”
If video games do cause violence, it’s not showing up in crime statistics. Violent crime in the U.S. has generally been in decline for decades: in 2025 the estimated murder rate was 4.1 per 100,000 people, the same as in 1955, according to FBI statistics. And the overall violent crime rate fell by 49 percent between 1993 and 2022, according to the Pew Research Center. That’s the same time period that saw a dramatic rise in the popularity of video games, culminating in 85 percent of teens saying they played video games in a poll conducted by Pew in late 2023. More than half of the poll’s respondents said that at least some of the games they played contained violent imagery.
“Why do we have this historical moment where we’re the most violent-video-game-playing we’ve ever been and the least violent-crime-committing we’ve been?” Ferguson muses.
Bushman, however, thinks video games may still be propping crime rates up. “I would argue that violent crime rates would be even lower” without violent video games, he says.
At the height of the panic over GTA 3 and other violent games, the fear was that the games would create a generation of children intent on re-creating what they had done in the games in real life. In the early 1990s Congress held hearings following the success of the ultragory Mortal Kombat, leading to a ratings system that, while not legally binding, is designed to limit children under age 17’s access to games with mature themes.
Those concerns have faded in the face of the psychological effects of cell phones and social media on adolescents, Ferguson notes. Researchers have also shifted their focus, with some looking at whether video games might have positive psychological and emotional effects. A growing body of literature shows that, under the right conditions, gaming may encourage prosocial behavior, although the connection to well-being remains unclear.
Regardless, video games can be “brilliant teachers,” Bushman says. But they’re also tools that, like many others, can be misused. “Video games are like an axe,” he says. “You can use an axe to cut down wood for your family to build a fire when it’s cold, or you can use an axe to kill someone.”

US judge repeats block on Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail

US judge repeats block on Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail
Judge blocks Trump’s mail voting rules for a second time, just days before ballots go out for the midterms.
A United States federal judge has for a second time blocked the Trump administration’s overhaul of election rules aimed at limiting voting by mail.
District Judge Indira Talwani late on Thursday blocked the US Postal Service’s new ballot rules for 14 days, hours after the agency said they had taken effect.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How the shape of a map can determine the US midterm elections
- list 2 of 3Trump tells Al Jazeera ‘not in a hurry’ for Iran to return to talks
- list 3 of 3US Postal Service says mail-in ballot restrictions now in effect
The ruling is part of an ongoing battle prompted by President Donald Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail, which is heating up as the US heads towards midterm elections in November that will decide control of Congress and the Senate.
Nearly a third of American voters cast votes by mail. The first ballots for the midterms are due to be sent out in about a week.
The new rules require states to submit approved voter lists and follow new ballot formatting before USPS can deliver voting slips. The restrictions were enacted on Thursday after the Supreme Court cleared the way for them.
Talwani wrote in a statement late on Thursday that states “have neither time nor funds” to redesign ballots, update election systems or train officials on the new USPS portal before the upcoming election.
The fight traces back to March, when Trump ordered the Postal Service to withhold ballots unless states supplied approved voter lists and new formatting rules.
Voting rights groups and democratic officials sued, arguing only states and Congress, not the president, can set election rules. Talwani agreed, blocking the rules over the summer.
On Monday, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority threw out that earlier ruling on a technicality, saying that the legal challenge on which it was based was filed too early.
Democratic officials and voting rights groups quickly refiled their challenge once the rules became official, allowing Talwani to block them once more in a late-night order.
Separately, attorneys general from 24 states filed a new lawsuit this week making the same core argument: that only the Senate and Congress, not the president, can have constitutional authority to set election rules.
A hearing on the refiled case is scheduled for September 3, just as ballots are set to go out. That timeline means whatever Talwani or a higher court decides next could take effect as voting begins, or after it is already under way.

The Endangered Species Act is getting weaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:45:26 UTC
19:45:26 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
What does it mean to cause “harm”? If someone walked into your house and slapped you across the face, I think just about anyone would agree that they had meant you harm—and caused it! But what if someone decided to say build their own house right where yours was, and they barrelled right in with a wrecking ball while you were eating your cornflakes? Most people would, I think, still consider that to be—harmful. Now, for humans, of course, we’re protected from both of these scenarios by numerous laws. But when it comes to other species? Not necessarily. And species at risk of extinction in the U.S. could have a lot more wrecking balls coming their way in the near future.
Since 1973 the Endangered Species Act, or ESA, has helped protect species at risk of extinction throughout the United States. Last month the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced some troubling changes to the way the ESA will be implemented, including a new definition of what it means to “harm” an endangered species.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Our guest today is Lynne Barre, who formerly worked as a marine biologist for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. She’s here to talk us through some of the revisions to the Endangered Species Act and what they could mean.
Feltman: Thank you so much for coming on to talk with us today.
Lynne Barre: Sure.
Feltman: So, uh, let’s start by talking a bit about the original goals of the Endangered Species Act and how the work you did contributed to that in your 25 years at NOAA.
Barre: Yeah, so the Endangered Species Act is there to protect endangered and threatened species and the habitats that they rely on. So it’s really about recovery of those species.
Feltman: How long has this act been in place, and has it been being enforced in the way that most of us are, are used to?
Barre: The Endangered Species Act was put in place in 1973, so it’s been in place for decades to protect those endangered and threatened species.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, on the one hand, I think many of our listeners would think that protecting endangered species is a universal goal. But what kind of pushback has the Endangered Species Act gotten, you know, over those decades?
Barre: Well, there have been so many lawsuits and court cases and regulations to help us implement the Endangered Species Act that, you know, create new definitions for terms in the Act, cases that set precedent that are then followed for subsequent years after those cases. So it’s, it—there’s been some evolution over time, and there definitely have been challenges in support of stronger protections under the ESA but also for, you know, less stringent restrictions under the ESA. Both have happened over the years.
Feltman: And are there any, you know, major success stories connected to the ESA that come to mind?
Barre: Well, there definitely have been species that have recovered. A species near and dear to my heart are gray whales. They were removed from the Endangered Species Act after recovering. And the Endangered Species Act was in place to protect them for many years. And there’s also other laws, like the Marine Mammal Protection Act that protects whales. So they’ve been fortunate to have other protection even without the ESA. But now, you know, there are definitely more recent challenges to the ESA starting in this new administration.
Feltman: Right. So the Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA announced a few major changes to the way the Endangered Species Act will be enforced, one pertaining to threatened animals. Can you tell us a little bit about that threatened designation and what’s changing here?
Barre: Yeah. There used to be an automatic protection that went into place for species listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, and that protection has been removed. So now new rules have to be promulgated to put those protections in place for threatened species.
Feltman: Mm. So it’s gonna be on more of a case-by-case basis, which I imagine will get pretty complicated and might prolong a lack of protections for these animals that are at great risk of becoming endangered?
Barre: Yeah. When there’s a, kind of, affirmative action that has to be taken to put those protections in place, you need people to do that work, and it needs to be a priority for the agency. And I’m concerned that, right now, there have been so many people who’ve left Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA that perhaps there aren’t the people to do that work, and also it’s not prioritized. Endangered species listings, protections, critical habitat designations—some of these important things under the Endangered Species Act that give those endangered and threatened species extra care and conservation effort are not a priority right now. And that’s one of the reasons I left NOAA, seeing those changes that recovery and conservation and protection of listed endangered and threatened species was no longer a priority.
Feltman: And another change was the very definition of the word “harm” when it comes to endangered species. So it refers to, if I’m understanding correctly, directly harming or killing an organism, as opposed to doing things to its habitat. So practically speaking, how do you expect this change to play out?
Barre: It’s complicated and legal, and it’s really the removal of something that was intended to provide clarity. And that was a definition of the term “harm” under the Endangered Species Act. So the recent rule rescinded the regulation with that definition. And so I expect that, again, it’s gonna be case by case in the courts of how that term is interpreted.
The rule really references a dissent opinion by [the late Supreme Court] Justice [Antonin] Scalia from a case back in the ’90s that had to do with timber harvest affecting habitat of Northern Spotted Owls. The Court upheld the definition of “harm” that included habitat modification. But Scalia’s dissent described “harm” as having to be that intentional, directed at the animals, affirmative. And so they are relying heavily on that dissent opinion and that interpretation of “harm” not including habitat as being the, sort of, best meaning of the word “harm.” And so without a definition, there’s a lot of interpretation; they have some guidance from Scalia’s dissent, but also, it’ll again be kind of a case by case and probably handled through the courts.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, I don’t know. If somebody knocked my house down, I certainly wouldn’t think that they had made my life any easier, so.
Barre: Yeah, there’s another important court case at play here. It’s known as the Chevron decision. And that was a case where the agencies, the agencies like NOAA and Fish and Wildlife Service that have experts and scientific expertise, they were given deference in some of that interpretation of terms that might be considered ambiguous, like “harm” and whether that includes habitat. And so that’s been overturned. And so now, again, the agencies don’t have that deference, and it’ll be up to courts to make those important decisions about what is the single best meaning of a word like “harm.”
Feltman: Yeah. Well, speaking of that, you know, pulling away from relying on the expertise of these agencies, could you tell us why you retired early and, and what that decision meant for you?
Barre: Yeah. I saw pretty early on in this administration that endangered species recovery—which I’d been working on for 25 years, and that includes habitat protection and also marine mammal conservation; those were all part of my job—that those things were no longer prioritized. And the work that, in general, that federal employees were doing to protect our environment was not valued. And so I saw a lot of changes and a lot of dismantling of programs, funding for these things, fewer people to do the work. People were fired that were on probationary status, things like that.
And a lot of partnerships were no longer a priority. Things that we did working with Canada on endangered species protection or even partnerships with industry, we were no longer able to do that work. Things like education and outreach of the public, which we know is so important for conservation, was not a part of our portfolios anymore and labeled as DEI work. And even internship programs that I spent years really helping develop to get our workforce engaged and energized with new people and new perspectives, all just dismantled and canceled. And it was really a toxic environment to work in.
And knowing that the agency was not gonna be supporting a lot of the work I had done—I really feel fortunate that I had the number of years and was of an age and financial means that I was able to take an early retirement. But it didn’t feel good, and I wasn’t ready to stop doing this important work.
Feltman: Yeah, and what was your reaction when you heard about these changes, you know, the “harm” rule in particular?
Barre: Yeah, I’m concerned about how habitat, which is so essential for recovery of endangered species, is probably in jeopardy now from economic drivers like development or—you know, I worked on killer whale recovery. We have an endangered group of orcas in the Pacific Northwest, the southern residents, and habitat’s really essential. And fortunately for these orcas and for other species, there is critical habitat, which identifies important aspects of habitat and protects them.
But not every endangered or threatened species has critical habitat. It’s just, again, like probably staff resources to get those designations in place, and I know Fish and Wildlife Service has backlogs of species to be listed and recovery plans to be written and critical habitat to be designated. So without some of that extra protection under the ESA, this removal of a definition of “harm” that includes habitat modifications could really put many species at risk.
Feltman: Well and, you know, I think many of us in the U.S. grew up with the conviction, you know, all around us that protecting endangered animals is an inherent good. But of course, it’s not just for the sake of our own consciences that it’s important to protect animals and their habitats. So, you know, maybe for listeners that haven’t given that a thought recently, could you share a little bit about, you know, what the potential impacts are of this on people and the economy?
Barre: The concerns about how this change in the ESA regulations could affect habitat protection for species does definitely tie into human health and the economy. I looked at some of the letters that people wrote, comment letters, including tribes here in the Pacific Northwest that were really concerned about how this could affect salmon habitat work that’s essential for their ability to exercise their treaty rights, their cultural practices around salmon—so essential. And yet, this could undo some of that. And also, there’s been a point made that there’s a restoration economy built around protecting and conserving and restoring these natural habitats for species but also for people. And so there’s concerns that this rule may undo some of that good work that’s ongoing, that’s been funded, that’s been supported. It includes jobs; it includes food safety; it includes industries and commercial businesses that rely on a healthy environment and ecosystem. So there’s a lot of potential impacts, not just for these listed species but for other species that aren’t listed that use the same habitats and for humans as well.
Feltman: I think that’s such an important point because a lot of the times it, it feels like, in these conversations, the focus is on what we can’t build because we’re protecting these, these organisms. But to your point, there are projects and jobs and endeavors that exist and, you know, support people and the economy as part of that, that conservation effort. I think one thing I would love to ask you before you go is: What can listeners do if they want to help protect threatened and endangered species, and they’re troubled by the news that they’re hearing about the ESA?
Barre: There’s a lot people can do who may be also concerned about
these changes to the regulations under the Endangered Species Act. Certainly people can go out and get their hands dirty and do habitat restoration or conservation, you know, on their own or with local nonprofit groups or
tribes or states or whoever is doing that work. It needs to continue, and I hope it will continue with that direct public support. But this is a lot of regulatory language and legal lawsuits. There are lawsuits by nonprofit groups and tribes that are fighting against this removal of the definition of “harm” including habitat—and so supporting one of those nonprofit groups. Or, uh, how you vote is something that empowers people. Make sure your elected officials are concerned about these changes and the environment. There’s actually a bipartisan [bill] in the House challenging this rule, and basically it’s a short one paragraph. There’s a lot people can do to stop contamination from going into our waters. You know, we have an issue with sound and some of our animals that are susceptible to that. The Easiest Ways to Share Anything Between Android and iOS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Whisper it quietly, but certain bricks in Apple’s walled garden might be getting taken away.
Thanks to some recent upgrades added to Android by Google, it's now easier than ever to share files between an iPhone and an Android phone, without installing any new apps (though that's still an option too).
So if you need to send a photo, contact card, web link, or anything else, these are the options you have available. As is often the case with Android, they may vary depending on the make and model of your handset, though you should find at least one of these methods works for you.
Share Files via AirDrop
This is the big one: Google recently figured out a way to add support for AirDrop—Apple's previously closed-off, device-to-device sharing protocol—to newer Pixel phones. It doesn't appear that Apple was involved in the process, but the company hasn't gotten in Google's way since, and the functionality has been rolled out to other phones (including the recent Pixel and Galaxy handsets).
Some prep work may be required. On Samsung phones, you need to open Settings, then choose Connected devices > Quick Share and enable Share with Apple devices—though there's no such toggle switch on Pixel phones—it'll just work right away. It needs enabling on iOS too: From Settings, tap General > AirDrop, and Everyone for 10 Minutes.
With that done, whenever you tap the share button anywhere in any Android app, you can choose Quick Share from the resulting pop-up panel to communicate with a nearby iPhone. The iPhone should show up in the available devices, so select it to start the transfer—which will still need to be accepted on the iPhone.
It will work the other way too, starting from AirDrop on an iPhone, as long as the Android device is set up to receive from any other device. From Settings, tap either Connection preferences (Google Pixel phones) or Connected devices (Samsung Galaxy phones), then select Quick Share > Who can share with you.
Share Files via QR code
Google hasn't stopped with AirDrop on Android. It has also recently pushed out a QR-code-based option for sharing from Android to iOS. It's a bit more clunky than AirDrop, but it'll work no matter what kind of Android phone you've got.
Again, you need to go through Quick Share, which pops up as an option whenever you try to share something in Android—no matter what the app or item you want to share. You won't see an iPhone appear if you don't have the AirDrop functionality, but you should see a Use QR code option on the right, under Share with iPhone and other devices, which after a few moments shrinks down to just a QR code symbol.
Tap this option to get your QR code on screen. On the iPhone side, AirDrop still needs enabling (via General > AirDrop > Everyone for 10 Minutes), and the iPhone camera can then be pointed at the QR code to get to a special Google web address. That will lead to a simple download page for the shared file or content.
Google says transferred files remain in the cloud for 24 hours, after which they'll be securely deleted. They don't count toward your Google Drive storage quota, and you can share up to 1,000 files in a single session, to a maximum of 20 iPhones (or iPads or Macs, which also support AirDrop).
Other Sharing Options
You do have a multitude of sharing options to pick from if you want to get something from Android to iOS. You can simply attach a file to an email, for example, or use a messaging app that supports both Android and iOS, like WhatsApp. Bear in mind that certain messaging apps compress photos and videos before sending, though many apps let you turn compression off in the settings.
Cloud storage apps are another helpful method you can use, though as with messaging apps you want something that works well on any platform (so not iCloud). Google Drive and Dropbox are two apps that are simple to use, run well on Android and iOS, and have smart sharing features built in, for example.
For iPhone-to-iPhone and Android-to-Android connections and file transfers, everything is much more straightforward: You can just use AirDrop or Quick Share through the relevant share panels, and the receiving device should pop up (assuming you've set the right availability options, as described above).
One option you can't use is Bluetooth: Apple locks down Bluetooth on the iPhone to some extent, so while you can connect accessories like wireless earbuds, you can't use it for wireless file transfers.

Xi, Modi, Putin to meet in Kyrgyzstan: What to watch at SCO summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:44:58 UTC
19:44:58 KST

Some of Eurasia's most powerful leaders will gather next week in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, bringing together a complicated mix of improving ties, longstanding rivalries and regional conflicts.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin will be among those attending the Sept. 1 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Heads of State summit, which marks the group's 25th anniversary.
The gathering comes amid a tentative thaw in China-India relations following years of border tensions, as India and Pakistan navigate the aftermath of their brief conflict last year.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will also attend as Tehran faces growing US economic pressure, while conflicts and instability stretching from the Middle East and Ukraine to Afghanistan are expected to feature in discussions.
The meeting also comes as SCO members seek to capitalize on shifting global economic and geopolitical dynamics by strengthening trade, transport links and economic cooperation across Eurasia.
The SCO traces its roots to the "Shanghai Five," established in 1996 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to reduce military tensions and address border disputes following the breakup of the Soviet Union.
Uzbekistan joined when the SCO was formally established in 2001, and the grouping remained largely centered on China, Russia and Central Asia for much of its early history.
Its international profile grew significantly with its expansion. India and Pakistan became full members in 2017, followed by Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.
For Iran, membership marked a major diplomatic opening after years of geopolitical isolation, while Belarus's accession reflected its broader pivot toward non-Western partners
Today, the organization has 10 members: Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus.
Turkmenistan is the only Central Asian country outside the SCO, reflecting its longstanding policy of permanent neutrality. Afghanistan and Mongolia have observer status, while dialogue partners include Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Saudi Arabia.
Together, SCO members have a population of around 3.4 billion, span a vast stretch of Eurasia and account for around 25% of global GDP.
Unlike NATO, the SCO is not a military alliance, nor is it an economic union like the EU. Instead, its consensus-based structure provides a forum for security cooperation, economic ties and diplomacy among countries that do not necessarily share the same interests.
One of the most closely watched encounters will be between Xi and Modi as Asia's two most populous countries seek to build on a tentative thaw after years of tensions over their disputed Himalayan border.
Senior Chinese and Indian officials held another round of boundary talks in Beijing on Aug. 25, agreeing to continue efforts toward a settlement and maintain stability along the frontier.
Relations deteriorated sharply after deadly border clashes in 2020, making the leaders' interactions in Bishkek an opportunity to gauge how far the recent improvement in ties has progressed.
The interaction between Xi and Putin will also offer a window into the increasingly close relationship between China and Russia and how the two powers coordinate within the SCO.
The gathering will also put the leaders of India and Pakistan in the same room just more than a year after the two nuclear-armed neighbors fought a brief conflict.
Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif is slated to attend, bringing him together with Modi as tensions persist between the two countries, primarily over Kashmir.
Another leader to watch will be Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is scheduled to meet Putin on the sidelines of the summit, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
His visit comes as the US threatens increased secondary sanctions against countries and entities that continue doing business with Tehran.
According to the SCO Secretariat, leaders are expected to discuss major regional and international security challenges, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, the situation in Afghanistan and India's relations with China and Pakistan.
The organization has taken a more visible collective position in 2026 on Iran and the broader Middle East, including the Palestinian issue, calling for restraint, dialogue and political and diplomatic solutions.
At a July meeting, SCO foreign ministers expressed particular concern over developments in the Middle East and around Iran, reiterating that international conflicts should be settled through political and diplomatic means in accordance with international law and the UN Charter.
Afghanistan remains a longstanding regional priority, particularly because of concerns over terrorism, drug trafficking and cross-border security.
Ukraine is also expected to feature in discussions, though there has been no indication that the war will be a separate focus of the summit.
Relations between India and China and India and Pakistan are also expected to be discussed, bringing some of the SCO's own internal tensions onto the agenda.
Counterterrorism remains a core area of cooperation through the SCO's Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure, based in Tashkent. The summit is expected to approve its plans for the coming year, including possible joint exercises.
Economic connectivity will be another major focus, with transport infrastructure and a proposed SCO Development Bank among the projects under discussion.
One major transport project involving SCO members is the 7,200-kilometer (4,474-mile) International North-South Transport Corridor, which links St. Petersburg with Mumbai through Iran and ports on the Persian Gulf.
The organization also agreed in 2025 to establish a network of Silk Road Stations to support international freight traffic across Eurasia.
Members are meanwhile continuing talks on establishing an SCO Development Bank. A fourth round of consultations was held in Shenzhen in June, though its structure and operating arrangements remain under negotiation.
The SCO enters its second quarter-century as economic activity shifts toward Asia, supply chains are reconfigured and countries seek new trade and diplomatic partnerships.
For some members, it offers a platform to strengthen regional security. For others, it provides opportunities to expand economic ties, develop transport links and coordinate positions on international issues.
The summit is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the SCO's 25th anniversary, alongside documents on the organization's development and regional and international issues.
It will also mark the end of Kyrgyzstan's chairmanship and the handover to Pakistan, which is set to lead the organization for the next year and host the 2027 leaders' summit.
The SCO lacks the binding commitments of a military alliance or economic union, but its scale has made it an increasingly significant forum for dialogue across Eurasia.
As leaders gather in Bishkek for its 25th anniversary, the summit underscores how an organization founded to resolve border disputes has grown into a major multilateral grouping.
Its next challenge will be turning that scale into influence while maintaining consensus among an increasingly diverse membership.

Education Ombudsman Nadiya Leshchyk is urging educational institutions to refrain from holding mass celebrations on the occasion of the start of the school year and during the educational process due to the security situation.
"Dear educators, parents, and students! The start of the new academic year is approaching. This is always an exciting moment, but in the conditions of the full-scale war launched by the Russian Federation, we must clearly set priorities. The most important of them is the life and health of every participant in the educational process. Considering the security situation in the country and real risks associated with potential shelling, I want to emphasize: holding mass events, particularly school assemblies, on September 1 and during the educational process is dangerous," Leshchyk wrote on Facebook.
She emphasized that mass gatherings create additional risks, as in the event of an "air alert" signal, ensuring a quick and safe evacuation of a large number of children in an open area is extremely difficult.
In this regard, she urges heads of educational institutions: to refrain from holding mass celebrations in educational institutions; to organize the start of the school year in formats that minimize risks for participants in the educational process; and to focus attention on conducting safety briefings, checking the readiness of shelters, and providing psychological support to children.
As reported, the new 2026-2027 academic year in secondary education institutions under martial law will start traditionally on September 1 and run until June 30, 2027. However, the actual end date of classes, holding of the last bell ceremony, and duration of summer holidays will be decided by the educational institutions themselves. They will be determined by the pedagogical council, taking into account the security situation and the needs of participants in the educational process.

Zimbabwean police have arrested a senior local official over the Lake Kariba ferry disaster that killed 97 people earlier this month.

“The ZRP confirms the arrest and subsequent appearance in court of Kariba RIDA District Coordinator, Ignatius Chiome (49),” the statement read.

The 41-year-old ferry was carrying up to 180 passengers and heavy cargo when it left Andora Harbour for the Chalala fishing camps, despite having an authorized capacity of 90 passengers, according to The Herald. The investigation is continuing, and prosecutors have indicated that further arrests could follow.
The RIDA-operated Mbuya Nehanda ferry capsized on Lake Kariba while traveling from the town of Kariba to communities and fishing camps along the lake. Local broadcaster ZBC News previously reported that the vessel encountered strong waves during the journey.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa declared the sinking a national disaster and ordered maritime safety agencies and security forces to address shortcomings in Zimbabwe’s maritime capabilities. The African Union also expressed condolences, with AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf saying the bloc stood “in solidarity with the people of Zimbabwe and the affected communities.”
Similar deadly boat accidents have occurred elsewhere in Africa. In September, at least 29 people were killed when a wooden boat carrying around 90 passengers capsized in Nigeria’s Niger State. Officials said the vessel was overloaded and struck a submerged tree stump.

From Tagore's thread of unity to booming trade opportunity - how Raksha Bandhan became Rs 25k-crore business
Aadrita Halder / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 28, 2026, 17:07 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
From Tagore's streets to 10-minute delivery: The business of Rakhi
In August 1905, as Bengal braced for a partition designed by the British to split its Hindu and Muslim population along communal lines, Rabindranath Tagore walked through the streets of Kolkata asking strangers to tie threads on each other's wrists. It was Raksha Bandhan, and Tagore had repurposed a domestic ritual, sisters protecting brothers, into a public act of protest. Hindus tied rakhis on Muslims, Muslims tied them on Hindus, and for one day at least, the colonial administration's attempt to engineer division through the Bengal Partition met a street-level answer in silk thread. The gesture was Tagore's response to a strategy of divide and rule that he saw threatening the nationalist movement at its foundations; the rakhi, in his hands, stopped being only a family custom and became a symbol of a shared, non-negotiable bond between communities.
When Tagore turned a ritual into protest
More than a century later, the thread has kept its symbolism but acquired a balance sheet. Raksha Bandhan is now one of the biggest festival-linked retail events in the Indian calendar, and the story of how it got there says as much about India's e-commerce boom, its gig economy and its small-manufacturing base as it does about siblings and sentiment.
A festival with a turnover
The Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT) estimates that India’s rakhi trade could reach nearly Rs 25,000 crore this year.
The broader Raksha Bandhan-related trade, including sweets, dry fruits, gifts, apparel, electronics, decorative items, puja articles and other festive products, is expected to cross Rs 30,000 crore nationally. Delhi alone is estimated to account for around Rs 4,000 crore, with major markets such as Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Karol Bagh, Lajpat Nagar, Kamla Nagar, Rajouri Garden, Gandhi Nagar, Khari Baoli and Laxmi Nagar seeing increased shopping activity ahead of Raksha Bandhan. These figures are CAIT estimates based on inputs from traders and trade associations, rather than audited market data.Much of the physical production still runs through India's traditional craft clusters. Kolkata remains a major wholesale and manufacturing hub, supplying rakhi traders across the country. Khadi rakhis from Nagpur, Sanganeri prints from Jaipur, seed rakhis from Pune, tea-leaf rakhis from Assam, jute rakhis from Kolkata, and bamboo and Madhubani-art rakhis from Bihar now sit alongside mass-produced options, driven in part by women's self-help groups and artisan collectives for whom the rakhi season is a source of supplementary household income.
Threads with a message, threads with a name
What has changed most visibly is the design vocabulary. This year's rakhi shelves carry threads built around Viksit Bharat, BrahMos and women's-empowerment themes alongside the more familiar Rudraksha, Swastik and Bhaiya-Bhabhi pairs, a sign of how quickly manufacturers now respond to the news cycle and government messaging, treating the rakhi as a wearable billboard as much as a ritual object. Superhero and cartoon-branded rakhis for children, evil-eye designs marketed as fashion accessories that can be worn past the festival, and premium metal or stone-studded pieces round out a market that has moved well beyond plain thread.Personalisation has become the dominant pitch, and not just at the top end.
A thread for every trend
Sellers now routinely offer rakhis with a brother's name sublimated onto acrylic or wood, or a sibling photograph printed directly onto the pendant, products that would have required a jeweller or an artist a decade ago and are now templated, priced from under Rs 50 apiece, and turned around in bulk by small manufacturing units in cities such as Ahmedabad, Delhi and Jaipur. The wider gifting trend has moved the same way: industry trackers this year note a decline in generic mass-market combo set, the standard thread-plus-sweets hamper, in favour of curated boxes that buyers can customise by age, taste or budget, from wellness kits to eco-friendly packaging.
Minutes, not days
The most disruptive change, though, has been in delivery. Quick-commerce platforms have turned the rakhi thali, once assembled by a sister at home or bought over a shop counter, into a same-day, sometimes same-hour order: thread, roli-chawal, sweets and a small gift bundled and dispatched from a neighbourhood dark store. For siblings living in different cities, or those who simply left the shopping too late, this has effectively replaced the courier parcels and last-minute market runs of previous years.That speed now comes with an asterisk. Since January this year, the quick-commerce platforms have all dropped explicit "10-minute" delivery claims from their branding, after the Union Labour Ministry pushed quick-commerce companies to stop advertising rigid delivery windows, citing rider safety concerns following gig-worker protests. Blinkit's tagline shifted from promising goods "in 10 minutes" to simply listing what it delivers; some of them now advertise "groceries in minutes" rather than a fixed number. The underlying model, dark stores, real-time inventory, delivery fleets built for speed, is unchanged, and rakhi orders still move fast during the festival rush; platforms have simply stopped putting a number on it.
The vendors left behind
For the street sellers who used to own this season, the shift has been harder to absorb than a change in app copy. Rakesh, who sells rakhi threads and thalis from a stall in one of Delhi's older markets, has watched the balance of the trade move online over the past few years."The availability of Rakhi threads and thalis online have changed things a lot for us," he said. "People get things delivered in minutes, there is also the aspect of personalisation. Customers can get their money back if they do not like a design but that is not the case for us. The demand has not dropped dramatically but we can definitely sense a shift now."His account captures something the trade-body turnover figures don't: this isn't a market in collapse so much as one being quietly redistributed. Total demand for rakhis hasn't fallen, traders' projections for this year are, if anything, higher than last year's, but a growing share of it is being captured by platforms that can offer instant refunds, endless design catalogues and delivery to a doorstep hundreds of kilometres away, none of which a pavement stall can match. A street vendor operates on thin, fixed margins and cannot offer the kind of no-questions-asked returns that have become standard on e-commerce and quick-commerce apps; a design that doesn't suit a customer is a sunk cost for him in a way it isn't for a platform with centralised inventory. What he is describing is less a festival in decline than a festival whose profits are migrating toward whoever controls speed, choice and convenience, the same forces reshaping most other categories of Indian retail.
Opportunity online, obstacles offline
The same platforms squeezing street vendors have opened a door for a different kind of small operator: the home-run, social-media-first rakhi business. Instagram and WhatsApp catalogues have made it possible for someone with no shop and little capital to sell personalised or handcrafted rakhis directly to customers, without a physical stall or a wholesaler in between.But reach isn't the same as revenue, says says a woman running an online rakhi business. "The biggest opportunity is using social media to reach more customers and promote products," she said. "But the biggest challenges for a new small business are building a customer base, increasing sales, competing with larger companies and recovering costs. When sales are low in the initial stages, profits can be very small, or there may be no profit at all.
"It's a reminder that the barriers for small players haven't disappeared with the shift online — they've simply moved. A social media page can put a home business in front of thousands of potential buyers, but it competes in the same feed as established D2C brands and marketplace sellers with bigger budgets, faster fulfilment and the cushion to absorb a slow first season. For someone starting out, the gap between visibility and an actual, sustainable customer base can take more than one festival cycle to close.
A hundred and twenty years of the same thread
The distance between Tagore's Kolkata processions and this year's app-driven rush is, on the surface, total: one was a deliberate refusal of commerce, staged to make a political point about unity in the face of engineered division; the other is commerce itself, organised around choice, speed and margin. But the thread running between them, literally, is the same one: an ordinary domestic ritual, elastic enough to be pressed into whatever a moment demands, whether that moment calls for resistance or for a same-day delivery slot. What has changed is not the rakhi but who gets to decide what it means, and increasingly, that decision is being made by whoever can get it to your wrist the fastest.
