Russia Launches 140 Drones in Rare Daylight Assault Across Ukraine — Kyiv Under Attack for Hours
Russian forces carried out a drone attack across Ukraine from 07:00 to 19:00, launching approximately 140 strike drones. The majority of the unmanned aerial vehicles targeted Kyiv.
Ukrainian air defense forces intercepted and shot down 120 of the incoming strike drones, with approximately 100 of the launched drones identified as jet-powered models. During the operation, Russian drones altered their flight behavior, making sharp 180-degree mid-flight turns—a maneuver rarely observed in previous attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In Kyiv on August 27, air raid sirens sounded 11 times, with the total duration of alerts exceeding 11 hours. This daytime targeting represents unusual timing for Russian forces, who typically launch strike drones at night.
The air strikes caused damage in multiple locations. In Kyiv, falling debris hit the roof of a dormitory in the Desnyanskyi district, while a four-story building was damaged in the Podilskyi district.
In Sumy, two drones hit the grounds of a civilian enterprise, and a 66-year-old woman was wounded in a separate strike in the Sumy region. Additional strikes were recorded in other areas.
In Kharkiv, a drone hit the Osnovyanskyi district. In the Kherson region, Russian forces launched an attack using aviation, artillery, and various types of drones, killing one man and injuring nine other people. The head of the regional military administration reported that significant damage to the local thermal power plant means it will likely be unable to operate normally.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, nine people were injured after Russian forces shelled the Nikopol and Synelnykove districts 40 times throughout the day. These daytime strikes followed overnight attacks on the capital.
Overnight, Russian forces launched at least four ballistic missiles at Kyiv, followed by continued drone activity into the day.
In the Holosiivskyi district, a drone fell onto a roadway and a non-residential building, causing a roof fire and injuring three people. In the Shevchenkivskyi district, falling debris damaged two educational institutions, including a gymnasium, and shattered windows at a municipal medical clinic.
Debris was also recorded falling in an open area and a residential courtyard in the Podilskyi district, while a grass fire was triggered in the Pecherskyi district. Emergency services, rescuers, and bomb disposal personnel were deployed to the affected sites.

Ugandan King Oyo Nyimba, once world's youngest monarch, dies at 34
KAMPALA, Aug 28 - Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king, who became the world's youngest reigning monarch when he took the crown in 1995, has died aged 34, the prime minister of his kingdom announced.
Uganda is a republic, ruled by an elected head of state, but it has several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms as they were constituted in the pre-colonial period. Their political power is largely symbolic, but they wield enormous cultural and social influence.
Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV was the King of Tooro, a small kingdom in Uganda's west near the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo.
"It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty the Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV," the prime minister of the kingdom, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said in a post on X late on Thursday.
The king died at around 10:00 p.m. local time on Thursday, Akiiki said, without revealing the cause of his death.
Rukidi IV was crowned at just three years old on September 12, 1995 after the death of his father, Rukirabasaija Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III.
Balaam Barugahara, a minister in the government of President Yoweri Museveni, said shortly before the announcement of the king's death that he was receiving treatment in the U.S.
"This is an immeasurable loss," the prime minister said, adding the king, who was unmarried, had left an heir and that "continuity of the Crown is assured."
His death triggered an outpouring of grief across social media platforms in Uganda and widespread media coverage nationally.
"Most devastating news! May His Majesty the King's soul rest in eternal peace," Bobi Wine, Ugandan pop star-turned-politician who is the country's leading opposition leader, said in a post on X.
In April, in a message to celebrate the King's birthday, Tooro's prime minister had said: "Our King is not distant from the realities of his people; he is part of this generation, part of this ecosystem, growing, learning, and leading... His youth is not a limitation; it is a strength. It brings energy, fresh perspective, and the courage to imagine a different future for Tooro." REUTERS

NEW DELHI: Penguin Random House India on Friday clarified that it is not the publisher of Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's memoir Belonging: A Journey of Love in India.The Publishing house rejected reports that it decided against publishing the book because the author declined editorial changes.

Embezzled over UAH 12 million in the procurement of 580 FPV drones - a group of criminals detained
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU detained a group for embezzling funds during the procurement of 580 FPV drones. The unmanned aerial vehicles intended for the military on the Kharkiv front were not handed over.
Military counterintelligence, in cooperation with the Department for the Protection of National Statehood of the Security Service of Ukraine, with the assistance of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the Commander of the Territorial Defense Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, exposed and detained a group of individuals who misappropriated budget funds during the procurement of unmanned systems for the Ukrainian army. The SBU press center reported this, UNN reports.
Details
The investigation established that the organizer of the scheme was a former commander of a Territorial Defense brigade in the Kyiv region, who was serving in the position at the time the crime was committed.
According to the case materials, he organized the procurement of 580 FPV drones worth a total of more than UAH 12 million, involving other individuals in the illegal activity. Subsequently, the unmanned aircraft were to be delivered to Ukrainian Armed Forces soldiers in the Kharkiv sector. However, according to the available information, the contracts for the supply of the weapons were fictitious. None of the "contracted" drones reached the Ukrainian defenders, which negatively affected the performance of tasks on the front line
It is also reported that the suspects prepared documents as if the drones had been handed over to the military. In particular, the official submitted falsified UAV acceptance and transfer certificates for signing without any actual delivery.
The suspect then demanded that personnel conceal the absence of the drones during an inspection and arrange for the property to be written off as lost on the battlefield
All the detainees were notified of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 114-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (obstruction of the lawful activities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and other military formations). The article provides for imprisonment for a term of 8 to 15 years.
Reminder
SBU counterintelligence exposed an FSB agent network that was adjusting air attacks. Four informants were detained in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Kirovohrad regions.

Russia’s mass-produced Kuryer combat robot can be controlled via smartphone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:02:35 UTC
18:02:35 KST

NOVOSIBIRSK, August 28. /TASS/. The Kuryer (Courier), Russia’s most widely deployed combat robot in the special military operation zone, is capable of firing weapons, laying and clearing mines, and evacuating the wounded - the platform, which an operator can control with a standard smartphone, was unveiled at the Technoprom forum, a TASS correspondent reports.
The ground robotic system was developed at the Kaps manufacturing company in collaboration with specialists from the Omsk Armored Engineering Institute (OABII). The Kuryer has a range of more than 10 km and is controlled via fiber-optic cable, cellular communication, or a radio channel. The robot is equipped with AGS-17 grenade launchers and 12.7-mm PKT and NSVT machine guns. It is capable of covertly laying mines on a road, carrying out diversionary maneuvers, and firing to destroy targets.
"The robot lays mines on a road in the evening while no one can see it, and by the morning, the enemy will already be driving along it. In addition to this turret, we can mount completely different add-on modules here. It could be a smoke-generating system, or it could be a laser device for mine clearance," Vyacheslav Kalabin, a cadet at the OABII, a corporal, and a member of the All-Russian Society of Inventors and Innovators (VOIR), told TASS.
The vehicle is also equipped with a thermal imager and 360-degree cameras, and can deploy TM-62 anti-tank mines. "This is the most combat-ready and most widely used robot to date," Nurzhan Rakimzhanov, a representative of the Omsk branch of VOIR, told TASS. The developers did not specify the exact number of systems deployed on the front line, but noted their widespread use in the combat zone.
To transport cargo and personnel, the robot is coupled with the Troyan modular transformer trailer. The platform’s adjustable width allows not only for the transport of soldiers but also for the covert delivery of other compact robotic systems under a tarp--they can be quickly unloaded via folding ramps just before carrying out a combat mission. The inventors also demonstrated to a TASS correspondent how the Kuryer operates when evacuating wounded personnel from the battlefield.
About the forum
The 13th International Forum for Technological Development -- Technoprom 2026 is taking place in Novosibirsk from August 26 to 28. Delegations from 40 countries are participating. The forum’s motto is "Russian Science is the Foundation of Technological Leadership." A major part of the program is devoted to the launch of the Siberian Circular Photon Source in Koltsovo and the operation of other megascience facilities. The program also includes the Intelligent Systems and Medicine of the Future tracks.
TASS is the general media partner of the Technoprom forum.

A corruption case involving senior figures in the Swiss financial sector is to be heard in court: Pierre Mirabaud, former president of the Swiss Bankers Association (SBA), is due to stand trial at the beginning of September before the Federal Criminal Court.
He is accused of bribing a senior Kuwaiti official in order to secure control of substantial public funds.
According to the indictment, a copy of which was obtained by the Swiss News Agency Keystone-ATS, the criminal investigation was launched in 2021 by the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland (OAG). The alleged offences date back to the period between 2000 and 2012.
Mirabaud is alleged to have promised undue kickbacks totalling CHF82 million ($102 million) to the chairman of Kuwait’s Public Institution for Social Security (PIFSS). In return, the man is alleged to have entrusted the Geneva-based private bank Mirabaud with a portion of the Kuwaiti institution’s funds, amounting to $500 million (CHF400 million).

Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:01:51 UTC
18:01:51 KST

Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
Hundreds of popular vegan and vegetarian foods may contain an unwanted extra ingredient: toxins naturally produced by fungi.
- Date:
- August 28, 2026
- Source:
- Cranfield University
- Summary:
- Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time.
- Share:
A large survey of plant-based foods and beverages sold in the UK has found that mycotoxins, toxic compounds naturally produced by fungi, are widespread across vegetarian and vegan products.
Researchers analyzed 212 plant-based meat alternatives (PMBAs) and plant-based beverages (PBBs) purchased from UK stores. Every product tested contained at least one of 19 mycotoxins, and some contained several.
The study was led by the University of Parma in Italy and coauthored by Cranfield University. Researchers examined a wide range of products commonly available to UK shoppers, including burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond and soy-based milks.
Why Mycotoxins Appear in Plant-Based Foods
Mycotoxins can be especially common in plant-based products because many of their ingredients, including grains, legumes and seeds, may be exposed to mould while they are being grown or stored.
Despite the widespread detection of mycotoxins, the levels measured in the UK products remained below recommended EU guideline levels. The researchers said this reflects the high quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.
Long-Term Exposure Could Still Matter
The concern is not necessarily the amount present in a single product. Previous research studies have indicated that repeated exposure to small amounts of mycotoxins can add up over time and may eventually create health concerns.
Eating individual plant-based products is therefore unlikely to cause problems on its own. However, the researchers say that a diet based entirely on plant foods could increase cumulative exposure to mycotoxins if that exposure is not properly managed. In severe cases, mycotoxin exposure has been associated with liver and kidney damage, suppression of the immune system, and cancer.
The findings provide new data that can be used to estimate dietary exposure and improve risk assessments for consumers in the UK.
Experts Call for Better Monitoring
Andrea Patriarca, Senior Lecturer in Mycology at Cranfield University, said:
"Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.
"However, a significant concern arises when new foods enter the market, as there are currently no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins. We collaborate closely with various sectors in the food industry, from farmers to food companies, to help implement effective mycotoxin management integrated within food safety standards. The data from our research helps food safety organisations in assessing risks, particularly in complex multi-ingredient products.
"We are currently collaborating with the University of Parma to evaluate the risks faced by the population based on different dietary habits. Our aim is to advise policymakers and raise awareness among vulnerable consumers."
The full research paper, "Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market," is published in Food Control.
This work was carried out under the Horizon Europe FunShield4Med project (HORIZON-WIDERA-2021-ACCESS-03) Grant Agreement No 101079173 funded by the European Union.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cranfield University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raquel Torrijos, Octavian Augustin Mihalache, Andrea Patriarca, Angel Medina, Chiara Dall’Asta. Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market. Food Control, 2026; 183: 111910 DOI: 10.1016/j.foodcont.2025.111910

How Sudan built the very force that destroyed it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:01:21 UTC
18:01:21 KST

Breadcrumb
How Sudan built the very force that destroyed it
For millions of Sudanese, the war has reduced life to one agonising question: when will it end? Peace is no longer a political luxury but an urgent necessity. It is the only thing that matters to families who lost their homes, to communities pushed into mass displacement, and to all those wondering whether their relatives are still alive.
I could feel the heaviness of our reality when Mahmoud and I met in Gallal café in Madinaty, Cairo. We chose the location simply because he lives in Badr and we wanted to head to Downtown Cairo eventually, so it made sense to meet near my place. It was the first time I had seen Mahmoud in three years.
The way we greeted each other was so intense that it made an Egyptian woman at the next table start crying.
Mahmoud was instantly embarrassed. He doesn’t know how to navigate a crying stranger, or emotions in general, so he simply stared at his phone. He muttered that she must be crying over a relationship as he watched a video of Khartoum burning on his social media feed.
We didn’t talk much after that. We have become exceptionally good at silence.
Massacre
Certainly, the war in Sudan did not appear out of nowhere on 15 April 2023. It was a long, carefully constructed project of violence becoming visible.
Before the first shot was even fired, politicians and elites spent years trying to reduce everything to a simple conflict between power blocs, or a transitional crisis that could be neatly resolved with yet another framework agreement.
Many external observers also tried to explain it away as two generals fighting over a shrinking pie. But for us, the real story was about a state that spent years systematically allowing more than one armed power to exist within its borders.
When I trace back to the exact moment I first noticed the collapse of our state’s institutions, my mind goes to May 2019, just after then-President Omar al-Bashir fell. It was the prelude to what would be known years later as the 8th of Ramadan massacre. I remember how we stood out there, trying to protect the sit-in with nothing but rocks.
We were acting as the neighbourhood committees, desperately trying to hold the fabric of our streets together, while the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) turned violence into a lucrative business.
I recall that day with brutal clarity because that is when they killed Ali Kisketa, a friend from my neighbourhood. Then my memory drags me to the aftermath, when they also killed Abdul Salam Kisha and Qusai Hammadtto.
I also lost loved ones indirectly. My friend Ali, who was a maxillofacial surgeon, died of a heart defect following three consecutive days of intensively treating injured migrants fleeing Khartoum in Atbara’s general hospital.
Another friend, Mazen, took his own life last year.
Intrinsically violent
There is a deep, structural flaw in how the army has communicated the meaning of this war. By framing its position around aggressive slogans like "no negotiation," the army has allowed the RSF — a force intrinsically built on violence — to absurdly pose as the side offering peace.
The army hasn’t just lost a media battle; it has ceded the moral language of the war itself. And that language matters, because the RSF’s violence is not incidental.
Those sitting in displacement tents, uprooted from their entire lives, don’t just want to know who will win; they need to know why all of this happened in the first place, and exactly what will take place after the shooting finally stops.
War requires clear communication, not hollow slogans. It requires a discourse that tells people: we fight because we had absolutely no choice when your existence was threatened, and if they put down their weapons today, peace will be our immediate priority.
The purpose of any legitimate army is not to perpetuate conflict, but to protect its people and end the war as soon as possible. For Sudan, the army must clearly position itself in stark contrast to the RSF.
For us, the RSF was never just an acronym in a geopolitical report. They were in our streets, occupying our neighbourhoods, sleeping in our houses. We watched first-hand how they turned the Khartoum we knew and loved into a place of total fear.
Compared to the army – which included individuals who chose to stand with the people when that choice carried genuine, fatal risk – the RSF has historically been intrinsically linked to violence against civilians.
Indeed, this was the role it was designed to play from its inception in the early 2000s when the state was facing a dilemma over how to deploy extreme violence with the least political cost. Given the formal army could theoretically be held accountable for every battle, a model was developed in which forces operated completely outside the traditional structure of the state.
These forces were given weapons and a mandate to carry out the brutal tasks the central authority sought to distance itself from.
The Janjaweed were used as a specific method of governance, produced by the centre and deployed whenever convenient. Yet many still make the fatal mistake of portraying the RSF as a marginal, rogue force that suddenly rose to power.
After Bashir fell, this force didn’t vanish with the regime that birthed it; it metastasised. It inherited the state's sprawling security networks, acquired massive corporate holdings, and cultivated its own external relations. It evolved into a fully realised political and economic project, fighting solely to protect its own interests.
In the case of the RSF, its weaponry was closely linked to money, gold smuggling, cross-border trade, and mercenaryism.
Gold became the ultimate source of power in a collapsed economy. Armed forces were able to translate physical resources directly into political influence, perfectly illustrating what Alex de Waal described as a “political marketplace” where loyalties are bought, and alliances are structured using raw capital.
In this marketplace, true power comes from the ability to finance weapons and turn immense wealth into regional influence.
When central state resources declined following South Sudan's secession, the RSF capitalised on the vacuum. They achieved financial independence, making them less reliant on the state and far more capable of challenging it. Even their deployment in the war in Yemen was part of a new political economy, in which exporting fighters abroad became a lucrative source of financing and regional leverage.
Therefore, framing the RSF as a "revolution of the marginalised" is a dangerous fallacy. There is a profound difference between acknowledging the tragic recruitment conditions of people from impoverished environments, and excusing a heavily armed project that weaponised this marginalisation to serve a new network of elite interests.
The Janjaweed were not outside the state; they were its harshest, most cynical product — and when this force grew large enough, it naturally wanted to consume the state entirely. For the RSF, the war was an existential battle over the very shape of that state.
From the barrel of a gun
How could a force that sprouted from an economy of violence turn, in the eyes of some politicians, into a potential democratic partner? Societies deep in crisis often delude themselves into believing they can control a violent force by pointing it at a specific opponent.
Karl Marx vividly described how a fractured society can produce a force that benefits from everyone’s collective fear. Elites, terrified of their rivals, look for an armed shortcut, convinced they hold the leash.
But a force that derives its legitimacy entirely from the barrel of a gun enters politics with a logic of coercion, not persuasion. Those who saw the RSF as a convenient tool to balance the army or bypass Islamists wilfully ignored the entire history of this weapon.
An entity accustomed to deriving its immense power from the informal economy and the active bypassing of institutions will never magically transform into a democratic national institution simply by signing a piece of paper.
This does not absolve the Sudanese army. Its long, troubled history of political intervention and systemic participation in authoritarian regimes demands sweeping reform of all state institutions. However, there is a fundamental, unbridgeable difference between an institution that desperately requires reform, and a militia whose very existence is predicated on undermining the concept of an institution itself.
An institution, regardless of its deep flaws, inherently assumes the existence of rules, structure, and a relationship between state power and the law. A militia represents an inverted reality where the law is entirely subordinate to brute force, and state institutions become mere tools in the hands of whoever possesses the most money and weapons.
Hence, this war was the violent expression of a state wrestling with what it seeks to be.
When military control is accompanied by the systematic looting and deliberate destruction of civil institutions, war becomes a calculated means to permanently rearrange who owns and who loses.
In Sudan, the war was engineered through the systematic dismantling of daily life. Crimes were deliberately filmed and broadcast to break the collective will of the people. The ultimate goal was total control over citizens’ sense of belonging.
After all, when a man loses his home, he loses his memory, his anchor, and his sense of the future.
As Lebanese psychologist Mustafa Hijazi pointed out, an oppressed individual who has been severely marginalised can, when suddenly handed absolute, unchecked authority, turn into a monster who practices the exact same logic of cruelty he once suffered from.
The true danger emerges when a deep-seated sense of historical injustice meets high-calibre weapons, a total absence of law, and a toxic discourse that reduces human beings to abstract enemies. Violence simply becomes a way to prove oneself.
Without an institution to hold the fighter accountable, the "other" transitions from a human being into a disposable object. This is exactly what we witnessed with the gleeful documentation of crimes and the online publication of civilian humiliation, framed as if it were a military victory.
We heard comfortable, lazy classifications that "the army are all kizan (a derogatory nickname for Islamists loyal to al-Bashir's National Congress Party)," that "the RSF are all gharaba (people from west Sudan)," and that "northerners are just local informants for the coloniser." These broad strokes make societies entirely incapable of seeing the complex, agonising truth.
The reality
It is entirely possible – and important – to acknowledge that deep corruption and the attempts of Islamists to return to power exist at the same time as an armed militia representing a parasitic project that actively wants to devour the state. Choosing the easier, binary explanation exempts us from facing our crushing reality.
Sudan reached this horrific moment due to decades of building a weak state, a hollowed-out economy, and the treatment of national institutions as disposable tools for personal conflict.
Nevertheless, the question now is what will become of Sudan after the war. Because for the side theoretically protecting the state, if it continues to refuse to recognise the nature of the project that dragged us into this catastrophe in the first place, there is little chance that our fractured country can be rebuilt.
But defending the state does not, and will not, justify repeating the catastrophic mistakes of the past. Sudan desperately needs a different kind of state—one where the military institution is firmly situated below society, and where a militia is never again viewed as a viable alternative.
Furthermore, we must be honest with ourselves that defeating the militia terrorising the people does not mean the end of Sudan’s problems. The hardest battle will be what follows this stage, including rebuilding legitimate institutions, holding the perpetrators of atrocities accountable, and permanently ending the politicisation of the army.
The message to the Sudanese people must not be one of blind hatred or endless revenge. It must be expressed with uncompromising honesty—that we will absolutely not accept armed aggression as a legitimate way to rule.
Peace will be possible if weapons are laid down, justice isn’t bypassed, and blanket amnesties are not granted. And certainly, whilst peace is the ultimate goal, it must never be left as a cynical political tool for those who invaded our houses and looted our cities.
Before we can move forward, Sudan needs to permanently destroy the idea that made this war possible in the first place.
Ahmed Ismat is a Sudanese writer, researcher and political activist currently based in Cairo. He previously served as a spokesperson for Khartoum resistance committees in Sudan. This essay is adapted from his upcoming book, The Republic of the Unimportant.

Castelion raises $1bn for hypersonic weapons
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
10:00:35 BST
18:00:35 KST

US defence technology company Castelion has announced a $1 billion Series C financing round intended to expand production of its Blackbeard hypersonic strike missile and fund work on longer-range strike and defensive systems, according to the company.
Castelion announced the financing on 19 August, saying the round values the California-headquartered company at $13 billion. The company describes the financing as a $1 billion Series C, comprising $800 million in equity investment and $250 million committed to a revolving credit facility.
The equity portion was co-led by JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group, Andreessen Horowitz and funds managed by Carlyle. Lightspeed Venture Partners, Lavrock Ventures, Altimeter, General Catalyst and Interlagos also participated alongside new investor T. Rowe Price Associates.
Castelion said the capital will be directed primarily towards increasing production capacity for Blackbeard, its first hypersonic strike weapon, while accelerating development of another longer-range precision strike system and expanding work on air and missile defence technologies. The company says it has secured more than $500 million in US military contracts during the past 18 months and moved Blackbeard from an initial design to a programme of record in less than four years. Fielding of the weapon is targeted for 2027, according to Castelion.
Bryon Hargis, co-founder and chief executive of Castelion, said in the company’s announcement: “Deterrence depends on unapologetic American strength; highly capable weapon systems that adversaries fear produced in quantities they can’t imagine at a price taxpayers can afford.”
He added: “There’s a manufacturing renaissance underway and this round turbocharges American production of Blackbeard. Designed in California, built in New Mexico, supplied from small and large businesses across the United States; Blackbeard is an example of what America can do when private capital and Government work together.”
A substantial part of the new investment is expected to go into manufacturing infrastructure in New Mexico. Castelion is developing Project Ranger, a 1,000-acre manufacturing campus in Sandoval County dedicated to hypersonic missile production. The company had already committed more than $250 million in private infrastructure investment at the site and said it will now commit hundreds of millions of dollars more to expand Blackbeard production capacity.
Castelion is also using technology developed for Blackbeard as the basis for a separate longer-range precision strike weapon. According to the company, the system has been under development for several years and will reuse core technologies, components and manufacturing methods developed for Blackbeard. The stated objective is to produce a longer-range hypersonic weapon at substantially greater volumes and lower cost than existing high-end systems. Castelion has not identified the new weapon by name in the announcement.
A third portion of the investment will support defensive systems. Castelion said these programmes will draw on technologies and manufacturing processes developed through Blackbeard, with an emphasis on air and missile defence and increasing available interceptor magazine depth.
Todd Combs, head of JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group, said in the release: “Castelion is helping to address a critical national security challenge by bringing greater speed, agility and manufacturing capacity to the development of next-generation defense technologies.”
Katherine Boyle, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said: “We backed Castelion when it was a small team that wanted to build what the department of War most needed faster and cheaper than the experts thought possible.” She added: “Four years later there is a factory in New Mexico and a production agreement with the Department of War.”
Castelion has moved through successive private funding rounds as it expands from development and flight testing into production. The company raised $350 million in a Series B financing round announced in December 2025, with that investment similarly directed towards manufacturing hypersonic weapons at scale.
Alongside its land-based production plans, Castelion is also working with autonomous vessel manufacturer Saronic on a proposed maritime launch demonstration. The companies announced in June that they intend to integrate Castelion hypersonic wepons with Saronic autonomous surface vessels, with a demonstration targeted for 2027. The latest financing will now support expansion at Project Ranger alongside continued Blackbeard production, development of the unnamed longer-range strike system and work on lower-cost defensive weapons.

How an Atlanta Suburb Ended Up Sharing Flock Data With More Than 2,000 Organizations

18:00:00 KST

Alpharetta, a prosperous suburb of Atlanta, Georgia, is home to about 67,000 people, served by about 120 local police officers. It also hosts several dozen cameras sold by Flock Safety, the increasingly controversial surveillance company that collects license plate data and other information and makes it searchable by police.
Data captured by those Flock cameras, WIRED has learned via public records requests, is accessible to more than 2,000 police departments, colleges, airports, and government agencies across the United States. These range from Morehouse College to Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Commission and include Medicare fraud investigators in Illinois, a drug task force focused on east-central Missouri, and the inspector general of a federal agency.
In return, Alpharetta receives Flock data from more than 1,300 entities, which span from the prosecutor’s office of Whitley County, Indiana, to the Metro Police Authority of Genesee County, Michigan.
The Alpharetta Police Department—which, as reported by WIRED, had an officer resign due to Flock misuse on August 5—also exchanges Flock data with several agencies that have been similarly rocked by recent incidents of officers misusing its technology, including Georgia’s Bibb County Sheriff’s Department, the Savannah Police Department, and the Dallas Police Department.
Alpharetta’s data-sharing network has expanded tremendously over the past year. Since June 2025, the number of entities receiving data from Alpharetta police has grown by about 42 percent, and the number of entities sending data to them has grown by about 125 percent. And, according to documents obtained via public records requests from several other cities around the country, Alpharetta is far from alone in having an expansive and complicated data-sharing system, providing a potent example of how pervasive Flock’s surveillance network has become.
One of Flock’s central selling points is its network of customers—mostly, though not entirely, law enforcement agencies. If a criminal suspect crosses city, county, or perhaps state lines, Flock tells its customers, a query can prevent them from falling through the cracks.
Data sharing across agencies is hardly novel. A police department can, for instance, share data from its automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) with state-run fusion centers, which centralize resources from law enforcement agencies in particular regions. They could also share it with a regional High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) program. (Alpharetta police agreed to do just that in 2025, according to a memorandum of understanding that WIRED obtained.)
Whereas HIDTAs are federally funded public programs, Flock is a private company that manages a sprawling, interconnected ALPR network governed by rules and restrictions that vary wildly from city to city. And if police departments don’t closely supervise their settings for data requests and sharing within Flock’s interface, they can unwittingly become nodes in a much larger surveillance network than they necessarily know or understand.
This can lead to situations like that in Alpharetta, where citizens and visitors are embedded in a data-sharing network that has propagated to more than 2,300 nodes. So, how does it happen?
Setting Boundaries
To understand how cities like Alpharetta can build such expansive data-sharing networks with Flock, it’s important to understand how Flock’s interface actually works.
WIRED analyzed a cache of files on Flock’s website that are served by its login pages to anyone who loads them. Some of the code that WIRED analyzed illustrates what a Flock administrator might see in their own Flock interface—specifically, in their settings and sharing preferences.
An administrator can automatically share their agency’s Flock data with any organization within a custom radius, within their home state, or within one or more other states. Alternatively, they can individually choose organizations to share data with.
Administrators can also limit specific data that other organizations can receive, like live or archived videos. They can also limit which organizations can ask them for data. They could restrict this, for instance, to organizations based in the same state, or within a 50-mile radius.
Lieutenant Jason Hiott of the Alpharetta Police Department tells WIRED that per the city’s Flock settings, the department will “automatically approve” requests for its Flock data from law enforcement agencies within 500 miles. If they’re outside that radius, the police department has to individually request access to Alpharetta’s data.
Hiott was unable to say what the Alpharetta police department’s default settings were, whether it altered the default settings, or how long the radius has been set to 500 miles—though he did note that the department “does not share any live feeds, analytics, etc. with anyone.”
Flock spokesperson Jess Montejano claims that data sharing is turned off by default for new and onboarding customers—so no law enforcement agencies automatically get access to another agency’s data. Flock did not specify whether that has always been the case.
Paris Lewbel, another Flock spokesperson, adds that “historically,” its customers have been able to request data from other customers that are within the same state, or within 50 miles—the precursor to actually sharing data.
Coast-to-Coast
Flock’s network settings allow agencies to set specific limits on what Flock data it shares and receives, but in some cases, police departments have been caught off guard by how expansive the search settings were for their officers.
Often, the confusion has been tied to Flock’s Nationwide lookup tool, which the company introduced in 2021 and is available to customers that opt in, according to the company. It allows any Flock customer to query any other Flock customer in the country, as long as they have a specific license plate. (Flock disabled the tool for federal agencies following backlash to the company’s pilot program with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.) In several cases, Flock customers had no idea this tool was enabled.
Chris Shook is the city attorney in Reynoldsburg, Ohio, where two officers recently resigned after the police department probed their alleged misuse of Flock’s technology. He tells WIRED that in June, the city’s police department made an unexpected discovery while attempting to complete a public records request: Per the department’s Flock settings, the Nationwide lookup tool was active. Police leadership, however, had been under the impression that officers could only search cameras within Ohio.
Shook says that the police department immediately changed the settings to enable only in-state camera searches. But they had no idea when, or why, nationwide searches may have been enabled. Lacking answers, Shook turned to Flock.
According to emails reviewed by WIRED, Flock customer success manager Caroline Bush could only say that Nationwide lookup “was enabled at some point before February 2025.” Due to an “event-log limitation” prior to that month, she could not say exactly when. But she added that, upon checking the police department’s audit, she “found nationwide searches as early as 03/2023.”
This came as a surprise to Shook. If nationwide search was enabled, he said, there must have been an error, “but we are unsure of how that error could have occurred.”
“The most likely explanation is that the setting was enabled during initial account setup or onboarding,” Bush replied. She said Nationwide lookup “was a common default configuration for agencies at that time, before Flock introduced stronger in-product disclosures and tighter controls around this feature.”
In California, the Palo Alto Police Department had a similar experience. In a city council “study session” led by city manager Ed Shikada on June 1, he claimed that Flock activated Nationwide lookup “for all customers” in mid-2023. Flock says this is a “false claim,” based on research that found “agencies across the country that have never been in the Nationwide Network including in the state of California.”
Notably, California law forbids sharing ALPR data with federal or out-of-state law enforcement. Shikada said that Flock quietly “disabled” Nationwide lookup for Palo Alto police in October 2024, and for all California law enforcement by March 2025.
However, Shikada said Palo Alto police didn't know Nationwide lookup had ever been active until December 2025.
Meanwhile, Commander David Hart of Minnesota’s Beltrami County Sheriff’s Office tells WIRED that while his office didn’t have a debacle with the Nationwide lookup tool, he had to reel in the permissions that were set up when the county started using Flock in early 2024.
For the first few months, his officers could send and receive data requests to any Flock customer in the country. But toward the end of 2024, Hart says, he limited outgoing and incoming data requests to in-state agencies. No data requests are approved automatically. (Minnesota’s ALPR statute sets specific standards that agencies must meet before capturing or receiving ALPR data.) Hart tells WIRED that on principle, he doesn’t believe in using Flock casually for wide-ranging searches.
“It’s gotten to the point where people want to search more agencies just to be able to search more agencies, without a real reason behind it,” Hart says.
When examining Flock audit logs, it’s not always obvious why an officer would want or need to expand the scope of their search.
WIRED filed a public records request to the Reynoldsburg Police Department and received 549 pages that log every Flock query its officers made from January 2024 through April 2026. The records show that even from query to query, the number of probed Flock networks can vary significantly.
On January 1, 2025, for instance, a Reynoldsburg police officer queried 53 Flock networks. The officer’s “reason” for the search, according to the log, was a potential criminal offense coded “30.” Just 40 minutes later, the same officer cited the same criminal offense code but, for reasons the log does not specify, instead queried 5,392 Flock networks. Similar examples appear regularly throughout the log, though most of the searches WIRED reviewed had probed fewer than 100 networks.
Flock users, as illustrated in a recent video on the company’s YouTube channel, can customize the number of networks they want to probe in a single query. A police officer can probe every single camera network their department has access to—or they can limit their search to their state, or simply their own jurisdiction. That decision is left up to the officer.
“The particular officer can narrow the networks they want to search, but typically they don't,” Shook tells WIRED. “Typically, they search every network they have access to.”
Mixed Company
Alpharetta’s Flock data-sharing network shows that it sends data to and receives it from agencies that, along with being geographically distant, are a far cry from the local police departments and county sheriff offices that represent Flock’s prototypical customers.
It’s often unclear, outside of a fluke circumstance, what the agencies would gain from exchanging data.
For instance, it’s not obvious why the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration, Region G of the Alabama Drug Enforcement Task Force, or the University of North Texas’ Denton campus police would need to have a mutual exchange of Flock data with the police department of Alpharetta, Georgia. (None of these agencies responded to requests for comment.)
WIRED contacted more than a dozen agencies sending or receiving data with the Alpharetta Police that are neither a police department nor a sheriff’s office, and most did not respond to requests for comment. Just one answered specific questions about its use of Flock: Kentucky’s Louisville Regional Airport Authority, a nearly seven-hour drive from Alpharetta.
Natalie Ciresi Chaudoin, the airport authority’s director of public relations, tells WIRED that the Louisville Regional Airport Authority has 13 Flock cameras across its properties. She says that the airport shares data from its cameras with 2,240 federal, state, and local agencies across the country and receives data from 1,124 agencies.
Chaudoin adds that the airport’s Flock settings are configured to “automatically accept a request for data-sharing with in-state law enforcement agencies, while out-of-state agencies’ requests are manually accepted or declined following their review.”
When asked about Alpharetta, Chaudoin says that the airport was “aware that it received data from an agency” in the city. The airport has not shared its data in return.
Limiting Factors
Twenty-four states, as well as Washington, DC, have statutes covering ALPR use. The regulations they impose differ widely from state to state, with some being quite specific: Since 2023, it’s been illegal for law enforcement in Illinois to use ALPR data in criminal cases related to immigration or abortion.
The effects of California’s restrictions are visible in records obtained via public records request from the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC), which are published publicly on Muckrock, a public records request facilitator. According to the records, the fusion center shares and receives data from fewer than 400 agencies—a fraction of the agencies in Alpharetta’s network—and they’re all based in California. However, that fact alone doesn’t paint the whole picture.
According to an audit of searches run on the NCRIC’s Flock network, NCRIC member agencies ran more than 57,000 Flock queries in the single month between November 26 and December 26, 2025. Many of the queries probed thousands of Flock networks, and more than 96 percent of them probed at least 100.
In other words, the scope of the NCRIC queries tended to be significantly larger than those of the Reynoldsburg Police Department—the police department in a state with no ALPR statute, where officers had access to the Nationwide lookup tool until June and from which two officers recently resigned due to allegedly misusing Flock.
On August 13, Flock announced a set of changes to how its software works, seemingly in response to a surge in news coverage about police officers misusing the technology. The company said that it is now “recommending a 7-day ALPR data retention period,” a reduction from 30 days. But Flock customers can pay for extended data retention, according to documents obtained via a public records request from St. Petersburg, Florida.
Flock also says that law enforcement can’t run a Flock search without entering a criminal case code and that by the end of the year, all customers must activate its Audit Assistance tool, which scans for “defined criteria for abnormal behavior” and “automatically” suspends Flock access if detected.
In Alpharetta, according to Lieutenant Hiott, police chief Trent Lindgren learned about the Audit Assistance tool in July and promptly activated it. By July 20, the department had opened an investigation into one of its officers. On August 5, the officer resigned.
Updated 8/28/2026 at 3:55 pm EDT: The year the Nationwide lookup tool was introduced and Caroline Bush’s title have been updated to reflect comment offered by Flock after publication.

Thieves snatch $5.1m diamond necklace from Vienna museum
Unknown

Thieves snatch $5.1m diamond necklace from Vienna museum
A historic diamond necklace originally designed for the Egyptian royal family and valued at about US$4 million (S$5.1 million) was stolen from a major Vienna museum, triggering a police manhunt for the two alleged thieves.
The men smashed a display case in Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts during opening hours on Aug 27 and fled on foot, according to a police statement. Their target was a Van Cleef & Arpels necklace designed for an Egyptian royal wedding in 1939.
Made for the marriage of Princess Fawzia of Egypt and the Crown Prince of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, Sotheby’s assessed its value at between US$3.6 and US$4.6 million at a 2015 auction. The piece is made of platinum and 673 diamonds with a total weight of 200 carats.
It is the highest value art heist in Vienna since Benvenuto Cellini’s gold-and-enamel Saliera was stolen from the Kunsthistorisches Museum in 2003. That piece, valued at €50 million (S$73.9 million), was recovered three years later.
The heist is poised to refocus attention on security protocols at museums, following the the theft of about US$100 million worth of jewels from the Louvre, conducted in broad daylight in 2025. That led to the replacement of the Paris-based museum’s director.
Thieves also made off this week with a collection of 3,000-year-old gold pieces in a museum in the Spanish town of Villena.
The thieves behind Aug 27’s caper in Vienna fled in an unknown direction, according to police. They were described as two slim men about 175cm tall, with dark hair and beards. CCTV images show both wearing black clothes and dark sneakers.
Curated in conjunction with the Parisian luxury brand, the exhibition at the museum on Vienna’s famous Ringstrasse, “Prime Pieces: Van Cleef & Arpels High Jewelry x Masterpieces from the MAK Collection,” was scheduled to run until Sept 27.
The museum said in a statement that visitors can still see its collection “with the exception of the affected exhibition”. BLOOMBERG

Philippine Roblox ban call sparks wider debate over children’s online safety
The online gaming platform has been blamed for the rise in school shootings and child sexual exploitation cases in Southeast Asia

Roblox has become a flashpoint in Southeast Asia’s debate over child safety online, as officials scrutinise whether young users are being exposed to harmful subcultures on the gaming platform. But analysts warn that it might just be a convenient scapegoat for wider failures in how children are protected online and offline.
Most recently, Roblox has been linked to the August 18 school shooting in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga, where a Grade 9 student brought two firearms to a private school, live-streamed the attack and killed one schoolmate before taking his own life.

It is the chat group … that is where the coaxing happens, where the radicalisation takes place.”

OPINION - What does Syria's removal from US State Sponsors of Terrorism list mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:58:38 UTC
17:58:38 KST

The writer is a researcher at the Türkiye Research Foundation.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has officially signed off on removing Syria from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list, following the expiration of a 45-day congressional review period. The move stems from US President Donald Trump's decision, which was made after meeting with Syrian President Ahmad Sharaa at the 36th NATO Summit in Ankara in July.
This marks a major victory for the Damascus administration, which has made significant strides in global diplomatic and economic integration since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. An Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur Airbase near Idlib reaffirmed that Israel remains the primary threat to Syria's reconstruction and post-civil war recovery in this new era. Meanwhile, in a separate domestic development, Ferhat Abdi Sahin – ringleader of the former SDF, operating under the code name Mazloum Abdi – announced the dissolution of the SDF on the evening of Aug. 25, declaring the integration process complete.
These developments, most notably Washington’s decision to remove Syria from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list, amount to much more than the mere lifting of sanctions. They signal that post-Assad Syria is rapidly gaining momentum as an integrated player in the new regional order.
The US removal of Syria from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list means the end of a status that has continued since 1979. While this decision reveals that Damascus is no longer classified by the US as part of state-sponsored terrorism, it removes a significant legal and political obstacle for Syria, particularly regarding financial transactions, international banking, investments, and economic relations.
Syria's removal from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list should be read as a political and diplomatic victory prior to its economic consequences. The significance of the decision can be understood more clearly when considering the list's other members, Cuba, Iran, and North Korea, and keeping in mind that Syria was the country that remained on the list the longest. Therefore, being on this list is valuable in terms of seeing how the US positions a country in the international system, even before economic sanctions. Consequently, Syria's removal from the list serves as a declaration of the kind of relationship the Trump administration wants to establish with Damascus.
For Syria, the second and perhaps most concrete dimension of the decision is economic. The US decision to remove Syria from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list constitutes one of the final major steps necessary for previously lifted sanctions to translate into meaningful economic gains. This is because a significant portion of the legal and financial uncertainties preventing the private sector and international capital from entering Syria has now been eliminated.
A new era is beginning for Syria, particularly regarding banking transactions and reintegration into the global financial system. Given that approximately $260 billion is needed for Syria's reconstruction, this decision is critical for implementing existing investment agreements, accelerating new ones, and allowing the economy to recover and erase the scars of the civil war.
However, it should be noted that the lifting of sanctions does not automatically guarantee an influx of investment into the country. This process must be built on a sound foundation through new legal regulations, particularly in banking, finance, and foreign investment.
The decision also entails the removal of significant barriers restricting US civilian aid, military sales, and the transfer of dual-use technologies to Syria. More importantly, it eliminates one of the primary legal hurdles preventing Washington from providing military assistance to Syria or signing a future military agreement. This demonstrates that beyond its economic impact, the decision opens a new door for Damascus's integration into the international system in the fields of security and defense.
Developments unfolding in and around Syria around the time the decision took effect indicate that this is also part of a broader struggle over the country's future. While the Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur Airbase revealed that security risks capable of undermining Syria's diplomatic integration and reconstruction process still persist, the US Congress's failure to raise any objections during the 45-day review period was a notable development regarding the political balance in Washington. This shows that no overt political resistance to the Trump administration's Syria policy materialized, even in a Congress influenced by pro-Israel circles. It can be argued that lawmakers, particularly those navigating a midterm election cycle, were hesitant to openly oppose or contradict Trump's decision.
The local dimension of these developments involves the decision to dissolve the SDF. In the face of the Damascus administration's efforts to restore the country's territorial integrity, the shift in US policy on Syria has created a new equation for the SDF as well.
In an equation where Washington prefers to work with the Syrian central government, it was no longer possible for the organization, having also lost its occupation zones east of the Euphrates, to maintain its existence as an independent political-military entity.
This process ultimately concluded with Abdi's announcement that the organization had been dissolved. Thus, while the SDF issue, which stood as one of the greatest threats to Syria's unitary state structure, has been largely resolved, the possibility of Israel operationalizing the terror organization in pursuit of its vision of an unstable Syria has also been largely eliminated.
Nevertheless, considering that Israel's occupation and offensive operations in southern Syria continue, the risks remain active. On the same day, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz's visit to the occupied Jabal al-Sheikh, the protests by separatist Druze circles in Suwayda, and Hikmat al-Hijri's statement that they are an "inseparable part" of Israel demonstrate that the issue facing Syria is not merely about economic restructuring.
The decision also holds distinct significance for Türkiye. The shift in US policy on Syria significantly aligns with Ankara's vision for Syria and the region. It is also symbolically noteworthy that the decision came following the meeting between Trump and Sharaa, who was in Ankara for the NATO Summit. Washington's policy of reintegrating Syria into the international system parallels Türkiye's goals of preserving Syria's territorial integrity, strengthening its central state structure, and economically revitalizing the country.
Reactions to the Abu al-Duhur strike reveal a growing divergence between Israel's approach and the strategic value the US assigns to Syria within its broader regional vision. Despite Israel lobbying over the past 18 months to tether the lifting of sanctions to specific conditions, Washington has consistently advanced measures favoring Damascus. The repeal of the Caesar Act and this latest delisting clearly underscore that Washington has made a strategic calculation to forge a new relationship with Damascus, effectively curtailing Israeli leverage over this decision. Furthermore, the critical posture adopted by Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Ankara and special envoy for Syria, toward the Abu al-Duhur strike, specifically his warning that the attack heightens the risk of conflict with Türkiye, can be read as an explicit pushback against Israel and the Netanyahu administration.
Ultimately, the removal of the final US sanctions on Syria constitutes a renewed diplomatic triumph for Damascus and Ankara, while signaling yet another setback for Tel Aviv's objectives in the Syrian arena. Looking ahead, augmented by diplomatic, economic, and potential military backing from Türkiye, the US, and regional actors, we are likely to witness substantial progress in Syria's national reconstruction, particularly concerning the separatist Druze challenge in Suwayda.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

tato architects suspends arc tent somewhere between a hammock and a campsite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:58:30 UTC
17:58:30 KST

Tato Architects rethinks the familiar camping tent with Arc Tent, a lightweight shelter that behaves almost as much like a hammock as a place to sleep. Instead of resting directly on the terrain, its tubular equilateral triangle is suspended within a folded circular frame, raising the occupant slightly above the ground and allowing the structure to accommodate uneven outdoor surfaces.
That suspension also gives Arc Tent its defining movement. The geometric structure gently swings as people climb inside, turning a practical shelter into something closer to playground equipment. Rather than trying to eliminate every wobble from outdoor living, Tato Architects makes it part of the experience, encouraging occupants to remain aware of their own bodies — and, when sharing the space, everyone else’s.
side view of the silver Arc Tent | all images by Daici Ano
A TRIANGLE SUSPENDED INSIDE A CIRCLE
The tent’s construction is deliberately legible: a triangular tubular frame hangs within the surrounding circular structure, while pegs and ropes anchor the assembly to the ground. The resulting composition looks more like a piece of temporary outdoor furniture than conventional camping equipment, with its basic geometries doing most of the visual work.
Elevating the inner space also separates its occupants from stones, roots, damp surfaces, and the other small inconveniences that usually come free with sleeping outdoors. At the same time, the structure retains the informal quality of a hammock, allowing the shelter to respond to movement instead of insisting on remaining perfectly still.
with the light-blue outer tent draped over the frame, the silver Arc Tent opens in the background
TECHNICAL FABRICS WRAP THE LIGHTWEIGHT SHELTER
Tato Architects develops Arc Tent with different outer skins suited to outdoor conditions. A light blue version uses Dyneema Composite Fabric, a highly durable material made with ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene fibers and known for its high tear strength relative to its weight. A silver version is wrapped in polyethylene fabric designed to reflect infrared radiation.
Inside, a mesh layer keeps insects out while allowing air to circulate through the shelter. Together, the suspended frame, breathable enclosure, and technical outer fabrics turn Arc Tent into a compact experiment in how little architecture it takes to change the feeling of being outside — apparently, getting a few centimeters off the ground already goes quite a long way.

Audit: Continued confusion in national defense hiking risks of state property misuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

Audit: Continued confusion in national defense hiking risks of state property misuse
The National Audit Office has identified numerous serious problems in the activities of institutions under the Ministry of Defense's administration, which it says increase the risk of misuse of state funds and assets.
"Society is making an effort to fund the country's growing defense capabilities, but the audit shows that the Ministry of Defense, the Estonian Defense Forces and the Estonian Center for Defense Investments have not made sufficient efforts in return to resolve the serious problems with the use of funds and the accounting of assets and inventories highlighted in the state's consolidated annual report for the previous fiscal year," Auditor General Janar Holm said.
According to Holm, these are not merely technical problems but have real-world consequences, giving incompetence or malicious actors within the system an easy opportunity to waste or misuse state funds and assets.
According to the audit, defense-related inventories have been incorrectly reported in the state's consolidated annual report.
The National Audit Office issued a qualification regarding the accuracy of €1.2 billion in inventories held by institutions under the Ministry of Defense's administration. Due to significant deficiencies in the Defense Forces' inventory accounting, it is unclear which inventories, in what quantities and at what value have been recorded on the balance sheet and which have been unjustifiably omitted.
Apart from this qualification, however, the state's 2025 financial statements fairly present, in all material respects, the state's financial position as well as its financial performance and cash flows for the reporting period.
In addition, according to the National Audit Office, the Ministry of Defense violated the state's general accounting rules by unilaterally establishing an exemption for inventory accounting and failing to recognize some inventories on the balance sheet.
The Defense Forces justified creating this exemption for itself by saying that inventory records had not been maintained in sufficient detail in previous periods, meaning some of the data did not reflect the actual situation.
The Defense Forces retroactively changed the composition and value of its inventories but is unable to explain the substance of the nearly €100 million adjustment.
After the Riigikogu approved the state's consolidated annual report for 2024, the Defense Forces retroactively increased its inventory balance by €99.7 million, from €723.9 million to €823.6 million.
According to explanations provided during the audit, the change resulted from a review of categories of materiel and the recognition of additional categories. However, the Defense Forces was unable to explain which categories were added or in what quantities.
Under the Accounting Act, every accounting entry must be supported by a source document that makes it possible to independently determine why and what was adjusted, what data the adjustment was based on and how the amount was calculated.
The Defense Forces did not prepare such a document for the inventory adjustment. As a result, it is impossible to assess whether the €99.7 million adjustment was made at fair value or whether it was justified.
In the case of Defense Forces inventories, it is impossible to determine what proportion of all inventories was physically counted during the reporting year, what the results of the inventory counts were or what shortages or surpluses were identified. Because there is no consolidated overview, the Defense Forces does not have a complete picture of the volume or condition of its inventories or whether physical quantities correspond to accounting records.
According to the National Audit Office, this means some inventories could remain outside physical inventory counts for extended periods.
"This increases the risk that inventory shortages, poor condition or expiration will not be detected in a timely manner or reflected in the accounts. There is also a significant risk that misuse of assets will go undetected."
The audit found that the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) and the Defense Forces continue to have serious financial management problems involving the accounting of expenses and receivables, the management of signed contracts, the accounting of advance payments and the tracking and recognition of delivered goods.
"Another major ongoing problem is that institutions within the ministry's area of administration are not following the principles and rules established by the minister," the audit found.
Contrary to what RKIK claimed last year, the audit found that agreements to facilitate defense-related assistance have resulted in obligations and risks for the state that were not accounted for in the state budget.
The National Audit Office was able to examine agreements for facilitating the provision of defense equipment and inventories to partner countries in defense cooperation that the Ministry of Defense had failed to provide to the National Audit Office during the previous audit of the state's annual accounts. It found that the agreements had resulted in obligations and risks for the state that were not accounted for in the state budget.
As a result of the audit, the National Audit Office issued recommendations to both the defense minister and the finance minister.
The defense minister was advised to take measures to improve financial management and ensure that financial transactions are recorded in accordance with the Estonian financial reporting standard.
"In cooperation with the director general of RKIK and the commander of the Defense Forces, the defense minister must resolve the problems identified in asset accounting, physical inventory procedures and other work processes."
Permanent secretary: We admit there's more to do
Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk said the National Audit Office's observations are relevant and provide further detail on shortcomings identified in previous audits.
"We have taken steps to address them, but we acknowledge that what we have done so far has not been sufficient or that resolving the shortcomings is taking longer than expected," Kuusk said.
According to Kuusk, inventory procedures have been changed, 10 dedicated inventory positions have been created within the Estonian Defense Forces, controls over advance payments and the movement of assets have been strengthened and institutions under the ministry's administration are transitioning to digital warehouse management.
"We can confirm that the defense budget entrusted to us by taxpayers has been used for its intended purpose of strengthening Estonia's defense capabilities," the secretary added.
The state's consolidated annual report, including the report on the implementation of the state budget, provides the Riigikogu and the public with information about financial transactions that have already taken place. The state's consolidated annual report is prepared in accordance with the State Budget Act and the Estonian financial reporting standard.
The article was updated to add comments from Kaimo Kuusk.

Dairy farmers' €30M debt fate unclear as Saudi buyer takes over E-Piim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:57:00 UTC
17:57:00 KST

Dairy farmers' €30M debt fate unclear as Saudi buyer takes over E-Piim
When Estonian farmers left in debt after the bankruptcy of the country's largest dairy producer will be paid is still unclear, Agriculture Minister Hendrik Terras (Eesti 200) said.
Aound €30 million in unpaid invoices remains, but the company's new Saudi owner has said at least future invoices will be paid in time.
AS E-Piim Tootmine was declared bankrupt in March and its Paide and Põltsamaa plants were earlier this month bought at auction by Saudi retailer BinDawood for over €135 million, a sum higher than anticipated.
E-Piim's Paide plant alone is capable of processing nearly 40 percent of Estonia's milk production, with raw input coming from dairy farmers nationwide; the company is also Estonia's largest cheesemaker.
The new owner says it plans to invest in expanding E-Piim's market share, but there is unfinished business over the €30 million owed to farmers in Estonia. A delegation from BinDawood was in Tallinn Thursday and met with Minister Terras.
"The debt situation is quite complicated. There was debt owed by the cooperative to its own producers. I am not currently familiar with the cooperative's proceedings; restructuring and bankruptcy proceedings have also been discussed there," Terras said.
BinDawood CEO Ahmad BinDawood has pledged dairy farmers' invoices will not go unpaid in the future and that payments would be made on time. "We want to build good relations with farmers because they are the foundation of our success," he said.
Terras was also confident the deal should ease the concerns of Estonian dairy farmers. "The fact that the Paide plant was bought up is surely very good news for the Estonian dairy market. It is a place where Estonian producers can deliver their milk," he said.
Ahmad BinDawood said the aim is to increase E-Piim's market share and to expand into EU markets, adding E-Piim's skilled workers will be instrumental in achieving these goals, meaning their jobs are not at risk.
Local investor Joakim Helenius took part in the auction. He, too, said the eventual buyer may be a boon. "It did end up in foreign hands, but in the hands of foreigners who could potentially be of great benefit to Estonian dairy farmers and the Estonian economy," Helenius said.
Helenius had been part of a consortium of Estonian companies hoping to keep E‑Piim in local hands, but the advantage of the new owner is that it may open the Middle Eastern market — which due mainly to climate relies heavily on imports despite its large dairy sector — to Estonian dairy farmers.
However, E-Piim's plants will need investment in equipment for producing higher-protein products, and this investment may be difficult to obtain in the short term due to a glut of orders, Helenius added. "All dairy processors want the same equipment right now. It will certainly take a year and a half or two years before the plant has the equipment installed."
Saudi retail giant BinDawood Holding won the auction for the two plants with a €135.25 million bid, well above the €80 million starting price. The deal, submitted through its Estonian subsidiary, marks BinDawood's first major move into Europe's dairy industry and is part of its strategy of expanding food-sector investments. A third E-Piim plant in Järva-Jaani, Järva County, with a starting price of €8 million, drew no buyers.

Norway’s King Harald V dies, succeeded by son
Harald V, who was Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, has died at the age of 89. His son will reign as King Haakon VIII.
Norway’s King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after being hospitalised with a rare blood condition.
The death of Europe’s oldest reigning monarch was announced on Friday by the Royal Palace of Norway.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Son of Norway’s crown princess denies rape as trial opens in Oslo
- list 2 of 3Epstein files set off Norwegian political storm: What we know
- list 3 of 3Norway’s King Harald in ‘extremely serious’ condition, palace says
“King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, Aug 28 at 6:35 a.m,” the palace said in a statement.
His son, Crown Prince Haakon, automatically succeeds him and is expected to reign as King Haakon VIII.
Royal family members had visited the king on Thursday, and crowds gathered outside the palace and laid flowers for the king after officials warned that his condition had turned “extremely serious”.
Harald was hospitalised on August 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne 35 years ago, has had multiple health problems in recent years, forcing him to have a pacemaker fitted and to scale back his official schedule.
But he had always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.
Harald was Norway’s first king born on Norwegian soil since the 14th century. Taking the throne in January 1991, after the death of his father, Olav V, he presided over decades of oil-fuelled prosperity.
He was born in February 1937, near Oslo. When the Nazis invaded Norway his mother fled with him and his sisters to Sweden and then the United States, while his father and grandfather, Haakon VII, sat out the war in Britain.
Harald won lasting public affection for his speech in 2011 after Anders Behring Breivik‘s bomb attacks which killed 77 people, telling mourners: “I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear.”
His death, however, comes at a fraught time for the monarchy, after documents published in January showed Crown Princess Mette-Marit corresponding with notorious US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, years after his conviction.
Her 29-year-old son, Marius Borg Høiby, the new King Haakon’s stepson, was sentenced in June to four years in prison on two counts of rape and 32 other charges, including domestic violence.

Fewer Estonians on subsistence benefits, but costs keep rising
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Fewer Estonians on subsistence benefits, but costs keep rising
Fewer people are applying for Estonia's subsistence benefits this year, but the rising cost of living and a higher income threshold are keeping spending on the aid high.
The Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture plans to provide 46 local governments with an additional €1.1 million to cover benefit payments through the end of the year.
Local governments spent €20.6 million on subsistence benefits in the first seven months of 2026, down 1 percent from the same period last year. Applications fell 7 percent in July, but the average monthly cost per application rose 6 percent.
Andrus Jõgi, an adviser at the ministry's Local Government Policy Department, said the increase reflects both inflation and the higher subsistence threshold introduced this year.
"On one hand, costs have risen because of inflation, such as heating and electricity costs," he said. "On the other hand, the subsistence threshold has also increased."
The additional funding will vary widely, from an extra €1,000 for some municipalities to €115,000 for the largest recipient. Smaller local governments generally need more help because even a small change in the number of applicants can significantly affect their budgets.
Kati Nõlvak, head of economic well-being policy at the Ministry of Social Affairs, said the subsistence threshold is also set to rise in line with the consumer price index (CPI) next year, under an agreement reached last year.
"Last year it was agreed that that figure should be €231 [a month] per adult and €277 per child," she added.
The 2026 state budget allocated €42.5 million to reimburse local governments for subsistence benefits, up from €36.7 million last year.
Next year's planned allocation is €36.5 million, but Nõlvak said the lower figure does not necessarily signal a major drop in spending. Not all of this year's allocation is expected to be used.
"You have to look at what's behind the numbers," she explained, noting that several legislative changes taking effect this year had prompted the ministry to budget a higher amount for the benefit.
"Even this year, we won't be spending all of the more than €40 million that was allocated," she added.
