Gaza war magnifies decades-long crisis over Palestinian remains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:48:50 UTC
17:48:50 KST

Palestinians marked the National Day for the Recovery of the Bodies of Palestinian and Arab Martyrs on Thursday as the number of Palestinian remains held by Israel reached unprecedented levels, underscoring a decadeslong struggle by families seeking the return of their loved ones.
The annual observance, held Aug. 27, highlights the plight of families whose relatives’ bodies are being kept in Israeli military morgues or buried in closed military cemeteries known as “graves of numbers.”
The issue has taken on new urgency since Israel launched its war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
Hundreds of unidentified bodies have been returned to Gaza, while thousands of Palestinians remain missing, leaving families uncertain about the fate of their relatives.
The Palestinian Cabinet designated Aug. 27 as a national occasion in 2008 to mobilize legal and popular efforts to establish the fate of missing Palestinians, recover their bodies and ensure they are returned to their families for burial.
The Palestinian National Campaign for the Retrieval of Martyrs’ Bodies and Disclosure of the Fate of the Missing, a nongovernmental organization, said Palestinian prisoners’ institutions have documented the names of 799 Palestinians whose bodies are being held by Israel.
The campaign said 256 of the bodies are buried in “graves of numbers,” while 99 belong to Palestinians who were prisoners. The list also includes 81 children under 18 and 10 women.
But recent Israeli reporting suggests the actual number could be significantly higher.
Haaretz reported Aug. 11, citing two Israeli security sources, that Israel is holding about 1,700 Palestinian bodies, most of them from Gaza, for possible use in future prisoner or hostage exchanges.
The discrepancy reflects the difficulty of establishing the full number of Palestinians whose remains are being held, particularly amid the destruction and mass displacement caused by the Gaza war.
“Graves of numbers” is the term Palestinians use for closed Israeli military cemeteries where Palestinian and Arab bodies have been buried without their names being publicly identified.
Instead, graves are marked with numbers corresponding to files containing information about the person buried there.
The practice in its modern form dates to the late 1960s and expanded after the 1967 war.
The cemeteries are generally located in restricted military zones, preventing families from visiting the graves or knowing precisely where their relatives are buried.
The cemeteries have historically held the remains of Palestinians and Arabs, including Lebanese nationals.
For Palestinian families, the graves represent more than the withholding of remains.
They are also a source of prolonged uncertainty, as relatives can spend years or decades without knowing exactly where a loved one is buried or being able to conduct a traditional funeral.
Israel has increasingly used the detention of Palestinian bodies as a tool in negotiations.
Since 2015, Israel has expanded its policy of retaining Palestinian remains. In 2017, its security Cabinet approved the continued detention of certain bodies for potential use in negotiations.
In September 2019, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that military authorities could hold Palestinian bodies under the 1945 Emergency Regulations, including for the purpose of negotiations over the return of Israelis or their remains.
The security Cabinet broadened the circumstances for holding Palestinian bodies again in 2020.
Palestinian officials and rights groups have condemned the practice, arguing that the dead should not be used as leverage in political or security negotiations.
International humanitarian law requires parties to armed conflicts to respect the dead and their graves and to facilitate the return of remains to families whenever circumstances permit.
The International Committee of the Red Cross has documented customary international humanitarian law rules requiring respect for the remains of people who die during armed conflict and efforts to facilitate their return.
Article 34 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions also calls for respect for the remains of people who died in connection with armed conflict or occupation and provides for their return when circumstances permit.
Israel’s war in Gaza has added a new and much larger dimension to the longstanding issue.
Israeli forces have transferred hundreds of bodies out of the enclave, while thousands of Palestinians remain missing amid widespread destruction and continued difficulties accessing areas where people were killed.
The National Campaign to Recover the Bodies said that, as of Feb. 4, 2026, Israel had returned 930 Palestinian bodies to Gaza, along with 66 boxes containing human remains.
The campaign said some of the remains were taken from cemeteries in Gaza and areas around the al-Shifa Medical Complex in Gaza City.
Identifying the remains has proved difficult because Palestinian authorities lack sufficient DNA-testing equipment and supplies. Teams have instead had to rely on traditional identification methods and information provided by families searching for missing relatives.
The National Campaign and Palestinian prisoners’ institutions said Wednesday that the number of detained bodies could rise as investigators obtain more information and identify additional victims. They said thousands of Palestinians remain missing in Gaza, while extensive destruction has made it difficult to reach areas where people may have been killed.
The crisis also extends beyond bodies removed from Gaza. Thousands of Palestinians are believed to remain buried beneath the rubble of destroyed buildings inside the enclave.
Zaher al-Wahidi, director of the Health Information Unit at Gaza’s Health Ministry, said Aug. 20 that about 7,400 bodies remained trapped beneath the rubble, with recovery teams unable to reach many of the sites.
The scale of the deaths has made identifying and recovering the missing an enormous challenge. Gaza’s Health Ministry says Israeli attacks have killed more than 73,400 Palestinians and injured more than 174,400 since October 2023.
Since a U.S.-brokered cease-fire took effect Oct. 10, 2025, Israeli attacks have killed 1,303 Palestinians and wounded 4,336, according to the ministry.

US judge rules Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:48:00 UTC
17:48:00 KST

US judge rules Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful
August 28, 2026
A United States federal judge has ruled in favor of the artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic in its dispute with the Pentagon over its labeling as a "supply chain risk."
California district judge Rita Lin concluded that the label constituted an attempt by the government to make an example of Anthropic after the company refused to allow unrestricted military use of its technology and criticized the Department of Defense's use of AI.
Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling that "the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics."
She said the government's actions were "based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its 'arrogance' in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model."
An Anthropic spokesperson said they welcomed the judge's ruling, saying in a statement: "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."
Anthropic AI: What is the Pentagon dispute all about?
The dispute between the San Francisco-based firm and the government broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security after the company declined to allow unrestricted military use of its technology.
"We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America's warfighters and civilians at risk," wrote CEO Dario Amodei in a blog post back in February, adding that AI wasn't reliable enough to be used in fully autonomous weapons systems and expressing concerns over mass surveillance.
In March, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk" – a highly unusual label to apply to a US firm. The company complained of an "unlawful campaign of retaliation," pointing out that the designation would have negative consequences for its business beyond defense deals.
Indeed, President Trump ordered all US government agencies to stop using Anthropic technology, calling it "a radical left, woke company" and "out-of-control" in a social media rant.
Defense Secretary Hegseth said companies would be expected to cut business links to Anthropic if they wanted to be considered for defense sector deals.
Shortly afterwards, OpenAI, Anthropic's primary tech industry rival and operator of ChatGPT, made its own deal to work with the Pentagon.
Anthropic ruling: What else did Judge Lin say?
In her ruling, Judge Lin, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote that neither the US Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows them to "impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."
Earlier in the legal proceedings, Lin had temporarily blocked the Pentagon from labeling the company as a supply chain risk and blocked enforcement of Trump's social media directive ordering all federal agencies to stop using Anthropic and its chatbot Claude.
In a preliminary hearing on July 30, Lin had said that the government's position was "really troubling" and seemed "at odds to me with the First Amendment."
The White House is yet to comment on the decision.
In the coming weeks, Anthropic is expected to launch on the US stock market with an initial public offering (IPO) that could potentially eclipse SpaceX's record Wall Street debut in June, which raised $86 billion (€74 billion).

Ukrainian eggs blamed for UK salmonella outbreak – Telegraph
Unknown

Ukrainian eggs blamed for UK salmonella outbreak – Telegraph
British health officials believe that eggs imported from Ukraine could be responsible for a major salmonella outbreak in the UK, The Telegraph has reported, citing a source.
A total of 259 people in the country have been infected with the bacteria over the past year, with one of them dying, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said in a statement on Thursday.
The agency stressed that the exact source of the contaminated products has yet to be established, but added that the outbreak “could all be associated with imported eggs.”
However, a senior official involved in the investigation of a salmonella outbreak in the Netherlands, where over a hundred cases have been registered, told The Telegraph that the “working hypothesis” among his British counterparts is that the unsafe eggs were of Ukrainian origin.
The cases, involving three closely related salmonella strains, were recorded over a year-long period, with a spike in recent weeks, UKHSA said.
Almost half of the victims, ranging from babies to people in their 90s, required hospitalization, the statement read.
Salmonella causes intestinal infection, typically resulting in diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal cramps. While most patients recover without specific treatment, the disease can be life-threatening for people with weakened immune systems.
Investigators believe the people were infected after consuming eggs served in “small cafes, restaurants, and takeaway businesses,” rather than eating at home, UKHSA said.
Chief Scientific Adviser at the Food Standards Agency Ian Young urged the British public to give up on traditional fried eggs with a runny yolk as long as the spread of salmonella continues.
The UK produces most of its eggs at home, with UKHSA assuring that they are perfectly safe. The country imports only 11% of its eggs, with Ukraine being the largest supplier, accounting for almost a third of them.
The exemption from tariffs on Ukrainian eggs exported to Britain, introduced after the escalation between Ukraine and Russia in February 2022, will remain in place until 2028, despite the EU reimposing barriers last year.
In July, EU health authorities linked Ukrainian-made instant noodles to a salmonella outbreak that affected more than 100 people across over a dozen member states.
A few months before that, Azerbaijan’s food safety agency reported discovering the bacteria in a 4.9-ton batch of frozen chicken coming from Ukraine.

Sanajy Raut on one-year extension for drivers to learn Marathi
NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut on Friday alleged that the BJP-led Maharashtra government extended by a year the deadline for auto and taxi drivers to learn Marathi as it was “under pressure from Delhi," referring to the BJP’s central leadership.“The Marathi proficiency initiative was not for the Marathi language but for non-Marathi people, including drivers. Delhi pressured the government to roll it back. We had been watching this move and anticipated pressure from Delhi for the rollback, which happened yesterday,” Raut told the media in Mumbai, according to PTI.
The Rajya Sabha member described the decision as a “message” from the BJP to its allies, including deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, that they would have to “listen” to whoever succeeds chief minister Devendra Fadnavis.“By extending the deadline for drivers to learn the language by a year, the chief minister has shown that he is the boss. The announcement was an arrangement to remind the allies and send a message that they have to listen to the person who succeeds the incumbent CM,” Raut said, referring to speculation about a possible central government role for Fadnavis.He also addressed speculation that the rollback was linked to the crucial assembly elections in BJP-led Uttar Pradesh, which are due early next year.
Uttar Pradesh accounts for a sizeable number of migrant and non-Marathi-speaking drivers settled in Maharashtra, including Mumbai."Elections may have dictated the decision, but the issue was of Marathi language," Raut stated.On Thursday, Fadnavis announced that autorickshaw and taxi drivers would be given one year to acquire functional knowledge of Marathi, following demands from representatives of migrant, non-native drivers.“The state government has accepted their demand and is giving them one year. No action will be taken during this period,” the chief minister said.Autorickshaw and taxi unions on Friday welcomed the decision, saying the extension removed the immediate threat to drivers’ livelihoods.
The move came a week after the Transport Department, headed by Shiv Sena minister Pratap Sarnaik, issued notices to drivers who failed Marathi “working knowledge” tests conducted by RTO officials on the roads.The BJP-led Maharashtra government had announced in April that drivers of commercial vehicles must have functional knowledge of Marathi. It said those failing the test would be given one month to acquire working knowledge of the language, failing which their badges would be suspended for three months.

U.S. Army orders $99 million worth of drone-detecting gadgets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:42:18 UTC
17:42:18 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Heaviside Industries Inc. a contract worth up to $99 million for its MOTH spectrum analyzer.
- The indefinite-delivery contract runs through August 27, 2031, with work locations determined by individual task orders.
The U.S. Army signed a deal worth up to $99 million for a small handheld gadget that can detect drones and other radio signals on the battlefield.
The device is called MOTH, short for a spectrum analyzer, and it’s made by a California company called Heaviside Industries. The Army’s contract runs through 2031, according to a Department of War announcement, and covers buying, fielding, upgrading and maintaining the devices over that period.
Heaviside Industries is based in Marina del Rey, California. The company won the contract after the Army opened bidding online and got 99 companies competing for it.
So what does MOTH actually do? Think of it as a pocket-sized radio detector for soldiers. It picks up signals anywhere between 5 MHz and 6 GHz, a wide enough range to catch most drone control links, walkie-talkies and other communications gear. It weighs less than a pound with the battery in, about the size of a large smartphone, and soldiers can wear it on a vest or carry it in a pack.
The device tells a soldier not just that a signal is present, but roughly which direction it’s coming from, using a built-in direction-finding feature. It also has GPS, a small screen, and vibrates to alert the user when it picks something up. It’s built to survive rain, dust and rough handling, rated to work anywhere from 14 to 131 degrees Fahrenheit.
A single MOTH unit runs about $4,950 through retailer Lumenier, which is inexpensive by military technology standards. That low price matters because it means the Army can hand these out widely instead of reserving expensive detection gear for specialists.
According to the trade outlet Soldier Systems Daily, MOTH is meant mainly for soldiers trained in electronic warfare, but it’s simple enough that almost anyone in a unit could use it to spot a nearby drone or radio signal without needing special training.

US court backs Anthropic over Pentagon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:40:55 UTC
17:40:55 KST

US court backs Anthropic over Pentagon
A US court has struck down the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic, ruling that it illegally sanctioned the AI developer for refusing to let its Claude model be used for certain military operations.
In a 59-page ruling issued on Thursday, US District Judge Rita Lin said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority by designating Anthropic a “supply-chain risk to national security.” She also argued that the move amounted to unlawful retaliation under the First Amendment and deprived Anthropic of due process under the Fifth. 
“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” she wrote.
Lin said the government had sought to make a public example of Anthropic for its “arrogance” in criticizing Washington, adding that Hegseth’s supply-chain designation violated the statute invoked by the Pentagon and was “arbitrary and capricious.”
The dispute grew out of the Pentagon’s push to provide the military with access to AI models for “any lawful use.” Before the standoff, Anthropic had been deeply involved with the Pentagon, with Claude being deployed for various operations. Anthropic also held a Pentagon agreement worth up to $200 million.
However, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued in February that while he supports the use of Claude for military ends, it should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or guiding fully autonomous weapons because its current frontier models are not reliable enough for the latter task.
As the tensions escalated, US President Donald Trump ordered federal agencies to cease using Anthropic technology on February 27, branding the company a “radical Left AI company.” Hegseth meanwhile announced the supply-chain-risk designation and declared that the Pentagon’s partners could no longer conduct commercial activity with Anthropic.
Anthropic vowed to challenge the designation, saying such treatment had historically only been reserved for US adversaries. It sued in March, alleging that Washington had retaliated against its protected speech and denied it a chance to contest the allegations before imposing the sanctions.
Hegseth, however, stood his ground, comparing Anthropic’s red lines to “Boeing giving us airplanes and telling us who we can shoot at,” and calling Amodei an “ideological lunatic.”
In the ruling, Lin stressed that the Pentagon “is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice” and remains free to abandon Claude if Anthropic’s conditions do not meet its requirements. Yet the Pentagon itself had been reluctant to lose access to the model, with one defense official telling Axios in February that “the problem for these guys is they are that good.”
A separate lawsuit from Anthropic is also pending in Washington, DC over a supply chain risk designation that could lead to its exclusion from civilian government contracts.

Norway Cleared for $270m 155mm ammunition sale
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:37:49 BST
17:37:49 KST

The United States has approved a possible $270 million Foreign Military Sale to Norway covering additional 155mm M795 high-explosive artillery projectiles and associated support, according to the US Department of State.
The State Department notification, issued on 5 August under Transmittal 26-82, covers further M795 ammunition to be added to an existing Foreign Military Sales case alongside technical assistance, documentation and engineering, logistics and programme support.
The original case was valued at $99.99 million and remained below the threshold requiring congressional notification. The latest approval brings the estimated value of the combined package to $270 million.
The notification does not specify the number of additional projectiles requested by Norway. The package is classified entirely as non-Major Defense Equipment and includes the ammunition itself together with the services required to support the programme.
The M795 is a conventional 155mm high-explosive artillery projectile used with NATO-standard 155mm artillery systems. It is designed as a general-purpose high-explosive round and forms part of the wider family of ammunition used by US and allied artillery forces.
Norway has been expanding and modernising its land-based fires capability in recent years, including through its operation of the South Korean-built K9 Vidar 155mm self-propelled howitzer. The NATO member has also placed greater emphasis on ammunition stocks and artillery capacity as European countries seek to replenish inventories and increase readiness.
The State Department said the proposed sale would improve Norway’s ability to meet current and future threats while increasing interoperability with American and other allied forces.
In the notification, the department stated: “The proposed sale will improve Norway’s capability to meet current and future threats and increase its interoperability with the U.S. and other allied forces.”
It added: “This proposed sale will enhance Norway’s artillery and mid-range fire capability. Norway will have no difficulty absorbing this equipment into its armed forces.”
The proposed transaction forms part of the US Foreign Military Sales process, through which approved defence equipment and services are supplied to foreign governments under government-to-government arrangements. Congressional notification is required when proposed sales exceed specified thresholds, depending on the equipment involved and the status of the purchasing country.
American Ordinance in Middletown, Iowa, and General Dynamics in Camden, Arkansas, have been identified by the State Department as the principal contractors for the proposed package.

Global Spirits is a major international alcohol holding company that includes the Khortytsia distillery (Zaporizhia), the Odesa Cognac Factory (Odesa) and the Ukrainian Distribution Company. Its head office is in New York, U.S. According to Opendatabot, the holding’s three legal entities were owned by Yevgen Chernyak until July 2022, after which ownership passed to Liechtenstein citizen Mikael Martin Wachter.
The holding owns more than 15 local, regional and international brands, including Khortytsia, Pervak, Shustov, Morosha, Oreanda, San Marino, Mikado and Medovukha. Global Spirits products are exported to more than 87 countries.
Global Spirits revoked its license to manufacture and distribute its products on the Russian market on February 24, 2022, in response to Russia’s military invasion of Ukraine.

Pegatron chair urges Taiwan to prioritize nuclear power over solar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:36:12 UTC
17:36:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should rely more on nuclear power because solar energy uses too much land and cannot provide steady electricity for industry, Pegatron Corporation Chair Tung Tzu-hsien (童子賢) said Thursday.
Speaking at an environment ministry event, Tung said advanced chips, AI computing, and electric vehicles require large and reliable amounts of electricity. He said the country has limited room for large-scale solar development because less than 30% of its land is flat or gently sloped, CNA reported.
Tung also questioned whether solar power should automatically be considered environmentally friendly. Solar panels generally need to be replaced after about 20 years, creating large amounts of waste, he said.
Even if Taipei, including Yangmingshan and the Keelung River area, were covered with solar panels, they would still provide less than 10% of domestic electricity demand, Tung said. He supported solar power as a supplementary source but said it should not form the core of the country’s energy system.
Tung also warned about the country’s dependence on imported solar equipment. He said China controls about 80% of the solar panel market, which could leave Taiwan vulnerable to supply disruptions.
Stable electricity is essential for continued industrial growth, Tung said. He argued that intermittent solar and wind power cannot provide the same steady supply as power sources that can operate continuously and said nuclear power offers a low-carbon alternative.
Tung pointed to Switzerland, which is similar in land area to Taiwan and gets more than 30% of its electricity from nuclear power. He said Taiwan should also consider a greater role for nuclear energy despite its mountainous terrain.
He said TSMC and its wider semiconductor supply chain depend on reliable electricity to keep growing. Tung described these industries as important parts of the domestic economy.
Tung also compared generation costs, saying nuclear power costs about NT$1 (3.2 cents) to NT$1.5 per kilowatt-hour, while solar power costs about NT$4.5. With the country using nearly 300 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, he said every NT$1 increase in generation costs would add about NT$300 billion in annual expenses.
Addressing safety concerns, Tung said newer nuclear reactor designs have improved cooling systems, stronger safety mechanisms, and better accident containment. He said these changes have significantly improved safety compared with older reactor designs.

The protests began as a fight for justice but ended up nearly becoming part of Fedorov's new political project, the expert says.
The cardboard protests, whose participants supported Mykhailo Fedorov, ended with an attempt to use them as the foundation for the former defense minister’s new political project. Political expert Oleksandr Chernenko wrote about this, analyzing the start of the new political season.
According to him, Fedorov himself ended the rallies by publishing a campaign video address.
"Paradoxically, Fedorov himself ended the protests. The politician whom the protesters were defending found time to record a campaign address, but did not find time to come out to the people. The participants in the Maidan emphasized that they were for Fedorov and against politics, elections, and speculation. But Fedorov said the opposite: he is for elections," Chernenko wrote.
The expert emphasized that after Fedorov’s video address, the organizers of the Maidan were forced to distance themselves from the politician and wind down the protest.
"The organizers of the Maidan quickly realized that Mikhail was no longer on the same path with them – he had received the political springboard he needed. And the statement about elections came as a complete surprise: people were still standing outside the Verkhovna Rada and demanding "Fedorov – to the Ministry of Defense!", while he was already campaigning for elections and preparing for a political tour of the United States. Under these conditions, the protest became pointless – and it was wound down," the expert wrote.
In the expert’s view, Fedorov was able to use the protests as the launchpad for his own political career.
"The former defense minister managed to appropriate the protest’s political capital, but did not take responsibility for the protest itself. People felt that they had been used: they came out against injustice, but nearly became extras in yet another political project," Chernenko concluded.
As previously reported, Mykhailo Fedorov published a video in which he named holding elections as one of his political demands. Maidan organizer Dmytro Koziatynskyi said that the demand for elections "is so ridiculous that I cannot imagine how anyone can even think about it now." Fedorov’s adviser Serhii Sternenko also rejected the idea of holding elections during the war: "Elections are unacceptable in any form while the full-scale aggression continues. More deposit bottles returned but still short of legal mandate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:34:33 UTC
17:34:33 KST

More deposit bottles returned but still short of legal mandate
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Although more people are returning their cans and bottles for recycling and cash back, the mandatory collection target of 90% is not being met, just as it hasn’t since the deposit scheme was first introduced five years ago.
According to Verpact, the foundation that oversees the statiegeld (deposit) system in the Netherlands, based on figures from the first half of the year, 78% of deposit bottles will be collected in 2026; for cans, that number jumps to 86%.
Since 2021, when the deposit scheme for bottles and cans was first introduced, producers and importers have been required by law to collect and recycle 90% of plastic bottles and cans.
While the percentages have been increasing – last year 77% of plastic bottles and 83% of cans were returned – the 90% target is unlikely to be reached again this year, according to Verpact’s preliminary 2025 annual report.
“We cannot continue doing what we have always done and expect to continue meeting our statutory targets in the future,” said Hester Klein Lankhorst, Verpact’s chair of the executive board, of the changing European landscape.
She said companies currently not taking a deposit should be obliged to and calls for more recycling capacity in Europe. She sees a ban on selling cans and bottles without deposits as a possible future step.
Fines
Following the Human Environment and Transport Inspectorate’s (ILT) threat of fines this year, Verpact came up with additional incentives for consumers: a national sweepstakes with cash prizes for those returning their bottles and cans and even a lottery to encourage people to do so.
Verpact also added 2,500 more drop-off points this year, saying it expects to meet its legal requirement to have 5,400 new collection points in supermarkets and public places before the end of the year.
Verpact invested more than €220 million in the deposit system last year and paid €626 million to consumers who returned their recyclables. But by failing to hand in all their bottles and cans, Dutch consumers left €129 million unclaimed. That money goes back into the deposit system and is spent on items like new return machines.
The Netherlands has some 9,900 deposit-return points and 23,000 donation points.
And although coffee capsules are not part of the cash-back scheme, since January 1, 2026, consumers can return them – along with household aerosols (think deodorant or whipped cream cans) – in the PMD bins (plastic packaging, metal packaging, and drink cartons) due to an agreement between Verpact and the Coffee Capsule Recycling Association, reports NU.nl.

Expert’s opinion to HC contradicts govt stand on patented cancer drug
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:31:44 UTC
17:31:44 KST

NEW DELHI: Contradicting the government claim that generic breast cancer drug palbociclib can be used as an alternative to patented drugs in the same group, noted oncologist and Magsaysay award winner Dr R Ravi Kannan has opined that these drugs are not interchangeable. He explained that ribociclib benefits early-stage breast cancer and can reduce recurrence and improve overall survival, while palbociclib trials have shown that it has no role in early breast cancer treatment.Dr Kannan, the director of Cachar Cancer Hospital and Research Centre, Silchar, a nonprofit hospital that provides free cancer treatment, gave his opinion in a case before the Kerala High Court filed by a patient seeking access to expensive patented breast cancer drugs. After the patient’s death, the court took it up suo moto in public interest. It concerned the most common breast cancer subtype, hormone receptor positive and HER2-negative tumors.
The petition sought a government use licence under section 100 of the Patent Act, to enable access to ribociclib, a patented drug, at affordable prices. However, government refused to issue a government use licence stating that breast cancer did not constitute a matter of national emergency and that the National Cancer Institute in Jhajjar, and Chittaranjan National Cancer Institute in Kolkata had said that generic palbociclib could be used as an alternative to ribociclib.
Dr Kannan’s letter stated that despite palbociclib, abemaciclib and ribociclib being CDK4/6 inhibitors, they “cannot be interchanged in the early breast cancer (adjuvant) setting”. He cited the trial which showed that adding abemaciclib to endocrine therapy significantly reduced recurrence, and extended follow up of seven years showed significant invasive disease-free survival and improved overall survival. He also cited trials that found that giving ribociclib for three years along with non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor, a type of hormone therapy drug used to treat hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, significantly improved the outcomes. The trial showed significant improvement in invasive disease-free survival and reduction in recurrence of the cancer in parts of the body far from the original breast tumor. He added that two large trials had shown that palbociclib in early breast cancer did not show similar advantages.Citing the trial results, Dr Kannan stated that the approval of generic palbociclib in India should not be seen as providing an equivalent adjuvant option. “Clinicians must use the evidence-based drugs--abemaciclib or ribociclib--when indicated for high risk early-stage patients, since palbociclib’s adjuvant trials showed no benefit,” stated the letter.He pointed out that the high cost of abemaciclib and ribociclib meant that vast numbers of high-risk patients who could benefit from these drugs simply could not obtain them. Ribociclib is over Rs 78,400 per month and Abemaciclib Rs 47,700 to 95,500 per month.“Generic entry has historically been the single most reliable lever for expanding access to targeted cancer therapies in resource-limited settings, and there is no clinical reason to expect abemaciclib and ribociclib to be an exception,” stated Dr Kannan adding that only by substantially lowering prices can the lifesaving benefits of these drugs reach the broad population of high-risk patients in India.The latest affidavit submitted on August 14 by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), the apex regulator for pharmaceuticals in India, includes tables that show that both palbociclib and ribociclib are approved for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer. But the affidavit also records a separate January 2026 approval for ribociclib for early-stage breast cancer in patients at high risk of recurrence. “CDSCO’s own data shows an additional early-stage breast cancer indication for ribociclib that is not shown for palbociclib. Yet the affidavit then says the two medicines have been approved for the same indications. This is a serious contradiction. A drug regulator has a responsibility to place clear and accurate information before the court, particularly when women’s access to life-saving treatment is at stake,” said Gargeya Telakapalli, co-ordinator, Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments.
“Nearly one lakh women are dying of breast cancer every year. If that is not a public health emergency, what is? This case has been going on since 2022. The woman who first approached the Court died before she could get the medicine she needed. Many more women have died while this case has continued. The government cannot keep treating access to breast cancer medicines as an ordinary pricing dispute. Women need the best available treatment when it can still save their lives,” said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group.

Dobrindt: Security task force and enhanced drone defense agreed at Baltic summit
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that Baltic and European leaders at a special hybrid security meeting agreed to plans to set up a new security task force and to enhance collective drone defense capabilities.
The assembled politicians discussed "urgent security policy questions for a shared future in the Baltic Sea region," Dobrindt said amid the meeting at the Mürwik naval training center in Flensburg on Germany's northeast coast
"Foreign powers are trying to attack our security with hybrid measures, to destabilize our democracies, to weaken our economy," he said. "Drone attacks, cyber attacks, spying, disinformation, arson attacks on critical infrastructure, covert operations and the use of 'disposable agents' are all rapidly increasing in number."
Dobrindt warned that the recent past had shown a pronounced increase in the "quality and intensity" of such attacks and surmised that "we must prepare ourselves for the hybrid threat situation continuing to intensify."
He said the shared goal was to bolster defense against such hybrid threats.
"We want to investigate, deter and defend altogether more quickly," Dobrindt said, saying they wanted to work together to transform the Balitc from a "collective risk area" into a "collective defensive area."
The assembled politicians from Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, Norway and Ireland — the current holder of the rotating EU presidency — had a working lunch at the Mürwik base amid the talks.
They were also taken out on the Baltic Sea in a German Federal Police motorboat.
Germany will stick to 'Lake Ontario' despite Trump's 'Lake America' renaming
Germany intends to continue referring to the body of water between the US and Canada as Lake Ontario, despite US President Donald Trump's decision to rename it as "Lake America" amid his growing rift with Canada.
"This is an American decision to refer to this lake by a different name. For the time being, it has no further implications for other countries," said a spokesman for the German Foreign Ministry on Friday. "As far as we are concerned, it remains Lake Ontario, which is the customary name."
The spokesman went on to argue that "in the US, football is called 'soccer,' but that doesn't mean it's called 'soccer' in other countries as well."
When asked whether the decision could culminate in fresh Trump resentment toward Berlin, the spokesman said that naming of waterways "should not be a reason to harbour political resentment toward anyone."

Berlin mayor: Hackers trying to blackmail city hall after data breach
Berlin's Mayor Kai Wegner says the city-state's government is being blackmailed by hackers who breached several sectors of its administration earlier in this month.
"Berlin has become a victim of a serious crime," Wegner said, albeit adding that the state "will not allow itself to be blackmailed."
German news magazine Spiegel reports that the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin or just over €2 million (roughly $2.3 million).
As a result of the cyber attack, departments like city planning, construction, housing, mobility, transportation and environment and climate protection were all isolated from the state government network for around a week, starting on August 14.
Among other things, it meant that it was not possible to apply for or pay out housing benefits for several days.
At first, officials said they did not believe sensitive data had been captured. Then on Wednesday of this week, the state government said it was possible that personalized or non-public information might be affected.
According to Spiegel, a ransomware group known as Rhysida is claiming responsibility in a post on the dark web, saying it had secured some 6 terabytes of data and putting a countdown to the time of its publication alongside a demand for 30 bitcoin.
Rhysida gained notoriety in 2023 when it hacked the online information systems of the British Library and published leaked material when it was not paid the bitcoin ransom it demanded.

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is the guest on this Friday's "Interview der Woche" political podcast by public broadcaster ARD.
Much of the interview revolves around domestic policies directly in Klingbeil's ministerial wheelhouse, like the sugar tax, planned income tax reforms, and Germany's difficult economic situation more generally.

Klingbeil said that the second issue should be to address oil companies "profiteering" as a result of the unrest in Iran and the Gulf, arguing that consumer prices were not a fair reflection of the oil prices or economic fundamentals.
He said he wanted the question of windfall taxes on oil companies to once again be discussed at an EU level.
"The oil companies are making gains on the back of this geopolitical situation," Klingbeil said. The leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the eastern German state of Thuringia, Björn Höcke, failed on Friday in an attempt to topple State Premier Mario Voigt of the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) with a vote of no-confidence.

Like on the first occasion, Höcke once again argued that Voigt's recently revoked doctorate renders him unsuitable to head up the state government. Voigt had an appeal rejected by the University of Chemnitz last month, prompting Höcke's latest no-confidence vote.
"You are a plagiarist," he told Voigt, and described his coalition with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the left-wing populist BSW as a "plunder gang."
Voigt, on the other hand, said the vote in his favor was a strong show of support and told Höcke: "I won't allow you to drag me down."
The vote in Thuringia came a week ahead of key local elections in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD have a significant lead in the polls and could potentially form a majority far-right government.
Star sprinter Owen Ansah to challenge NADA doping ban in court
European 200 meter champion Owen Ansah plans to challenge the German Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) proposal to suspend him for failing to provide a sample on demand.
Ansah faced a 20-day deadline to accept a doping ban of four years, with a possibility of it being shortened to three, or to seek a court hearing at Germany's sports arbitration court.
NADA announced Ansah's decision on Friday as the deadline expired but said it could provide no further information on the trial or its timeline.
The case is unusual as Ansah is not accused of failing a doping test. He's accused of refusing to provide a sample, which is treated as a direct indication of guilt.
But Ansah has previously argued that the tester came to his hotel room out of the agreed timeframe, when he was running late for a plane, and so he refused to comply. He also argues that him providing a clean sample the next day to the World Anti-Doping Agency in a separate test rendered the issue moot.
Most recently his lawyer said the sprinter would be making no further comments on the issue amid the likelihood of an appeal.
Ansah has continued to compete this summer amid the dispute, winning gold in the 200 meters at the European Championships and bronze in the 100 meters, as well as 100 and 200 meter gold in the German championships. Accepting the ban would disqualify him from these competitions retroactively.
The German with Ghanaian heritage is 25, so a lengthy suspension could effectively mean the end of his career — making it prohibitively difficult for him to maintain his performance level, and with his physical peak potentially passing amid the ban.

Germany risks missing 2026 climate target
Germany is on course to miss its legally binding climate target this year, according to preliminary calculations by the Agora Energiewende think tank.
Greenhouse gas emissions fell by only around 7 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent in the first half of 2026, a decline of about 2% compared with the same period last year.
Agora estimates that Germany will emit around 635 million tons of CO2 equivalent over the full year. That would exceed the country's 2026 limit of 625 million tons.
Germany emitted 648.9 million tons in 2025.
Agora said the decline so far this year was driven largely by weak economic activity and high fossil fuel prices rather than structural progress on cutting emissions.
The think tank said the energy price shock triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had pushed up oil and gas prices and contributed to lower fossil fuel use.
Germany is required to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 65% from 1990 levels by 2030, equivalent to annual emissions of no more than 439 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent.
Agora said meeting that goal would require emissions to fall by an average of around 40 million tonnes a year.

German unemployment remains above 3 million
The number of unemployed people in Germany remained above three million in August despite signs of an improving economy, official figures showed on Friday.
Germany's Federal Employment Agency said 3.061 million people were unemployed, 54,000 more than in July and 36,000 more than a year earlier.
The unemployment rate rose to 6.5% from 6.4% in July.
Adjusted for seasonal effects, unemployment increased by 4,000.
"Even in August, there is little momentum in the labor market beyond the usual seasonal pattern," Federal Employment Agency head Andrea Nahles said, adding that the subdued trend of recent months was continuing.
Unemployment first climbed back above three million in July. Joblessness typically rises during the summer, while Germany's weak economy has also weighed on employment.
There have recently been signs that the economic outlook is improving. The Ifo business climate index rose for a fourth consecutive month in August to its highest level in a year, while German exporters have also become more optimistic.
Germany sees earliest-ever start to grape harvest
Germany's grape harvest has begun earlier than ever recorded following an exceptionally hot summer, according to the German Wine Institute.
"It was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions," institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. "Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays for it."
The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also the first grapes destined for premium wines.
Harvesting is expected to begin "on a large scale" next week.
Büscher said the main harvest was starting one to two weeks earlier than in recent years, which was already earlier than it was decades ago.
"Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it's certainly four weeks earlier," he said.
The harvest could be completed as early as September because many grape varieties are ripening at roughly the same time.
"This will be a very fast harvest," Büscher said.
Growers are also picking grapes early to prevent sugar levels from becoming too high. More sugar generally produces wines with a higher alcohol content, while demand is increasingly for lighter wines with less alcohol.
Prolonged heat can also reduce the fruit acidity characteristic of many German wines.

Iran’s unseen supreme leader fuels questions over who is in charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

Six months after the airstrikes that triggered the war and thrust a badly wounded Mojtaba Khamenei into the role of Iran’s supreme leader, he remains almost completely absent from public view, creating an unusual vacuum at the center of the country’s leadership.
Questions about Khamenei’s health and ability to govern are becoming increasingly sensitive as Iran faces critical decisions over a war that has destabilized the Middle East and further battered its already fragile economy.
Iranian officials and senior sources familiar with the leadership say Khamenei remains firmly in control, governing largely from the shadows because of security concerns while recovering from injuries that have reportedly left him disfigured.
They say he has delegated much of the day-to-day running of the country to a small group of senior officials.
But Khamenei has not appeared in a photograph or video, nor has he delivered a recorded audio message, since he was appointed supreme leader about a week into the war. His prolonged absence has fueled growing skepticism among Iranians in a political system where the supreme leader is expected to project authority and remain the ultimate voice on matters of state.
“The question is no longer whether Mojtaba is alive, but whether Iran still has a functioning supreme leader,” said Alex Vatanka of the Middle East Institute in Washington.
Khamenei has communicated with the Iranian public only through a small number of written statements read by state broadcasters. He was also notably absent from the elaborate weeklong funeral rites held for his father last month, further intensifying speculation about his health and whereabouts.
Iranian officials and insiders attribute his continued absence to fears of assassination. They insist, however, that he remains actively involved in governing, holding frequent meetings with senior officials, receiving reports on major developments and making the final decisions on key national issues.
President Masoud Pezeshkian said Aug. 10 that he had held a seven-hour meeting with Khamenei.
But even among the Islamic Republic’s most hard-line supporters, doubts are creeping in.
“We need to hear our leader’s voice, or see any sign that he is there on top and leading the country to give us more confidence,” said a member of the Basij volunteer militia in Qom, the seminary city at the heart of Iran’s theocratic state.
The Basij member, who requested anonymity to discuss such a sensitive subject, said he believed Khamenei was still making key decisions. But he said the lack of even a photograph was damaging morale and not in Iran’s interest.
Among Iranians who oppose the ruling hierarchy or want broad reforms, the message is blunter.
“How do we know that Mojtaba has not been killed?” said Shahrokh, a pro-reform businessman in Tehran who also requested anonymity.
“It is not logical that there is not a single sign proving he is alive, let alone evidence that he is involved in decision-making,” he added.
Iran has weathered six months of war with its most powerful enemies to emerge battered but still standing. Its political system has held. Its military retains the ability to choke off global energy supplies and strike U.S. Gulf allies.
The clerical establishment has shown it can absorb the loss of a supreme leader and senior commanders without collapsing, maintaining a political and military chain of command loyal to its theocratic ideology.
But Iran’s economy is buckling under the cost of the conflict and a months-long blockade of its oil exports, which has cratered the rial currency, risking a resumption of the mass protests that authorities crushed in January by killing thousands of demonstrators.
Meanwhile, the ruling establishment has reorganized around a clear imperative: preserve the state, restore deterrence and stop the economic fallout from destabilizing the country.
The Revolutionary Guards, long a powerful force, grew in influence from the start of the war and remain central to strategic thinking at the top of a reconfigured ruling system centered on the Supreme National Security Council, the sources said.
That upper echelon includes top Guards commanders as well as senior political figures such as Pezeshkian and parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf.
Several senior sources reached by Reuters in Iran said Khamenei was holding meetings with those top figures, was fully involved in deliberations and had the final say on all major questions.
A senior Iranian official said only a small number of officials retained direct contact with Khamenei in person and that no details about him had been published for fear of leaking information that could allow the U.S. to target him.
His health is meanwhile improving significantly, said a person close to Khamenei’s inner circle, describing him as sharp and involved in decision-making.
“Despite all the pressures, services to the people have not stopped. Our foreign policy line is unified and our decisions are coherent. All of this shows the supreme leader is in charge,” a second official said.
Even before the war, Khamenei preferred a backroom role as his father’s top aide, shunning public attention. His wounds in the early hours of Feb. 28, when Israel and the United States launched their war with airstrikes that killed his late father, disfigured his face, according to senior sources.
But now elevated to a role seen as conferring divine guidance, and at the country’s moment of greatest crisis since the 1979 revolution, such considerations look unconvincing.
“A genuine deal with Washington requires Mojtaba’s unmistakable approval and so does any decision to sustain a long and costly conflict with the United States,” said Vatanka.
“His prolonged absence has created a dangerous situation in which rival factions can all claim to know what the leader really wants,” he added.

New paraglider could give British troops an innovative way to strike from the sky
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:30:02 BST
17:30:02 KST

New paraglider could give British troops an innovative way to strike from the sky
A MOD-backed UK start-up has developed the UK's first foot-launched military paraglider, which can take off with no runway, helicopter or drop aircraft required.
- UK’s first foot-launched military paraglider systems could give British troops the freedom to take to the skies independently, with no runway, helicopter or drop aircraft required.
- The gliders can be assembled in under eight minutes, in darkness, and are capable of travelling up to 200 miles on their own power.
- British start-up Blakcro expands workforce with MOD support, showing defence is an engine for growth.
British soldiers could be equipped with rucksack-sized powered paragliders for covert missions in hostile territory, following a new invention by a UK start-up this year.
Backed by around £6 million from the Ministry of Defence (MOD), British start-up Blakcro has developed the UK’s first foot-launched military paraglider systems. A pilot can launch the system by running, powered only by their own legs and the glider’s engine. The gliders will enable troops to fly covertly into hostile territory without a runway, helicopter or drop aircraft.
Supported by UK Defence Innovation (UKDI) – the MOD’s ‘front door’ for companies that have not previously worked with defence – Wiltshire-based Blakcro has designed the unique gliders specifically for military use, with the company supplying systems this year and into 2027.
The glider folds into a case approximately the size of a large rucksack and can be assembled in under eight minutes in complete darkness, with a low acoustic, visual and radar signature designed to support stealth insertions into hostile territory.
Built around a UK-made titanium airframe, the glider can travel up to 200 miles under its own power, and accommodates body armour, night vision equipment and weapon mounts. The technology is already in operational use, with contracts held across the UK and with NATO allies. The Royal Marines and Parachute Regiment are now looking to trial this individual approach to air mobility in the coming months.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP, said:
  With UK Defence Innovation supporting SMEs like Blakcro from the drawing board through to deployment, we are building a more resilient, homegrown defence supply chain and ensuring our armed forces receive the pioneering equipment that can give them the edge on the battlefield.
Defence has a new way of working with industry, backing British innovation to deliver cutting-edge capability for our armed forces and good jobs in regions like Wiltshire.
Blakcro first engaged with UKDI, part of MOD’s National Armaments Director Group, through its Open Call for Innovation and has since received support across two other projects. One such project has received a Defence Innovation Loan, enabling the company to scale from a single product to full production.
Blakcro’s growth reflects the wider ambition of UKDI to strengthen the UK’s sovereign defence supply chain. Since receiving UKDI support, the company has grown from 3 to 11 employees and now holds 3 prime contracts with the UK and with NATO allies.
Sam Wedgwood, Founder and Chief Executive Officer at Blakcro, said:
  From a UKDI success story perspective, we have very rapidly moved from base technology in 2024, through UKDI-supported rapid innovation, through to purchase, through to operational use by 2026. We could not have done that at this pace without the support we have received – not just the funding, but the commercialisation support and the access to the right people. UKDI kept telling us we were special. I think it’s mutual.
The partnership between Blakcro and UKDI is an example of the government backing agile, homegrown innovators to deliver cutting-edge military capability and sustainable growth, strengthening the UK’s defence industrial base while keeping our armed forces ahead of emerging threats.

Ukraine maps supply chain behind Russian Iskander missiles
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:29:41 BST
17:29:41 KST

Ukraine’s military intelligence has published new data identifying components, companies and individuals it says are connected to production of Russia’s 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile, including dozens of foreign-made electronic parts found in recovered weapons.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence, known as the GUR, said in a statement published on Telegram that the latest release adds information on 140 Russian and foreign components, 35 enterprises and 108 officials and employees associated with the missile’s production chain.
The information has also been added to Ukraine’s War&Sanctions database, where the GUR is beginning a wider series examining Russian ballistic missile production and the industrial networks supporting it.
The combined database presented by Ukrainian intelligence is broader than the newly released material. According to the GUR, it now contains an interactive model of the 9M723 and information on more than 170 identified components, 82 Russian and two Belarusian companies involved in the production chain, 108 officials and employees, and 121 pieces of foreign-made manufacturing equipment used by the companies concerned.
Of the 140 components newly disclosed, Ukrainian intelligence said only around a quarter were manufactured by Russian companies. It attributed 63 components to US manufacturers, eight each to Switzerland and Belarus, four each to Germany and Taiwan, and three to China.
The GUR drew particular attention to electronics used in a flight-information processing unit associated with the missile’s laser gyroscope. According to the Ukrainian agency, five of 43 identified components in that unit were Russian-made.
Foreign components identified by the GUR include microprocessors, field-programmable gate arrays, memory devices and digital-to-analogue and analogue-to-digital converters. Manufacturers named by the agency include DM&P Electronics, Xilinx, now part of AMD, Atmel, now part of Microchip Technology, Winbond Electronics, Micron Technology and Analog Devices.
The presence of a commercially produced component inside a Russian weapon does not by itself establish that the manufacturer supplied the Russian defence industry directly. Electronic components can move through distributors, intermediaries and secondary markets before reaching their eventual end user, while Western governments have progressively tightened export controls intended to restrict Russian access to sensitive technology since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Ukrainian intelligence said the latest disclosure was intended to provide governments with additional information for sanctions and export-control measures targeting Russia’s ballistic missile supply chain.
The GUR also used the publication to make new claims about an updated version of the Iskander missile. It said Russian forces had employed an upgraded weapon designated 9M723-2 during a combined missile attack on Kyiv during the summer, describing the missile as also being known as “Iskander-1000” and associating it with a system called “Bora-M”.
According to the Ukrainian intelligence assessment, the modified missile uses a larger propulsion section and launcher and has a claimed range of up to 550 kilometres, compared with approximately 390 kilometres for the 9M723-1 configuration cited by the agency. The GUR said other elements of the missile remained largely identical to those of the earlier version.
Those details represent the Ukrainian intelligence service’s assessment of the recovered weapon and have been presented by the agency as part of its analysis of Russian ballistic missile development.
The 9M723 is the ballistic missile associated with Russia’s road-mobile Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system. Russia has used Iskander ballistic missiles extensively against targets in Ukraine, alongside air-launched missiles, cruise missiles and increasingly large numbers of uncrewed attack aircraft.

In the Kyiv region, rescue workers extinguished a fire involving 13 vehicles.

IN BRIEF: Damaged house in Sevastopol, supermarket in Moscow Region, 512 UAV attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:27:10 UTC
17:27:10 KST

MOSCOW, August 28. /TASS/. Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 512 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry reported.
As a result of a drone attack in the Yaroslavl Region, one person was killed and 27 were injured.
A supermarket in Moscow Region's Pavlovsky Posad was attacked by a drone, and the shock wave damaged a nearby clinic. In Sevastopol, a five-story building and two kindergarten buildings were damaged by a drone attack.
TASS has compiled key information on the aftermath of the attacks.
Scale
- From 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on August 27 to 8:30 a.m. Moscow time on August 28 (from 5:00 p.m. GMT on August 27 to 5:30 a.m. GMT on August 28), air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 512 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry said.
- The drones were destroyed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Vladimir, Voronezh, Kursk, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Oryol, Penza, Rostov, Ryazan, Saratov, Tambov, Tula, Yaroslavl, Moscow, and Krasnodar Regions, Crimea, and the Black Sea water.
- More than 70 Ukrainian drones were destroyed last night in seven districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar reported.
- A total of 67 Ukrainian drones attacked the Yaroslavl Region, Governor Mikhail Yevrayev reported on his Max channel.
Consequences
- A drone struck a supermarket in Pavlovsky Posad, near Moscow, regional head Andrey Vorobyov reported.
- A nearby clinic was damaged by the blast wave.
- Forty-six windows were shattered, and two examination rooms were damaged.
- The clinic in Pavlovsky Posad remains open despite the damage caused by the blast wave from the drone attack, Vorobyov noted.
- The governor added that all damaged windows will be replaced "as soon as possible."
- A power line was damaged in the Voronezh Region as a result of falling debris, Governor Alexander Gusev stated.
- Two villages and a farmstead remain without electricity.
- Two residential buildings burned down in the Tambov Region as a result of an enemy drone attack, the regional government’s press service reported on its Max channel. There were no fatalities or injuries.
- Two kindergartens in Yaroslavl were closed while authorities addressed the aftermath of a drone attack, regional head Mikhail Yevrayev reported on his Max channel.
- As a result of the Ukrainian attack on the Yaroslavl Region, debris struck industrial infrastructure, residential areas, and commercial facilities, he noted.
- All fires that broke out are being quickly extinguished.
- As a result of the drone attack, one person was killed and 27 were injured in the Yaroslavl Region.
- Some ten people were injured when debris fell on an intercity bus.
- In addition, 17 others sustained injuries of varying severity.
Attack on Sevastopol
- A five-story apartment building in Sevastopol was severely damaged by a drone strike, city governor Mikhail Razvozhayev said.
- The blast wave also damaged two buildings of a kindergarten that was preparing to reopen on September 1 following renovations.
- In addition, more than 15 cars were damaged.
- The drone was loaded with metal pellets and explosives, Razvozhayev specified.
- The blast wave shattered windows and window frames and damaged balconies throughout the building. Furniture and walls were damaged in many apartments.
- In addition, drone debris caused a grass fire.
- Two people were injured, and two others sustained minor injuries as a result of the drone attack in Sevastopol.
- According to preliminary reports, an elderly woman suffered a closed head injury and a man sustained back lacerations from shrapnel.
Reaction
- The Russian Investigative Committee have opened criminal cases over the terrorist attacks (Article 205 of the Criminal Code) following Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets in the Belgorod Region and Sevastopol, Spokeswoman Svetlana Petrenko told TASS.

Türkiye’s economic confidence index rose 0.8 percent month-on-month in August to 100.6, according to official data released on Aug. 28.
The index has now increased for four consecutive months and moved back above the 100 threshold, which indicates an optimistic outlook on the general economic situation. In 2026, the index last exceeded the 100 threshold in February, when it stood at 100.7.
The increase was driven by gains in consumer and manufacturing sector sentiment. The consumer confidence index rose 1 percent from the previous month to 90.8, while the real sector (manufacturing industry) confidence index increased 1.2 percent to 102.4, the data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) showed.

17:26:49 KST

Russian investigators have released Ilya Traber, a prominent St. Petersburg businessman with alleged ties to President Vladimir Putin, from pre-trial detention, the news outlet Fontanka reported Friday.
The investigation reportedly justified the decision to release Traber based on a “sharp decline” in his health. The businessman, however, still faces charges of organized murder and arms trafficking.
Traber, 75, was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention in mid-June. He and his longtime business partner, Vladimir Danilenko, are accused of hiring two men to carry out the 2020 contract killing of businessman and politician Alexander Petrov.
Traber first drew public scrutiny for his ties to the Russian president during Putin’s early political career.
In 2011, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that Traber had met with the Kremlin leader in the 1990s to discuss an oil terminal project. At the time, Putin was working in the St. Petersburg mayor’s office.
Years later, Peskov said Putin knew Traber but could not confirm if the two were on friendly terms.
Traber, who had built a shipping and port empire in northwestern Russia during the 1990s, has reportedly surrendered ownership stakes in at least four major companies during his two months in detention.
There has been no official confirmation of Traber’s release from law enforcement agencies.
According to Fontanka, he walked out of Moscow’s Lefortovo prison on Thursday evening and was traveling back to St. Petersburg.

Russian drone hits warehouse storing books from Readeat, Book.ua and Ukrainian publishers
A Russian drone struck a warehouse in Kyiv on 27 August, where books belonging to the Readeat and Book.ua bookshops and a number of Ukrainian publishing houses were stored. Some of the print runs were destroyed in the fire.
Source: Dmytro Feliksov, founder of Readeat
Details: Due to the damage to the warehouse, orders will not be dispatched from there on 28 August. Ukrainian publishers that stored part of their print runs there also reported losing books.
The Ouroboros publishing house said that its books stored in warehouses operated by Readeat and Book.ua partners were likely destroyed.
Osnovy also reported losses. The publisher said it was currently awaiting official information about the extent of the damage and possible losses. Meanwhile, their orders continue to be dispatched from a backup warehouse in another region.
Yuliia Orlova, CEO of Vivat, also reported that the Kyiv warehouse where the publisher's books were stored was destroyed by fire as a result of the attack. According to Orlova, the exact scale of the losses is still being assessed.
"We lost in this lottery of where the strike would land tonight. So today, the Kyiv warehouse where Vivat's books were stored burned down," Orlova wrote.
She noted that the publisher had previously begun moving some print runs to other regions. Some books were transported to Lviv and distributed among bookshops.
Nonetheless, many new releases and books by Ukrainian authors remained in the Kyiv warehouses. The publisher had been preparing for the Book Country festival, so Vivat's participation in the event is now also in question.
"We are still counting the losses because these are essentially books destroyed by fire in three warehouses: ours and our partners'," Orlova said.
Two publishers – KSD and KnyhoLand – cancelled their participation in this autumn's Book Country festival, which will take place from 17 to 20 September.
KSD said that, in addition to its book stalls, it would not hold the planned events with authors and readers. The decision to cancel was prompted by the security situation in the capital.
Two weeks ago, KnyhoLand also announced that it was cancelling its participation. The company said it could not take part because it had lost a large number of books as a result of Russian attacks.
Background:
- On 1 August, the warehouses of the Ranok publishing house in Kharkiv were destroyed. As a result, the following publishers were also affected: Readberry, Zhorzh, Fabula, Shche Odna Storinka, Varvar Publishing, Osnova, Svoie, Korali Books, Kenhuru and 4mamas, as well as the KnyhoLand bookshop chain. Nearly 8 million copies of books – 28,800 titles – were destroyed.
- As a result of the Russian attack on Kyiv on 16 August, the publishers RM and BookChef at the Pochaina book market were also affected.
- Overall, Russia destroyed around 13 million books in summer 2026.

Türkiye’s exports rise 2.9 percent to $25.6 billion in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
08:25:31 UTC
17:25:31 KST

Türkiye’s exports increased 2.9 percent year-on-year to $25.62 billion in July, according to official data released on Aug. 28.
Imports rose at a faster pace of 5.1 percent to $32.97 billion, provisional data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK and the Trade Ministry showed.
The country’s foreign trade deficit consequently widened 13.6 percent from a year earlier to $7.34 billion.
The export-to-import coverage ratio declined to 77.7 percent from 79.4 percent in July 2025.
Excluding energy products and non-monetary gold, exports grew 3.1 percent to $23.79 billion, while imports advanced 3.6 percent to $26.19 billion.
The resulting foreign trade deficit excluding those categories stood at $2.41 billion, with the export coverage ratio at 90.8 percent.
On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, exports increased 2.6 percent from June, while imports fell 7.2 percent.
Manufacturing products accounted for 94.4 percent of Türkiye’s total exports in July, followed by agriculture, forestry and fishing at 3 percent and mining and quarrying at 1.8 percent.
High-technology products made up 4.4 percent of manufacturing exports, up from 4.2 percent a year earlier. Their value rose 4.7 percent to nearly $1.06 billion.
Intermediate goods represented 69.4 percent of total imports, followed by consumer goods at 16 percent and capital goods at 14.5 percent.
Germany remained Türkiye’s largest export market in July, receiving goods worth $2.04 billion. It was followed by the U.S. at $1.68 billion, the U.K. at $1.35 billion, Iraq at $1.11 billion and Italy at $1.11 billion.
China was the largest source of imports, with shipments valued at $5.04 billion, followed by Russia at $3.23 billion, Germany at $2.52 billion, the U.S. at $1.89 billion and Italy at $1.55 billion.
In January-July, Türkiye’s exports rose 3.4 percent year-on-year to $161.54 billion, while imports increased 4.7 percent to $222.09 billion.
The seven-month trade deficit grew 8.3 percent to $60.55 billion, while the export-to-import coverage ratio slipped to 72.7 percent from 73.6 percent.
{HH] Energy import bill rises 13 percent
According to official data, Türkiye’s energy import bill increased by 13.1 percent year-on-year in July, reaching $5.83 billion.
The figure, which covers imports of mineral fuels, mineral oils and products of their distillation, bituminous substances and mineral waxes, stood at $5.15 billion in July last year.
Crude oil imports rose by 0.3 percent year-on-year to 2.93 million metric tons in July.
In the January-July period, Türkiye’s energy imports totaled $40.1 billion, up 7.2 percent compared with the same period of the previous year.

China exports first homegrown F-class heavy-duty gas turbine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:25:30 CST
17:25:30 KST

Workers check a 50-megawatt (MW) G50 turbine to be exported to Kazakhstan at a factory of Dongfang Turbine Co., Ltd. in Deyang City, southwest China's Sichuan Province, on June 22, 2026. China shipped its first domestically developed F-class heavy-duty gas turbine for overseas use on Friday, marking a step forward in its push to enter a global market long ruled by a handful of international manufacturers. (Xinhua/Xu Bingjie)
CHENGDU, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China shipped its first domestically developed F-class heavy-duty gas turbine for overseas use on Friday, marking a step forward in its push to enter a global market long ruled by a handful of international manufacturers.
A truck carrying the 50-megawatt (MW) G50 turbine, developed by Dongfang Turbine Co., Ltd., left Deyang City in southwest China's Sichuan Province for Kazakhstan.
The delivery is part of an order signed in November 2025 to supply three G50 units for a power generation project in Kazakhstan. It is the first overseas order for a Chinese-developed F-class heavy-duty gas turbine.
Li He, deputy general manager of the company, said it will also provide lifecycle services for the units and has customized components, including air intake and rotor systems, to meet local operating requirements.
Heavy-duty gas turbines are critical equipment for power generation and mechanical drive applications.
F-class turbines, among the most widely used heavy-duty gas turbines globally, operate at temperatures of around 1,400 degrees Celsius. Their development involves expertise in more than 100 fields, including high-temperature alloys, precision casting and aerodynamics.
China has expanded its domestic capabilities in heavy-duty gas turbines in recent years, with independently developed models now covering capacities of up to 550 MW, said Fang Yu, head of a national laboratory for clean and efficient turbine power equipment at Dongfang Turbine Co., Ltd.
The export comes amid rising global demand for gas turbines, driven in part by growing electricity consumption from artificial intelligence data centers and changes in the global energy mix.
Feng Zhenping, a professor at Xi'an Jiaotong University, said China's manufacturing supply chain, delivery capacity and cost competitiveness could help its turbine manufacturers gain a larger foothold in the international market. ■

Ukrainian Railways report on situation with train delays from Russian attacks
Passengers on several Ukrzaliznytsia trains (Ukrainian Railways) will be transferred to other routes travelling to their destinations, while some trains from Przemyśl, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Kyiv and Lviv will depart with significant delays.
Source: Ukrzaliznytsia
Details: According to the company, no long-distance trains have been cancelled, and delays are gradually being reduced. However, the consequences of prolonged air-raid warnings and Russian attacks will continue to affect services for at least another day.
Transfers on the final section of routes are necessary to speed up the turnaround of carriages and locomotives and return services to schedule, Ukrzaliznytsia explained.
Until the morning of 29 August, passengers may use paid waiting lounges at railway stations free of charge. Passengers can warm up, drink tea and charge their phones there.
Background:
- Due to the aftermath of combat operations, Ukrzaliznytsia trains experienced significant delays – for example, the Kharkiv-Chełm train was running 11 hours and 30 minutes late in the morning, while the Sumy-Kyiv train was 17 hours and 15 minutes late.
- Ukrzaliznytsia reported that on trains delayed by more than five hours due to Russian attacks, meals are being organised for passengers and railway workers at intermediate stations together with World Central Kitchen.
- The company also advises passengers to bring a supply of water and snacks before setting off, as journeys may take longer than planned due to the security situation.
