UN rights office condemns US designation of Palestine Action as 'terrorist' group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:59:14 UTC
06:59:14 KST

UN rights office condemns US designation of Palestine Action as ‘terrorist’ group
- The UN rights office condemned the US designation of Palestine Action as a terrorist group, calling it a disproportionate restriction on free speech and civic rights.
- Palestine Action has targeted Israel-linked defence firms with disruptive protests, claiming to oppose Israel’s military actions and save lives.
- Experts warn the designation aims to silence critics, with similar bans in the UK sparking protests and legal challenges.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The UN human rights office said on Aug 27 that the Trump administration’s designation of the Palestine Action group as a terrorist organisation was “a disproportionate and unnecessary restriction” on free speech rights that amounted to an expansive use of the term terrorism and will have a chilling effect.
Washington designated Palestine Action on Aug 26 as a terrorist group, saying the step was part of US President Donald Trump’s effort to crack down on left-wing groups in its counter-terrorism efforts. Israel’s Foreign Ministry welcomed the designation.
The designation “appears to be both a disproportionate and unnecessary restriction on the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association as well as the right to participate in public affairs”, the office of United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said.
“Expansive use of the term ‘terrorism’ has been documented to have a chilling effect on civic space.”
Britain previously banned Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation, which was also condemned by Turk’s office. The UK’s Supreme Court has said it will hear an appeal against a lower court ruling that Britain’s decision to ban the campaign group as a terrorist organisation was lawful.
Palestine Action has targeted Israel-linked defence companies in Britain, especially Israel’s largest defence firm Elbit Systems, often blocking entrances or spraying red paint.
It was banned by Britain shortly after a break-in at the Royal Air Force’s Brize Norton base in June 2025 in which activists damaged two military planes. The UK ban on the group had prompted protests in which about 3,000 people were arrested.
The group says its activities “have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine” and opposing Israel’s assault on Gaza. It says it uses “disruptive tactics” to target “corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex.”
The Trump administration has attempted to deport pro-Palestinian foreign protesters, threatened a funding freeze for universities over protests, enforced social media screening for immigrants and sanctioned critics of US ally Israel.
Ben Saul, UN special rapporteur on human rights and counter-terrorism, and Francesca Albanese, a UN expert on the occupied Palestinian territories, also raised concerns about Washington’s designation.
Such steps aim to silence critics, said Albanese, who herself has been sanctioned by the US after she called Israel’s military actions in Gaza a “genocidal campaign” and called for war crime prosecutions.
Sarah McLaughlin, senior scholar of global expression at free speech group FIRE, said that “we must reject that censorship – not import it”. REUTERS

The Trump administration has attempted to deport pro-Palestinian foreign protesters, threatened a funding freeze for universities over protests, enforced social media screening for immigrants and sanctioned critics of US ally Israel.
Ben Saul, UN special rapporteur on human rights and counter-terrorism, and Francesca Albanese, a UN expert on the occupied Palestinian territories, also raised concerns about Washington’s designation.
Such steps aim to silence critics, said Albanese, who herself has been sanctioned by the US after she called Israel’s military actions in Gaza a “genocidal campaign” and called for war crime prosecutions.
Sarah McLaughlin, senior scholar of global expression at free speech group FIRE, said that “we must reject that censorship – not import it”. REUTERS

Australia faces 'sliding doors' moment to turn AI boom into local wealth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:51:40 UTC
06:51:40 KST

Australia in a 'sliding doors' moment to determine who reaps rewards of AI boom
In short:
Australia's growing appeal as a destination for data centres has given it rare bargaining power as global tech giants race to build AI infrastructure.
Local AI companies want the federal government to use that leverage to secure affordable computing power so Australian businesses can capitalise on the boom.
What's next?
The government says this is a "sliding doors" moment as it launches a new partnership to get major Australian companies buying more locally developed AI technology.
Christopher Sampson had to take his Australian artificial intelligence (AI) startup Tiliter overseas before customers at home would take it seriously.
For Michael Gately, scaling up his AI company from Australia has meant competing in a global scramble for expensive and increasingly sought-after computing power.
Both chief executives have found ways around these business constraints. Still, their experiences highlight the challenges Australia faces as it tries to capture more of the economic gains from AI.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton has declared Australia is at a "sliding doors" moment to ensure the country becomes a "creator" rather than a "renter" of AI.
The nation's AI startups agree and want Australia to leverage its advantage as an attractive destination for data centres to negotiate guaranteed and affordable access to computing power.
How Australia can get a 'return' for hosting data centres
Australian companies currently are heavily reliant on the small number of tech businesses that control the world's advanced computing capacity.
That capacity is generated by large electricity-hungry data centres. Australia has become a very attractive place to host these centres.
The federal government is in the process of developing national standards to govern the approval of data centre projects, which have increasingly attracted community backlash.
Working with states and territories, the government will establish rules around their location and their use of electricity and water.
Once built, data centres employ relatively few people directly, which means simply hosting them does not guarantee Australia a large share of the economic benefits they enable.
But Mr Charlton has argued Australia does have the bargaining power to dictate better terms.
"If you want to build a data centre in Australia, you should be prepared to make some of that compute available to Australian businesses, researchers and startups," he said in a speech this month.
Mr Charlton said this would ensure Australia got a greater "return" from the AI boom.
Australian companies urged to buy local AI technology
Computing power is not the only hurdle, however, with many Australian AI startups struggling to find domestic buyers to support their companies.
Yesterday, the federal government unveiled a new "Buy Australian AI Partnership" backed by the nation's Big Four banks to help local AI companies win customers.
Mr Charlton said the more than 1,500 Australian AI companies were already building "world-class" technology, but the challenge was getting in front of the organisations that could buy their product.
"We are in a sliding doors moment for Australia's AI industry," he said.
"As the importance of this technology grows, we need to ensure Australia is a creator and not just renter of AI."
The difficulty convincing Australian businesses to buy local AI products is well known to the Tiliter co-chief executive Mr Sampson, whose company creates vision software widely used by retailers, including for self-checkouts.
He said it took proving his technology in international markets to get "validity" back in Australia.
"Fortunately, I had a German co-founder, which gave us access to that market," Mr Sampson told the ABC.
"If I didn't, I'm not sure I would have taken that step.
"So I do wonder how many great Australian companies get stifled because they just can't get over that threshold in the early days in the Australian market."
Mr Sampson said there must be "leadership and risk taking" at a corporate level.
"If we're willing to back Australian companies, we do have capability here that we can unlock," he said.
Mr Sampson said while subsidies could help Australian AI companies develop their technology, nothing compared with winning an early customer at home.
"Compute support helps you build, but customers prove the value," he said.
"The first serious Australian customer can be worth more than any grant because they provide the real-world validation and credibility a company needs to compete."
Australia at risk of being 'squeezed out' of AI race
The Buy Australian AI partnership is an initiative of startup accelerator Stone & Chalk, with chief executive Stela Solar saying it is key to helping local tech companies succeed.
"Australian enterprises really need to lean in a little bit more and open the door to Australian innovation," she told the ABC.
Local companies are developing tools for medical diagnosis, speech and image recognition, agriculture, mining, finance and retail uses.
Along with encouraging more Australian businesses to purchase these tools, Ms Solar said it was critical the government worked to secure domestic computing power for startups to grow.
"If we don't secure compute capability for homegrown technologies, we actually risk being squeezed out of the very sovereign AI foundations that we're building here," she said.
"That means while we might experience productivity gains from AI, we won't gain from the wealth growth that AI is bringing because that will land in other countries."
Ms Solar, who has previously worked for tech giants in the US, said there was also a need for deeper investment, research and development partnerships between major tech players and Australian startups.
"Australia can sometimes be treated like a sales office, and that's something with the data centre wave we actually have every chance to reshape," she said.
Australian-owned technology key to solving AI 'trust issue'
It is a sentiment shared by Mr Gately, who is the chief executive of Trellis Data, an AI firm based in Canberra.
Mr Gately said the computing power his company needs can take months to secure, while its price can change by as much as 50 per cent in the space of a week.
"Given the amount of investment that Australia is accepting from the US tech suppliers, such as Nvidia or Dell, we should provision a 'set aside' for Australian companies to be able to have price certainty for a period of time," he said.
Mr Gately said Australia's negotiating position was particularly strong due to the backlash of the poorly managed rollout of data centres in the US.
He said there was clearly a "very big trust issue" with AI at the moment and believed establishing a strong Australian industry was key to gaining community support.
"There is a substantial fear among Australians broadly around AI,"
"They definitely know they need to use it. And those who know there's a future of massive benefit are very pro Australia having its own capability in this space."
Mr Gately said he often found people were relieved to learn Australia was producing globally competitive AI models.
"I think people go, 'Well, thank goodness for that, that someone is out there able to compete,'" he said.

August 19, 1953: A turning point in Iran’s struggle for sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:45:00 UTC
06:45:00 KST

August 19, 1953: A turning point in Iran’s struggle for sovereignty
TEHRAN — August 19, 1953, remains a pivotal and deeply contested date in Iran’s modern history. The events surrounding the overthrow of Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh and the subsequent political developments have continued to shape Iranian perceptions of foreign intervention, national sovereignty and independence.
Mosaddegh, who had led the nationalization of Iran’s oil industry, was removed from power following Operation Ajax, a covert operation involving the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and Britain’s MI6. The coup marked a major turning point in Iran’s political history and paved the way for the consolidation of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi’s rule.
For many Iranians, the events of 1953 remain a symbol of foreign interference and the struggle to safeguard the country’s political and economic sovereignty. The subsequent decades of the Pahlavi monarchy were marked by growing political repression, including the activities of SAVAK, the monarchy’s intelligence and security organization.
The 1953 coup also left a lasting legacy in Iran’s relations with Western powers. The episode continues to feature prominently in Iranian political discourse, particularly in discussions over foreign intervention, control of national resources and the right of nations to determine their own political future.
More than seven decades later, Operation Ajax remains a reference point in debates over Iran’s independence and resistance to external pressure. From Tehran’s perspective, the experience of 1953 reinforced the conviction that national sovereignty must be protected against attempts by foreign powers to influence Iran’s internal affairs.
The legacy of August 19, 1953, therefore extends beyond the events of a single day. It remains part of a broader historical narrative in Iran concerning sovereignty, independence and resistance to foreign domination.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres expressed support for the victims of the war crimes committed by former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladić, who died in a prison hospital in The Hague. LRT reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The Secretary-General expresses his solidarity with the victims, survivors, and their families

Westpac's economic growth forecast ahead of GDP
Westpac has now provided us with its gross domestic product (GDP) preview ahead of Wednesday's ABS publication.
Senior economist Pat Bustamante is the author.
Growth remained stuck in the slow lane, with GDP expected to rise 0.2%qtr and 1.7%yr in Q2. Aussie dollar also stronger against euro, pound and yen on higher chance of RBA interest rate hike
The Australian dollar is performing well today as the odds of an interest rate hike continue to increase.
There's a 48% chance the Reserve Bank board will lift interest rates when it next meets in late-September, according to the latest market pricing data from Bloomberg.
That's slightly higher than yesterday's 40% probability.
So that's why the local currency has risen to 72 US cents, its highest level in three months.
And it's also doing well against other currencies, having risen to:
- 61.8 euro cents — its highest since May
- 53 British pence — the strongest it has been since June
On top of that, the Aussie dollar has jumped to a 36-year high against the Japanese yen.
But it's mainly because Japan is grappling with serious economic problems of its own.
The last time the AUD was worth 114.8 yen was back in September 1990 when Japan's asset price bubble had burst, leading to huge falls in the nation's share market and property prices.
That led to a long period of economic stagnation for Japan, known as the "lost decades".
Bad news for Japan and the US
So the fact the Aussie dollar is this strong against the Asian currency is a bad sign for Japan.
That's because Japan buys much of its food and energy from overseas and a weaker yen makes these essential goods a lot more expensive, and is bad for inflation/cost of living. Though it's great for tourists on a short holiday there.
It also means recent attempts by the United States and Japan to buy more yen to prop up its value appear to have failed.
The US framed its rare intervention as a goodwill gesture to "support a key ally".
But it's more likely because the Trump administration is worried that Japan is the largest foreign holder of US Treasury bonds.
If Japan continues to sell off large amounts of its dollar assets to prop up the yen, it could lead to a huge spike in American bond yields.
That could push up US interest rates, especially for those paying off a mortgage in America, and make the Trump administration's interest bill in repaying its $US40 trillion national debt even higher.

Australia is a ‘short duration nation’
You're forgiven if you have no idea what that means.
Here's commentary from Luci Ellis to get you up to speed:
- High bond yields have spurred the US government into manoeuvres to contain debt-servicing costs. They also matter for the US mortgage market, where mortgages are mostly fixed-rate. Existing borrowers by definition do not face higher repayments when bond yields rise, but they can feel ‘trapped’ by the high cost of moving or refinancing.
- The US model of 30-year fixed rate mortgages that are cheap to refinance is unlikely to be replicated in Australia. It only exists because of significant government intervention. Our tax, prudential regulation and superannuation systems also favour floating interest rates, even for loans with long contractual maturity like mortgages.
- Long yields still matter for fiscal policy, and our corporate bond market is attractive to both domestic and offshore (Kangaroo) issuers and investors. But when thinking about financial conditions from a monetary policy perspective, the short end of the yield curve matters far more than in some countries.
"For all these reasons, Australia is a ‘short duration nation’," Luci Ellis wrote.
"[But] long yields still matter for asset valuations, hurdle rates, fiscal policy and some forms of private financing activity.
"Our corporate bond market is attractive to both domestic and offshore (Kangaroo) issuers.
"But organic domestic demand and supply for fixed interest securities is lower than in some countries.
"Long yields therefore matter less for monetary policy transmission and should receive less weight in considerations of financial conditions than in, say, the US or Japan."

CIA chief did not threaten Russia with consequences for continuing war during Moscow visit – NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
00:34:00 EEST
06:34:00 KST

CIA chief did not threaten Russia with consequences for continuing war during Moscow visit – NYT
CIA Director John Ratcliffe did not make any threats during his visit to Moscow about possible consequences for Russia if Vladimir Putin decides to continue the war against Ukraine.
Source: The New York Times, citing current and former senior US officials
Details: The NYT said that the CIA chief had given a pessimistic assessment of the course of the war for the Russians during talks with Federal Security Service (FSB) Director Alexander Bortnikov. Ratcliffe urged the Kremlin to begin genuine negotiations to end the war before Russia's military and economic position deteriorates further. However, he made no threats regarding the possible consequences if Putin ignored this assessment and decided to continue the war against Ukraine.
US intelligence analysts have long questioned whether Putin's advisers are giving him an accurate account of the scale of Russia's losses and the actual situation on the battlefield. The US hopes that, as a former intelligence officer, the Russian leader will regard information from the CIA chief as more urgent and credible than conventional diplomatic signals.
The NYT noted that Ratcliffe's channel of communication with Bortnikov operates in parallel with those established by US President Donald Trump's Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with other Putin advisers.
Despite the expectation among some members of Trump's circle that Russia would achieve a quick victory, Russian forces' heavy losses and Ukraine's determination to continue fighting have changed Washington's assessment of the situation.
Quote: "Before Mr. Ratcliffe met with Mr. Bortnikov in Moscow, he spoke with his Ukrainian counterparts, assuring them that he would be exploring Russian positions, not making concessions on behalf of the Ukrainians."
Background:
- In November 2021, the then CIA director William Burns visited Moscow to meet Bortnikov and personally warn the Russian leadership against launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
- In November 2022, Burns met Sergei Naryshkin, head of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, in the Turkish capital of Ankara following intercepted intelligence suggesting that Russia might use nuclear weapons during a Ukrainian counteroffensive.
- On 25 August 2026, it became known that Ratcliffe had made a secret visit to Moscow for talks with the Russian leadership.
- On 27 August, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service reported that the Russian General Staff had prepared a plan for the additional mobilisation of 600,000 people in 2026-2027. They are primarily intended to replenish units fighting against Ukraine.

Argentina has named the same starting side that was defeated by world champions South Africa earlier this month.
Los Pumas enter this two-Test series against the Wallabies with several key players unavailable after facing the Wallabies in 2025.
Captain Julián Montoya, flanker Marcos Kremer and backs Mateo Carreras, Santiago Chocobares, Bautista Delguy are all unavailable.
Juan Martin Gonzalez, Juan Cruz Mallia and Pedro Rubiolo, who also faced the Wallabies in 2025, are injured.
The Wallabies are on a three-Test winning streak after two wins over Japan earlier this month, and a thumping 57-10 win over Italy in Perth in July.
Argentina has played four Tests in 2026, all at home, with just one win.
Los Pumas were defeated by Scotland and England, but defeated Wales during July's Nations Championship.
The South Americans then lost a standalone Test match to South Africa, pushing the world champions to a 17-10 defeat.
The Wallabies and Los Pumas each claimed a victory in the two matches played on Australian soil during last year's Rugby Championship.
In 2024, both nations also traded victories in the two matches played in Argentina.

6 Takeaways From the GTA VI Extended Look
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:30:28 UTC
06:30:28 KST

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.
And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.
The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.
It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.
It Sure Is Pretty
GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.
There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.
You Play as 2 Characters Simultaneously
The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.
The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.
GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.
There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.
Maybe Don’t Hit and Run
The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.
In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.
Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.
At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.
So Much Room for Activities
Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.
One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.
You Can Pet the Dog
A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.
User-Generated Content
In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.
The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.

Armed raiders kill 49 in South Sudan cattle raid: local official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:28:29 UTC
06:28:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Armed raiders kill 49 in South Sudan cattle raid: local official
At least 49 people were killed and 33 wounded in northwestern South Sudan on Thursday after armed attackers raided a cattle camp and a village, a local official said, in the latest deadly cattle raid.
The young nation has long been plagued by violent cattle raids but is now also seeing clashes between troops loyal to President Salva Kiir and forces loosely allied with the opposition.
The attack took place at 5:00 a.m. local time Thursday, with the attackers targeting the Machar-Pakuek cattle camp and Mading Juer Boma in Majak Payam, Tonj North County, Warrap State, according to an official statement.
"The attack was perpetuated by an armed cross-border, criminal network," said Warrap spokesperson William Wol Mayom Bol in the statement.
Last year, Kiir declared a six-month state of emergency in the state after a surge of violent inter-communal cattle raids.
The attack comes barely three weeks after another cattle raid in the area left 60 people dead and 50 wounded.
"We extend heartfelt condolences to the families that lost loved ones in the attack and appeal for restraint," Bol said.
The local government condemned the attack and called on humanitarian organisations to help respond to the "humanitarian catastrophe resulting from conflict-induced displacement."
Earlier this month, the head of the UN mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), Anita Kiki Gbeho, expressed concerns over the cycle of communal violence in places such as Warrap.
Gbeho said humanitarian workers were also facing growing dangers in South Sudan, with 36 killed in 2026 alone.

Iran threatens US economic interests if maritime blockade continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:26:18 UTC
06:26:18 KST

Rania Abushamala
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Iran will target US economic interests if the maritime blockade against the country continues, a senior Iranian official warned Thursday.
“If the blockade continues, we will target US economic interests fully and with intensity and force,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
Rezaei said Iran had “broken the maritime blockade” during the ceasefire and exported between 70 million and 80 million barrels of oil.
He added that Iranian oil sales had returned to their pre-sanctions level.
“In addition to clearing floating stocks, we have established new export routes that are gradually expanding,” Rezaei said.
Addressing developments in Lebanon, Rezaei said Beirut and its southern suburbs were a “red line” for Tehran.
“No one has the right to move toward Beirut or its southern suburbs,” he said. “We are closely monitoring the situation with complete seriousness.”
Rezaei added that Israel “will be forced to withdraw from the occupied areas in Lebanon.”
Earlier, US President Donald Trump claimed in remarks at the White House: “The strait is open. The Strait of Hormuz is open. We have control, and we have the blockade.”
In mid-June, Iran and the US -- with Pakistani and Qatari mediation -- signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding in Islamabad.
The memorandum included provisions for ending hostilities, reopening the strait, lifting a US naval blockade and beginning a 60-day negotiation process.
Tehran has accused the US of failing to implement key provisions of the memorandum, insisting that the strait will not fully reopen until Washington fulfills its commitments.

Guangfu cultural exchange tour hosted in Indonesia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
05:24:27 CST
06:24:27 KST

JAKARTA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- A cultural exchange tour was held in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Thursday, showcasing the rich history, traditions, and legacy of Guangfu culture, a regional culture from southern China, through Cantonese opera, stand-up comedy, and a flash mob.
At the event, titled "From Zhuji Lane to the World," opera performers brought the ancient stories of Zhuji Lane to life through melodic singing and stylized movements. Located in Shaoguan city, south China's Guangdong Province, Zhuji Lane is celebrated as one of the best-preserved ancient alleys dating back to the Song Dynasty.
Adding a contemporary touch, a stand-up comedian shared traditional Cantonese customs, linguistic humor, and moving tales of Cantonese emigrants who crossed the seas to build new lives abroad.
Beyond the theater, performers staged a lively flash mob at a historic square in Jakarta's old town, drawing enthusiastic crowds of local residents. Spectators captured the impromptu performance on their phones, with several joining the artists in dance.
Que Sumei, deputy director of the Shaoguan-based Nanling International Communication Center, said the tour brought Cantonese culture to Indonesia while strengthening emotional ties among overseas Chinese communities.
She expressed hope that culture could continue to serve as a bridge, tracing the journey from departing Zhuji Lane to returning to it, and that these enduring bonds of friendship would flourish through ongoing exchanges. ■

PHNOM PENH, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- The fourth Cambodia Asian Film Festival (CAFF) is currently underway in the Cambodian capital, showcasing a captivating selection of movies from China and across the region.
Running from Aug. 24 to 28, the festival features roughly 30 shortlisted films screened for free at Fable Cinema and Legend Cinema Olympia. Selected from dozens of submissions, the lineup includes entries from China, Cambodia, India, Japan, Malaysia, and Nepal, with China contributing almost 20 of the featured films.
Speaking at an awards ceremony on Thursday evening, Cambodian Minister of Culture and Fine Arts Phoeurng Sackona highlighted the powerful role of cinema in global connection.
"Films serve as a bridge connecting nations and bringing them closer to the international community," she said. "In the context of rapid technological and media advancements, cinema has increasingly become an effective tool for promoting tourist destinations, enhancing their appeal, and encouraging travel."
Sackona praised the CAFF as a vital platform for celebrating Asian cinema and fostering industry connections.
"It serves as a meeting place for screenwriters, directors, producers, artists, and film professionals to exchange perspectives, build networks, and explore co-production opportunities," she said.
The minister emphasized that the festival strengthened regional friendship and cultural cooperation, expressing hope that the partnerships forged during the event would pave the way for future technical exchanges and creative collaborations, ultimately driving sustainable growth in the film sector while preserving diverse cultural heritages.
Pok Borak, director of the Department of Cinema and Cultural Promotion at Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, said the festival created a vibrant atmosphere for the local film industry by bringing together outstanding films from across Asia to screen in Cambodia.
"We shortlisted about 30 famous films for this year's screening, and more than half -- nearly 20 of them -- are Chinese films," he told Xinhua. "This festival will boost cooperation between Cambodia and China, with a specific focus on the film industry."
Borak said that Chinese movies are very popular in Cambodia. He explained that this popularity stems not only from advanced technical production standards but also from compelling storytelling and engaging scripts.
"Cambodians really love watching Chinese movies," he added.
Ling Liya, a 27-year-old Cambodian actress, shared that she is an avid fan of Chinese films. She noted that screening famous Chinese movies at the festival helps bring China and Cambodia closer together.
"I like Chinese films because they reflect modern society, the economy, and education, while giving me deep insights into the culture," she told Xinhua.
"Chinese films are really popular and receive substantial support from Cambodian film enthusiasts," Liya added. ■

China deploys satellites, drones for rescue efforts in mudslide-hit county in SW China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
05:24:11 CST
06:24:11 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China has deployed satellites and drones to aid the rescue efforts in the mudslide-hit area in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region after a mudslide struck a port along the China-Nepal border.
The China National Space Administration (CNSA) said on Thursday that immediately after the disaster, it coordinated and deployed satellite resources to conduct emergency imaging of the mudslide-hit area and retrieve historical imagery of the area.
As of 5 p.m. (Beijing Time) Thursday, the CNSA had delivered five pre-disaster images and 10 post-disaster images to relevant emergency response and disaster relief departments, providing timely and effective satellite data support for disaster assessment and mitigation efforts.
A large unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) Wing Loong took off from adjacent Sichuan Province and arrived over the disaster-hit area at 2 a.m. on Thursday. Equipped with high-definition cameras for comprehensive reconnaissance of the area, the UAV also carried mobile base stations from China's three major telecommunications operators and a satellite communication system to support emergency communications work.
Meanwhile, rescue personnel also used small UAVs in rescue operations. Using the high-definition cameras, the UAVs can help construct 3D real-scene models of the mudslide-hit area, providing data support for the rescue command center to understand the overall situation and mark priority search zones.
In addition, rescue personnel utilized UAVs' thermal imaging equipment to capture human heat-source signals, helping to identify the locations of missing persons in vegetated terrains and mud-covered zones.
The mudslide, which occurred on the Nepalese side, struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. ■

China

2026-08-28
05:24:03 CST
06:24:03 KST

Experts and rescuers head to the area of a barrier lake for inspection on Aug. 28, 2026. China's Ministry of Water Resources on Thursday activated a level-IV emergency flood response in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region as a barrier lake that formed after a mudslide hitting the border port of Gyirong faces a high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream. The mudslide that occurred on Wednesday caused a barrier lake to form near the confluence of two rivers, which had accumulated an estimated 2 million cubic meters of water as of Thursday morning. According to forecasts, inflows into the lake could reach about 3 million cubic meters over the next three days amid continued rainfall, increasing the risk of a breach that could send floodwaters downstream and potentially cause further damage in areas including Gyirong Port and elsewhere downstream. In response, the ministry has instructed local authorities to closely monitor the barrier lake and rainfall, strengthen forecasting and risk assessments, and accurately identify people living in areas that could be affected downstream. (Xinhua/Jigme Dorje)
BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Water Resources on Thursday activated a level-IV emergency flood response in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region as a barrier lake that formed after a mudslide hitting the border port of Gyirong faces a high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream.
The mudslide that occurred on Wednesday caused a barrier lake to form near the confluence of two rivers, which had accumulated an estimated 2 million cubic meters of water as of Thursday morning.
According to forecasts, inflows into the lake could reach about 3 million cubic meters over the next three days amid continued rainfall, increasing the risk of a breach that could send floodwaters downstream and potentially cause further damage in areas including Gyirong Port and elsewhere downstream.
In response, the ministry has instructed local authorities to closely monitor the barrier lake and rainfall, strengthen forecasting and risk assessments, and accurately identify people living in areas that could be affected downstream.
The authorities should issue timely risk warnings and evacuate threatened residents in advance, according to the ministry.
The ministry has dispatched an expert team to Gyirong County to assist with the emergency response, while a hydrological emergency monitoring team deployed earlier is closely monitoring the situation at the site. ■

WUHAN, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhao Xintong became the second Chinese player to reach the top of the world snooker ranking after beating Neil Robertson 5-1 on Thursday, while fellow Chinese Chang Bingyu and Xiao Guodong also advanced at the World Snooker Wuhan Open.
Zhao opened his quarterfinal against Robertson with breaks of 106 and 91 to take a 2-0 lead. Robertson capitalized on a mistake by Zhao to pull one frame back, but Zhao responded by winning the next three frames to seal the victory.
With world No. 1 Judd Trump and No. 2 Robertson both eliminated on the same day, Zhao moved to the top of the live rankings.
Zhao said he felt "quite calm" about reaching No. 1. "Maybe if I think about this again later, I will be very happy," he said after the match. "But I think I still have a long way to go to become a top-level player."
Asked about his next goal, Zhao said fans might hope he wins a Grand Slam or more titles, but he viewed those achievements as part of a longer process. "The most important thing is to enjoy the happiness that snooker brings me," he said.
Zhao will face Xiao in the semifinals after Xiao defeated Mark Williams 5-3, ensuring that a Chinese player will reach the final.
Earlier on Thursday, China's Chang Bingyu stunned Trump 5-1. Chang opened a 2-1 lead before winning the final three frames in succession. He sealed his first professional victory over Trump with a break of 132 in the final frame.
The win was an unexpected boost for Chang, who said he experienced some nerves after taking the 2-0 lead.
"When I was 2-0 up, I thought there was a chance I could win the match, and I did have some fluctuations mentally," Chang said. "Fortunately, I managed to adjust in the end."
"He is my role model because he is also left-handed, and he is world No. 1 now," Chang added. "Being able to beat him gives me a lot of confidence."
In the English derby between seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan and Mark Selby, the latter took the opening two frames, while O'Sullivan responded with breaks of 87 and 96 to level the match at 2-2. O'Sullivan then moved ahead 3-2 after a tactical fifth frame in which he forced Selby into conceding after a snooker.
Selby leveled with a break of 53, but O'Sullivan then produced breaks of 80 and 129 to close out the match.
O'Sullivan said he was surprised to come through against Selby and praised his upcoming opponent.
"Chang Bingyu is very talented and has the potential to become one of the best players of his generation in China because his game is very complete," O'Sullivan said.
Chang has previously noted O'Sullivan as the player he wants to emulate the most. And the two will meet Friday for a place in the final. ■

UN chief regrets lack of int'l attention to Ebola, calls for action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
05:23:33 CST
06:23:33 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres (1st L) speaks to reporters on Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), at the UN headquarters in New York, Aug. 27, 2026. Guterres on Thursday lamented the lack of international attention to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and made an urgent appeal to step up action. (Mark Garten/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)
UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday lamented the lack of international attention to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and made an urgent appeal to step up action.
"My main message is this: The outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it. But it can be stopped," Guterres told reporters. "We know how to contain Ebola -- how to interrupt transmission -- and how to save lives. But we must also overcome another virus -- the virus of indifference. Because international attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground."
Noting that the Ebola crisis is a human tragedy affecting families and communities on an extraordinary scale, Guterres said the outbreak, the largest in the history of the DRC, continues to expand across a vast area, with women and children particularly hard hit. As of Aug. 25, 5,713 cases had been confirmed, claiming 2,744 lives, with about 500 new cases reported each week.
"Every gap in funding and operational support makes the Ebola response more challenging," Guterres said, adding that the UN has put forward a detailed 2.13 billion U.S.-dollar humanitarian needs and response plan, 48 percent of which is funded.
The current resources will last weeks, not months, he said, adding that without additional funding, vital operations will run out of money just when they need to expand.
"The world still has an opportunity to get ahead of this crisis. But time is not on our side. The Ebola outbreak deserves far greater attention than it is receiving today. The communities affected deserve far greater assistance. And the response deserves far greater support," said Guterres.
Calling to stop the outbreak, Guterres said it is time to summon the collective determination to act before the cost becomes more deadly, more difficult, and more expensive. ■

Türkiye condemns Israel’s attacks on Syria, welcomes US decision on terrorism list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:22:19 UTC
06:22:19 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ahmet Yildiz on Thursday condemned Israel’s continued attacks on Syria, saying they violate the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, while welcoming the US decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
Addressing a UN Security Council meeting on the latest developments in the Middle East, Yildiz said Syria was steadily advancing toward stabilization despite continuing challenges.
He welcomed progress by Syria’s People’s Assembly toward becoming a fully functioning legislative institution and said recent developments in the judicial process concerning transitional justice and accountability were also important.
“Sustaining momentum in these areas will be essential to strengthening public confidence in the state institutions and advancing an inclusive political process,” Yildiz said.
He also welcomed the recent visit to Syria by International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi and commended the Syrian government for its cooperation with the agency.
Yildiz also welcomed the US decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
“We commend the constructive approach of the US administration and congratulate the Syrian government and people,” he said.
He said the decision would give further impetus to Syria’s economic recovery and reconstruction, strengthen its position in the international community and contribute to lasting security and stability.
Yildiz, however, warned that Israel continued to undermine Syria’s positive trajectory through what he described as destabilizing actions.
“The recent airstrikes on the Abu al-Duhur airbase constitute yet another example of such actions,” he said.
“We condemn Israel’s relentless attacks targeting Syria’s infrastructure and capabilities in blatant violation of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity,” Yildiz added.
He said Israel’s aggression, which continues to affect civilians and undermine stability, “must cease.”
Yildiz reiterated Türkiye’s call on Israel to fully comply with the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement, refrain from further escalation and reverse its encroachments into Syrian territory.
“The international community and this council, in particular, must use all means at its disposal to bring an end to Israel’s aggression against Syria and its occupation of Syrian territory,” he said.
Yildiz also addressed Türkiye’s military cooperation with Syria, stressing that Ankara’s activities in the country are conducted with the consent of the Syrian government.
“Türkiye's military cooperation with Syria is conducted with the consent of the Syrian government,” he said.
“None of our activities in Syria are directed against or pose a threat to any third country,” he said.
He warned that attempts to obstruct efforts to build Syria’s security capacity could create conditions conducive to the resurgence of terrorist organizations such as ISIS (Daesh).
Yildiz added that Türkiye’s relations with countries in the region are guided by a firm commitment to stability, security and prosperity, which he described as essential to Türkiye’s national, regional and international security.

LeBlanc praised the move in a post on Thursday on X and added that Canada is looking “forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement”.

Explosive-Laden Drone Found Near Ukrainian Cargo Plane in Germany Had Russian GRU Hallmarks
An explosive-laden drone discovered near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport earlier in August showed characteristics associated with devices used by Russia’s military intelligence agency (GRU).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This was reported by ABC News on August 27, citing a US intelligence assessment.
A US intelligence official briefed on the investigation into the suspected sabotage plot said both the explosives attached to the drone and the construction of the device were “typical” of those previously associated with the GRU.
According to the official, the assessment was reached in coordination with German security and intelligence agencies investigating the incident.
The US assessment comes as German investigators continue examining several drones potentially connected to the suspected sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Most recently, another drone bearing traces of explosives was discovered in a field near the airport in Kabelsketal on August 14. The drone, reportedly the third linked to the case, was found ten days after the first drone was discovered, Süddeutsche Zeitung reported on August 25.
Investigators examining the site subsequently detected a substance that, according to preliminary analysis, may have contained traces of RDX, a powerful military-grade explosive.
The investigation stems from an earlier incident involving a Ukrainian An-124 cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Overnight on August 5, a drone believed to have been fitted with an explosive device was discovered near the Ukrainian transport plane.
According to German newspaper Bild, the drone was found on the airport apron shortly before midnight, directly beside the Ukrainian Antonov aircraft.

From Abbey Gate to today: How five years reshaped the Middle East and world policy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:11:18 UTC
06:11:18 KST

It has been five years since the attack at Abbey Gate in Kabul, Afghanistan. US President Donald Trump put out a proclamation on August 26, the anniversary. “The terrorist was one of the thousands of prisoners released by the Taliban just 2 months earlier. As a result, 13 American service members were killed, 45 were wounded, and more than 160 civilians were injured,” President Trump said.
He noted that on August 26, “a lone ISIS-K terrorist pressed into the crowd at Abbey Gate in Kabul, Afghanistan, and detonated a body-worn bomb.”
Trump called on the nation to honor the fallen. “On the fifth anniversary of the attack at Abbey Gate, we solemnly honor their selflessness and valor.” He noted that for 20 years Americans fought in Afghanistan.
He then got to the tragedy of the 2021 withdrawal. “Yet within months, President Biden squandered those hard-fought gains, putting politics over strategy and rushing through a poorly executed withdrawal that would soon become one of the worst military disasters in our Nation’s history.”
The Wall Street Journal’s Opinion section also released a new video documentary about the withdrawal. It is called The Path to Zero: The Withdrawal From Afghanistan.
The Journal described this as “an unflinching account of America's disastrous withdrawal from Afghanistan, told by the people who lived it. Structured around President Biden's 2021 decision to draw down to "zero" troops, the film traces how one choice cascaded into a chaotic, deadly ending - the closure of Bagram, the collapse of the Afghan army, and a frantic evacuation through three Kabul airport gates, culminating in the tragic Abbey Gate suicide bombing attack.” It includes “candid interviews with the diplomats, generals, and soldiers who were there, the film tells the riveting story of the unfolding tragedy - and gives voice to the moral injury many young Marines who manned the gates still carry.”
Withdrawal from the airfield was tragic chaos
The video illustrates how the withdrawal became a tragic chaos and led to death and suffering.
The US left Bagram Airfield in July, before the final date of withdrawal. That withdrawal was supposed to go on through September but was accelerated. The Afghan security forces collapsed, and Afghanistan rapidly fell to the Taliban. This fall was likely envisioned in talks that had taken place in Doha. The first Trump administration had wanted to withdraw from Afghanistan. In fact, it was never clear why US troops had stayed so long.
The problem is that it’s easier to get into wars like Afghanistan than it is to leave.
The US has seen this before in Vietnam or other conflicts. However, the 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan had large ramifications. Trump said this week that the withdrawal from Bagram “surrendered our largest military base in the country, lost billions of dollars of military equipment, and left our remaining forces without their strategic advantages as the Taliban rapidly advanced.” He described the collapse in Afghanistan as the result of the previous Biden administration’s incompetence.
The WSJ video reminds us of how the tragedy unfolded. It also sheds a concerning light on the failed planning for withdrawal and a sense that no one was accountable for the failure. It also leads to questions about whether other countries looked at the withdrawal and drew lessons about a weakened America that couldn’t deter enemies.
Geopolitical crisis, faltered international agreements that followed
In February 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine. The Biden administration had warned that Russia would invade. However, when the chips were down, many Western governments evacuated Kyiv and appeared to believe half of Ukraine would fall to Russia. In the end, the Ukrainians held on, and Russia failed to take Kyiv. Russia felt that it could get away with the invasion because it was not deterred. Did the Afghanistan chaos of withdrawal lead to that sense?
Other crises followed. In April, a civil war broke out in Sudan. Did the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) feel it could get away with launching a conflict in Sudan after there had been hope of transition to democracy? The civil war has been brutal and has included massacres. Did the US try to stop the civil war? It’s not clear, but it appears the Biden White House failed to do much. The Trump administration has called for a ceasefire, but it still hasn’t happened.
In Yemen, the administration also failed to make much progress, despite talks in Oman. A UN-backed truce in Yemen in March 2023 was a rare silver lining.
On other fronts, the US continued to appear to lose leverage around the world. Armenians in Nagorno-Karabakh were cut off throughout much of 2023 and under siege. This had followed a previous short conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia in 2020. In September 2023, a new offensive led to 50,000 Armenians fleeing the enclave. Here, again, the US appeared absent.
On October 7, Hamas launched its attack on Israel, murdering 1,000 people and taking 251 hostages. Did Hamas feel emboldened by the Taliban victory? Hamas leaders were hosted in Doha, as the Taliban had been hosted. The Taliban had been careful not to carry out massive massacres when they marched on Kabul, instead handing the US a fait accompli. Hamas believed it could carry out a massacre and get away with it. It apparently believed it could then take over the West Bank and spread war across the region. What was the Hamas calculus? Didn’t it know Israel would launch a major war in response? Did it think the massive hostage taking would prevent the war?
We know that Hamas released two elderly Israelis and also several Americans soon after October 7, apparently hoping to achieve some kind of deal. This didn’t work, but it raises some questions. It has never been fully explained about the two Americans released by Hamas in October, before the Israeli offensive on October 27. At the time Reuters reported on October 21, 2023 that “U.S. President Joe Biden thanked Qatar and Israel” after the women were released. “Hamas said the two women, who Israel's Kan public broadcaster reported were dual Israeli-American nationals, were freed ‘for humanitarian reasons’ in response to Qatari mediation.”
Trends that emerged since Kabul 2021
Is there any connection to the US withdrawal from Afghanistan? Did that withdrawal lead to Russia assuming that the US wouldn’t stop its march on Kyiv? Did that lead to Hamas assuming it could get away with an unprecedented attack? Was US deterrence weakened? We may never know, unless we have access to internal documents of the Putin administration or Hamas leadership. What is clear is that the years after 2021 were ones of accelerating global chaos as the world order has shifted. Many countries want to weaken the US-led world order that emerged in the 1990s. Russia, China, and others have been clear about this.
Other trends were clear in the period 2021-2024. Economic blocs such as BRICS and the SCO expanded, as Russia and China grew their power. Many US partners and allies began hedging their bets by working with China.
The Abraham Accords also appeared to stagnate. No new countries joined. Concepts such as I2U2, meant to bring together India, the UAE, Israel, and the US, didn’t progress as much as hoped. Neither did the Negev Forum. Regional integration didn’t happen as planned. Instead, October 7 derailed hopes of peace. Iran also prodded its militias in Iraq to increase attacks. They targeted US forces in Erbil, and Iran also targeted ships using drones.
Iran also moved its Shahed 136 drones to the Houthis in Yemen in 2020, foreshadowing how it would send them to Russia. As such, it is clear that the years around the fall of Kabul became ones in which there were serious setbacks for the US and the US-led world order.
We now live in the aftermath of that era. The war in Ukraine and Sudan continues. The war in Gaza and the Middle East that began on October 7 has continued for more than 1,000 days with no end in sight. China continues to position itself as a more powerful country. The war with Iran, which began in February, has shifted US focus to the Middle East. This may embolden China.
Many trends that began years ago are continuing. The Trump administration has deterred US enemies and has had successes, such as in Venezuela. However, it remains to be seen if all the lessons of Kabul will be learned.

From Sept 4, businesses will also get access to a self-serve ChatGPT ads manager (File photo)
NEW DELHI: OpenAI has started showing ads on ChatGPT in India. The company has rolled out advertising for logged-in adult users on its Free and Go plans, while paid subscriptions including Plus and Pro remain ad-free. Over 50 brands are expected to begin advertising on the platform this week, with WPP and Omnicom among the initial agency partners.From Sept 4, businesses will also get access to a self-serve ChatGPT ads manager, with daily campaign budgets starting at Rs 725, potentially opening the platform to smaller advertisers alongside large brands.An OpenAI spokesperson told TOI that the company expects early advertiser interest across travel, financial services, retail, and health and beauty. “India’s particular opportunity lies in its combination of large enterprises, a sophisticated agency ecosystem, and a long tail of small and medium-sized businesses that can access the platform through self-serve tools,” he said.OpenAI is positioning ChatGPT advertising differently from conventional search ads, arguing that relevance will come from the immediate intent expressed during a conversation rather than keyword bidding or long term advertising profiles.
According to the company, when a user’s request shows commercial intent, a separate advertising system can determine whether an eligible and relevant ad should appear. The ad will be displayed independently below the organic ChatGPT response and clearly labelled. OpenAI said advertisers will not receive users’ conversation text or profile details. Instead, they will get conventional campaign metrics such as impressions, clicks, click-through rates, conversions and return on investment.OpenAI also plans to support action-based buying models, conversion tools and integration with independent measurement partners.

Due to the costs of the war, Russia cut budget expenditures by 35% amid a growing deficit

Due to the costs of the war, Russia cut budget expenditures by 35% amid a growing deficit
Kyiv • UNN
Russia cut most budget expenditures by 35%, leaving defense and social payments untouched. On August 24, the deficit reached 8.654 trillion rubles.
The Russian authorities have imposed strict restrictions on budget spending due to the rapid growth of the deficit and a shortage of funds. UNN writes about this, citing The Moscow Times.
Details
Since April, spending under most budget items has been cut by 35%. The restrictions do not apply to defense, social payments, salaries for public-sector employees, subsidies to regions, or servicing the national debt. Agencies were also instructed to postpone nonessential spending and prepare to reduce staff by 15%.
According to Bloomberg, the decision was made after Russia's Finance Minister Anton Siluanov warned Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin that the budget might not have enough funds to make all payments on time. At that point, the federal treasury deficit had already reached 5.5 trillion rubles.
The deficit exceeded the annual plan
When planning the 2026 budget, Russia's Finance Ministry expected to reduce last year's deficit of 5.7 trillion rubles to 3.7 trillion through increases in VAT and taxes for small businesses. However, by the end of the first quarter, the deficit had already exceeded the plan for the entire year and amounted to 4.5 trillion rubles.
By the end of the second quarter, the budget "hole" had grown to 5.7 trillion rubles, and by early August—to 6.5 trillion. According to Russia's Electronic Budget system, as of August 24, the deficit had reached 8.654 trillion rubles.
Russia continues to spend on the war
According to Bloomberg sources' estimates, by the end of the year the deficit could grow to approximately 9 trillion rubles, or 3.2–3.8% of GDP. This would exceed even the Russian central bank's most pessimistic forecast of 8.2 trillion rubles.
Despite its financial problems, the Russian authorities do not currently consider the situation critical and expect that the country will be able to finance the continuation of the war against Ukraine for several more years. At the same time, cuts in civilian spending are already being used to contain further growth in the budget deficit.

Supreme Court issues directions to expedite dowry trials
TNN / Aug 28, 2026, 02:36 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
All trial courts shall consider framing of charges within 60 to 90 days, the SC bench said.
NEW DELHI: Expressing concern that many engaging in the practice of dowry are not getting punished, Supreme Court has passed a series of directions to streamline and expedite trial in such cases.A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih said there was a need for time-bound completion of trial in dowry cases and directed the high courts to periodically review pending criminal appeals.“Many who openly seek and give dowry go scot-free. It has been noted time and again, in various judicial pronouncements, that Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, suffers from various difficulties in its implementation. This Court further acknowledged that when it comes to the giving and taking of dowry in particular, this practice unfortunately has deep roots in society; hence, it being not a matter of swift change, a concentrated effort is needed on the part of all the involved parties, be it Legislature, Judiciary, law enforcement agencies, civil society organisations, etc,” the apex court said.It said that all trial courts shall endeavour, as far as is practicable and subject to compliance with statutory safeguards under CrPC/BNSS, to secure prompt appearance of the accused after the filing of a chargesheet, and thereafter, consider the framing of charges within 60 to 90 days.
“Trial Courts/High Courts shall discourage unnecessary adjournments and ensure that adjournments are granted only after recording reasons in writing. Where counsel for the accused repeatedly remains absent without sufficient cause, appropriate Legal Aid Counsel or Amicus Curiae may be appointed to ensure that proceedings are not unnecessarily delayed. Additionally, where the Investigating Officer has been transferred or has retired, a substitute or holding officer shall be nominated sufficiently in advance to avoid adjournments,” it said.
The bench also directed states/Union territories and high courts to conduct periodic training and sensitisation programmes for judicial officers, police officials, prosecutors, protection officers, counsellors through judicial academies, police training institutions and other appropriate bodies.

India’s petroleum products’ exports surge 8% in July

India’s petroleum products’ exports surge 8% in July
Atul Mathur / TNN / Updated: Aug 28, 2026, 20:36 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Govt data showed India exported 2.4 million tonnes (MT) of diesel in July this year.
NEW DELHI: India’s export of petroleum products recorded a year-on-year surge of over 8 percent in July, as margins improved amid a global supply shortage following Russia’s ban on diesel exports and ample supplies of crude to India during the US-Iran ceasefire.Govt data showed India exported 2.4 million tonnes (MT) of diesel in July this year, up from 2.2 MT in the corresponding month last year, while total petroleum product exports rose from 5 MT to 5.5 MT. Diesel is currently commanding nearly 70 percent premium over crude, making exports lucrative for refiners despite the windfall gains tax govt brought in to ensure adequate domestic stocks.While the Indian basket of crude averages $90 per barrel this month, diesel averages $150 per barrel. Windfall tax imposed by govt, however, has ensured refiners meet domestic demand before exporting the surplus.India is the second-largest crude importer, but it has stepped up fuel exports, consolidating its position as a major supplier of refined petroleum products to neighbouring countries as well as South Asian, African and European nations. Indian refiners import 40-45 percent of their crude requirements, but they export a significant part of refined products, with experts pointing out that they have also sent cargo of refined fuel to Russia, whose refining capacity has come down drastically because of damage from drone attacks by Ukraine.
Russian refineries were processing around 3.8-3.9 million barrels per day (mbd) in July, down from 5.3 mbd a year ago, forcing the country to ban diesel exports and start importing.“A renewed wave of Ukrainian drone attacks since March, following a brief pause over the winter months, has significantly disrupted Russia’s refining system, pushing refinery runs to multi-decade lows of around 3.8 million barrels per day. Persistent attacks on refining infrastructure have tightened domestic product availability and prompted Russia to impose restrictions on exports of key fuels, including diesel, gasoline and jet fuel,” said Nikhil Dubey, lead analyst with Kpler.He added that cargoes of refined fuel from India, Turkey and Morocco have moved towards Russia. “Some Indian-origin cargo, such as volumes from Nayara Energy, have moved through traders and involved ship-to-ship (STS) transfers,” he added.According to S&P Global Commodities at Sea, India’s clean product exports, excluding LPG, averaged around 1.4 mbd in July and 1.1 mbd in Aug, with nearly 70 percent of volumes loaded from Sikka port, the key gateway for Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery. Nayara Energy’s Vadinar refinery also emerged as a major exporter following its turnaround, supported by continued access to Russian crude.Abhishek Ranjan, Lead South Asia Fuels & Refining, S&P Global Energy, said that diesel exports became more profitable in July as the export tax fell by about $3 per barrel and profit margins rose 44 percent over the previous month, creating a strong incentive to ship more diesel overseas. Diesel accounted for roughly 43 percent of total exports, reflecting strong international demand for middle distillates and India’s ability to redirect cargo towards these markets.“Indian refiners were able to capture stronger margins and gain market share in export destinations despite broader global supply challenges,” Ranjan said.
Analysts suggested that crude oil refining in West Asia, which catered to several African countries, has also declined by nearly 1.6 mbd from 2025 levels to about 8 mbd in 2026, opening an additional market for India.“East Africa, which has traditionally sourced a large share of its refined products from the Middle East, has seen those supply routes disrupted by constraints around the Strait of Hormuz and, more recently, the Bab el-Mandeb. The resulting supply gap has opened up additional outlets for Indian diesel, with refiners redirecting barrels towards African markets to replace some of the disrupted Middle Eastern supply,” Dubey said.

The stockpiles of U.S. Patriot interceptor missiles in Europe have fallen to a critical level due to their active use in the war with Iran. This could weaken NATO's ability to counter a potential Russian missile attack, UNN reports, citing the Associated Press.
Details
According to U.S. and NATO officials, the greatest concern is the shortage of Patriot missiles capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles. A U.S. official said that the stockpiles in Europe are insufficient to repel a prolonged ballistic attack, while the ability to defend against even a single missile is "very limited."

The situation is causing additional concern over the prospect of potential Russian aggression against NATO countries. At the same time, Western officials do not expect a Russian attack in the near future and believe that Patriot stockpiles should be replenished by 2030.
NATO denies that the Alliance has already lost the necessary level of protection. NATO representative Martin O'Donnell said that the Alliance has enough air defense munitions for self-defense and to support Ukraine.

PM Modi’s bilateral with Russia President Putin will follow EAM Jaishankar’s visit to Moscow this week
NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi will have a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the margins of the upcoming SCO summit in Bishkek, said govt while announcing Modi’s two-nation central Asia tour to Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan that begins Saturday. The summit meeting of the Eurasian bloc will take place on Aug 31-Sept 1.In Bishkek, Modi will also come face to face with Chinese President Xi Jinping before he hosts him for the Brics summit here on Sept 12-13. Modi’s other bilateral engagements are still being finalised.
Modi’s bilateral with Putin, the first since the Russian President visited India in Dec 2025 for the annual summit, will follow external affairs minister S Jaishankar’s visit to Moscow this week for a meeting of the 27th India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation during which he also called on Putin.While discussing trade and investment, energy and nuclear cooperation, Putin assured Jaishankar of continued supply of fertilisers, saying Russia is doing everything to help Indian farmers. Jaishankar told him Modi is looking forward to hosting him for the Brics summit in Sept.
This year’s summit marks the 25th anniversary of the SCO, of which India has been a full member since 2017 along with Pakistan. With Islamabad watching, India is again likely to remind the grouping that the original SCO mandate was to fight terrorism, extremism and separatism.
“The Prime Minister will address the summit where he will highlight India’s priorities of security, connectivity and opportunity at the forum. He will also hold bilateral meets with SCO leaders on the sidelines of the summit,” said MEA, adding that Modi will also attend the opening ceremony of the 6th World Nomad Games, a celebration of the rich cultural heritage of central Asia, in Kyrgyzstan.

Nine-man Trabzonspor eliminated from Europa League after 4-0 loss to Ferencvaros
Unknown

Halis Sunnetci
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Nine-man Trabzonspor were eliminated from the UEFA Europa League after suffering a 4-0 defeat at Ferencvaros in the second leg of their playoff tie on Thursday.
The Hungarian side advanced to the Europa League league phase with a 5-0 aggregate victory, having won the opening leg 1-0 in Trabzon.
Trabzonspor were reduced to 10 players in the 13th minute when Ruslan Malinovskyi was shown a straight red card for violent conduct.
Ferencvaros quickly increased the pressure, with Lenny Joseph firing wide before Trabzonspor goalkeeper Andre Onana denied Marius Corbu.
The hosts broke the deadlock in the 19th minute when Callum O'Dowda headed Adam Nagy's cross into the center of the net.
Trabzonspor responded through Ernest Muci in the 26th minute, but goalkeeper Denes Dibusz produced a fine save to keep out his effort from outside the penalty area.
Ferencvaros thought they had doubled their lead through Cadu in the 39th minute, but the goal was ruled out for offside.
Bamidele Yusuf then missed a clear opportunity before Onana denied Kristoffer Zachariassen as Ferencvaros entered halftime with a 1-0 lead.
Corbu doubled the advantage in the 55th minute, firing a right-footed shot into the bottom corner.
Trabzonspor were reduced to nine players in the 57th minute when Sidny Cabral received a second yellow card for bringing down Bamidele Yusuf inside the penalty area.
Yusuf converted the resulting penalty to make it 3-0 before Krisztian Lisztes struck the post in the 72nd.
Lisztes completed the scoring in the 86th minute, finishing Oliver Nagy's pass with a left-footed shot into the bottom corner.
Ferencvaros will compete in the Europa League league phase, while Trabzonspor will continue their European campaign in the UEFA Conference League league phase.

Nepal floods: No adverse impact of flash floods on Indian side, says NDRF
TNN / Updated: Aug 28, 2026, 08:04 IST

Large
NDRF has deployed 20 teams — 11 in UP and nine in Bihar.
NEW DELHI: National Disaster Response Force Thursday said there is no adverse impact of Nepal’s glacial lake outburst floods on Indian side even as Centre and states are monitoring the situation in bordering districts of UP and Bihar to mitigate any risk from excessive river waters flowing into India.NDRF has deployed 20 teams — 11 in UP and nine in Bihar — for evacuation, relief and rescue operations in case these areas experience floods and waterlogging. These include an NDRF team deployed in Kushinagar district, near Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh.
In a media briefing, NDRF IG Narendra Bundela said floods have caused massive destruction in Nepal with hundreds of people, including Indian tourists, reported missing.Govt is monitoring the excessive flow of water in the first barrage along India-Nepal border in Bihar’s Valmiki Nagar (West Champaran district) on Gandak river, and the situation is under control. On humanitarian assistance offered to Nepal, Bundela said India despatched two planeloads of assistance and relief cargo, including medicines, to Kathmandu Wednesday and Thursday.

Russia threatens strikes on British military targets over Ukraine’s use of Storm Shadow
Kyiv • UNN
Moscow threatened strikes on British military facilities over Ukraine’s use of Storm Shadow missiles. London was accused of escalation.
Russia has stated that it could strike British military targets in Ukraine and beyond in response to Kyiv’s use of British long-range Storm Shadow missiles. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that the United Kingdom was allegedly "one step" away from legal involvement in what Moscow calls "terrorism" against Russian civilians.
According to her, if London does not change its policy toward Ukraine, this could have "inevitable catastrophic consequences."
We have repeatedly warned that any British military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become targets in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory carried out using British weapons
She also called on the British leadership to reconsider its policy and warned of the risk of escalating the conflict "to an entirely new level."
Russia criticizes London-Kyiv missile cooperation
Moscow’s statements came after the United Kingdom decided to provide Ukraine with access to classified technologies for launching its own production of Storm Shadow cruise missiles. Such missiles are capable of striking deep inside Russian territory.
Zakharova said that the United Kingdom and France, which are involved in transferring missile technologies to Ukraine, were "playing with fire."
The day before, Russia also accused Ukraine of using Storm Shadow missiles to strike a shopping center in occupied Donetsk. Moscow said that civilians, including children, had been injured. Reuters notes that it was unable to independently verify these claims.
