Six months into Iran war: Does US have one last economic card to play?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:29:05 UTC
04:29:05 KST

The US Treasury has moved to cut Banque Misr UAE off from the American financial system, accusing the Egyptian bank’s Emirates branch of processing $1.8 billion for companies potentially linked to Iran’s shadow banking network.
The action comes just four days after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent launched “Operation Economic Outcast,” a sanctions campaign that aims to sever all of Iran’s economic ties around the world.
Washington intensified its pressure this week, nearly six months into the war without a lasting settlement, as it turns to economic pressure in its campaign against Iran, seeking to further squeeze Tehran's access to the global financial system.
“Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in announcing the measures.
The campaign, dubbed ‘economic D-Day’, comes as Iran is already under intense economic pressure.
Its Central Bank says oil exports have stopped, the rial has fallen to a record low, and the International Monetary Fund expects the economy to contract 6.1% this year.
But Iran has endured decades of US sanctions and economic isolation without abandoning policies Washington has sought to change, raising a larger question: What economic cards does the US still have to play, and how much leverage can they give Washington over Tehran?
Oil, naval blockade
At the centre of Washington's economic pressure is Iran's oil trade, one of Tehran's main sources of export revenue and foreign currency.
Iran’s Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said last week that Tehran's oil exports had fallen to zero amid the war and sanctions.
"There is no doubt that we face restrictions on oil exports," Hemmati said in a televised interview. "It is a reality that we are not exporting oil."
The US restored its naval blockade against vessels travelling to and from Iranian ports on July 14 after a temporary easing of restrictions.
According to commodities intelligence firm Kpler, Iranian crude loadings fell from an average of 893,000 barrels per day in July to just 156,000 barrels per day through August.
Hemmati's statement that exports have since fallen to zero suggests the pressure on Tehran's oil revenues has intensified further.
Max Gillman, Friedrich A. Hayek Professor of Economic History at the University of Missouri-St. Louis, said the blockade is likely to remain Washington's main instrument of economic pressure.
"I think the main enforcement measure will be the naval blockade on Iranian trade. I expect this to continue indefinitely," Gillman told Anadolu.
"The continued blockade serves to pressure the economic resources available to the ruling Iranian regime," he said.
Foreign reserves, access to dollars
Restricting Iran's ability to sell oil is only one side of Washington's strategy.
Washington can also make it more difficult for Tehran to access foreign currency it has already earned.
Hemmati said the Iranian government and Central Bank had prepared for the loss of revenue, but stressed that Iran faced an additional constraint because its foreign currency reserves remained blocked by Washington.
"The Americans have frozen our foreign currency reserves and do not allow us to withdraw them," he said.
He also said Iranian funds expected to be released under the Islamabad Memorandum, the framework agreement reached with Washington in June, had not yet been freed.
Access to those reserves has become increasingly important as pressure mounts on Iran's currency.
Iran has increasingly relied on alternative payment mechanisms, shadow banking networks, cryptocurrency and intermediaries in third countries to move export revenues and bypass sanctions.
US authorities have repeatedly targeted those channels, seeking to make it harder for Tehran to convert trade and energy earnings into usable foreign currency.
Secondary sanctions
Washington can also target foreign companies, banks and individuals that do business with sanctioned Iranian entities, potentially threatening their access to the US financial system.
This week, the US Treasury announced new categories of Iranian economic activity that can expose foreign companies and individuals to sanctions, including digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
The Treasury also said it was developing sanctions against more than 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world that it accused of helping Iran.
Teams from the Treasury and State departments and the US military are meeting foreign counterparts and setting deadlines for them to halt activities identified by Washington, he said.
"Every country has a defined timeline to shut down activities we have identified. If they do not take action, we will do so unilaterally through Treasury authorities," Bessent said.
He singled out Iran's Bank Melli, saying every branch must be shuttered, and issued a broader warning to institutions facilitating transactions Washington considers illicit.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock is ticking," he said.
How much more can Iran’s economy take?
Washington is tightening restrictions at a difficult moment for Iran's economy.
The IMF expects the economy to contract 6.1% in 2026, a downward revision of 7.2 percentage points from its January forecast, while average inflation is projected at 68.9%, up from 50.9% in 2025.
Labour-market conditions have also deteriorated. Iran's official unemployment rate rose to 9.1% in the spring, while the number of employed people fell by around 450,000 from a year earlier.
Meanwhile, the rial fell to a record low of about 2 million against the US dollar on the informal market this week, while figures from the Statistical Centre of Iran showed point-to-point consumer inflation reached 87.9% in July.
The weaker rial increases the local cost of imported goods, adding to pressure on households already confronting rapidly rising prices.
Limits of US economic pressure
There are limits both to how far Washington can push its economic leverage and what that pressure can ultimately achieve.
Asked why the US was giving Iran's business partners an opportunity to halt targeted activities rather than immediately penalising them, Bessent pointed to potential consequences for the wider financial system.
"We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour," he said. "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?"
Restrictions on Iranian trade can also have consequences beyond Iran, particularly through their impact on energy markets.
Gillman said continued economic pressure could nevertheless prove less disruptive than renewed large-scale warfare, arguing that Washington appears to be seeking to pressure Tehran while avoiding sharper increases in oil prices.
Although the blockade itself puts upward pressure on oil prices, Gillman said keeping crude within the $70-$80 range would support wider economic stability and limit additional export revenues for Russia.
But the bigger question is whether even severe economic pressure can produce the political concessions Washington is seeking.
Iran has lived under varying degrees of US sanctions and economic isolation for decades, developing ways to circumvent restrictions while resisting pressure to abandon policies opposed by Washington.
The Trump administration argues that stronger enforcement can change Tehran's calculation.
Yet despite the economic strain already facing Iran, nearly six months of war and pressure have so far failed to produce a lasting settlement.

Austria museum heist: Thieves snatch diamond necklace
August 28, 2026
Two men walked into Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) as visitors only to storm out with a priceless 200-carat platinum and diamond necklace worth several million dollars, police said on Friday.
The broad-daylight heist on Thursday, the latest in a series of high-profile thefts to have hit European museums in the past year, triggered a search that grew beyond Austria's borders.
What do we know about the heist?
The two robbers bought tickets to enter the museum.
But once inside, they made their way to the temporary exhibition for French designers Van Cleef and Arpels and "smashed a glass display case" with a hammer before "fleeing with the jewelry in an unknown direction," according to a police statement.
Police added that they did not wear masks and could be clearly seen on surveillance cameras.
A police spokeswoman told the German DPA news agency that one of the robbers was carrying what is believed to be a real firearm.
She said visitors and security staff were in the room when the display case was smashed, adding that it was understandable that the security staff did not stand in the way of the armed perpetrator.
The MAK museum confirmed the theft but did not comment further. On its website, the museum continues to promote its exhibition, which is due to run until September 27.
What do we know about the stolen necklace?
The stolen necklace belonged to Egypt's now-deposed Queen Nazli and was designed for her in 1939 for her daughter's marriage to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose family has also since been removed from power.
It is made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats.
Van Cleef and Arpels describes the necklace on its website as a "triumph of white jewelry."
The case is only the latest in a string of heists to have hit European museums in recent month.
The most high profile was last October's Louvre museum break-in in Paris, which saw thieves snatching in jewellery worth $102 million (roughly €88 million) in under eight minutes. Museum thefts have also been reported in Italy and Spain.

MELITOPOL, August 28. /TASS/. Ukraine’s attacks on the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant’s (ZNPP) dry spent nuclear fuel (SNF) storage facility pose a threat to nuclear security, the plant’s said.
A Ukrainian drone attacked the ZNPP’s dry SNF storage site on August 26. No serious damage was done, no casualties were reported. The radiation background is within the normal levels, the plant said.
"Any attacks in the vicinity of such a facility are inadmissible as they pose a potential threat to nuclear security. An attack on the dry SNF storage site is dangerous primarily due to the potential damage to the complex’s infrastructure and containers holding spent nuclear fuel. The consequences of such actions cannot be ignored - they could create additional risks and require complex measures to ensure the facility’s security," according to a post on the ZNPP’s channel in messaging app Max.
The dry SNF storage site is a "reliable and unique facility, built with a large safety margin and designed for the long-term safe storage of fuel," it said. August 24 marked the 25th anniversary of the installation of the first container of spent nuclear fuel at the storage site and the start of pilot operation of this ZNPP facility.
Currently, the facility holds 173 containers. The site is designed to safely store up to 380 containers for 50 years, the ZNPP said, adding that the site is regularly checked by specialists and International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors deployed to the nuclear plant.
Earlier in the day, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called for the utmost restraint following three Ukrainian drone attacks on the ZNPP on August 25 and 26. On August 25, a drone exploded near the plant’s cooling pond. Two Zaporozhye NPP employees were injured in the incident. The next day, another drone exploded on the grounds of the plant’s dry spent nuclear fuel storage facility. On the same day, a third drone struck a sprinkler system at the plant’s power units. On August 27, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that Russian calls on the IAEA to take measures against the Kiev regime in connection with the strikes on the Zaporozhye NPP.

I work with children every day. This is what I want people to know about a growing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:38:34 UTC
05:38:34 KST

IN BRIEF
- Nearly 40 per cent of all sexual assault victims in Australia are young people aged between 10 and 17.
- Love Bites is a primary prevention program working with young Australians to reduce rates of violence and misogyny.
This article contains references to child sexual abuse and sexual assault.
The death of a 16-year-old girl after a suspected sexual strangulation act has unearthed major concerns about the increasing rate of young people experiencing and perpetrating sexual violence.
Consent educator Sarnia Ralston told SBS News that sexual strangulation is "not a freak occurrence" in young people's sexual experiences.
"We need young people to know that sexual strangulation is not something that you can ever do safely," she said.
"The exposure to online pornography has a direct correlation to young people's expectations of sex."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The girl's death comes days after three students were charged with the sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl in Bondi, and three boys were charged with the sexual assault of a 17-year-old girl in Sydney's McCarthur region.
"Escalating rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are a huge concern that we need to address," Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said in parliament.
"Almost 40 per cent of victims of sexual assault are between the ages of 10 and 17, and we know that online harms are spilling into real-life harm."
Plibersek said "sexual strangulation is becoming more commonplace" due to children being exposed to "violent and degrading pornography".
"It's where they're getting their sex education from."
According to the Breathless Campaign, 57 per cent of young Australians have been strangled by a partner during sex and 51 per cent have strangled a partner during sex.
Ralston is the Queensland and Northern Territory projects executive manager and facilitator trainer for a primary prevention program called Love Bites.
She told SBS News about what actually works.
What is the Love Bites program?
Operated by the National Association for Prevention of Child Abuse and Neglect, Love Bites is a trauma-informed and evidence-based respectful relationships program teaching young people across Australia since 2003.
A national network of grassroots facilitators delivers it to young people aged 11 to 17.
Designed in line with Australia’s consent curriculum, it’s "scaffolded according to their developmental needs" and addresses topics like consent, technology-facilitated abuse, pornography and coercive control.
"It's a universal program that really challenges the drivers of violence ... we unpack what the attitudes and beliefs are that form somebody’s actions or behaviours," said Ralston.
What do young people know about sex?
In 2022, almost 40 per cent of young people had already encountered online pornography by the age of 13.
Ralston said pornography and its effects are so pervasive that the Love Bites senior program is now being delivered to the youngest cohort.
"We're now having these conversations in the younger years around coercive control, around consent and more explicit consent conversations,” she said.
“We're hearing about the impact of AI, sextortion, sexual images, technology-facilitated abuse — all of these conversations that we didn't even have words for a few years ago.”
She said there’s been a significant rise in language and content associated with the "manosphere" — and it’s happening in primary schools.
Manosphere is an umbrella term for a mix of online spaces that talk about men, masculinity and gender relations. Such spaces frequently advocate narrow and rigid ideas about what it means to be a "real" man.
But most Love Bites graduates are pushing back.
"We see so many incredible young men in our Love Bite programs that are genuinely trying to navigate their way through this harmful space and they're asking really great questions, they're showing respect in relationships and in their actions,” said Ralston.
“We can’t pretend this isn’t happening at all, but we can highlight the incredible young people, men and women, who are really recognising harm and standing by each other.”
How do you challenge a harmful sexual behaviour or attitude in a young person?
When a concerning opinion or behaviour is identified in the Love Bites program, it’s met with "curious questioning”.
She said facilitators are trained to “provide opportunities to have conversations around how things could look different”.
The approach varies by age.
“When we’re working with little kids, up to 10 years old, developmentally they need us to be their manager. We can run the program and feed the information to them,” Ralston said.
“When we work with adolescents, 11 years and up ... we’re hired as a contractor ... we come into the room with a perspective, tell them what we know, and they can choose if they want to contract our services.”
She said it’s a method that has enabled complex and progressive conversations and helped young people self-determine what safe, respectful sex is.
What's the right way to talk to young people about sex?
Ralston said being delicate isn’t necessary when talking to young people about sex.
She said many young people in the Love Bites program have expressed a desire to be able to talk to the adults in their lives about sex and relationships.
“It’s just providing that safe space and beginning the conversation,” she said.
“The really important thing is being curious and having solid, informed, evidence-based research.”
What to do if a young person needs help?
Conversations about sex can feel shameful at any age, Ralston said it’s important to “get comfortable and confident”.
"If we are not comfortable having a conversation about some explicit materials, we need to start with ourselves,” she said.
"We’ve done really well in Australia to normalise conversations around the prevention of domestic and family violence. We need to get that with sexual violence and sexual abuse.”
Consent education can cause some to reflect on experiences they deemed healthy — and realise otherwise.
Ralston said it’s a common occurrence.
She said when a young person discloses an experience of sexual assault, believing them is crucial.
If a young person has recognised they’ve perpetrated harmful sexual behaviour, they must be met with support.
"We need to help them understand that everybody has capability to change,” Ralston said.
“The first step in understanding how to change is understanding that your behaviour has crossed the line.”
Readers seeking support can ring Lifeline crisis support on 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467 and Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800 (for young people aged 5 to 25). More information is available at beyondblue.org.au and lifeline.org.au.
Anyone seeking information or support relating to sexual abuse can contact Bravehearts on 1800 272 831 or Blue Knot on 1300 657 380.
If you or someone you know is impacted by sexual assault, call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732, text 0458 737 732, or visit 1800RESPECT.org.au. In an emergency, call 000.
The Men’s Referral Service, operated by No to Violence, can be contacted on 1300 766 491.
